q: Which compound is the strongest Brønsted acid?
h: All four acidic hydrogens sit on atoms in the same molecule type (CH<sub>3</sub>–X–H). Compare the atoms X: across a row, then down a group.
w: Going down a group, atom size outweighs electronegativity: the S–H bond is longer and weaker, and the negative charge of CH3S− is spread over a larger, more polarizable atom. CH3SH (pKa ≈ 10) is therefore more acidic than CH3OH (≈ 15.5). Across the second row, acidity follows electronegativity: O–H > N–H (CH3NH2, ≈ 40) > C–H (ethane, ≈ 50).
x: Methanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.5) is the most acidic of the second-row compounds, but sulfur is below oxygen and size wins down a group, so methanethiol is about 10<sup>5</sup> times more acidic.
Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>−</sup> is much less stable than CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>; methylamine (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 40) is a very weak acid.
Ethane (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50) puts the negative charge on carbon, the least electronegative atom here, so it is the weakest acid of the four.

q: Rank compounds I–IV in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
h: Ask what stabilizes each conjugate base: which atom carries the charge, and can it be delocalized by resonance?
w: Ethane (II, pKa ≈ 50) leaves the charge on carbon. Ethanol (IV, ≈ 16) puts it on oxygen with no resonance. Phenol (III, ≈ 10) puts it on oxygen with delocalization into the ring (onto carbons). Acetic acid (I, ≈ 4.8) delocalizes the charge over two oxygens, the best case. Order: II < IV < III < I.
x: This places ethanol above phenol. Ethoxide has no resonance, while phenoxide spreads its charge into the ring, so phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10) is about a million times more acidic than ethanol (16).
Ethane cannot be more acidic than ethanol: a carbanion on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50) is far less stable than an alkoxide (≈ 16).
Phenoxide delocalizes charge onto ring carbons, but acetate delocalizes it onto a second oxygen, which is better; acetic acid (4.8) is more acidic than phenol (10).

q: Which labeled hydrogen (on atom a, b, c or d) is the most acidic?
h: Recall the approximate pK<sub>a</sub> of each type: terminal alkyne C–H, alcohol O–H, ketone α-C–H, phenol O–H.
w: Approximate pKa values: a terminal alkyne ≈ 25; b primary alcohol ≈ 16; c ketone α-hydrogen ≈ 20; d phenol ≈ 10. The phenoxide ion has the charge on oxygen and delocalized into the aromatic ring, so the phenol O–H on d is the most acidic, about 106 times more acidic than the alcohol.
x: Atom b is an ordinary alcohol (pKa ≈ 16); its alkoxide has no resonance stabilization, unlike phenoxide.
The ketone α-hydrogen (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 20) gives a resonance-stabilized enolate, but the charge starts on carbon; it is about 10<sup>10</sup> times less acidic than the phenol.
The sp C–H of a terminal alkyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is acidic for a hydrocarbon, but far weaker than any O–H in this molecule.

q: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8) is mixed with one equivalent of sodium ethoxide; ethanol has pK<sub>a</sub> 16. Which best describes the equilibrium shown?
c: It lies far to the right; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>11</sup>
It lies far to the left; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−11</sup>
It lies to the right; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 3
It lies far to the right; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>21</sup>
h: Find the acid on each side. The equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid, and K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of reactant acid)</sup>.
w: The reactant acid is acetic acid (4.8); the product acid is ethanol (16). Equilibrium favors the weaker acid (and weaker base), so it lies to the right. Keq = 10(16 − 4.8) = 1011.2, so far to the right, Keq ≈ 1011. The Na+ counterion is a spectator and is not written.
x: This subtracts in the wrong order. The stronger acid (acetic acid) is on the left, so the reaction proceeds forward and K<sub>eq</sub> > 1.
This divides the pK<sub>a</sub> values (16/4.8 ≈ 3). pK<sub>a</sub> values are logarithms, so K<sub>eq</sub> comes from their difference as a power of ten.
This adds the two pK<sub>a</sub> values. K<sub>eq</sub> depends on the difference, 16 − 4.8 = 11.2.

q: Which base can deprotonate 1-hexyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) essentially completely?
h: A base works well only if its conjugate acid is a weaker acid (higher pK<sub>a</sub>) than the compound being deprotonated.
w: For complete deprotonation, the conjugate acid of the base must have a higher pKa than the alkyne. Only NaNH2 qualifies: NH3 (≈ 38) is a much weaker acid than the alkyne (25), so Keq ≈ 1013. This is why acetylide ions are made with NaNH2.
x: Water (15.7) is a stronger acid than the alkyne (25), so hydroxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−9</sup>; almost no acetylide forms.
Methanol (≈ 15.5) is a stronger acid than the alkyne, so methoxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−10</sup>.
Bicarbonate is a very weak base (its conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> 6.4); it can deprotonate carboxylic acids but not alkynes.

q: Solid NaNH<sub>2</sub> is added to water. Which statement best describes the result?
c: NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> is converted essentially completely to NH<sub>3</sub>, and OH<sup>−</sup> becomes the strongest base present.
NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> stays the strongest base present, because Na<sup>+</sup> stabilizes it as an ion pair.
Very little reaction occurs, because NH<sub>3</sub> is a stronger acid than water.
NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> removes a proton from H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> only, so the solution stays neutral.
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of water (15.7) with that of NH<sub>3</sub> (≈ 38). What is the strongest base that can survive in water?
w: Water (pKa 15.7) is a far stronger acid than NH3 (≈ 38), so NH2− + H2O → NH3 + OH− has Keq ≈ 1022. This is the leveling effect: any base stronger than OH− is converted to OH− in water, so OH− becomes the strongest base present. Strong bases such as NaNH2 must be used in solvents that are weaker acids than their conjugate acids (for example liquid NH3).
x: Na<sup>+</sup> is a spectator counterion; it does not change which side of a proton transfer is favored. Amide ion is destroyed by water.
This reverses the acidities: water (15.7) is about 10<sup>22</sup> times more acidic than NH<sub>3</sub> (≈ 38).
The H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> concentration in neutral water is tiny (10<sup>−7</sup> M); NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> reacts with water itself and the solution becomes strongly basic.

q: Boron trifluoride dissolves in diethyl ether to form the adduct shown. Which statement is correct?
c: Diethyl ether is the Lewis base, and boron in the adduct has a formal charge of −1.
Diethyl ether is the Lewis base, and boron in the adduct has a formal charge of +1.
BF<sub>3</sub> is the Lewis base, and oxygen in the adduct has a formal charge of −1.
Diethyl ether is the Lewis acid, and boron in the adduct has a formal charge of −1.
h: Which species has an empty orbital, and which has a lone pair? Then find formal charges: B (four bonds, no lone pairs) and O (three bonds, one lone pair).
w: BF3 has an empty 2p orbital on boron (only six valence electrons), so it is the electron-pair acceptor (Lewis acid). The ether oxygen donates a lone pair, so ether is the Lewis base. In the adduct, boron has four bonds and no lone pairs: FC = 3 − 4 = −1; oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair: FC = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.
x: The donor/acceptor roles are right, but boron with four bonds and no lone pairs has formal charge 3 − 0 − 4 = −1, not +1; the +1 belongs to oxygen.
BF<sub>3</sub> accepts the electron pair, so it is the Lewis acid; the fluorine lone pairs are not used in this bond. Oxygen in the adduct is +1.
The ether gives up a lone pair to boron, which makes it the Lewis base, not the Lewis acid.

q: Rank phenols I–IV in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
h: In the phenoxide ion, the negative charge reaches the ortho and para carbons by resonance, but not the meta carbons. Which substituents can accept that charge, and from which position?
w: Phenoxide charge is delocalized to the ortho and para carbons. A para-NO2 (II, pKa ≈ 7.2) can take the charge directly onto its oxygens by resonance and withdraw inductively. A meta-NO2 (IV, ≈ 8.4) withdraws only inductively, because the charge never reaches the meta carbon. Phenol itself (I) is ≈ 10. A para-OCH3 (III, ≈ 10.2) donates electron density by resonance, destabilizing the anion slightly. Order: III < I < IV < II.
x: This makes meta-nitrophenol more acidic than para. Only the para nitro group can delocalize the phenoxide charge onto its own oxygens by resonance, which outweighs the slightly closer inductive effect of a meta group.
Methoxy oxygen is electronegative, but at the para position its resonance donation dominates; 4-methoxyphenol is slightly less acidic than phenol, not more.
This is the order of decreasing acidity (strongest first), the reverse of what was asked.

q: Which ranking lists acids I–IV from most acidic to least acidic?
h: All four are carboxylic acids, so the carboxylate resonance is the same. Look at where (or whether) the electron-withdrawing Cl sits relative to the COOH.
w: An electronegative chlorine stabilizes the carboxylate by inductive withdrawal, and induction falls off quickly with the number of bonds. Chlorine on C2 (III, pKa ≈ 2.9) has the largest effect, on C3 (I, ≈ 4.1) less, on C4 (IV, ≈ 4.5) little, and butanoic acid (II, ≈ 4.8) has none: III > I > IV > II.
x: This reverses the distance effect. Induction weakens with each bond, so a Cl far from the carboxylate (IV) helps least, not most.
This swaps I and IV. Chlorine on C3 is one bond closer to the carboxylate than chlorine on C4, so I is more acidic than IV.
Butanoic acid has no electron-withdrawing group and is the weakest acid of the set, not the strongest.

q: Which carbanion is the most stable (the weakest base)?
h: Each lone pair sits in a hybrid orbital on carbon. More s character holds electrons closer to the nucleus.
w: The acetylide ion (HC≡C−) holds its lone pair in an sp orbital (50% s character), close to the nucleus, which stabilizes it. That is why ethyne (pKa 25) is far more acidic than ethene (≈ 44) or ethane (≈ 50). Its conjugate acid is the strongest, so the anion is the weakest base.
x: The vinyl anion's lone pair is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital (33% s); it is more stable than an alkyl anion but much less stable than acetylide (pK<sub>a</sub> of ethene ≈ 44).
The ethyl anion has its lone pair in an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital (25% s), far from the nucleus; ethane's pK<sub>a</sub> is about 50.
Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating, so a tertiary carbanion is even less stable than a primary one; carbanion stability runs opposite to carbocation stability.

q: Which labeled hydrogen is the most acidic?
h: Deprotonate each carbon in your head. Over how many electronegative atoms can the resulting charge spread?
w: Removing H from carbon b, between two C=O groups, gives an anion delocalized onto both carbonyl oxygens (pKa ≈ 9, like 2,4-pentanedione). Carbon c is α to only one carbonyl (pKa ≈ 20), the alkyne C–H on a is ≈ 25 (no resonance, only sp character), and the CH3 on d is β to the carbonyl, so its anion has no resonance (≈ 50). Answer: carbon b.
x: Carbon c is α to only one carbonyl, so its enolate spreads the charge onto one oxygen (pKa ≈ 20). Carbon b is α to two.
The terminal alkyne C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is stabilized only by sp hybridization, which is weaker than delocalizing the charge onto two oxygens.
Carbon d is β to the carbonyl, not α; the anion cannot be delocalized onto oxygen, so this is an ordinary alkane C–H.

q: Ethanol reacts with sodium hydride to give sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas. Why does this reaction go essentially to completion?
c: H<sup>−</sup> is a very strong base (pK<sub>a</sub> of H<sub>2</sub> ≈ 36), and H<sub>2</sub> escapes as a gas.
Na<sup>+</sup> binds ethoxide tightly, which drives an otherwise unfavorable proton transfer.
H<sup>−</sup> attacks carbon as a nucleophile and displaces ethoxide from ethanol.
Ethanol is a stronger acid than water, so any base deprotonates it completely.
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of ethanol with that of the conjugate acid of hydride. Then ask what happens to that conjugate acid once it forms.
w: The conjugate acid of H− is H2 (pKa ≈ 36), far weaker than ethanol (≈ 16), so Keq ≈ 1020. In addition, H2 bubbles out, so the reverse reaction cannot occur. NaH therefore makes alkoxides cleanly; Na+ is just the counterion.
x: Na<sup>+</sup> is a spectator counterion. The large pK<sub>a</sub> difference, not the cation, makes the reaction favorable.
Hydride from NaH acts as a base, not a nucleophile, and ethanol has no leaving group at carbon (OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group anyway). The products are ethoxide and H<sub>2</sub>.
Ethanol (≈ 16) is in fact slightly weaker than water (15.7), and a weak base such as NaHCO3 does not deprotonate it at all.

q: A tert-butyl carbocation reacts with water to give the oxonium ion shown. In this step, which species acts as the Lewis acid?
c: The carbocation, which accepts an electron pair
Water, which donates an electron pair to carbon
Water, which donates a proton to the carbocation
The oxonium ion, which accepts a proton from water
h: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. Which reactant has an empty orbital?
w: The carbocation has an empty p orbital and accepts a lone pair from the water oxygen, so the carbocation is the Lewis acid (electrophile) and water is the Lewis base (nucleophile). No proton moves in this step.
x: Donating an electron pair makes water the Lewis base, not the Lewis acid.
No proton is transferred in this step; a bond forms from an oxygen lone pair to the carbocation carbon.
The oxonium ion is the product of this step; it loses a proton later, acting as a Brønsted acid, not as a Lewis acid that accepts one.

q: Phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.0) is mixed with sodium acetate (pK<sub>a</sub> of acetic acid 4.8). What is the approximate K<sub>eq</sub> for the reaction shown?
h: K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of the product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of the reactant acid)</sup>.
w: The reactant acid is phenol (10.0) and the product acid is acetic acid (4.8). Keq = 10(4.8 − 10.0) = 10−5.2 ≈ 10−5. The stronger acid (acetic acid) is on the right, so the equilibrium lies to the left: acetate is too weak a base to deprotonate phenol.
x: This has the sign reversed. The weaker acid (phenol) is on the reactant side, so the equilibrium favors reactants and K<sub>eq</sub> < 1.
This adds the pK<sub>a</sub> values (10 + 4.8 ≈ 15). K<sub>eq</sub> uses their difference.
This divides the pK<sub>a</sub> values (4.8/10). pK<sub>a</sub> values are logarithms; their difference becomes an exponent of 10.

q: Which anion is the strongest base?
h: The strongest base has the weakest conjugate acid (highest pK<sub>a</sub>). Recall the pK<sub>a</sub> of ethanol, acetic acid, ammonia and ethyne.
w: Conjugate-acid pKa values: ethanol ≈ 16, acetic acid ≈ 4.8, NH3 ≈ 38, ethyne ≈ 25. The highest belongs to NH3, so the amide ion, NH2−, is the strongest base. This is why NaNH2 deprotonates terminal alkynes.
x: Ethoxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) is a strong base but about 10<sup>22</sup> times weaker than amide ion.
Acetate is resonance-stabilized; its conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8, making it the weakest base here.
Acetylide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is a strong base, but amide is stronger; that is exactly why NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> can make acetylide ions.

q: Acetone is deprotonated at an α-carbon. Which structure is the major resonance contributor of the resulting anion?
h: Draw both resonance forms of the anion. Which atom is better at carrying a negative charge?
w: The enolate has two resonance forms: one with the charge on the α-carbon and one with the charge on oxygen and a C=C bond. Both have full octets, so the better contributor is the one with the negative charge on the more electronegative atom, oxygen. That oxyanion form is the major contributor, which is why the α-H of a ketone (pKa ≈ 19–20) is far more acidic than an alkane C–H.
x: This carbanion form is a real resonance contributor of the enolate, but a minor one: carbon is less able than oxygen to carry the negative charge.
This neutral enol is a tautomer of acetone (a different compound with an O–H bond), not a resonance form of the anion.
This is the isopropoxide ion, the conjugate base of 2-propanol; forming it would need a hydride added to the carbonyl, not removal of an α-proton.

q: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8) is about 10<sup>11</sup> times more acidic than ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> 16). What is the main reason?
c: In acetate the negative charge is delocalized by resonance over two oxygen atoms.
The methyl group of acetic acid donates electrons and weakens the O–H bond.
The acidic oxygen of acetic acid is sp-hybridized, so it holds the charge closer to the nucleus.
Inductive withdrawal by the carbonyl group alone; resonance plays no part in acetate.
h: Both acids lose a proton from oxygen. Compare how the negative charge is distributed in acetate and in ethoxide.
w: In both conjugate bases the charge starts on oxygen (same atom), so the difference comes from resonance: acetate spreads its charge equally over two oxygens (both C–O bonds are the same length), whereas ethoxide holds it on one oxygen. The carbonyl group's inductive withdrawal adds a smaller contribution.
x: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating, which would destabilize the anion and make the acid weaker, not stronger; ethanol has an alkyl group too.
The OH oxygen of acetic acid is not sp-hybridized; in acetate both oxygens share the charge through a conjugated system. Orbital (hybridization) arguments apply to C–H acids such as alkynes.
Induction contributes, but the main factor is resonance; the two C–O bonds of acetate are identical in length, which shows the charge is shared.

q: Rank compounds I–IV from most basic to least basic (as Brønsted bases in water).
h: A nitrogen lone pair is most basic when localized. Is each lone pair delocalized into a ring or a C=O group? Is an alkyl group donating to it?
w: Basicity follows the pKa of each conjugate acid. Ethylamine (II, pKaH ≈ 10.7): localized sp3 lone pair with an electron-donating alkyl group. Ammonia (IV, ≈ 9.2): localized but no alkyl group. Aniline (III, ≈ 4.6): the lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring. Acetamide (I, ≈ −0.5): the lone pair is strongly delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen, so the amide is barely basic. Order: II > IV > III > I.
x: In water, ethylamine (pK<sub>a</sub>H 10.7) is more basic than ammonia (9.2) because the ethyl group donates electron density and stabilizes the ammonium ion.
Amide nitrogen lone pairs are delocalized onto a C=O oxygen, which is far more effective than delocalization into a benzene ring; acetamide is much less basic than aniline.
Aniline's aromatic ring does not make it a strong base; delocalizing the lone pair into the ring lowers its basicity by about a million-fold compared with alkylamines.

q: When this compound is treated with one equivalent of HCl, which labeled atom is protonated?
h: Compare a localized amine lone pair with the lone pairs of an amide (both N and O) and an ether oxygen. Which conjugate acid has the highest pK<sub>a</sub>?
w: The tertiary amine nitrogen c has a localized sp3 lone pair; its conjugate acid has pKa ≈ 10. An amide is protonated (when at all) on its carbonyl oxygen d (pKaH ≈ −0.5); the amide nitrogen b is even less basic because its lone pair is delocalized into the C=O. The ether oxygen a has pKaH ≈ −3.5. So atom c, the amine, is protonated.
x: The amide N–H nitrogen looks like an amine, but its lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl; it is the least basic site of an amide.
The amide oxygen is the more basic site within the amide, but its conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> near −0.5, about 10<sup>10</sup> times more acidic than a protonated amine.
Ether oxygens are very weak bases (pK<sub>a</sub>H ≈ −3.5); an amine in the same molecule is protonated first.

q: Use the table to find K<sub>eq</sub> for: CF<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>O<sup>−</sup> ⇌ CF<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>O<sup>−</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH
h: Identify the acid on each side. K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of the product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of the reactant acid)</sup>.
w: The reactant acid is 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (12.4); the product acid is ethanol (16.0). Keq = 10(16.0 − 12.4) = 103.6 ≈ 4 × 103, products favored. The three fluorines stabilize the alkoxide inductively, so ethoxide deprotonates trifluoroethanol.
x: This uses the exponent with the wrong sign. The stronger acid (CF<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is on the left, so K<sub>eq</sub> > 1.
This divides the pK<sub>a</sub> values (16.0/12.4). Since pK<sub>a</sub> is a logarithm, K<sub>eq</sub> = 10 raised to the difference.
This adds the pK<sub>a</sub> values. K<sub>eq</sub> depends only on their difference, 3.6 units.

q: At equal concentrations in water, HCl (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −7) and HBr (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −9) give solutions with the same pH. Why?
c: Both transfer their protons essentially completely to water, so H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> is the strongest acid present in each.
Chloride and bromide are both stabilized by hydrogen bonding to the same extent, which cancels the difference.
Water is a stronger acid than both HCl and HBr, so neither ionizes significantly.
The pK<sub>a</sub> values are too close to give any measurable difference in K<sub>eq</sub>.
h: What is the strongest acid that can exist in significant amounts in water? (pK<sub>a</sub> of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ≈ −1.7)
w: Any acid much stronger than H3O+ (pKa −1.7) protonates water completely, giving H3O+ + X−. Water levels the strong acids: H3O+ is the strongest acid present in each solution, so their difference only shows up in a less basic solvent (such as acetic acid).
x: Solvation of the anions does not cancel out; the true reason is that both acids ionize completely, so only H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> remains as the acid.
This reverses the acidities. HCl and HBr are far stronger acids than water (15.7) or H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (−1.7), so they ionize completely.
Two pK<sub>a</sub> units is a 100-fold difference in K<sub>a</sub>, which would be measurable; it disappears in water only because both ionize completely.

q: Which base/solvent combination converts 1-hexyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) essentially completely to its acetylide ion?
h: Two conditions: the base's conjugate acid must be weaker than the alkyne, and the solvent must not be a stronger acid than the alkyne.
w: NH2− (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 38) deprotonates the alkyne with Keq ≈ 1013, and the solvent NH3 is a weaker acid than the alkyne, so it cannot reprotonate the acetylide. NaNH2 in liquid NH3 works.
x: Hydroxide is too weak a base (water pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7), and water as solvent would reprotonate any acetylide formed.
Ethoxide is too weak (ethanol pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16), and ethanol solvent is about 10<sup>9</sup> times more acidic than the alkyne.
Butyllithium is a strong enough base, but methanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.5) is a far stronger acid than the alkyne; BuLi is destroyed by the solvent, giving butane and lithium methoxide.

q: Which structure is the conjugate acid of acetone?
h: A conjugate acid has one more H<sup>+</sup> (one more proton and one more positive charge) than the base.
w: Adding H+ to a lone pair of the carbonyl oxygen gives protonated acetone, (CH3)2C=OH+ (pKa ≈ −7). Its formula is acetone + H+.
x: This is the enolate, the conjugate base of acetone (one H+ removed).
This is the enol, a tautomer of acetone with the same formula; nothing was added.
This is 2-propanol, which has two more hydrogens than acetone and no charge; it is a reduction product, not a conjugate acid.

q: Using the table, which base converts acetone (pKa 19.2) almost completely to its enolate?
h: For each base, compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of its conjugate acid with 19.2. K<sub>eq</sub> must be much larger than 1.
w: Keq = 10(pKa of conjugate acid − 19.2). For LDA: 10(36 − 19.2) ≈ 1017, essentially complete. tert-Butoxide: 10−1.2 ≈ 0.06; ethoxide: 10−3.2; hydroxide: 10−3.5. Those alkoxide and hydroxide bases form only small equilibrium amounts of enolate.
x: tert-Butoxide is a strong, bulky base, but tert-butanol (18) is a slightly stronger acid than acetone (19.2), so Keq ≈ 0.06; most acetone stays protonated.
Ethanol (16.0) is more acidic than acetone, so ethoxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−3</sup>; only a small fraction of enolate forms.
Water (15.7) is more acidic than acetone, so hydroxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−3.5</sup>; it makes only traces of enolate.

q: Fluorine is more electronegative than iodine, yet HI (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −10) is a far stronger acid than HF (pK<sub>a</sub> 3.2). Which explanation is best?
c: Iodide is much larger, so its charge is spread over more volume, and the H–I bond is weaker.
Iodine is more electronegative than fluorine in water, because of hydrogen bonding to the solvent.
Fluoride is stabilized by resonance, which makes HF less likely to ionize in water.
HI has an sp-hybridized iodine, while HF has an sp<sup>3</sup>-hybridized fluorine.
h: Within a row of the periodic table electronegativity controls acidity. What factor dominates down a column?
w: Down a group, atom size dominates: I− spreads its charge over a much larger, more polarizable volume than F−, and the long H–I bond is weak. Both factors favor ionization of HI. Electronegativity is the deciding factor only across a row (C < N < O < F).
x: Iodine is less electronegative than fluorine in any medium; electronegativity would actually predict HF to be the stronger acid.
Fluoride has no resonance; it is a single atom. Its small size concentrates the charge, which makes F<sup>−</sup> less stable, not more.
Hybridization arguments compare acids with the same atom (such as sp vs sp<sup>3</sup> C–H). It is not the reason for the HF/HI difference.

q: Rank the labeled hydrogens from most acidic to least acidic.
h: All three are C–H bonds with no resonance stabilization of the anion. What is different is the hybridization of each carbon.
w: With the atom the same and no resonance, the orbital holding the lone pair decides. The anion from a (sp, 50% s) is most stable (pKa ≈ 25), then b (sp2, 33% s, ≈ 44), then c (sp3, 25% s, ≈ 50): a > b > c. Carbon c is neither allylic nor propargylic, so it gets no resonance help.
x: This reverses the trend. More s character holds the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilizes the carbanion, so the sp C–H is the most acidic.
A vinylic sp<sup>2</sup> C–H (≈ 44) is far less acidic than a terminal alkyne C–H (≈ 25).
The sp3 C–H on c has the least s character, so it is less acidic than the sp2 vinylic C–H on b.

q: In the phenoxide ion, resonance places the negative charge on oxygen and on which ring carbons?
c: The two ortho carbons and the para carbon
Only the ring carbon bonded to oxygen
h: Push the oxygen lone pair into the ring and move the π electrons one step at a time. Which carbons pick up the lone pair?
w: Each resonance step moves the negative charge two atoms along the ring, so from the oxygen it reaches the carbons at the ortho, para and other ortho positions. The meta carbons and the ipso carbon never carry the charge. This is why groups at ortho/para positions (such as NO2) affect phenol acidity most.
x: The meta carbons are skipped: charge alternates around the ring and never lands on them.
The charge is not spread over all six carbons; it alternates, reaching only ortho and para.
The ipso carbon forms a C=O double bond in the contributors that carry ring charge; it never holds the negative charge itself.

q: Which species is the strongest acid? (Remove the proton from each and compare the hybridization of the atom that held it.)
h: The strongest acid has the weakest conjugate base. Compare how tightly each neutral base holds its lone pair: what is the hybridization of the atom being protonated?
w: Remove the proton to get each conjugate base: CH3OH, CH3NH2, acetone and acetonitrile. The nitrile nitrogen's lone pair is in an sp orbital (50% s), held tightly, so acetonitrile is the weakest base and protonated acetonitrile (pKa ≈ −10) is the strongest acid. Protonated acetone (sp2 O, ≈ −7) and protonated methanol (sp3 O, ≈ −2.5) are weaker; methylammonium (≈ 10.6) is weakest.
x: Protonated acetone is a very strong acid (≈ −7), but the sp lone pair of a nitrile is held even more tightly than the sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair of a carbonyl oxygen.
Protonated methanol (≈ −2.5) is a strong acid, but its sp<sup>3</sup> oxygen lone pair is a better base than the sp nitrogen of a nitrile, so it gives up its proton less readily.
Methylammonium (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10.6) is the weakest acid here because methylamine is a good base; a positive charge alone does not make a strong acid.

q: Ethylmagnesium bromide is added to ethanol. What are the main products?
c: No reaction; Grignard reagents are stable in alcohols
h: The C–Mg bond is highly polarized toward carbon, so the ethyl group behaves like a carbanion (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50). What does ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) offer it?
w: A Grignard reagent is an extremely strong base. Ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is about 1034 times more acidic than ethane (≈ 50), so a fast proton transfer gives ethane and the magnesium alkoxide CH3CH2OMgBr. For this reason Grignard reagents must be prepared and used in dry, aprotic ethers.
x: Grignard reagents do not couple with alcohols to form new C–C bonds; proton transfer from the O–H is much faster.
An ether would require the alkyl group to attack oxygen and displace OH, which does not happen; the fast reaction is proton transfer.
Grignard reagents are destroyed by any O–H, N–H or S–H acid; that is why they are made in dry ether or THF.

q: Rank these species in order of increasing acidity: NH3, H2O, NH4+, H3O+
h: Two trends work together: O–H bonds are more acidic than N–H bonds (electronegativity), and a positively charged acid gives up H<sup>+</sup> far more easily than its neutral form.
w: pKa values: NH3 ≈ 38, H2O 15.7, NH4+ 9.2, H3O+ −1.7. Order: NH3 < H2O < NH4+ < H3O+. Two trends combine: O–H is more acidic than N–H (electronegativity), and a positive charge on the acid makes it much more acidic than its neutral form.
x: Ammonium (9.2) is more acidic than water (15.7): the positive charge makes losing H<sup>+</sup> much easier.
Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so water is more acidic than ammonia, and H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> is more acidic than NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
This puts the cations as the weakest acids. Positively charged acids lose a proton far more readily than their neutral counterparts.

q: Which compound dissolves in aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub> by forming a water-soluble salt? (pK<sub>a</sub> of H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> ≈ 6.4)
h: Bicarbonate is a weak base. It can deprotonate only acids stronger than its conjugate acid, H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.
w: HCO3− deprotonates an acid to a large extent only if that acid has pKa below about 6.4. Benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) qualifies: it forms sodium benzoate, which dissolves, and CO2 bubbles off. Phenol (10) and cyclohexanol (≈ 18) are too weak, and aniline is a base, not an acid.
x: Phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10) is weaker than H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, so bicarbonate gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−3.6</sup>; phenol needs NaOH.
Cyclohexanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 18) is far too weak an acid to be deprotonated by bicarbonate or even by NaOH to a large extent.
Aniline is a weak base; it dissolves in aqueous acid (as the anilinium ion), not in aqueous base.

q: A diethyl ether solution contains compounds I, II and III. Which extraction sequence separates all three, leaving one compound in each of two aqueous extracts and one in the ether?
c: Extract with aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, then extract the ether with aqueous NaOH
Extract with aqueous NaOH, then extract the ether with aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>
Extract with aqueous HCl, then extract the ether with aqueous NaOH
Extract with aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, then extract the ether with aqueous HCl
h: Match each compound's pK<sub>a</sub> to the base strength: benzoic acid ≈ 4.2, 4-methylphenol ≈ 10.3, naphthalene has no acidic H. Which base takes only the strongest acid?
w: NaHCO3 (conjugate acid pKa 6.4) deprotonates only the carboxylic acid I, moving sodium benzoate into the first aqueous layer. NaOH (water pKa 15.7) then deprotonates the phenol II, moving the phenoxide into the second aqueous layer. Naphthalene III, with no acidic or basic group, stays in the ether. So: NaHCO3 first, then NaOH.
x: NaOH is strong enough to deprotonate both the carboxylic acid and the phenol, so the first extract would contain I and II together.
None of the three compounds is basic, so HCl removes nothing; NaOH would then pull I and II into one extract together.
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> removes I correctly, but HCl cannot remove the phenol (it is an acid, not a base); II and III would stay together in the ether.

q: Rank the indicated C–H acids I–IV from least acidic to most acidic.
h: In each conjugate base, where can the negative charge go by resonance, and how electronegative is that atom? A nitro group puts a positive nitrogen next to the carbanion.
w: Methane (II, pKa ≈ 50) has no stabilization. Acetonitrile (IV, ≈ 25) delocalizes the charge onto nitrogen. Acetone (I, ≈ 19–20) delocalizes it onto oxygen, which is more electronegative. Nitromethane (III, ≈ 10) delocalizes it onto two oxygens of a group that also carries a formal positive charge on nitrogen, giving very strong stabilization. Order: II < IV < I < III.
x: This makes acetonitrile more acidic than acetone. A carbanion stabilized onto nitrogen (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is less stable than an enolate with the charge on oxygen (≈ 19–20).
Acetone (≈ 19–20) is far less acidic than nitromethane (≈ 10); the nitro group spreads the charge onto two oxygens next to a positive nitrogen.
Acetonitrile is not less acidic than methane: its anion is resonance-stabilized onto nitrogen, while the methyl anion has no stabilization at all.

q: In water, methanol (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.5) is more acidic than tert-butyl alcohol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 18). What is the best explanation?
c: Methoxide is less hindered, so solvent molecules can stabilize its charge more effectively.
Methoxide is stabilized by resonance, while tert-butoxide is not.
The three methyl groups of tert-butoxide withdraw electron density and destabilize the anion.
The oxygen in methanol is sp<sup>2</sup>-hybridized, while in tert-butyl alcohol it is sp<sup>3</sup>.
h: Both alkoxides put the charge on an oxygen with no resonance. Think about what surrounds the anion in solution.
w: Neither alkoxide has resonance, and the hybridization is the same. The difference is solvation: the small methoxide ion is easily surrounded by hydrogen-bonding water molecules that spread out its charge, while the bulky tert-butyl group blocks solvent from the oxygen. Poorer solvation leaves tert-butoxide less stabilized, so tert-butyl alcohol is the weaker acid (and tert-butoxide the stronger base).
x: Neither methoxide nor tert-butoxide has resonance; the charge sits on a single sp<sup>3</sup> oxygen in both.
Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating, not withdrawing; and the main effect here is solvation, not induction.
Both oxygens are sp<sup>3</sup>-hybridized; hybridization is not the source of the difference.

q:
For which of these equilibria do the products predominate?
I. CH3COOH + NH3 ⇌ CH3COO− + NH4+
II. HC≡CH + NaOH ⇌ HC≡CNa + H2O
III. CH3OH + NaNH2 ⇌ CH3ONa + NH3
h: In each equation, find the acid on the left and the acid on the right. The equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid (higher pK<sub>a</sub>).
w: I: acetic acid (4.8) → NH4+ (9.2); weaker acid on the right, products favored. II: ethyne (25) → water (15.7); stronger acid on the right, reactants favored. III: methanol (15.5) → NH3 (38); products strongly favored. Answer: I and III only. The Na+ counterions are spectators.
x: Equilibrium II lies to the left: water (15.7) is a much stronger acid than ethyne (25), so hydroxide cannot make acetylide.
Equilibrium III also favors products: amide ion is a far stronger base than methoxide (NH<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> 38 vs CH<sub>3</sub>OH 15.5).
Equilibrium I favors products too (acetic acid 4.8 is stronger than ammonium 9.2), while II does not.

q: Each sodium salt is dissolved in ethanol (pKa 16). Which one is converted essentially completely to sodium ethoxide?
h: Ethoxide is the strongest base that can persist in ethanol. Which salts contain a base stronger than ethoxide? Compare conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> values with 16.
w: A base is leveled by a solvent when its conjugate acid is much weaker than the solvent. NH3 (≈ 38) is 1022 times weaker than ethanol, so NaNH2 + EtOH → NH3 + NaOEt goes to completion. For NaOH, water (15.7) and ethanol (16) are nearly equal acids, so Keq ≈ 0.5 and both bases are present. Phenoxide (10) and acetate (4.8) are much weaker bases than ethoxide and stay unchanged.
x: Water (15.7) and ethanol (16) have nearly the same pK<sub>a</sub>, so hydroxide and ethoxide coexist (K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 0.5); the conversion is far from complete.
Phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10) is a much stronger acid than ethanol, so phenoxide does not deprotonate ethanol (K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−6</sup>).
Acetate is a weak base (acetic acid pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8); it cannot deprotonate ethanol at all to a useful extent.

q: Which species is a Lewis acid but not a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
h: A Brønsted acid must have a proton to donate. A Lewis acid needs only a vacant orbital to accept an electron pair.
w: AlCl3 has an aluminum with only six valence electrons and an empty orbital, so it accepts electron pairs (it is the Lewis acid catalyst in many reactions), but it has no hydrogen to donate. The other three each donate a proton, so they are Brønsted acids.
x: Water donates protons (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7), so it is a Brønsted acid; it is also commonly a Lewis base.
Ammonium donates a proton (pK<sub>a</sub> 9.2), so it is a Brønsted acid.
HCl is a strong Brønsted acid (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −7).

q: Rank alcohols I–IV in order of increasing acidity (weakest first).
h: Each alkoxide puts the charge on oxygen with no resonance. Count the fluorine atoms near the oxygen.
w: Fluorine withdraws electron density inductively and stabilizes the alkoxide; more fluorines give a larger effect. Ethanol (II, pKa ≈ 16) has none; 2-fluoroethanol (IV, ≈ 14.4) has one; 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (I, 12.4) has three; hexafluoro-2-propanol (III, ≈ 9.3) has six. Order: II < IV < I < III.
x: This is the order of decreasing acidity (strongest first), the reverse of what was asked.
This places one fluorine above three. Inductive effects add, so CF<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH is more acidic than FCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
A fluorine substituent stabilizes the alkoxide, so 2-fluoroethanol is more acidic than ethanol, not less.

q: The cationic form of alanine is shown. When one equivalent of NaOH is added, which labeled site loses its proton?
h: Compare a carboxylic acid with an ammonium ion. A positive charge on an acid helps, but which conjugate base is more stabilized, and which pK<sub>a</sub> is lower?
w: The carboxylic acid O–H (b, pKa ≈ 2.3, lowered by the nearby positive NH3+) is far more acidic than the ammonium N–H (a, ≈ 9.7). One equivalent of base removes the most acidic proton first, giving the zwitterion. The C–H bonds are not acidic under these conditions. The key is therefore the O–H on atom b.
x: The ammonium N–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 9.7) is acidic because of its positive charge, but the carboxylic acid (≈ 2.3) is about 10<sup>7</sup> times more acidic, so it is deprotonated first.
The α-C–H is next to both the carbonyl and NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, but its pK<sub>a</sub> is still above 20; hydroxide removes the O–H (2.3) first.
The methyl C–H is an ordinary sp<sup>3</sup> C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50) with no stabilizing group next to it.

q: Which compound is the strongest base?
h: Protonate each compound at its most basic site and look at the conjugate acid. Can the positive charge be delocalized?
w: Guanidine is protonated on its sp2 (=NH) nitrogen to give the guanidinium ion, whose positive charge is shared equally by three nitrogens through resonance. That large stabilization of the conjugate acid (pKa ≈ 13.6) makes guanidine more basic than an ordinary alkylamine such as methylamine (pKaH 10.6). In urea and aniline the lone pairs are delocalized in the neutral base, which lowers basicity.
x: Methylamine is a good base (pK<sub>a</sub>H 10.6), but its conjugate acid has no resonance; guanidinium's charge is spread over three nitrogens.
Urea's nitrogen lone pairs are delocalized into the C=O, as in an amide; urea is a very weak base (pK<sub>a</sub>H ≈ 0.1).
Aniline's lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring in the neutral base, which makes it a weak base (pK<sub>a</sub>H 4.6).

q: Rank compounds I–IV in order of increasing acidity of their most acidic C–H (weakest first).
h: Two questions: is the C–H α to one carbonyl or to two? And is that carbonyl a ketone or an ester? An ester's OR group donates into its C=O.
w: A CH2 between two carbonyls is far more acidic than one next to a single C=O, because the anion spreads over two oxygens. Within each pair, ketones beat esters: the ester's alkoxy oxygen donates electron density into the C=O, so the carbonyl is less able to accept the enolate charge. Values: ethyl acetate (I) ≈ 25, acetone (III) ≈ 19, diethyl malonate (IV) ≈ 13, 2,4-pentanedione (II) ≈ 9. Order: I < III < IV < II.
x: This makes the ester α-H more acidic than the ketone α-H. The alkoxy group of an ester donates into the C=O, so ester enolates are less stabilized (25 vs 19).
This places the diester above the diketone. As with the monocarbonyl pair, ester groups stabilize the anion less than ketone groups do (13 vs 9).
This reverses both pairs: ketones are more acidic than the corresponding esters in each case.

q: Ethyne (pK<sub>a</sub> 25) reacts with a base B<sup>−</sup> with K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>13</sup>: HC≡CH + B<sup>−</sup> ⇌ HC≡C<sup>−</sup> + HB. Which base B<sup>−</sup> fits these data?
h: K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of HB − 25)</sup>. Solve for the pK<sub>a</sub> of HB, then recognize the acid.
w: 13 = pKa(HB) − 25, so pKa(HB) ≈ 38, the value for NH3. The base is therefore NH2−, the standard reagent for making acetylide ions.
x: HB would be water (15.7), giving K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(15.7 − 25)</sup> ≈ 10<sup>−9</sup>, not 10<sup>13</sup>.
HB would be butane (≈ 50), giving K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>25</sup>, far larger than 10<sup>13</sup>.
HB would be propyne (≈ 25), essentially the same acidity as ethyne, giving K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 1.

q: Which compound is not deprotonated to a significant extent by aqueous NaOH (pKa of H2O 15.7)?
h: NaOH deprotonates an acid substantially only when that acid's pK<sub>a</sub> is lower than 15.7. Recall the pK<sub>a</sub> of each type.
w: Approximate pKa values: 1-hexyne ≈ 25, acetic acid 4.8, phenol 10, ethanethiol 10.6. Only 1-hexyne is weaker than water, so Keq ≈ 10(15.7 − 25) ≈ 10−9; hydroxide leaves it essentially untouched. Terminal alkynes need NaNH2.
x: Acetic acid (4.8) is about 10<sup>11</sup> times more acidic than water; NaOH converts it completely to acetate.
Phenol (10) is more acidic than water, so NaOH converts it to sodium phenoxide (K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>5.7</sup>).
Thiols (≈ 10.6) are much more acidic than alcohols because of the larger sulfur atom; NaOH converts ethanethiol to the thiolate.

q: Sodium acetylide (HC≡CNa) is mixed with an equimolar amount of each compound below. With which one does essentially no proton transfer occur?
h: The acetylide ion removes a proton only from an acid stronger than ethyne (pK<sub>a</sub> 25).
w: Water (15.7), ethanol (16) and tert-butyl alcohol (≈ 18) are all stronger acids than ethyne, so each converts acetylide back to ethyne. Ammonia (pKa ≈ 38) is 1013 times weaker, so Keq ≈ 10−13 and nothing happens. This is why liquid NH3 is the usual solvent for acetylide reactions.
x: Water (15.7) is far more acidic than ethyne, so it protonates acetylide immediately (K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>9</sup>).
Ethanol (16) is more acidic than ethyne by about 9 pK<sub>a</sub> units, so it protonates acetylide.
tert-Butyl alcohol is the weakest of the alcohols (≈ 18), but it is still about 10<sup>7</sup> times more acidic than ethyne, so it protonates acetylide.

q:
Which statements are correct?
I. Ethanethiol (CH3CH2SH) is a stronger acid than ethanol.
II. Ethanethiolate (CH3CH2S−) is a stronger base than ethoxide.
III. The S–H bond is longer and weaker than the O–H bond, and sulfur spreads the negative charge over a larger volume.
h: If an acid is stronger, what must be true of its conjugate base? Then check whether the size argument in III is the right reason.
w: Ethanethiol (pKa ≈ 10.6) is far more acidic than ethanol (≈ 16), so I is true, and the reason is the size effect described in III (true). Because the thiol is the stronger acid, its conjugate base, ethanethiolate, must be the weaker base, so II is false. Answer: I and III only. (Thiolates are excellent nucleophiles, but nucleophilicity is not the same as basicity.)
x: Statement II is false: the stronger acid has the weaker conjugate base, so ethanethiolate is a weaker base than ethoxide.
Statement I is true (thiols are about 10<sup>5</sup> times more acidic than alcohols) and II is false, so this combination fails on both.
Statement III is also true; it gives the reason thiols are more acidic, so it must be included.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Protonate the alkene so that the more stable carbocation forms, then let bromide bond to that carbon.
w: HBr adds by Markovnikov's rule. H+ bonds to the CH carbon of the C=C, which leaves the positive charge on the carbon bearing two methyl groups (a tertiary cation). Bromide traps that cation to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. Protonating the other alkene carbon would give a less stable secondary cation.
x: 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane places Br on the less substituted alkene carbon; that would require the secondary cation, not the tertiary one.
1-Bromo-2-methylbutane has Br on a CH<sub>2</sub> that was a methyl group, not one of the two alkene carbons.
1-Bromo-3-methylbutane puts Br on a primary carbon that was never part of the C=C; HBr adds only across the double bond.

q: What is the major product of this reaction? (Assume the carbocation rearranges whenever a more stable cation can form.)
h: Draw the first carbocation, then ask whether a neighboring hydrogen can shift to make a more stable one.
w: Protonation of the terminal CH2 gives a secondary cation at C2. The neighboring C3 carries a hydrogen and two methyls, so a 1,2-hydride shift converts the secondary cation into a tertiary cation. Chloride traps the tertiary cation: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane is the major product. The unrearranged 2-chloro-3-methylbutane forms only as a minor product.
x: 2-Chloro-3-methylbutane is the unrearranged Markovnikov product; it forms, but most of the secondary cation rearranges before chloride traps it.
1-Chloro-3-methylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product; HCl adds through a carbocation, which never forms on the terminal carbon.
1-Chloro-2-methylbutane has Cl on a primary carbon; no step of the mechanism produces a primary cation there.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: The first carbocation sits next to a quaternary carbon. What can migrate from that carbon?
w: Protonation gives a secondary cation at C2, next to the quaternary C3 that has three methyls and no hydrogen. A 1,2-methyl shift moves one methyl (with its bonding pair) to C2 and leaves a tertiary cation on C3. Bromide traps it to give 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.
x: 3-Bromo-2,2-dimethylbutane is the unrearranged product; the secondary cation rearranges to the tertiary one faster than most of it is trapped.
1-Bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product, which needs radical conditions (HBr with peroxides).
1-Bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane has Br on a primary carbon; the methyl shift leaves the charge on a tertiary carbon, not a primary one.

q: Which species is the intermediate in this reaction?
h: HBr adds in two steps; the first step is protonation of the C=C.
w: Protonation of the CH carbon of 1-methylcyclohexene puts the positive charge on the ring carbon that carries the methyl, giving the tertiary 1-methylcyclohexyl cation. Bromide then adds to it to give 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.
x: The secondary cation forms only if H<sup>+</sup> adds to the methyl-bearing carbon, which is the less stable choice.
A bridged bromonium ion forms when Br<sub>2</sub> adds to an alkene; HBr adds H<sup>+</sup> first, not Br<sup>+</sup>.
A carbanion would need a nucleophile to add first; the alkene is the nucleophile here and H<sup>+</sup> is the electrophile.

q: What is the product of this two-step sequence? (Chiral products form as racemates; one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: Decide which carbon gets boron, then remember that H and B add to the same face and oxidation keeps the configuration.
w: BH3 adds in one concerted step: boron bonds to the less substituted alkene carbon (C2) and hydrogen to the methyl-bearing carbon (C1), both from the same face (syn). H2O2/NaOH replaces C–B with C–OH with retention. The new H on C1 and the OH on C2 are cis, so the methyl and OH are trans: trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, formed as a racemate.
x: cis-2-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol would require H and OH on opposite faces; hydroboration is syn and oxidation occurs with retention.
1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is the Markovnikov alcohol from acid hydration or oxymercuration, not from hydroboration.
Cyclohexylmethanol would come from hydroboration of methylenecyclohexane, whose C=C is outside the ring.

q: What is the product of this reaction sequence?
h: Oxymercuration follows the same regiochemistry as acid hydration but without rearrangement.
w: Hg(OAc)2 forms a mercurinium ion; water opens it at the more substituted carbon (C2), and NaBH4 replaces the C–HgOAc bond with C–H. Net Markovnikov addition of H and OH: hexan-2-ol.
x: Hexan-1-ol is the anti-Markovnikov alcohol from hydroboration–oxidation.
Hexan-3-ol would need a hydride shift; the mercurinium ion does not rearrange, and a shift would only give another secondary cation anyway.
A 1,2-diol comes from dihydroxylation (OsO<sub>4</sub>); NaBH<sub>4</sub> puts H, not OH, where mercury was.

q: Which reagents carry out this conversion in good yield?
h: The target is the Markovnikov alcohol with the carbon skeleton unchanged. Which method avoids a free carbocation?
w: The target, 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, is the Markovnikov alcohol with no change to the skeleton. Oxymercuration–demercuration gives Markovnikov addition through a bridged mercurinium ion, so the methyl shift that plagues this substrate cannot occur.
x: Acid-catalyzed hydration goes through the secondary cation, which undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift and gives mainly 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov and gives the primary alcohol 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups and gives 3,3-dimethylbutane-1,2-diol, not a mono-alcohol.

q: What is the product? The two new stereocenters form as a racemate; one enantiomer is drawn.
h: Both alkene carbons are tertiary, so focus on stereochemistry: which two groups are delivered to the same face?
w: Hydroboration is a syn addition: H goes to one alkene carbon and B to the other from the same face, and oxidation replaces B with OH with retention. So the OH on C1 and the new H on C2 are cis. Each original methyl is pushed to the face opposite the group that added to its carbon: with OH up at C1, the C1 methyl is down; with H up at C2, the C2 methyl is down. The product is 1,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol with the two methyl groups cis (OH trans to the C2 methyl).
x: This diastereomer has the two methyls trans, which would require H and OH to add to opposite faces (anti addition).
A cis-1,2-diol forms with OsO<sub>4</sub>; hydroboration–oxidation introduces only one OH.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane is the product of catalytic hydrogenation (H<sub>2</sub>, Pt), not hydroboration–oxidation.

q:
Which statements correctly explain why hydroboration–oxidation of propene gives propan-1-ol rather than propan-2-ol?
I. Boron, the electron-poor end of the B–H bond, bonds to the less substituted alkene carbon.
II. In the four-center transition state, partial positive charge builds on the more substituted carbon, which supports it better.
III. Putting the bulky boron group on the terminal CH2 minimizes steric strain.
IV. A secondary carbocation forms and is trapped by hydride from boron.
h: Hydroboration is concerted. Check each statement for both electronic and steric reasoning.
w: Statements I, II and III are all correct and work together: boron is the electrophile, it bonds to the terminal carbon, the slight δ+ in the transition state is on the secondary carbon, and the larger BH2 group goes to the less hindered carbon. Statement IV is false because hydroboration is concerted and has no carbocation intermediate. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement II is also correct: the electronic preference (δ+ on the more substituted carbon) reinforces the steric one.
Statement IV is false; no carbocation forms, which is also why hydroboration never rearranges.
Statement IV is false, and statement I (boron as the electrophile bonding to the terminal carbon) is a key part of the explanation.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Draw the first carbocation and look at the carbon next to it. Is there a hydrogen on a more substituted neighbor?
w: Protonation of the terminal CH2 gives a secondary cation next to the ring CH. A 1,2-hydride shift from that ring carbon gives the tertiary 1-ethylcyclohexyl cation, and bromide traps it: 1-bromo-1-ethylcyclohexane.
x: (1-Bromoethyl)cyclohexane is the unrearranged product; the secondary cation shifts a hydride to reach a tertiary cation first.
(2-Bromoethyl)cyclohexane is anti-Markovnikov; it needs HBr with peroxides (a radical mechanism).

1-Bromo-1-methylcycloheptane would need a ring expansion (which gives only a secondary cycloheptyl cation, no gain) and then a second shift; the single 1,2-hydride shift to the tertiary 1-ethylcyclohexyl cation is faster.

q: In the acid-catalyzed hydration of 2-methylpropene (H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>), which step is rate-determining?
c: Protonation of the alkene to form the tert-butyl cation
Attack of water on the tert-butyl cation
Deprotonation of the oxonium ion to give the alcohol
Simultaneous addition of H and OH in one concerted step
h: Which step creates a high-energy intermediate from a neutral, stable starting material?
w: The slow step is protonation of the alkene: it breaks the π bond and creates a carbocation. Water capturing the cation and the final proton transfer are both fast.
x: Water attack on a carbocation is a fast combination of a nucleophile with a reactive cation.
Proton transfer from the oxonium ion to water is fast and nearly thermoneutral.
Acid-catalyzed hydration is stepwise through a carbocation; it is not a concerted addition.

q: For which alkene do acid-catalyzed hydration and hydroboration–oxidation give the same constitutional isomer of the alcohol?
h: Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov products are the same only if the two alkene carbons are equivalent and no rearrangement is possible.
w: In cyclohexene the two alkene carbons are equivalent, so Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov addition both give cyclohexanol, and the secondary cyclohexyl cation has no better cation to shift to.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene gives 1-methylcyclohexanol by acid hydration but trans-2-methylcyclohexanol by hydroboration.
Methylenecyclohexane gives 1-methylcyclohexanol by acid hydration but cyclohexylmethanol by hydroboration.
3-Methylbut-1-ene gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol (after a hydride shift) by acid hydration but 3-methylbutan-1-ol by hydroboration.

q:
Which statements about oxymercuration–demercuration (1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 2. NaBH4) are correct?
I. A bridged mercurinium ion forms, so carbocation rearrangements do not occur.
II. Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the mercurinium ion.
III. NaBH4 replaces the C–HgOAc bond with a C–H bond.
IV. The H and OH are always added syn to each other.
h: Think separately about the oxymercuration step (stereospecific) and the demercuration step.
w: I, II and III are correct. The mercurinium ion has no free carbocation, so no shifts; water opens it at the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov); NaBH4 replaces mercury with hydrogen. Statement IV is false: the demercuration step goes through a radical and is not stereospecific, so the overall addition of H and OH is not reliably syn or anti. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement IV is false (demercuration is not stereospecific), and II and III are true.
Statement I is also true; the bridged ion is exactly why this method avoids rearrangement.
Statement IV is false; replacing Hg with H goes through a radical, so the H can end up on either face.

q: What is the major product of this sequence?
h: The solvent is the nucleophile that opens the mercurinium ion.
w: Hg(OAc)2 forms the mercurinium ion; the solvent, methanol, attacks the more substituted carbon (the one bearing the methyl). NaBH4 then replaces mercury with H. The result is Markovnikov addition of H and OCH3: 1-methoxy-1-methylcyclohexane.
x: 1-Methoxy-2-methylcyclohexane has OCH<sub>3</sub> on the less substituted carbon; the nucleophile opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon.
1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol would form if water were the solvent; here methanol is the nucleophile.
(Methoxymethyl)cyclohexane puts OCH<sub>3</sub> on a carbon that was not part of the C=C.

q: Hydroboration–oxidation (1. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  2. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH) of which alkene gives racemic trans-2-methylcyclopentan-1-ol (shown) as the only constitutional isomer?
h: Work backward: OH marks where boron went; the H added to the neighboring carbon, which carries the methyl.
w: Boron (and later OH) goes to the less substituted alkene carbon, and H goes to the other carbon, syn. For the OH to sit next to the methyl-bearing carbon, the C=C must join those two carbons: 1-methylcyclopentene. Syn addition puts H and OH cis, so methyl and OH are trans, as in the target.
x: Methylenecyclopentane gives cyclopentylmethanol; the OH ends up on the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>.
3-Methylcyclopentene has two similar secondary alkene carbons, so boron adds to both and gives a mixture of 2- and 3-methylcyclopentanols.
4-Methylcyclopentene gives only 3-methylcyclopentan-1-ol; its OH is two carbons from the methyl.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylpropene is treated with H<sub>2</sub>O and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Which carbocation forms when the alkene is protonated?
w: Protonation of the CH2 carbon gives the tert-butyl cation; water adds and loses a proton to give 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol), the Markovnikov product.
x: 2-Methylpropan-1-ol is the anti-Markovnikov alcohol from hydroboration–oxidation.
A diol needs a dihydroxylation reagent such as OsO<sub>4</sub>; aqueous acid adds only H and OH.
2-Methylpropane would require H<sub>2</sub> and a metal catalyst; water adds OH, not H.

q: (R)-3-Methylhex-1-ene is treated with H2O and catalytic H2SO4. Which best describes the major product?
c: 3-Methylhexan-3-ol, formed as a single enantiomer because C3 keeps its configuration
3-Methylhexan-2-ol, formed as a mixture of diastereomers
h: Follow the carbocation: does it rearrange, and what happens to the original stereocenter?
w: Protonation gives a secondary cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 (the stereocenter) gives the more stable tertiary cation at C3, which is planar, so the original configuration is lost. Water attacks either face equally, giving 3-methylhexan-3-ol as a racemic mixture (C3 bears CH3, ethyl, propyl and OH, so it is a stereocenter).
x: C3 becomes the sp<sup>2</sup> cation carbon after the hydride shift, so its configuration cannot be retained.
3-Methylhexan-2-ol is the unrearranged product; the secondary cation shifts a hydride to reach the tertiary cation.
The primary alcohol is the hydroboration product; acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov.

q:
Rank these alkenes by rate of acid-catalyzed hydration (slowest to fastest).
I. ethene II. propene III. 2-methylpropene
h: The rate-determining step forms a carbocation. Apply the Hammond postulate.
w: Protonation is rate-determining and its transition state resembles the carbocation. Ethene gives a primary cation, propene a secondary, and 2-methylpropene a tertiary cation, so the rate order is I < II < III.
x: This reverses the order; more substituted cations form faster, not slower.
Ethene cannot be faster than propene: it would have to form a primary (essentially methyl-like) cation.
2-Methylpropene forms the tertiary cation, so it reacts fastest, not in the middle.

q: What is the product of this reaction? (Chiral products form as racemates; one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: Br<sub>2</sub> adds through a bridged bromonium ion. From which face does bromide attack?
w: Br2 forms a bromonium ion on one face of the ring; bromide must attack from the opposite face (backside, SN2-like). Anti addition gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane, formed as a racemate.
x: cis-1,2-Dibromocyclohexane would need syn addition; the bromonium ion blocks the face that Br<sup>−</sup> would need.
A geminal dibromide would require both Br atoms on one carbon; Br<sub>2</sub> adds one Br to each alkene carbon.
3-Bromocyclohexene is an allylic substitution product from NBS and light, a radical reaction, not Br<sub>2</sub> in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>.

q: What is the stereochemical outcome when (Z)-but-2-ene reacts with Br2 in CH2Cl2?
h: Anti addition to a cis alkene: is the product the like (R,R/S,S) or unlike (R,S) diastereomer?
w: Br2 adds anti. For a cis alkene, anti addition gives the (R,R)/(S,S) pair; bromide opens the achiral bromonium ion equally at either carbon, so the two enantiomers form equally: racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane. (The meso compound comes from the E alkene.)
x: The meso dibromide comes from anti addition to (E)-but-2-ene, or syn addition to the Z alkene.
Achiral reactants with no chiral catalyst cannot give a single enantiomer; attack at the two bromonium carbons is equally likely.
Bromine addition is stereospecific: one alkene isomer gives one diastereomer, not a mixture of both.

q: Which alkene and reagent combination gives meso-butane-2,3-diol (shown)?
h: Pair cis/trans with syn/anti: which pairing gives the meso (unlike) diol?
w: For a symmetric 1,2-disubstituted alkene, cis + syn addition or trans + anti addition gives the meso product. OsO4/NMO adds both OH groups syn, so (Z)-but-2-ene with OsO4, NMO gives meso-butane-2,3-diol. (The E alkene with mCPBA then H3O+ would also work, but that pairing is not offered.)
x: Syn addition to the E alkene gives the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) diol.
Epoxidation then acid opening is an anti dihydroxylation; anti addition to the Z alkene gives the racemic diol.
Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C and gives two molecules of acetaldehyde, not a diol.

q: What is the major product? (Chiral products form as racemates; one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: Water is the nucleophile that opens the bromonium ion. Which carbon does it attack, and from which face?
w: Br2 forms a bromonium ion. Water, present in large excess, attacks the carbon that carries more positive charge, the tertiary C1, from the face opposite the bridging Br. The result is OH on C1 and Br on C2, trans: trans-2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (racemic).
x: In this diastereomer Br and OH are cis, which would require syn addition; bromonium opening is anti.
This regioisomer puts OH on the secondary carbon; water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bromonium ion.
The dibromide is a minor product; water, the solvent, vastly outnumbers bromide and captures the bromonium ion.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: The solvent is the nucleophile, and it opens the bromonium ion where the positive charge is best supported.
w: Br2 forms a bromonium ion. Methanol (the solvent) attacks the tertiary carbon, which carries more δ+, and loses a proton. Product: 1-bromo-2-methoxy-2-methylpropane.
x: This regioisomer has OCH<sub>3</sub> on the primary carbon; the solvent attacks the more substituted carbon.
The dibromide would form in an inert solvent such as CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>; in methanol the solvent outcompetes bromide.
A bromohydrin requires water as the nucleophile; here the solvent is methanol.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Anti addition to a trans alkene with identical ends: like (R,R) or unlike (R,S)?
w: Br2 adds anti. Anti addition to a trans alkene whose two ends are identical gives the meso (unlike) product: (3R,4S)-3,4-dibromohexane, which has an internal mirror plane.
x: (3R,4R)-3,4-Dibromohexane is one enantiomer of the racemate formed from the Z alkene.
4-Bromohex-2-ene is an allylic bromination product (NBS, light); Br<sub>2</sub> in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=C.
A geminal dibromide would need both Br atoms on one carbon; each alkene carbon receives one Br.

q: Which species is the intermediate when cyclopentene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>?
h: The intermediate explains why the two Br atoms end up trans.
w: Br2 is polarized by the π bond; the alkene attacks one Br and the same Br uses a lone pair to bond to the second carbon, giving a cyclic bromonium ion. Bromide then attacks from the back face, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane.
x: An open β-bromo carbocation would be planar and could be attacked from either face, giving cis and trans products; the observed anti addition rules it out.
The cyclopentyl cation is the intermediate in HBr addition, not Br<sub>2</sub> addition.
A carbanion is not formed; the alkene acts as the nucleophile, not the electrophile.

q:
2-Methylpropene reacts with Br2 in water to give 1-bromo-2-methylpropan-2-ol. Which statements about the opening of the bromonium ion are correct?
I. Water attacks the more substituted carbon because that carbon carries more of the positive charge.
II. Water attacks from the face opposite the bridging bromine.
III. Water attacks the less hindered CH2 carbon, as in an SN2 reaction.
IV. The OH ends up on the tertiary carbon.
h: The bromonium ion is unsymmetrical: the C–Br bond to the tertiary carbon is longer and weaker.
w: In the unsymmetrical bromonium ion, the tertiary carbon bears more δ+ and its C–Br bond is weaker, so water attacks there (I), from the back face (II), and the OH ends up on the tertiary carbon (IV). Statement III describes the opposite regiochemistry. Answer: I, II and IV only.
x: Statement IV is also true: it is the result of the attack described in I.
Statement III is false; electronic effects (δ+ on the tertiary carbon) outweigh steric hindrance in bromonium opening.
Statement III is false, and it contradicts IV: attack at CH<sub>2</sub> would put OH on the primary carbon.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Both H atoms come from the catalyst surface.
w: Catalytic hydrogenation adds both H atoms to the same face (syn). The two methyl groups are pushed together to the other face, giving cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane (a meso compound).
x: trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane needs H atoms on opposite faces (anti addition), which a metal surface cannot deliver.
1,2-Dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol adds H and OH, as in hydration; H<sub>2</sub>/Pd adds only hydrogen.
1,1-Dimethylcyclohexane would require a methyl to migrate; hydrogenation does not change the carbon skeleton.

q: Which alkene gives a meso compound when hydrogenated with H2 over Pt?
h: A meso product needs two stereocenters. Syn addition to which geometry gives the unlike (R,S) product?
w: Hydrogenation is syn. In (Z)-3,4-dimethylhex-3-ene, the two ethyl groups are on the same side (and so are the two methyls). Adding H to both carbons from one face gives (3R,4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane, which has an internal mirror plane: the Z alkene gives the meso product.
x: Syn addition to the E isomer gives racemic (3R,4R)/(3S,4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane, which is chiral.
2,3-Dimethylbutane is achiral but has no stereocenters, so it is not a meso compound.
This alkene gives 3-methylhexane, which has one stereocenter and forms as a racemate.

q: What is the product of this two-step sequence? (Chiral products form as racemates; one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: Step 1 makes an epoxide on one face; in step 2 water opens it from the other face.
w: mCPBA delivers O to one face to give cyclohexene oxide. In aqueous acid the protonated epoxide is opened by water from the back face (anti), so the two OH groups end up trans: trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol (racemic).
x: cis-Cyclohexane-1,2-diol (meso) comes from syn dihydroxylation with OsO4.
The epoxide is the product after step 1 only; H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> opens it.
Cyclohexanol would form from hydration; this sequence adds two oxygens.

q: What is the product of this reaction? (Chiral products form as racemates; one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: OsO<sub>4</sub> forms a cyclic osmate ester with both oxygens on one face.
w: OsO4 adds both oxygens to the same face through a cyclic osmate ester; NMO reoxidizes the osmium. The diol is syn: cis-1-methylcyclohexane-1,2-diol (racemic).
x: The trans diol forms by anti dihydroxylation (mCPBA, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>).
6-Oxoheptanal is the ozonolysis product; OsO<sub>4</sub>/NMO does not cleave the C–C bond.
1-Methylcyclohexanol has only one OH; it is the Markovnikov hydration product.

q: Which reagents convert cyclopentene into racemic trans-cyclopentane-1,2-diol?
h: A trans diol needs the two oxygens added to opposite faces.
w: Epoxidation puts one O on one face; acid-catalyzed opening by water attacks from the opposite face. The net anti dihydroxylation gives trans-cyclopentane-1,2-diol: 1. mCPBA, 2. H3O+.
x: OsO4 is a syn dihydroxylation and gives the cis (meso) diol.
Cold, dilute basic KMnO<sub>4</sub> also adds both OH groups syn through a cyclic manganate ester, giving the cis diol.
Ozonolysis cleaves the ring C=C and gives pentanedial, not a diol.

q: 1-Methylcyclohexene is converted to a diol in two separate experiments: (a) OsO<sub>4</sub>, NMO; (b) 1. mCPBA  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. How are the diol products of (a) and (b) related?
h: Both give 1-methylcyclohexane-1,2-diol. Compare the relative positions of the two OH groups.
w: Both give OH groups on C1 and C2, so they have the same connectivity. OsO4 is syn (cis diol) and epoxidation/acid opening is anti (trans diol). Cis and trans isomers of the same ring compound are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers.
x: Enantiomers are mirror images; cis and trans diols are not, since a mirror image keeps the OH groups on the same relative faces.
Syn and anti dihydroxylation put the second OH on different faces, so the products differ.
Both reactions put OH on the two former alkene carbons, so the connectivity is the same.

q: (E)-But-2-ene reacts with Br2 in water. Which describes the product?
h: Use the dibromide as a model: anti addition to the E alkene gives the meso dibromide. Now replace one Br by OH without moving any atoms.
w: Anti addition to (E)-but-2-ene with Br2 would give meso-(2R,3S)-dibromide. Replacing one Br with OH (water attacks the bromonium ion anti) keeps the same spatial arrangement, and OH outranks carbon just as Br does, so the descriptors stay unlike: (2R,3S). Water attacks the two equivalent carbons of the achiral bromonium ion equally, giving the mirror image too: racemic (2R,3S)/(2S,3R)-3-bromobutan-2-ol.
x: The (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair comes from anti addition to the Z alkene.
A meso compound needs identical halves; C2 carries OH and C3 carries Br, so no internal mirror plane is possible.
Achiral starting materials give a racemate; the two carbons of the bromonium ion are attacked equally.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Which carbon of the bromonium ion carries more positive charge: the CH<sub>2</sub> or the benzylic CH?
w: Water opens the bromonium ion at the benzylic carbon, where the δ+ is stabilized by the ring. OH goes to the benzylic carbon and Br to the CH2: 2-bromo-1-phenylethan-1-ol (racemic).
x: This regioisomer puts OH on CH<sub>2</sub>; water attacks the carbon that better supports positive charge, the benzylic one.
The dibromide forms in an inert solvent; in water the solvent captures the bromonium ion.
1-Phenylethanol is the product of hydration (H and OH), not of Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O.

q: What is the final product of this two-step sequence?
h: Step 1 gives a trans bromohydrin. In base, which nucleophile is right next door, and where is it relative to Br?
w: Step 1 gives trans-2-bromocyclohexan-1-ol. NaOH deprotonates the OH; because OH and Br are trans, the alkoxide can reach the back side of the C–Br bond (both diaxial), and an intramolecular SN2 closes the three-membered ring: cyclohexene oxide.
x: Hydroxide does not substitute Br directly here; the neighboring alkoxide closes the epoxide much faster. A diol would need a later acid step.
Cyclohexanone would need an oxidation; no oxidizing agent is present.
Elimination of HBr toward the CH<sub>2</sub> side is slow compared with the intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2 that forms the epoxide.

q: Why does catalytic hydrogenation (H<sub>2</sub>, Pt) add both hydrogen atoms to the same face of an alkene?
c: Both H atoms are delivered from the metal surface to the alkene face bound to the catalyst
A carbocation forms and is then attacked by hydride from the less hindered face of the alkene
A bridged three-membered ring intermediate blocks one face of the alkene from the second H
H<sub>2</sub> adds in one step through a cyclic osmate-like ester
h: Picture where the alkene and the hydrogen atoms are when they react.
w: H2 dissociates into H atoms on the metal surface, and the alkene adsorbs on the surface through one face of its π bond. Both H atoms are transferred from the surface to that face: syn addition.
x: No carbocation forms in catalytic hydrogenation; there is no acid and no cation intermediate.
Bridged intermediates (bromonium, mercurinium) explain anti addition, not the syn addition of H<sub>2</sub>.
Cyclic esters explain syn dihydroxylation with OsO<sub>4</sub>; H<sub>2</sub> is activated on the metal surface.

q: Which products form when 2-methylbut-2-ene is treated with 1. O<sub>3</sub>, 2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S?
h: Cut the C=C and put a C=O on each carbon. Reductive workup stops at the aldehyde.
w: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C; each alkene carbon becomes a C=O. The carbon bearing two methyls becomes acetone, and the CH carbon becomes acetaldehyde. Dimethyl sulfide is a reductive workup, so the aldehyde is not oxidized: acetone and acetaldehyde.
x: Acetic acid would form with an oxidative workup (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) or hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>; (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S leaves the aldehyde intact.
Butan-2-one and formaldehyde come from 2-methylbut-1-ene, whose C=C is at the end of the chain.
Propanal and acetaldehyde come from pent-2-ene, which has no branching methyl on the alkene carbon.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: When the C=C is in a ring, ozonolysis opens the ring and both carbonyls stay in one molecule.
w: Cleaving the ring C=C opens the ring into one chain. The methyl-bearing carbon becomes a ketone (CH3C=O) and the CH carbon becomes an aldehyde, with four CH2 groups in between: 6-oxoheptanal.
x: 6-Oxoheptanoic acid has a carboxylic acid; that needs an oxidative workup or hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>, not (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S.
Cyclohexanone (plus formaldehyde) comes from methylenecyclohexane, whose C=C is outside the ring.
Heptane-2,6-dione would need methyl groups on both alkene carbons; the CH carbon becomes an aldehyde, not a ketone.

q: Alkene X (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) reacts with 1. O<sub>3</sub>, 2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S to give octane-2,7-dione (shown) as the only organic product. What is X?
h: One product containing two C=O groups from a C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>14</sub> alkene means a ring. Join the two carbonyl carbons back together with a C=C.
w: C8H14 has two degrees of unsaturation: one C=C and one ring. A single product with both carbonyls means the C=C was in a ring. Reconnecting the two ketone carbons (C2 and C7) with a double bond gives a six-membered ring with a methyl on each alkene carbon: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene.
x: 1,3-Dimethylcyclohexene gives 2-methyl-6-oxoheptanal (one aldehyde), because one alkene carbon is a CH.
1-Methylcycloheptene gives 7-oxooctanal, a keto aldehyde, because one of its alkene carbons is a CH.
(2E,6E)-Octa-2,6-diene gives two acetaldehyde molecules and butanedial, three products instead of one.

q: What is the organic product of this reaction?
h: Hot, acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves C=C, and any aldehyde formed is oxidized further.
w: Hot KMnO4 cleaves the C=C like ozonolysis, but the CH carbon is oxidized all the way to a carboxylic acid. The methyl-bearing carbon has no H, so it stops as a ketone: 6-oxoheptanoic acid.
x: 6-Oxoheptanal is the reductive ozonolysis product; hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidizes the aldehyde to an acid.
The cis diol forms with cold, dilute, basic KMnO<sub>4</sub>; hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the C–C bond.
Hexanedioic acid would require cutting off the methyl carbon; a ketone carbon has no H and is not oxidized further.

q: An alkene C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> is heated with acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>; the products are butan-2-one and CO<sub>2</sub>. What is the alkene?
h: CO<sub>2</sub> comes from a terminal =CH<sub>2</sub>. Rebuild the C=C from the ketone carbon.
w: A =CH2 group is oxidized all the way to CO2. The other alkene carbon became the C=O of butan-2-one, so it carried a methyl and an ethyl: 2-methylbut-1-ene.
x: 2-Methylbut-2-ene gives acetone and acetic acid; neither carbon is a =CH<sub>2</sub>.
Pent-1-ene gives butanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>; its internal alkene carbon is a CH, which becomes an acid, not a ketone.
Pent-2-ene gives acetic acid and propanoic acid; it has no =CH<sub>2</sub> to make CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Compound Y (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) gives heptanedioic acid, HO<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, as the only product when heated with acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>. What is Y?
h: All seven carbons stay in one product, and both ends are COOH. Where was the C=C?
w: The single product keeps all seven carbons, so the C=C was in a ring, and both alkene carbons were CH (each became a COOH). Joining the two acid carbons with a C=C gives a seven-membered ring: cycloheptene.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene gives 6-oxoheptanoic acid; the methyl-bearing carbon becomes a ketone, not an acid.
Methylenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and CO<sub>2</sub>.
Hepta-1,6-diene gives pentanedioic acid plus two CO<sub>2</sub>; the terminal CH<sub>2</sub> carbons are lost.

q: Which reagents convert hex-1-ene into pentanal?
h: You need to cut the C=C and stop at the aldehyde.
