w: Ozonolysis with a reductive workup cleaves the C=C into two carbonyl compounds and leaves aldehydes as aldehydes: hex-1-ene gives pentanal and formaldehyde. Answer: 1. O3, 2. (CH3)2S.
x: Hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidizes the aldehyde further and gives pentanoic acid (and CO<sub>2</sub>).
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups (hexane-1,2-diol) without breaking the C–C bond.
An H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> workup is oxidative and gives pentanoic acid.

q: Which reagents carry out this conversion?
h: The OH ends up on the less substituted alkene carbon.
w: The OH is on the former =CH2, the less substituted alkene carbon: anti-Markovnikov hydration. That is hydroboration–oxidation.
x: Acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
Oxymercuration–demercuration is also Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
Ozonolysis removes the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon as formaldehyde; reducing cyclohexanone then gives cyclohexanol, which has one fewer carbon.

q: Which sequence converts 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene into 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene as the major product?
h: The skeleton must change. Which step rearranges it, and which base gives the more substituted alkene?
w: The target has a different carbon skeleton, so a rearrangement is needed. HBr gives the secondary cation, which undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to the tertiary cation, giving 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane. Ethoxide, a small base, then gives the Zaitsev (tetrasubstituted) alkene, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene: 1. HBr, 2. NaOCH2CH3, heat.
x: tert-Butoxide is bulky and removes a primary CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogen, giving the Hofmann product 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene as the major alkene.
With peroxides HBr adds anti-Markovnikov by a radical path with no rearrangement; the primary bromide then gives the ether or 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, never the new skeleton.
Oxymercuration–demercuration does not rearrange and gives 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, not an alkene.

q:
Which of these alkene reactions go through a carbocation intermediate?
I. HBr (no peroxides)
II. H2O, H2SO4 (cat.)
III. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH
IV. 1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 2. NaBH4
h: Reactions that can rearrange go through free carbocations.
w: HBr addition and acid-catalyzed hydration both begin with protonation to give a carbocation, which is why both can rearrange. Hydroboration is concerted, and oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion instead of a free carbocation. Answer: I and II only.
x: Oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, not a free carbocation; that is why it does not rearrange.
HBr addition (I) does go through a carbocation, and oxymercuration (IV) does not.
Hydroboration is a concerted syn addition and oxymercuration uses a bridged ion; neither has a free carbocation.

q: What is the product when (E)-hex-3-ene is treated with 1. mCPBA, 2. H3O+?
c: A 1:1 mixture of meso and racemic hexane-3,4-diol
h: Epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition. Combine anti with trans.
w: mCPBA gives the trans epoxide, and water opens the protonated epoxide with inversion at one carbon: overall anti addition of two OH groups. Anti addition to a trans alkene with identical ends gives the unlike (3R,4S) product: meso-hexane-3,4-diol.
x: The racemic (R,R)/(S,S) diol comes from syn dihydroxylation (OsO4) of this E alkene, or anti addition to the Z alkene.
Achiral reactants cannot give a single enantiomer, and the anti addition to the E alkene gives the meso diastereomer anyway.
Epoxidation and acid opening are both stereospecific, so only one diastereomer forms.

q:
Which statements about epoxidation of alkenes with mCPBA are correct?
I. The oxygen is transferred in a single concerted step.
II. A cis alkene gives a cis epoxide.
III. A carbocation intermediate forms, so methyl and hydride shifts can occur.
IV. More highly substituted (more electron-rich) alkenes react faster.
h: The peroxy acid is an electrophile, and the reaction has no intermediate.
w: mCPBA transfers O in one concerted step (I), so the alkene geometry is kept (II) and no cation forms to rearrange (III is false). The peroxy acid is electrophilic, so electron-rich, more substituted alkenes react faster (IV). Answer: I, II and IV only.
x: Statement IV is also true: alkyl groups make the π bond more nucleophilic toward the electrophilic peroxy acid.
Statement III is false; the concerted mechanism has no carbocation and no rearrangement.
Statement III is false, and statement II (stereospecific, cis stays cis) is true.

q: Br2 is added separately to (E)-but-2-ene and to (Z)-but-2-ene. How is the product from the E alkene related to either product from the Z alkene?
h: Work out each product first: anti addition to E and to Z.
w: Anti addition to the E alkene gives meso-(2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane; anti addition to the Z alkene gives racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S). The meso compound and either chiral enantiomer are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers.
x: A meso compound is its own mirror image, so it cannot be the enantiomer of a chiral compound.
The reaction is stereospecific: the two alkene isomers give different stereoisomers.
Both products are 2,3-dibromobutane, so the connectivity is the same.

q: Limonene is treated with excess O<sub>3</sub>, then (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S. Besides formaldehyde, what is the organic product?
h: Both C=C bonds react with excess O<sub>3</sub>. The ring C=C opens the ring; the side-chain C=CH<sub>2</sub> loses its CH<sub>2</sub>.
w: Both alkenes are cleaved. The ring C=C opens: the methyl-bearing carbon becomes a methyl ketone and the CH carbon an aldehyde. The isopropenyl group loses CH2 as formaldehyde and becomes an acetyl group. Product: 3-acetyl-6-oxoheptanal (C9H14O3).
x: With excess O<sub>3</sub> the side-chain C=C is also cleaved; leaving it intact ignores the second alkene.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S is a reductive workup; the aldehyde is not oxidized to a carboxylic acid.
With excess O<sub>3</sub> the ring C=C is also cleaved, so the ring does not survive.

q: An alkene C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> gives propanoic acid as the only product when heated with acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>. What is the alkene?
h: A single product means the two halves of the alkene are identical.
w: Each CH alkene carbon becomes a COOH. Two identical propanoic acid molecules mean the alkene was symmetric, CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3: hex-3-ene (either isomer gives the same product; the E isomer is shown).
x: 2-Methylpent-2-ene gives acetone and propanoic acid: the carbon with two methyls becomes a ketone.
2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene gives only acetone, a ketone, because neither alkene carbon carries an H.
Hex-1-ene gives pentanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: What is the first intermediate formed when 2-methylbut-2-ene reacts with H<sub>2</sub>O and catalytic H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: The first step is protonation of the C=C. Which carbon should get the proton?
w: H+ adds to the CH carbon so that the positive charge ends up on the carbon bearing two methyls: the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation. Water then traps it.
x: The secondary cation forms only if H<sup>+</sup> adds to the more substituted carbon, which is the less favorable choice.
The primary cation is not formed by protonating this alkene; it would be far less stable anyway.
A carbanion would need a nucleophile to attack the alkene; in acid the alkene is the nucleophile.

q: Pent-4-en-1-ol reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (no water present) to give a cyclic product, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>BrO. What is it? (It forms as a racemate; one structure is drawn without stereochemistry.)
h: The molecule carries its own nucleophile. Which carbon of the bromonium ion does the OH attack, and what ring size results?
w: Br2 forms a bromonium ion on C4–C5. The OH group, held in the same molecule, attacks the more substituted carbon C4 (the one that carries more δ+), forming a five-membered ring, then loses H+. Br stays on C5: 2-(bromomethyl)oxolane (2-(bromomethyl)tetrahydrofuran).
x: Attack at the terminal CH<sub>2</sub> would form a six-membered ring, but that carbon carries less δ+ and the five-membered ring closes faster.
The dibromide forms when no internal nucleophile competes; here the OH captures the bromonium ion intramolecularly, and the product formula has only one Br.
The formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>BrO requires a ring; this open-chain bromohydrin would be C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>BrO<sub>2</sub> and needs water.

q: Which reaction gives a product that is a racemic mixture?
h: Draw each product and look for an internal mirror plane.
w: Br2 adds anti to cyclohexene, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane, which is chiral; both enantiomers form equally, so the product is racemic (cyclohexene + Br2). The other three reactions give achiral meso products.
x: Anti addition to the E alkene gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane, which is achiral.
Syn dihydroxylation of the Z alkene gives meso-butane-2,3-diol, which is achiral.
Syn dihydroxylation of cyclohexene gives cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, a meso compound.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Add H to the alkene carbon that already has more hydrogens.
w: Protonation of the CH carbon gives the tertiary 1-methylcyclohexyl cation; chloride adds to it, giving 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane (Markovnikov addition).
x: 1-Chloro-2-methylcyclohexane would come from the less stable secondary cation (anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry).
(Chloromethyl)cyclohexane puts Cl on the methyl carbon, which was not part of the C=C.
1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is the hydration product; HCl adds H and Cl, not H and OH.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Number so the multiple bonds as a set get the lowest locants. If both directions tie, which multiple bond wins the lower number?
w: Both numbering directions give the multiple bonds locants {1,4}. When there is a tie, IUPAC gives the double bond the lower number, so the name is pent-1-en-4-yne. In an enyne name the "-en-" always comes before the "-yne" (alphabetical order of the endings), and the final "e" of "-ene" is dropped.
x: This numbering gives the same locant set {1,4} but puts the lower number on the triple bond; on a tie the double bond gets the lower number.
In an enyne name "-ene" is cited first and "-yne" last; "-yn-...-ene" is never used.
Every multiple bond needs its own locant, written next to its own ending; a combined "1,4-enyne" ending is not used.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: First find the lowest locant set for both multiple bonds; only use the "double bond gets the lower number" rule if the sets tie. Then assign E/Z.
w: Numbering from the alkyne end gives locants {1,3}; from the other end {2,4}. The first point of difference decides, so C1 is the alkyne carbon: (E)-pent-3-en-1-yne. The double-bond tiebreaker only applies when the locant sets are equal, which they are not here. At C3=C4 the higher-priority groups (the alkynyl carbon on C3 and the CH3 on C4) are on opposite sides, so the alkene is E.
x: The two higher-priority groups (C≡CH on C3, CH3 on C4) are on opposite sides of the double bond, which is E, not Z.
Locants {2,4} are higher than {1,3}; the double bond gets the lower number only when the two sets tie.
The ending order is always "-en-...-yne"; "-yn-...-ene" is not an IUPAC form.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Settle the numbering using the multiple bonds first (lowest set, then the double bond lower). Substituent locants are considered only after that.
w: The six-carbon chain holds both multiple bonds. From either end the multiple bonds get {1,5}, a tie, so the double bond gets C1. Numbering from the alkene end puts the methyl on C4: 4-methylhex-1-en-5-yne. The ene-before-substituent priority means you cannot renumber just to give the methyl a lower locant (3).
x: This numbers from the alkyne end to give the methyl locant 3, but the double-bond tiebreaker outranks substituent locants.
Locant 3 for the methyl would require numbering from the alkyne end, which would make the alkene C5, not C1; the name mixes two numberings.
Numbering from the alkyne end makes the alkene C5 and the methyl C3, not C4; and the double bond should get the lower number anyway.

q: A terminal alkyne (pKa ≈ 25) must be converted completely to its acetylide ion before an alkylation. Which base is suitable?
h: An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid. Compare the pKa of the alkyne with the pKa of each base's conjugate acid.
w: Deprotonation is favorable only if the conjugate acid of the base is a weaker acid (higher pKa) than the alkyne. NH3 (38) is far weaker than the alkyne (25), so NaNH2 deprotonates it essentially completely (Keq ≈ 1013). Hydroxide, ethoxide and bicarbonate all have conjugate acids stronger than the alkyne, so the equilibrium lies on the alkyne side.
x: Water (15.7) is a much stronger acid than the alkyne (25), so hydroxide leaves the alkyne almost entirely protonated (Keq ≈ 10−9).
Ethanol (16) is a stronger acid than the alkyne, so ethoxide gives only a trace of acetylide; this is the classic "close enough" trap.
Bicarbonate is a very weak base; carbonic acid (6.4) is about 10<sup>18</sup> times more acidic than the alkyne.

q:
Which list puts these compounds in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first)?
ethane, ethene, ethyne, ammonia
h: For the hydrocarbons, think about the s character of the orbital holding the lone pair in each conjugate base. Then place NH3 using its pKa (≈ 38).
w: Approximate pKa values: ethane ≈ 50 (sp3, 25% s), ethene ≈ 44 (sp2, 33% s), ammonia ≈ 38, ethyne ≈ 25 (sp, 50% s). More s character holds the carbanion lone pair closer to the nucleus, stabilizing the base. So ethane < ethene < ammonia < ethyne. This ordering is why NH2− deprotonates a terminal alkyne but not an alkene.
x: Ethyne (25) is far more acidic than ammonia (38); if ammonia were the stronger acid, NaNH<sub>2</sub> could not make acetylides.
Ammonia (38) is more acidic than ethane (50) and ethene (44); N is more electronegative than C.
Ethene (sp2, pKa ≈ 44) is more acidic than ethane (sp3, ≈ 50), not less.

q: Which statement best describes the equilibrium shown (pKa: ethyne ≈ 25, ethanol ≈ 16)?
c: It lies far to the left; Keq ≈ 10−9
It lies far to the right; Keq ≈ 109
It lies far to the left; Keq ≈ 10−41
It is roughly balanced; Keq ≈ 1, because both acids are weak
h: For HA + B− ⇌ A− + HB, log Keq = pKa(HB) − pKa(HA).
w: The acid on the left is ethyne (25); the acid on the right is ethanol (16). Keq = 10(16 − 25) = 10−9, far to the left. Equilibrium favors the weaker acid (ethyne) and weaker base (ethoxide). That is why ethoxide cannot be used to make acetylide ions for alkylation.
x: This inverts the subtraction; equilibrium favors the weaker acid, and ethyne (25) is weaker than ethanol (16).
The exponent comes from the difference of pKa values (16 − 25 = −9), not their sum.
Both are weak acids, but they differ by 9 pKa units, so Keq is nowhere near 1.

q: What is the major organic product of this sequence?
h: Step 1 makes a carbon nucleophile at the terminal carbon. Where does the new C–C bond form, and how many carbons does each piece bring?
w: NaNH2 removes the terminal ≡C–H of propyne. The acetylide carbon attacks the primary carbon of 1-bromobutane by SN2, joining C3 + C4 = 7 carbons with the triple bond kept where it was: CH3C≡C–CH2CH2CH2CH3, hept-2-yne.
x: Hept-1-yne would need the butyl group on the internal carbon; the new bond forms at the deprotonated terminal carbon, so the triple bond ends up internal (C2).
This has the triple bond at C3, which would require an ethyl acetylide and a propyl halide; propyne + butyl gives the triple bond between C2 and C3.
A branched product would require attack at a secondary carbon; S<sub>N</sub>2 at the primary C–Br gives an unbranched chain.

q: Sodium propynide is treated with 2-bromopropane in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the main outcome?
c: E2: propene forms and propyne is regenerated
S<sub>N</sub>1: 4-methylpent-2-yne forms through an isopropyl cation
No reaction: acetylides do not react with alkyl halides
h: An acetylide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile. What does a strong base usually do with a secondary alkyl halide?
w: Acetylide ions are strong bases (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 25). With a secondary (or tertiary) halide, backside attack is hindered and E2 wins: the acetylide removes a β-H from 2-bromopropane, giving propene, Br−, and propyne (the acetylide is protonated). Acetylide alkylation is used only with methyl and primary halides.
x: S<sub>N</sub>2 at a secondary carbon is slow, and the strongly basic acetylide prefers E2 there, so little or no 4-methylpent-2-yne forms.
A secondary halide does not ionize in NH<sub>3</sub> with a strong base present; the strong base reacts bimolecularly (E2) instead.
Acetylides do react with alkyl halides: S<sub>N</sub>2 with methyl/primary halides and E2 with secondary/tertiary ones.

q: Which route gives the best yield of the alkyne shown?
h: There are two ways to disconnect the target at a C(sp)–C(sp<sup>3</sup>) bond. Which disconnection puts the halide on a carbon that can do S<sub>N</sub>2?
w: The target is 4,4-dimethylpent-2-yne, (CH3)3C–C≡C–CH3. Disconnecting the CH3–C≡ bond uses the tert-butyl acetylide (from 3,3-dimethylbut-1-yne and NaNH2) plus CH3I, a methyl halide that reacts cleanly by SN2: 3,3-dimethylbut-1-yne; 1. NaNH2 2. CH3I. The other disconnection would need a tert-butyl halide, which gives only E2 with acetylides.
x: A tertiary halide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; the acetylide acts as a base and gives isobutylene (E2).
Neopentyl bromide is primary but too hindered for S<sub>N</sub>2, and it would add an extra CH<sub>2</sub> (C8 product, not the C7 target).
Hydroxide cannot deprotonate a terminal alkyne (water, pKa 15.7, is the stronger acid), so almost no acetylide forms.

q: Pent-1-yne is made from 1,2-dibromopentane with 3 equivalents of NaNH<sub>2</sub>, followed by H<sub>2</sub>O. Why are 3 equivalents of base needed rather than 2?
c: Pent-1-yne (pKa ≈ 25) is deprotonated by NaNH2, using a third equivalent; H2O then reprotonates it.
The third equivalent isomerizes the pent-2-yne that forms first into the terminal alkyne, pent-1-yne.
Each E2 step needs two equivalents of base because NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> removes both a proton and a bromide.
The third equivalent converts the vinyl bromide intermediate into an amine, which then eliminates NH<sub>3</sub>.
h: Count the base used by the two eliminations. Then ask what NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> does to the product itself.
w: Two E2 reactions (each uses one NH2−) convert the vicinal dibromide to the alkyne. But a terminal alkyne (pKa 25) is far more acidic than NH3 (38), so the product is immediately deprotonated by a third equivalent. The final H2O workup protonates the acetylide to release pent-1-yne. (For an internal alkyne, 2 equivalents suffice.)
x: From a 1,2-dibromide the triple bond forms between C1 and C2 directly; no isomerization step is needed or intended.
Each E2 uses one base: the base takes the β-H and bromide leaves on its own as Br<sup>−</sup>.
Amide is not acting as a nucleophile on the vinyl bromide here; the second step is another E2.

q: Which dibromide gives pent-1-yne as the main product with 3 equiv NaNH2, then H2O?
h: Double dehydrohalogenation forms the triple bond between the carbons that carry the bromines (vicinal) or between the C–Br carbon and its neighbor (geminal).
w: The two E2 steps create the triple bond between the two carbons that lose the H–Br pairs. For a C1≡C2 triple bond, the bromines must be on C1 and C2 (vicinal) or both on C1 or C2 (geminal). 1,2-Dibromopentane fits. 2,3- and 3,3-dibromopentane place the triple bond at C2–C3 (pent-2-yne), and 1,3-dibromopentane cannot form a triple bond at all because its bromines are not on the same or adjacent carbons.
x: Bromines on C2 and C3 give the triple bond between C2 and C3: pent-2-yne, not pent-1-yne.
A geminal dibromide at C3 can eliminate only toward C2 or C4; both give pent-2-yne.
The bromines are on C1 and C3, so the two eliminations cannot build two π bonds between one pair of carbons; a diene or other products form instead.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Lindlar's catalyst is a "poisoned" catalyst. How many H<sub>2</sub> add, and from which face?
w: Lindlar's catalyst (Pd on CaCO3, poisoned with lead acetate and quinoline) adds one equivalent of H2 syn from the metal surface and stops at the alkene. Hex-3-yne gives (Z)-hex-3-ene.
x: The E alkene comes from dissolving-metal reduction (Na, NH3), not from syn addition on a catalyst surface.
Full reduction to the alkane happens with an active catalyst such as Pt or Pd/C; the poisoned Lindlar catalyst stops at the alkene.
Hydrogenation adds H atoms to the two alkyne carbons; it does not move the double bond to C2.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Dissolving-metal reductions add electrons one at a time. Which alkene geometry results, and how is the alkene numbered?
w: Na in liquid NH3 adds two electrons and two protons anti, giving the trans (E) alkene and stopping there. 4-Methylpent-2-yne gives CH3CH=CH–CH(CH3)2; numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives (E)-4-methylpent-2-ene.
x: The Z (cis) alkene is the Lindlar (H2, syn) product; Na/NH3 gives the E alkene.
Na/NH<sub>3</sub> does not reduce isolated alkenes, so the reaction stops at the alkene.
This is the correct alkene numbered from the wrong end; the double bond must get the lower locant (2, not 3).

q: Which sequence converts but-2-yne into meso-2,3-dibromobutane?
h: Br2 adds anti to an alkene. For a symmetric alkene, does anti addition to the cis or the trans isomer give the meso product?
w: Bromine adds anti through a bromonium ion. Anti addition to trans-but-2-ene gives the meso (2R,3S) dibromide, while anti addition to cis-but-2-ene gives the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair. So make the trans alkene first with dissolving metal: 1. Na, NH3(l) 2. Br2.
x: Lindlar gives cis-but-2-ene; anti addition of Br2 to the cis alkene gives the racemic (R,R)/(S,S) dibromide, not meso.
H<sub>2</sub>/Pt reduces the alkyne all the way to butane, which has no π bond for Br<sub>2</sub> to add to.
Two equivalents of HBr add Markovnikov to give the geminal 2,2-dibromobutane, not a vicinal dibromide.

q: What is the major product when pent-1-yne reacts with 2 equivalents of HBr (no peroxides)?
h: Each HBr adds Markovnikov. After the first addition, which carbocation is stabilized by the bromine already present?
w: The first HBr adds Markovnikov to give 2-bromopent-1-ene. In the second addition, H+ adds to C1 so the cation forms at C2, where the bromine lone pair stabilizes it by resonance. Bromide then adds to C2, giving the geminal dihalide 2,2-dibromopentane.
x: A vicinal (1,2) dibromide comes from Br<sub>2</sub> addition, not from two HBr additions.
Putting both Br on C1 is anti-Markovnikov; without peroxides H adds to C1 each time.
This is the product of only one equivalent of HBr; with 2 equivalents the vinyl bromide adds a second HBr.

q: What is the final organic product of this reaction?
h: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov, and the first product is not stable. What does it tautomerize to?
w: HgSO4/H2SO4 adds water Markovnikov: OH goes to C2 of hex-1-yne, giving the enol CH2=C(OH)C4H9. The enol tautomerizes to the more stable keto form, hexan-2-one.
x: An aldehyde comes from anti-Markovnikov hydration (disiamylborane or 9-BBN, then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/NaOH), not from HgSO<sub>4</sub>.
Alkyne hydration gives a carbonyl compound, not an alcohol; nothing reduces the C=O here.
This enol is the first-formed intermediate, but it tautomerizes to the ketone under the acidic conditions.

q: Which alkyne gives a single ketone on hydration with HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O?
h: For an internal alkyne, the OH can end up on either sp carbon. When do both choices give the same compound?
w: An internal alkyne with two different alkyl groups has no strong Markovnikov preference, so it gives a mixture of two ketones. A symmetric internal alkyne gives the same ketone either way. Hex-3-yne gives only hexan-3-one.
x: Hex-2-yne gives both hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one, because its two sp carbons are both disubstituted.
The isopropyl and ethyl groups differ, so 2-methylhex-3-yne gives a mixture of 2-methylhexan-3-one and 5-methylhexan-3-one.
Oct-3-yne has an ethyl and a butyl group, so it gives octan-3-one and octan-4-one.

q: What is the final organic product of this sequence? (Sia<sub>2</sub>BH = disiamylborane)
h: Hydroboration puts boron on the less substituted carbon. After oxidation, the OH is on a C=C carbon. What happens to that?
w: Disiamylborane adds once, with boron on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov, syn). H2O2/NaOH replaces B with OH, giving the enol CH3CH2CH2CH=CH–OH, which tautomerizes to the aldehyde: pentanal.
x: The methyl ketone is the Markovnikov product of HgSO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> hydration.
No reducing agent is present; the enol tautomerizes to an aldehyde, which is not reduced to the alcohol.
This enol is the intermediate formed by oxidation; it tautomerizes to the aldehyde.

q: 3-Methylbut-1-yne is treated separately with (I) H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, HgSO<sub>4</sub> and (II) 1. disiamylborane 2. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH. Which pair names the products correctly?
h: Decide Markovnikov vs anti-Markovnikov for each, then remember both reactions pass through an enol.
w: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: OH on C2, then the enol tautomerizes to the methyl ketone, 3-methylbutan-2-one. A bulky dialkylborane puts boron on C1 (anti-Markovnikov); oxidation gives the enol HO–CH=CH–, which tautomerizes to the aldehyde, 3-methylbutanal.
x: The regiochemistry is reversed: HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration is Markovnikov (ketone), hydroboration is anti-Markovnikov (aldehyde).
Hydroboration–oxidation of an alkyne gives an enol that tautomerizes to the aldehyde; an alcohol would need a reduction step.
Alkyne hydration gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone, not an alcohol.

q: Why is a bulky dialkylborane such as disiamylborane or 9-BBN used, instead of BH<sub>3</sub>, to hydroborate a terminal alkyne?
c: The vinylborane still has a π bond; a bulky borane adds only once, so oxidation gives the aldehyde.
BH<sub>3</sub> adds with Markovnikov regiochemistry to alkynes, so oxidation would give a ketone, not the aldehyde.
BH<sub>3</sub> cannot add to C≡C bonds; only dialkylboranes react with alkynes.
The bulky borane is needed to make the enol tautomerize to the aldehyde after oxidation.
h: Think about what is left after the first B–H adds across the triple bond.
w: Hydroboration of a triple bond leaves a C=C (a vinylborane), which can react with a second B–H. A small borane like BH3 can add twice and has three B–H bonds that react further. The steric bulk of Sia2BH or 9-BBN stops the reaction after one addition (and reinforces boron on the terminal carbon), so H2O2/NaOH gives the enol and then the aldehyde.
x: BH<sub>3</sub> also adds boron to the less substituted carbon; the problem with BH<sub>3</sub> is double addition, not regiochemistry.
BH<sub>3</sub> does react with alkynes; it just does not stop cleanly after one addition.
Enol-to-aldehyde tautomerization occurs on its own under the basic oxidation conditions; the borane plays no part in it.

q: What is the major product of but-2-yne with one equivalent of Br2 in CH2Cl2?
h: Halogen addition to a π bond goes through a bridged bromonium ion. Which face does Br<sup>−</sup> attack, and how many equivalents add?
w: As with alkenes, Br2 adds to an alkyne mainly anti, so the two Br atoms end up on opposite sides of the new C=C. With one equivalent the product is the dibromoalkene (E)-2,3-dibromobut-2-ene.
x: The Z isomer would require syn addition; bromination is mainly anti.
The tetrabromide forms only with two (or more) equivalents of Br<sub>2</sub>.
A saturated vicinal dibromide would need an extra H<sub>2</sub>; Br<sub>2</sub> adds only Br atoms, leaving a C=C.

q: An alkyne C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub> is treated with 1. O<sub>3</sub> 2. H<sub>2</sub>O. The only products are propanoic acid and butanoic acid. Which alkyne was it?
h: Ozonolysis cuts the triple bond and turns each sp carbon into a COOH carbon. Rejoin the two acid carbons with a triple bond.
w: Ozonolysis of an internal alkyne breaks C≡C completely, giving two carboxylic acids (a terminal ≡CH becomes CO2). Joining the carboxyl carbons of CH3CH2COOH (C3) and CH3CH2CH2COOH (C4) gives CH3CH2C≡CCH2CH2CH3, hept-3-yne.
x: Hept-2-yne would give acetic acid (C2) and pentanoic acid (C5).
This alkyne would give propanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid, a branched C4 acid, not butanoic acid.
A terminal alkyne gives one carboxylic acid (here hexanoic acid) plus CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Compound X (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) takes up 2 equiv H<sub>2</sub> over Pt to give C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>. Treatment of X with 1. O<sub>3</sub> 2. H<sub>2</sub>O gives a single product, octanedioic acid, HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>COOH. Which structure is X?
h: Count degrees of unsaturation and how many are π bonds. If the product keeps all 8 carbons with a COOH at each end, where was the cleaved bond?
w: C8H12 has 3 degrees of unsaturation; 2 equiv H2 removes two π bonds, so X has one ring plus a triple bond (or two C=C). Ozonolysis giving a single C8 diacid means one multiple bond was cut inside a ring, leaving both cut carbons as COOH groups on the same chain. Both new COOH carbons come from a triple bond (alkyne ozonolysis gives acids). That is cyclooctyne, the smallest isolable cycloalkyne.
x: Ethynylcyclohexane fits the formula and H<sub>2</sub> uptake, but ozonolysis gives cyclohexanecarboxylic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>, not an open-chain diacid.
Cycloocta-1,5-diene also fits the formula, but cutting both C=C bonds gives two C<sub>4</sub> fragments, not one C<sub>8</sub> product.
Cleaving both C=C bonds of 1-vinylcyclohexene gives a C<sub>7</sub> fragment and a one-carbon fragment, not a single C<sub>8</sub> diacid.

q: Which sequence, starting from acetylene (HC≡CH), gives hexanal?
h: Count carbons: acetylene brings 2. Then decide which hydration puts the C=O on the terminal carbon.
w: Hexanal, CH3(CH2)4CHO, has 6 carbons with the carbonyl at C1. Acetylene (2 C) + a butyl group (4 C) gives hex-1-yne. Anti-Markovnikov hydration with the bulky borane then gives the aldehyde: 1. NaNH2 2. butyl bromide 3. Sia2BH 4. H2O2, NaOH.
x: HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration of hex-1-yne is Markovnikov and gives hexan-2-one, not hexanal.
Hydroxide is too weak a base to make the acetylide (water, pKa 15.7, is far more acidic than acetylene, 25).
A pentyl halide gives hept-1-yne, so the final aldehyde is heptanal (7 C), one carbon too many.

q: Which sequence converts acetylene into the alkene shown?
h: Build the full carbon skeleton as an alkyne first (two alkylations), then choose the reduction that sets the alkene geometry.
w: The target is (E)-oct-4-ene: two propyl groups on a trans C=C. Alkylate acetylene twice with 1-bromopropane (deprotonate before each alkylation) to make oct-4-yne, then reduce with Na, NH3(l), which gives the trans (E) alkene.
x: Lindlar hydrogenation is syn and gives (Z)-oct-4-ene, the wrong stereoisomer.
Reducing too early turns the terminal alkyne into an alkene, which has no acidic C–H for NaNH<sub>2</sub>, so the second alkylation fails.
Isopropyl bromide is secondary; acetylides do E2 with it (propene forms), and even S<sub>N</sub>2 would give a branched skeleton.

q: Which route is best for preparing the ketone shown as a single product?
c: HC≡CH; 1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>  2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  4. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
h: A methyl ketone comes cleanly from Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne. What happens when an unsymmetrical internal alkyne is hydrated?
w: The target is 5-methylhexan-2-one, CH3CO–CH2CH2CH(CH3)2. Alkylating acetylide with the primary halide 1-bromo-3-methylbutane gives the terminal alkyne 5-methylhex-1-yne; HgSO4 hydration is Markovnikov and gives only the methyl ketone. So the best route is HC≡CH; NaNH2; (CH3)2CHCH2CH2Br; HgSO4/H2SO4/H2O.
x: This makes the internal alkyne 5-methylhex-2-yne; hydration of an unsymmetrical internal alkyne gives a mixture of the 2-one and the 3-one.
Hydroboration–oxidation of the terminal alkyne gives the aldehyde, 5-methylhexanal, not the methyl ketone.
Acid-catalyzed hydration of the alkene gives an alcohol (5-methylhexan-2-ol), not a ketone.

q: Which reagent converts hept-1-yne into heptane?
h: Which reducing conditions do not stop at the alkene stage?
w: An active metal catalyst (Pd/C or Pt) with excess H2 adds two equivalents of H2 and does not stop at the alkene: hept-1-yne → heptane. The other conditions either stop at the alkene or do not reduce C≡C.
x: Lindlar's poisoned catalyst stops after one H<sub>2</sub>, giving hept-1-ene.
Dissolving-metal reduction stops at the alkene (and a terminal alkyne is largely deprotonated under these conditions).
NaBH<sub>4</sub> delivers hydride to polar C=O bonds; it does not reduce nonpolar C≡C bonds.

q: Which statement correctly describes the reduction of an internal alkyne by Na in NH<sub>3</sub>(l)?
c: Electrons add one at a time; the vinyl radical and anion prefer the trans geometry before NH3 protonates them.
Hydrogen atoms are delivered to one face from the surface of the sodium metal, so the product is the trans alkene.
NH3 first protonates the alkyne to give a vinyl cation, which Na then reduces to the trans alkene.
The cis alkene forms first and then isomerizes to the more stable trans alkene in the liquid NH3.
h: The sequence is electron, proton, electron, proton. Which intermediate decides the geometry?
w: Na donates an electron to give a radical anion; NH3 protonates it to a vinyl radical, which adopts the less crowded trans arrangement; a second electron gives a vinyl anion that keeps the trans geometry and is protonated by NH3. The trans product therefore comes from the preferred geometry of these intermediates.
x: Na is not a hydrogenation surface; it supplies electrons, and the H atoms come from NH<sub>3</sub>. (Surface delivery would be syn and give cis.)
NH<sub>3</sub> is far too weak an acid to protonate an alkyne; the first step is electron transfer from Na.
No cis alkene forms; the geometry is set in the vinyl radical/anion stage, and simple alkenes do not isomerize under these conditions.

q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene gives a methyl-shift product. What is the final product when 3,3-dimethylbut-1-yne is treated with H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4?
h: Mercury-catalyzed alkyne hydration does not go through a free carbocation. Where does OH go, and what does the enol become?
w: Hg2+ activates the triple bond without forming a free carbocation, so no methyl shift occurs. Water adds Markovnikov (OH on C2), and the enol tautomerizes to the ketone: 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one.
x: The aldehyde is the anti-Markovnikov product, obtained by hydroboration–oxidation, not by HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration.
This rearranged alcohol is what the alkene gives through a free carbocation; the alkyne hydration gives a ketone with no rearrangement.
This enol is the first-formed intermediate; under the acidic conditions it tautomerizes to the ketone.

q: Which compounds give 2,2-dichlorobutane as the major product with excess HCl?
h: HCl adds Markovnikov. In a vinyl chloride, a cation next to Cl is stabilized by the Cl lone pair.
w: I (but-1-yne): two Markovnikov additions put both Cl on C2 → 2,2-dichlorobutane. II (but-2-yne): the first HCl gives 2-chlorobut-2-ene; the second protonates C3 so the cation sits on the Cl-bearing C2 → 2,2-dichlorobutane (C2 and C3 are equivalent at the start). III is that same vinyl chloride: protonation at C3 gives the Cl-stabilized cation at C2, and Cl− adds there. So I, II, and III all give 2,2-dichlorobutane.
x: III is a vinyl chloride; HCl adds so the cation forms on the Cl-bearing carbon, giving the same geminal 2,2-dichloride.
The symmetric internal alkyne II also gives the geminal dichloride at C2 (equivalent to C3), so I alone is incomplete.
Terminal alkyne I adds HCl Markovnikov twice, putting both Cl on C2, so it must be included.

q: What is the major product when pent-1-yne reacts with one equivalent of HCl?
h: Markovnikov: H goes to the carbon that already has more H atoms. How many HCl add?
w: H+ adds to terminal C1 so the vinyl cation forms on C2 (the more substituted sp carbon). Cl− adds to C2, giving the vinyl halide 2-chloropent-1-ene. Only one equivalent adds, so the product keeps a C=C.
x: Cl on C1 is the anti-Markovnikov product; HCl does not add anti-Markovnikov, even with peroxides.
The double bond stays between C1 and C2; HCl addition does not move it to C2–C3.
The geminal dichloride needs a second equivalent of HCl.

q: Sodium acetylide is to be alkylated with 1-bromopropane. Which solvent must not be used?
h: Compare the acidity of each solvent with that of acetylene (pKa ≈ 25).
w: Acetylide is the conjugate base of an acid with pKa ≈ 25. Ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is a much stronger acid, so it protonates the acetylide immediately (Keq ≈ 109) and destroys the nucleophile. NH3 (38), THF and ether are far weaker acids and are suitable.
x: NH3 (pKa 38) is a weaker acid than acetylene, so it does not protonate acetylide; it is the usual solvent for these reactions.
THF has no O–H and its C–H bonds are far less acidic than acetylene, so it is a suitable aprotic solvent.
Diethyl ether is aprotic and does not protonate acetylide ions.

q: Pent-4-yn-1-ol is treated with 2 equiv NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then 1 equiv CH<sub>3</sub>I, then H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the major product?
h: Two equivalents remove both the most acidic H (O–H, pKa ≈ 16) and the next (≡C–H, ≈ 25). Which anion of the dianion is the stronger base and nucleophile?
w: NaNH2 first removes the O–H proton, then the terminal ≡C–H, giving a dianion. The acetylide carbanion (conjugate acid pKa 25) is a much stronger base and better nucleophile than the alkoxide (conjugate acid pKa 16), so the one equivalent of CH3I alkylates carbon. Water then protonates the alkoxide: hex-4-yn-1-ol.
x: Alkylation at oxygen would require the alkoxide to outcompete the more reactive acetylide; the more basic anion of a dianion reacts first.
Only 1 equiv of CH<sub>3</sub>I is present, and the alkoxide is the less reactive site, so dimethylation is not the major outcome.
The propargylic CH2 is not deprotonated by NaNH2 (pKa well above 38), so no carbanion forms there.

q: Which sequence converts hex-1-yne into hexan-1-ol?
c: 1. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  2. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  3. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
h: Hydroboration of an alkyne stops at a carbonyl compound. To reach a primary alcohol in one oxidation step, what must the hydroboration substrate be?
w: Partial hydrogenation (Lindlar) gives hex-1-ene; hydroboration–oxidation of the alkene is anti-Markovnikov and gives the primary alcohol hexan-1-ol. Hydroborating the alkyne directly gives an enol that becomes hexanal, which would still need a reduction.
x: Hydroboration–oxidation of the alkyne gives hexanal (via the enol), an aldehyde rather than the alcohol.
Acid-catalyzed hydration of hex-1-ene is Markovnikov and gives hexan-2-ol.
HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration gives hexan-2-one, and NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces it to the secondary alcohol hexan-2-ol.

q: Alkyne X (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) gives the same single ketone with either H<sub>2</sub>O/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/HgSO<sub>4</sub> or 1. Sia<sub>2</sub>BH 2. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH. Ozonolysis of X (1. O<sub>3</sub> 2. H<sub>2</sub>O) gives one carboxylic acid and no CO<sub>2</sub>. Which structure is X?
h: A terminal alkyne gives different products with the two hydration methods and loses its ≡CH carbon as CO<sub>2</sub> on ozonolysis. What internal alkyne gives one product from each?
w: Getting the same single ketone from Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov hydration requires the two sp carbons to be equivalent, and a single acid with no CO2 on ozonolysis also requires an internal, symmetric alkyne. Hex-3-yne gives hexan-3-one by both methods and two molecules of propanoic acid on ozonolysis.
x: Hex-1-yne gives hexan-2-one with HgSO<sub>4</sub> but hexanal with Sia<sub>2</sub>BH, and its ozonolysis releases CO<sub>2</sub>.
Hex-2-yne is unsymmetric: each hydration gives a mixture of hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one, and ozonolysis gives two different acids (acetic and butanoic).
This terminal alkyne gives a methyl ketone with HgSO<sub>4</sub> but an aldehyde with Sia<sub>2</sub>BH, and ozonolysis gives CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: The Newman projection shows butane viewed along the C2–C3 bond. Which conformation is drawn?
c: Eclipsed, with each CH<sub>3</sub> eclipsing an H
h: Find the front CH<sub>3</sub> and the back CH<sub>3</sub>, then estimate the dihedral angle between them. Are the back bonds lined up with the front bonds or in between them?
w: The back bonds sit between the front bonds, so the projection is staggered. The front CH3 points straight up and the back CH3 points straight down: a 180° dihedral angle. That is the anti conformation, the lowest-energy conformation of butane.
x: Gauche would put the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on neighboring positions, 60° apart; here they are on opposite sides of the circle.
In the totally eclipsed conformation the back CH<sub>3</sub> would sit directly behind the front CH<sub>3</sub>; the back bonds here are offset, so nothing is eclipsed.
An eclipsed conformation has every back bond hidden behind a front bond; this drawing is staggered.

q: Four conformations of butane about the C2–C3 bond are shown. Rank them from lowest to highest energy.
h: First sort staggered from eclipsed (eclipsing always costs torsional strain). Then, within each group, ask how close the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are.
w: I is gauche (staggered, CH3/CH3 60°), II is totally eclipsed (CH3 behind CH3), III is anti (180°), IV is eclipsed with each CH3 behind an H. Staggered conformations are lower than eclipsed ones; anti beats gauche by about 3.8 kJ/mol of steric strain. Among the eclipsed forms, two CH3/H eclipsings (about 16 kJ/mol) cost less than a CH3/CH3 eclipsing plus two H/H (about 19 kJ/mol). Order: III < I < IV < II.
x: This places an eclipsed conformation (IV) below a staggered one (I); any eclipsed form carries torsional strain far larger than the 3.8 kJ/mol gauche penalty.
Gauche (I) is not lower than anti (III): bringing the CH<sub>3</sub> groups to 60° adds steric strain.
The totally eclipsed conformation (II), with CH<sub>3</sub> directly behind CH<sub>3</sub>, is the highest point on the butane energy curve, not IV.

q: The Newman projection shows 2-methylbutane viewed along the C2–C3 bond (C2 in front). Using the strain values in the table, what is the total strain energy of this conformation (relative to a hypothetical strain-free one)?
h: Pair each front bond with the back bond directly behind it. There are exactly three eclipsing pairs; add their costs.
w: Read the three eclipsed pairs: CH3 (top, front) with CH3 (top, back) = 11; CH3 (lower left, front) with H = 6.0; H (lower right, front) with H = 4.0. Total = 11 + 6.0 + 4.0 = 21 kJ/mol. The gauche value does not apply because nothing here is staggered.
x: 17 kJ/mol leaves out the H/H eclipsing; H/H eclipsing is still torsional strain and must be counted.
15 kJ/mol skips the CH<sub>3</sub>/H eclipsing between the lower-left front CH<sub>3</sub> and the H behind it.
26 kJ/mol treats the lower-left pair as a second CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> eclipsing, but the back carbon (C3) carries only one CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Three staggered conformations of 2-methylbutane about the C2–C3 bond are shown (C2 in front). A CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> gauche interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol. Which conformation is highest in energy, and by how much does it lie above the most stable one?
h: Find the single CH<sub>3</sub> on the back carbon in each drawing and count how many front CH<sub>3</sub> groups sit 60° from it.
w: The back carbon (C3) has one CH3. In I it lies between a front CH3 and the front H (one gauche); in II it lies between the front H and the other front CH3 (one gauche); in III it sits between both front CH3 groups (two gauche, anti to H). I and II are equal (3.8 kJ/mol); III has 7.6 kJ/mol. So III is highest, 3.8 kJ/mol above I (and II).
x: 7.6 kJ/mol is the total gauche strain in III, not the difference from I, which already has one gauche interaction (3.8 kJ/mol).
I has only one gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> interaction; III, with the back CH<sub>3</sub> between both front CH<sub>3</sub> groups, has two.
II and I each have one gauche interaction, so they have the same energy; II is not higher than I.

q: Which Newman projection represents 2-bromobutane viewed along the C2–C3 bond (C2 in front)?
h: Write out C2 and C3 of 2-bromobutane. List the three groups on C2 other than C3, and the three groups on C3 other than C2.
w: 2-Bromobutane is CH3–CHBr–CH2–CH3. C2 carries Br, CH3 (C1) and H; C3 carries CH3 (C4) and two H. Only I has a front carbon with Br, CH3, H and a back carbon with CH3, H, H.
x: II is BrCH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane: the bromine-bearing carbon has two H and the back carbon has two CH<sub>3</sub>.
III has two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the back carbon, so it is 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (five carbons), not 2-bromobutane.
IV is BrCH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> viewed along C1–C2: 1-bromobutane, a constitutional isomer.

q: The Newman projection shows an alkane viewed along one C–C bond. What is the IUPAC name of the alkane?
h: Rebuild the condensed formula: front carbon with its three groups, bonded to back carbon with its three groups. Find the longest chain; number from the end nearer a branch.
w: Front carbon: CH bearing CH2CH3 and CH3. Back carbon: CH bearing two CH3. The molecule is (CH3)2CH–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3, C7H16. Longest chain = 5 carbons; numbering from the isopropyl end gives methyls at C2 and C3: 2,3-dimethylpentane.
x: A four-carbon parent misses the longest chain: the ethyl group extends the main chain to five carbons.
Numbering from the wrong end gives 3,4; the lowest locants are 2,3.
The molecule has seven carbons (front C, back C, ethyl, and three methyls); a hexane parent with two methyls would need eight.

q: Rotation about the C–C bond of ethane has a barrier of about 12 kJ/mol. This barrier is attributed mainly to
c: torsional strain in the eclipsed conformation
steric strain from H atoms pressed inside their van der Waals radii
angle strain from H–C–C angles bent away from 109.5°
partial breaking of the C–C σ bond during rotation
h: Ethane's hydrogens are small and far apart even when eclipsed. Which kind of strain comes from bonds being lined up, rather than atoms bumping?
w: In the eclipsed conformation each C–H bond is aligned with a C–H bond on the neighboring carbon; the electron pairs repel and the stabilizing σ(C–H)→σ*(C–H) overlap of the staggered form is lost. That energy cost is torsional strain, about 4.0 kJ/mol per H/H eclipsing (3 × 4.0 ≈ 12).
x: The eclipsed H atoms of ethane are about 2.3 Å apart, slightly outside the sum of their van der Waals radii, so steric strain is minor; that term matters for larger groups such as CH<sub>3</sub>.
Bond angles stay near tetrahedral during rotation about a single bond; angle strain arises in small rings, not in ethane.
The C–C σ bond is cylindrically symmetric, so rotation does not break or weaken it; the barrier comes from interactions among the C–H bonds.

q:
Which statements about the conformations of butane about the C2–C3 bond are correct?
I. The gauche conformation is staggered but has steric strain.
II. The anti conformation is lower in energy than gauche by about 3.8 kJ/mol.
III. At 25 °C, rotation is too slow for the anti and gauche conformers to interconvert.
IV. The two gauche conformations are mirror images and have the same energy.
h: Compare butane's largest rotational barrier (about 19 kJ/mol) with room-temperature thermal energy; conformers can be isolated only when the barrier is about 80 kJ/mol or more.
w: I is true: in gauche the CH3 groups are 60° apart and crowd each other, but no bonds are eclipsed. II is true: the gauche penalty is about 3.8 kJ/mol. III is false: barriers of about 15–19 kJ/mol are crossed billions of times per second at 25 °C. IV is true: the +60° and −60° gauche forms are nonsuperimposable mirror images of equal energy. Answer: I, II, and IV only.
x: Statement IV is also correct: the two gauche conformations (CH<sub>3</sub> groups at +60° and −60°) are mirror images, so they have identical energy.
Statement III is false; butane's rotational barriers are small, so conformers interconvert rapidly at room temperature and cannot be separated.
Statement II is also correct: anti is more stable than gauche by about 3.8 kJ/mol of steric strain.

q: Two staggered conformations of ethane-1,2-diol (HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) are shown. In the gas phase, which conformation predominates, and why?
c: II, because an intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bond is possible only in the gauche form
I, because steric strain between the two OH groups is smallest when they are anti
I, because the two C–O bond dipoles cancel in the anti arrangement
II, because the gauche conformation has less torsional strain than the anti conformation
h: Butane prefers anti because its CH<sub>3</sub> groups only repel. What attractive interaction can two OH groups have when they are close together?
w: In the gauche form (II) the two OH groups are close enough for one O–H to hydrogen-bond to the other oxygen. That attraction outweighs the small steric cost, so II predominates, because of an intramolecular hydrogen bond. In the anti form the OH groups are too far apart to interact.
x: OH groups are small, so the gauche steric penalty is minor; it is outweighed by the intramolecular hydrogen bond available only in the gauche form.
Dipole cancellation does favor anti in the gas phase for 1,2-dihalides, but in the diol the hydrogen bond dominates, so the gauche form is preferred.
Both conformations are staggered, so neither has torsional strain; the preference must come from another interaction.

q: Heats of combustion per CH<sub>2</sub> group are given. An unstrained acyclic CH<sub>2</sub> releases 658.6 kJ/mol. What is the total ring strain of cyclobutane?
h: Find the extra heat released per CH<sub>2</sub>, then remember how many CH<sub>2</sub> groups the ring has.
w: Excess per CH2 = 686.2 − 658.6 = 27.6 kJ/mol. Cyclobutane has four CH2 groups: 4 × 27.6 = 110 kJ/mol of ring strain (angle strain from 90° angles plus torsional strain).
x: 27.6 kJ/mol is the strain per CH<sub>2</sub>; total ring strain multiplies by the four CH<sub>2</sub> groups in the ring.
88.8 kJ/mol uses cyclopentane (664.0) as the strain-free reference; the stem gives 658.6 kJ/mol as the unstrained value.
115 kJ/mol is the strain of cyclopropane: 3 × (697.1 − 658.6). Cyclobutane is the 686.2 row.

q: Cyclobutane is not planar; one carbon is folded about 25° out of the plane of the other three. What does this puckering accomplish?
c: It staggers neighboring C–H bonds to lower torsional strain, at the cost of slightly more angle strain
It lowers angle strain by opening the C–C–C angles from 90° toward the ideal 109.5°
It relieves steric strain between the 1,3-carbons, which move farther apart across the ring
It allows the ring carbons to rehybridize toward sp<sup>2</sup>, which shortens and strengthens the C–C bonds
h: In planar cyclobutane every C–H bond is eclipsed with its neighbor. What happens to the C–C–C angle when the ring folds?
w: Planar cyclobutane would have all eight C–H bonds eclipsed. Folding the ring partially staggers them, reducing torsional strain. The price is that the C–C–C angles shrink slightly below 90° (about 88°), so angle strain rises a little. The net effect is a lower-energy puckered ring.
x: Puckering makes the C–C–C angles slightly smaller (about 88°), not closer to 109.5°; angle strain increases a little.
The 1,3-carbons actually move closer together when the ring folds; the benefit comes from staggering the C–H bonds.
Ring carbons in cyclobutane remain sp<sup>3</sup>; puckering is a conformational change, not a change in hybridization.

q: Cyclopropane undergoes ring-opening reactions (for example, with H<sub>2</sub>/Ni) that do not occur with propane. The main reason is that cyclopropane
c: has bent, poorly overlapping C–C bonds and high ring strain
has sp<sup>2</sup>-hybridized carbons and a reactive C=C π bond, like propene
has staggered C–H bonds that weaken the ring C–C bonds
has axial hydrogens that crowd each other, as in a chair
h: Compare the 60° internuclear angle with the angle sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals prefer. How well can such orbitals overlap?
w: The C–C–C internuclear angle is 60°, far below 109.5°, so the sp3-like orbitals overlap off-axis in bent (banana) bonds. These bonds are weak, and the ring carries about 115 kJ/mol of angle and torsional strain that is released when the ring opens.
x: Cyclopropane has no π bond; its carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>-like with extra p character in the ring bonds, and it is a saturated C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.
All six C–H bonds in planar cyclopropane are eclipsed, not staggered; eclipsing adds torsional strain.
Axial and equatorial positions belong to chair cyclohexanes; cyclopropane is a flat ring.

q: Rank these C6H14 isomers from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: All three have the same molar mass. Which shape gives the largest contact area for London dispersion forces?
w: Isomeric alkanes differ only in shape. Branching makes a molecule more compact and spherical, reducing surface contact and London dispersion forces. Hexane (I, bp 69 °C) > 2-methylpentane (II, 60 °C) > 2,2-dimethylbutane (III, 50 °C). Order: III < II < I.
x: This is reversed: branching lowers, not raises, the boiling point of isomeric alkanes because it shrinks the surface area.
2,2-Dimethylbutane (III) is the most branched and most compact, so it boils lowest, below 2-methylpentane.
Unbranched hexane (I) has the largest surface area and the strongest dispersion forces, so it boils highest.

q: Which alkane defines a rating of 100 on the octane scale for gasoline?
h: The reference compound is highly branched and resists premature ignition (knocking). It is often called isooctane.
w: The octane scale is anchored by heptane (0) and 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (isooctane, 100). Highly branched alkanes burn smoothly under compression; straight-chain alkanes knock.
x: Octane is the straight-chain C<sub>8</sub> alkane; it knocks badly and has an octane number below zero, despite the name of the scale.
Heptane is the zero point of the octane scale, not the 100 point.
2-Methylheptane is only lightly branched and knocks readily; its octane number is far below 100.

q: In a petroleum refinery, catalytic cracking is used mainly to
c: break large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes for gasoline
separate crude oil into fractions by their boiling points
convert straight-chain alkanes into aromatic hydrocarbons for gasoline
remove sulfur compounds from crude oil fractions
h: Gasoline demand is higher than the amount of the C<sub>5</sub>–C<sub>10</sub> fraction found in crude oil. What process makes more of it from heavier fractions?
w: Catalytic cracking heats heavy fractions (such as gas oil) over zeolite catalysts, breaking C–C bonds to give smaller alkanes and alkenes in the gasoline range, plus small alkenes used as chemical feedstocks.
x: Separating crude oil by boiling point is fractional distillation, which does not break any bonds.
Converting alkanes into aromatics (and branched isomers) is catalytic reforming, a different refinery process.
Removing sulfur is hydrodesulfurization (hydrotreating), not cracking.

q: Which C8H18 isomer releases the least heat on complete combustion?
h: All isomers burn to the same products (8 CO<sub>2</sub> + 9 H<sub>2</sub>O). The isomer that starts lowest in energy releases the least heat. How does branching affect alkane stability?
w: Isomers that give the same combustion products differ in heat of combustion only by their own stability. Branched alkanes are more stable than unbranched isomers, so the most highly branched isomer, 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane, starts lowest in energy and releases the least heat.
x: Octane is the least branched isomer and the least stable, so it releases the most heat of these four.
2-Methylheptane has only one branch; it is less stable than the highly branched 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane and releases more heat.
3-Methylheptane has only one branch, so it releases more heat than the most branched isomer.

q: The rotational barrier about the C–C bond in propane is 14 kJ/mol. If each H/H eclipsing interaction costs 4.0 kJ/mol, what does one CH<sub>3</sub>/H eclipsing interaction cost?
h: In the eclipsed conformation of propane, list the three pairs of eclipsed bonds. How many are H/H, and how many involve the CH<sub>3</sub>?
w: Viewed along C1–C2, the front carbon (CH3) has three H; the back carbon (CH2) has CH3, H, H. Eclipsing gives one CH3/H pair and two H/H pairs: 14 = 2(4.0) + x, so x = 6.0 kJ/mol.
x: 4.7 kJ/mol divides the barrier evenly over three pairs, ignoring that the CH<sub>3</sub>/H pair costs more than an H/H pair.
10 kJ/mol subtracts only one H/H interaction; there are two H/H eclipsings in eclipsed propane.
2.0 kJ/mol would make a CH<sub>3</sub>/H eclipsing cheaper than H/H, which contradicts the larger size of CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Two staggered conformations of 1,2-dichloroethane are shown. Which conformation has zero net dipole moment, and how does the fraction of the gauche form change on going from the gas phase to a polar solvent?
c: I; the gauche fraction increases in a polar solvent
I; the gauche fraction decreases in a polar solvent
II; the gauche fraction increases in a polar solvent
II; the gauche fraction decreases in a polar solvent
h: Add the two C–Cl bond dipoles as vectors in each conformation. Then ask which conformer a polar solvent stabilizes more.
w: In the anti form (I) the two C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so I has μ = 0. In the gauche form (II) they partly add, so II is polar. A polar solvent stabilizes the polar conformer more through dipole–dipole solvation, so I is nonpolar, and the gauche fraction increases in a polar solvent.
x: A polar solvent preferentially stabilizes the polar gauche conformer, so its share goes up, not down.
The gauche conformer has the C–Cl dipoles at 60°, so they add to a net dipole; the dipoles cancel only in the anti form.
The gauche form is the polar one, not the nonpolar one, and polar solvents raise rather than lower its population.

q: Consider the staggered conformations of 2,3-dimethylbutane about the C2–C3 bond. A CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> gauche interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol. How many gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> interactions does the most stable staggered conformation have, and how much more stable is it than the other staggered conformations?
h: C2 and C3 each carry two CH<sub>3</sub> and one H. Draw the Newman with the two H anti, then with H anti to CH<sub>3</sub>; count gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> pairs.
w: With the two H atoms anti, each back CH3 sits between one front CH3 and the front H: 2 gauche interactions (7.6 kJ/mol). In either of the other two staggered conformations (H anti to CH3), one back CH3 sits between both front CH3 groups and the other is next to one: 3 gauche interactions (11.4 kJ/mol). The most stable has 2 gauche interactions and is 3.8 kJ/mol more stable.
x: With four CH<sub>3</sub> groups on two adjacent carbons, no staggered arrangement puts every CH<sub>3</sub> pair anti; at least two gauche interactions remain.
Placing the H atoms anti leaves two, not one, gauche interactions: each back CH<sub>3</sub> is gauche to one front CH<sub>3</sub>.
7.6 kJ/mol is the total gauche strain of the best conformer; the other staggered conformers have 11.4 kJ/mol, so the difference is 3.8 kJ/mol.

q: Which conformation of butane (about C2–C3) has steric strain but no torsional strain?
h: Torsional strain comes from eclipsed bonds. Which staggered conformation still brings the CH<sub>3</sub> groups close together?
w: Torsional strain requires eclipsing, so only staggered conformations are free of it. Of the staggered ones, gauche puts the CH3 groups 60° apart, close enough to cause steric strain (about 3.8 kJ/mol).
x: Anti has neither torsional strain (staggered) nor steric strain (CH<sub>3</sub> groups 180° apart).
The totally eclipsed conformation has both steric strain and large torsional strain.
Any eclipsed conformation has torsional strain from the lined-up bonds.

q: The chair shows methylcyclohexane with the CH<sub>3</sub> group axial. After a ring flip, the CH<sub>3</sub> group is
c: equatorial and still on the top face; this conformer is lower in energy
equatorial and now on the bottom face; this conformer is lower in energy
still axial, because a ring flip only rotates the whole molecule
equatorial and still on the top face; this conformer is higher in energy
h: A ring flip interconverts axial and equatorial positions. Does it break any bonds, and can a group that pointed up end up pointing down?
w: A ring flip swaps every axial position for an equatorial one, but no bonds break, so each group stays on the same face (up stays up). The CH3 becomes equatorial, still on the top face, and the flipped chair is lower in energy (by about 7.3 kJ/mol) because the two 1,3-diaxial CH3/H interactions are gone.
x: Up/down (wedge/dash) cannot change without breaking a bond; the CH<sub>3</sub> stays on the top face after the flip.
A ring flip is not a rigid rotation: each carbon moves, and axial positions become equatorial.
Equatorial CH<sub>3</sub> avoids the 1,3-diaxial interactions with axial H atoms, so the flipped chair is more stable, not less.

q: The A-value of a methyl group is 7.3 kJ/mol (ΔG° for equatorial ⇌ axial). What percentage of methylcyclohexane molecules have the CH<sub>3</sub> equatorial at 25 °C?
h: Use ΔG° = −RT ln K with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T in kelvin. Then convert K (equatorial : axial) into a percentage.
w: K = [equatorial]/[axial] = eΔG°/RT = e7300/(8.314 × 298) = e2.95 ≈ 19. Fraction equatorial = 19/(19 + 1) = 95%.
x: 75% corresponds to K = 3, which would need an A-value of only about 2.7 kJ/mol.
99.9% needs K ≈ 1000 (about 17 kJ/mol); that level of preference is typical of tert-butyl, not methyl.
5% is the axial fraction; the larger share is equatorial because that conformer is lower in energy.

q: Which monosubstituted cyclohexane has the largest fraction of molecules with the substituent equatorial at 25 °C?
h: Compare A-values: which group cannot avoid pointing a CH<sub>3</sub> at the axial hydrogens when it is axial?
w: The equatorial preference grows with the A-value: Br (about 2.0 kJ/mol) < CH3 (7.3) < isopropyl (9.2) < tert-butyl (about 21). tert-Butylcyclohexane is more than 99.9% equatorial and is effectively locked.
x: Isopropyl can rotate so its C–H points toward the ring, keeping its A-value (9.2 kJ/mol) far below tert-butyl's.
Methyl has an A-value of 7.3 kJ/mol, so about 5% of molecules are still axial at 25 °C.
Br has a small A-value (about 2 kJ/mol) because the long C–Br bond keeps it away from the axial H atoms.

q: The A-value of Br (about 2.0 kJ/mol) is much smaller than that of CH<sub>3</sub> (7.3 kJ/mol). Which explanation is best?
c: The C–Br bond is much longer than a C–C bond, so an axial Br sits farther from the 3- and 5-axial H atoms
Br is more electronegative than C, so it pulls electron density away from the axial H atoms and reduces their repulsion
An axial Br forms weak hydrogen bonds to the 3- and 5-axial H atoms, which offsets its steric strain
Br is so polarizable that its 1,3-diaxial interactions are attractive, so axial Br is preferred
h: A-values measure 1,3-diaxial crowding. Compare the C–Br bond length (about 1.94 Å) with a C–C bond (1.54 Å).
w: Steric strain depends on distance. The longer C–Br bond places an axial Br farther from the axial H atoms on C3 and C5, so the 1,3-diaxial interactions are weak even though the Br atom is large. A CH3 on a short C–C bond also carries three H atoms that crowd the ring.
x: Electronegativity does not reduce steric repulsion; Cl and Br have nearly equal A-values despite different electronegativities, because the larger Br atom is offset by its longer bond.
C–H bonds in cyclohexane are not hydrogen-bond donors; there is no hydrogen bonding between axial H and Br.
Br still prefers the equatorial position (its A-value is positive), so axial Br is not favored.

q: The chair conformation shown is one conformer of which compound?
h: Count ring positions between the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Then decide whether each points up or down; one axial and one equatorial alone does not decide cis or trans.
w: The CH3 groups are on carbons separated by two ring carbons on each side: a 1,4 relationship. One is axial pointing up; the other is equatorial on a carbon whose axial bond points down, so its equatorial bond tilts up. Both point up: cis-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane. (The ring-flipped chair has the same energy.)
x: In trans-1,4 one group is up and the other down, which in a chair means both axial or both equatorial; here one is axial and one equatorial.
The substituents are across the ring (1,4), not separated by a single CH<sub>2</sub> (1,3).
The substituents are 1,4, and in any case one up and one down is not what the chair shows.

q: The two chair conformations of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane are shown. Which statement is correct?
c: II is much more stable, because both CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equatorial
I is more stable, because cis groups must both be axial to stay on the same face
I and II have equal energy, because each has one axial and one equatorial CH<sub>3</sub>
II is more stable only because it has less torsional strain than I
h: Identify each CH<sub>3</sub> as axial or equatorial in I and in II. In I, how close are the two axial groups to each other?
w: In I both CH3 groups are axial on the same face, 1,3 to each other: a severe CH3/CH3 1,3-diaxial interaction plus two CH3/H interactions. In II both are equatorial with no 1,3-diaxial strain. II is much more stable (both equatorial); cis-1,3 is the diequatorial-capable isomer.
x: Cis groups can both be equatorial: equatorial bonds also point up or down. In 1,3-cis both up positions are equatorial in chair II.
Equal energy (one axial, one equatorial in each chair) describes trans-1,3 or cis-1,2/cis-1,4, not cis-1,3.
Both chairs are fully staggered, so torsional strain is the same; the difference is steric 1,3-diaxial strain.

q: The chair shows one conformation of a 4-methylcyclohexanol stereoisomer. Using the A-values in the table, which chair is favored at equilibrium, and by how much?
c: Neither; both chairs have one axial group, so they are equal in energy
h: Decide which group is axial in the drawing and which will be axial after the flip. The energy difference is the difference between the two A-values.
w: In the drawing the OH is equatorial and the CH3 is axial (both on the top face, so this is the cis isomer). After the flip the CH3 becomes equatorial and the OH axial. Axial CH3 costs 7.3; axial OH costs 3.9. The ring-flipped chair is favored by 7.3 − 3.9 = 3.4 kJ/mol.
x: The chair shown has the larger group (CH<sub>3</sub>) axial, so it is the higher-energy conformer.
11.2 kJ/mol adds the two A-values; each chair has only one axial group, so the difference is 7.3 − 3.9.
Each chair has one axial group, but not the same group; the A-values differ, so the energies differ.

q: Which chair is the most stable conformation of trans-1-tert-butyl-3-methylcyclohexane?
h: First discard any chair that is not the trans compound (one group up, one down). Then, between the two chairs of the trans compound, put the larger group equatorial.
w: III and IV have both groups on the same face: they are cis-1,3, a different compound. I and II are the two chairs of the trans isomer: in I tert-butyl is axial and CH3 equatorial; in II tert-butyl is equatorial and CH3 axial. A trans-1,3 compound must have one group axial, so the bulky tert-butyl (A ≈ 21 kJ/mol) takes the equatorial site: II.
x: I puts the tert-butyl group axial (A-value about 21 kJ/mol) instead of CH<sub>3</sub> (7.3 kJ/mol), so it is much higher in energy than II.
III has both groups equatorial, but both are on the top face: that is cis-1-tert-butyl-3-methylcyclohexane, not the trans isomer.
IV has both groups on the top face (cis isomer) and both axial, the worst possible arrangement.

q: The chair conformation shown is one conformer of which compound?
h: The two Cl atoms are on adjacent carbons and both axial. Do adjacent axial bonds point to the same face or to opposite faces?
w: Axial bonds alternate up, down, up… around the ring, so axial groups on adjacent carbons point to opposite faces. One Cl is up and the other down: trans-1,2-dichlorocyclohexane in its diaxial chair. Its ring flip gives the diequatorial chair.
x: Both axial does not mean same side: on adjacent carbons one axial bond points up and the other down, which is trans.
The Cl atoms are on neighboring carbons (1,2), not separated by a CH<sub>2</sub> (1,3).
The Cl atoms are on neighboring carbons, and they point to opposite faces, so the compound is neither 1,3 nor cis.

q: Which dimethylcyclohexane can adopt a chair with both methyl groups equatorial?
h: Read each drawing as cis or trans. Then recall which cis/trans pattern lets both groups be equatorial for 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-substitution.
w: Both-equatorial is possible for trans-1,2, cis-1,3 and trans-1,4. The choices are trans-1,4 (wedge and dash), cis-1,4, cis-1,2 and trans-1,3. Only trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane qualifies: in one chair both CH3 groups are equatorial.
x: cis-1,4: in a chair one 1,4 position is axial and the other equatorial when both point up, so one CH<sub>3</sub> is always axial.
cis-1,2: adjacent groups on the same face are always one axial and one equatorial.
trans-1,3: one group up and one down on 1,3 carbons means one axial and one equatorial in either chair.

q: For which constitutional pattern of dimethylcyclohexane is the cis isomer more stable than the trans isomer?
c: For all three, the trans isomer is more stable
h: The more stable isomer is the one that can put both CH<sub>3</sub> groups equatorial. Work out which (cis or trans) allows that for each pattern.
w: Diequatorial requires trans for 1,2 and 1,4 but cis for 1,3. So cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane (diequatorial chair) is more stable than trans-1,3 (always one CH3 axial), by about 7 kJ/mol.
x: For 1,2, trans can be diequatorial, while cis always has one axial CH<sub>3</sub>; trans is more stable.
For 1,4, trans can be diequatorial, while cis always has one axial CH<sub>3</sub>; trans is more stable.
1,3 is the exception: there the cis isomer is the diequatorial one.

q: The two chairs of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane are shown. Each CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol, and a gauche CH3/CH3 interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol. What is the energy difference between the two chairs?
h: Count the 1,3-diaxial CH<sub>3</sub>/H interactions in the diaxial chair. In the diequatorial chair, are the adjacent CH<sub>3</sub> groups anti or gauche to each other?
w: Chair I is diaxial: each axial CH3 has two CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interactions, 4 × 3.8 = 15.2 kJ/mol; the axial CH3 groups are anti to each other, so no gauche term. Chair II is diequatorial: no diaxial strain, but adjacent equatorial CH3 groups are gauche (60°), 3.8 kJ/mol. Difference = 15.2 − 3.8 = 11.4 kJ/mol, favoring II.
x: 15.2 kJ/mol is the strain of the diaxial chair alone; the diequatorial chair is not strain-free because its CH<sub>3</sub> groups are gauche.
7.6 kJ/mol counts only one axial CH<sub>3</sub>; in the diaxial chair both CH<sub>3</sub> groups are axial.
3.8 kJ/mol is only the gauche term of the diequatorial chair, not the difference between the chairs.

q: Using 3.8 kJ/mol for each CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interaction and 3.8 kJ/mol for a gauche CH3/CH3 interaction, by how much is trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane more stable than the cis isomer (each in its best chair)?
h: The best chair of trans is diequatorial; any chair of cis has one axial and one equatorial CH<sub>3</sub>. Do adjacent axial/equatorial groups also have a gauche relationship?
w: trans (diequatorial): one gauche CH3/CH3 = 3.8 kJ/mol. cis (axial/equatorial): two CH3/H 1,3-diaxial interactions = 7.6 kJ/mol, plus the adjacent CH3 groups are still gauche = 3.8 kJ/mol; total 11.4. Difference = 11.4 − 3.8 = 7.6 kJ/mol in favor of trans.
x: 3.8 kJ/mol ignores the gauche interaction in cis: adjacent axial and equatorial groups are also 60° apart.
11.4 kJ/mol is the total strain of cis, not its difference from trans, which still has one gauche interaction.
The two chairs of cis are equal to each other, but cis and trans are different compounds with different strain.

q: Which property of a substituent on a cyclohexane ring is unchanged by a chair–chair ring flip?
c: Whether it points up or down (its wedge/dash sense)
Whether it is axial or equatorial
The energy of the conformer that contains it
h: A ring flip involves only rotations about C–C single bonds. What would have to happen for a substituent to move to the other face?
w: A ring flip converts every axial position to equatorial and vice versa, but because no bonds break, a group on the top face stays on the top face. The up/down (wedge/dash) sense, and therefore cis/trans relationships, never change.
x: Axial and equatorial are exactly what a ring flip interchanges.
Axial groups have 1,3-diaxial interactions and equatorial groups do not, so this count changes when the ring flips.
The energy usually changes, because groups that move from equatorial to axial pick up 1,3-diaxial strain.

q: Rank these conformations of cyclohexane from lowest to highest energy: boat, chair, half-chair, twist-boat.
h: The boat has flagpole crowding and eclipsed bonds; twisting relieves some of both. The half-chair, with several carbons nearly coplanar, is the transition state for ring flipping.
w: Chair (0, strain-free) < twist-boat (about 23 kJ/mol) < boat (about 29 kJ/mol, flagpole steric strain plus eclipsed C–H bonds) < half-chair (about 45 kJ/mol, the energy maximum on the ring-flip path). Order: chair < twist-boat < boat < half-chair.
x: The boat is higher than the twist-boat: twisting partly relieves the flagpole interaction and the eclipsing, so the boat is a local maximum between twist-boats.
The half-chair is the highest point on the ring-flip path, not the second-lowest conformation.
The chair has no angle, torsional or flagpole strain and is lower in energy than the twist-boat.

q: Which Newman projection, viewed along the C1–C2 bond, represents the diequatorial chair of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane? (C3 and C6 are the ring CH2 carbons attached to C2 and C1.)
h: In a chair, ring bonds C6–C1 and C2–C3 are gauche. Axial groups on adjacent carbons are anti; an equatorial group is anti to a ring C–C bond.
w: In every chair the two ring bonds (to C6 and C3) are gauche. Axial bonds on C1 and C2 are anti; each equatorial bond is anti to a ring bond. In I the two H atoms are anti (both axial), each CH3 is anti to a ring carbon (equatorial), and the CH3 groups are gauche: I is the diequatorial trans chair.
x: II has the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups anti to each other: both are axial. That is the diaxial chair of the trans isomer, not the diequatorial one.
III has the front CH<sub>3</sub> anti to the back H (axial) and the back CH<sub>3</sub> anti to C6 (equatorial): one axial and one equatorial, which is the cis isomer.
IV puts C6 and C3 anti to each other (180°), which is impossible in a six-membered ring, where these ring bonds are gauche.

q: The chair shows a stereoisomer of 3,5-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol. Which statement is correct?
c: The OH is trans to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the chair shown is the more stable chair
The OH is trans to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the ring-flipped chair is more stable because the OH becomes equatorial
The OH is cis to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the chair shown is the more stable chair
The OH is cis to both CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the ring-flipped chair is more stable because the OH becomes equatorial
h: Assign up or down to each group (an equatorial bond tilts opposite the axial bond on its carbon). In the flipped chair, which groups become axial, and are any 1,3-diaxial?
w: The OH on C1 is axial and up. The CH3 groups on C3 and C5 are equatorial; the axial bonds on C3 and C5 point up, so their equatorial bonds tilt down. The OH is up and both CH3 are down: OH trans to both CH3 groups. Ring flipping would make both CH3 groups axial on the same face, 1,3 to each other (a severe CH3/CH3 diaxial clash plus four CH3/H interactions), far worse than one axial OH. The chair shown is the more stable chair.
x: The flip moves the OH to equatorial but forces both CH<sub>3</sub> groups axial and 1,3-diaxial to each other, which costs far more than one axial OH.
The equatorial CH<sub>3</sub> groups on C3 and C5 tilt down (their axial bonds point up), so they are on the opposite face from the axial-up OH: trans, not cis.
The CH<sub>3</sub> groups are on the opposite face from the OH (trans), and the flipped chair is the less stable one.

q: Which statement about cis- and trans-decalin (bicyclo[4.4.0]decane) is correct?
c: trans-Decalin cannot undergo a chair–chair ring flip, but cis-decalin can
cis-Decalin cannot undergo a chair–chair ring flip, but trans-decalin can
cis-Decalin is more stable than trans-decalin because its ring-fusion H atoms are on the same face
In trans-decalin both rings must adopt boat conformations
h: In trans-decalin, the bonds from each fusion carbon into the second ring are both equatorial. What would a ring flip require of those bonds?
w: In trans-decalin the second ring is attached through two equatorial bonds of the first ring (trans-1,2-diequatorial). A ring flip would make both bonds axial and anti (180° apart), too far apart to be bridged by a four-carbon chain. So trans-decalin is conformationally locked, while cis-decalin (one axial, one equatorial fusion bond) flips freely.
x: It is the reverse: cis-decalin, joined through one axial and one equatorial bond, can flip, because flipping just swaps which fusion bond is axial.
trans-Decalin is the more stable isomer (by about 11 kJ/mol); cis-decalin has extra gauche interactions.
Both rings of trans-decalin are chairs; it is rigid, but in a strain-free double-chair shape.

q: In the preferred chair conformation of the compound shown, the Br atom is
c: axial, because the tert-butyl group occupies an equatorial position
equatorial, because Br is larger than a hydrogen and avoids 1,3-diaxial strain
axial half the time and equatorial half the time, because the two chairs are equal in energy
axial, because Br has a larger A-value than the tert-butyl group
h: Is this cis or trans? Then decide which group controls the conformation.
w: Both Br and tert-butyl are wedged: this is cis-1-bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane. In a cis-1,4 compound one group is axial and one equatorial. tert-Butyl (A ≈ 21 kJ/mol) insists on equatorial, which forces Br axial, because the tert-butyl group is equatorial.
