This locked axial Br is why the cis isomer undergoes E2 much faster than the trans isomer.
x: Br would prefer equatorial on its own, but in this cis-1,4 isomer the Br can be equatorial only if tert-butyl is axial, which costs far more.
The A-values differ greatly (tert-butyl about 21 vs Br about 2 kJ/mol), so the two chairs are not equal; the tert-butyl-equatorial chair dominates.
The conclusion is right but the reason is wrong: Br's A-value (about 2 kJ/mol) is much smaller than tert-butyl's.

q: A-values (kJ/mol): CH<sub>3</sub> 7.3, CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> 7.5, CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> 9.2, C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> about 21. Why does the A-value rise only slightly from methyl to isopropyl but jump sharply for tert-butyl?
c: Ethyl and isopropyl can rotate to point a C–H over the ring; axial tert-butyl must point a CH<sub>3</sub> at the 3- and 5-axial H atoms
Isopropyl is smaller than ethyl, so the two groups’ A-values nearly cancel the effect of the extra carbon
tert-Butyl is the only group that adds torsional strain to the ring C–C bonds, even when it is equatorial
Branched groups are more electron-donating, and tert-butyl donates enough to destabilize the axial C–H bonds of the ring
h: Picture each group axial and spin it about its bond to the ring. Can it always find an orientation that aims only an H toward the ring?
w: An axial group interacts mainly with the 3- and 5-axial H atoms through whatever it points toward the ring. Ethyl and isopropyl can rotate so that a small H faces the ring and the CH3 groups point outward, so their A-values stay near methyl's. tert-Butyl has three CH3 groups and no H, so one CH3 must always point at the axial H atoms, causing severe steric strain and a large A-value.
x: Isopropyl is larger than ethyl; the small change in A-value comes from rotational freedom, not size.
The jump comes from axial tert-butyl's steric clash with the 3- and 5-axial H atoms; equatorial tert-butyl is nearly strain-free.
A-values reflect steric 1,3-diaxial interactions; electron donation by alkyl groups does not explain the jump.

q: What is the major organic product when 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is heated with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol?
h: A tertiary halide with a strong, small base reacts by E2. Which β hydrogen gives the more substituted C=C?
w: A 3° bromide cannot undergo SN2, and ethoxide is a strong base, so the reaction is E2. Ethoxide is small, so it can reach the internal CH2 hydrogens and the Zaitsev product, 2-methyl-2-butene (trisubstituted, more stable) is major. 2-Methyl-1-butene (disubstituted) is the minor Hofmann product.
x: 2-Methyl-1-butene is the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene; it becomes major only with a bulky base such as tert-butoxide.
3-Methyl-1-butene would need the C=C between C3 and C4 of the original chain; neither carbon carries the leaving group, so it cannot form by E2 here.
The ether is the substitution product. A 3° carbon blocks backside attack, and with a strong base and heat elimination dominates.

q: 2-Bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butyl alcohol. What is the major product?
h: Think about which β hydrogens a very bulky base can reach most easily.
w: tert-Butoxide is a strong but bulky base. With a 3° bromide it does E2, and it removes the most accessible hydrogen: one of the six equivalent CH3 hydrogens on C1, not the single hindered C–H on C3. The Hofmann product, 2,3-dimethyl-1-butene, is therefore major, even though 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene (tetrasubstituted) is more stable.
x: 2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene is the Zaitsev product; it is major with a small base such as ethoxide, not with tert-butoxide.
3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene has a different carbon skeleton; making it would require a methyl shift, which does not happen in a concerted E2.
tert-Butoxide is a very poor nucleophile, and the 3° carbon cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2, so this ether does not form.

q: Which reagent converts 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane mainly into methylenecyclohexane?
h: The target is the less substituted (exocyclic) alkene. What kind of base favors that?
w: Methylenecyclohexane is the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene, formed by removing a hydrogen from the CH3 group. A bulky base removes the exposed CH3 hydrogens faster than the ring CH2 hydrogens, so (CH3)3COK in (CH3)3COH gives mainly the exocyclic alkene.
x: Ethoxide is small, so E2 gives mainly the Zaitsev product, 1-methylcyclohexene (trisubstituted).
Hot water gives S<sub>N</sub>1/E1 through the 3° carbocation; the alcohol and 1-methylcyclohexene (the more stable alkene) dominate.
Iodide is a good nucleophile but a very weak base, and a 3° carbon cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; no elimination to the exocyclic alkene occurs.

q: (2R,3R)-2-Bromo-3-methylhexane is heated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. What is the major product?
h: Zaitsev decides which carbon loses H; the anti-periplanar geometry then decides E or Z, because C3 has only one hydrogen.
w: Ethoxide is small, so the trisubstituted Zaitsev alkene (C2=C3) is major. C3 has only one H, so only one conformation puts that H anti-periplanar to Br, and the geometry of the alkene is fixed. Put Br and the C3–H anti in a Newman projection along C2–C3: for the (2R,3R) isomer the C2 methyl ends up anti to the C3 propyl group, so those two become trans. On C2, CH3 > H; on C3, CH2CH2CH3 > CH3. The higher-priority groups are trans, so the product is (E)-3-methylhex-2-ene. (The (2R,3S) diastereomer gives the Z alkene.)
x: The Z alkene comes from the (2R,3S)/(2S,3R) diastereomer; E2 is stereospecific, so this isomer cannot give it.
3-Methylhex-1-ene is the Hofmann product; with a small base like ethoxide it is minor.
The S<sub>N</sub>2 ether is minor: the 2° carbon is next to a branched carbon, and ethoxide with heat favors E2.

q: The Newman projection shows 2-bromo-3-phenylbutane viewed along C2–C3 (C2 in front) in the conformation that reacts. What is the product of E2 elimination with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Br and the back H are anti. Groups that are gauche (60°) to each other in this conformation end up cis on the alkene.
w: In the drawn conformation the back-carbon H is anti to Br, so E2 removes it and the C=C forms between C2 and C3. The remaining groups keep their sides: the front CH3 (lower left) is next to the back C6H5 (upper left), and the front H is next to the back CH3. So CH3 on C2 and C6H5 on C3 are cis. Priorities: CH3 > H on C2; C6H5 > CH3 on C3, so the product is (Z)-2-phenyl-2-butene.
x: The E isomer would need the front CH3 and the phenyl on opposite sides; in the anti-periplanar conformation they are gauche, so they end up cis.
3-Phenyl-1-butene would need removal of a C1 hydrogen, but the drawn anti-periplanar H is on C3, and the conjugated trisubstituted alkene is strongly favored.
2-Phenyl-1-butene needs a C=C between the phenyl-bearing carbon and its methyl group; neither carbon carries the Br, so E2 cannot form it.

q: meso-2,3-Dibromobutane is treated with one equivalent of NaOCH2CH3. Which monobromoalkene forms?
h: Draw a Newman projection with one Br anti to the H on the other carbon, and see where the two methyl groups end up.
w: In the meso isomer, the conformation with Br on C2 anti to H on C3 places the two CH3 groups gauche (on the same side), so they are cis in the alkene. On C2, Br > CH3; on C3, CH3 > H. Br and the C3 methyl are therefore trans: (E)-2-bromo-2-butene. The racemic (2R,3R) isomer gives the Z isomer instead.
x: The Z isomer comes from the chiral (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) dibromide; E2 from the meso isomer cannot give it.
3-Bromo-1-butene needs loss of a C1 hydrogen; the C3 hydrogen, which gives the more substituted vinyl bromide, is removed instead.
2-Butyne needs a second elimination, which requires excess very strong base such as NaNH<sub>2</sub>; one equivalent of ethoxide stops at the vinyl bromide.

q: On E2 with NaOCH2CH3, which compound gives (E)-2-phenyl-2-butene with no (Z) isomer?
h: The C=C must form between the carbon with Br and a carbon that has only one H, so the anti-periplanar requirement fixes E/Z.
w: 2-Bromo-3-phenylbutane eliminates toward C3 (one H, gives the conjugated trisubstituted alkene). With Br and that H anti, the (2R,3R) isomer puts the C2 methyl gauche to the C3 methyl, so the methyls end up cis and the phenyl trans to the C2 methyl: the E alkene. So (2R,3R)-2-bromo-3-phenylbutane gives only the E isomer. (Its enantiomer, (2S,3S), would too.)
x: This is the (2R,3S) diastereomer; in its anti-periplanar conformation CH3 and C6H5 are gauche, so it gives only the Z alkene.
This is (2S,3R), the enantiomer of the (2R,3S) isomer; it also gives only the Z alkene.
Here Br is on the carbon bearing the phenyl, and the neighboring CH2 has two hydrogens, so either can be anti to Br: both E and Z form (plus the 1-alkene).

q: trans-1-Bromo-2-methylcyclohexane is shown in its more stable chair. What is the major product of E2 with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol? (Stereochemistry at ring carbons is not shown in the choices.)
h: Cyclohexane E2 needs Br axial and an axial H on the neighboring carbon (trans-diaxial). Flip the ring and check both β carbons.
w: E2 on a cyclohexane requires the leaving group and the β H to be trans-diaxial. In the drawn chair both groups are equatorial, so the ring must flip; then Br and CH3 are both axial (trans-1,2 = diaxial). On C2 the axial position is taken by CH3, so the C2 H is equatorial and cannot be anti to Br. Only C6 has an axial H, so the C=C forms between C1 and C6: 3-methylcyclohexene, even though it is the less substituted alkene.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene is the Zaitsev product, but it needs an axial H on C2; in the diaxial conformer C2 has an axial CH<sub>3</sub> and only an equatorial H.
Methylenecyclohexane would need Br on the carbon bearing the methyl; here Br is on C1 and the methyl on C2, so that C=C cannot form.
S<sub>N</sub>2 (with inversion, giving this cis ether) on a hindered 2° ring carbon with a strong base and heat is minor; E2 is the main pathway.

q:
Consider E2 reactions of the cis and trans isomers of 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane with NaOCH2CH3. Which statements are true?
I. The cis isomer gives mainly 1-methylcyclohexene.
II. The trans isomer gives mainly 3-methylcyclohexene.
III. The trans isomer reacts faster than the cis isomer.
h: For each isomer, find the chair with Br axial and ask how much of the molecule is in that chair and which neighbors have axial H.
w: cis: Br axial / CH3 equatorial is the preferred chair (CH3 has the larger A-value), and both C2 and C6 have axial H, so E2 is fast and Zaitsev gives 1-methylcyclohexene (I true). trans: Br is axial only in the diaxial chair, a small fraction of molecules, and there only C6 has an axial H, so it reacts more slowly and gives 3-methylcyclohexene (II true, III false). Answer: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: in the reactive diaxial chair of the trans isomer only C6 has an axial H, so 3-methylcyclohexene forms.
Statement III is false: the trans isomer must flip into its diaxial chair before it can react, so it is the slower one.
Statement III is false: the cis isomer, with Br already axial in its preferred chair, reacts faster.

q: The chair below (a neomenthyl-type bromide) is heated with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol. What is the major E2 product? (Ring stereochemistry is not shown in the choices.)
c: The ethyl ether from S<sub>N</sub>2 at C1
No E2 product; an axial C–Br bond cannot react
h: Is Br already axial in this chair? Which neighboring carbons have an axial H?
w: In this chair Br is axial while the ethyl and methyl groups are both equatorial, so the reactive conformation is also the stable one. C2 (with an equatorial ethyl) has an axial H, and C6 has an axial H, so E2 can go either way. With a small base, Zaitsev wins: the trisubstituted alkene from loss of the C2 H, 1-ethyl-4-methylcyclohexene, is major.
x: 3-Ethyl-6-methylcyclohexene (C1=C6) is the minor, less substituted alkene here because C2 also has an axial H.
Substitution at a hindered 2° ring carbon with a strong base and heat is minor compared with E2.
An axial leaving group is exactly what cyclohexane E2 needs; it is anti-periplanar to the axial H atoms on C2 and C6.

q: Chairs I and II are diastereomers (shown in their more stable chairs). Compared with II, how does I behave in E2 with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
c: I reacts more slowly and gives only 3-ethyl-6-methylcyclohexene
I reacts more slowly and gives mainly 1-ethyl-4-methylcyclohexene
I reacts faster and gives only 3-ethyl-6-methylcyclohexene
I reacts faster and gives mainly 1-ethyl-4-methylcyclohexene
h: Where is Br in the stable chair of I? What must happen before I can eliminate, and what is axial on C2 after that?
w: In I all three groups are equatorial. To make Br axial the ring must flip, putting ethyl and methyl axial too, a high-energy chair present in tiny amounts, so I reacts more slowly. In that diaxial chair, C2 has an axial ethyl and only an equatorial H, so the only anti-periplanar H is on C6: I gives only 3-ethyl-6-methylcyclohexene (the non-Zaitsev alkene). II already has Br axial with axial H on both C2 and C6, so it reacts fast and gives mainly the Zaitsev alkene.
x: I does react slowly, but it cannot give the Zaitsev alkene: in its reactive chair C2 bears an axial ethyl, so the C2 H is not anti to Br.
The product is right, but I is slower: the conformer with Br axial is the minor triaxial chair.
This describes neither isomer correctly: II is the fast one (and gives mainly the Zaitsev alkene); I is slow and gives only the C1=C6 alkene.

q: Which isomer of 1-bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane undergoes E2 with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> much faster, and why?
c: cis, because its Br is axial and anti-periplanar to axial H on C2 and C6
trans, because its equatorial Br is less hindered for the approaching base
trans, because its equatorial Br is anti-periplanar to the ring C–C bonds
cis, because its Br is equatorial and eclipses the H on C2
h: The tert-butyl group locks the ring. Which isomer has Br axial in that locked chair?
w: The tert-butyl group stays equatorial, so neither ring flips. In the cis isomer Br is axial and is anti-periplanar to the axial H atoms on C2 and C6, so E2 is fast. In the trans isomer Br is locked equatorial; an equatorial C–Br is anti to ring C–C bonds, not to any H, so E2 is very slow.
x: Steric access to Br is not the issue in E2; the base attacks a β H, and that H must be anti-periplanar to Br, which an equatorial Br cannot satisfy.
Being anti to a C–C bond does not help: E2 needs an anti-periplanar C–H, whose electrons form the new π bond.
In the cis isomer (with the tert-butyl equatorial) Br is axial, not equatorial, and E2 needs anti, not eclipsed, geometry here.

q: The E2 reaction of 2-bromopropane with ethoxide follows rate = k[RBr][EtO−]. If [RBr] is doubled and [EtO−] is tripled, the rate changes by what factor?
h: E2 is bimolecular: both concentrations appear to the first power.
w: Rate = k[RBr][EtO−]. New rate = k(2[RBr])(3[EtO−]) = 6 × old rate, so 6 times faster. Both species are in the single, concerted step.
x: Doubling [RBr] alone would double the rate, but E2 is also first order in base, so tripling [EtO<sup>−</sup>] multiplies it by 3 more.
That counts only the base; the substrate is also in the rate law (E2 is bimolecular).
The factors multiply (2 × 3), they do not add.

q: 2-Bromopropane reacts with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> about 7 times faster than (CD<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHBr, in which all six β hydrogens are deuterium. What does this show?
c: The β C–H bond is broken in the rate-determining step
A carbocation forms in the rate-determining step
The C–Br bond breaks in a fast step after deprotonation
Ethoxide attacks the carbon bearing the bromine
h: C–D bonds are stronger than C–H bonds. When does that matter for the rate?
w: A primary deuterium kinetic isotope effect (kH/kD ≈ 7) appears only when the C–H (or C–D) bond is being broken in the rate-determining step. This supports the concerted E2 mechanism: the β C–H bond breaks in the rate-determining step, together with the C–Br bond.
x: Carbocation formation (E1) breaks only the C–Br bond in the slow step; deuterium on the β carbons would have little effect on that rate.
If C–Br broke in a later fast step, the rate would not be set by C–Br cleavage at all; E2 is concerted, so C–H and C–Br break together.
Attack at the C–Br carbon is S<sub>N</sub>2, which does not break a β C–H bond and would show no large isotope effect.

q: Rank these 2-halo-2-methylpropanes by E2 rate with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (slowest → fastest).
h: The C–X bond breaks in the rate-determining step. Which halide is the best leaving group?
w: Leaving-group ability follows the weakness of the conjugate base (and the weakness of the C–X bond): I− > Br− > Cl− > F−. Since C–X breaks in the E2 transition state, the order is I < II < III < IV (fluoride slowest, iodide fastest).
x: This is reversed: the strong C–F bond and basic F<sup>−</sup> make fluoride the worst leaving group, not the best.
Chloride is a better leaving group than fluoride; HCl is a far stronger acid than HF.
Bromide is a better leaving group than chloride; the C–Br bond is weaker and Br<sup>−</sup> is a weaker base.

q: 2-Bromobutane gives 1-butene and 2-butene by E2. Which base gives the highest percentage of 1-butene?
h: Which base is too crowded to reach the internal CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogens easily?
w: 1-Butene is the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene. A sterically bulky base removes the more exposed CH3 hydrogens, so potassium tert-butoxide gives the most 1-butene. The small bases all favor the Zaitsev product, 2-butene.
x: Ethoxide is a small base and gives mainly 2-butene (Zaitsev).
Methoxide is even smaller than ethoxide and gives mainly 2-butene.
Hydroxide is small; with it 2-butene (Zaitsev) is again the main alkene.

q: E2 of 2-bromobutane with NaOCH2CH3 gives more (E)-2-butene than (Z)-2-butene. Which statement best explains this?
c: Both C3 H atoms can be anti to Br; the conformer leading to E keeps the methyls anti and is lower in energy
E2 is not stereospecific, so the more stable alkene forms after the double bond equilibrates under the conditions
Only one C3 hydrogen can be anti-periplanar to Br, and that hydrogen always gives the E alkene
The Z alkene forms first and then isomerizes to E under the basic conditions
h: How many C3 hydrogens can be anti to Br? Compare the two conformations that put each one there.
w: C3 is a CH2, so either H can be anti-periplanar to Br. In the conformer leading to E, the two methyls are anti; in the one leading to Z, they are gauche. The E-forming transition state has less steric strain and is lower in energy, so E-2-butene is major. E2 is stereoselective here (not stereospecific, since both geometries are possible).
x: E2 is concerted and irreversible; the alkenes do not equilibrate under these conditions. The ratio is set by the two competing transition states.
Both C3 hydrogens can be placed anti to Br, one in each of two conformers, which is why both E and Z form.
Alkenes do not isomerize with alkoxide bases; each geometry comes directly from its own conformer.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylcyclohexanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Acid-catalyzed dehydration goes through a carbocation (E1) and gives the most stable alkene.
w: Protonation of OH and loss of water give a 2° carbocation at C1; a 1,2-hydride shift from C2 gives the 3° cation, and loss of a proton from either cation can form the trisubstituted C=C. E1 dehydration gives the most stable alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexene (disubstituted) forms, but as a minor product; E1 favors the more substituted alkene.
Methylenecyclohexane is a less stable exocyclic, disubstituted alkene and is minor.
4-Methylcyclohexene has the C=C away from the original carbocation site; it would need extra hydride shifts to unproductive 2° cations.

q: 3,3-Dimethyl-2-butanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: The first carbocation is secondary and sits next to a quaternary carbon. What can migrate?
w: Loss of water gives a 2° carbocation at C2. A 1,2-methyl shift from the neighboring quaternary carbon makes a more stable 3° cation, (CH3)2C+–CH(CH3)2. Loss of the lone C–H proton gives the tetrasubstituted alkene 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene, the most stable possible product, as the major product.
x: 3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene is the unrearranged alkene; it is minor because the 2° cation rearranges by a methyl shift before losing a proton.
2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene does come from the rearranged cation, but it is only disubstituted; the tetrasubstituted isomer is major.
With concentrated acid and heat the rearranged cation loses a proton to give the alkene (which leaves the mixture); capture by water is reversed under these conditions.

q: The same alcohol, 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol, is instead treated with POCl<sub>3</sub> in pyridine. What is the major product?
h: Does this reagent pair form a carbocation? Which β carbon still has hydrogens?
w: POCl3 converts OH into a dichlorophosphate leaving group, and pyridine removes a β H in a concerted E2 step. No carbocation forms, so no methyl shift is possible. The only β carbon with hydrogens is C1 (C3 is quaternary), so the product is 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene.
x: 2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene needs a methyl shift, which happens only via a carbocation (acid-catalyzed E1), not in this E2 reaction.
2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene also requires the rearranged skeleton, which a concerted E2 cannot give.
Pyridine is a base, and the phosphate ester is eliminated, not substituted; the alkyl chloride is not the main product.

q: 1-Cyclobutylethanol is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: A carbocation next to a strained four-membered ring can relieve strain by an alkyl (ring bond) shift.
w: Loss of water gives a 2° cation next to the cyclobutane. A ring C–C bond migrates to the cation carbon, expanding the ring to a less strained cyclopentyl cation: the former cation carbon (with its CH3) is now a ring carbon, and the positive charge sits on the neighboring former ring CH. A hydride shift (or direct loss of the H on the methyl-bearing carbon) then gives the trisubstituted ring alkene 1-methylcyclopentene.
x: Vinylcyclobutane is the unrearranged, monosubstituted alkene; ring expansion relieves strain and the product is more stable.
Ethylidenecyclobutane keeps the strained four-membered ring and an exocyclic C=C; the ring-expansion pathway wins.
Cyclohexene would need the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon to join the ring as well; ring expansion adds only one carbon (the cation carbon), giving a five-membered ring.

q: Rank the alcohols by rate of acid-catalyzed dehydration (slowest → fastest).
h: The rate-determining step forms a carbocation. Which alcohol gives the most stable one?
w: E1 dehydration is limited by loss of water to form the carbocation, so the rate follows carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1°. I is 3°, II is 2°, III is 1° (which reacts slowly, by an E2-like path). Order: III < II < I.
x: This is reversed; tertiary alcohols dehydrate fastest because they form the most stable carbocations.
The primary alcohol III is the slowest, not the secondary alcohol II.
The tertiary alcohol I is the fastest; 2° alcohol II is slower than I.

q: The energy diagram is for the acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-methyl-2-propanol. Which labeled point is the transition state of the rate-determining step?
h: Match each step: protonation of OH, loss of water, loss of a proton. Which barrier is highest?
w: Step 1 (A) is fast protonation of the OH. Step 2 is loss of water to form the 3° carbocation; its transition state, point B, is the highest point, so this is the rate-determining step. C is the carbocation intermediate (a minimum), and D is the transition state for removal of the β proton.
x: C is an energy minimum, the carbocation intermediate, not a transition state.
A is the transition state for proton transfer to the OH, a fast step with a small barrier.
D is the transition state for loss of the β proton from the carbocation, which is fast compared with ionization.

q: Why is an alcohol dehydrated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> rather than concentrated HBr?
c: Bromide is a good nucleophile and traps the carbocation as an alkyl bromide
HBr is too weak an acid to protonate the alcohol’s OH group
Bromide is a strong base that removes the β proton too slowly to form much alkene
HBr adds water back to the alkene faster than H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> does
h: Compare the conjugate bases: what else can they do to a carbocation?
w: Both acids form the same carbocation. HSO4− and H2PO4− are very poor nucleophiles, so the cation loses a proton (E1). Br− is a good nucleophile and traps the carbocation, so HBr converts alcohols into alkyl bromides (SN1/SN2), not alkenes.
x: HBr (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −9) is a very strong acid and protonates alcohols readily.
Br<sup>−</sup> is a very weak base; the problem is its nucleophilicity, not its basicity.
HBr does not hydrate alkenes; it adds H–Br across the C=C to give an alkyl bromide.

q: Alkene hydration and alcohol dehydration are the reverse of each other. Which set of conditions best favors dehydration to the alkene?
c: Concentrated acid, high temperature, distilling off the alkene
Dilute aqueous acid, low temperature, excess water added to the flask
Concentrated acid, low temperature, excess water added at the start
Dilute aqueous acid, high temperature, a sealed flask so nothing escapes
h: Use Le Châtelier: which side has more molecules, and how can you remove a product?
w: Dehydration makes two molecules from one (ΔS > 0), so high temperature makes −TΔS more favorable. Concentrated acid supplies little water, and distilling the lower-boiling alkene removes a product. So concentrated acid, heat, and removal of the alkene drive the equilibrium to the right.
x: Dilute acid, low temperature and excess water are hydration conditions; they push the equilibrium toward the alcohol.
Excess water and low temperature both favor the alcohol, even with concentrated acid.
In a sealed flask with lots of water, the products cannot leave and water pushes the equilibrium back toward the alcohol.

q: 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide) is heated with AgNO<sub>3</sub> in ethanol. What is the major alkene formed?
c: No alkene forms; this bromide has no β hydrogen
h: Ag<sup>+</sup> pulls off bromide. What does the developing primary cation do next to a quaternary carbon?
w: Ag+ forces ionization; as Br− leaves, a methyl group shifts from the quaternary carbon, giving the 3° 2-methyl-2-butyl cation (no free 1° cation forms). That cation loses a proton (E1) or is trapped by ethanol (SN1). The major alkene is the trisubstituted Zaitsev product, 2-methyl-2-butene.
x: 2-Methyl-1-butene also comes from the rearranged cation, but it is disubstituted and minor.
3-Methyl-1-butene has its C=C two carbons away from the 3° cation center; forming it would require further shifts to less stable 2° and 1° cations.
It is true that the starting bromide has no β H (so no direct E2), but after the methyl shift the 3° cation has β hydrogens and loses one.

q: 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane undergoes E1 when heated in ethanol. Which change would make this reaction faster?
c: Using hexane as the solvent instead of ethanol
h: The rate-determining step of E1 is ionization. What makes ionization easier?
w: E1 rate = k[RX]; the slow step is C–X ionization to the carbocation. A better leaving group speeds this up, so 2-bromo-2-methylbutane reacts faster (Br− is a weaker base and a better leaving group than Cl−).
x: 1-Chloro-3-methylbutane is primary; a 1° carbocation is far too unstable, so it does not undergo E1.
Hexane is nonpolar and cannot stabilize the ions formed in the ionization step, so E1 would be much slower.
2-Chloro-3-methylbutane is secondary; its 2° carbocation forms more slowly than the 3° cation.

q:
Which statements about E1 and E2 reactions are true?
I. E2 normally requires the β H and the leaving group to be anti-periplanar.
II. The rate of an E1 reaction increases when the base concentration is doubled.
III. With small bases, both E1 and E2 usually give mainly the more substituted alkene.
h: Write the rate law for each mechanism, and recall what the transition state of each needs.
w: I is true: the anti-periplanar arrangement lets the C–H σ bond overlap with the C–X σ* orbital in the concerted step. II is false: E1 is first order, rate = k[RX]; the base acts only after the slow step. III is true: E1 goes through a carbocation that loses a proton to give the more stable alkene, and E2 with a small base gives the Zaitsev product. Answer: I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: both pathways favor the Zaitsev alkene when the base is small.
Statement II is false; base is not in the E1 rate-determining step, so rate = k[RX].
Statement II is false; doubling the base does not change an E1 rate.

q: Rank these C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkenes from least stable to most stable.
h: More alkyl groups on the C=C stabilize it; for disubstituted alkenes, compare cis and trans.
w: Alkene stability increases with substitution (hyperconjugation, stronger sp2–sp3 bonds), and trans beats cis because cis has steric strain between the groups. III is cis-disubstituted, I is trans-disubstituted, II is tetrasubstituted: III < I < II.
x: The cis isomer (III) is less stable than the trans isomer (I) because its alkyl groups crowd each other.
This is reversed; the tetrasubstituted alkene II is the most stable.
The tetrasubstituted alkene II is more stable than either disubstituted alkene.

q: 1-Butene, (Z)-2-butene and (E)-2-butene all hydrogenate to butane. Their heats of hydrogenation are −127, −120 and −116 kJ/mol (not in order). Which assignment is correct?
h: All three give the same alkane, so the less stable alkene releases more heat.
w: Because all three give the same product, differences in heat released reflect differences in alkene stability: the least stable alkene releases the most heat. Stability: monosubstituted < cis-disubstituted < trans-disubstituted. So 1-butene −127, (Z)-2-butene −120, (E)-2-butene −116 kJ/mol; the E isomer is about 4 kJ/mol more stable than Z.
x: This gives the most heat to the most stable alkene; a more stable alkene sits lower in energy and releases less heat.
The cis isomer is less stable than the trans isomer, so it releases more heat, not less.
1-Butene, the least substituted alkene, is the least stable and releases the most heat.

q: All four alkenes hydrogenate (H2, Pd) to methylcyclohexane. Which one releases the least heat?
h: Same product for all four, so the least heat comes from the most stable alkene.
w: With a common product, the most stable alkene has the smallest heat of hydrogenation. 1-Methylcyclohexene is trisubstituted; the others are disubstituted (3- and 4-methylcyclohexene) or a disubstituted exocyclic alkene (methylenecyclohexane), so 1-methylcyclohexene releases the least heat.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexene is only disubstituted, so it is less stable and releases more heat than the trisubstituted isomer.
4-Methylcyclohexene is disubstituted and releases more heat than 1-methylcyclohexene.
Methylenecyclohexane is a disubstituted exocyclic alkene; it is less stable than 1-methylcyclohexene and releases more heat.

q: Which alkyl bromide gives no E2 product when heated with (CH3)3COK?
h: Every choice has β hydrogens. Where would the new C=C have to be, and can its p orbitals line up?
w: 1-Bromobicyclo[2.2.1]heptane has β hydrogens, but any C=C would have to include the bridgehead carbon. In a small bicyclic ring the bridgehead p orbital cannot overlap with its neighbor's (Bredt's rule), so no E2 occurs. The other three give cyclohexene, methylenecyclohexane (bulky base), and methylenecyclohexane respectively.
x: Bromocyclohexane has axial β H atoms anti to an axial Br in the ring-flipped chair, so it gives cyclohexene.
This 3° bromide eliminates readily; with tert-butoxide it gives mainly methylenecyclohexane.
This 1° bromide has one β H on the ring carbon; the bulky base favors E2 over S<sub>N</sub>2, giving methylenecyclohexane.

q: The heats of hydrogenation of 2,3-dimethyl-1-butene and 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene are about −117 and −111 kJ/mol. Both give 2,3-dimethylbutane. What is ΔH for the isomerization below?
h: Build a Hess's-law cycle through the common alkane.
w: 1-ene → alkane: ΔH = −117; alkane → 2-ene is the reverse of the 2-ene's hydrogenation: ΔH = +111. Sum: −117 + 111 = −6 kJ/mol. The isomerization is exothermic because the tetrasubstituted alkene is more stable.
x: The sign is wrong: going to the more stable (tetrasubstituted) alkene releases energy.
Adding the two heats of hydrogenation double-counts; one of them must be reversed in the cycle.
This both adds the values and flips the sign; reverse only the second hydrogenation, then add.

q: 2-Butanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which product is formed in the largest amount?
h: Through the carbocation, which C=C is most substituted, and which geometry has less strain?
w: Loss of water gives the 2-butyl cation. Removing a C3 proton gives 2-butene (disubstituted), favored over 1-butene; of the two 2-butenes, the trans isomer has no cis steric strain. E1 picks the most stable alkene, so (E)-2-butene is major.
x: (Z)-2-Butene forms too, but the cis methyl groups make it less stable than the E isomer, so it is minor.
1-Butene is monosubstituted and least stable; it is a minor product of E1.
The ether forms when an alcohol attacks the cation at lower temperature; with heat, elimination dominates.

q: What is the major product when 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is treated with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> in methanol?
h: Tertiary substrate plus a strong base: which mechanisms are possible?
w: A 3° carbon cannot undergo SN2, and methoxide is a strong base, so E2 dominates: 2-methylpropene.
x: tert-Butyl methyl ether would need S<sub>N</sub>2 at a 3° carbon (blocked) or S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis, which is far slower than E2 with a strong base present.
Isobutyl methyl ether has the oxygen on a different carbon; nothing here moves the reaction site.
No water is present, so tert-butyl alcohol cannot form.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is dissolved in methanol at 25 °C with no added base. What happens mainly?
c: S<sub>N</sub>1, giving mainly tert-butyl methyl ether (with some 2-methylpropene by E1)
E2, giving mainly 2-methylpropene, with methanol as the base
S<sub>N</sub>2, giving mainly tert-butyl methyl ether by backside attack
E1, giving mainly 2-methylpropene (with some tert-butyl methyl ether by S<sub>N</sub>1)
h: Methanol is a weak nucleophile and weak base in a polar protic solvent. What does a 3° bromide do there at room temperature?
w: With no strong base, the 3° bromide ionizes in the polar protic solvent (solvolysis). The carbocation is captured mostly by solvent at 25 °C: SN1 gives mainly tert-butyl methyl ether, with a smaller amount of 2-methylpropene from E1. Heating would increase the alkene fraction.
x: E2 needs a strong base; methanol is far too weak a base for E2 to compete with ionization.
A 3° carbon is too hindered for backside attack; the ether forms by S<sub>N</sub>1, not S<sub>N</sub>2.
At room temperature, capture of the carbocation by the solvent beats loss of a proton; E1 is the minor path.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with NaN3 in DMSO. What is the major product?
h: Azide is an excellent nucleophile but a weak base, and DMSO is polar aprotic.
w: N3− is a strong nucleophile and weak base, and DMSO leaves it unsolvated, so a 2° bromide reacts by SN2 with backside attack and inversion: (S)-2-azidobutane. (N3 and Br both have top priority, so inversion changes R to S here.)
x: Retention would need front-side attack; S<sub>N</sub>2 goes with inversion of configuration.
Azide is a weak base (HN<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4.7), so E2 to 2-butene is minor.
1-Butene would need a strong, bulky base; azide gives substitution.

q: 2-Bromopentane is heated with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol at 55 °C. What is the major product?
h: A 2° halide with a strong, small base and heat: substitution or elimination? Then pick the alkene.
w: With a 2° halide, a strong base such as ethoxide (and heat) favors E2 over SN2. Small bases give the Zaitsev alkene, and of the two 2-pentenes the trans isomer is formed faster (less steric strain in its transition state): (E)-2-pentene.
x: The S<sub>N</sub>2 ether forms, but with a 2° halide, a strong base and heat it is the minor product.
1-Pentene is the Hofmann product; ethoxide is small, so the more substituted 2-pentene dominates.
(Z)-2-Pentene forms in smaller amount; its anti-periplanar conformer puts the alkyl groups gauche.

q: 1-Bromobutane is treated separately with (I) NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol and (II) (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COK in tert-butyl alcohol. What is the main product in each case?
h: A primary carbon is easy to attack from the back. Which base is too bulky to act as a nucleophile?
w: With an unhindered 1° bromide, ethoxide acts mainly as a nucleophile (SN2), giving 1-ethoxybutane. tert-Butoxide is too bulky to reach the carbon, so it removes a β H instead (E2), giving 1-butene.
x: Ethoxide with an unhindered 1° bromide gives mainly S<sub>N</sub>2; E2 is minor.
tert-Butoxide is a poor nucleophile because of its bulk; with a 1° bromide it gives mainly E2.
2-Butene cannot form directly from 1-bromobutane by E2; the C=C must include C1, which bore the Br.

q: Which reagent converts bromocyclohexane mainly into a substitution product?
h: For a 2° substrate you need a nucleophile that is strong but only weakly basic.
w: Secondary substrates give E2 with strong bases and SN2 with good nucleophiles that are weak bases. CH3S− in DMF (polar aprotic) is highly nucleophilic but much less basic than alkoxides, so it gives cyclohexyl methyl sulfide by SN2.
x: Methoxide is a strong base; with a 2° ring halide and heat it gives mainly cyclohexene by E2.
tert-Butoxide is a strong, bulky base that gives E2 (cyclohexene).
DBU is a non-nucleophilic amidine base used specifically to promote E2.

q: Which combination is the best way to prepare tert-butyl ethyl ether, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: The Williamson synthesis is S<sub>N</sub>2. Which partner must be the alkyl halide?
w: The C–O bond must be made by SN2, so the halide must be unhindered. tert-Butoxide + bromoethane works: a 1° bromide with no β-branching undergoes SN2 readily. Putting the halogen on the 3° carbon makes the alkoxide act as a base and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.
x: Ethoxide with a 3° bromide gives E2 (2-methylpropene), because the 3° carbon cannot undergo backside attack.
Changing the solvent or leaving group does not help: the 3° chloride still cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2, and ethoxide eliminates.
A neutral alcohol is a weak nucleophile; without converting it to the alkoxide, S<sub>N</sub>2 on bromoethane is extremely slow.

q: Which reaction gives mainly an elimination product?
h: Classify each substrate (1° or 2°) and each reagent (strong base, good nucleophile/weak base, or weak nucleophile/weak base).
w: 2-Bromopropane with ethoxide and heat: a 2° substrate with a strong base gives mainly E2 (propene, roughly 80%). The 1° bromide with ethoxide gives mainly SN2; cyanide in DMSO is a good nucleophile and weaker base, so the 2° bromide gives SN2; in ethanol with no base at room temperature, the slow solvolysis gives mainly the ether.
x: A 1° unhindered bromide gives mainly S<sub>N</sub>2 with ethoxide; E2 is minor.
Cyanide is a good nucleophile and much weaker base than ethoxide, and DMSO speeds S<sub>N</sub>2; substitution dominates.
Ethanol alone is a weak base; solvolysis of a 2° bromide at room temperature gives mainly substitution, not alkene.

q:
Assign the main mechanism to each reaction.
I. (S)-2-iodooctane + NaCN, DMSO
II. 2-bromo-2-methylpentane in 80% aqueous acetone, 25 °C
III. 2-bromo-2-methylpentane + NaOCH2CH3, ethanol, heat
c: I S<sub>N</sub>2; II S<sub>N</sub>1; III E2
I S<sub>N</sub>2; II E1; III S<sub>N</sub>1
I S<sub>N</sub>1; II S<sub>N</sub>1; III E1
I E2; II S<sub>N</sub>1; III S<sub>N</sub>2
h: Match substrate class with reagent strength: good nucleophile/weak base, weak nucleophile/weak base, strong base.
w: I: a 2° iodide with a strong nucleophile/weak base in a polar aprotic solvent: SN2 with inversion. II: a 3° bromide in a polar protic solvent with only water as nucleophile at room temperature: ionization, mainly SN1 (some E1). III: the same 3° bromide with a strong base and heat: E2. Answer: I SN2; II SN1; III E2.
x: A 3° substrate with a strong base (III) gives E2, not S<sub>N</sub>1; and II at 25 °C gives mainly substitution.
I has a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent, which favors S<sub>N</sub>2, and III has a strong base, which makes it E2, not E1.
Cyanide is a weak base and a 2° iodide is not hindered enough for E2 to win; S<sub>N</sub>2 dominates. A 3° carbon cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: For a 2° alkyl bromide with ethoxide, raising the temperature increases the fraction of alkene relative to ether. Which explanation is best?
c: Elimination makes more molecules, so its ΔS is more positive and −TΔS matters more when hot
Elimination has the lower activation energy, so heating speeds it up more than substitution
At high temperature the ether product is converted into the alkene by further elimination
Heating makes the ethoxide ion a weaker base and a stronger nucleophile
h: Count the particles on each side for substitution and for elimination.
w: Substitution: 2 reactants → 2 products. Elimination: 2 reactants → 3 products (alkene, alcohol, halide). Elimination has a more positive ΔS, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS becomes more favorable for elimination as T rises; heating therefore increases the alkene fraction.
x: Heating helps the reaction with the higher barrier more, not the lower one; elimination generally has the higher barrier and is the one helped.
Ethers are stable to ethoxide; the ether does not convert to alkene under these conditions.
Temperature does not turn ethoxide into a better nucleophile; if anything, the elimination pathway gains.

q: What is the IUPAC name of this compound?
h: The C=C carbons are C1 and C2. Then choose the direction that gives the lowest set of substituent locants.
w: The double bond must be C1=C2. Starting at the methyl-bearing alkene carbon (C1) and going through C2 puts the other methyl at C5: {1,5}. Starting at the other alkene carbon gives {2,4}. Compare at the first point of difference: 1 < 2, so the name is 1,5-dimethylcyclohexene.
x: {2,4} loses to {1,5} at the first point of difference (1 < 2).
1,3-Dimethylcyclohexene would have the second methyl on the carbon right after C2; here two CH<sub>2</sub> groups separate them going that way.
Locants 3 and 5 would place both methyls off the double bond; one methyl is on an alkene carbon.

q: What is the IUPAC name of this alkene?
h: Two five-carbon chains contain the C=C; choose the one with more substituents. Then rank the two groups on C3 by CIP.
w: Chains through the ethyl or through the isopropyl both have five carbons; the one through the isopropyl carries two substituents (ethyl and methyl), so the parent is 3-ethyl-4-methylpent-2-ene. For E/Z: on C2, CH3 > H; on C3, isopropyl (C,C,H) > ethyl (C,H,H). The C2 methyl and the isopropyl are on the same side, so the name is (Z)-3-ethyl-4-methylpent-2-ene.
x: Isopropyl outranks ethyl at the first atom (C,C,H vs C,H,H); it is cis to the C2 methyl, which is Z.
The E/Z label is right, but when two chains are equally long, the parent is the one with more substituents (two vs one).
Both the parent chain and the E/Z label are wrong.

q: Which structure is (Z)-2-chloro-2-butene?
h: Rank the two groups on each alkene carbon by atomic number. Do not judge by where the methyl groups are.
w: On C2, Cl (Z = 17) > CH3; on C3, CH3 > H. Z means Cl and the C3 methyl are on the same side, so the two methyl groups are trans to each other. The structure with Cl cis to the C3 methyl (methyls trans) is (Z)-2-chloro-2-butene.
x: Here Cl and the C3 methyl are on opposite sides: this is the E isomer, even though the two methyls look cis.
This is (Z)-1-chloro-2-butene; the Cl is on C1, not on an alkene carbon.
This is 2-chloro-1-butene, which has two H on C1 and no E/Z isomers.

q: Which alkene can exist as E and Z isomers?
h: Each alkene carbon needs two different groups.
w: 3-Methylpent-2-ene: C2 has CH3 and H, and C3 has CH3 and CH2CH3, so both alkene carbons carry two different groups and E/Z isomers exist.
x: In 2-methylpent-2-ene, C2 carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so no E/Z isomers exist.
In 3-ethylpent-2-ene, C3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so no E/Z isomers exist.
In 2-methylpent-1-ene, C1 is =CH<sub>2</sub> with two H atoms, so no E/Z isomers exist.

q: (3R,4S)-3-Bromo-4-methylhexane is heated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. What is the major product?
h: First pick the Zaitsev carbon. It has one H, so the anti-periplanar conformation fixes the alkene geometry.
w: Ethoxide is small, so the trisubstituted C3=C4 alkene (Zaitsev) is major. C4 has a single H, so only one conformer has it anti to Br. In that conformer the C3 ethyl is gauche to the C4 ethyl, so they become cis. Priorities: on C3, ethyl > H; on C4, ethyl > methyl. Higher priorities on the same side: (Z)-3-methylhex-3-ene. The (3R,4R) diastereomer would give the E alkene.
x: The E isomer comes from the (3R,4R)/(3S,4S) diastereomer; E2 from this isomer gives only Z.
4-Methylhex-2-ene comes from loss of a C2 hydrogen; it is only disubstituted and is minor with a small base.
The S<sub>N</sub>2 product (with inversion at C3) is minor: the 2° carbon is next to a branch point, and a strong base with heat favors E2.

q: Which alkyl bromide gives a single alkene (no constitutional or E/Z isomers) on E2 with NaOCH2CH3?
h: List every β carbon with H and the alkene each would give; then check each for E/Z.
w: In 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane the three β carbons are equivalent CH2 groups, and each gives CH3CH=C(CH2CH3)2, 3-ethylpent-2-ene. Its C3 bears two identical ethyl groups, so it has no E/Z isomers: a single product.
x: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane gives both 2-methyl-2-butene and 2-methyl-1-butene.
3-Bromo-3-methylpentane gives (E)- and (Z)-3-methylpent-2-ene plus 2-ethylbut-1-ene.
2-Bromo-3-methylbutane gives 2-methyl-2-butene and 3-methyl-1-butene.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown? (There is no significant absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> or between 1600 and 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>.)
h: A medium, sharp band in the triple-bond region (2100–2260 cm<sup>−1</sup>) with no band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> narrows it down quickly.
w: The only band beyond the C–H stretches is a medium, sharp absorption at 2250 cm−1, the C≡N stretch of a nitrile. The polar C≡N bond gives a stronger band than a C≡C stretch. The answer is butanenitrile. Nothing above 3000 cm−1 rules out O–H, N–H and ≡C–H, and nothing at 1700 cm−1 rules out C=O.
x: A terminal alkyne shows a strong, sharp ≡C–H stretch near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a weak C≡C stretch near 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup>; neither is in this spectrum.
Butanal would show a strong C=O band near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the aldehyde C–H pair near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Butylamine (a primary amine) would show two N–H stretches between 3300 and 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup> and has no triple bond to absorb at 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown?
h: Look at the two regions that decide most problems: 3200–3600 cm<sup>−1</sup> and 1650–1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
w: A strong, broad band centered near 3340 cm−1 is a hydrogen-bonded alcohol O–H, and the strong band near 1070 cm−1 is the C–O stretch. There is no C=O band, and all C–H stretches are below 3000 cm−1 (sp3 only). The answer is cyclohexanol.
x: Cyclohexanone has a strong C=O stretch near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no O–H band.
Cyclohexene shows a vinylic =C–H stretch just above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=C stretch near 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no broad O–H band.
A carboxylic acid shows an O–H band so broad it spans about 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, plus a strong C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>; there is no C=O band here.

q: The IR spectrum shown has an extremely broad O–H absorption that spans about 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> (it overlaps the C–H stretches) and a strong band at 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which compound is it?
h: Several choices have an O–H or a C=O. What makes an O–H band reach all the way down to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
w: Carboxylic acids exist as strongly hydrogen-bonded dimers, so the O–H stretch is spread over roughly 2500–3300 cm−1 and buries the C–H bands. Together with the C=O stretch at 1710 cm−1 (typical of a dimeric acid), this identifies butanoic acid.
x: 4-Hydroxy-2-butanone has both an alcohol O–H and a ketone C=O, but an alcohol O–H band is centered near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup> and does not extend down to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Methyl propanoate is an ester: strong C=O near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and strong C–O bands near 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no O–H at all.
1,4-Butanediol has a broad alcohol O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> but no C=O, so it cannot explain the strong 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup> band.

q: An amine-containing compound gives the IR spectrum shown. The only band between 1500 and 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup> is a medium band at 1600 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which compound is it?
h: Count the N–H stretching bands, then ask whether a C=O band is present.
w: Two medium N–H bands (3370 and 3290 cm−1, the asymmetric and symmetric stretches of an NH2 group) mean a primary amine or a primary amide. The medium 1600 cm−1 band is the N–H bend; there is no strong C=O band. The answer is butylamine (1-butanamine).
x: Diethylamine is a secondary amine with one N–H, so it shows only a single weak N–H band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Triethylamine is a tertiary amine with no N–H bond, so there is no absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Butanamide also shows two N–H bands, but its amide C=O gives a strong band near 1650–1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which is missing here.

q: Rank the C=O stretching wavenumbers of compounds I–IV from highest to lowest.
h: Electron-withdrawing groups on the carbonyl carbon stiffen the C=O bond; lone-pair donation into the C=O gives it single-bond character.
w: A higher C=O wavenumber means more double-bond character (larger force constant). Chlorine withdraws inductively and donates poorly, so the acid chloride absorbs highest (~1800 cm−1). In the ester the inductive pull of the extra oxygen outweighs its resonance donation (~1740 cm−1). A ketone is the reference (~1715 cm−1). Nitrogen donates its lone pair strongly, so the amide C=O is lowest (~1650–1690 cm−1). The order is I > II > III > IV.
x: This reverses the trend: resonance donation from N lowers, not raises, the C=O bond order, so the amide is lowest.
The acid chloride is above the ester; chlorine withdraws electrons and is a much poorer π donor than the ester oxygen.
Esters absorb above ketones (about 1740 vs 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>) because the ester oxygen's inductive withdrawal dominates its resonance donation.

q: Which compound has the lowest C=O stretching wavenumber?
h: Two effects matter: conjugation with a C=C and ring strain in small rings. Which way does each move the C=O band?
w: Conjugation with a C=C lets the C=O π electrons delocalize, lowering the C=O bond order and its stretching wavenumber by about 30–40 cm−1. 2-Cyclohexen-1-one absorbs near 1680 cm−1. Ring strain does the opposite: the smaller the ring, the higher the C=O band.
x: Cyclohexanone is the unstrained, unconjugated reference, absorbing near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, higher than the conjugated enone.
Cyclopentanone's ring strain raises the C=O stretch to about 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Cyclobutanone is even more strained and absorbs near 1780 cm<sup>−1</sup>, the highest of the four.

q: The reaction shown is followed by IR. Which change shows that the starting alkene has been completely converted to product?
c: A broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, and the weak bands near 3020 and 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup> disappear
A strong band near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, and the weak band near 3020 cm<sup>−1</sup> disappears completely
A broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, while the weak bands near 3020 and 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup> remain
A sharp band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a weak band near 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> appear
h: First decide what functional group hydroboration–oxidation makes; then decide which starting-material bands must vanish.
w: Hydroboration–oxidation converts the alkene into an alcohol (trans-2-methylcyclohexanol). The product shows a broad O–H band near 3350 cm−1. Completion means the alkene bands are gone: the vinylic =C–H stretch near 3020 cm−1 and the C=C stretch near 1670 cm−1. So the best evidence is a broad 3350 cm−1 band appearing while the 3020 and 1670 cm−1 bands disappear.
x: A 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> band would mean a ketone; hydroboration–oxidation gives an alcohol, not a carbonyl compound.
If the =C–H and C=C bands are still there, some alkene remains, so the reaction is not complete.
A sharp 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> band belong to a terminal alkyne, which is neither reactant nor product.

q: 1-Hexyne is treated as shown. How does the IR spectrum change on going from the starting material to the isolated product?
c: The sharp 3300 and weak 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> bands disappear; a strong band appears near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>
The sharp 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears; a strong band near 1730 and a pair near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> appear
The 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears; a broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears and stays
The sharp 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> band remains; a strong band appears near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>
h: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov, and the first-formed enol does not survive.
w: Hg2+-catalyzed hydration adds water Markovnikov to give an enol that tautomerizes to the methyl ketone, 2-hexanone. The terminal alkyne bands (strong, sharp ≡C–H at 3300 cm−1; weak C≡C at 2120 cm−1) vanish and a strong ketone C=O appears near 1715 cm−1. The answer is loss of 3300 and 2120 cm−1, gain of 1715 cm−1.
x: A 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> C=O with 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> bands is an aldehyde, the anti-Markovnikov product of hydroboration–oxidation, not of HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration.
The enol is only an intermediate; it tautomerizes to the ketone, so no lasting O–H band appears.
Both alkyne carbons react, so the terminal ≡C–H (3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is gone in the product.

q: A compound with formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O shows no IR absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and none between 1600 and 1700 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its strongest band is at 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O has two degrees of unsaturation. If one is a C=O and there is no C=C, what is the other? Then think about where the C=O band falls.
w: DBE = (2·5 + 2 − 8)/2 = 2. The strong 1745 cm−1 band is a C=O, and with no =C–H above 3000 cm−1 and no C=C near 1650 cm−1 the second unsaturation must be a ring. Ring strain in a five-membered ring raises a ketone C=O from 1715 to about 1745 cm−1. The compound is cyclopentanone.
x: 3-Penten-2-one is conjugated, so its C=O is lowered to about 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup>; it would also show a C=C band near 1630 cm<sup>−1</sup> and =C–H above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Pentenal would show the aldehyde C–H pair (2720, 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a vinylic =C–H near 3080 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=C near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
3-Cyclopenten-1-ol has a broad O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=O; its =C–H stretch also lies above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which compound shows C–H stretching absorptions both just above and just below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
h: sp<sup>3</sup> C–H absorbs below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, sp<sup>2</sup> C–H just above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and sp C–H near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
w: The compound needs both sp2 C–H (3000–3100 cm−1) and sp3 C–H (2850–3000 cm−1) and no sp C–H (3300 cm−1). Cyclohexene has two vinylic C–H bonds and eight allylic/ring CH2 hydrogens, so it fits.
x: Cyclohexane has only sp<sup>3</sup> C–H bonds, so all of its C–H stretches are below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
1-Hexyne has a terminal ≡C–H, which gives a strong, sharp band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Benzene has only aromatic sp<sup>2</sup> C–H bonds, so it has no C–H stretch below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Neat liquid 1-butanol shows a broad O–H band centered near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>. In a very dilute CCl<sub>4</sub> solution, the same compound shows a sharp O–H band near 3620 cm<sup>−1</sup>. What is the best explanation?
c: Hydrogen bonding in the neat liquid weakens the O–H bonds by varying amounts; in dilute solution the O–H is free
CCl<sub>4</sub> absorbs strongly near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and hides the O–H band, leaving only a weak overtone near 3620 cm<sup>−1</sup>
In the neat liquid some alcohol is ionized to alkoxide, and the O<sup>−</sup> absorbs at a lower wavenumber than a free O–H does
Dilution increases the O–H bond dipole of each isolated molecule, which raises the O–H stretching wavenumber
h: Which intermolecular interaction is present in the pure liquid but nearly absent when the molecules are far apart?
w: An O–H that donates a hydrogen bond is slightly weakened (smaller force constant), so it absorbs at lower wavenumber. In the neat liquid there is a range of hydrogen-bonded clusters, which smears the band out and centers it near 3350 cm−1. In very dilute CCl4 most molecules are isolated, so the free, non-hydrogen-bonded O–H gives a sharp band near 3620 cm−1.
x: CCl<sub>4</sub> has no C–H or O–H bonds and is nearly transparent above 1600 cm<sup>−1</sup>; that is why it is used as an IR solvent.
An alcohol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) is not ionized to alkoxide to any detectable extent in the pure liquid, and an alkoxide has no O–H stretch at all.
Bond dipole affects band intensity, not position; the position depends on the force constant and the reduced mass.

q: Which IR feature best distinguishes 1-hexyne (I) from 3-hexyne (II)?
c: A strong, sharp band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> in I only
A strong C≡C band near 2200 cm<sup>−1</sup> in II only
A C=C band near 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup> in I only
A broad band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> in II only
h: A vibration must change the molecule's dipole moment to absorb IR light. Look at the symmetry of each alkyne.
w: 1-Hexyne has a terminal ≡C–H bond, which gives a strong, sharp band near 3300 cm−1 (plus a weak C≡C near 2120 cm−1). 3-Hexyne has no ≡C–H, and its C≡C is symmetrically substituted, so stretching it hardly changes the dipole and the band is absent. The answer is the sharp 3300 cm−1 band, present in I only.
x: The symmetric C≡C of 3-hexyne is IR-inactive (no dipole change); if anything, the weak C≡C band belongs to 1-hexyne.
Neither compound has a C=C double bond, so neither absorbs near 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
A broad band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> signals a hydrogen-bonded O–H or N–H; 3-hexyne has neither.

q: Which compound's C=C stretching band in the 1600–1680 cm<sup>−1</sup> region is absent or nearly absent?
h: IR intensity depends on how much the dipole moment changes during the vibration.
w: A vibration absorbs IR light only if it changes the dipole moment. In (E)-3-hexene the C=C carries identical groups arranged symmetrically (a center of symmetry), so stretching the C=C produces no dipole change and the band is IR-inactive. Unsymmetrical or polarized C=C bonds give visible bands.
x: 1-Hexene is monosubstituted and unsymmetrical, so its C=C stretch (about 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is a clear medium band.
In ethyl vinyl ether the oxygen donates electron density into the C=C, polarizing it strongly, so its C=C band (about 1620 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is strong.
In 2-cyclohexenone the C=C is conjugated with and polarized by the C=O, so it gives a medium-to-strong band near 1620 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR spectrum shown. There is no absorption between 3100 and 3600 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: The strong 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup> band suggests an amide. Then count the N–H bonds each candidate has.
w: A strong band at 1650 cm−1 is the low-frequency C=O of an amide (nitrogen lone-pair donation lowers the C=O bond order). The absence of any N–H stretch (3100–3600 cm−1) requires a tertiary amide with no N–H bond. The answer is N,N-dimethylacetamide.
x: Butanamide is a primary amide: its NH<sub>2</sub> gives two N–H bands near 3350 and 3180 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
N-Ethylacetamide is a secondary amide with one N–H, which gives a band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Morpholine is a secondary amine and ether: it shows an N–H band near 3330 cm<sup>−1</sup> and has no C=O to absorb at 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown?
h: Besides the C=O band, look for a pair of medium bands just to the right of the ordinary C–H stretches.
w: The strong 1730 cm−1 band is a C=O, and the two medium bands at 2820 and 2720 cm−1 are the characteristic aldehyde C–H stretches (a Fermi-resonance doublet). Together they identify an aldehyde: hexanal.
x: 2-Hexanone is a ketone; its C=O is near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and it has no aldehyde C–H, so no 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> pair.
Ethyl butanoate is an ester: C=O near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus strong C–O bands near 1180 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> aldehyde C–H band.
Hexanoic acid would show a very broad O–H spanning 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which this spectrum lacks.

q: Which pair of compounds would be hardest to tell apart using only the functional-group region (above 1500 cm<sup>−1</sup>) of their IR spectra?
h: IR identifies functional groups. Which pair has exactly the same functional group in nearly the same environment?
w: 2-Pentanone and 3-pentanone are both saturated acyclic ketones: each shows a strong C=O near 1715 cm−1 and only sp3 C–H stretches. Their differences are confined to the fingerprint region, which is why IR alone is a poor tool for telling such isomers apart (NMR does it easily).
x: Pentanal shows the aldehyde C–H pair at 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup>; 2-pentanone has neither feature.
1-Pentanol has a strong, broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>; the ether has none, so they are easy to distinguish.
1-Pentyne has a strong, sharp ≡C–H band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>; the internal alkyne 2-pentyne does not.

q: A C–H stretch appears at 2950 cm−1. Hooke's law gives ν̃ ∝ √(k/μ), where μ = m1m2/(m1 + m2). Assuming the force constant k is unchanged, at about what wavenumber should the corresponding C–D stretch appear? (Use masses 12, 1 and 2.)
h: Compute the reduced mass for C–H and for C–D, then scale the wavenumber by the square root of their ratio.
w: μ(C–H) = (12·1)/13 = 0.923; μ(C–D) = (12·2)/14 = 1.714. Since ν̃ ∝ 1/√μ, ν̃(C–D) = 2950 × √(0.923/1.714) = 2950 × 0.734 ≈ 2165 cm−1. This is why deuterated solvents and C–D labels show bands near 2100–2200 cm−1.
x: A heavier isotope must lower the wavenumber, not raise it; 4170 cm<sup>−1</sup> comes from multiplying by √2 instead of dividing.
1475 cm<sup>−1</sup> halves the wavenumber, as if ν̃ were proportional to 1/μ and μ doubled; the dependence is on the square root, and μ does not double.
2085 cm<sup>−1</sup> divides by √2, using the H/D mass ratio instead of the reduced masses; because carbon also moves, μ rises by less than a factor of 2.

q: The ≡C–H stretch of a terminal alkyne (about 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is higher than the =C–H stretch of an alkene (about 3080 cm<sup>−1</sup>) or the C–H stretch of an alkane (about 2900 cm<sup>−1</sup>). Why?
c: Greater s character in the sp carbon orbital makes the C–H bond shorter and stiffer
The ≡C–H hydrogen forms hydrogen bonds, which raise its stretching wavenumber
The sp carbon is lighter than an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, which lowers the reduced mass
The ≡C–H bond is the weakest of the three, so it vibrates fastest
h: All three bonds join the same two atoms, so the reduced mass is the same. What about the force constant?
w: Wavenumber depends on the force constant and the reduced mass. The masses are identical (C and H), so the difference comes from k. An sp orbital has 50% s character (sp2 33%, sp3 25%), so the ≡C–H bond is shorter and stronger, with a larger force constant. The answer is greater s character gives a stiffer bond.
x: Hydrogen bonding weakens the X–H bond and lowers its stretching wavenumber, and alkyne C–H is only a very weak hydrogen-bond donor anyway.
Hybridization does not change an atom's mass; the reduced mass of every C–H bond is the same.
The ≡C–H bond is the strongest of the three, and a weaker bond (smaller k) vibrates at lower, not higher, wavenumber.

q: The mass spectrum of 2-butanone is shown. Which peak is the molecular ion?
h: Add up the nominal mass of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O. The molecular ion is not necessarily the tallest peak.
w: 2-Butanone is C4H8O: 4(12) + 8(1) + 16 = 72. The molecular ion (the radical cation of the intact molecule) is at m/z 72. The small peak at 73 is M+1 (about 4.4% of M, from 13C), and the base peak at 43 is the acylium ion CH3C≡O+.
x: m/z 43 is the base peak (most abundant ion), the CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> acylium ion from α-cleavage; the base peak is not the molecular ion.
m/z 73 is the M+1 peak, from molecules that contain one <sup>13</sup>C atom.
m/z 57 is M − 15, the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> ion formed by α-cleavage loss of a methyl radical.

q: An unknown aromatic compound shows a molecular ion at m/z 156 and a peak of almost equal height at m/z 158 (spectrum shown). Which element does this pattern indicate?
h: Which halogen has two isotopes, two mass units apart, in nearly equal amounts?
w: Bromine is about 50.7% 79Br and 49.3% 81Br, so a compound with one bromine shows M and M+2 peaks of nearly equal height. Here M = 156 fits bromobenzene, C6H579Br (72 + 5 + 79), and m/z 77 (C6H5+) is M − 79, loss of a Br atom.
x: One chlorine gives M : M+2 ≈ 3 : 1 (<sup>35</sup>Cl : <sup>37</sup>Cl), not 1 : 1.
Two chlorines give M, M+2 and M+4 in about 9 : 6 : 1; the M+2 peak would be smaller than M and an M+4 peak would appear.
Sulfur's <sup>34</sup>S is only about 4.4% abundant, giving a small M+2 peak, not one as tall as M.

q: Which compound gives the mass spectrum shown?
h: Find the highest-mass cluster and look at the height ratio of its two peaks.
w: The highest-mass peaks are m/z 78 and 80 in a 3 : 1 ratio, the signature of one chlorine (35Cl/37Cl). C3H735Cl = 36 + 7 + 35 = 78. The 63/65 pair (also 3 : 1) is M − CH3, which still contains Cl. The compound is 1-chloropropane.
x: 1-Bromopropane would show M at 122 and 124 in about a 1 : 1 ratio.
1-Chlorobutane would show its 3 : 1 molecular-ion pair at 92 and 94.
1,1-Dichloroethane (two Cl) would show M at 98, 100 and 102 in about 9 : 6 : 1.

q: Chlorine is about 75% <sup>35</sup>Cl and 25% <sup>37</sup>Cl. For a compound containing two chlorine atoms, what are the approximate relative intensities of the M, M+2 and M+4 peaks (ignore <sup>13</sup>C)?
h: Treat each Cl independently: P(35) = 3/4 and P(37) = 1/4. How many ways can you get one of each?
w: M (both 35Cl) = (3/4)2 = 9/16. M+2 (one of each) can arise two ways: 2(3/4)(1/4) = 6/16. M+4 (both 37Cl) = (1/4)2 = 1/16. The ratio is 9 : 6 : 1, a pattern seen for CH2Cl2 at m/z 84, 86 and 88.
x: 9 : 3 : 1 forgets that the mixed isotopologue can form two ways (<sup>35</sup>Cl/<sup>37</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl/<sup>35</sup>Cl).
1 : 2 : 1 is the pattern for two bromines, whose isotopes are nearly 1 : 1.
3 : 1 with no M+4 is the pattern for a single chlorine; a second Cl adds an M+4 peak.

q: A dihalomethane CH<sub>2</sub>XY gives the mass spectrum shown, with molecular-ion peaks at m/z 128, 130 and 132 in about a 3 : 4 : 1 ratio. Which halogens does it contain?
h: Combine Br (about 1 : 1) with Cl (about 3 : 1) and work out the probabilities for M, M+2 and M+4.
w: With one Br (½ : ½) and one Cl (¾ : ¼): M = (½)(¾) = 3/8; M+2 = (½)(¼) + (½)(¾) = 4/8; M+4 = (½)(¼) = 1/8, so one Br and one Cl gives 3 : 4 : 1. The mass fits too: CH279Br35Cl = 12 + 2 + 79 + 35 = 128. The fragments agree: 49/51 (3 : 1) is CH2Cl+ (loss of Br) and 93/95 (1 : 1) is CH2Br+ (loss of Cl).
x: Two bromines give a 1 : 2 : 1 pattern, and CH<sub>2</sub>Br<sub>2</sub> would appear at m/z 172, 174 and 176.
Two chlorines give 9 : 6 : 1, and CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> would appear at m/z 84, 86 and 88.
Fluorine has only one isotope (<sup>19</sup>F), so Br + F would give just M and M+2 at 1 : 1 (m/z 112 and 114), with no M+4.

q: An unknown containing only C, H, N and/or O shows M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 86 (relative intensity 15%) and an M+1 peak at m/z 87 (1.0%). Which molecular formula best fits? (Each carbon contributes about 1.1% to M+1.)
h: Number of carbons ≈ (M+1 intensity ÷ M intensity) ÷ 0.011.
w: (M+1)/M = 1.0/15 = 0.067, and 0.067/0.011 ≈ 6 carbons. All four formulas have nominal mass 86, but only C6H14 has six carbons. The fragments (57, 43, 71) fit a hexane, which loses alkyl radicals to give C4H9+, C3H7+ and C5H11+.
x: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O has five carbons, so its M+1 would be about 5.5% of M (0.8% here), not 6.7%.
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has four carbons, giving an M+1 of only about 4.4% of M.
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>2</sub> has four carbons; even adding about 0.4% per <sup>15</sup>N, M+1 would be only about 5% of M.

q: An unknown that contains only C, H, N and O gives the mass spectrum shown, with M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 73. What does the odd molecular mass tell you?
c: It contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms
It contains an odd number of oxygen atoms
Its molecular ion is an even-electron cation
It contains an odd number of carbon atoms
h: Think about the nitrogen rule: which of C, H, N, O has an even mass but an odd valence?
w: The nitrogen rule: a molecule made of C, H, O, N (and halogens) has an odd nominal mass only if it contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms. Nitrogen has even mass (14) but odd valence (3), which forces an odd number of hydrogens. Here C4H11N (diethylamine) = 73, and its base peak at 58 is M − CH3 from α-cleavage next to nitrogen.
x: Oxygen has even mass (16) and even valence (2), so the number of oxygens never changes whether M is odd or even.
Every molecular ion formed by electron impact is a radical cation (odd-electron), whatever its mass.
Carbon has even mass (12) and even valence (4), so the number of carbons has no effect on whether M is odd.

q: α-Cleavage of the molecular ion (m/z 100) of 2-methyl-3-pentanone gives two different acylium ions. At what m/z values do they appear?
h: α-Cleavage breaks a bond between the carbonyl carbon and one of its neighbors; the positive charge stays on the C≡O<sup>+</sup> fragment.
w: Breaking the C(=O)–CH(CH3)2 bond expels an isopropyl radical (43) and leaves CH3CH2C≡O+, m/z 100 − 43 = 57. Breaking the C(=O)–CH2CH3 bond expels an ethyl radical (29) and leaves (CH3)2CHC≡O+, m/z 100 − 29 = 71. The acylium ions are at m/z 57 and 71.
x: 43 and 29 are the masses of the radicals lost (isopropyl and ethyl); when they appear as ions they are alkyl cations, not acylium ions.
58 and 72 would be McLafferty ions, which need a hydrogen on a γ carbon; neither alkyl group here has a γ carbon.
85 is M − CH<sub>3</sub>; loss of a methyl from the isopropyl group breaks a bond β to the carbonyl, so it is not α-cleavage, and the ion is not an acylium.

q: A C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O carbonyl compound gives the mass spectrum shown: M<sup>+</sup> 100, base peak 43, and a strong peak at m/z 58. Which isomer is it?
h: An even-mass fragment from a C, H, O compound usually means a neutral molecule was lost. Which rearrangement does that, and what does it need?
w: The even-mass ion at 58 is a McLafferty fragment: a γ-hydrogen moves to the carbonyl oxygen and the α–β bond breaks, expelling an alkene. For 2-hexanone, the butyl chain has γ-hydrogens; loss of propene (42) gives the enol radical cation CH2=C(OH)CH3+• at 100 − 42 = 58. The base peak 43 is CH3C≡O+ from α-cleavage (loss of ·C4H9), and 85 is loss of ·CH3.
x: 3-Hexanone undergoes McLafferty cleavage on the propyl side, losing ethene (28) to give m/z 72, not 58; its acylium ions are at 57 and 71.
3,3-Dimethyl-2-butanone has no γ-hydrogen (the quaternary α carbon carries only methyls), so it cannot undergo a McLafferty rearrangement; its base peak is the tert-butyl cation at 57.
Hexanal's McLafferty fragment is CH<sub>2</sub>=CHOH<sup>+•</sup> at m/z 44, after loss of 1-butene (56).

q: The mass spectrum of 1-pentanol shows a very weak M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 88 and a peak at m/z 70. Which process gives the m/z 70 ion?
h: Subtract: 88 − 70 = ? Which small neutral molecule has that mass?
w: 88 − 70 = 18, the mass of water. Alcohols commonly show an M − 18 peak from loss of H2O (dehydration of the molecular ion), and their M+ is often weak or missing. The peak at 31 is the α-cleavage ion CH2=OH+.
x: Loss of a hydroxyl radical (17) would give m/z 71, not 70.
α-Cleavage losing a butyl radical (57) gives CH<sub>2</sub>=OH<sup>+</sup> at m/z 31, not 70.
Loss of a methyl radical (15) would give m/z 73.

q: Which m/z value is expected for the base peak in the mass spectrum of 2-methyl-2-butanol (M = 88)?
h: Alcohols cleave at the C–C bond next to the C–OH carbon. When there is a choice, which radical leaves most easily?
w: α-Cleavage of an alcohol breaks a C–C bond on the carbinol carbon and gives a resonance-stabilized oxonium ion. Here the carbinol carbon carries two methyls and one ethyl. Loss of the larger ethyl radical (29) is favored and gives (CH3)2C=OH+ at 88 − 29 = 59, the base peak. Loss of ·CH3 gives a smaller peak at 73.
x: m/z 73 comes from α-cleavage loss of a methyl radical; it is observed, but loss of the larger ethyl radical is preferred.
m/z 70 is M − H<sub>2</sub>O; dehydration occurs, but for a tertiary alcohol the α-cleavage ion dominates.
m/z 71 would be loss of ·OH; C–O cleavage is minor compared with α-cleavage, which gives a much more stable oxonium ion.

q: An amine C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>11</sub>N shows a weak M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 73 and a base peak at m/z 58. Which structure fits best?
h: Amines undergo α-cleavage: a C–C bond on the carbon attached to N breaks, giving an iminium ion. 73 − 58 = 15. Which radical is lost?
w: The base peak at 58 means loss of a methyl radical (15) by α-cleavage. In tert-butylamine the carbon bearing N carries three methyls, so every α-cleavage loses ·CH3 and gives (CH3)2C=NH2+ at m/z 58.
x: 1-Butanamine loses a propyl radical by α-cleavage, giving CH<sub>2</sub>=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 30 as the base peak.
2-Butanamine preferentially loses the larger ethyl radical, giving CH<sub>3</sub>CH=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 44 as the base peak.
N-Methylpropylamine loses an ethyl radical from the propyl side, giving CH<sub>2</sub>=NHCH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 44.

q: The mass spectrum of 2,2-dimethylpropane (M = 72) is shown. The base peak is at m/z 57, and almost no molecular ion is seen. What is the best explanation?
c: The molecular ion easily loses ·CH<sub>3</sub> to give the tertiary (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> cation
The molecular ion loses a hydrogen atom to give the primary (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> cation
The molecular ion undergoes a McLafferty rearrangement and expels a neutral CH<sub>4</sub> molecule
The molecular ion loses ·CH<sub>3</sub> to give a primary carbocation stabilized by hyperconjugation
h: Alkanes fragment where the most stable cation can form. What cation is left when a methyl leaves the central carbon?
w: Alkane molecular ions cleave preferentially at branch points, because the resulting carbocation is more substituted. Breaking any C–CH3 bond in neopentane leaves the tertiary tert-butyl cation, m/z 72 − 15 = 57. This is so favorable that the molecular ion barely survives.
x: Loss of H would give m/z 71, not 57, and a primary cation is far less stable than a tertiary one.
McLafferty rearrangement needs a C=O (or similar π bond) and a γ-hydrogen; neopentane has neither, and 72 − 16 = 56, not 57.
The ion left after losing CH<sub>3</sub> is (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>, whose charged carbon bears three alkyl groups: it is tertiary, not primary.

q: A mixture of 1-chlorobutane (bp 78 °C) and 1-bromobutane (bp 101 °C) is analyzed by GC-MS on a nonpolar column. Which describes the mass spectrum recorded for the first peak to elute?
c: Molecular-ion peaks at m/z 92 and 94 in about a 3 : 1 ratio
Molecular-ion peaks at m/z 136 and 138 in about a 1 : 1 ratio
Molecular-ion peaks at m/z 92 and 94 in about a 1 : 1 ratio
Peaks at m/z 92/94 and 136/138 together, because the MS records the whole mixture at once
h: The GC separates the components first; on a nonpolar column they come off roughly in order of boiling point. Then work out the M<sup>+</sup> pattern of that component.
w: In GC-MS the gas chromatograph separates the mixture, and the mass spectrometer records a separate spectrum for each component as it elutes. On a nonpolar column the lower-boiling 1-chlorobutane elutes first. C4H935Cl = 48 + 9 + 35 = 92, and one Cl gives M : M+2 ≈ 3 : 1, so the first spectrum shows m/z 92 and 94 in about 3 : 1.
x: 136/138 at 1 : 1 is 1-bromobutane, which boils higher and elutes second on a nonpolar column.
92/94 is the right mass for 1-chlorobutane, but one chlorine gives a 3 : 1 pattern; 1 : 1 is the bromine pattern.
The point of GC-MS is that the components reach the mass spectrometer at different times, so each chromatographic peak has its own spectrum.

q: A C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub> aromatic hydrocarbon gives the mass spectrum shown (M<sup>+</sup> 120, base peak 91). Which structure fits?
h: Alkylbenzenes break at the benzylic bond. 120 − 91 = 29: which radical is lost, and which isomer can lose it at the benzylic position?
w: Alkylbenzenes cleave at the bond β to the ring (the benzylic C–C bond), because the cation formed is a resonance-stabilized benzyl cation (which rearranges to the tropylium ion, C7H7+, m/z 91). A base peak at 91 means an ethyl radical (29) left from a benzylic CH2: propylbenzene.
x: Isopropylbenzene loses a methyl radical at the benzylic carbon, giving C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sup>+</sup> at m/z 105 as the base peak.
4-Ethyltoluene loses a methyl radical from the benzylic CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, giving a methylbenzyl cation at m/z 105.
1,3,5-Trimethylbenzene has only methyl groups; its main fragment is M − CH<sub>3</sub> at m/z 105 (with M − H at 119), not 91.

q: For a compound that contains only C, H and O (so M is even), which statement about fragment ions from the molecular ion is correct?
c: Loss of a radical gives an odd-m/z ion; loss of a neutral molecule (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O) gives an even-m/z ion
Loss of a radical (e.g. α-cleavage) gives an even-m/z ion; loss of a neutral molecule gives an odd-m/z ion
All fragment ions have odd m/z, because every fragment ion carries a single positive charge
Fragment ions have even m/z only when the radical lost contains an oxygen atom
h: Every C, H, O radical has an odd mass (CH<sub>3</sub>· 15, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>· 29, ·OH 17). Every neutral C, H, O molecule has an even mass (H<sub>2</sub>O 18, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> 28).
