w: An even-mass molecular ion that loses an odd-mass radical leaves an even-electron cation of odd m/z (e.g. 2-butanone 72 → CH3CO+ 43). Losing an even-mass neutral molecule leaves a radical cation of even m/z (e.g. 2-hexanone 100 → 58 by McLafferty; an alcohol M − 18). So radical loss gives odd m/z; neutral loss gives even m/z, a useful flag for spotting rearrangements.
x: This reverses the rule: subtracting an odd-mass radical from an even M gives an odd number.
Charge does not decide m/z parity; even-mass radical cations such as the McLafferty ion at m/z 58 are common.
Any radical made of C, H and O, with or without oxygen (·OH 17, ·OCH<sub>3</sub> 31), has an odd mass, so its loss still gives an odd-m/z ion.

q: A compound containing only C, H and O gives the IR and mass spectra shown (IR: strong band at 1717 cm<sup>−1</sup>, nothing above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> or at 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>; MS: M<sup>+</sup> 86, base peak 43, other peaks at 58 and 71). Which structure fits?
h: The IR says what kind of carbonyl. In the MS, 43 and 71 come from α-cleavage, and the even-mass 58 needs a γ-hydrogen.
w: IR: 1717 cm−1 with no aldehyde C–H (2720 cm−1) and no O–H means a saturated ketone; M = 86 fits C5H10O. MS: 43 (CH3CO+) and 71 (M − CH3, C3H7CO+) are α-cleavage ions of a methyl ketone, and the even-mass 58 is a McLafferty ion (loss of ethene, 28), which requires a γ-hydrogen on a propyl chain. Only 2-pentanone fits all three.
x: 3-Pentanone has two ethyl groups: α-cleavage gives CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at 57 (its base peak), and with no γ-hydrogen it gives no McLafferty ion at 58.
Pentanal would show the aldehyde C–H band near 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup>; its McLafferty ion appears at m/z 44.
3-Methyl-2-butanone gives 43 and 71 by α-cleavage, but its α carbon bears only methyl groups, so there is no γ-hydrogen and no McLafferty ion at 58.

q: Propene reacts with HBr in the gas phase to give 2-bromopropane. What are the signs of ΔH° and ΔS° for this reaction?
h: Count the molecules on each side, and compare the bonds broken (one π bond, one H–Br) with the bonds formed (two σ bonds).
w: An addition breaks a weak C=C π bond and the H–Br bond and makes two stronger σ bonds (C–H and C–Br), so heat is released: ΔH° < 0. Two gas molecules become one, so disorder drops: ΔS° < 0. ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0. Additions like this are favored at low temperature, where the −TΔS° penalty is small.
x: Two molecules combine into one, which lowers the entropy; ΔS° is negative, not positive.
Two σ bonds formed are stronger than the π bond plus H–Br bond broken, so the reaction is exothermic.
Both signs are reversed: this describes the reverse reaction, the elimination of HBr from 2-bromopropane.

q: The Diels–Alder reaction of 1,3-butadiene with ethylene has ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0. How does K<sub>eq</sub> for this reaction change as the temperature is raised?
c: K<sub>eq</sub> decreases, because the −TΔS° term becomes more unfavorable
K<sub>eq</sub> increases, because molecules collide more often at high temperature
K<sub>eq</sub> stays the same, because ΔH° and ΔS° do not depend on temperature
K<sub>eq</sub> increases, because the −TΔS° term becomes more favorable
h: Write ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. With ΔS° negative, what does a larger T do to the −TΔS° term?
w: With ΔS° < 0, the term −TΔS° is positive and grows with temperature, so ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° becomes less negative (and eventually positive). Since ΔG° = −RT ln K, a less negative ΔG° means a smaller K. Keq decreases with temperature, which is why the retro-Diels–Alder reaction takes over when these adducts are heated strongly.
x: Collision frequency affects the rate (how fast equilibrium is reached), not the position of equilibrium.
Even if ΔH° and ΔS° are constant, ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° contains T, so K must change.
With ΔS° < 0, −TΔS° is positive; it grows more unfavorable, not more favorable, as T rises.

q: An equilibrium A ⇌ B at 25 °C (298 K) has K<sub>eq</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>. What is ΔG° for A → B? (R = 8.314 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Use ΔG° = −RT ln K with the natural log, and keep the units of R in mind.
w: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −(8.314 J mol−1 K−1)(298 K)(ln 1000) = −(2478 J/mol)(6.91) = −17 100 J/mol = −17.1 kJ/mol. A handy rule: at 25 °C each factor of 10 in K is worth about 5.7 kJ/mol, and 3 × 5.7 = 17.1.
x: This uses log<sub>10</sub>(1000) = 3 instead of ln(1000) = 6.91; the equation needs the natural log.
K > 1 means products are favored, so ΔG° must be negative.
This is only −RT (2.48 kJ/mol); it leaves out the ln K factor.

q: For methylcyclohexane, ΔG° = −7.3 kJ/mol for the ring flip of chair I to chair II at 25 °C. About what percent of the molecules have the methyl group equatorial at equilibrium?
h: First find K from ΔG° = −RT ln K (watch kJ vs J), then turn K = [II]/[I] into a fraction.
w: K = e−ΔG°/RT = e7300/(8.314 × 298) = e2.95 ≈ 19. In chair II the methyl is equatorial, so the fraction equatorial = K/(1 + K) = 19/20 = 95%.
x: This comes from using 10<sup>2.95</sup> instead of e<sup>2.95</sup>; ΔG° = −RT ln K uses the natural log.
This results from dividing 7.3 (kJ) by RT in J (2478), which gives K ≈ 1; convert ΔG° to 7300 J/mol first.
This is the axial percentage: a negative ΔG° for I → II favors chair II, which has the methyl equatorial.

q: The SN2 reaction CH3I + CH3S− → CH3SCH3 + I− in DMF follows rate = k[CH3I][CH3S−]. If [CH3I] is tripled and [CH3S−] is halved, the initial rate becomes
h: Multiply the factor for each concentration by its order in the rate law.
w: Both reactants appear to the first power, so the rate changes by (3)(½) = 1.5.
x: A factor of 3 ignores the change in [CH<sub>3</sub>S<sup>−</sup>]; the reaction is first order in the nucleophile too.
A factor of 6 multiplies by 2 for the nucleophile instead of by ½.
A factor of 0.5 ignores the tripling of [CH<sub>3</sub>I], which also appears in the rate law.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with NaN<sub>3</sub> in aqueous acetone by an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. If [alkyl bromide] is halved and [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] is doubled, the initial rate
h: Which species are present in the rate-determining step of an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction?
w: The rate-determining step of SN1 is ionization of the C–Br bond, so rate = k[RBr]; azide is not in the rate law. Halving [RBr] halves the rate, and doubling [N3−] has no effect.
x: Unchanged would be right for rate = k[RBr][N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] (an S<sub>N</sub>2 rate law), where ½ × 2 = 1.
Doubling assumes the rate depends only on azide; azide attacks after the slow step and does not appear in the rate law.
One-quarter treats the reaction as second order in RBr; S<sub>N</sub>1 is first order in substrate.

q:
Which changes increase the rate constant k (not just the rate) of a reaction?
I. Raising the temperature
II. Increasing the concentration of a reactant
III. Adding a catalyst that provides a lower-energy pathway
h: The Arrhenius equation, k = A e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, contains no concentration term.
w: From k = A e−Ea/RT, k grows when T rises (I) or when Ea falls, which is what a catalyst does (III). Concentration changes the rate (rate = k[...]) but not k itself. I and III only.
x: Concentration (II) changes the rate through the rate law, but k is a constant at a given temperature.
II changes the rate, not k; and I and III do change k.
A catalyst lowers Ea, which also increases k, so III belongs with I.

q: How many transition states and how many intermediates are shown in this reaction energy diagram?
h: Transition states are maxima; intermediates are local minima between maxima. Reactants and products are not intermediates.
w: The maxima A and C are transition states, and the valley B between them is an intermediate. 2 transition states and 1 intermediate, so this is a two-step reaction.
x: This swaps the definitions: maxima (A, C) are transition states and the minimum (B) is the intermediate.
Reactants and products are not transition states or intermediates; only A, B and C count.
There is only one valley between the two peaks; reactants and products are not intermediates.

q: Which step of the reaction in this energy diagram is rate-determining, and why?
c: Step 2, because its transition state C is the highest-energy point on the path
Step 1, because its barrier (reactants to A) is larger than the barrier from B to C
Step 1, because it is endothermic while step 2 is exothermic
Step 2, because exothermic steps are always slower than endothermic steps
h: Intermediate B lies above the reactants and can fall back over A easily. What is the highest point every molecule must pass?
w: Every molecule that becomes product must pass C, the highest point on the diagram (20 units above the reactants). Intermediate B can return over A (barrier 4) more easily than it goes on over C (barrier 10), so B and the reactants equilibrate and the overall barrier is reactants → C. Step 2 is rate-determining because C is the highest transition state.
x: Comparing individual barriers misleads here: B lies above the reactants, so the overall barrier to product is reactants → C (20), larger than 14.
Whether a step is endothermic does not decide the rate-determining step; the highest transition state does.
Step 2 is the right step, but the reason is wrong: exothermic steps are not slower in general; C is simply the highest point.

q: The first step of the S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is a strongly endothermic ionization. According to the Hammond postulate, the transition state of this step most resembles
c: the tert-butyl cation and bromide ion
an equal blend of the alkyl bromide and the substitution product
h: The Hammond postulate says a transition state resembles the species (reactant or product of that step) closest to it in energy.
w: For an endothermic step the transition state lies close in energy to the higher-energy side, the products of that step. Here those are (CH3)3C+ and Br−, so the TS is late and has much carbocation character: it resembles the tert-butyl cation and bromide. That is why factors that stabilize the cation speed up SN1 reactions.
x: An early, reactant-like TS goes with an exothermic step; this ionization is endothermic.
The Hammond postulate compares a TS with the reactant and product of that one step; the final product forms in a later step.
A TS halfway between is expected only for a thermoneutral step; this step is strongly uphill.

q: Radical bromination of propane gives about 97% 2-bromopropane, while chlorination gives only about 55% 2-chloropropane. Which explanation uses the Hammond postulate correctly?
c: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so its late, radical-like transition state feels the 2° vs 1° radical stability difference
H abstraction by Br• is exothermic, so its transition state is early and resembles propane, which makes bromination more selective
Br• is more reactive than Cl•, so it attacks the more crowded 2° hydrogens of propane more often
H abstraction by Cl• is endothermic, so its transition state is late and cannot tell the 2° and 1° hydrogens of propane apart
h: Compare the H–Br and H–Cl bond strengths with a C–H bond to decide which abstraction step is uphill.
w: H–Br (366 kJ/mol) is weaker than a C–H bond (about 410–420 kJ/mol), so H abstraction by Br• is endothermic; H–Cl (431 kJ/mol) is stronger, so abstraction by Cl• is exothermic. An endothermic step has a late, product-like TS with nearly formed radical character, so the 2° radical's extra stability lowers its TS a lot. The late TS for bromination makes it selective. The early TS for chlorination resembles propane and shows little preference.
x: Abstraction by Br• is endothermic, not exothermic; and an early, reactant-like TS would make a reaction less selective.
Br• is less reactive than Cl•; lower reactivity (a later TS) goes with higher selectivity.
Abstraction by Cl• is exothermic with an early TS; that is why chlorination is unselective.

q:
Which statements about the reaction shown in this energy diagram are true?
I. The overall reaction is endothermic.
II. There are two intermediates.
III. The second step is rate-determining.
h: Count the valleys between peaks, compare products with reactants, and find the highest peak.
w: There are three peaks (transition states) and two valleys between them (energies 5 and 9): two intermediates, so II is true. Products lie below reactants, so the reaction is exothermic and I is false. The highest peak (18) is the second transition state, so step 2 is rate-determining and III is true. II and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: the second peak is the highest point on the diagram.
Statement I is false: the products end below the reactants, so the overall reaction is exothermic.
Statement II is true and I is false; the products lie below the reactants.

q: Which labeled atom in acetyl chloride is the most electrophilic site, the atom a nucleophile attacks?
h: Look for the atom with the largest partial positive charge, bonded to more than one electronegative atom.
w: The carbonyl carbon is bonded to both O and Cl, which pull electron density away, and resonance (C+–O−) puts a positive charge on it. Atom b, the carbonyl carbon, is the electrophile; nucleophiles add there in acyl substitution.
x: The methyl carbon carries little positive charge and has no leaving group or π bond; it is not electrophilic.
The oxygen is electron-rich (δ−, lone pairs); it is a nucleophilic/basic site, not an electrophilic one.
Chlorine is δ− and holds lone pairs; it leaves as chloride but is not where a nucleophile attacks.

q: In the first step of the addition of HBr to propene, a carbocation forms. Which statement identifies the nucleophile and electrophile in that step?
c: The C=C π bond is the nucleophile; the H of HBr is the electrophile
The Br of HBr is the nucleophile; an alkene carbon is the electrophile
The H of HBr is the nucleophile; the C=C π bond is the electrophile
The C=C π bond is the nucleophile; the Br of HBr is the electrophile
h: Electrons flow from the electron-rich site to the electron-poor atom. Which atom of H–Br is δ+?
w: The π electrons of the alkene attack the δ+ hydrogen of HBr, and the H–Br bond electrons leave with bromide. The π bond is the nucleophile and the H is the electrophile. Bromide acts as the nucleophile only in the second step, when it attacks the carbocation.
x: This describes the second step (bromide attacking the cation), and it is bromide ion, not HBr, that attacks.
This reverses the electron flow: the H of HBr is δ+ and electron-poor, so it accepts electrons.
The Br in HBr is δ−; the alkene bonds to the H, which is the δ+ atom, and Br leaves as bromide.

q: Rank these carbocations from most stable to least stable.
h: Alkyl groups stabilize a cation by hyperconjugation and induction. A vinyl cation has its positive charge on an sp-hybridized carbon.
w: More alkyl groups give more hyperconjugation, so 3° (I) > 2° (II) > 1° (III). The vinyl cation (IV) puts the charge on an sp carbon, which holds electrons tightly (50% s character), and the empty p orbital lies in the molecular plane, perpendicular to the π orbitals, so the π bond cannot donate into it. Vinyl cations are even less stable than primary cations. I > II > III > IV.
x: A vinyl cation is not stabilized by its π bond (the empty orbital is perpendicular to it) and is less stable than a primary cation.
A vinyl cation is not allylic; its π bond cannot delocalize the charge, so it does not rank first.
The vinyl cation, not the primary cation, is the least stable; it does not rank above the 2° and 1° alkyl cations.

q: Rank these secondary carbocations from most stable to least stable.
h: Ask whether the neighboring atom can donate a lone pair into the empty p orbital, or instead withdraws electron density.
w: In I, an oxygen lone pair donates into the empty p orbital (resonance form C=O+–CH3 where every atom has an octet), a strong stabilization that outweighs oxygen's inductive pull. II is an ordinary 2° alkyl cation. In III the carbonyl group next to the cationic carbon withdraws electrons (its carbon is δ+), destabilizing it. I > II > III.
x: Oxygen's inductive withdrawal is outweighed by lone-pair donation (resonance), so I is more stable than II.
The carbonyl in III cannot donate electrons to the cation; its δ+ carbon makes III the least stable.
I is the most stable, not the least: the oxygen lone pair gives a resonance form with full octets.

q: 3-Methyl-2-butanol reacts with concentrated HBr to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product. Which carbocation is attacked by bromide to form this product?
h: The first cation forms where the OH was. Is there a hydrogen on a neighboring carbon whose shift would make the cation more substituted?
w: Loss of water from the protonated alcohol gives a 2° cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 (which carries one H and two methyls) moves the positive charge to C3, giving the more stable 3° cation. Bromide then attacks the 3° carbon, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
x: This is the first-formed 2° cation; bromide attacking it would give 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, not the observed product.
This is a 2° cation on an unbranched chain; no 1,2-shift turns a branched skeleton into a straight one.
This is a primary cation; hydride shifts go toward more stable cations, never from 2° to 1°.

q: 3,3-Dimethyl-2-butanol is heated with HCl. The first-formed carbocation undergoes a 1,2-shift. Which carbocation does that shift produce?
h: The carbon next to the cationic center has no hydrogen. What group can migrate from it instead?
w: Loss of water gives the 2° cation (CH3)3C–CH+–CH3. The neighboring quaternary carbon has no H, so a 1,2-methyl shift moves a CH3 with its bonding electrons to the cationic carbon, leaving a 3° cation (CH3)2C+–CH(CH3)2. Chloride then gives 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane.
x: This is the unrearranged 2° cation that forms first, not the product of the shift.
This is a primary cation; a hydride shift from a methyl group to the cation would trade a 2° cation for a less stable 1° one.
D has a different carbon skeleton (3-methylpentane); a single 1,2-methyl shift keeps the 2,3-dimethylbutane skeleton.

q: When 1-cyclobutylethanol is treated with HBr, the 1-cyclobutylethyl cation forms first. A ring C–C bond then migrates to the cationic carbon. Which carbocation is produced directly by that migration?
h: Follow the atoms: the ring carbon attached to the cationic carbon loses one ring bond, and the cationic carbon becomes a ring member. Where is the positive charge left?
w: In the alkyl shift, a ring C–C bond on the carbon next to the cation moves to the cationic carbon. The former exocyclic carbon (with its CH<sub>3</sub>) becomes part of a five-membered ring, and the positive charge is left on the old ring carbon next to it. The product is the 2-methylcyclopentyl cation: still 2°, but the 4-membered ring strain is relieved. A later 1,2-hydride shift can turn it into the 3° 1-methylcyclopentyl cation, which is how 1-bromo-1-methylcyclopentane forms.
x: This is formed only after a second step (a hydride shift from A); it is not the direct product of the ring bond migration.
C would come from a hydride shift without ring expansion; it keeps the strained four-membered ring.
D would require the methyl carbon to enter the ring too; only the cationic carbon joins the ring, so the ring grows from 4 to 5, not 6.

q: A reaction can give two products, P and Q. At low temperature and short reaction time it gives mostly P; after long heating it gives mostly Q. Which statement is correct?
c: P forms through the lower-energy transition state, and Q is the more stable product
P is the more stable product, and Q forms through the lower-energy transition state
P and Q form through the same transition state but differ in stability
Q forms faster, and P is the more stable product
h: Under kinetic control the product ratio reflects relative rates; under thermodynamic control it reflects relative product stabilities.
w: At low temperature the products cannot revert, so the faster-forming product (lower ΔG‡) dominates: kinetic control favors P. With heating and time, the reactions become reversible and the mixture equilibrates to the more stable product: thermodynamic control favors Q. P has the lower-energy transition state; Q is the more stable product.
x: This reverses the two kinds of control: the product formed at low temperature is the kinetic (faster) one.
Different products form through different transition states; that difference is what allows kinetic control.
Q dominates only after equilibration; it is the more stable product, while P is the one formed faster.

q: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with one equivalent of HBr at 40 °C, conditions under which the products equilibrate. Which compound is the major product?
h: Protonation at C1 gives an allylic cation with positive charge shared by C2 and C4. Which of the two possible bromides has the more substituted (more stable) alkene?
w: Protonation of C1 gives a resonance-stabilized allylic cation (charge on C2 and C4). Bromide can add at C2 (1,2-addition, 3-bromo-1-butene) or at C4 (1,4-addition, 1-bromo-2-butene). At 40 °C the products interconvert, so the more stable one wins: A, (E)-1-bromo-2-butene, whose internal disubstituted alkene is more stable than the monosubstituted alkene of the 1,2-product.
x: This is the 1,2-product: it forms faster and dominates at low temperature (kinetic control), but it is less stable.
C would require protonation at C2 to give a primary, non-allylic cation; protonation at C1 gives the allylic cation instead.
D, a vinyl bromide, would need bromide to add to a vinyl cation; the allylic cation never puts charge there.

q: A mixture rich in 3-bromo-1-butene, made from 1,3-butadiene and HBr at −80 °C, is warmed to 40 °C and becomes mostly 1-bromo-2-butene. What is the best explanation?
c: At 40 °C the allylic C–Br bond ionizes reversibly, so the mixture equilibrates to the more stable product
At 40 °C the activation energy for forming 1-bromo-2-butene becomes lower than that for 3-bromo-1-butene
3-Bromo-1-butene becomes the less stable isomer only at higher temperatures
Bromide ion is a stronger nucleophile at higher temperature and attacks only the terminal carbon
h: Both products share the same allylic cation. What does added heat allow the kinetic product to do?
w: At −80 °C the products form irreversibly, so the faster-forming 1,2-product dominates (kinetic control). On warming, the allylic C–Br bond can ionize back to the same allylic cation and bromide; repeated ionization and recombination let the system reach equilibrium, which favors the more stable 1,4-product with its more substituted alkene. Reversible ionization leads to thermodynamic control.
x: Temperature changes how many molecules can cross each barrier, not which barrier is lower; the 1,2-pathway still has the lower TS.
Relative stability does not flip on warming: 1-bromo-2-butene is the more stable isomer at both temperatures.
Product ratios under equilibrium control are set by stabilities, not by nucleophile strength; bromide attacks both cation termini.

q: Use the bond dissociation energies in the table to estimate ΔH° for CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl.
h: ΔH° = (energy of bonds broken) − (energy of bonds formed).
w: Bonds broken: CH3–H (439) + Cl–Cl (242) = 681 kJ/mol. Bonds formed: CH3–Cl (350) + H–Cl (431) = 781 kJ/mol. ΔH° = 681 − 781 = −100 kJ/mol.
x: This is formed − broken; breaking bonds costs energy, so ΔH° = broken − formed.
+8 kJ/mol is only the first propagation step (CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl• → CH<sub>3</sub>• + HCl), not the overall reaction.
−108 kJ/mol is only the second propagation step (CH<sub>3</sub>• + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl•).

q: Use the table to estimate ΔH° for the step CH<sub>4</sub> + Br• → CH<sub>3</sub>• + HBr. What does the Hammond postulate then say about its transition state?
c: +73 kJ/mol; the transition state is late and resembles CH<sub>3</sub>• + HBr
+73 kJ/mol; the transition state is early and resembles CH<sub>4</sub> + Br•
−73 kJ/mol; the transition state is early and resembles CH<sub>4</sub> + Br•
−101 kJ/mol; the transition state is early and resembles CH<sub>4</sub> + Br•
h: Only one bond breaks and one forms in this step. Then: does an uphill step have a reactant-like or product-like TS?
w: Broken: CH3–H, 439 kJ/mol. Formed: H–Br, 366 kJ/mol. ΔH° = 439 − 366 = +73 kJ/mol, an endothermic step. The Hammond postulate places the TS of an endothermic step close to its higher-energy products, so the TS is late and resembles CH3• + HBr, with the C–H bond nearly broken.
x: The ΔH° is right, but an endothermic step has a late, product-like TS, not an early one.
The sign is reversed: breaking a 439 kJ/mol bond and forming a 366 kJ/mol bond costs energy.
−101 kJ/mol is the other propagation step (CH<sub>3</sub>• + Br<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Br + Br•), not this one.

q: Which labeled C–H bond in 4-methyl-1-pentene has the lowest bond dissociation energy?
h: The weakest C–H bond is the one whose homolysis gives the most stable radical.
w: Breaking a C–H at c gives an allylic radical, delocalized over two carbons by resonance with the C=C, so this bond is the weakest (about 350 kJ/mol). Homolysis at d gives an ordinary 3° radical (about 400 kJ/mol), and vinylic C–H bonds at a and b are the strongest (about 460 kJ/mol) because the sp2 vinyl radical is unstable. The C–H bond at c.
x: A 3° radical is stabilized by hyperconjugation, but less than the resonance-delocalized allylic radical from c.
This is a vinylic C–H; vinyl radicals are very unstable, so this bond is among the strongest.
This is a vinylic C–H on an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon; its homolysis gives an unstable vinyl radical.

q: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction by 11.4 kJ/mol without changing the pre-exponential factor. At 25 °C (298 K), the rate constant increases by a factor of about
h: From k = A e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, the ratio k<sub>new</sub>/k<sub>old</sub> = e<sup>ΔEa/RT</sup>.
w: knew/kold = e11 400/(8.314 × 298) = e4.60 ≈ 100. At room temperature every 5.7 kJ/mol of barrier is worth a factor of 10 in rate.
x: A factor of 10 corresponds to only 5.7 kJ/mol; 11.4 kJ/mol is twice that, so the factor is 10<sup>2</sup>.
4.6 is the exponent (ΔEa/RT), not the ratio; the ratio is e<sup>4.6</sup>.
A factor of 1000 would need about 17 kJ/mol of barrier lowering.

q: A reaction A → B + C has ΔH° = +20 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +80 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>. Which describes ΔG° and K<sub>eq</sub> at 25 °C (298 K)?
h: Convert ΔS° to kJ before using ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; then recall the sign link between ΔG° and K.
w: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 20 − (298)(0.080) = 20 − 23.8 = −3.8 kJ/mol. A negative ΔG° means Keq > 1 (here e3800/2478 ≈ 4.6). ΔG° = −3.8 kJ/mol and Keq > 1: the entropy gain from making two molecules outweighs the endothermic bond breaking at this temperature.
x: The sign is flipped; −TΔS° (−23.8) outweighs +20, so ΔG° is negative.
This adds TΔS° instead of subtracting it; ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
ΔG° is right, but a negative ΔG° gives K > 1, since ΔG° = −RT ln K.

q: Which reaction has ΔS° > 0?
h: Count molecules on each side; making more independent molecules raises entropy.
w: Dehydration turns one molecule into two, increasing the number of ways energy and matter can be distributed: ΔS° > 0 for the dehydration. The other three combine two molecules into one, so ΔS° < 0. This is why eliminations are favored at high temperature.
x: Hydrogenation joins two molecules into one, so entropy decreases.
The Diels–Alder reaction joins two molecules into one ring, so entropy decreases.
HBr addition joins two molecules into one, so entropy decreases.

q: Which reaction is best described by this energy diagram?
h: How many transition states are there, and is there any intermediate?
w: The diagram has one transition state and no intermediate: a single concerted step. The SN2 reaction of a primary bromide with cyanide in a polar aprotic solvent breaks C–Br as C–CN forms in one step. CH3CH2Br + NaCN in DMSO.
x: Solvolysis of a 3° bromide is S<sub>N</sub>1, with a carbocation intermediate, so its diagram has at least two transition states.
Acid-catalyzed dehydration (E1) has several steps (protonation, loss of water, deprotonation) and two intermediates.
HBr addition goes through a carbocation intermediate, so its diagram shows two transition states.

q: This diagram represents the acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-methyl-2-propanol by the E1 mechanism. Which point corresponds to the tert-butyl cation?
h: List the steps in order: protonation of OH, loss of water, loss of H<sup>+</sup>. Which valleys are intermediates, and which comes second?
w: E1 dehydration has three steps. Step 1 (TS A) protonates the OH to give the oxonium ion, intermediate B. Step 2 (TS C, the highest point, rate-determining) loses water to give the carbocation, intermediate D. Step 3 (TS E) removes a β-hydrogen to give the alkene. The carbocation is higher in energy than the oxonium ion, as the diagram shows.
x: B is the first intermediate, the protonated alcohol (alkyloxonium ion), formed before water leaves.
C is a transition state (a maximum), the point where the C–O bond is partly broken; the cation is the valley after it.
E is the transition state for removing a proton from the carbocation, not an intermediate.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane ionizes in water far faster than 2-bromopropane. Which explanation is best?
c: Ionization is endothermic, so its transition state resembles the carbocation, and the more stable 3° cation lowers it more
The 3° bromide has a stronger C–Br bond, so its transition state is reached earlier along the path
The ionization step is exothermic, so its transition state resembles the alkyl bromide, which is more stable for the 3° compound
Water attacks the 3° carbon more easily because it is less hindered
h: Use the Hammond postulate: an uphill step has a transition state that looks like its product.
w: Ionization of an alkyl bromide to a carbocation is strongly endothermic, so the TS is late and has much carbocation character. Whatever stabilizes the carbocation (here, three alkyl groups giving more hyperconjugation in the 3° cation) also stabilizes the TS and lowers Ea. The more stable 3° cation lowers the TS.
x: A stronger bond would slow ionization; the rate difference comes from carbocation stability, not bond strength.
Ionization is endothermic, not exothermic; and a more stable reactant would raise, not lower, the barrier.
A 3° carbon is more hindered, not less; and water does not attack in the rate-determining step of S<sub>N</sub>1.

q: Which two labeled carbons of 3-buten-2-one are electrophilic sites, where a nucleophile can add?
h: Draw the resonance form that moves the C=C π electrons toward the oxygen. Which carbons carry the + charge?
w: The carbonyl carbon c is δ+ (C=O ↔ C+–O−). Because the C=C is conjugated with C=O, a second resonance form moves the C=C π electrons toward the carbonyl and places the + charge on the terminal β carbon a. Carbons a and c are electrophilic (1,2- and 1,4-addition sites).
x: Carbon b (the α carbon) never carries + charge in any resonance form; the charge alternates to a.
b is not electrophilic, and the conjugate (β) site a pairs with the carbonyl carbon c.
The methyl carbon d is not electrophilic; it is not part of the conjugated system.

q: Diethyl ether and BF<sub>3</sub> combine as shown. Which statement describes the roles of the reactants?
c: The ether oxygen is the nucleophile (Lewis base); boron is the electrophile (Lewis acid)
Boron is the nucleophile (Lewis base); the ether oxygen is the electrophile (Lewis acid)
A fluorine of BF<sub>3</sub> is the nucleophile; the ether oxygen is the electrophile
The ether oxygen is the electrophile because it ends up with a positive formal charge
h: Which atom has a lone pair to donate, and which has an empty orbital?
w: Boron in BF3 has only six valence electrons and an empty p orbital, so it accepts an electron pair: electrophile (Lewis acid). The ether oxygen donates a lone pair: nucleophile (Lewis base). O is the nucleophile, B is the electrophile. The formal charges in the adduct (O+, B−) result from that electron donation.
x: The roles are reversed: boron has an empty orbital and no lone pair to donate.
Fluorine's lone pairs are held tightly and the new bond in the product is O–B, not F–O.
The + formal charge on oxygen in the product is the result of donating its lone pair; that is what a nucleophile does.

q: Which carbocation is the least stable?
h: Where is the empty orbital in each cation, and can it overlap with a π system?
w: In the phenyl cation A the positive charge sits in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, at right angles to the aromatic π system, so there is no resonance stabilization, and the high s character of the empty orbital makes it very unstable. The benzyl and allyl cations are stabilized by resonance, and the cyclohexyl cation is an ordinary 2° cation.
x: The allyl cation is resonance stabilized: its empty p orbital overlaps with the C=C π bond.
The benzyl cation is strongly resonance stabilized by the ring, unlike the phenyl cation.
The cyclohexyl cation is an ordinary secondary cation with hyperconjugation; it is far more stable than an aryl cation.

q: 3-Methyl-1-butene reacts with HCl to give two alkyl chlorides. Which product comes from a carbocation that underwent a 1,2-hydride shift?
h: Protonate the alkene to give the more substituted cation first. Is there a neighboring hydrogen whose shift gives a more stable cation?
w: Markovnikov protonation at C1 gives the 2° cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 gives the 3° cation at C3, and chloride capture there gives A, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Capture before the shift gives B, the other product of the reaction.
x: This is the unrearranged Markovnikov product, formed when chloride traps the 2° cation before any shift.
This is the anti-Markovnikov product; it would need a primary cation, which HCl addition does not form.
This is a primary chloride (1-chloro-2-methylbutane); it would need a primary cation, which neither protonation nor a hydride shift produces here.

q: Which carbocation is expected to rearrange by a 1,2-shift to a more stable carbocation?
h: For each cation, ask what a 1,2-hydride or methyl shift would produce, and whether the new cation is more substituted.
w: In A, a 1,2-methyl shift from the neighboring quaternary carbon turns the 2° cation into a 3° cation, so it rearranges. B is already 3°. In C (2-butyl cation), a hydride shift from C3 gives another 2-butyl cation, no gain. In D (cyclohexyl), any hydride shift gives another 2° cyclohexyl cation.
x: This is already a 3° cation; any 1,2-shift would give a less stable 2° or 1° cation.
A hydride shift in the 2-butyl cation gives an identical 2° cation, so there is no driving force.
Every carbon next to the cyclohexyl cation is a CH<sub>2</sub>; a hydride shift gives another 2° cation of the same kind.

q: An alkyl bromide (RBr) reacts with sodium azide. Based on the initial-rate data, what is the rate law?
h: Compare pairs of experiments in which only one concentration changes.
w: Experiments 1 → 2: doubling [RBr] (azide fixed) doubles the rate, so the reaction is first order in RBr. Experiments 1 → 3: tripling [N3−] (RBr fixed) leaves the rate unchanged, so it is zero order in azide. rate = k[RBr], the rate law expected for an SN1 reaction whose slow step is ionization.
x: Tripling [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] did not change the rate, so azide does not appear in the rate law.
The rate depends on [RBr] (experiments 1 and 2) and not on [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>].
Doubling [RBr] doubled the rate; second order would have quadrupled it.

q: Two irreversible pathways from the same intermediate give products X and Y. The transition state leading to X is 4.0 kJ/mol lower than the one leading to Y. At 25 °C (298 K), what is the approximate X : Y ratio?
h: Under kinetic control, [X]/[Y] = k<sub>X</sub>/k<sub>Y</sub> = e<sup>ΔΔG‡/RT</sup>.
x: This uses 10<sup>1.61</sup> ≈ 41 instead of e<sup>1.61</sup>; rate ratios from ΔΔG<sup>‡</sup> use the natural exponential.
This comes from dividing 4.0 (kJ) by RT in J, giving e<sup>0.0016</sup> ≈ 1; convert to 4000 J/mol first.
The ratio is reversed: the pathway with the lower transition state is faster, so X is the major product.

q: An intermediate can form product A or product B. The table gives energies relative to the intermediate. Which statement is correct?
c: A dominates at low temperature (kinetic product); B dominates when the system can equilibrate (thermodynamic product)
B dominates at low temperature (kinetic product); A dominates when the system can equilibrate (thermodynamic product)
A dominates under all conditions because its transition state is lower
B dominates under all conditions because it is the more stable product
h: Kinetic control compares transition-state energies; thermodynamic control compares product energies.
w: A has the lower transition state (60 vs 70 kJ/mol), so it forms faster and dominates when products cannot revert (low temperature, short times). B is lower in energy (−25 vs −10 kJ/mol), so it dominates once the reactions are reversible and equilibrium is reached. A is the kinetic product; B is the thermodynamic product.
x: This swaps the definitions: the lower transition state (A) makes A the kinetic product.
When the reactions become reversible, the more stable product B accumulates, so A does not win under all conditions.
Under irreversible, low-temperature conditions the faster-forming A wins, so B does not dominate under all conditions.

q: A mixture of methane and oxygen can sit unchanged at 25 °C for years even though combustion has a very negative ΔG°. What is the reason?
c: The activation energy is very high, so the rate at 25 °C is extremely small
K<sub>eq</sub> for combustion is less than 1 at 25 °C
ΔS° for combustion is negative, which makes the reaction non-spontaneous
Exothermic reactions do not start unless their ΔH° is positive
h: Thermodynamics says whether a reaction is favorable; kinetics says how fast it goes.
w: A very negative ΔG° means Keq is huge, so combustion is favorable. But the rate depends on the activation energy, and breaking the strong C–H and O=O bonds requires a large Ea. The barrier is high, so the reaction is extremely slow at 25 °C until a spark supplies energy.
x: A very negative ΔG° means K<sub>eq</sub> is much greater than 1.
ΔG° already includes the entropy term; a very negative ΔG° means spontaneous whatever the sign of ΔS°.
This is not a rule; reaction rates depend on E<sub>a</sub>, not on the sign of ΔH°.

q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of the ether shown?
h: Sort the hydrogens into sets that are interchanged by symmetry or by fast rotation. Each set gives one signal.
w: Ethyl isopropyl ether has four sets of equivalent H: the ethyl CH3 (3H, triplet), the OCH2 (2H, quartet), the OCH (1H, septet) and the two isopropyl CH3 groups (6H, doublet). The two isopropyl methyls are swapped by a mirror plane, so they count once. Answer: 4 signals.
x: Three signals would require two of the sets to coincide, but the ethyl CH<sub>3</sub> (next to CH<sub>2</sub>) and the isopropyl CH<sub>3</sub> groups (next to CH) are in different environments.
Five counts the two isopropyl methyls separately. They are related by a mirror plane through O–CH, so they are equivalent and give one 6H doublet.
Six is more signals than there are carbons bearing H (five). The two isopropyl CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent, so there are only four sets of H.

q: How many signals appear in the broadband-decoupled <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of methylcyclohexane?
h: Find the mirror plane of the ring, then pair up carbons that it reflects onto each other.
w: A mirror plane passes through C1 (bearing CH3) and C4. It makes C2 = C6 and C3 = C5. The unique carbons are CH3, C1, C2/C6, C3/C5 and C4: 5 signals.
x: Seven counts every carbon separately and ignores the mirror plane through C1 and C4.
Four would require C4 to match another carbon, but C4 lies on the mirror plane and has no partner.
Six pairs only one set (C2/C6 or C3/C5); the same mirror plane relates both pairs.

q: Which C6H12 isomer gives exactly two signals in its 13C NMR spectrum?
h: Look for the isomer with the most symmetry: how many different kinds of carbon does each one have?
w: 2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2, has only two kinds of carbon: four equivalent CH3 (≈20 ppm) and two equivalent alkene C (≈123 ppm). Two signals. (E)-3-Hexene gives 3, 1,1-dimethylcyclobutane gives 4 and 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene gives 4.
x: (E)-3-Hexene is symmetric end to end but still has three kinds of carbon: CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub> and =CH (3 signals).
1,1-Dimethylcyclobutane has CH<sub>3</sub> (both equivalent), the quaternary C, C2/C4 and C3: 4 signals.
3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene has CH<sub>3</sub> (three equivalent), the quaternary C, =CH and =CH<sub>2</sub>: 4 signals.

q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of 1-bromo-3-methylbutane?
h: Walk along the chain and ask which hydrogens are interchanged by rotation or symmetry.
w: BrCH2–CH2–CH(CH3)2: the BrCH2 (2H), the middle CH2 (2H), the CH (1H) and the two equivalent CH3 groups (6H). 4 signals. No stereocenter is present, so each CH2 pair is equivalent.
x: Five counts the two terminal CH<sub>3</sub> groups separately; they are attached to the same CH and are interchanged by a mirror plane.
Three merges the two CH<sub>2</sub> groups, but one is bonded to Br (≈3.4 ppm) and the other is not (≈1.8 ppm).
Six is more signals than the molecule has carbons (five). The two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the same CH are one set, so there are only four sets of H.

q: How many chemically different kinds of hydrogen does (S)-2-chlorobutane have? Count diastereotopic protons as different (as a high-field 1H spectrum would show).
h: Replace each H of the CH<sub>2</sub> group in turn by D. What is the relationship between the two products?
w: C1 CH3 (doublet), C2 CH–Cl, C4 CH3 (triplet) and the C3 CH2. Because C2 is a stereocenter, replacing one C3 H by D gives (2S,3R) and replacing the other gives (2S,3S): diastereomers. The two C3 H are therefore diastereotopic and inequivalent, giving 5 kinds of H in all.
x: Four is the count if the CH<sub>2</sub> pair is treated as one set. Next to a stereocenter, the two CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogens are diastereotopic, not equivalent.
Six would require the H within a CH<sub>3</sub> group to differ, but fast C–C rotation averages each methyl into one environment.
Three merges the two methyl groups. The C1 methyl sits on the stereocenter (doublet) and the C4 methyl sits on CH<sub>2</sub> (triplet).

q: In which compound are the two hydrogens on the tagged carbon a diastereotopic?
h: Use the substitution test: replace one H, then the other, by X. Identical products = homotopic, enantiomers = enantiotopic, diastereomers = diastereotopic.
w: Only in 2-bromobutane does C3 sit next to an existing stereocenter (C2). Replacing either C3 H by X creates a second stereocenter, so the two products are diastereomers: the C3 hydrogens are diastereotopic and can give separate signals. In the other compounds the products are identical or enantiomers.
x: In 1-bromobutane, replacing either H on C1 gives the two enantiomers of BrCHX–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, so these H are enantiotopic (equivalent in NMR).
In propane, replacing either H on C2 gives the same 2-X-propane (no stereocenter), so these H are homotopic.
In 3-pentanone, replacing either H on C2 creates one new stereocenter and no other, so the products are enantiomers: the H are enantiotopic.

q: Which tagged hydrogens give the 1H signal farthest downfield?
h: An oxygen attached directly to the carbon deshields more than a C=O one bond away.
w: Typical shifts: a CH3C=O ≈ 2.2, b CH2C=O ≈ 2.7, c OCH2 ≈ 3.7, d CH3 of ethyl ≈ 1.2 ppm. Hydrogens on a carbon bonded directly to an electronegative O (3.3–4.2 ppm) are more deshielded than hydrogens α to a carbonyl (2–2.6 ppm). c is farthest downfield.
x: H b is α to the C=O (≈2.7 ppm). The carbonyl deshields, but less than an oxygen bonded directly to the carbon.
H a is a methyl ketone CH3 (≈2.2 ppm), upfield of both CH2 groups.
H d is an ordinary alkyl CH3 two bonds from O (≈1.2 ppm), the most upfield of the set.

q: Which tagged hydrogens give the 1H signal farthest upfield (lowest δ)?
h: Upfield means most shielded: hydrogens far from O and not on an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon.
w: a CH3 ≈ 1.2, b OCH2 ≈ 3.5, c OCH2 (also allylic) ≈ 4.0, d =CH ≈ 5.9 ppm. The alkyl CH3 a is not on a carbon attached to O or to a π bond, so it is the most shielded.
x: H b is on a carbon bonded to O, which deshields it to ≈3.5 ppm.
H c is on a carbon bonded to O and next to C=C, so it is even more deshielded (≈4.0 ppm).
H d is a vinyl H (≈5.9 ppm), deshielded by the π-electron circulation; it is the farthest downfield, not upfield.

q: What is the splitting pattern and integration of the tagged hydrogens a in the 1H NMR spectrum of 1-bromopropane? (Assume all neighboring J values are similar.)
h: Count every H on the carbons on both sides of C2, then apply the n + 1 rule.
w: The C2 hydrogens have 3 neighbors on C1 (CH3) and 2 on C3 (CH2Br): n = 5. With similar coupling constants, n + 1 = 6 lines, a sextet, and the signal integrates for 2H (≈1.9 ppm).
x: A quintet (n = 4) undercounts the neighbors: C1 has three H and C3 has two, giving five.
A quartet counts only the CH<sub>3</sub> neighbors and ignores the CH<sub>2</sub>Br hydrogens on the other side.
A triplet counts only the CH<sub>2</sub>Br neighbors and ignores the CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Which description fits the signal of the tagged hydrogen a?
h: Does the O atom pass on coupling from the OCH<sub>3</sub> group? Which atom is the CH bonded to?
w: The CH of 2-methoxypropane is bonded to O, so it appears near 3.5 ppm. Its only coupled neighbors are the six H of the two methyls on adjacent carbons; the OCH3 hydrogens are four bonds away through O and do not split it. n = 6 → septet, 1H, δ ≈ 3.5.
x: δ 1.1 is the shift of the isopropyl CH<sub>3</sub> groups; the CH bonded to O is deshielded to about 3.5 ppm.
Ten lines would count the OCH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens as neighbors, but they are separated by an O atom and do not couple measurably.
The 6H doublet at 1.1 ppm belongs to the two CH3 groups, not to a.

q: In the 1H NMR spectrum of 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene, how is the signal of the tagged vinyl H a split?
c: Triplet (J ≈ 14 Hz), from the two =CH2 hydrogens
h: Are the two H of the =CH<sub>2</sub> group equivalent? One is cis to H<sub>a</sub> and one is trans.
w: The two =CH2 hydrogens are not equivalent: one is trans to Ha (Jtrans ≈ 17 Hz) and one is cis (Jcis ≈ 10 Hz). The other neighbor of C2 is the quaternary C with no H. Two different couplings give a doublet of doublets (4 lines). The full spectrum therefore has 4 signals: t-Bu (9H, s), Ha (1H, dd) and two separate =CH2 signals (each 1H, dd).
x: A triplet would need two equivalent neighbors with equal J; the cis and trans =CH2 hydrogens differ and couple with different J values.
A doublet counts only the trans neighbor; the cis =CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogen also couples (≈10 Hz).
A singlet would be true only if no H were on adjacent carbons; C1 carries two H that couple to H<sub>a</sub>.

q: An alkene shows two separate vinyl signals (1H each) in its 1H NMR spectrum, and they split each other with J = 15.6 Hz. Which compound fits?
h: Recall typical J: trans vinyl 12–18 Hz, cis vinyl 6–12 Hz, geminal =CH2 0–3 Hz. Also ask whether the two vinyl H are even different from each other.
w: A 15.6 Hz vinyl coupling is a trans (E) coupling, and the two vinyl H must be non-equivalent to show splitting. (E)-4,4-Dimethyl-2-pentene fits: H3 appears as a doublet (J ≈ 15.6 Hz, next to the t-Bu C with no H) and H2 as a doublet of quartets.
x: The (Z) isomer has its vinyl H cis to each other, with J ≈ 11–12 Hz, smaller than 15.6 Hz.
In symmetric (E)-2,2,5,5-tetramethyl-3-hexene the two vinyl H are equivalent; equivalent H do not split each other, so they appear as one 2H singlet.
This 1,1-disubstituted alkene has a =CH<sub>2</sub> group; geminal vinyl coupling is only about 0–3 Hz.

q: Which C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> compound gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: Where would a CH<sub>2</sub> bonded to O appear, and where would a CH<sub>2</sub> next to C=O appear?
w: Three signals in a 2:3:3 ratio: an ethyl group (q + t) and an isolated CH3 (s). The quartet at 4.12 ppm means the CH2 is bonded to O; the singlet at 2.04 ppm is a CH3 next to C=O. That is CH3C(=O)OCH2CH3, ethyl acetate.
x: Methyl propanoate has an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near 3.7 ppm and its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near 2.3 ppm (next to C=O), the reverse of what is observed.
Butanoic acid has four signals including the COOH H at 10–12 ppm and a CH<sub>2</sub> sextet; no singlet near 2 ppm.
Propyl formate shows the formyl H near 8 ppm and four signals (s, t, sextet, t).

q: A C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O ether gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: A doublet and a septet together signal an isopropyl group. How many isopropyl groups does a 12H : 2H ratio require?
w: Only two signals: a 12H doublet at 1.12 ppm and a 2H septet at 3.65 ppm (CH on O). Each CH has six methyl neighbors, and four equivalent CH3 groups give 12H. Two isopropyl groups on one O: diisopropyl ether.
x: Dipropyl ether gives three signals: OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet (≈3.4, 4H), CH<sub>2</sub> sextet (≈1.6, 4H) and CH<sub>3</sub> triplet (≈0.9, 6H).
tert-Butyl ethyl ether gives a 9H singlet (≈1.2), a 2H quartet (≈3.4) and a 3H triplet; no septet.
This ether gives three singlets (9H, 2H, 3H), because none of its carbons with H are next to another carbon with H.

q: Which C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br isomer gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: The 2H doublet near 3.3 ppm is a CH<sub>2</sub>Br. What must it be attached to for it to be a doublet?
w: A 6H doublet (two equivalent CH3 on one CH), a 1H multiplet (that CH, with 8 neighbors) and a 2H doublet at 3.30 ppm (CH2Br next to one H). That is (CH3)2CH–CH2Br, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.
x: 1-Bromobutane has a CH<sub>2</sub>Br triplet (next to CH<sub>2</sub>) and a 3H triplet; it has no 6H doublet.
2-Bromobutane has a 1H CHBr signal near 4.1 ppm, a 3H doublet and a 3H triplet, not a 6H doublet.
2-Bromo-2-methylpropane gives a single 9H singlet near 1.8 ppm.

q: Which C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub> aromatic compound gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: A 5H signal near 7.2 ppm tells you how the ring is substituted. Then read the alkyl pattern.
w: 5 aromatic H → a monosubstituted benzene. The alkyl part shows a 6H doublet and a 1H septet at 2.90 ppm (benzylic CH): an isopropyl group. Isopropylbenzene (cumene).
x: Propylbenzene has a monosubstituted ring too, but its alkyl signals are a triplet (2H), a sextet (2H) and a triplet (3H), not a doublet and septet.
4-Ethyltoluene is disubstituted (4 aromatic H) and shows a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet, an ethyl quartet and triplet.
1,3,5-Trimethylbenzene shows only two singlets: 3 aromatic H near 6.8 and 9H near 2.3 ppm.

q: Which <sup>1</sup>H NMR data set belongs to the ketone shown?
h: Find each set of H, its neighbors (n + 1), and whether it sits next to C=O (2–2.6 ppm) or on an O-bearing carbon (3.3–4.2 ppm).
w: 3-Methyl-2-butanone: the acetyl CH3 has no neighbors (s, 3H, ≈2.1); the CH is next to C=O and has six methyl neighbors (septet, 1H, ≈2.6); the two CH3 each see the one CH (d, 6H, ≈1.1). δ 2.58 (septet, 1H), 2.13 (s, 3H), 1.10 (d, 6H).
x: The multiplicities are swapped: the 1H signal has 6 neighbors (septet) and the 6H signal has 1 neighbor (doublet).
This is the pattern of 2-pentanone (a propyl chain), which has 4 signals; the drawn ketone has an isopropyl group.
3.6 ppm is too far downfield for a CH next to C=O (2–2.6 ppm); that shift fits an O–CH, as in an ester or ether.

q: A C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O compound gives the broadband-decoupled <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: Count the signals first, then use the shift above 200 ppm to decide between a ketone and an aldehyde.
w: Three signals for five carbons means symmetry. The peak at 211.8 ppm is a ketone C=O (an aldehyde C=O is usually 195–205 ppm and the CHO carbon is CH). 3-Pentanone, (CH3CH2)2C=O, has three kinds of C: C=O, two equivalent CH2 (35.4) and two equivalent CH3 (7.9).
x: 2-Pentanone has no symmetry: all five carbons differ, so 5 signals.
Pentanal has 5 different carbons (5 signals), with the CHO carbon near 202 ppm.
3-Methyl-2-butanone has 4 kinds of carbon (C=O, CH, acetyl CH<sub>3</sub>, two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub>), so 4 signals.

q: Predict the DEPT spectra of 3-methyl-1-butanol (shown). In DEPT-135, CH and CH<sub>3</sub> peaks point up (positive) and CH<sub>2</sub> peaks point down (negative).
h: First count the distinct carbons and classify each as C, CH, CH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>. DEPT-90 shows only CH.
w: HOCH2–CH2–CH(CH3)2 has 4 distinct carbons: CH2O, CH2, CH and one signal for both equivalent CH3. DEPT-90 shows only the CH (1 peak). DEPT-135 shows CH and CH3 up (2 positive) and the two CH2 down (2 negative). DEPT-90: 1 peak; DEPT-135: 2 positive, 2 negative.
x: The two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent (both on the same CH), so they give one positive peak, not two.
DEPT-90 shows only CH carbons; CH<sub>3</sub> carbons do not appear in it.
In DEPT-135, CH<sub>2</sub> carbons give negative peaks; the CH<sub>2</sub>O and CH<sub>2</sub> carbons point down.

q: A C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> compound gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown; the DEPT result (C, CH, CH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>) is written over each peak. Which structure is it?
h: Use DBE = 1 and the two peaks above 100 ppm. Which alkene carbon is quaternary, and which kind is the sp<sup>3</sup> CH?
w: DBE = 1 and two sp2 peaks (154.6 C, 107.0 CH2) → a 1,1-disubstituted alkene, R2C=CH2. The sp3 carbons are one CH (35.7) and two kinds of CH3, with no CH2. Five signals for six carbons means two CH3 are equivalent: an isopropyl group. 2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene, CH2=C(CH3)CH(CH3)2.
x: 4-Methyl-1-pentene has five signals too, but its alkene carbons are =CH (≈138, CH) and =CH<sub>2</sub>, and it has an sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>; no quaternary C.
2-Ethyl-1-butene has a quaternary alkene C and =CH<sub>2</sub>, but only 4 signals and its sp<sup>3</sup> carbons are CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub> (no CH).
2-Methyl-2-pentene has a trisubstituted alkene with an sp<sup>2</sup> CH (≈125) and 6 signals (the two methyls on C2 are cis and trans to the ethyl, so they differ).

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: DBE first. Then: what does a 1H signal near 9.6 ppm mean, and why is it a doublet rather than a triplet?
w: DBE = 1. The 1H signal at 9.62 ppm is an aldehyde H; it is a doublet, so the α carbon carries one H. A 6H doublet plus a 1H multiplet (that α-CH) is an isopropyl group. (CH3)2CH–CHO, 2-methylpropanal.
x: Butanal also has a CHO, but its α carbon is CH<sub>2</sub>: its CHO would be a triplet, and it would give 4 signals including a 3H triplet.
2-Butanone has no H above 3 ppm; its signals are a 2H quartet, a 3H singlet and a 3H triplet.
3-Buten-1-ol has vinyl H at 5–6 ppm (3H total), an OCH<sub>2</sub> near 3.7 and an OH; nothing near 9.6 ppm.

q: An ester C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: Two candidate esters have an isopropyl group and an isolated CH<sub>3</sub>. The shift of the septet tells you which side of the ester O the isopropyl is on.
w: 1H septet + 6H doublet = isopropyl; 3H singlet = isolated CH3. The septet is at 4.99 ppm, so the CH is bonded to the ester O (O–CH, strongly deshielded), and the singlet at 2.02 ppm is CH3C=O. Isopropyl acetate, CH3CO2CH(CH3)2.
x: Methyl 2-methylpropanoate has the same three signal types, but its septet (CH next to C=O) is near 2.5 ppm and its singlet (OCH<sub>3</sub>) near 3.7 ppm.
Propyl acetate has a propyl group: an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, a CH<sub>2</sub> sextet and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet (4 signals).
Ethyl propanoate shows two ethyl groups (two quartets and two triplets), no septet or singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown, with DEPT results written over the peaks. Which structure is it?
h: Three of the choices give three signals. Use DEPT: which carbon is bonded to O, and is it C, CH or CH<sub>2</sub>?
w: DBE = 0. Three signals for five carbons: a CH2 bonded to O (73.4), a quaternary C (32.6) and CH3 (26.0, three equivalent methyls). (CH3)3C–CH2OH, 2,2-dimethyl-1-propanol, fits.
x: tert-Butyl methyl ether also gives three signals, but its O-bearing carbon is quaternary (≈73, C) and it has an OCH<sub>3</sub> near 49 ppm; it has no CH<sub>2</sub>.
3-Pentanol gives three signals, but its O-bearing carbon is a CH (≈74), with CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub> upfield; no quaternary C.
2-Methyl-2-butanol has four kinds of carbon (C–O quaternary, CH<sub>2</sub>, two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub>, and the ethyl CH<sub>3</sub>): 4 signals.

q: How can <sup>1</sup>H NMR best distinguish isomers I and II?
c: I shows a 1H vinyl signal near 5.2 ppm; II shows 2H of vinyl signals near 4.7 ppm.
I shows 2H of vinyl signals near 4.7 ppm; II shows a 1H vinyl signal near 5.2 ppm.
Neither has vinyl H, so only <sup>13</sup>C NMR can tell them apart.
They have the same molecular weight, so NMR cannot tell them apart.
h: Count the H on the sp<sup>2</sup> carbons of each isomer and integrate the 4.5–6.5 ppm region.
w: I, 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, has one vinyl H (≈5.2 ppm, 1H). II, 2-methyl-1-butene, CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3, has a =CH2 group (≈4.7 ppm, 2H). The integration of the vinyl region (1H vs 2H) distinguishes them.
x: The assignments are reversed: the trisubstituted alkene I has one vinyl H, and the 1,1-disubstituted alkene II has two.
Both are alkenes with H on sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, so both show vinyl signals in the 4.5–6.5 ppm region.
Isomers always share a molecular weight; NMR distinguishes them by their different H environments.

q: An aromatic hydrocarbon C8H10 gives five signals in its 13C NMR spectrum. Which compound is it?
h: Draw the symmetry element of each isomer and count the distinct ring carbons, then add the alkyl carbons.
w: 1,3-Dimethylbenzene has a mirror plane through C2 and C5: ring carbons C1/C3, C2, C4/C6 and C5 (4 signals) plus one CH3 signal = 5 signals.
x: 1,2-Dimethylbenzene: ring carbons C1/C2, C3/C6, C4/C5 (3) + CH<sub>3</sub> = 4 signals.
1,4-Dimethylbenzene: ring carbons C1/C4 and the four CH (2) + CH<sub>3</sub> = 3 signals.
Ethylbenzene: four ring signals (ipso, ortho, meta, para) + CH<sub>2</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub> = 6 signals.

q: An ester C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives only two singlets in its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum, as shown. Which structure is it?
h: Two choices give a 9H singlet and a 3H singlet. Which CH<sub>3</sub> is on O (3.3–4.2 ppm) and which is next to C=O (≈2 ppm)?
w: A 9H singlet (t-Bu) and a 3H singlet. The 3H singlet at 3.66 ppm is an O–CH3, and the t-Bu at 1.20 ppm is on the carbonyl side. Methyl 2,2-dimethylpropanoate, (CH3)3CCO2CH3.
x: tert-Butyl acetate also gives two singlets (9H, 3H), but its CH<sub>3</sub> is next to C=O (≈2.0 ppm) and its t-Bu is on O (≈1.45 ppm); no peak near 3.7.
Isobutyl acetate gives four signals: OCH<sub>2</sub> doublet, acetyl singlet, CH multiplet and 6H doublet.
Ethyl butanoate shows two ethyl-type patterns (quartet, triplets, sextet), not just singlets.

q: The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of ethanol in CDCl<sub>3</sub> is shown. A drop of D<sub>2</sub>O is added and the tube is shaken. What change is seen?
c: The broad singlet near 2.6 ppm disappears; the rest are unchanged.
The quartet at 3.69 ppm becomes a triplet; the other signals stay the same.
The triplet at 1.22 ppm disappears; the other signals stay the same.
The broad singlet near 2.6 ppm becomes a triplet from coupling to the CH<sub>2</sub>.
h: Which H in ethanol is acidic enough to swap with deuterium? Deuterium does not appear in a <sup>1</sup>H spectrum.
w: The O–H proton exchanges with D2O (ROH + D2O ⇌ ROD + HOD), and O–D gives no 1H signal, so the broad OH singlet disappears. The CH2 quartet was never split by the OH (fast exchange already removed that coupling), so it stays a quartet.
x: The CH<sub>2</sub> was not coupled to the OH in the first place (fast exchange), so removing the OH H does not change its quartet.
C–H hydrogens do not exchange with D<sub>2</sub>O; only the O–H proton does.
The OH becomes OD, which has no <sup>1</sup>H signal at all; it cannot become a triplet.

q: Which tagged hydrogens give a 2H signal near δ 2.3?
h: Allylic H (on a carbon next to C=C) appear near 1.6–2.4 ppm; vinyl H at 4.5–6.5; H on O-bearing carbons at 3.3–4.2.
w: a =CH2 ≈ 5.0, b =CH ≈ 5.8, c allylic CH2 ≈ 2.3, d OCH2 ≈ 3.4 ppm. The 2H signal near 2.3 ppm is the allylic CH2, c.
x: H a are terminal vinyl H, near 5.0 ppm.
H b is a single vinyl H (1H) near 5.8 ppm.
H d are on a carbon bonded to O, near 3.4 ppm.

q: A <sup>13</sup>C NMR signal at δ 208 ppm most likely comes from which kind of carbon?
c: An sp<sup>3</sup> carbon bonded to O
h: Recall the <sup>13</sup>C regions: sp<sup>3</sup> C 0–50, C–O 50–90, C=C 100–150, ester/acid C=O 160–185, ketone/aldehyde C=O 190–220.
w: Ketone and aldehyde carbonyl carbons appear at 190–220 ppm. A signal at 208 ppm is a ketone C=O.
x: Ester C=O carbons are shielded by the extra O lone pair donation and appear near 165–175 ppm.
Alkene carbons appear at roughly 100–150 ppm.
sp<sup>3</sup> carbons bonded to O (alcohols, ethers) appear at about 50–90 ppm.

q: How does the tagged CH2 (a) of 2-butanone appear in the 1H NMR spectrum?
h: Neighbors are H on adjacent carbons only. Does the carbonyl carbon carry any H?
w: C2 is the C=O carbon and carries no H, so the CH2 couples only to the 3 H on C4: n + 1 = 4, a quartet, 2H. Being α to the C=O, it appears near 2.4 ppm.
x: A sextet counts the acetyl CH<sub>3</sub> as a neighbor, but it is on the far side of the C=O carbon (4 bonds away) and does not split the CH<sub>2</sub>.
A triplet would mean 2 neighbors; the adjacent carbon is a CH<sub>3</sub> with 3 H.
3.6 ppm is typical of a CH<sub>2</sub> bonded to O; a CH<sub>2</sub> next to C=O appears at 2–2.6 ppm.

q: Which C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> isomer gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: Only two signals, 4H : 2H. Which isomer has two equivalent CH<sub>2</sub>Cl groups?
w: A 4H triplet at 3.70 ppm (two equivalent CH2Cl, each next to a CH2) and a 2H quintet at 2.21 ppm (the middle CH2, with 4 neighbors). 1,3-Dichloropropane, ClCH2CH2CH2Cl.
x: 1,2-Dichloropropane gives three signal groups: a CHCl multiplet (1H), a CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (2H) and a 3H doublet near 1.6 ppm.
1,1-Dichloropropane shows a CHCl<sub>2</sub> triplet near 5.8 ppm (1H), a CH<sub>2</sub> multiplet and a 3H triplet.
2,2-Dichloropropane gives a single 6H singlet near 2.2 ppm.

q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown (DEPT results over the peaks). All four choices give three <sup>13</sup>C signals. Which one is it?
h: DBE = 2. Ask what the 127 ppm peak is (sp or sp<sup>2</sup>, and how many H), and what the two upfield CH<sub>2</sub> signals require.
w: The only low-field peak (127.3) is an sp2 CH; there are no other sp2 or sp carbons, so there is just one C=C, and DBE = 2 requires a ring. Two kinds of sp3 CH2 and no CH3: cyclohexene (C1/C2, C3/C6, C4/C5).
x: 3-Hexyne has sp carbons near 81 ppm with no H (DEPT: absent, quaternary) and a CH<sub>3</sub> signal; no sp<sup>2</sup> CH.
1,5-Hexadiene shows two sp<sup>2</sup> peaks (≈138 CH and ≈115 CH<sub>2</sub>) and only one sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>.
(E,E)-2,4-Hexadiene has two sp2 CH peaks and a CH3 near 18 ppm; it has no CH2.

q: Which C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Cl isomer gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: Nothing appears between 3 and 4.5 ppm. What does that say about the carbon bearing Cl?
w: No signal near 3.4–4 ppm means the C–Cl carbon has no H: a tertiary chloride. A 6H singlet (two CH3 on the C–Cl carbon) plus an ethyl group (2H quartet, 3H triplet): 2-chloro-2-methylbutane.
x: 1-Chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane has a CH<sub>2</sub>Cl singlet near 3.4 ppm and a 9H singlet; no ethyl pattern.
2-Chloro-3-methylbutane has a CHCl near 3.9 ppm (1H) and two different CH<sub>3</sub> doublets.
3-Chloropentane has a CHCl near 3.8 ppm (1H) and a 6H triplet; no 6H singlet.

q: Which chloroalkane gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: The 1H signal is a triplet and the 2H signal is a doublet: how many neighbors does each set have?
w: A 1H triplet (2 neighbors) at 5.77 ppm, deshielded by two Cl (CHCl2), and a 2H doublet (1 neighbor) at 3.96 ppm (CH2Cl). Cl2CH–CH2Cl, 1,1,2-trichloroethane.
x: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane has only a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet (3H) near 2.7 ppm.
1,2-Dichloroethane has four equivalent H: one singlet near 3.7 ppm.
1,1-Dichloroethane gives a 1H quartet (≈5.9) and a 3H doublet (≈2.1), the reverse multiplicities and a different ratio.

q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of 4-ethyltoluene (shown)? Assume the aromatic H that are not related by symmetry give separate signals.
h: The para-disubstituted ring has a mirror plane through C1 and C4. How many kinds of ring H does that leave?
w: Ring H: two ortho to CH3 (equivalent pair) and two ortho to the ethyl (equivalent pair) = 2 signals (they appear as two doublets). Plus Ar–CH3 (s), CH2 (q) and the ethyl CH3 (t) = 5 signals.
x: Four treats all four ring H as one set; the H next to CH<sub>3</sub> and the H next to ethyl are different.
Six would need one more set; the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are already counted separately and the ring has only two kinds of H.
Seven counts each ring H separately, ignoring the mirror plane that makes them pairwise equivalent.

q:
Which pairs of compounds can be distinguished by the number of signals in their 13C NMR spectra alone?
I. cyclohexane and methylcyclopentane
II. pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane
III. 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane
h: Count the <sup>13</sup>C signals for each of the six compounds. A pair is distinguished only if the counts differ.
w: I: cyclohexane 1 signal, methylcyclopentane 4 → different. III: 1-chlorobutane 4, 2-chlorobutane 4 → same count (shifts differ, but the count does not). II: pentane 3 (C1/C5, C2/C4, C3), 2,2-dimethylpropane 2 → different. I and II only.
x: Pair II is also distinguished: pentane gives 3 signals and 2,2-dimethylpropane gives 2.
Pair III gives the same count (4 and 4), while pair I is distinguished (1 vs 4 signals).
Pair III fails: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane each give 4 signals.

q: An ester C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR data below, with raw integral areas. How many hydrogens does the δ 0.93 signal represent?
h: Add the areas, divide by the total number of H, then divide each area by that value.
w: Total area = 21.0 + 31.6 + 10.4 + 63.0 = 126.0 for 12 H, or 10.5 per H. The signals are 2H, 3H, 1H and 63.0/10.5 = 6H. (This fits isobutyl acetate: OCH2 d, CH3C=O s, CH m, (CH3)2 d.)
x: 3H assumes the 0.93 signal is one CH<sub>3</sub>, but its area is twice that of the 3H singlet at 2.05 ppm (63.0 vs 31.6), so it is 6H.
9H would require 63.0 to be 75% of the total area, but it is 50% (63.0 of 126.0).
4H does not match any whole-number ratio of the areas; 63.0/10.5 = 6.

q: Which alkane gives exactly three signals in its 1H NMR spectrum?
h: For each structure, group the H into equivalent sets (same carbon type, related by symmetry).
w: 2,2-Dimethylbutane, (CH3)3C–CH2CH3: the t-Bu methyls (9H, s), the CH2 (2H, q) and the CH3 (3H, t). Three signals.
x: 2-Methylbutane has 4 sets: two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> (6H), CH, CH<sub>2</sub> and the ethyl CH<sub>3</sub>.
2,3-Dimethylbutane is highly symmetric: four equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> and two equivalent CH give only 2 signals.
2,2,4-Trimethylpentane has 4 sets: t-Bu (9H), CH<sub>2</sub>, CH and two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> (6H).

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O shows the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR data below. Its IR spectrum has no O–H band. Which structure is it?
h: DBE = 1. Is there any carbon above 100 ppm? If not, where does the degree of unsaturation go?
w: DBE = 1, but no 13C peak above 100 ppm, so there is no C=O or C=C: the unsaturation is a ring. Only two carbon environments (67.9, C–O; 25.7) and two 4H signals mean a symmetric ring with two OCH2 and two CH2: tetrahydrofuran.
x: 2-Butanone has a C=O carbon near 209 ppm and four <sup>13</sup>C signals.
Ethyl vinyl ether has two sp<sup>2</sup> carbons (≈150 and ≈87 ppm) and vinyl H at 4–6.5 ppm.
3-Buten-1-ol has sp<sup>2</sup> carbons (≈135, 117 ppm), vinyl H and an O–H (IR ≈3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>).

q: The H of a terminal alkyne (≈2 ppm) appears well upfield of a vinyl H (4.5–6.5 ppm). Why?
c: Circulation of the cylindrical π electrons around the C≡C axis creates a local field that shields the alkyne H.
The sp carbon is less electronegative than an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, so the C–H bond is more electron-rich.
The alkyne H exchanges rapidly with the solvent, which moves its signal upfield.
The alkyne H has no neighbors to couple with, and uncoupled H appear upfield.
h: Think about magnetic anisotropy: where does the induced field of the π cloud reinforce or oppose the applied field?
w: The applied field drives the π electrons of a triple bond to circulate around the bond axis. The induced field opposes the applied field along the axis, exactly where the alkyne H sits, so the H is shielded by the induced π-electron field. In an alkene the H lies in the deshielding region of the π circulation.
x: The trend runs the other way: an sp carbon (50% s character) is more electronegative than sp<sup>2</sup>, which by itself would deshield the H.
Terminal alkyne C–H does not exchange quickly with CDCl<sub>3</sub>; exchange affects O–H and N–H protons.
Coupling changes the splitting of a signal, not its chemical shift.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkane shown?
h: Find every seven-carbon chain. When two chains tie in length, pick the one carrying more substituents; then number for the lowest locant set and list prefixes alphabetically.
w: Two different seven-carbon chains exist: one runs through the ethyl branch, the other through the isopropyl end. When chains tie in length, the parent is the one with more substituents. Running through the isopropyl end gives three substituents (methyl, ethyl, methyl), while running through the ethyl gives only two. Numbering from the isopropyl end gives locants {2,3,5}, lower than {3,5,6} from the other end. Prefixes are listed alphabetically, with di/tri ignored, so ethyl comes before methyl: 3-ethyl-2,5-dimethylheptane.
x: The locants are right, but prefixes must be listed alphabetically (ethyl before methyl). The multiplier “di” does not count when alphabetizing.
This numbers from the wrong end. {3,5,6} loses to {2,3,5} at the first point of difference.
This heptane chain runs through the ethyl group and carries only two substituents. Among equally long chains, the one with more substituents is the parent.

q: A student names a compound “2-ethylpentane.” What is the correct IUPAC name for the structure the student had in mind?
h: Draw the structure the student described, then look for a longer continuous chain.
w: Draw it: a pentane chain with CH2CH3 on C2. Following the ethyl branch gives a six-carbon chain, so the parent is hexane, not pentane. The one-carbon branch (the old C1 of pentane) then sits on C3 of the hexane chain when numbered from the nearer end: 3-methylhexane. An ethyl group on C2 always signals a missed longer chain.
x: An ethyl group on C2 extends the chain by two carbons, so pentane is not the longest chain and the name is wrong.
This numbers the hexane from the far end. The methyl must get the lowest locant, 3.
3-Ethylpentane is a different isomer of C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>: its ethyl is on the central carbon, so no longer chain exists. The student's ethyl is on C2, which creates a six-carbon chain.

q: Which name describes the compound shown, including its relative configuration?
h: Decide whether the two groups point to the same face of the ring (both wedged or both dashed). With a tie in locants, the group cited first alphabetically gets C1.
w: The two ring bonds to the substituents use the same wedge/dash sense, so both groups are on the same face: cis. The ring locants are {1,3} either way, so the tie is broken alphabetically: ethyl is cited first and gets C1. The name is cis-1-ethyl-3-methylcyclohexane.
x: Both substituents are drawn on the same face of the ring, which is cis. Trans would need one wedge and one dash.
Prefixes are cited in alphabetical order, so ethyl comes before methyl in the name.
When the locant set ties ({1,3} both ways), the alphabetically first prefix (ethyl) gets the lower number, C1.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkene shown?
h: Two five-carbon chains contain the C=C. Choose the one with more substituents, then rank the groups on each alkene carbon by CIP rules.
w: Both five-carbon chains contain the double bond (one runs into the ethyl group, one into the isopropyl group). The tie is broken by the number of substituents: the chain through the isopropyl carbon carries an ethyl and a methyl (two) versus one isopropyl group for the other chain. Number from the end nearer the C=C: pent-2-ene with 3-ethyl and 4-methyl. For E/Z: on C2, CH3 > H; on C3, CH(CH3)2 (C,C,H) > CH2CH3 (C,H,H). The CH3 on C2 and the isopropyl carbon are on the same side, so the alkene is (Z)-3-ethyl-4-methylpent-2-ene.
x: The higher-priority groups (CH<sub>3</sub> on C2 and the isopropyl carbon on C3) are on the same side of the double bond, which is Z.
This chain is as long but carries only one substituent. With equal chains, the parent is the one with more substituents.
The double bond must get the lowest locant, so numbering starts at the CH<sub>3</sub>CH= end (pent-2-ene, not pent-3-ene).

q: How many degrees of unsaturation (rings + π bonds) does a compound with formula C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>ClNO<sub>2</sub> have?
h: Treat a halogen like H, ignore O, and let each N add one to the H count allowed.
w: DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2 = (18 + 2 + 1 − 10 − 1)/2 = 10/2 = 5. Oxygen does not change the count. 4-Chlorophenylalanine (a benzene ring, 4, plus a C=O, 1) is one compound with this formula.
x: This comes from subtracting the nitrogen instead of adding it. Each N raises the number of H atoms a saturated molecule can hold by one.
This adds the Cl to the allowed H count instead of subtracting it. A halogen takes the place of an H, so it is subtracted like H.
This counts oxygen as if it lowered the H count. Divalent O does not change the DBE.

q: Capsaicin, the compound that makes chili peppers hot, is shown. Which functional group is not present in capsaicin?
h: Look at what is attached to each oxygen and to the carbonyl carbon.
w: Go group by group. The C=O carbon is bonded to N, so that unit is an amide (a secondary amide, N–H). The OH sits directly on the benzene ring, which makes it a phenol. The OCH3 on the ring is an aryl methyl ether. There is also a trans C=C. No carbonyl carbon is bonded to an O–C, so there is no ester.
x: The C(=O)–NH unit is an amide; capsaicin has one.
The OH bonded directly to the aromatic ring is a phenol; capsaicin has one.
The CH<sub>3</sub>O– group on the ring is an ether (an aryl methyl ether); capsaicin has one.

q: Cocaine is shown. Which choice correctly lists its functional groups (ignore the benzene ring)?
c: two esters and a tertiary amine
two esters and a secondary amine
an ester, a ketone, and a tertiary amine
an ester, an ether, and a tertiary amide
h: For each C=O, ask what the carbonyl carbon is bonded to. For the nitrogen, count its carbon neighbors and check whether any is a C=O.
w: Both carbonyl carbons are bonded to an O–C: one is a methyl ester (CO2CH3) and one is a benzoate ester. The nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and a CH3) and none is a carbonyl carbon, so it is a tertiary amine. Answer: two esters and a tertiary amine.
x: The N carries a CH<sub>3</sub> and two ring carbons, three carbon groups in all, which makes it tertiary.
Neither carbonyl carbon is flanked by two carbons; each is bonded to an oxygen that carries a carbon, so both are esters.
The nitrogen is not bonded to a carbonyl carbon, so it is an amine, not an amide; and the O–C single bonds belong to esters, not a simple ether.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the bicyclic compound shown?
h: Count the carbons in each bridge between the two bridgeheads. Number from a bridgehead around the longest bridge, then the next longest, and the shortest bridge last.
w: The bridgeheads are joined by bridges of 3, 2 and 1 carbons (8 carbons total), so the ring system is bicyclo[3.2.1]octane, with the numbers in decreasing order. Numbering starts at a bridgehead (C1), runs around the 3-carbon bridge (C2–C4) to the other bridgehead (C5), continues through the 2-carbon bridge (C6, C7) and ends on the 1-carbon bridge (C8). The methyl is on the 2-carbon bridge next to a bridgehead. Choosing C1 so that this carbon is reached first in the 2-carbon bridge gives it locant 6 (the other choice gives 7): 6-methylbicyclo[3.2.1]octane.
x: This starts at the wrong bridgehead. Both numberings are allowed by the bridge order, so pick the one giving the methyl the lower locant, 6.
C2–C4 belong to the longest (3-carbon) bridge. The methyl is on the 2-carbon bridge, which is numbered after the 3-carbon bridge.
Bridge sizes are cited in decreasing order: [3.2.1], not [2.3.1].

q: Which structure is (R)-4-chloropent-1-ene?
h: First find structures with the right chain and Cl position (C=C at C1, Cl at C4). Then assign R/S at C4: Cl > CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> > CH<sub>3</sub> > H.
w: Only two choices have five chain carbons with C=C at C1–C2 and Cl at C4. At C4 the priorities are Cl > CH2CH=CH2 > CH3 > H. Viewed with H pointing away, Cl → CH2CH=CH2 → CH3 must run clockwise for R; only one of those two structures does. Its mirror image is the S enantiomer.
x: This is the enantiomer, (S)-4-chloropent-1-ene: the Cl is on the opposite wedge/dash.
The Cl here is on C3, next to the double bond: this is (R)-3-chloropent-1-ene.
This chain has six carbons: (R)-4-chlorohex-1-ene, not a pentene.

q: What is the IUPAC (substitutive) name of the ether shown?
h: Name the larger alkyl group as the parent alkane and the smaller one as an alkoxy prefix.
w: The oxygen joins an ethyl group and an isopropyl group. The larger group (three carbons) is the parent, propane; the smaller becomes the ethoxy prefix. The O is on the middle carbon of propane: 2-ethoxypropane (common name ethyl isopropyl ether).
x: 1-Ethoxypropane has the O on the end carbon of a straight propyl group; here the O is on the central CH carbon.
That compound has a methyl on oxygen and a four-carbon chain; the drawing has an O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> group and a three-carbon branch.
The parent here has only three carbons. A butane parent would need four carbons on one side of the oxygen.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the amine shown?
h: The parent is the longest carbon chain attached to N. The other groups on N are named with the prefix N-.
