w: The nitrogen carries two CH3 groups and a four-carbon sec-butyl group. The longest carbon chain bonded to N is butane, with N on C2 when numbered from the nearer end. The two methyls on nitrogen are cited as N,N-dimethyl: N,N-dimethylbutan-2-amine.
x: The amine suffix must get the lowest possible locant: 2, not 3.
This is an isomer: it has an ethyl and a methyl on N and an isopropyl group. The drawn compound has two N-methyls and a four-carbon chain.
This uses a three-carbon parent and treats a chain carbon as a methyl branch. The parent must be the longest chain, butane.

q: How many degrees of unsaturation does the compound shown have?
h: Each ring counts 1, each double bond 1 and each triple bond 2. Check your count with the formula.
w: Count: one ring (1) + one C=C (1) + the C≡C (2) + the C≡N (2) = 6. Check with the formula C9H9N: (18 + 2 + 1 − 9)/2 = 6.
x: This misses one unit, usually by counting the ring C=C but forgetting the ring itself, or by counting a triple bond as one.
This counts each triple bond as only one degree. A triple bond has two π bonds and counts 2.
This double-counts something. One ring + one C=C + two triple bonds (2 each) gives 6.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Pick the longest chain containing the C=C; Cl is only a prefix. For E/Z, compare the two groups on each alkene carbon by first atoms, then the atoms attached.
w: The longest chain containing the double bond runs CH3–CH=C–CH2CH2CH3 (six carbons), numbered so the C=C gets locant 2. The CH2Cl on C3 is a chloromethyl prefix. On C2, CH3 > H. On C3, CH2Cl outranks the propyl group because its first atom bears (Cl,H,H) versus (C,H,H). The CH3 on C2 and the CH2Cl are on opposite sides, so the alkene is E, even though the main chain itself is drawn cis: (E)-3-(chloromethyl)hex-2-ene.
x: Z would require the two top-priority groups on the same side. Here the CH<sub>2</sub>Cl, not the propyl chain, is the higher-priority group on C3, and it is opposite the CH<sub>3</sub>.
The double bond must get the lowest locant, so number from the CH<sub>3</sub>CH= end (hex-2-ene).
This parent has only five carbons. Halogens are prefixes and do not have to be in the parent chain, so the six-carbon chain wins.

q: The enyne shown gives its multiple bonds the same locants from either end of the chain. What is its correct IUPAC name?
h: Give the multiple bonds, taken together, the lowest locants. If both directions tie, the double bond gets the lower number.
w: Numbering from the alkene end puts the multiple bonds at {1,5}; numbering from the alkyne end also gives {1,5}. When the ene/yne set ties, the rule gives the double bond the lower locant, so C1 is the CH2= carbon. The methyl is then on C4: 4-methylhex-1-en-5-yne. This rule outranks the substituent locant, so the methyl does not get 3.
x: This gives the alkyne locant 1. With a tie in the multiple-bond set, the double bond gets the lower number.
With the C=C at C1, the methyl lands on C4, not C3. Count again from the CH<sub>2</sub>= end.
With the C≡C at C1, the methyl would be on C3. In any case the alkyne end should not be C1 here.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Number so the double bond gets the lowest locant, list halogens alphabetically, then rank each alkene carbon's two groups by atomic number.
w: The double bond must be at C1, so C1 is the CHCl carbon and C2 bears Br and the ethyl group. Prefixes are listed alphabetically: bromo before chloro. On C1, Cl > H; on C2, Br > CH2CH3. Cl and Br are on the same side, so the alkene is Z: (Z)-2-bromo-1-chlorobut-1-ene.
x: Cl and Br, the higher-priority atoms on each alkene carbon, are on the same side. That is Z.
The prefixes must be in alphabetical order: bromo before chloro.
This numbers from the wrong end. The double bond must get the lowest locant, 1.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: OH is the principal group, so it is the suffix and its carbon must be in the parent chain, lowest locant. For E/Z, compare CH<sub>2</sub>OH and isopropyl atom by atom.
w: The OH is the principal characteristic group, so the parent must contain the CH2OH carbon and the name ends in -ol. From that carbon, two four-carbon chains are possible; the one containing the C=C is preferred (more multiple bonds). Number from the OH carbon: but-2-en-1-ol with an isopropyl group on C2. For E/Z, on C2: CH2OH (O,H,H) beats CH(CH3)2 (C,C,H) at the first point of difference, because O > C. On C3: CH3 > H. CH2OH and CH3 are on the same side: (Z)-2-isopropylbut-2-en-1-ol.
x: The isopropyl group has more carbons, but CIP compares atoms one at a time: CH<sub>2</sub>OH carries an O, which beats the C,C,H set of isopropyl. The top groups are on the same side, so Z.
An alcohol is named with the -ol suffix, not as a hydroxy- prefix, and its carbon must be in the parent chain.
The OH carbon must get the lowest locant (C1), not C4.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The OH carbon is C1. Go around the ring in the direction that gives the double bond the lower locant.
w: The alcohol is the principal group, so the OH carbon is C1. Going toward the C=C gives the double bond locants 2,3 (cyclohex-2-ene); the other direction gives 5,6. The methyl then sits on C3: 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
x: The OH carbon must be C1 because the alcohol is the suffix. Here the alkene was numbered first.
This numbers around the ring the long way. The double bond should get the lower locants, 2 and 3.
Here the methyl would be on the C=C carbon next to C1. In the drawing it is on the far alkene carbon, C3.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Assign each center separately. At C2: Cl > C3 (bears Br) > CH<sub>3</sub> > H. At C3: Br > C2 (bears Cl) > CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> > H.
w: Numbering from the left gives locants {2,3}; from the right {3,4}, so the Cl carbon is C2 and the Br carbon is C3 (bromo is cited first alphabetically). At C2: Cl > C3 (Br,C,H) > CH3 > H; as drawn this center is R. At C3: Br > C2 (Cl,C,H) > CH2CH3 > H; also R. Name: (2R,3R)-3-bromo-2-chloropentane.
x: Both descriptors are reversed. This is the enantiomer; recheck which way the H points before reading the direction.
C2 is right but C3 is not. At C3 the C2 branch (Cl,C,H) outranks the ethyl group (C,H,H).
C3 is right but C2 is not. At C2 the C3 branch, which carries Br, outranks CH<sub>3</sub>, and the result is R.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Number the bicyclic system first (C1 bridgehead, then the longer bridges, the one-carbon bridge last). Among the allowed numberings, the double bond gets the lowest locants before the substituent.
w: The ring system is bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (bridges of 2, 2 and 1 carbon). The double bond comes before the substituent in numbering, so the C=C is placed at C2–C3. That leaves two choices of starting bridgehead. Starting at the bridgehead not next to the methyl carbon, the numbering runs C2=C3, C4 (bridgehead), C5 (methyl carbon), C6, and C7 (one-carbon bridge). The other start puts the methyl on C6. Lowest locant: 5-methylbicyclo[2.2.1]hept-2-ene.
x: This starts at the other bridgehead. Both numberings put the C=C at C2, so choose the one giving the methyl the lower locant, 5.
The double bond takes precedence over the substituent for low locants, so it must be at C2, not C5.
C7 is the one-carbon bridge. The methyl in the drawing is on a two-carbon bridge.

q: Which structure is cis-1-bromo-3-methylcyclohexane?
h: First check the positions (1,3 means one carbon between them). Then check that both groups are on the same face (both wedged or both dashed).
w: Two choices are 1,3-disubstituted and two are 1,2. Of the 1,3 pair, the correct one has Br and CH3 on the same face of the ring (both wedges or both dashes), which is cis.
x: This is the 1,3 compound with Br and CH3 on opposite faces: trans-1-bromo-3-methylcyclohexane.
The groups are on adjacent carbons: this is cis-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane.
The groups are on adjacent carbons and on opposite faces: trans-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane.

q: Which of these names is a correct IUPAC name?
h: Draw each one. Check for a longer chain hiding in a branch, then check numbering and alphabetical order.
w: 2,3-Dimethylpentane uses the longest chain (five carbons), the lowest locants ({2,3} beats {3,4}) and a single kind of prefix. Each of the others breaks a rule.
x: An ethyl on C2 extends the chain: the compound is 3-methylpentane.
Prefixes must be alphabetical: 3-ethyl-4-methylhexane.
A methyl on C1 lengthens the chain: the compound is 2-methylbutane.

q: To which functional groups do the carbons labeled a and b belong?
h: Look at what each carbonyl carbon is bonded to besides its C=O oxygen.
w: Carbon a is a C=O carbon single-bonded to a ring oxygen that also carries carbon: that is an ester, and because it is part of a ring it is called a lactone. Carbon b is a C=O carbon bonded to two carbons: a ketone.
x: Carbon a is bonded to an O–C oxygen, which makes it an ester, not a ketone; and b carries no H, so it is not an aldehyde.
A carboxylic acid needs an O–H on the carbonyl carbon. Here the oxygen carries a ring carbon instead, which is an ester.
Carbon a has a C=O, so it is part of an ester, not a plain ether; carbon b is bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone.

q: Epinephrine (adrenaline) is shown. Which choice correctly describes its functional groups?
c: a secondary amine, a secondary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
a primary amine, a primary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
a secondary amine, a tertiary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
an amide, a secondary alcohol, and two phenol OH groups
h: Classify an alcohol by how many carbons are on the C–OH carbon; classify an amine by how many carbons are on N.
w: The nitrogen carries a CH3 and a CH2 (two carbons) and an H: a secondary amine. The side-chain OH carbon is bonded to two carbons (the ring carbon and the CH2), so it is a secondary alcohol. The two OH groups bonded directly to the benzene ring are phenols.
x: The N has two carbon groups (secondary), and the C–OH carbon has two carbon neighbors (secondary).
The C–OH carbon still has one H and two carbon neighbors, which makes it secondary, not tertiary.
There is no carbonyl group, so there is no amide. The nitrogen is an amine.

q:
Morphine is shown. Which statements about its functional groups are correct?
I. It contains a phenol and a secondary alcohol.
II. It contains a tertiary amine.
III. It contains an ester.
h: Find each oxygen and decide what it is bonded to. Then count the carbons on nitrogen.
w: Morphine has three oxygens. One OH is on the benzene ring (phenol). One OH is on a ring CH carbon bonded to two other carbons (secondary alcohol, also allylic). The third O bridges an aromatic carbon and an sp3 carbon with no C=O anywhere, so it is a cyclic ether, not an ester. The N carries three carbons (CH3 and two ring carbons): a tertiary amine. So I and II are true and III is false: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: the nitrogen is bonded to three carbons, which makes it a tertiary amine.
Statement III is false: the ring oxygen is an ether. An ester needs a C=O carbon bonded to the O, and morphine has no C=O.
Statement III is false: morphine has no carbonyl group, so it cannot contain an ester.

q: How many degrees of unsaturation does nicotine (shown, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>14</sub>N<sub>2</sub>) have?
h: Count rings and π bonds, or use the formula: each N adds one to the allowed H count.
w: From the structure: two rings (2) + three π bonds in the pyridine ring (3) = 5. From the formula: (2·10 + 2 + 2 − 14)/2 = 10/2 = 5.
x: This counts the three pyridine π bonds but only one of the two rings. Both rings count.
Three is the π-bond count alone; the two rings each add one more.
This adds an extra unit, as if the formula had two fewer H. Check with (2C + 2 + N − H)/2.

q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>10</sub> takes up 2 equivalents of H<sub>2</sub> over Pt to give C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>. How many rings does it contain?
h: Find the total degrees of unsaturation, then subtract the π bonds that hydrogenation removed.
w: C7H10 has DBE = (14 + 2 − 10)/2 = 3. Hydrogenation over Pt saturates C=C and C≡C bonds but does not open ordinary rings. Two equivalents of H2 account for 2 π bonds, and the product C7H14 still has DBE 1, so the compound has 1 ring.
x: With no rings, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>10</sub> would add three H<sub>2</sub> to reach C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>. Only two were taken up.
Two rings would leave only one π bond, so only one H<sub>2</sub> would add.
Three rings would leave no π bonds, so no H<sub>2</sub> would add.

q: Which structure is (E)-4-methylpent-2-en-1-ol?
h: Build the five-carbon chain from the OH carbon (C1), put the C=C between C2 and C3 and the methyl on C4, then check the chain continues trans across the C=C.
w: C1 bears the OH, the double bond is C2=C3 and C4 carries a methyl, so C4 is a CH(CH3)2 unit. On C2 the higher group is CH2OH and on C3 it is the isopropyl group (each partner is H). For E they must be on opposite sides of the double bond, as in the correct structure.
x: This is the Z isomer: CH<sub>2</sub>OH and the isopropyl group are on the same side.
This is (E)-hex-2-en-1-ol, a straight chain with no methyl branch.
Here the branch is on C3 (an alkene carbon): this is 3-methylpent-2-en-1-ol.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The locants are {1,2} either way, so the prefix cited first alphabetically gets C1. Compare “methoxy” and “methyl” letter by letter. Then assign each center.
w: Both numberings give {1,2}. The tie goes to the prefix cited first alphabetically: m-e-t-h-o-xy comes before m-e-t-h-y-l, so the OCH3 carbon is C1. At C1: OCH3 > C2 (C,C,H) > C6 (C,H,H) > H, giving R. At C2: C1 (O,C,H) > C3 (C,H,H) > CH3 > H, also R. The two groups are trans. Name: (1R,2R)-1-methoxy-2-methylcyclohexane.
x: This is the enantiomer: both centers are inverted.
(1R,2S) is the cis diastereomer. In the drawing the groups are trans, and C2 is R.
This describes the same molecule but numbers it wrongly. With tied locants, methoxy (cited first) must get C1.

q: Which compound is a secondary amine?
h: Amines are classified by the number of carbons bonded to nitrogen, not by the kind of carbon the N is attached to.
w: Count the carbons on N. The correct choice, N-methylcyclohexanamine, has N bonded to a CH3 and a ring carbon (two carbons, one N–H): a secondary amine. This is different from alcohols, where the class depends on the carbon bearing the OH.
x: The NH<sub>2</sub> is on a carbon that has three other carbons, but the N itself bears only one carbon: this is a primary amine (1-methylcyclohexan-1-amine).
The N bears only one carbon (the CH<sub>2</sub>): cyclohexylmethanamine is a primary amine.
The N bears three carbons: N,N-dimethylcyclohexanamine is a tertiary amine.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkane shown?
h: Find the longest chain. Then compare the two locant sets term by term and take the set that is lower at the first point of difference.
w: The longest chain has seven carbons, running from a CH3 of the tert-butyl end to the isopropyl end. Numbering from the tert-butyl end gives substituents at {2,2,4,6}; from the other end {2,4,6,6}. At the first point of difference (second term) 2 < 4, so number from the tert-butyl end. Alphabetical order (ignoring tri-) puts ethyl first: 4-ethyl-2,2,6-trimethylheptane.
x: This numbers from the wrong end. {2,2,4,6} beats {2,4,6,6} at the second term. The sum of locants is not the rule.
Prefixes must be in alphabetical order. The multiplier “tri” is ignored, so ethyl precedes methyl.
This uses a six-carbon chain. A seven-carbon chain exists, and the longest chain is the parent.

q: A student named a compound “3-ethyl-2-methylhex-4-ene.” What is the correct IUPAC name of that compound (ignore E/Z)?
h: Draw the student's structure. The double bond must get the lowest locant, and among equally long chains the one with more substituents is the parent.
w: The student's structure is CH3–CH(CH3)–CH(C2H5)–CH=CH–CH3. The chain is right (six carbons, two substituents; the alternative six-carbon chain through the ethyl group carries only one isopropyl substituent), but it must be numbered from the end nearer the C=C. Renumbered: hex-2-ene with ethyl on C4 and methyl on C5: 4-ethyl-5-methylhex-2-ene.
x: The locants are right, but prefixes must be alphabetical: ethyl before methyl.
This chain runs through the ethyl group and carries one substituent. The equally long chain with two substituents is preferred.
This is a different compound, with the double bond moved to C2–C3 in the original numbering.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The parent is the longest chain (the Br carbon need not be a branch). At the stereocenter, compare CH<sub>2</sub>Br, CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The longest chain is four carbons and includes the CH2Br carbon, which is C1 (lowest locants {1,2}). At C2: CH2Br (Br,H,H) > CH2CH3 (C,H,H) > CH3 > H. As drawn, the center is S: (S)-1-bromo-2-methylbutane.
x: R is the mirror image. Recheck with the H pointing away: the descriptor for the drawn molecule is S.
Halogens are prefixes on the longest chain. The CH<sub>2</sub>Br carbon is part of a four-carbon chain, so it is C1, not a bromomethyl branch.
An ethyl branch on C2 means the chain was too short: the longest chain is butane.

q: Which structure is (2E,4R)-4-bromohex-2-ene?
h: Check three things in turn: Br on C4 (next to the alkene), a trans C=C, and R at C4 (Br > CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> > CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> > H).
w: At C4 the priorities are Br > CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> (C,C,H, counting the duplicate C for the double bond) > CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (C,H,H) > H. Only one structure has the Br on C4, a trans (E) double bond and the R configuration.
x: The double bond is Z here: the C1 methyl and C4 are on the same side.
This is the C4 epimer: the double bond is E, but C4 is S.
The Br is on C5 (two carbons from the alkene): this is (2E,5R)-5-bromohex-2-ene.

q: What is the von Baeyer name of the compound shown?
h: A fused ring system has a zero-carbon bridge. Number from a bridgehead around the largest bridge, then the next, and choose the start that gives the substituent the lowest locant.
w: Nine ring carbons, with bridges of 4, 3 and 0 carbons between the shared bridgeheads: bicyclo[4.3.0]nonane. Numbering: C1 (bridgehead), C2–C5 (four-carbon bridge), C6 (bridgehead), C7–C9 (three-carbon bridge). The methyl is on a five-ring carbon next to a bridgehead. Starting at the bridgehead not attached to it, that carbon becomes C7; the other start makes it C9. Lowest locant: 7-methylbicyclo[4.3.0]nonane (the fusion name is 1-methyloctahydro-1H-indene).
x: This starts at the other bridgehead. Both are allowed, so choose the start that gives the methyl the lower number, 7.
C8 is the middle carbon of the three-carbon bridge. The methyl is on a carbon next to a bridgehead.
Bridge lengths are cited in decreasing order: [4.3.0], not [3.4.0].

q: α-Pinene, a major component of turpentine, is shown. What is its molecular formula?
h: Count the carbons, then use rings + π bonds to find the H count: H = 2C + 2 − 2(DBE).
w: There are 10 carbons (seven in the bicyclic skeleton plus three methyls). The molecule has two rings and one C=C, so DBE = 3. H = 2(10) + 2 − 2(3) = 16. Formula: C10H16, a typical monoterpene.
x: C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub> has DBE 2. α-Pinene has two rings and a C=C, so DBE 3.
C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>14</sub> has DBE 4, one more than the two rings and one C=C present.
This misses a carbon. The gem-dimethyl bridge carbon carries two methyls, and the alkene carbon carries a third.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: In a cycloalkene the C=C carbons are C1 and C2, numbered through the double bond. Then compare the two possible substituent locant sets at the first point of difference.
w: The double-bond carbons must be C1 and C2, with numbering continuing through the C=C. Two directions are possible. If the methyl-bearing alkene carbon is C1, the methyls are at {1,6}. If the other alkene carbon is C1, the methyls are at {2,3}. At the first point of difference 1 < 2, so 1,6-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene is correct, even though {2,3} has the smaller sum.
x: The rule is first point of difference, not the smallest sum. {1,6} beats {2,3} because 1 < 2.
The double bond must be C1=C2, so “6-ene” is never correct in a cycloalkene.
In a cycloalkene the numbering runs through the C=C so it gets locants 1 and 2; a “2-ene” name with these methyl locants does not describe the drawn compound.

q: Which name breaks the IUPAC numbering rules?
h: The triple bond, as part of the parent, gets a lower locant than any substituent.
w: Draw 2-methylpent-3-yne: (CH3)2CH–C≡C–CH3. Numbering from the other end puts the triple bond at C2 instead of C3, so the correct name is 4-methylpent-2-yne. The alkyne locant takes precedence over the methyl locant. 2-Methylpent-3-yne is the incorrect name; the other three are numbered correctly.
x: HC≡C–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: the alkyne already has locant 1, so this name is correct.
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C–C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>: the alkyne gets 2 from this end (3 from the other), so this name is correct.
CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C–CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>: the alkyne gets 2 from this end (4 from the other), so this name is correct.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The OH is the suffix and gets the lowest locant. At the stereocenter, compare CH<sub>2</sub>Br with CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> by the first atoms attached.
w: The alcohol is the principal group (suffix -ol), so number to give the OH carbon the lowest locant: C2 from the CH2Br end (C3 from the other end). Bromo and methyl are prefixes: 1-bromo-3-methylbutan-2-ol. At C2: OH > CH2Br (Br,H,H) > CH(CH3)2 (C,C,H) > H, because Br outranks C at the first point of difference. As drawn the center is R: (R)-1-bromo-3-methylbutan-2-ol.
x: S is the enantiomer. Note that CH<sub>2</sub>Br outranks isopropyl even though isopropyl has more carbons.
The OH suffix must get the lowest locant (2, not 3), even if the prefixes then get higher numbers.
OH is the highest-priority group here, so it must be named as the -ol suffix, not as a hydroxy prefix.

q: Linalool, a fragrant terpene in lavender oil, is shown. Which choice correctly describes it?
c: a tertiary alcohol; 2 degrees of unsaturation
a secondary alcohol; 2 degrees of unsaturation
a tertiary alcohol; 3 degrees of unsaturation
a primary alcohol; 2 degrees of unsaturation
h: Count the carbons bonded to the C–OH carbon. For unsaturation, count rings and π bonds.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (a CH3, the vinyl carbon and the chain CH2), so it is a tertiary alcohol (also allylic). There are no rings and two C=C bonds, so DBE = 2 (formula C10H18O: (20 + 2 − 18)/2 = 2).
x: The C–OH carbon has no H and three carbon neighbors, which makes it tertiary.
There are only two C=C bonds and no rings, so the DBE is 2.
A primary alcohol needs OH on a CH<sub>2</sub> bonded to one carbon. Here the OH carbon has three carbon neighbors.

q: A student named the compound shown “4-ethoxy-2-methylpentane.” What is the correct IUPAC name?
h: The ethoxy group is a prefix like methyl. If both directions give the same locant set, the prefix cited first alphabetically gets the lower number.
w: An ether is named as an alkoxy-substituted alkane. The parent is the five-carbon chain, with substituents at {2,4} from either end. To break the tie, the prefix cited first in alphabetical order (ethoxy) gets the lower locant: 2-ethoxy-4-methylpentane.
x: The locants are right, but prefixes must be cited alphabetically: ethoxy before methyl.
This uses a four-carbon parent. The longest chain has five carbons.
The locant sets tie ({2,4} both ways), so alphabetical order decides: ethoxy is cited first and gets 2.

q: The light-initiated chlorination of methane is a radical chain reaction. Which step is a termination step?
h: Count the radicals on each side of the arrow. Which kind of step lowers the number of radicals?
w: A termination step combines two radicals into a nonradical product, so the number of radicals drops by two and the chain stops. CH3• + Cl• → CH3Cl has two radicals on the left and none on the right. Homolysis of Cl2 makes radicals (initiation), and the two steps that consume one radical and make another are propagation steps.
x: Homolysis of Cl<sub>2</sub> by light creates two radicals from a nonradical; that is initiation.
One radical in, one radical out: this is the second propagation step, which regenerates the Cl• chain carrier.
One radical in, one radical out: this is the first propagation step (H abstraction).

q: Which radical is the most stable?
h: Two effects stabilize a carbon radical: delocalization into a π system and the number of alkyl groups on the radical carbon.
w: Radicals are stabilized by resonance (allylic, benzylic) and by alkyl substitution (hyperconjugation). The 2-phenyl-2-propyl radical, C6H5–C•(CH3)2, is both benzylic (the odd electron is delocalized into the ring) and tertiary, so it has both effects. Benzyl is benzylic but only primary; tert-butyl is tertiary but has no resonance; the vinylic radical is the least stable of the four.
x: Benzyl is resonance-stabilized, but it is primary; adding two methyl groups to the same benzylic carbon stabilizes it further.
tert-Butyl is tertiary but not delocalized; a benzylic radical gains much more from resonance than from hyperconjugation alone.
The odd electron of a vinylic radical sits in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital perpendicular to the π orbitals, so it is not delocalized; vinylic radicals are very unstable.

q:
Rank these radicals from least stable to most stable.
I. CH2=CH•
II. CH3CH2CH2•
III. (CH3)3C•
IV. CH2=CH–CH•–CH3
h: Place the vinylic radical first, then compare a tertiary alkyl radical with a secondary allylic one.
w: Vinylic radicals (I) are the least stable: the odd electron is in an sp2 orbital and cannot be delocalized. Among alkyl radicals, 3° (III) is more stable than 1° (II). The secondary allylic radical IV is delocalized over two carbons, and allylic resonance outweighs one extra alkyl group, so IV is the most stable (a 2° allylic C–H bond is roughly 50 kJ/mol weaker than a 3° C–H). Order: I < II < III < IV.
x: A primary alkyl radical is still more stable than a vinylic radical, whose odd electron sits in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital with no hyperconjugative or resonance help.
This puts the 3° alkyl radical above the allylic radical; resonance delocalization in IV stabilizes more than the extra alkyl group in III.
The vinylic radical is the least stable, not the most; sp<sup>2</sup> character does not stabilize a radical the way it stabilizes a carbanion.

q: Which hydrogen is abstracted most easily by a bromine atom? (The labels mark the carbons; consider an H on each labeled carbon.)
h: The easiest H to remove is the one whose C–H bond is weakest, which is the one that leaves the most stable radical.
w: Removing an H on carbon b gives a radical next to the C=C, an allylic radical delocalized onto the terminal CH2. Allylic C–H bonds (roughly 350–370 kJ/mol) are weaker than a 3° C–H (about 400 kJ/mol), so the H on carbon b goes first. Carbon c is tertiary but not allylic; a is vinylic (strong sp2 C–H); d is a primary C–H.
x: Carbon c gives a 3° alkyl radical, but an allylic radical is more stable than a 3° radical because the odd electron is delocalized.
Carbon a is a vinylic C–H: an sp2 C–H is strong, and the vinylic radical cannot be delocalized.
Carbon d is a methyl group; a primary C–H gives the least stable alkyl radical.

q: 2-Methylbutane is treated with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light at 25 °C. Using relative rates per H of 1° : 2° : 3° = 1 : 3.8 : 5, what percentage of the monochlorinated product is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane?
h: For each kind of H, multiply the number of hydrogens by the rate per H, then divide the 3° share by the total.
w: Count H: two equivalent CH3 on C2 (6 H, 1°), C2–H (1 H, 3°), C3 CH2 (2 H, 2°), C4 CH3 (3 H, 1°). Relative amounts: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane 6 × 1 = 6; 2-chloro-2-methylbutane 1 × 5 = 5; 2-chloro-3-methylbutane 2 × 3.8 = 7.6; 1-chloro-3-methylbutane 3 × 1 = 3. Total 21.6. Tertiary chloride = 5/21.6 = 23%. Chlorination is fast and unselective, so the statistical factor (number of H) matters a lot.
x: 35% is the share of 2-chloro-3-methylbutane (7.6/21.6), the 2° product, not the 3° product.
46% comes from 5/(1 + 3.8 + 5 + 1), which uses rates but ignores how many H of each kind there are.
8.3% is 1/12, a purely statistical count that ignores that a 3° H reacts 5 times faster than a 1° H.

q: 3-Methylpentane is brominated with Br<sub>2</sub> and light. Using relative rates per H of 1° : 2° : 3° = 1 : 82 : 1600, what percentage of the monobromide is 3-bromo-3-methylpentane?
h: Classify all 14 hydrogens first (how many 1°, 2° and 3° H are there?), then weight each class by its rate.
w: 3-Methylpentane has 9 primary H (three CH3 groups), 4 secondary H (two CH2 groups) and 1 tertiary H. Weighted amounts: 1°: 9 × 1 = 9; 2°: 4 × 82 = 328; 3°: 1 × 1600 = 1600. Total = 1937. 3-Bromo-3-methylpentane = 1600/1937 = 83%. Bromination is far more selective than chlorination (compare about 17% for the same 3° product with Cl2), but the four 2° H still take a noticeable share.
x: 90% (1600/1773) counts only 2 secondary H; there are two CH<sub>2</sub> groups, so 4 secondary H.
95% (1600/1683) uses the rates per H without multiplying by the number of each kind of H.
17% is what the chlorination rates (1 : 3.8 : 5) give; the question uses the bromination rates.

q: Why is radical bromination of alkanes much more selective than radical chlorination?
c: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so its transition state is late and radical-like, and radical stability differences show up strongly in the activation energies.
H abstraction by Br• is exothermic, so its transition state is early and resembles the alkane, which makes the different C–H bonds react at very different rates.
Br• is more reactive than Cl•, so it reacts with the weakest C–H bond before it can reach the stronger ones.
The Br–Br bond is weaker than the Cl–Cl bond, so more Br• forms and the most stable radical is reached faster.
h: Use the Hammond postulate: is the H-abstraction step uphill or downhill for each halogen, and what does that say about where its transition state lies?
w: The selectivity-determining step is H abstraction. For Br• it is endothermic (H–Br is weaker than most C–H bonds), so by the Hammond postulate the transition state is late and looks like the alkyl radical; the 3° > 2° > 1° stability gap is largely felt in Ea. For Cl• the step is exothermic, the TS is early and alkane-like, and the rates differ little. Hence the endothermic, late-TS step for Br• makes bromination selective.
x: This reverses the energetics: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, and an early, reactant-like TS would make a reaction less selective, not more.
Br• is less reactive than Cl•. The lower reactivity (higher E<sub>a</sub>) is the reason it can discriminate between C–H bonds.
The Br–Br bond strength affects initiation, not which C–H bond is broken; selectivity is set in the H-abstraction step.

q:
Use the bond dissociation energies in the table. What is ΔH for the first propagation step of the bromination of propane at C2?
Br• + CH3CH2CH3 → HBr + (CH3)2CH•
h: ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed). Which bond breaks and which forms in this one step?
w: One bond breaks, (CH3)2CH–H (413 kJ/mol), and one forms, H–Br (366 kJ/mol). ΔH = 413 − 366 = +47 kJ/mol. This endothermic step is why bromination is slow and selective. The second step, (CH3)2CH• + Br2, is 193 − 299 = −106 kJ/mol, so the chain is still downhill overall.
x: Sign error: subtract energy of bonds formed from bonds broken (413 − 366), not the reverse.
−18 kJ/mol is the same step for chlorination (413 − 431), using H–Cl instead of H–Br.
−59 kJ/mol is ΔH for the overall bromination (sum of both propagation steps), not the first step alone.

q: (S)-3-Methylhexane is treated with Br2 and light. Which describes the major product, 3-bromo-3-methylhexane?
c: A single enantiomer with the same spatial arrangement as the starting alkane
A single enantiomer with the inverted arrangement
Two diastereomers formed in unequal amounts
h: Which H is removed, and what is the shape of the radical carbon that forms?
w: Br• removes the 3° H, which is on the stereocenter itself. The resulting 3° radical is planar (or rapidly inverting), so the original configuration is lost, and Br2 delivers Br to either face equally. The product is racemic 3-bromo-3-methylhexane.
x: Retention would require the radical to stay pyramidal with a fixed shape; the stereocenter is destroyed when its H is removed.
Inversion is the SN2 outcome (backside attack). A radical halogenation has no backside attack; the planar radical reacts on both faces.
Diastereomers need a second stereocenter that survives the reaction. Here the only stereocenter is the carbon that becomes the radical.

q: (S)-2-Chlorobutane is chlorinated with Cl2 and light. Considering only the 2,3-dichlorobutane formed, which statement is correct?
c: It is a mixture of meso-2,3-dichlorobutane and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane in unequal amounts.
It is a mixture of meso-2,3-dichlorobutane and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane in exactly equal amounts.
It is a racemic mixture of (2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane.
It is only (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane, because C2 blocks one face of the radical completely.
h: C2 is not touched when the H on C3 is removed. Which configurations can the new stereocenter at C3 have, and how are the two products related?
w: Abstraction of an H from C3 leaves C2 unchanged (still S; its priorities Cl > CHClCH3 > CH3 > H keep the same order). Cl adds to either face of the planar C3 radical, giving C3 = R or S. (2S,3R) is the meso compound; (2S,3S) is chiral. The two faces of the radical are diastereotopic (C2 is a nearby stereocenter), so the transition states are diastereomeric and the products form in unequal amounts: meso + (2S,3S).
x: The two faces of the C3 radical are not mirror images because C2 is a stereocenter; diastereomeric transition states have different energies, so 50:50 is not expected.
C2 keeps its S configuration, so no (2R,3R) product can form from (S)-2-chlorobutane.
A neighboring stereocenter biases the two faces but does not block one completely; both diastereomers form.

q: What is the major product?
h: With peroxide present, which species adds to the alkene first: H<sup>+</sup> or Br•?
w: Peroxides start a radical chain in which Br• adds to the less substituted carbon (CH2) to give the more stable 3° radical, which then takes H from HBr. Br ends up on the less substituted carbon: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, the anti-Markovnikov product.
x: tert-Butyl bromide is the Markovnikov product of the ionic (no peroxide) HBr addition via a 3° carbocation.
An anti-Markovnikov alcohol comes from hydroboration–oxidation; no oxygen is added here.
A vicinal dibromide comes from Br<sub>2</sub> addition, not from HBr.

q: In the radical chain addition of HBr (with ROOR) to 1-methylcyclohexene, what happens in the first propagation step?
c: Br• adds to carbon b, leaving a 3° radical on carbon a
Br• adds to carbon a, leaving a 2° radical on carbon b
H• adds to carbon b, leaving a 3° radical on carbon a
H+ adds to carbon b, leaving a 3° carbocation on carbon a
h: The chain carrier is made when RO• takes H from HBr. Which radical is that, and where must it add to leave the more stable radical?
w: Initiation: RO• + HBr → ROH + Br•. Propagation step 1: Br• adds to carbon b (the CH end), leaving the 3° radical on carbon a. Step 2: that radical takes H from HBr, giving 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane and a new Br•. The regiochemistry is set by radical stability, which is why Br ends up on the less substituted carbon.
x: Adding Br• to carbon a would leave the less stable 2° radical; the favored path gives the 3° radical.
H• is not a chain carrier; RO• abstracts H from HBr (forming the strong O–H bond), so Br• is what adds.
That is the ionic (Markovnikov) mechanism without peroxide; it gives 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

q: 1-Methylcyclohexene is treated with HBr in the presence of a peroxide. Which best describes the product?
c: 1-Bromo-2-methylcyclohexane, as a mixture of cis and trans isomers (each racemic)
1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane, a single achiral product with Br on the tertiary carbon
h: Decide the regiochemistry from the radical mechanism first, then count the new stereocenters and ask whether anything in the reaction is chiral.
w: Br• adds to the CH carbon to give the 3° radical, which then picks up H from HBr. The product, 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane, has two stereocenters (C1 and C2). H can be delivered to either face of the radical, so both cis and trans diastereomers form, and because all reagents are achiral each is racemic: a mixture of cis and trans 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane.
x: Br on the more substituted carbon is the Markovnikov product of the ionic mechanism; peroxide switches to the radical path.
Achiral starting materials and reagents cannot give a single enantiomer, and the radical intermediate does not enforce one relative stereochemistry.
Allylic substitution needs a low, steady Br<sub>2</sub> concentration (NBS); with HBr the radical chain adds across the C=C bond.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: NBS keeps the Br<sub>2</sub> concentration very low. Which C–H bond in cyclohexene is weakest?
w: NBS supplies Br2 at a very low concentration, so addition to the C=C is too slow and radical substitution wins. Br• removes an allylic H (the weakest C–H), the allylic radical takes Br from Br2, and the product is 3-bromocyclohexene. In cyclohexene both ends of the allylic radical give the same compound.
x: Vinylic C–H bonds are strong and the vinylic radical is not stabilized, so the H on the double bond is not removed.
The 1,2-dibromide forms when Br<sub>2</sub> is present at high concentration (Br<sub>2</sub> in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>), not with NBS.
Bromocyclohexane would need HBr addition; NBS substitutes an allylic H and keeps the C=C.

q: But-1-ene is treated with NBS and light. Which set of products forms?
c: 3-Bromobut-1-ene (racemic) only, with Br at the allylic carbon
h: Draw the allylic radical from C3 and its resonance form. Where can Br attach?
w: Br• removes a 2° allylic H at C3. The radical is delocalized: CH2=CH–CH•–CH3 ↔ •CH2–CH=CH–CH3. Br2 can trap either end. At C3 the product is 3-bromobut-1-ene (new stereocenter, racemic); at C1 the allylic shift gives 1-bromobut-2-ene, whose new C2=C3 bond can be E or Z. Answer: 3-bromobut-1-ene and (E/Z)-1-bromobut-2-ene.
x: This ignores the resonance form of the allylic radical; Br can also bond at C1, with the double bond shifting to C2=C3.
4-Bromobut-1-ene would need abstraction at the C4 methyl, which is not allylic and gives a less stable 1° radical.
Addition of Br<sub>2</sub> across the C=C is suppressed by the very low Br<sub>2</sub> concentration NBS provides.

q: Use the bond dissociation energies in the table. What is ΔH for the overall reaction CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl + HCl, obtained by adding the two propagation steps?
h: Write the two propagation steps, find ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed) for each, and add them.
w: Step 1: Cl• + C–H → H–Cl + R•, ΔH = 413 − 431 = −18 kJ/mol. Step 2: R• + Cl–Cl → R–Cl + Cl•, ΔH = 242 − 354 = −112 kJ/mol. Sum = −130 kJ/mol. The same value comes from the net equation: broken C–H + Cl–Cl (655) minus formed H–Cl + C–Cl (785). Both chlorination steps are exothermic, which is why chlorination is fast and unselective.
x: −18 kJ/mol is only the first propagation step (H abstraction).
−112 kJ/mol is only the second propagation step (Cl transfer from Cl<sub>2</sub>).
Sign error: bonds formed (785) are stronger than bonds broken (655), so energy is released and ΔH is negative.

q: Methylenecyclohexane is treated with NBS and light. Which pair of constitutional isomers forms?
h: Find the allylic hydrogens, draw the allylic radical, and draw its resonance form. Each radical carbon can take Br.
w: The allylic H are on the ring CH2 groups next to C1 (C2 and C6 are equivalent). Removing one gives a radical delocalized between ring C2 and the exocyclic CH2: Br at C2 gives 1-bromo-2-methylidenecyclohexane; Br at the exocyclic carbon (allylic shift, C=C moves into the ring) gives 1-(bromomethyl)cyclohexene. Those two products form; the shifted product has the more substituted (trisubstituted) alkene.
x: These are HBr-addition products (saturated). NBS substitutes an allylic H and keeps a C=C in the product.

3-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexene would need a radical at C3 of 1-methylcyclohexene, which is not formed from this starting alkene; the radical here is spread over ring C2 and the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon only.
A dibromide with the C=C gone is a Br<sub>2</sub>-addition product, which the low Br<sub>2</sub> concentration from NBS suppresses.

q: (E)-Pent-2-ene is treated with 1 equiv of NBS and light. Ignoring stereoisomers, what is the major product?
c: 4-Bromopent-2-ene (formed as a mixture of its stereoisomers)
1-Bromopent-2-ene, because the CH<sub>3</sub> group has more allylic H (3 vs 2)
h: There are two sets of allylic H. Which gives the more stable allylic radical, and are the two ends of that radical different?
w: Allylic H are on C1 (CH3, would give a 1° allylic radical) and C4 (CH2, gives a 2° allylic radical). Br• removes the C4 H because the radical is more stable. That radical, CH3–CH=CH–CH•–CH3 ↔ CH3–CH•–CH=CH–CH3, is symmetric: both ends are CH next to a CH3. Br at either end gives the same constitution, 4-bromopent-2-ene (as stereoisomers: a stereocenter and E/Z).
x: Statistics (3 H vs 2 H) are outweighed by radical stability; a 2° allylic C–H is clearly weaker than a 1° allylic C–H, and Br• is selective.
These two products come from the C1 (1° allylic) radical, which is the minor pathway.
A vicinal dibromide comes from Br<sub>2</sub> addition, which NBS suppresses by keeping Br<sub>2</sub> very low.

q: Radical polymerization of which monomer gives the polymer with repeat unit –[CH2–CH(CN)]n–?
h: In chain-growth polymerization the C=C becomes the backbone; every other atom of the monomer becomes a side group.
w: Each monomer adds through its C=C, which becomes two backbone carbons; substituents on those carbons become side groups. –[CH2–CH(CN)]– comes from CH2=CH–CN, acrylonitrile (polyacrylonitrile, used in acrylic fibers).
x: Propanenitrile has no C=C, so it cannot undergo chain-growth radical polymerization.
Methacrylonitrile would give –[CH<sub>2</sub>–C(CH<sub>3</sub>)(CN)]–, with an extra methyl on every other carbon.
A CN on both alkene carbons would give –[CH(CN)–CH(CN)]–, with a nitrile on every backbone carbon.

q: During radical polymerization of styrene, where does the growing chain radical add to a styrene molecule, and why?
c: To the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, because the new radical is benzylic and resonance-stabilized
To the CH carbon, because that carbon is less hindered
To the CH carbon, because the new radical is primary and more reactive toward the next monomer
To an aromatic ring carbon, because the ring has the most π electrons
h: Compare the two radicals you could make by adding to either end of the C=C.
w: Adding R• to the CH2 end leaves the odd electron on the carbon bearing the phenyl group, a benzylic radical delocalized into the ring. Adding to the CH end would give an unstabilized 1° radical. So addition occurs at CH2, giving the benzylic radical, and the chain grows head-to-tail with phenyl groups on alternating carbons.
x: The CH carbon carries the phenyl group, so it is the more hindered end, and attack there gives a poorly stabilized 1° radical.
Chain growth follows the more stable radical (lower E<sub>a</sub>), not the more reactive one; a 1° radical is formed much more slowly.
Adding to the ring would destroy aromaticity; the vinyl C=C is far more reactive toward radicals.

q: A small amount of a thiol (RSH) is added to the radical polymerization of styrene. The polymer still forms at nearly the same rate, but its average molar mass is much lower. What explains this?
c: A growing chain radical abstracts H from S–H, ending that chain, and RS• starts a new chain.
RSH combines with two growing chain radicals at once, stopping polymerization.
RSH adds across the C=C of styrene and turns monomer into an unreactive sulfide.
RSH breaks into H• and RS• on its own, adding more initiator and speeding up the reaction.
h: The number of radicals stays about the same, yet each chain is shorter. Which process ends one chain and immediately starts another?
w: This is chain transfer: P• + RS–H → P–H + RS•. The weak S–H bond gives up its H, so the growing chain stops, but the radical count is unchanged because RS• adds to styrene and starts a new chain. More, shorter chains form at about the same overall rate. Thiols are used as chain-transfer agents to control molar mass.
x: Removing radicals (termination) would slow the polymerization; the observation is that the rate hardly changes.
Converting monomer to an inert compound would lower yield, not specifically shorten each chain; the small amount of thiol works catalytically through its S–H bond.
Extra initiation would speed up the reaction; here the rate is nearly unchanged. RSH does not undergo homolysis on its own under these conditions.

q: Polyethylene made by high-pressure radical polymerization has many short branches (mostly butyl groups). Which process creates these branches?
c: The chain-end radical takes an H from the fifth carbon of its own chain (1,5-H shift), and the new mid-chain radical adds ethylene.
The chain-end radical adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon of a butene impurity, which is then built into the growing chain.
Two chain-end radicals combine head-to-head, forming a branch point at the junction of the chains.
The chain-end radical rearranges by a 1,2-methyl shift to a more stable 2° radical, which keeps growing.
h: A primary chain-end radical can become a more stable 2° radical without adding monomer. Which kind of intramolecular step does that, and why would it favor a four-carbon branch?
w: This is intramolecular chain transfer ("backbiting"). The 1° chain-end radical reaches back through a six-membered cyclic transition state and abstracts an H from C5 (counting the radical carbon as C1; a 1,5-H shift), giving a more stable 2° radical within the chain. Ethylene then adds at that site, so the four carbons past it (C1–C4) become a butyl branch. Intermolecular H transfer between chains gives the long branches.
x: Butyl branches form in pure ethylene polymerization; they come from the chain itself, not from an impurity.
Combination of two radicals is termination: it joins two chains end-to-end into a linear chain, not a branched one.
A polyethylene chain end has no methyl group to shift, and 1,2-shifts are typical of carbocations, not radicals.

q: Di-tert-butyl peroxide is used as a radical initiator. Which bond breaks homolytically when it is heated?
h: Initiators contain one unusually weak bond.
w: The O–O bond of a peroxide is very weak (about 155 kJ/mol), far weaker than C–O, C–H or C–C bonds (about 350–420 kJ/mol). Heating breaks the O–O bond homolytically to give two (CH3)3CO• radicals, which start the chain.
x: C–O bonds are much stronger than the peroxide O–O bond, so they do not break at typical initiation temperatures.
C–H bonds are strong (about 400 kJ/mol or more); they are broken later by radicals in propagation, not in initiation.
C–C bonds are strong (about 350 kJ/mol); the initiator is designed with a much weaker bond elsewhere that breaks first.

q: Ethane is chlorinated with Cl2 and light. A trace of which product can form only by a termination step?
h: Which product needs two carbon radicals to meet each other?
w: Termination joins two radicals. Two ethyl radicals combine: 2 CH3CH2• → CH3CH2CH2CH3. Butane contains a new C–C bond that no propagation step can make, so traces of it are evidence for the radical chain mechanism. Chloroethane and HCl come from propagation; 1,1-dichloroethane comes from further propagation on chloroethane.
x: Chloroethane forms mainly in the propagation step CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>• + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + Cl•.
1,1-Dichloroethane forms when chloroethane goes through the same propagation steps again (polychlorination).
HCl forms in every first propagation step, Cl• + C–H → H–Cl + C•.

q: Methylcyclohexane is monochlorinated with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light at 25 °C. Using relative rates per H of 1° : 2° : 3° = 1 : 3.8 : 5, what percentage of the product is 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane?
h: Count every H as 1°, 2° or 3° (there are 14 H). Weight each class by its rate, then find the 3° share.
w: Methylcyclohexane has 3 primary H (CH3), 1 tertiary H (C1) and 10 secondary H (five ring CH2 groups). Weighted amounts: 1°: 3 × 1 = 3; 2°: 10 × 3.8 = 38; 3°: 1 × 5 = 5. Total = 46. 1-Chloro-1-methylcyclohexane = 5/46 = 11%. The many 2° H swamp the single more reactive 3° H.
x: 51% is 5/(1 + 3.8 + 5), which uses the rates but not the number of each kind of H.
7.1% is 1/14, the purely statistical share that ignores the higher reactivity of a 3° H.
33% (15.2/46) is the share of 1-chloro-2-methylcyclohexane (the four C2/C6 H), not of the 3° chloride.

q: Chlorination of propane with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light gives 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane in a 45 : 55 ratio. What is the reactivity of a secondary H relative to a primary H (per hydrogen)?
h: Divide each product amount by the number of hydrogens that lead to it, then take the ratio.
w: Propane has 6 primary H (giving 1-chloropropane) and 2 secondary H (giving 2-chloropropane). Per H: primary 45/6 = 7.5; secondary 55/2 = 27.5. Ratio 2° : 1° = 27.5/7.5 = 3.7.
x: 1.2 is 55/45, the product ratio without correcting for 6 primary vs 2 secondary H.
0.41 corrects the wrong way (55/45 × 2/6); the product from the fewer H must be divided by the smaller number.
7.3 divides only the primary amount by 6 and forgets to divide the secondary amount by 2.

q: Which sequence converts 2-methylbutane into 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product with the best selectivity?
c: 1. NBS, hν, CCl<sub>4</sub>  2. NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, heat
h: Step 1 must put the halogen on one specific carbon; step 2 must remove H to give the more substituted alkene.
w: Br2/hν is highly selective for the 3° C–H, giving mainly 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. A small, unhindered base (ethoxide) then performs Zaitsev E2 to give the trisubstituted alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene. Br2, hν, then NaOEt is the best route.
x: Cl<sub>2</sub> is unselective and gives a mixture of four monochlorides (only about 23% 3°), so many alkenes would form.
tert-Butoxide is bulky and gives mainly the Hofmann product, 2-methylbut-1-ene, from the 3° bromide.
NBS brominates allylic or benzylic positions; an alkane has no allylic H, so NBS is not the right reagent for this step.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Light means radicals. Which C–H bond in ethylbenzene gives the most stable radical?
w: Under radical conditions Br• removes the weakest C–H bond, the benzylic C–H (about 356 kJ/mol), giving a resonance-stabilized secondary benzylic radical. Br2 then delivers Br to that carbon: (1-bromoethyl)benzene, formed racemic because the planar radical reacts on both faces.
x: The terminal CH<sub>3</sub> gives a 1° radical that is not benzylic; that C–H bond is much stronger.
Ring bromination is electrophilic aromatic substitution and needs a Lewis acid such as FeBr<sub>3</sub>, not light.
Ortho ring bromination also requires FeBr<sub>3</sub> (electrophilic substitution); hν leads to radical substitution at the benzylic carbon.

q: cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane (a meso compound) is treated with Br2 and light. Which statement best describes the 1-bromo-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane formed?
c: Two diastereomers (Br cis or trans to the C2 methyl), each formed as a racemic mixture
One meso compound, because the starting alkane is meso
Two diastereomers, each formed as a single enantiomer, because C2 keeps its configuration
One diastereomer, as a racemic mixture, because Br always adds trans to the C2 methyl
h: Which H is removed? Look at the two tertiary H: how are they related in a meso compound? Then ask what the planar radical can do.
w: Br• removes a 3° H (on C1 or C2). In the meso alkane those two H are enantiotopic, so they react at the same rate, giving enantiomeric radicals in equal amounts. Each planar radical takes Br from either face, so Br ends up cis or trans to the remaining methyl-bearing stereocenter: two diastereomers, and because the two radicals are mirror images, each diastereomer forms as a 1:1 pair of enantiomers. Answer: two diastereomers, each racemic. (The product is chiral; it has no internal mirror plane.)
x: 1-Bromo-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane has two different stereocenters (C1 bears Br, C2 bears H), so no stereoisomer of it is meso.
C2 keeps its configuration within one radical, but the H at C1 and the H at C2 are mirror-image (enantiotopic) and react equally, so every product forms together with its enantiomer.
Neither face of the radical is fully blocked; both diastereomers form, though not necessarily in equal amounts.

q: Radical iodination of alkanes (I<sub>2</sub>, hν) does not occur to a useful extent. Given BDEs of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–H = 413, H–I = 297, I–I = 151 and (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–I = 234 kJ/mol, what is the main reason?
c: H abstraction by I• is endothermic by about 116 kJ/mol, too slow to sustain a chain.
The I–I bond is too strong to be broken by light, so no I• forms to start the chain.
Transfer of I from I<sub>2</sub> to the alkyl radical is endothermic by about 83 kJ/mol.
I• is so reactive that it abstracts every kind of H equally and gives only product mixtures.
h: Calculate ΔH for each propagation step. Which one is the problem?
w: Step 1: I• + R–H → H–I + R•, ΔH = 413 − 297 = +116 kJ/mol, steeply uphill, so Ea is at least 116 kJ/mol and the step is far too slow for a chain. Step 2: R• + I–I → R–I + I•, ΔH = 151 − 234 = −83 kJ/mol, which is fine. The endothermic H-abstraction step stops iodination.
x: I–I (151 kJ/mol) is the weakest of the halogen–halogen bonds, so visible light splits it easily; initiation is not the problem.
Sign error: ΔH = 151 − 234 = −83 kJ/mol; the iodine-transfer step is exothermic.
I• is the least reactive halogen atom; the problem is too little reactivity, not too much.

q: What is the configuration at carbon a, and which priority order supports it?
h: Rank by atomic number of the attached atoms; for the two carbons, list what each one is bonded to (a double bond counts its partner twice).
w: Cl (Z = 17) is first. The vinyl carbon carries (C, C, H) because the C=C partner is duplicated, which beats CH3 (H, H, H). H is last. Viewing with H pointed away from you, Cl → CH=CH2 → CH3 runs clockwise, so carbon a is R.
x: The priority order is right, but the direction was read with H toward the viewer without reversing it; correctly viewed, the path is clockwise (R).
CH<sub>3</sub> (H, H, H) cannot outrank the vinyl carbon (C, C, H); the duplicated C from the double bond wins the first point of difference.
CH<sub>3</sub> does not outrank CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, and with that wrong order the path would also be read as S, not R.

q: What is the configuration at carbon a, and which priority order supports it?
h: Compare the two carbon branches one atom at a time. The first point of difference decides; you never jump ahead to the double bond.
w: OH is first. Next compare the atoms attached to carbon a: the isopropyl CH carries (C, C, H) and the allyl CH2 carries (C, H, H). The first point of difference already favors isopropyl, so the C=C further out never matters. With H pointing away, OH → CH(CH3)2 → CH2CH=CH2 runs counterclockwise: S.
x: This ranks the allyl group above isopropyl because of its double bond, but the double bond is two atoms out; at the first atom isopropyl (C, C, H) beats CH<sub>2</sub> (C, H, H).
The priority order is right, but the direction is reversed; with H pointing away the path is counterclockwise.
The allyl group does not outrank isopropyl, so this order is wrong even though the letter matches.

q: Carbon a carries no hydrogen. What is its configuration?
c: It is not a chirality center, because it has no hydrogen
It cannot be assigned until the sign of optical rotation is measured
h: A chirality center needs four different groups, not a hydrogen. Here the lowest-priority group is a carbon group.
w: Carbon a has four different groups: OH, CH=CH2, CH2CH3 and CH3. Priorities: OH > CH=CH2 (C, C, H) > CH2CH3 (C, H, H) > CH3 (H, H, H). With the CH3 (priority 4) pointing away, OH → vinyl → ethyl runs counterclockwise, so the center is S.
x: R comes from reading the circle with the methyl (lowest priority) toward you without reversing, or from ranking ethyl above vinyl.
A chirality center needs four different groups, not an H; this carbon has OH, vinyl, ethyl and methyl.
R/S comes from the CIP rules and the 3-D arrangement; it has no fixed relation to the sign of rotation.

q: What is the configuration at carbon a of this 2-methylcyclohexanone, and which priority order supports it?
h: Treat the two ring directions as two different substituents and list the atoms attached to each neighbor of carbon a.
w: The carbonyl carbon carries (O, O, C) because the C=O oxygen is duplicated; the ring CH2 carries (C, H, H); CH3 carries (H, H, H). So C=O > ring CH2 > CH3 > H. With H pointing away, the path runs counterclockwise: S.
x: The priorities are right but the direction is reversed; check whether H is toward or away from you before reading the circle.
CH<sub>3</sub> (H, H, H) loses to the ring CH<sub>2</sub> (C, H, H) at the first point of difference.
The carbonyl carbon (O, O, C) outranks the ring CH<sub>2</sub> (C, H, H), so this order is wrong even though the letter matches.

q: Assign the configurations of carbons a and b.
h: At each center the heteroatom is first, and the neighboring ring carbon that carries the other heteroatom is second.
w: At a: NH2 > Cb (O, C, H) > ring CH2 (C, H, H) > H; the path is clockwise with H away, so a is R. At b: OH > Ca (N, C, H) > ring CH2 > H; also clockwise, so b is R. The answer is a = R, b = R (the trans isomer).
x: This is the enantiomer; both directions were read with H toward the viewer without reversing.
Carbon b was misread; at b the OH is first and Ca (N, C, H) is second, which gives R.
Carbon a was misread; at a the NH2 is first and Cb (O, C, H) is second, which gives R.

q: What is the configuration at carbon a, and which priority order supports it?
h: Write the three attached atoms for each carbon branch. One oxygen beats any number of carbons at the first point of difference.
w: The attached sets are CH2OH (O, H, H), C≡CH (C, C, C, the triple bond duplicated twice) and CH(CH3)2 (C, C, H). Compare highest atoms first: O beats C, so CH2OH is first; then (C, C, C) beats (C, C, H). Order: CH2OH > C≡CH > CH(CH3)2 > H. With H pointing away the path is counterclockwise, so S.
x: C≡CH has more attached atoms, but CIP compares the highest atom first: the O on CH<sub>2</sub>OH beats every C.
Group size or mass does not set priority; isopropyl (C, C, H) is last among the three carbon groups.
With C≡CH ranked first the circle would read R, so this combination is internally inconsistent as well as misranked.

q: Carbon a in this labeled ethanol carries one H and one deuterium (D = 2H). What is its configuration?
c: Not a chirality center, because H and D are the same element
h: When atomic numbers tie, the CIP rules use atomic mass. Then ask where D ranks relative to a carbon.
w: Isotopes are different groups: D (mass 2) outranks H (mass 1), but both rank below carbon. Priorities: OH > CH3 > D > H. With H pointing away, OH → CH3 → D is clockwise, so the center is R. Compounds like this are chiral and are used to follow the stereochemistry of reactions.
x: The priority order is right but the direction is reversed; read the path with H away from you.
D has atomic number 1, so it ranks below carbon (Z = 6); mass only breaks ties between the same element.
H and D differ in mass, which the CIP rules use to break the tie, so carbon a has four different groups.

q: The natural (L) form of the amino acid cysteine is drawn. What is the configuration at carbon a?
c: S, because every L amino acid is S
h: Compare the first atoms attached to the two carbon branches: CH<sub>2</sub>SH has (S, H, H) and CO<sub>2</sub>H has (O, O, O).
w: NH2 is first. CH2SH (S, H, H) beats CO2H (O, O, O) because S (Z = 16) beats O (Z = 8) at the first point of difference. The order NH2 > CH2SH > CO2H > H gives clockwise with H away, so L-cysteine is R. It is the common exception to "L = S".
x: D/L is a Fischer-projection label and R/S is a CIP label; they usually line up for amino acids but not for cysteine, where sulfur changes the priorities.
CO<sub>2</sub>H has three oxygens, but CIP compares the highest atom first, and one S beats any O.
If CO<sub>2</sub>H did outrank CH<sub>2</sub>SH, this drawing would be S, so the reason and the letter do not fit together.

q: Which structure is (2S,3R)-3-chlorobutan-2-ol?
h: Number from the end nearer the OH (C2 carries OH, C3 carries Cl), then assign each center separately.
w: At C2: OH > C3 (Cl, C, H) > CH3 > H. At C3: Cl > C2 (O, C, H) > CH3 > H. Only one structure gives S at the OH carbon and R at the Cl carbon, so it is (2S,3R). The other three are its enantiomer (2R,3S) and the two diastereomers (2S,3S) and (2R,3R).
x: This is (2R,3S), the enantiomer: both centers are inverted.
This is (2S,3S); the OH carbon is right but the Cl carbon is S.
This is (2R,3R); the Cl carbon is right but the OH carbon is R.

q: Rank these substituents in CIP priority, highest first: −CO<sub>2</sub>H, −CHO, −CH<sub>2</sub>OH, −CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.
h: Write the set of three atoms on each attached carbon (count a double-bonded O twice) and compare highest atom first.
w: Attached sets: CO2H (O, O, O); CHO (O, O, H); CH2OH (O, H, H); CH(CH3)2 (C, C, H). All three oxygen-bearing carbons start with O, so compare the next atom; the isopropyl group loses at the first atom. Order: −CO2H > −CHO > −CH2OH > −CH(CH3)2.
x: CHO has (O, O, H) and CO<sub>2</sub>H has (O, O, O); the third atom decides, and O beats H.
CH<sub>2</sub>OH has an O on its first carbon, which beats the (C, C, H) of isopropyl regardless of how many carbons follow.
Size and mass do not set priority; isopropyl has no O on its first carbon, so it is last.

q: What is the relationship between compounds I and II?
h: Assign R/S to both centers of each compound and compare: are both inverted, one inverted, or none?
w: Both are 3-chlorobutan-2-ol, so they are stereoisomers. I is (2R,3R) and II is (2S,3R): the OH carbon differs and the Cl carbon is the same. Stereoisomers that differ at some but not all centers are diastereomers.
x: Enantiomers differ at every chirality center; here the Cl-bearing carbon is R in both.
The OH-bearing carbon is R in I and S in II, so they are not the same compound.
The atoms are connected in the same order in both (OH on C2, Cl on C3), so they are not constitutional isomers.

q: Compounds I and II are both 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol. What is their relationship?
h: Do not judge by the orientation on the page. Assign R/S at the OH carbon and at the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon of each.
w: In both drawings the OH carbon is R (OH > C–CH3 ring carbon > ring CH2 > H) and the CH3 carbon is R. Same configuration at every center means the drawings are the same molecule turned on the page: identical (both are the trans isomer, (1R,2R)).
x: Enantiomers would show opposite configurations at both centers; here both centers match.
Diastereomers would differ at exactly one of the two centers; neither center differs.
Both have OH and CH<sub>3</sub> on adjacent ring carbons, so the connectivity is the same.

q: What is the relationship between drawings I and II of 2,3-dibromobutane?
h: Assign both centers in each drawing. If a molecule has R and S at two equivalently substituted centers, ask what its mirror image is.
w: Each drawing has one R and one S center. For 2,3-dibromobutane, (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are the same molecule because the two halves are equivalent and an internal mirror plane exists. Both drawings are the meso compound, so they are identical.
x: A meso compound is its own mirror image, so it has no enantiomer; the mirror-image look of the drawings is misleading.
Diastereomers would differ at only one center, but here (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) describe the same achiral molecule.
The two drawings are identical, but each has one R and one S center, so neither is (2R,3R).

q: What is the relationship between compounds I and II?
h: Decide cis or trans first. Only the cis isomer has an internal mirror plane.
w: Both are trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane (one Br wedged, one dashed). I is (1R,2R) and II is (1S,2S). Trans-1,2-disubstitution with identical groups has no mirror plane, so the molecule is chiral and I and II are enantiomers.
x: Only the cis isomer of 1,2-dibromocyclopentane is meso; the trans isomer has no internal mirror plane.
Both are trans with opposite configurations at both centers, which makes them mirror images, not diastereomers.
Both have Br on adjacent ring carbons, so the connectivity is the same.

q: Menthol (peppermint) has three chirality centers. Assign carbons a, b and c.
h: At each ring carbon, the two ring directions are different groups: follow each until they differ.
w: a (C–OH): OH > ring C bearing the isopropyl (C, C, H) > ring CH2 (C, H, H) > H → R. b (C–isopropyl): Ca (O, C, H) > isopropyl CH (C, C, H) > ring CH2 (C, H, H) > H → S. c (C–CH3): both ring neighbors are CH2 (C, H, H) and tie; one atom further, the path toward Ca reaches a carbon bearing O, which beats the CH2 on the other path. So ring path toward a > other ring path > CH3 > H → R. Natural menthol is (1R,2S,5R): a = R, b = S, c = R.
x: This is the enantiomer (all three inverted), which comes from reading every center with H toward you without reversing.
At b, Ca (with its O) outranks the isopropyl carbon (C, C, H); swapping them gives the wrong letter R.
At a, OH is first and the isopropyl-bearing ring carbon is second; that order gives R, not S.

q: Which of the tagged carbons is a chirality center (four different groups)?
h: For each ring carbon, compare the two paths around the ring. If they are identical, that carbon has two identical groups.
w: Carbon a carries H, CH3, CH2CH3 and the cyclohexyl ring: four different groups, so it is a chirality center. Carbons b and c sit at C1 and C4 of a 1,4-disubstituted ring; the two ring paths from each are identical, so neither is a chirality center (they do make cis/trans isomers possible, but cis and trans here are achiral diastereomers). Carbon d is a CH2. a only.
x: Carbons b and c each have two identical ring paths (C1 and C4 of the ring), so they lack four different groups.
Being able to show cis/trans isomerism does not make b and c chirality centers; each still has two identical ring branches.
Carbon d is a CH2 with two hydrogens, so it cannot be a chirality center.

q: A wedge-and-dash drawing shows one chirality center. Which operation on the drawing turns it into a drawing of the enantiomer?
c: Exchange the positions of two groups on the chirality center
Rotate the whole drawing 180° in the plane of the page
Make two separate exchanges of groups on the chirality center
Rotate the whole drawing 90° in the plane of the page
h: Which of these changes is a real motion of a molecule, and which one breaks and remakes bonds?
w: Any single exchange of two groups inverts a center: one swap gives the enantiomer, a second swap restores the original. Rotating a wedge-and-dash drawing in the page is just moving the molecule, so it leaves the configuration unchanged at any angle.
x: Rotating a molecule never changes its configuration; the wedges stay wedges and the dashes stay dashes.
Two exchanges invert the center twice, which returns the original configuration.
A 90° turn inverts a Fischer projection, but a wedge-and-dash drawing is a true 3-D picture, so it can be turned in the page by any angle without change.

q: (2R,3R)-2,3-Dibromopentane has [α]D = +x. What can be said about [α]D of (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromopentane?
c: It cannot be predicted; it must be measured
It is 0, because the compound is meso
h: Decide first how the two compounds are related, then recall which relationship fixes the rotation.
w: Changing one of two centers gives a diastereomer, and diastereomers have unrelated physical properties, including optical rotation; the value must be measured. Only the enantiomer, (2S,3S), is required to show −x. 2,3-Dibromopentane has different groups (CH3 and CH2CH3) on its two ends, so no stereoisomer is meso.
x: −x belongs to the enantiomer (2S,3S), where both centers are inverted.
Meso needs equivalent halves; with CH<sub>3</sub> on one end and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the other, (2R,3S) is chiral.
Diastereomers are different compounds, so there is no reason for their rotations to match.

q: In a Fischer projection, how are the bonds at each chirality center (the cross) oriented in space?
c: Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer; vertical bonds point away
Vertical bonds point toward the viewer; horizontal bonds point away
All four bonds lie in the plane of the page
The left bond points toward the viewer and the right bond points away
h: Picture the carbon chain curling back away from you, like a bow tie at each center.
w: A Fischer projection draws the main chain vertically, curving back behind the page, so vertical bonds go away from the viewer and horizontal bonds come toward the viewer. That is why it may be rotated 180° in the plane but not 90°.
x: This is reversed; the carbon chain (vertical) recedes behind the page and the horizontal groups project out.
A tetrahedral carbon cannot have all four bonds in one plane; the cross is shorthand for a 3-D arrangement.
Both horizontal bonds point toward the viewer; neither horizontal bond goes back.

q: What is the configuration of the chirality center in this Fischer projection of 2-bromopropanoic acid?
c: R: Br → CO<sub>2</sub>H → CH<sub>3</sub> is counterclockwise, reversed because H is on a horizontal bond
S: Br → CO<sub>2</sub>H → CH<sub>3</sub> is counterclockwise, and the H position does not matter
S: CO<sub>2</sub>H → Br → CH<sub>3</sub> is clockwise, reversed because H is on a horizontal bond
R: CO<sub>2</sub>H → Br → CH<sub>3</sub> is clockwise, and the H position does not matter
h: Rank the groups, trace 1 → 2 → 3, then check whether H is on a vertical (away) or horizontal (toward you) bond.
w: Priorities: Br > CO2H > CH3 > H. On the page Br (right) → CO2H (top) → CH3 (bottom) runs counterclockwise. H is on a horizontal bond, pointing toward you, so the true sense is the reverse: R.
x: When H is on a horizontal bond it points toward the viewer, so the direction read on the page must be reversed.
Br (Z = 35) outranks the carbon of CO<sub>2</sub>H; atomic number of the attached atom comes first.
Br outranks CO<sub>2</sub>H, and the H on a horizontal bond requires reversing the direction; this choice makes both errors.

q: Give the configuration of this stereoisomer of 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane (C2 carries Br, C3 carries Cl).
h: Treat each cross separately. The other stereocenter is just a substituent: at C2 it is CH(Cl)CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: C2: Br > C3 (Cl, C, H) > CH3 > H. Br (right) → C3 (down) → CH3 (up) is clockwise on the page; H is horizontal, so reverse: S. C3: Cl > C2 (Br, C, H) > CH3 > H. Cl (left) → C2 (up) → CH3 (down) is clockwise; H is horizontal, so reverse: S. The compound is (2S,3S).
x: This is the enantiomer; both centers were read on the page without reversing for the horizontal H.
C2 was read without reversing for the horizontal H; only C3 was handled correctly.
C3 was read without reversing for the horizontal H; only C2 was handled correctly.

q: Which Fischer projection represents a meso compound?
h: A meso compound needs identical top and bottom halves and a horizontal mirror line through the middle of the projection.
w: In III (tartaric acid) the top and bottom halves are the same, and the two OH groups are on the same side, so a horizontal mirror line maps the top half onto the bottom. It has two chirality centers but is achiral: III is meso.
x: I has the same ends as III, but the OH groups are on opposite sides, so there is no internal mirror line; it is one enantiomer of chiral tartaric acid.
II has OH groups on the same side but different ends (CHO and CH<sub>2</sub>OH), so the halves are not equivalent and the compound is chiral.
IV has identical ends, but OH and Cl make the two centers different, so no internal mirror plane is possible.

q: What is the relationship between Fischer projections I and II?
h: Try rotating I by 180° in the plane of the page. Which operations are allowed for a Fischer projection?
w: Rotating I by 180° in the plane puts CH2OH on top and CHO on the bottom, and every horizontal group swaps sides, giving exactly II. A 180° in-plane rotation keeps horizontal bonds toward the viewer, so it is allowed: the two are identical (both are (2R,3R)-2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal, D-erythrose).
x: The OH groups appear on the left in II, but that is the result of the 180° turn, not reflection; both centers are R in both projections.
Diastereomers would differ at one center; assigning R/S shows both centers match.
Both are 2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal with the same connectivity; only the drawing orientation differs.

q: Fischer projection II was made by rotating I by 90° clockwise in the plane of the page. What is the relationship between I and II?
h: After the turn, which groups now sit on the vertical bonds, and which way do vertical bonds point?
w: A 90° turn moves the horizontal groups (toward the viewer) onto vertical bonds, which by convention point away, and vice versa. That reverses the center: I is R (OH > CHO > CH3), II reads as S. So I and II are enantiomers. Only 180° in-plane turns are allowed.
x: A rotation is harmless for a 3-D model, but a Fischer projection has a fixed meaning for vertical and horizontal bonds; a 90° turn breaks it.
With only one chirality center there are just two stereoisomers, which are mirror images, so diastereomers are impossible.
The connectivity (2-hydroxypropanal) is unchanged; only the configuration is inverted.

q: Which Fischer projection (OH-bearing carbon in the upper row) represents the compound drawn?
h: Assign R/S to the drawn compound first, then assign each Fischer projection and look for the match.
w: The drawing is (2R,3S)-3-chlorobutan-2-ol. In the Fischer projections, with H horizontal, read each center and reverse. IV: C2 (OH left) is R and C3 (Cl left) is S, so IV matches. I is (2R,3R), II is (2S,3R) (the enantiomer) and III is (2S,3S).
x: I is (2R,3R): the OH carbon matches, but the Cl carbon is inverted.
II is (2S,3R), the enantiomer of the drawn compound; both centers are inverted.
III is (2S,3S): the Cl carbon matches, but the OH carbon is inverted.

q: Assign C2 and C3 of this aldotetrose (D-threose).
h: At C2, the CHO carbon (O, O, H) outranks C3 (O, C, H). At C3, C2 (O, C, H) outranks CH<sub>2</sub>OH (O, H, H).
w: C2: OH > CHO > C3 > H. OH (left) → CHO (up) → C3 (down) is clockwise on the page; H is horizontal, so reverse: S. C3: OH > C2 > CH2OH > H. OH (right) → C2 (up) → CH2OH (down) is counterclockwise; reverse: R. D-Threose is (2S,3R).
x: This is L-threose, the enantiomer; both centers were read without reversing for the horizontal H.
C2 was read without reversing for its horizontal H; C3 is correct.
C3 was read without reversing for its horizontal H; C2 is correct.

q: Which compound is meso?
h: Meso: two or more chirality centers and an internal mirror plane (so the molecule is achiral).
w: The 2,3-dibromobutane with opposite configurations (R and S) at two identically substituted centers has an internal mirror plane, so it is meso.
x: This is (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane (or its mirror image); like-configured centers with identical substituents give a chiral compound.
The two centers carry different halogens (Br and Cl), so no internal mirror plane is possible; the compound is chiral.
This is a like-configured 2,4-pentanediol ((2R,4R) or (2S,4S)), which is chiral; only the (2R,4S) isomer is meso.

q: Which compound is a meso compound?
h: A meso compound must contain chirality centers and still be achiral. Check both requirements for each ring.
w: cis-1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane has two chirality centers (C1 and C2 each carry H, Cl, CH2 and CHCl) and a mirror plane through the CH2 carbon: it is meso.
x: trans-1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane has no mirror plane; it is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers.
cis-1,3-Dichlorocyclobutane is achiral, but it is not meso: C1 and C3 each have two identical ring paths, so the molecule has no chirality centers.
trans-1,2-Dichlorocyclobutane is chiral; only the cis-1,2 isomer has an internal mirror plane.

q: A pure compound has two chirality centers, is optically inactive, and cannot be resolved into enantiomers. It is best described as:
c: a conformational isomer of a chiral compound
h: Which kind of sample is optically inactive because of the molecule itself rather than a 50:50 mixture?
w: A meso compound has chirality centers but an internal mirror plane, so the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image: no rotation, and nothing to resolve.
x: A racemic mixture is also optically inactive, but it is a 50:50 mixture of enantiomers that can be resolved, not a single pure compound.
A pair of diastereomers is a mixture of two different compounds, not one pure compound, and each may rotate light.
Conformers of a chiral compound remain chiral and optically active.

q: How many stereoisomers exist for pentane-2,3,4-triol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH(OH)CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Use symmetry. When C2 and C4 have the same configuration, is C3 still stereogenic? When they are opposite?
w: The molecule is symmetric end to end. If C2 and C4 match ((2R,4R) or (2S,4S)), the two halves at C3 are identical, so C3 is not stereogenic: one pair of enantiomers. If C2 and C4 are opposite ((2R,4S)), C3 becomes pseudoasymmetric and can be either of two forms, giving two different meso compounds. Total: 2 + 2 = 4.
x: 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 is only the maximum; symmetry makes several of those combinations the same molecule.
3 is the count for a two-center symmetric molecule such as 2,3-butanediol; here C3 adds a second meso form.
Six would require three pairs of enantiomers; the opposite-configured C2/C4 forms are meso, not pairs.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 2-bromo-3-chloropentane?
h: Count the chirality centers, then check whether any symmetry could reduce 2<sup>n</sup>.
w: C2 and C3 are both chirality centers, and the molecule has no symmetry that could create a meso form (the groups differ). So 22 = 4: two pairs of enantiomers.
x: 2 would be correct for a single chirality center; this molecule has two.
3 applies only when a meso form exists, which needs identically substituted centers.
8 would require three chirality centers.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 2,4-dibromopentane?
