h: Two chirality centers, but look at the symmetry of the carbon chain.
w: C2 and C4 are chirality centers with identical substituent sets, and C3 is a CH2. (2R,4R) and (2S,4S) are enantiomers; (2R,4S) has an internal mirror plane through C3 and is meso. Total 3.
x: 2<sup>2</sup> = 4 counts (2R,4S) and (2S,4R) separately, but they are the same meso compound.
2 counts only the chiral pair and misses the meso isomer.
With only two chirality centers there cannot be more than four stereoisomers.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for hex-4-en-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Look for every stereogenic unit, not just chirality centers.
w: There are two stereogenic units: the chirality center at C2 (R or S) and the C4=C5 double bond (E or Z). They are independent, so 2 × 2 = 4 stereoisomers: (2R,4E), (2S,4E), (2R,4Z), (2S,4Z).
x: 2 counts only the chirality center and ignores E/Z isomerism of the double bond.
No meso form is possible here, so nothing reduces the count below 2 × 2.
8 would require three stereogenic units; the molecule has only two.

q: This Fischer projection shows one stereoisomer of 3-chlorobutan-2-ol. How is it best described?
h: Erythro: the similar groups (here OH and Cl) on the same side of the Fischer projection. Then ask if a mirror line could exist when OH ≠ Cl.
w: OH and Cl are both on the right, so this is the erythro isomer. Because the two centers carry different groups (OH and Cl), there is no internal mirror plane: it is chiral ((2S,3R)). Erythro resembles meso in layout, but it is only meso when the two centers are identical.
x: Threo means the similar groups are on opposite sides; here OH and Cl are on the same side.
Erythro is a layout term; this molecule cannot be meso because OH and Cl make the halves different.
The groups are on the same side (erythro), and the molecule is chiral, not meso.

q: Which pair of stereoisomers of 3-bromobutan-2-ol is the threo pair?
h: Draw the Fischer projection with OH and Br on opposite sides, assign both centers, then find its mirror image.
w: Put CH3 top and bottom, OH on the right at C2 and Br on the left at C3 (threo, opposite sides). C2: OH > C3 > CH3; with H horizontal it reads S. C3: Br > C2 > CH3; it reads S. So threo = (2S,3S) and its enantiomer (2R,3R). The erythro pair is (2R,3S)/(2S,3R).
x: This is the erythro pair: in the Fischer projection, OH and Br are on the same side.
These two differ at only one center, so they are diastereomers (one threo, one erythro), not a pair.
These two differ at only one center, so they are one erythro and one threo isomer, not a pair of enantiomers.

q: The amino acid drawn is 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanoic acid. Which description fits it?
h: Assign R/S from the drawing, then build the Fischer projection (CO<sub>2</sub>H on top) and see whether NH<sub>2</sub> and OH fall on the same side.
w: C2: NH2 > CO2H > C3 > H gives S. C3: OH > C2 (N, C, H) > CH3 > H gives R. In the Fischer projection with CO2H up and CH3 down, NH2 is on the left at C2 and OH is on the right at C3: opposite sides, so threo, (2S,3R). This is natural L-threonine (its name, like the threo label, comes from threose).
x: In the Fischer projection NH<sub>2</sub> and OH fall on opposite sides, which is threo, not erythro.
C3 is R: OH > C2 (N, C, H) > CH<sub>3</sub>. (2S,3S) is allothreonine, a diastereomer.
(2S,3S) is allothreonine, which is erythro, but it is not the compound drawn; C3 here is R.

q: Which dimethylcyclohexane is chiral?
h: Treat the ring as flat and look for a mirror plane through the ring (perpendicular to it).
w: trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane has chirality centers at C1 and C2 and no mirror plane, so it is chiral (it exists as the (1R,2R)/(1S,2S) pair). Ring flipping cannot remove chirality, because both chairs of one enantiomer are still that enantiomer.
x: cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane has a mirror plane between C1 and C2 in the flat-ring view; it is meso.
trans-1,4-Dimethylcyclohexane has a mirror plane through C1 and C4 and no chirality centers; it is achiral.
cis-1,3-Dimethylcyclohexane has a mirror plane through C2 and C5; it is meso.

q: Which compound is achiral?
h: For the carbon bearing the methyl, are the two paths around the ring the same or different?
w: In 4-methylcyclohexanone the methyl carbon (C4) has two identical ring paths to the C=O, so it is not a chirality center, and a mirror plane passes through C1 and C4: achiral.
x: In 3-methylcyclohexanone the two ring paths from C3 differ (one reaches C=O after one carbon, the other after three), so C3 is a chirality center.
In 2-methylcyclohexanone C2 has C=O on one side and CH<sub>2</sub> on the other, so it is a chirality center.
In 3-methylcyclopentanone the two ring paths from C3 differ in length to the C=O, so C3 is a chirality center.

q: Which compound is chiral?
h: Find the chirality centers first (if any), then look for a mirror plane in the flat ring.
w: trans-1,3-Dimethylcyclopentane has chirality centers at C1 and C3 (each ring path differs in length to the other CH(CH3)). The only possible mirror plane, through C2 and the C4–C5 bond, would need both methyls on the same face. With one up and one down there is none: chiral.
x: cis-1,3-Dimethylcyclopentane has a mirror plane through C2 and the middle of the C4–C5 bond; it is meso.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclopentane has a mirror plane between C1 and C2; it is meso.
In trans-1,3-dimethylcyclobutane, C1 and C3 each have two identical ring paths, so there are no chirality centers, and a mirror plane contains both methyls: achiral.

q: Each chair conformation of cis-1,2-dichlorocyclohexane, taken alone, is chiral. Why is the compound nevertheless optically inactive and not resolvable at room temperature?
c: The ring flip converts one chair into its mirror image, and it is fast at room temperature
The axial C–Cl dipole cancels the equatorial C–Cl dipole
C1 and C2 are not chirality centers in the cis isomer
The two chairs have different energies, so only the achiral one is populated
h: Draw the chair with Cl axial at C1 and equatorial at C2, flip it, and compare the result with the mirror image of the starting chair.
w: In the cis isomer one Cl is axial and one equatorial. Flipping the ring swaps them, and the flipped chair is the mirror image of the first. Because the flip is fast at room temperature, the two enantiomeric chairs are always present 50:50 and cannot be separated: the compound behaves as the achiral (meso) cis isomer.
x: Dipole cancellation has nothing to do with optical activity, which depends on chirality, not polarity.
C1 and C2 each carry H, Cl, CHCl and CH<sub>2</sub>, so they are chirality centers; the cis compound is meso, not center-free.
Both chairs have one axial and one equatorial Cl, so they have equal energy; and neither single chair is achiral.

q: How many stereoisomers exist for 1,4-dimethylcyclohexane, and how many of them are chiral?
h: Are C1 and C4 chirality centers? Compare the two ring paths from C1.
w: The two ring paths from C1 (and from C4) are identical, so there are no chirality centers. The only stereoisomerism is cis/trans, and each has a mirror plane through C1 and C4. So there are 2 stereoisomers (cis and trans), neither chiral; they are diastereomers.
x: This counts the 1,2- or 1,3-isomer pattern (meso + a pair); 1,4-substitution has no chirality centers.
2<sup>2</sup> = 4 assumes two chirality centers, but C1 and C4 each have two identical ring paths.
There are two stereoisomers, but each has a mirror plane through C1 and C4, so neither is chiral.

q: A sample contains 80% of the (R) enantiomer and 20% of the (S) enantiomer. What is its enantiomeric excess?
h: ee = % major enantiomer − % minor enantiomer.
w: ee = 80% − 20% = 60% in favor of R. Equivalently, 40% of the sample is racemic (20% R + 20% S) and 60% is excess R.
x: 80% is the fraction of R, not the excess of R over S.
40% is the racemic part of the sample (20% R + 20% S), not the excess.
The excess is in favor of the major enantiomer, R, and is 60%, not 20%.

q: A solution of 0.250 g of a pure chiral compound in 10.0 mL of ethanol gives an observed rotation of −1.30° in a 100-mm cell. What is the specific rotation?
h: [α] = α / (l × c), with l in decimeters and c in g/mL.
x: This uses l = 10 (centimeters); the path length must be in decimeters.
This uses c = 2.50 (g per 100 mL); the formula needs g/mL.
This uses l = 0.100 (meters); the path length must be in decimeters.

q: The pure (+) enantiomer of a compound has [α]<sub>D</sub> = +40.0. A synthetic sample has [α]<sub>D</sub> = +12.0. What percentage of the sample is the (+) enantiomer?
h: First find the optical purity (ee) from the rotations, then split the racemic remainder evenly.
x: 30% is the enantiomeric excess, not the percentage of the (+) enantiomer.
70% is the racemic portion of the sample.
35% is the percentage of the (−) enantiomer.

q: Pure (S)-X has [α]D = −24.0. A sample of X (0.300 g/mL, 0.500-dm cell) shows an observed rotation of +1.80°. What is the composition of the sample?
h: Convert the observed rotation to a specific rotation first. Then decide which enantiomer gives a positive sign.
w: [α] = +1.80 / (0.500 × 0.300) = +12.0. Since (S) is −24.0, (R) is +24.0, so a positive rotation means R is in excess. ee = 12.0 / 24.0 = 50% R. Composition: 50% + 25% = 75% R, 25% S.
x: The sign is positive, and (S) is levorotatory, so R must be the major enantiomer.
This divides by the concentration but not the path length (1.80 / 0.300 = 6.0, 25% ee); l = 0.500 dm must be included.
This both drops the path length and gives the excess to the wrong (levorotatory) enantiomer.

q: Pure (S)-Y has [α]D = +15.0. What observed rotation do you expect for a 90:10 mixture of (S)-Y and (R)-Y at 0.200 g/mL in a 2.00-dm cell?
h: Only the enantiomeric excess contributes to rotation. Find ee, then the sample specific rotation, then α = [α] × l × c.
w: ee = 90 − 10 = 80%, so the sample [α] = 0.80 × 15.0 = +12.0. α = 12.0 × 2.00 × 0.200 = +4.80°. The racemic 20% contributes nothing.
x: This uses 90% instead of the ee; the 10% R cancels an equal 10% of S.
This is the rotation of pure (S)-Y; the 10% R lowers it.
This leaves out the 2.00-dm path length.

q: A chemist mixes 3.0 g of the pure (R) enantiomer of a compound with 1.0 g of the racemate. What is the enantiomeric excess of the mixture?
h: Split the racemate into its R and S halves, then total R and S.
w: The racemate is 0.5 g R + 0.5 g S. Totals: R = 3.5 g, S = 0.5 g, out of 4.0 g. ee = (3.5 − 0.5)/4.0 = 75%. (Or: 3.0 g of the 4.0 g is unpaired R.)
x: 87.5% is the percentage of R (3.5/4.0), not the excess of R over S.
This treats the 1.0 g of racemate as if it were all S.
25% is the racemic fraction of the mixture (1.0/4.0).

q: An asymmetric reduction gives an alcohol in 90% ee. What is the ratio of the major to the minor enantiomer?
h: Convert ee to percentages: major = (100 + ee)/2.
x: 9:1 is 90:10, which is 80% ee.
10:1 is about 91:9, which is about 82% ee.
90:1 reads the ee as a percentage of one enantiomer and divides by 1; the minor enantiomer is 5%, not 1%.

q: Which property is different for the two enantiomers of 2-butanol?
c: The sign of the specific rotation
The IR spectrum of the pure liquid
h: Enantiomers differ only in interactions with something chiral.
w: Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment; they differ only toward chiral things, such as plane-polarized light. They rotate light by the same magnitude in opposite directions.
x: Boiling point depends on intermolecular forces, which are identical for mirror-image molecules.
Hexane is achiral, so both enantiomers dissolve in it equally.
IR absorptions depend on bond vibrations, which are identical in mirror-image molecules.

q: Which sample is optically active?
h: A sample rotates light only if it contains an excess of one enantiomer of a chiral compound.
w: The 70:30 mixture has a 40% excess of the (R) enantiomer, so it rotates light at 40% of the pure value: optically active.
x: A meso compound is achiral, so it does not rotate plane-polarized light.
A racemate has equal amounts of both enantiomers, whose rotations cancel.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane is a meso compound (achiral), so it is optically inactive.

q: Racemic 2-phenylpropanoic acid is treated with one equivalent of enantiopure (S)-1-phenylethylamine. Which statement about the product is correct?
c: It is a mixture of two diastereomeric salts, which can be separated by crystallization
It is a mixture of two enantiomeric salts, which cannot be separated by crystallization
It is a single salt, because the (S)-amine reacts with only the (S)-acid
It is a racemic salt, which must be separated by chiral chromatography
h: Write the two salts as (R)-acid·(S)-amine and (S)-acid·(S)-amine. What is their relationship?
w: The amine deprotonates both acid enantiomers, giving (R)-acid·(S)-amine and (S)-acid·(S)-amine salts. These are not mirror images (the mirror of the first would be (S)-acid·(R)-amine), so they are diastereomers, with different solubilities that allow separation by fractional crystallization.
x: The two salts share the same (S)-amine, so they are not mirror images; enantiomeric salts would need the (R)-amine as well.
An acid–base reaction is not selective enough to leave one enantiomer untouched; with one equivalent, both acid enantiomers form salts.
Diastereomeric salts are separable by ordinary methods; chiral chromatography is not required.

q: Which reagent could be used to resolve racemic butan-2-amine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Resolution of a base needs a partner that (1) forms a salt with an amine and (2) is a single enantiomer of a chiral compound.
w: (2R,3R)-Tartaric acid is an enantiopure chiral acid. With the racemic amine it forms two salts, (R)-amine·(R,R)-acid and (S)-amine·(R,R)-acid, which are diastereomers and can be separated by crystallization. Treating each salt with NaOH then frees the single amine enantiomer. The answer is (2R,3R)-tartaric acid.
x: meso-Tartaric acid is achiral, so its salts with the (R) and (S) amine are enantiomers and cannot be separated by crystallization.
1-Phenylethylamine is enantiopure but is a base; it does not form a salt with another amine. It is used to resolve racemic acids.
Acetic acid is achiral, so the two acetate salts are enantiomers with identical solubility.

q: In a classical resolution, 10.0 g of a racemic acid is converted to diastereomeric salts and separated, without recycling the unwanted enantiomer. What is the maximum mass of the pure (R)-acid that can be recovered?
h: How much of the racemate is the (R) enantiomer to begin with?
w: A racemate is 50% R. Resolution only separates what is present; it does not convert S into R. The maximum is 5.0 g (50% yield), and in practice less is recovered.
x: Getting 10.0 g of R would require converting the S enantiomer into R (racemizing and recycling it), which this process does not do.
2.5 g is half of the R that is present; a perfect separation recovers all 5.0 g.
7.5 g exceeds the 5.0 g of R that the racemate contains.

q: The less soluble salt, (R)-acid·(S)-amine, is collected from a resolution and shaken with aqueous HCl and ether. What is in the ether layer?
c: The (S)-acid, because protonation inverts the chirality center
The racemic acid, because the HCl racemizes it
h: Strong acid protonates the carboxylate. Which species stays neutral (ether-soluble), and which becomes a charged salt (water-soluble)?
w: HCl protonates the carboxylate, giving the neutral carboxylic acid, which moves into the ether. The amine becomes its water-soluble hydrochloride. No bond to the chirality center is made or broken, so the ether holds the (R)-acid, enantiomerically enriched; the (S)-amine can be recovered from the water with NaOH.
x: Proton transfer happens at the carboxylate oxygen, not at the chirality center, so the configuration is unchanged.
Racemization would require breaking a bond at the chirality center; a quick acid–base extraction does not.
In aqueous HCl the amine is protonated to an ammonium salt, which stays in the water layer.

q: Which compound contains chirality centers but is achiral?
h: You need a molecule with two or more chirality centers and an internal mirror plane.
w: cis-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane has two chirality centers (C1 and C2) and a mirror plane between them: it is a meso compound, achiral despite its chirality centers.
x: 3-Methylcyclopentene has one chirality center (C3) and no mirror plane, so it is chiral.
trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclopropane has two chirality centers but no mirror plane; it is chiral.
1,1-Dimethylcyclohexane is achiral, but it has no chirality centers (C1 carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups).

q: Dimethyl ether donates a lone pair to BF<sub>3</sub> to form the Lewis acid–base adduct (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>O–BF<sub>3</sub>. In this adduct every second-row atom has an octet. What are the formal charges on O and B?
h: Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons). Count bonds and lone pairs on each atom after the new O–B bond forms.
w: Oxygen now has three bonds and one lone pair: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. Boron has four bonds and no lone pairs: 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. The adduct is neutral overall, so the two charges must cancel. The donor atom (O) always becomes more positive and the acceptor (B) more negative when a dative bond forms.
x: This reverses the electron flow. O gave away a share of its lone pair, so it loses electron density and becomes +1; B gains a share and becomes −1.
Before the reaction both atoms are 0, but forming a fourth bond to B and a third bond to O changes the electron count on each.
The adduct is neutral, so a +1 on O must be balanced by a −1 somewhere. Boron with four bonds and no lone pairs is 3 − 4 = −1.

q: What is the hybridization of the tagged carbons a, b and c?
h: Count the σ-bonded neighbors (steric number) of each carbon. Two π bonds on one carbon leave it with two σ bonds.
w: Carbon a is the central carbon of an allene (C=C=C): it makes two σ bonds and two π bonds, so it is sp (linear). Carbon b has three σ bonds (to a, H and c) and one π bond, so it is sp2. Carbon c is a nitrile carbon with two σ bonds and two π bonds, so it is sp. A good shortcut: hybridization depends on the number of σ bonds plus lone pairs, not on how many double bonds you see in the drawing.
x: Carbon a has two double bonds, which means only two σ bonds; two σ domains give sp, not sp2.
Carbon b has three σ bonds (C, H, C) and only one π bond, so it is sp2; it is not part of two π bonds.
Carbon b is part of a C=C double bond, so it cannot be sp3, and the C≡N carbon has two π bonds, so it is sp.

q: Which statement correctly describes the three-dimensional shape of penta-2,3-diene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=C=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
c: The H–C–CH<sub>3</sub> plane at one end is perpendicular to the H–C–CH<sub>3</sub> plane at the other end
All five carbons and both alkene hydrogens lie in a single plane, as in a conjugated diene
The central carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, so the C=C=C bond angle is about 120°
The two π bonds use parallel p orbitals and are conjugated with each other
h: The central carbon uses one p orbital for each π bond. How are those two p orbitals oriented relative to each other?
w: The central allene carbon is sp with two unhybridized p orbitals at 90° to each other. One p orbital makes the π bond to C2, the other makes the π bond to C4. Each terminal carbon's p orbital must line up with one of them, so the substituent planes at the two ends are twisted 90° apart: the two H–C–CH3 planes are perpendicular. The C=C=C unit is linear (180°), and because the π bonds are orthogonal they are cumulated, not conjugated.
x: A planar arrangement would require both π bonds to use parallel p orbitals on the central carbon, but one carbon has no two parallel p orbitals; the ends are twisted 90°.
The central carbon has only two σ bonds, so it is sp and the C=C=C angle is 180°, not 120°.
The two π bonds are perpendicular, so they cannot overlap; cumulated double bonds are not conjugated.

q: Which species has a trigonal pyramidal geometry at the central atom?
h: Count electron domains (bonds plus lone pairs) on the central atom, then name the shape from the atoms only.
w: Trimethylamine has three σ bonds and one lone pair on N: four electron domains (tetrahedral electron geometry), but with only three atoms attached the shape is trigonal pyramidal. Trimethylborane has three bonds and no lone pair (trigonal planar), the tetramethylammonium ion has four bonds (tetrahedral), and the iminium N has three σ bonds plus a π bond (trigonal planar).
x: Boron in B(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> has only three bonding domains and no lone pair, so it is trigonal planar with an empty p orbital.
N in (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>N<sup>+</sup> has four bonds and no lone pair, so the shape is tetrahedral, not pyramidal.
The iminium N has three σ bonds and one π bond and no lone pair, so it is sp<sup>2</sup> and trigonal planar.

q: In which species is the tagged carbon a sp2 hybridized with an empty unhybridized p orbital?
h: An empty p orbital means the carbon has fewer than eight electrons around it.
w: The tert-butyl cation has three σ bonds and only six valence electrons at the cationic carbon. It is sp2 and trigonal planar, and the leftover p orbital is empty; this is the LUMO that nucleophiles attack. The alkene carbon is also sp2, but its p orbital holds the π electrons.
x: The carbanion carbon has a lone pair, so its orbitals are all filled; a simple alkyl carbanion is roughly sp<sup>3</sup> and pyramidal.
This carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, but its p orbital is used for the C=C π bond, so it is filled, not empty.
The C–H carbon of isobutane has four σ bonds; it is sp<sup>3</sup> and has no unhybridized p orbital.

q: Which molecule has the smallest H–X–H bond angle at its central atom X?
h: Lone pairs take up more room than bonding pairs and squeeze the bond angles.
w: Water has two lone pairs on an sp3-like oxygen; they push the O–H bonds together to about 104.5°. Ammonia has one lone pair (about 107°), methane none (109.5°), and formaldehyde has an sp2 carbon with an H–C–H angle near 116–120°.
x: NH<sub>3</sub> has only one lone pair, so its H–N–H angle (about 107°) is larger than water's.
CH<sub>4</sub> has no lone pairs, so it keeps the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°.
The carbon in H<sub>2</sub>C=O is sp<sup>2</sup>, so its H–C–H angle is near 120°, the largest of the four.

q: How many σ bonds and how many π bonds are in acrylonitrile, shown below?
h: Every bond between two atoms has one σ bond; each extra line in a double or triple bond is a π bond. Count the hydrogens hidden in a line drawing.
w: Acrylonitrile is H2C=CH–C≡N (C3H3N). σ bonds: three C–H, the C=C, the C–C and the C≡N give 6 σ. π bonds: one in C=C and two in C≡N give 3 π.
x: The C≡N triple bond contains two π bonds, not one; together with the C=C that makes three.
This misses one of the three C–H bonds that a line drawing does not show.
A triple bond is one σ plus two π, not three σ bonds; multiple bonds add only one σ each.

q: Each tagged nitrogen has one lone pair. Which nitrogen(s) hold that lone pair in an sp2 hybrid orbital?
h: First decide each N's hybridization. Then ask whether the lone pair can sit in an unhybridized p orbital and overlap with a neighboring π bond.
w: Nitrogen a is an imine N: one σ bond to each carbon, a π bond, and a lone pair. The p orbital is used by the C=N π bond, so the lone pair lies in the plane in an sp2 orbital. Nitrogen b is an amide N: it is also sp2 (trigonal planar), but its lone pair sits in the p orbital so it can overlap with the C=O π bond (amide resonance). Nitrogen c is an ordinary amine N, sp3, with the lone pair in an sp3 orbital. Only a fits.
x: The amide N is sp<sup>2</sup>, but its lone pair is delocalized into the C=O π system, which requires a p orbital, not an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital.
Nitrogen a also qualifies, and b's lone pair is in a p orbital, not an sp2 orbital.
Nitrogen c is an amine with no adjacent π bond; it is sp3, and b's lone pair is in a p orbital.

q: The σ bond between carbons a and b in but-1-en-3-yne is formed by overlap of which orbitals?
h: Determine the hybridization of each carbon from the multiple bonds it is part of; the single bond between them uses one hybrid orbital from each.
w: Carbon a is part of the C=C double bond, so it is sp2. Carbon b is part of the C≡C triple bond, so it is sp. The single bond between them is a σ bond made from an sp2 orbital on a and an sp orbital on b. Because both orbitals have high s character, this C–C bond (about 1.43 Å) is shorter than the sp3–sp3 bond in ethane (1.54 Å).
x: Carbon b is part of a triple bond and has only two σ bonds, so it uses sp, not sp2, orbitals.
Carbon a is in the double bond, not the triple bond, so it is sp2.
Carbon a has a π bond, so it cannot be sp3.

q:
Consider each species drawn with all second-row atoms obeying the octet rule.
I. In BH4−, boron has a formal charge of −1.
II. In (CH3)3O+, oxygen has a formal charge of +1.
III. In carbon monoxide (C≡O), carbon has a formal charge of 0.
Which statements are true?
h: Apply valence − nonbonding − ½ bonding to each atom. For C≡O, count the lone pair on carbon.
w: I: B has 4 bonds, no lone pairs: 3 − 0 − 4 = −1 (true). II: O has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1 (true). III: in :C≡O:, carbon has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, and O is +1, so III is false. Answer: I and II only. The carbon of CO bears the negative formal charge even though O is more electronegative, which is why CO binds metals through carbon.
x: Statement II is also true: an oxygen with three bonds and one lone pair is +1, just like hydronium.
Statement III is false: the octet structure of CO puts −1 on carbon and +1 on oxygen.
Statement III is false; C in :C≡O: is 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, not 0.

q: In which compound is the lone pair on the tagged nitrogen a delocalized by resonance?
h: A lone pair is delocalized only if its atom is directly attached to a π bond (or an empty p orbital). An sp<sup>3</sup> carbon in between breaks the connection.
w: In N-methylacetamide the nitrogen is bonded directly to the carbonyl carbon, so its lone pair overlaps with the C=O π bond (a second resonance form puts C=N+ and O−). In allylamine, benzylamine and 4-aminobutan-2-one there is at least one sp3 CH2 between N and the π system, so the lone pair is localized and the N is a normal sp3 amine.
x: In allylamine the N is attached to an sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>, not to the alkene carbon; the lone pair cannot overlap with the C=C π bond (only an N on the sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, as in an enamine, would be conjugated).
Benzylamine's N sits on a CH<sub>2</sub> next to the ring, so the lone pair is not conjugated with the aromatic π system; that is why benzylamine is about as basic as an alkylamine.
The C=O is two sp<sup>3</sup> carbons away from N, so the lone pair is localized; there is no resonance form moving it toward oxygen.

q: In the best Lewis structure of methyl isocyanate (shown), how many lone pairs are there in total, and what is the hybridization of the carbon bonded to both N and O?
h: Give N and O octets with the double bonds shown, then count σ bonds on the N=C=O carbon.
w: With CH3–N=C=O and no formal charges, N (two bonds) has one lone pair and O (one double bond) has two lone pairs: 3 lone pairs. The N=C=O carbon makes two σ bonds and two π bonds, so it is sp and the N=C=O unit is linear, like CO2.
x: The central carbon has two double bonds and therefore only two σ bonds; two σ domains make it sp, not sp<sup>2</sup>.
N with two bonds needs only one lone pair to complete its octet; giving it two would make it −1.
Oxygen with one double bond needs two lone pairs, and the N=C=O carbon is sp because it has only two σ bonds.

q: In N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) the two N–CH3 groups give separate 1H NMR signals at 25 °C because rotation about the C–N bond is slow (barrier about 85 kJ/mol). What is the best explanation for this large barrier?
c: Resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character; rotation breaks the N lone pair’s overlap with C=O
Steric clash between the N-methyl groups and the carbonyl oxygen locks the molecule in one fixed conformation
Hydrogen bonds from the N-methyl hydrogens to the carbonyl oxygen hold the methyl groups in place
The nitrogen is sp<sup>3</sup>, and slow pyramidal inversion at N keeps the methyl groups apart
h: Draw the second resonance contributor of an amide. What kind of bond does it show between C and N?
w: An amide has a contributor with C=N+ and O−. In the hybrid the N is sp2 and planar and its lone pair (in a p orbital) overlaps with the C=O π bond, so the C–N bond has partial double-bond character. Rotating 90° about that bond would twist the N p orbital out of alignment and destroy the delocalization, which costs much more energy than rotating about an ordinary single bond (about 12 kJ/mol). The two methyl groups are therefore locked cis and trans to O on the NMR time scale.
x: Steric strain from small methyl groups is only a few kJ/mol; it cannot account for a barrier near 85 kJ/mol.
C–H bonds of methyl groups are not hydrogen-bond donors; H bonding requires H on N, O or F.
Amide nitrogens are sp<sup>2</sup> and planar, not sp<sup>3</sup>; N inversion is fast and would not separate the methyl signals anyway.

q: Which compound has no net molecular dipole moment?
h: Add the C–Cl bond dipoles as vectors. Do any two point in exactly opposite directions?
w: In trans-1,2-dichloroethene the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions across a center of symmetry and cancel, so μ = 0. In the cis isomer and in 1,1-dichloroethene both C–Cl dipoles point toward the same side, and in CH2Cl2 the tetrahedral arrangement leaves a net dipole.
x: In the cis isomer both chlorines are on the same side of the double bond, so their bond dipoles add to a net dipole.
Both C–Cl bonds in 1,1-dichloroethene point away from the same carbon at about 120°; they partly reinforce, giving a net dipole.
In tetrahedral CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> the two C–Cl dipoles are about 110° apart and do not cancel.

q: In which molecule do all of the atoms lie in one plane?
h: Any sp<sup>3</sup> carbon has hydrogens out of the plane. In allene, think about the two perpendicular π bonds.
w: In acrylonitrile every atom is sp2 or sp: the vinyl group is planar and the C–C≡N unit is linear and lies in that plane, so all seven atoms are coplanar. Propene and acetaldehyde contain a CH3 group whose tetrahedral hydrogens cannot all lie in the plane. In allene the two CH2 groups are twisted 90° from each other.
x: Allene's two π bonds are perpendicular, so the H–C–H plane at one end is perpendicular to the one at the other end.
The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon of propene is sp<sup>3</sup>; at most one of its hydrogens can lie in the plane of the alkene.
The methyl group of acetaldehyde is sp<sup>3</sup>, so two of its hydrogens sit above and below the plane of the C=O group.

q: Starting from N-methylacetamide as drawn, one curved arrow is drawn from the nitrogen lone pair to the C–N bond, and a second arrow from the C=O π bond onto oxygen. What are the formal charges on N and O in the new resonance contributor?
h: Follow the electrons: which atom loses a share of a lone pair, and which atom gains a lone pair?
w: The first arrow turns the N lone pair into a C=N π bond, so N goes from three bonds + one lone pair (0) to four bonds and no lone pair: +1. The second arrow moves the C=O π electrons onto oxygen, giving O one bond and three lone pairs: −1. Carbon keeps four bonds and stays neutral, and the contributor stays neutral overall.
x: The arrows move electron density away from N and toward O, so N becomes positive and O negative, not the reverse.
That pattern (C<sup>+</sup>, O<sup>−</sup>) would come from the C=O arrow alone; the N lone-pair arrow gives carbon a new bond, so carbon stays neutral and N becomes +1.
Oxygen gains the π electrons as a third lone pair, so it must become −1; a net +1 charge would also make the neutral amide charged.

q: A nucleophile adds to formaldehyde at carbon, while a proton or Lewis acid binds at oxygen. Which molecular-orbital description best explains this pattern?
c: The nucleophile donates into the π*<sub>C=O</sub> LUMO, which is larger on carbon; the acid accepts a nonbonding lone pair on oxygen
The nucleophile donates into the π<sub>C=O</sub> bonding orbital, which is concentrated on carbon; the acid accepts the π* electrons on oxygen
The nucleophile donates into the σ*<sub>C–H</sub> orbital, and the acid accepts the C=O π bonding electrons
The nucleophile donates into the π*<sub>C=O</sub> LUMO, which is larger on oxygen; the acid binds the lone pair on carbon
h: Nucleophiles fill an empty orbital (a LUMO); acids take electrons from a filled one. Where is each orbital concentrated in a polar C=O?
w: Formaldehyde's LUMO is π*C=O. Because O is more electronegative, the bonding π orbital is concentrated on O and the antibonding π* has its larger lobe on carbon, so nucleophiles attack C (roughly 107° from the C=O axis). The highest filled orbitals are the nonbonding lone pairs on oxygen, so protons and Lewis acids bind at O.
x: The π bonding orbital is already full and is larger on oxygen; a nucleophile must add electrons to an empty orbital.
σ*<sub>C–H</sub> is high in energy and attack there would be an S<sub>N</sub>2-like hydride displacement, which does not happen; acids bind the oxygen lone pairs.
In a polar π bond the antibonding orbital is larger on the less electronegative atom (carbon), and carbon in formaldehyde has no lone pair.

q: Structures I and II are the two resonance contributors of the methoxymethyl cation. Which statement is correct?
c: II is the major contributor because every atom has a complete octet
I is the major contributor because the positive charge is on the less electronegative carbon
I and II contribute equally because they are equivalent structures
II is not a valid contributor because oxygen cannot carry a positive charge
h: Rank contributors by the octet rule first; charge placement on the more or less electronegative atom is a later tiebreaker.
w: The first criterion for the major contributor is that the most atoms have full octets. In II every C and O has an octet (O has three bonds and one lone pair, +1). In I the CH2+ carbon has only six electrons. So II is the major contributor, even though it puts + on oxygen. This oxygen stabilization is why α-alkoxy carbocations (oxocarbenium ions) form easily.
x: Charge placement is only a tiebreaker between structures with equal numbers of octets; I has an electron-deficient carbon, so it is the minor contributor.
The two structures are not equivalent: they differ in octets and in where the charge sits, so they do not contribute equally.
Oxygen often carries +1 (hydronium, protonated alcohols, oxonium ions); with three bonds and one lone pair, + is the correct formal charge.

q: Rank the three resonance contributors of N,N-dimethylacetamide from least to most important (stable).
h: Use the rules in order: full octets first, then fewest formal charges.
w: I has full octets and no formal charges, so it is the most important. II has full octets but separated charges (N+, O−), so it is next. III also has separated charges and a carbon with only six electrons, so it is least important. Order: III < II < I. II is still a significant contributor, which is why amides are planar with a short C–N bond.
x: II has an octet at every atom while III has an electron-deficient carbon, so II is more important than III.
Charge separation makes II and III less stable than neutral I; I is the most important contributor, not the least.
Neutral I with all octets outranks charge-separated II; the octet rule and fewest charges both favor I.

q: Which carbocation is stabilized by resonance?
h: Resonance needs the empty p orbital directly next to a π bond, with the orbitals parallel.
w: The but-3-en-2-yl cation is allylic: the cationic carbon is directly bonded to the C=C, so the π electrons can shift to give a second contributor with + on the terminal CH2. In the homoallylic cation an sp3 CH2 separates the π bond from the cation. In the vinyl cation the empty orbital lies in the plane of the molecule, perpendicular to the C=C π bond, so no overlap is possible. The sec-butyl cation has no π bond at all.
x: The CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is one carbon removed from the alkene; with an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon in between, the π bond cannot overlap with the empty p orbital.
In a vinyl cation the empty orbital is perpendicular to the C=C π bond, so the two cannot overlap; vinyl cations are especially unstable.
The sec-butyl cation is stabilized only by hyperconjugation and induction; it has no π bond to delocalize the charge.

q: How many significant resonance contributors (including the one shown) can be drawn for the anion of pentane-2,4-dione?
h: The lone pair on the central carbon can push into either C=O bond.
w: The central carbanion can delocalize into the left C=O (putting − on that oxygen) or the right C=O (putting − on the other oxygen). With the drawn carbanion form that is 3 contributors, two of which place the charge on an electronegative oxygen. This extra delocalization is why the C3–H of pentane-2,4-dione has pKa ≈ 9, far lower than a simple ketone (about 19).
x: Two contributors would describe a simple ketone enolate; here there are two carbonyls, so the charge can reach either oxygen.
There is no fourth reasonable contributor: the CH<sub>3</sub> groups and C=O carbons have no further π bonds or lone pairs to shift.
Five would require moving σ bonds or hydrogens, which changes the compound rather than drawing a resonance form.

q: Number the cation below C1 (the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon) through C6 (the CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> carbon). Considering all of its resonance contributors, which carbons share the positive charge?
c: C2, C3, C4, C5 and C6
h: Push one π bond at a time toward the cationic carbon and see where the + moves each time.
w: Moving the C4=C5 π electrons toward C6 forms C5=C6 and puts + on C4. Then moving the C2=C3 π electrons toward C4 forms C3=C4 and puts + on C2. So the charge is shared by C2, C4 and C6: in a conjugated cation the + appears on alternating carbons, never on two adjacent ones.
x: This skips the middle contributor; you cannot get from + at C6 to + at C2 without passing through + at C4.
Charge in a conjugated π system alternates; C3 and C5 always keep a π bond in every contributor and never carry the +.
C3 and C5 keep a π bond in every contributor, so they are exactly the carbons that never bear the charge.

q:
Consider the acetate ion.
I. The ion rapidly flips back and forth between its two resonance contributors.
II. The two C–O bonds have the same length.
III. Each oxygen carries about half of the negative charge.
Which statements are true?
h: A resonance hybrid is a single real structure, not a mixture of structures in equilibrium.
w: Acetate has two equivalent contributors, so the real ion is their average: both C–O bonds are equal (about 1.26 Å, between C=O and C–O) and each oxygen carries about −½. Statement I describes resonance incorrectly: contributors are not separate species interconverting; the hybrid exists all the time. Answer: II and III only.
x: III is also true: equivalent contributors share the charge equally, so each O is about −½.
I is the classic misconception; the ion never exists as either contributor, so nothing flips.
I is false; resonance contributors are imaginary pictures, and the actual ion is always the hybrid.

q: Which structure is a resonance contributor of protonated acetone (shown), rather than a different compound?
h: All four have the formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. Resonance forms may move only π electrons and lone pairs; every atom, including every H, must stay put.
w: Moving the C=O π electrons onto oxygen gives (CH3)2C+–OH: the same atoms with the same connections, only electrons moved. Each of the other structures has a hydrogen or a carbon in a new place, so each is a constitutional isomer. The real ion is a hybrid with + shared between C and O, which explains why acid makes a carbonyl carbon more electrophilic.
x: Here a hydrogen has moved from a CH<sub>3</sub> to the central carbon; changing where an H is attached makes a different compound, not a resonance form.
This is the O-protonated enol (a tautomer pathway): an H moved from carbon to oxygen, so it is a different compound.
Oxygen is now on a terminal carbon and a hydrogen has moved, so this is a constitutional isomer (a cation derived from propan-1-ol), not a form of protonated acetone.

q: Structures I and II are resonance contributors of the enolate of acetone. Which statement is correct?
c: II is the major contributor because the negative charge is on the more electronegative oxygen
I is the major contributor because a negative charge is more stable on the less electronegative carbon
I and II contribute equally because both have full octets
Neither is valid, because I and II differ in the position of a hydrogen atom
h: Both have full octets and one formal charge. Use the tiebreaker: where is a negative charge most comfortable?
w: Both contributors obey the octet rule and each has a single −1 charge. The tiebreaker is electronegativity: a negative charge is better on the more electronegative atom, so II (the oxyanion) is the major contributor. Most of the charge density sits on oxygen, though the carbon still reacts as a nucleophile because its HOMO coefficient is large.
x: Carbon is less electronegative than oxygen, so it holds negative charge less well; I is the minor contributor.
Equal octets do not mean equal weight; charge location breaks the tie in favor of oxygen.
No hydrogen moves between I and II; only the π electrons and a lone pair shift, so they are valid resonance forms.

q: In the phenoxide ion, on which tagged ring carbons does the negative charge appear in resonance contributors?
h: Push an oxygen lone pair into the ring and follow the charge around one double bond at a time.
w: An O lone pair forms C=O, and the ring π bond moves to put − on the ortho carbon (a). Shifting the next π bond moves the charge to the para carbon (c), then to the other ortho carbon. The meta carbons (b) never carry the charge, because charge moves to alternating atoms. Answer: a and c.
x: The meta position is the one carbon type that never receives the charge.
Charge in a conjugated system alternates; it skips the meta carbon b.
Carbon b is meta and never bears the charge; the para carbon c does.

q: Based on resonance, which tagged carbons of pent-3-en-2-one carry a partial positive charge?
h: Draw the contributor with C<sup>+</sup>–O<sup>−</sup>, then move the C=C π bond toward the cation.
w: Polarizing the C=O gives + on the carbonyl carbon a. The adjacent C=C π electrons can shift to form a C=C between a and b, leaving + on the β-carbon c. So both a and c are electrophilic, which is why α,β-unsaturated carbonyls accept nucleophiles at the β-carbon (conjugate addition).
x: The β-carbon c also gets a + in a contributor; this is the basis of conjugate (1,4-) addition.
The α-carbon b never carries the + charge; charge alternates and skips it.
Carbon a, the carbonyl carbon, is δ+, and b is not.

q: In methyl acetate, rank the three bonds from shortest to longest: I = a–b, II = a–c, III = c–d.
h: A double bond is shortest. Then compare the two C–O single bonds: one has partial double-bond character from resonance and an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, the other does not.
w: I is the C=O double bond (about 1.20 Å). II, the acyl C–O bond, is shortened because the ester oxygen's lone pair donates into the C=O (a contributor with C=O+–CH3) and because the carbon is sp2 (about 1.34 Å). III, the O–CH3 bond, is an ordinary single bond to an sp3 carbon (about 1.44 Å). Order: I < II < III.
x: The acyl C–O bond (II) has partial double-bond character from resonance, so it is shorter, not longer, than the O–CH<sub>3</sub> bond.
A C=O double bond is shorter than any C–O bond with only partial double-bond character.
This is the reverse order; the full double bond I is the shortest.

q: In the allyl anion as drawn, the carbon bearing the negative charge is best described as:
c: sp<sup>2</sup>, with the lone pair in a p orbital that is part of the π system
sp<sup>3</sup>, with the lone pair in an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital
sp, with the lone pair in an sp orbital
sp<sup>2</sup>, with the lone pair in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital in the plane of the molecule
h: A lone pair next to a π bond is delocalized only if it sits in an orbital parallel to the π bond.
w: Because the lone pair can delocalize onto the other terminal carbon, the charged carbon rehybridizes to sp2 and places the lone pair in a p orbital that overlaps with the C=C π bond. All three carbons are then sp2, and the two terminal carbons share the negative charge equally. Rule: an atom with a lone pair adjacent to a π bond uses a p orbital for that lone pair.
x: Counting domains as drawn (three bonds + one lone pair) gives sp<sup>3</sup>, but that ignores resonance; an sp<sup>3</sup> lone pair could not overlap with the π bond.
The carbon has three σ bonds, so it needs three hybrid orbitals; sp would leave too few.
A lone pair in an in-plane sp<sup>2</sup> orbital would be perpendicular to the π bond and could not be delocalized.

q: Which statement about nitromethane is correct?
c: Both N–O bonds have the same length, between that of an N–O single bond and an N=O double bond
Nitrogen is +1 in one resonance contributor and neutral in the other
The best Lewis structure has two N=O double bonds and no formal charges on any atom
The negative charge stays on one oxygen, while the other oxygen remains neutral and double-bonded to N
h: Draw the second contributor by swapping which oxygen has the double bond. Are the two structures equivalent?
w: Nitromethane has two equivalent contributors that differ only in which oxygen holds the double bond. N is +1 in both, and each O is −½ in the hybrid. So the two N–O bonds are identical (about 1.22 Å) with a bond order of about 1.5.
x: N has four bonds and no lone pairs in both contributors, so it is +1 in each.
Two N=O bonds would give N five bonds (10 electrons); second-row atoms cannot exceed an octet.
Because the two contributors are equivalent, the negative charge is shared equally by both oxygens.

q: Methyl azide is often drawn as CH<sub>3</sub>–N=N<sup>+</sup>=N<sup>−</sup> (shown). In the other octet contributor, CH<sub>3</sub>–N–N≡N (N1 bonded to CH<sub>3</sub>), what are the formal charges on N1, N2 and N3?
h: Give each N an octet in CH<sub>3</sub>–N–N≡N, then use valence − nonbonding − ½ bonding.
w: In CH3–N–N≡N, N1 has two bonds and two lone pairs: 5 − 4 − 2 = −1. N2 has four bonds and no lone pairs: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. N3 has three bonds and one lone pair: 5 − 2 − 3 = 0. The middle nitrogen of an azide is +1 in every octet contributor, while the −1 charge moves between N1 and N3.
x: These are the charges in the contributor that was drawn, not the triple-bonded one; moving electrons shifts the −1 from N3 to N1.
N2 has four bonds and no lone pair in both contributors, so it is always +1, and N3 with a triple bond and a lone pair is 0.
N1 has two lone pairs and two bonds, which makes it −1, and N2 with four bonds is +1.

q: Which set of curved arrows converts the oxyanion contributor of the acetone enolate (shown) into the carbanion contributor?
c: One arrow from an O lone pair to the C–O bond, and one from the C=C π bond onto the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon
One arrow from an O lone pair directly to the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon
One arrow from the C=C π bond to the C–O bond, and one from an O lone pair onto the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon
One arrow from a C–H σ bond of the CH<sub>3</sub> to the C–O bond
h: Arrows start at electrons (lone pairs or π bonds) and end where those electrons become a new bond or lone pair. Make sure no carbon ends up with five bonds.
w: The O lone pair moves in to make the C=O π bond (arrow 1, lone pair → C–O bond). The central carbon would then have five bonds, so the C=C π bond must leave as a lone pair on the CH2 carbon (arrow 2, π bond → CH2). This gives CH3C(=O)CH2−. Resonance arrows move only π electrons and lone pairs.
x: Electrons cannot jump across an atom to a non-adjacent atom; the charge is relayed by two arrows through the central carbon.
The arrows' origins are swapped: the C=C π electrons cannot go to oxygen's bond while the O lone pair goes to a distant carbon.
Resonance never breaks σ bonds; moving a C–H σ bond would change the structure (a different compound), not draw a resonance form.

q: Which statement about the guanidinium ion (shown) is correct?
c: It has three equivalent resonance contributors, so all three C–N bonds have the same length
It has two resonance contributors, and the positive charge rests on carbon in the major one
One C–N bond is a double bond and is shorter than the other two C–N bonds
The two NH<sub>2</sub> nitrogens are sp<sup>3</sup> because each has a localized lone pair
h: Each NH<sub>2</sub> lone pair is next to the C=N bond. How many ways can you place the double bond?
w: The C=N+ can be drawn to any of the three nitrogens, with the other two NH2 lone pairs adjacent to it. The three contributors are equivalent, so the hybrid has three identical C–N bonds (bond order 1⅓), each N carries about +⅓, and all three nitrogens are sp2 and planar. This exceptional delocalization makes guanidine one of the strongest neutral organic bases (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 13.6).
x: There are three equivalent contributors, and in each one the + is on a nitrogen with four bonds; carbon keeps its octet.
Since all three contributors are equivalent, no single C=N exists in the real ion; all three bonds are the same length.
Each NH<sub>2</sub> lone pair is delocalized into the C=N π system, so those nitrogens are sp<sup>2</sup> with the lone pair in a p orbital.

q: Rank the C–H bonds on the tagged carbons a, b and c from weakest to strongest (homolytic bond dissociation energy).
h: More s character in the carbon orbital makes a shorter, stronger C–H bond. Also ask whether the radical left behind could be resonance-stabilized.
w: C–H bond strength rises with s character: sp3 (25% s) < sp2 (33%) < sp (50%). The alkyne C–H on a is the strongest (about 556 kJ/mol), the vinyl C–H on b is next (about 465 kJ/mol), and the CH3 C–H on c is weakest. Carbon c is also allylic, so breaking its C–H gives a resonance-stabilized radical, which lowers its BDE even further (about 370 kJ/mol). Order: c < b < a.
x: This reverses the trend; higher s character holds the bonding electrons closer to carbon and makes the C–H bond stronger, so the sp C–H is the strongest.
The allylic CH<sub>3</sub> C–H is weaker than a vinyl C–H: it is sp<sup>3</sup> and its radical is resonance-stabilized, while a vinyl radical is not.
The alkyne C–H (sp, 50% s) is the strongest of the three, not weaker than the vinyl C–H.

q:
Rank the molecular dipole moments from smallest to largest.
I. CH2Cl2   II. CHCl3   III. CCl4
h: More polar bonds do not always mean a larger molecular dipole. Think about how the C–Cl vectors cancel in a tetrahedron.
w: CCl4 is perfectly tetrahedral, so its four C–Cl dipoles cancel (μ = 0). In CHCl3 three C–Cl dipoles partly cancel one another, leaving about 1.0 D. In CH2Cl2 only two C–Cl dipoles at about 112° add, and they reinforce more than they cancel, giving about 1.6 D. Order: III < II < I.
x: Adding chlorines adds polar bonds, but in a tetrahedron the extra C–Cl dipoles point in opposing directions and cancel; CCl<sub>4</sub> has μ = 0.
CCl<sub>4</sub> is the smallest (zero), but CHCl<sub>3</sub> (about 1.0 D) is smaller than CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (about 1.6 D), because a third C–Cl bond partly cancels the other two.
CCl<sub>4</sub> has zero dipole by symmetry, so it must be the smallest, not in the middle.

q: Rank these C5H12 isomers from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Only London dispersion forces act here. Which shape gives the most surface contact between neighboring molecules?
w: All three isomers have the same mass, so the difference comes from shape. Branching makes a molecule more compact (closer to a sphere), which lowers the contact area and the London dispersion forces. Neopentane (III, 9.5 °C) < isopentane (II, 28 °C) < pentane (I, 36 °C): III < II < I.
x: This is reversed: the linear isomer has the most surface contact and the strongest dispersion forces, so it boils highest.
Isopentane is less branched than neopentane, so it boils higher than III, not lower.
Pentane, with the most surface area, has the highest boiling point, not the middle one.

q: These compounds have similar molar masses (72–74 g/mol). Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each pure liquid: dispersion only, dipole–dipole, or hydrogen bonding.
w: Diethyl ether (I) has a small dipole and no O–H, so it relies mostly on dispersion (bp 35 °C). Butanal (II) has a strongly polar C=O and dipole–dipole attractions (bp 75 °C). Butan-1-ol (III) can hydrogen-bond to itself through O–H (bp 117 °C). Order: I < II < III.
x: The C=O group of an aldehyde is much more polar than the C–O–C of an ether, so the aldehyde boils higher than the ether.
Butan-1-ol hydrogen-bonds to itself; the aldehyde cannot (it has no O–H), so the alcohol boils highest.
This is the reverse; the alcohol, with H bonding, has the highest boiling point.

q: Which compound is miscible with water in all proportions?
h: Both ethers accept hydrogen bonds from water. Which oxygen is easier for a water molecule to reach?
w: Water dissolves an ether by donating H bonds to the oxygen lone pairs. In tetrahydrofuran the ring ties the alkyl groups back, leaving the oxygen lone pairs exposed, so THF is completely miscible with water. In diethyl ether the freely rotating ethyl groups crowd the oxygen, and the compound dissolves only to about 7 g per 100 mL. Pentane and 1-chlorobutane cannot accept H bonds well and are nearly insoluble.
x: Diethyl ether has the same number of carbons and an O atom, but its ethyl groups shield the oxygen; it is only partly soluble (about 7 g/100 mL).
Pentane has only C–C and C–H bonds; it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor and is insoluble in water.
The C–Cl bond is polar, but chlorine is a very weak H-bond acceptor, so 1-chlorobutane is nearly insoluble in water.

q: Which compound can form hydrogen bonds with other molecules of itself in the pure liquid?
h: A hydrogen bond needs both a donor (H on N, O or F) and an acceptor (a lone pair on N, O or F).
w: N-Methylacetamide has an N–H donor and a C=O acceptor, so its molecules hydrogen-bond to each other (as in protein backbones). Trimethylamine, acetone and ethyl acetate have lone-pair acceptors but no H on N or O, so they can accept H bonds from water but cannot H-bond to themselves.
x: All three N substituents are methyl groups; with no N–H, trimethylamine has no donor.
Acetone's oxygen is an acceptor, but its hydrogens are on carbon and C–H is not an H-bond donor.
The ester has two oxygen acceptors but no O–H or N–H donor.

q: cis-1,2-Dichloroethene boils at 60 °C, while the trans isomer boils at 48 °C. What is the best explanation?
c: The cis isomer has a net dipole and dipole–dipole attractions; the trans isomer’s bond dipoles cancel
The cis isomer can hydrogen-bond through its C–H bonds, while the trans isomer cannot do so
The cis isomer has a larger molar mass and therefore stronger London dispersion forces between molecules
The trans isomer is more strained, which weakens its attractions to neighboring molecules
h: The isomers have the same mass and formula. What property differs because of how the C–Cl bonds are arranged?
w: Both isomers have the same atoms and nearly the same surface area. In the trans isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel (μ = 0), while in the cis isomer they add to a net dipole (about 1.9 D). The cis molecules attract each other through dipole–dipole forces in addition to dispersion, so the cis isomer boils higher.
x: C–H bonds are not hydrogen-bond donors; neither isomer can H-bond to itself.
Stereoisomers have identical formulas and molar masses, so mass cannot explain the difference.
Ring or steric strain is an intramolecular energy term and does not set boiling point; trans-alkenes are actually the less strained isomers.

q: Acetic acid (60 g/mol) boils at 118 °C, while propan-1-ol (60 g/mol) boils at 97 °C. What is the best explanation?
c: Acetic acid forms cyclic dimers held by two strong hydrogen bonds
Acetic acid has more hydrogen-bond donors per molecule than propan-1-ol
Propan-1-ol is nonpolar because its O–H dipole is canceled by the alkyl chain
Acetic acid is ionized in the pure liquid, so ion–ion forces raise its boiling point
h: Count donors and acceptors in a carboxylic acid, and picture two molecules facing each other.
w: Both compounds have one O–H donor. A carboxylic acid also has a C=O oxygen that is a strong acceptor, so two molecules can line up head-to-head and form a cyclic dimer held by two hydrogen bonds. The resonance in the COOH group makes its O–H more polarized and its C=O oxygen more electron-rich, so these H bonds are stronger than an alcohol's. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so acetic acid boils higher.
x: Each molecule has exactly one O–H donor, so the difference is not the number of donors but the strength and pairing of the H bonds.
Propan-1-ol is polar and hydrogen-bonds to itself; that is why it boils far above propane or butane of similar mass.
Pure acetic acid is a weak acid and is almost entirely un-ionized; the liquid is held together by hydrogen bonds, not ions.

q: Which statement about the π and π* molecular orbitals of ethene is correct?
c: π* has a nodal plane between the two carbons, perpendicular to the C=C axis, and is the LUMO
π has a nodal plane between the two carbons, and that is why it is lower in energy than π*
π* holds the two π electrons in the ground state and is the HOMO
The π electron density is concentrated along the C–C internuclear axis
h: Combine two parallel p orbitals in phase and out of phase. Which combination puts a node between the nuclei?
w: Adding the two p orbitals in phase gives the bonding π MO, with electron density above and below the C–C axis and no node between the carbons; it holds both π electrons and is the HOMO. The out-of-phase combination is π*, which has a nodal plane between the carbons perpendicular to the bond axis. It is empty, higher in energy, and is the LUMO. (Both MOs also share the nodal plane of the molecule itself.)
x: The bonding π MO has no node between the carbons; a node between nuclei raises the energy, which is why π* is higher.
The two π electrons fill the lower-energy bonding π MO, which is the HOMO; π* is empty in the ground state.
Density along the internuclear axis describes a σ bond; π density lies above and below the plane of the molecule.

q: Why does cis-but-2-ene not convert to trans-but-2-ene at room temperature?
c: Rotating about the C=C bond would twist the p orbitals apart and break the π bond
The two methyl groups are too large to pass each other during rotation
Both carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>, and their σ bond cannot rotate
The cis isomer is more stable than the trans isomer, so there is no driving force
h: What holds the two halves of a double bond in one orientation that a single bond does not have?
w: The π bond exists only while the two p orbitals are parallel. Rotating one carbon 90° makes the p orbitals perpendicular, so the overlap drops to zero and the π bond breaks, which costs roughly 250–270 kJ/mol. That is far more energy than is available at room temperature, so cis and trans alkenes are separate, isolable compounds.
x: Methyl groups pass each other easily in butane (single-bond rotation barrier only about 25 kJ/mol); the problem is the π bond, not size.
The alkene carbons are sp<sup>2</sup>; σ bonds alone rotate freely, so a pure σ bond would not prevent isomerization.
The trans isomer is actually the more stable one, so there is a driving force; the barrier, not thermodynamics, prevents the change.

q: The C=C bond of ethene is stronger than the C–C bond of ethane, but less than twice as strong. Why?
c: The π bond is formed by side-on p-orbital overlap, which is weaker than the head-on overlap of a σ bond
The π bond is formed by head-on overlap of sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals, which is weaker than p-orbital overlap
The two carbons of ethene are farther apart than those of ethane, so both bonds are weakened
The π electrons are shared with the hydrogens, so less of their density is between the carbons
h: Compare how much overlap two orbitals get when they meet end-to-end versus side-by-side.
w: A double bond is one σ bond plus one π bond. The σ component forms by head-on overlap of sp2 orbitals, which concentrates density between the nuclei. The π component forms by side-on overlap of parallel p orbitals, which is less effective, so the π bond is weaker than a σ bond. The total is therefore less than twice a C–C single bond. This weak π bond is the reactive site of alkenes.
x: Head-on overlap of hybrid orbitals makes the σ bond; the π bond uses unhybridized p orbitals overlapping side by side.
The C=C bond (about 1.34 Å) is shorter than the C–C bond in ethane (1.54 Å), not longer.
The π MO is made only from the two carbon p orbitals; the hydrogens bond through σ bonds and are not part of the π system.

q: What is the LUMO of the tert-butyl cation, the orbital that accepts electrons from an incoming nucleophile?
c: The empty 2p orbital on the central carbon
An sp<sup>3</sup> orbital on the central carbon holding a lone pair
A σ*<sub>C–H</sub> orbital of one methyl group
An sp<sup>2</sup> orbital on the central carbon in the plane of the methyl groups
h: The cationic carbon is sp<sup>2</sup> with three σ bonds. Which of its orbitals is left over and how many electrons does it hold?
w: The cationic carbon uses three sp2 orbitals for its three C–C σ bonds and has one unhybridized 2p orbital that is empty. This low-energy empty orbital is the LUMO, and nucleophiles attack it from either face of the planar cation (which is why SN1 at a stereocenter gives racemization).
x: A carbocation has no lone pair, and its carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, not sp<sup>3</sup>.
σ*<sub>C–H</sub> orbitals are much higher in energy than the empty p orbital; neighboring C–H bonds donate into the p orbital (hyperconjugation), not the reverse.
All three sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals are already used in C–C σ bonds; the only empty orbital is the p orbital perpendicular to that plane.

q: Which tagged carbon of chloroacetone carries the largest partial positive charge?
h: Count bonds to electronegative atoms, and remember that a C=O π bond is also polarized toward oxygen (C<sup>+</sup>–O<sup>−</sup> contributor).
w: The carbonyl carbon a is bonded to oxygen by both a σ and a π bond, and the resonance contributor C+–O− places a full + on it. Its partial positive charge is the largest, which is why nucleophiles add to C=O carbons. Carbon b is δ+ from one C–Cl bond, and the CH3 carbon c is only slightly affected. Answer: a.
x: The C–Cl bond makes b δ+, but one polar σ bond to Cl withdraws less than a σ + π bond to oxygen with a C+–O− contributor.
The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has no bond to an electronegative atom; it is only weakly δ+ by induction through the carbonyl carbon.
Carbon b has a polar C–Cl bond and c does not, so they cannot be equal; neither matches the carbonyl carbon.

q:
Consider the carbon–halogen bonds in CH3F, CH3Cl, CH3Br and CH3I.
I. The C–F bond is the shortest and strongest.
II. The C–I bond is the most polar.
III. The C–Br bond is longer than the C–Cl bond.
Which statements are true?
h: Bond length follows the size of the halogen; bond polarity follows the electronegativity difference.
w: Down group 17 the halogen atoms grow larger, so bond length increases (C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I) and orbital overlap with carbon decreases, so bond strength decreases. That makes I and III true. Polarity follows electronegativity: F (4.0) gives the most polar bond, while I (2.7) is barely more electronegative than C (2.5), so the C–I bond is the least polar. Answer: I and III only.
x: II is false: iodine's electronegativity is close to carbon's, so C–I is the least polar C–X bond, not the most.
II is false, and I is true; C–F is both the shortest and the strongest C–X bond.
II is false: C–F is the most polar bond and C–I the least.

q: These C8H10 isomers have similar boiling points (136–144 °C). Which one has by far the highest melting point?
h: Boiling depends on attractions in the liquid; melting also depends on how well the molecules fit together in a crystal.
w: Melting point depends strongly on how efficiently molecules pack in the solid. p-Xylene is the most symmetrical isomer (a center of symmetry), so it packs tightly and melts at about 13 °C. o-Xylene (−25 °C), m-xylene (−48 °C) and ethylbenzene (−95 °C) are less symmetrical and pack poorly. The boiling points, which depend on liquid-phase forces, are all similar. This symmetry effect is used to purify p-xylene industrially by crystallization.
x: o-Xylene has the largest dipole and the highest boiling point, but its lower symmetry gives poorer packing; it melts near −25 °C.
m-Xylene is less symmetrical than the para isomer and melts at about −48 °C.
The flexible ethyl group packs worst of all; ethylbenzene melts near −95 °C.

q: These compounds have nearly the same molar mass (58–60 g/mol). Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Two of these hydrogen-bond. Which bond, N–H or O–H, is more polar?
w: Butane (I) has only dispersion forces (bp −1 °C). Propan-1-amine (II) hydrogen-bonds through N–H (bp 48 °C). Propan-1-ol (III) hydrogen-bonds through O–H, which is more polar because O is more electronegative than N, so its H bonds are stronger (bp 97 °C). Order: I < II < III.
x: N–H bonds are less polar than O–H bonds, so the amine forms weaker H bonds and boils lower than the alcohol.
The amine hydrogen-bonds while butane does not, so the amine boils well above butane.
This is the reverse; butane, with dispersion forces only, boils lowest.

q: Rank the three carbon–carbon bonds of (E)-hex-3-en-1-yne from shortest to longest: I = a–b, II = c–d, III = d–e.
h: Bond order matters most. For single bonds, compare the hybridization (s character) of the two carbons.
w: III is the C≡C triple bond (about 1.20 Å), the shortest. II is a single bond, but it joins an sp2 carbon to an sp carbon; the high s character of both orbitals pulls the nuclei together (about 1.43 Å). I is an ordinary sp3–sp3 single bond (about 1.53 Å). Order: III < II < I.
x: This is the reverse; higher bond order and higher s character both shorten a bond, so the triple bond is shortest.
The single bond II cannot be shorter than the triple bond III, even with sp<sup>2</sup>–sp hybridization.
The sp<sup>2</sup>–sp single bond (II) is shorter than the sp<sup>3</sup>–sp<sup>3</sup> single bond (I) because of its greater s character.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated in ethanol, and the substitution product forms by an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. Which rate law describes this reaction?
h: Only species that appear in or before the rate-determining step show up in the rate law. What is the slow step of an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction?
w: In an SN1 reaction the slow step is ionization of the C–Br bond to give the tertiary carbocation and Br−. Ethanol attacks the cation only afterward, in a fast step, so it does not appear in the rate law: rate = k[RBr]. (Ethanol is also the solvent, so its concentration barely changes anyway.)
x: A second-order rate law with the nucleophile is the S<sub>N</sub>2 rate law. Here ethanol adds after the rate-determining step, so its concentration does not enter.
The substrate must appear: its ionization is the rate-determining step. The nucleophile alone cannot control the rate.
No step involves two substrate molecules colliding; ionization is unimolecular, so the order in RBr is one.

q: The reaction of 1-bromopropane with NaCN in DMSO is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction. If [NaCN] is tripled and [1-bromopropane] is halved, what happens to the initial rate?
c: It increases by a factor of 1.5
It increases by a factor of 3
It decreases to half of the original rate
It increases by a factor of 6
h: Write the rate law for an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction, then multiply the factor for each concentration change.
w: SN2 is a single concerted step involving both partners, so rate = k[RBr][CN−]. New rate = (½)(3) = 1.5 × the original rate.
x: Tripling the rate would be correct only if the substrate concentration did not appear in the rate law; in S<sub>N</sub>2 it does, and it was halved.
Halving the rate ignores the cyanide term; an S<sub>N</sub>2 rate is first order in the nucleophile too.
A factor of 6 comes from multiplying 3 × 2, treating "halved" as "doubled". Halving [RBr] contributes a factor of ½.

q: Initial rates were measured for the reaction of an alkyl bromide (RBr) with sodium azide in 80% aqueous ethanol. Which conclusion fits the data?
c: Rate = k[RBr]; an SN1 mechanism, as expected for a tertiary RBr
Rate = k[RBr][N3−]; an SN2 mechanism, as expected for a primary RBr
Rate = k[N3−]; an SN2 mechanism in which azide attack is slow
Rate = k[RBr]2; an SN1 mechanism with two ionizations
h: Compare experiments that change only one concentration at a time: 1 vs 2 for RBr, 1 vs 3 for azide.
w: Experiments 1 → 2: doubling [RBr] doubles the rate, so the reaction is first order in RBr. Experiments 1 → 3: doubling [N3−] leaves the rate unchanged, so it is zero order in azide. Rate = k[RBr], the signature of an SN1 mechanism (rate-determining ionization). That fits a tertiary (or other cation-stabilizing) substrate in a polar protic solvent.
x: An S<sub>N</sub>2 rate law would double when [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] doubles; experiment 3 shows no change.
Experiment 2 shows the rate depends on [RBr], and experiment 3 shows it does not depend on azide; this choice has both backwards.
Doubling [RBr] would quadruple a second-order rate; the data show only a doubling.

q: Rank these alkyl bromides from slowest to fastest in an SN2 reaction with NaI in acetone.
h: S<sub>N</sub>2 needs backside access to the carbon bearing Br. Look at branching on that carbon (α) and on the next carbon (β).
w: SN2 rates fall as the backside of the electrophilic carbon gets crowded. Methyl (I) is fastest, then the unbranched primary 1-bromopropane (II), then the secondary 2-bromopropane (III). Neopentyl bromide (IV) is primary, but the tert-butyl group on the β carbon blocks the backside so completely that it reacts about 105 times slower than a simple primary halide, slower even than a secondary one. Order: IV < III < II < I.
x: This treats neopentyl bromide as a "normal" primary halide. Its β-tert-butyl group makes it slower than the secondary bromide III.
This is the S<sub>N</sub>1 (carbocation-stability) order turned around; for S<sub>N</sub>2 the least hindered methyl halide is fastest, not slowest.
Secondary III has an extra α-methyl group, so it is slower than the unbranched primary II, not faster.

q: Which compound undergoes S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis fastest in 80% aqueous ethanol?
h: The rate-determining step makes a carbocation. Which cation is stabilized by both alkyl groups and resonance?
w: SN1 rates follow carbocation stability. 2-Bromo-2-phenylpropane ionizes to a cation that is both tertiary and benzylic: the positive charge is delocalized into the ring and also stabilized by two methyl groups. 2-Bromo-2-phenylpropane is fastest.
x: The tert-butyl cation is tertiary but has no resonance; adding benzylic delocalization (the key) makes the cation more stable still.
The benzyl cation is resonance stabilized but primary; the tertiary benzylic cation has extra alkyl stabilization.
A secondary cyclohexyl cation has neither resonance nor tertiary substitution; it ionizes far more slowly.

q: Rank the halide ions from most to least nucleophilic toward CH3Br in methanol.
h: Methanol is a protic solvent. Which anion does it hydrogen-bond to most strongly?
w: In a polar protic solvent, small anions with concentrated charge are tightly hydrogen-bonded and must shed part of that solvent shell to react. F− is held most tightly and I− least; iodide is also the most polarizable. Nucleophilicity therefore runs I− > Br− > Cl− > F−, opposite to basicity.
x: This is the basicity order, and roughly the order in a polar aprotic solvent where anions are not hydrogen-bonded. Methanol is protic.
Iodide is not weaker than chloride in methanol; it is the least solvated and most polarizable halide, so it is the strongest of the four.
Bromide and iodide are reversed. Iodide, larger and more polarizable, is the better nucleophile in a protic solvent.

q: KCN reacts with 1-chlorobutane much faster in DMSO than in methanol. Which explanation is correct?
c: DMSO solvates K<sup>+</sup> well but cannot hydrogen-bond to CN<sup>−</sup>, leaving the anion poorly solvated and more reactive
DMSO hydrogen-bonds to CN<sup>−</sup>, which pulls electron density onto carbon and makes it more nucleophilic
DMSO stabilizes the butyl carbocation, so ionization of the C–Cl bond is faster
DMSO protonates the chlorine, turning it into a better leaving group
h: Think about what each solvent can do to an anion. Does DMSO have an O–H or N–H bond?
w: DMSO is polar aprotic: its partly negative oxygen solvates cations strongly, but it has no O–H to hydrogen-bond to anions. In methanol, CN− sits in a hydrogen-bonded cage that must be partly removed before it can attack. In DMSO the "naked" cyanide is higher in energy, so the SN2 barrier is lower. DMSO solvates K+ but not CN−.
x: DMSO has no O–H or N–H bond, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to anions; and hydrogen-bonding would lower, not raise, nucleophilicity.
A primary butyl cation is far too unstable to form; 1-chlorobutane reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2, which has no carbocation.
DMSO is not an acid; it cannot protonate an alkyl chloride.

q: Rank the anions from best to worst leaving group.
h: A good leaving group is a weak base. Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> values of the conjugate acids.
w: Leaving-group ability tracks the stability of the departing anion, i.e., how weak a base it is. Conjugate-acid pKas: CF3SO3H ≈ −14, CH3SO3H ≈ −2, CH3CO2H 4.8, H2O 15.7. Triflate (II) has the charge spread over three oxygens and pulled further by the CF3 group. Order: II > III > I > IV.
x: The CF<sub>3</sub> group withdraws electron density inductively and makes triflate a weaker base than mesylate, so triflate leaves better.
Acetate is a much stronger base than either sulfonate (its acid has pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8); it is a poor leaving group compared with them.
Hydroxide (from water, pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) is a far stronger base than acetate, so it is the worst leaving group, not third.

q: Which set of conditions converts 2-bromobutane mainly into a substitution product by an SN2 pathway?
h: A secondary substrate goes S<sub>N</sub>2 only with a good nucleophile that is a weak base, in a polar aprotic solvent.
w: With a secondary halide, strong bases (alkoxides) favor E2 elimination. Azide is an excellent nucleophile but a weak base (HN3 pKa 4.7), and DMSO leaves it unsolvated, so NaN3 in DMSO gives mainly 2-azidobutane by SN2 with inversion.
x: Ethoxide is a strong base; with a secondary bromide and heat, E2 (butenes) is the major pathway.
tert-Butoxide is a bulky strong base; it gives almost entirely E2 product with a secondary bromide.
Methanol is a weak nucleophile; with heat, a secondary bromide reacts slowly by S<sub>N</sub>1/E1, not S<sub>N</sub>2.

q:
Which changes would increase the rate of SN1 solvolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane in ethanol?
I. Adding 0.1 M NaN3, a much stronger nucleophile than ethanol
II. Using 50% aqueous ethanol as the solvent
III. Replacing the chloride with bromide (2-bromo-2-methylpropane)
h: Ask what each change does to the energy of the ionization transition state.
w: The SN1 rate depends only on ionization. II: water is more polar and a better hydrogen-bond donor than ethanol; it stabilizes the developing carbocation and chloride, so ionization is faster. III: Br− is a weaker base and better leaving group than Cl−, so the C–Br bond ionizes faster. I: the nucleophile is not in the rate law, so adding azide changes which product forms (some tert-butyl azide) but not how fast the chloride ionizes. II and III only.
x: I does not raise the rate: any nucleophile, azide included, reacts only after the rate-determining ionization.
Adding a stronger nucleophile is the S<sub>N</sub>2 lever; S<sub>N</sub>1 is zero order in the nucleophile, and II and III do speed ionization.
A better leaving group also speeds the rate-determining ionization, so III belongs with II.

q: The energy diagram is for the S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction of a tertiary alkyl bromide with water. Which point is the carbocation intermediate?
c: B, the local minimum between two maxima
A, the highest point on the curve
The reactant energy level at the far left
h: Intermediates sit in energy wells; transition states sit at peaks.
w: An SN1 diagram has two steps: ionization (TS A, highest, rate-determining) and capture of the cation by water (TS C, low). The carbocation sits in the valley between them, at B. It is a real species with a finite lifetime, unlike a transition state.
x: A is the transition state for ionization, the rate-determining step. A transition state is a maximum, not an intermediate.
C is the transition state for nucleophile capture of the cation; it is a maximum.
The far-left level is the starting alkyl bromide plus water, before any bond breaks.

q: Which description of the S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state for CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is correct?
c: The carbon is roughly trigonal bipyramidal, with O and Br partly bonded on opposite sides
The central carbon is a planar carbocation, with Br<sup>−</sup> fully detached and CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup> not yet bonded
O and Br are partly bonded on the same side of the central carbon, about 90° apart
The central carbon is tetrahedral, with five full bonds to its five groups
h: S<sub>N</sub>2 is concerted and goes with inversion. Where must the nucleophile be relative to the leaving group?
w: In the SN2 transition state the nucleophile enters from the back while the leaving group departs from the front: O···C···Br is nearly linear (180°), and the three other groups lie flat in a plane, like an umbrella turning inside out. Trigonal bipyramidal, O and Br partly bonded on opposite sides. This geometry is why SN2 inverts configuration.
x: A free carbocation is the S<sub>N</sub>1 intermediate. S<sub>N</sub>2 has no intermediate; bond making and breaking happen together.
Frontside attack would give retention; S<sub>N</sub>2 uses backside attack, with the nucleophile 180° from the leaving group.
Carbon cannot have five full bonds; in the transition state the C–O and C–Br bonds are both partial.

q: Which list contains only polar aprotic solvents?
h: Protic solvents have an H on O or N. Polar solvents have a sizable dipole.
w: Dimethyl sulfoxide, N,N-dimethylformamide, acetone and acetonitrile all have strong dipoles (S=O, C=O, C≡N) but no O–H or N–H bonds. DMSO, DMF, acetone, acetonitrile is the all-aprotic polar list.
x: Methanol has an O–H bond; it is polar protic.
