Water, acetic acid and ethanol are all polar protic; only DMF is aprotic.
Hexane and toluene are nonpolar, and diethyl ether is only weakly polar; DMSO is the only polar aprotic solvent in the list.

q: 3-Bromo-2,2-dimethylbutane is heated in ethanol. Which compound is the major substitution product?
h: A secondary carbocation next to a quaternary carbon can become more stable by a 1,2-shift. Which group can move?
w: Ionization gives a secondary cation at C3. The adjacent C2 carries three methyl groups (no H), so a 1,2-methyl shift moves the cation to C2, where it is tertiary. Ethanol captures this tertiary cation: 2-ethoxy-2,3-dimethylbutane. (E1 alkenes also form, but the question asks for the substitution product.)
x: This is the unrearranged ether. The secondary cation rearranges to a tertiary one faster than ethanol captures it.
This is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, an E1 elimination product, not a substitution product.
D would need the cation on a primary carbon; shifts go toward the more stable cation, not away from it.

q: 3-Chloro-3-methylbut-1-ene is dissolved in aqueous acetone. Which statement best describes the alcohol products of S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis?
c: Both 2-methylbut-3-en-2-ol and 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol, from water attacking either end of the allylic cation
Only 2-methylbut-3-en-2-ol forms, because water attacks only the tertiary carbon that lost Cl<sup>−</sup>
Only 3-methylbutan-2-ol forms, after a hydride shift
Only 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol forms, by direct S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of water at the less hindered primary carbon atom
h: Draw the cation formed by ionization. Is the positive charge on one carbon only?
w: Loss of Cl− gives a cation that is both tertiary and allylic. Resonance spreads the positive charge over C3 (tertiary) and C1 (primary end of the old alkene). Water can attack either site, giving 2-methylbut-3-en-2-ol and 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol. The second product has a trisubstituted (more stable) C=C, so it is an important product even though attack occurs at a primary carbon.
x: The allylic cation is delocalized, so water can also attack C1; ignoring the second resonance form misses a major product.
That product is saturated: a hydride shift cannot remove a C=C, and the allylic tertiary cation has no reason to rearrange.
The starting material has no leaving group on a primary carbon; C1 is sp<sup>2</sup>. The primary alcohol comes from the resonance-delocalized cation, not from S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: Rank the nucleophiles from most to least reactive toward CH3I in methanol.
h: Two rules: an anion beats its neutral conjugate acid, and in a protic solvent a larger, more polarizable atom beats a smaller one in the same group.
w: Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen and is less tightly hydrogen-bonded by methanol, so CH3S− is the best. Among the oxygen nucleophiles, methoxide (localized charge, strong base) beats acetate (charge delocalized over two oxygens), and neutral methanol is weakest. Order: CH3S− > CH3O− > CH3CO2− > CH3OH.
x: This follows basicity. In a protic solvent, the more polarizable, less solvated thiolate is the better nucleophile even though methoxide is the stronger base.
Acetate is resonance stabilized, which makes it a weaker nucleophile than methoxide, not a stronger one.
Thiolate is the strongest of the four in methanol; placing it below acetate ignores polarizability.

q: Which compound reacts readily both by S<sub>N</sub>1 (ethanol, heat) and by S<sub>N</sub>2 (NaI in acetone)?
h: S<sub>N</sub>1 needs a stabilized cation; S<sub>N</sub>2 needs an unhindered carbon. Which substrate offers both?
w: Benzyl bromide is primary, so the backside is open for SN2; it is also benzylic, so the SN2 transition state and the SN1 cation are both stabilized by the ring π system. Benzyl bromide reacts quickly by either path.
x: tert-Butyl bromide ionizes easily (S<sub>N</sub>1) but its crowded tertiary carbon blocks backside attack, so it does not undergo S<sub>N</sub>2.
1-Bromobutane is a fine S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate, but a primary unstabilized cation is too high in energy for S<sub>N</sub>1.
Bromobenzene reacts by neither: backside attack would go through the ring, and an aryl cation is very unstable.

q: (S)-2-Bromopentane is treated with NaSCH3 in DMF. What is the major product?
h: Thiolate is a strong nucleophile and a weak base, and DMF is polar aprotic. What happens to the configuration in that mechanism?
w: CH3S− is an excellent nucleophile but a weak base, so this secondary bromide reacts by SN2: backside attack with inversion at C2. Priorities in the product are SCH3 > propyl > CH3 > H, the same pattern as Br > propyl > CH3 > H in the reactant, so inversion changes the label: (R)-2-(methylthio)pentane.
x: This is the (S) product, formed with retention. SN2 goes by backside attack and inverts the stereocenter.
C has SCH<sub>3</sub> on C3. S<sub>N</sub>2 has no carbocation and no shift; the nucleophile bonds to the carbon that held Br.
This is an E2 alkene. Thiolates are weak bases, so elimination is minor with this secondary bromide.

q: (R)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane is warmed in methanol. What is the stereochemical outcome for the substitution product, 3-methoxy-3-methylhexane?
c: Only (S), by inversion at the stereocenter
h: Which mechanism does a tertiary bromide follow in a weakly nucleophilic protic solvent? What is the shape of its intermediate?
w: A tertiary bromide in methanol reacts by SN1. Ionization gives a planar (sp2) tertiary carbocation, and methanol can add to either face, so both enantiomers form: a racemic (or nearly racemic) mixture. In practice a small excess of inversion is often seen because the departing Br− briefly shields the front face (ion pairing), but the product is essentially racemized.
x: Clean inversion is the S<sub>N</sub>2 outcome. A tertiary carbon is too hindered for backside attack.
Retention would need the nucleophile to approach only the face the bromide left; a planar cation has two equally open faces.
The product has a single stereocenter, so it cannot be meso; meso compounds need two or more stereocenters and an internal mirror plane.

q: (2R,3R)-2-Bromo-3-methylpentane reacts with NaN3 in DMSO. Which product forms?
h: Only one stereocenter is touched by the nucleophile. What happens there, and what happens at the other one?
w: Azide in DMSO is a strong nucleophile and weak base, so the reaction is SN2 at C2: backside attack inverts C2. N3 takes the top priority that Br had, so the C2 label flips from R to S. C3 is not involved, and its substituent priorities (C2 branch > ethyl > CH3 > H) are unchanged, so it stays R: (2S,3R). It is a diastereomer of the retention product.
x: This is retention at C2, which would need frontside attack. S<sub>N</sub>2 inverts the carbon that is attacked.
C3 is not attacked and no bond to it breaks, so its configuration (and label) stays R; inverting both gives the enantiomer of the retention product.
This keeps C2 and inverts C3, the wrong carbon. The reaction occurs at C2, which bears the bromine.

q: cis-1-Bromo-4-methylcyclohexane is treated with NaN3 in DMSO. What is the major product?
c: a 1:1 mixture of the cis and trans azides
h: Backside attack puts the nucleophile on the opposite face of the ring from where the leaving group was.
w: Azide/DMSO gives SN2. The nucleophile enters from the face opposite the C–Br bond, so the azide ends up on the opposite face of the ring from the original bromine. The bromide was cis to the methyl, so the azide is trans: trans-1-azido-4-methylcyclohexane.
x: This is the cis azide, the retention product. Backside attack moves the substituent to the other face of the ring.
This is 4-methylcyclohexene, the E2 product. Azide is a weak base, so elimination is minor.
A cis/trans mixture would come from a planar carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1). Azide in DMSO with a secondary bromide reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: The tosylate shown is treated with NaSCH<sub>3</sub> in DMF. What is the major product?
h: Tosylate is an excellent leaving group; thiolate is a strong nucleophile and weak base. Track which carbon changes and which does not.
w: SN2 at the carbon bearing OTs inverts that carbon only; the carbon bearing CH3 is untouched. The starting (1R,2R) tosylate has OTs and CH3 trans; after inversion SCH3 and CH3 are cis, with the methyl-bearing carbon still in its original configuration: A.
x: B keeps the trans relationship, i.e., retention at the carbon attacked. SN2 inverts.
This is cis, but it is the enantiomer of A: the methyl-bearing carbon has also been inverted, and no bond to that carbon is made or broken.
D comes from a carbocation and hydride shift (S<sub>N</sub>1). A strong nucleophile in DMF reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 without rearrangement.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Which step breaks the C–O bond, and which only changes the oxygen?
w: Step 1 converts the OH into OTs. The C–O bond is not broken (the oxygen attacks sulfur), so the tosylate keeps the (R) configuration. Step 2 is SN2 by cyanide with inversion. In the nitrile, C≡N (C attached to N,N,N) > ethyl > CH3, the same priority pattern as the alcohol, so inversion gives (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile.
x: This is the (R) nitrile: net retention. Only the cyanide step touches the stereocenter, and it inverts.
This is the tosylate intermediate, the product of step 1 only. Cyanide then displaces the tosylate.
Racemization would need a carbocation. Cyanide in DMSO with a secondary tosylate reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q:
(R)-Butan-2-ol is converted to 2-methylbutanenitrile by two routes.
Route 1: 1. PBr3 2. NaCN, DMSO
Route 2: 1. TsCl, pyridine 2. NaCN, DMSO
Which statement about the products is correct?
h: Count inversions. Does PBr<sub>3</sub> break the C–O bond? Does TsCl?
w: PBr3 activates the OH and Br− then displaces it by SN2: inversion, giving (S)-2-bromobutane. Cyanide inverts again, so route 1 shows two inversions = net retention: (R) nitrile. TsCl makes the tosylate without touching the C–O bond (retention); cyanide then inverts once: (S) nitrile. Priorities are OH/Br/CN > ethyl > CH3 throughout, so each inversion flips the label. Route 1 → (R), route 2 → (S).
x: PBr<sub>3</sub> is not a retention reagent like TsCl; the bromide forms by S<sub>N</sub>2 with inversion, so route 1 has two inversions.
Tosylation leaves the stereocenter unchanged, so route 2 has only one inversion and gives (S), not (R).
This swaps the two routes: the PBr<sub>3</sub> route has two inversions (net retention), the TsCl route only one.

q: (S)-Pentan-2-ol is treated with SOCl2 in pyridine. What is the product?
h: In pyridine, the chlorosulfite intermediate is attacked by free chloride. From which side?
w: SOCl2 turns the OH into a chlorosulfite (–OS(O)Cl), an excellent leaving group. With pyridine present, free Cl− attacks from the back (SN2), giving inversion. Cl > propyl > CH3, like OH > propyl > CH3, so the label flips: (R)-2-chloropentane.
x: This is the retention product. Retention is seen with SOCl<sub>2</sub> alone (no pyridine) in some cases; with pyridine the chloride attacks from the back.
C, 3-chloropentane, would require a carbocation and hydride shift. The pyridine conditions avoid a free carbocation.
Racemization requires an S<sub>N</sub>1 carbocation. SOCl<sub>2</sub>/pyridine on a secondary alcohol goes by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: (R)-Pentan-2-ol is treated with TsCl in pyridine. What is the configuration of the tosylate formed?
c: (R), because the C–O bond is not broken
(S), because tosylation is an SN2 reaction at carbon
(S), because the priority of OTs is lower than that of OH
h: In tosylation, which atom does the alcohol oxygen attack?
w: The alcohol oxygen attacks the sulfur of TsCl and displaces chloride from sulfur; pyridine removes the proton. Nothing happens at the stereocenter: the C–O bond stays intact, and OTs (O attached) still has top priority. The tosylate is (R), with retention. Inversion comes only later, when a nucleophile displaces the tosylate.
x: The substitution in this step happens at sulfur, not at the stereocenter. The carbon is untouched.
No carbocation forms: the C–O bond does not break during tosylation.
OTs is attached through oxygen, just like OH, so it keeps the highest priority; the label does not change.

q: (S)-5-Bromohexan-1-amine is warmed in dilute solution. A cyclic amine forms. What is it?
h: Count the ring atoms: the nitrogen plus every carbon from C1 to the carbon that bears Br. Then decide what happens at that carbon.
w: The amine nitrogen attacks C5 intramolecularly. The ring contains N, C1, C2, C3, C4 and C5: six atoms, a piperidine with the C6 methyl on the carbon next to N. Intramolecular SN2 is backside attack, so C5 is inverted. N replaces Br as the top priority (N > ring CH2 > CH3), so (S) becomes (R)-2-methylpiperidine. Dilute solution favors ring closure over intermolecular reaction.
x: This is (S)-2-methylpiperidine, the retention product. The nitrogen must approach from the back of the C–Br bond.
This is a five-membered ring, which would need N to bond to C4, a carbon with no leaving group.
This is an elimination product. A neutral amine is a weak base, and ring closure to a six-membered ring is fast.

q: 4-Chlorobutan-1-ol is treated with NaH in DMF. What is the major organic product?
h: NaH removes the O–H proton. The alkoxide can now reach the carbon that holds Cl. How big is that ring?
w: NaH deprotonates the alcohol. The alkoxide attacks C4 from the back in an intramolecular SN2 (an intramolecular Williamson synthesis). The ring contains O, C1, C2, C3 and C4: five atoms, so the product is tetrahydrofuran. Five-membered rings close fastest.
x: This is a six-membered ring, one atom too many; there are only four carbons between O and Cl, counting both ends.
This is a four-membered ring (oxetane); it would need the alkoxide to attack C3, which has no leaving group.
This is an elimination product. The alkoxide finds the nearby carbon intramolecularly far faster than it removes a β-hydrogen from a primary chloride.

q: Two stereoisomers of 2-chlorocyclohexanol (each racemic) are treated with NaOH. Only one gives cyclohexene oxide rapidly. Which one, and why?
c: I (trans), because O− and Cl can both be axial, anti to each other, for backside attack
II (cis), because O− and Cl are on the same face and close together
I (trans), because its O− is equatorial and attacks the front of the C–Cl bond
II (cis), because its more stable chair puts Cl axial
h: Epoxide formation is an intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2. Where must the nucleophile be relative to the C–Cl bond?
w: Ring closure is an intramolecular SN2, so the alkoxide must reach the back of the C–Cl bond. In the trans isomer, a ring flip puts OH and Cl both axial, pointing in opposite directions (anti-periplanar); the O− then sits directly behind the C–Cl bond and closes the epoxide quickly. In the cis isomer one group is always axial and the other equatorial, so the O− can never reach the backside. Answer: I, the trans isomer.
x: Being on the same face is exactly wrong for S<sub>N</sub>2; the alkoxide would attack the front of the C–Cl bond.
An S<sub>N</sub>2 nucleophile must attack the back of the C–Cl bond, which requires the diaxial (anti) arrangement, not frontside attack.
An axial Cl alone is not enough; in the cis isomer the O<sup>−</sup> is then equatorial and points away from the backside of the C–Cl bond.

q: (2R,3S)-3-Bromobutan-2-ol is treated with aqueous NaOH. What is the major product?
h: Deprotonated OH attacks the neighboring C–Br carbon from the back. Which carbon is inverted and which keeps its configuration?
w: The alkoxide at C2 attacks C3 from the back (intramolecular SN2), closing an epoxide. C2 keeps its configuration (its C–O bond is not broken); C3 is inverted. Working this through gives the trans-epoxide (2R,3R)-2,3-dimethyloxirane. The intramolecular reaction is much faster than attack by external hydroxide.
x: This is cis-2,3-dimethyloxirane (meso). It would require retention at C3, i.e., frontside attack.
This is the (2S,3S) enantiomer of the product; it would require inverting C2 as well, but no bond to C2 is broken.
This is the diol from intermolecular S<sub>N</sub>2 by HO<sup>−</sup>. With an alkoxide held right next to the C–Br carbon, ring closure wins.

q: The single stereoisomer of 1-chloro-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane shown is heated in methanol. Which statement describes the substitution products?
c: A mixture of both ring stereoisomers of 1-methoxy-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane
Only the stereoisomer with OCH<sub>3</sub> on the face opposite where Cl was
Only the stereoisomer with OCH<sub>3</sub> on the same face where Cl was
h: A tertiary chloride in methanol forms a carbocation. Can the nucleophile reach both faces of it?
w: The tertiary chloride ionizes (SN1) to a planar carbocation at C1. Methanol can add to the top or bottom face, so OCH3 ends up either cis or trans to the C4 methyl: a mixture of both stereoisomers. (The ratio need not be 1:1, since the two faces of the ring cation are not equivalent, but both form.)
x: Exclusive inversion is the S<sub>N</sub>2 result; a tertiary carbon cannot be attacked from the back.
A planar cation has no memory of which face the chloride left from, so retention alone is not expected.
The cation at C1 is already tertiary; a hydride shift to C2 would make a less stable secondary cation, and no rearrangement is favored.

q: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated HBr. What is the major alkyl bromide?
h: A secondary alcohol in strong acid loses water. Is the resulting cation the most stable one available?
w: Protonation and loss of water give a secondary cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 gives a tertiary cation, which Br− captures (SN1): 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
x: This is the unrearranged bromide. The secondary cation rearranges to the adjacent tertiary site faster than bromide traps it.
C would need the cation at a primary carbon; shifts go toward more stable cations.
This is the E1 alkene, which is not an alkyl bromide; with concentrated HBr, bromide capture gives the substitution product.

q: Which reagent converts 3-methylbutan-2-ol into 2-bromo-3-methylbutane without rearrangement?
h: You need a way to turn OH into a leaving group that bromide displaces directly, without forming a carbocation.
w: PBr3 converts the OH into an –OPBr2 leaving group, and bromide displaces it by SN2 (with inversion). No carbocation forms, so no hydride shift occurs: PBr3.
x: HBr protonates the OH and water leaves to give a secondary cation, which shifts to the tertiary cation: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
NaBr/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> generates HBr in situ, so it gives the same carbocation and the same rearrangement.
Without activation, HO<sup>−</sup> is far too poor a leaving group; bromide in DMSO does not react with the alcohol.

q: Butan-1-ol reacts with concentrated HBr to give 1-bromobutane. Which statement about the mechanism is correct?
c: Br<sup>−</sup> displaces water from the protonated alcohol in one step (S<sub>N</sub>2)
The protonated alcohol loses water to form a primary carbocation, which Br<sup>−</sup> traps
Br<sup>−</sup> displaces hydroxide directly from the neutral alcohol
The primary cation rearranges to the 2-butyl cation before Br<sup>−</sup> adds
h: Which leaving group is present after protonation? Can a primary carbocation form?
w: Strong acid first protonates the OH, converting the very poor leaving group HO− into neutral H2O. A primary cation is too unstable to form, so Br− attacks the CH2 from the back as water departs: SN2 on the protonated alcohol. That is why 1-bromobutane is obtained without rearrangement.
x: A primary carbocation is too high in energy to form under these conditions; primary alcohols react with HBr by S<sub>N</sub>2.
Hydroxide is a strong base and a very poor leaving group; the alcohol must be protonated first.
No free primary cation forms, so there is nothing to rearrange; the product is 1-bromobutane, not 2-bromobutane.

q: 1-Bromo-3-chloropropane is treated with one equivalent of NaCN in DMSO. What is the major product?
h: Both carbons bearing halogens are primary. What differs between the two leaving groups?
w: Both C–X carbons are primary and equally unhindered, so selectivity comes from the leaving group. Br− is a weaker base and a better leaving group than Cl−, so with one equivalent of cyanide the C–Br carbon reacts first (SN2): 4-chlorobutanenitrile.
x: B would require displacing chloride while leaving the better leaving group, bromide, in place.
C needs two equivalents of cyanide; with one equivalent, the faster C–Br displacement dominates.
D would require deprotonating the CH<sub>2</sub> next to the nitrile (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 31) and closing a ring; cyanide is far too weak a base for that.

q: (R)-1,3-Dibromobutane is treated with one equivalent of NaN3 in DMF at 25 °C. What is the major product?
h: Same leaving group at both sites: compare the steric environment. Then ask whether the stereocenter is touched.
w: Both carbons carry Br, so sterics decide: SN2 at the primary C1 is much faster than at the secondary C3. With one equivalent of azide, the product is the primary azide. The stereocenter C3 is not attacked, so it keeps its configuration, and the priority order (Br > CH2CH2X > CH3 > H) is unchanged: (R)-1-azido-3-bromobutane.
x: This is substitution at the secondary carbon (with inversion). The primary CH<sub>2</sub>Br is less hindered and reacts much faster.
C puts azide at the secondary carbon with retention, which is wrong on both counts: wrong site, and S<sub>N</sub>2 would invert.
D needs two equivalents of azide; with one, the faster primary displacement dominates.

q: Which combination is the best way to prepare 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl methyl ether) by a Williamson ether synthesis?
c: CH<sub>3</sub>OH + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr in the presence of NaOH
h: The Williamson synthesis is S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon must be the electrophile?
w: The alkoxide attacks the alkyl halide by SN2, so the halide should be methyl or primary. Putting the bulky group on the alkoxide and the methyl on the halide gives clean substitution: (CH3)3CO− + CH3I. CH3I has no β-hydrogens, so elimination is impossible.
x: A tertiary bromide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; methoxide acts as a base and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.
Hydroxide with a tertiary bromide again gives mainly E2 alkene; and neutral methanol is a weak nucleophile.
An alcohol has no leaving group; HO<sup>−</sup> cannot be displaced by methoxide.

q: A student makes butan-1-amine from 1-bromobutane by the route shown instead of heating 1-bromobutane with NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the main advantage of the azide route?
c: Azide adds only once, so no di- or trialkylated amines form
Azide is a stronger base than ammonia, so it suppresses elimination
The azide route forms a carbocation, which speeds the reaction
Ammonia would give the product with inverted configuration, but azide gives retention
h: What happens to butan-1-amine once it forms in the presence of more 1-bromobutane?
w: With NH3, the product amine is itself a good nucleophile (often better than NH3) and reacts with more alkyl halide, giving a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and even the ammonium salt. The alkyl azide formed with N3− is not nucleophilic, so it stops cleanly after one alkylation, and LiAlH4 then reduces it to the primary amine. No overalkylation.
x: Azide is a weak base (HN<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4.7), and the point is not basicity; it is that the azide product cannot alkylate again.
Both routes are S<sub>N</sub>2 at a primary carbon; no carbocation forms.
The substrate carbon (CH<sub>2</sub>) is not a stereocenter, and both nucleophiles would react by S<sub>N</sub>2 with inversion anyway.

q: 1-Chlorobutane is heated with NaI in acetone. Why does this reaction go nearly to completion?
c: NaCl is insoluble in acetone and precipitates, driving the equilibrium to 1-iodobutane
The C–I bond is much stronger than the C–Cl bond, so 1-iodobutane is the more stable product
I<sup>−</sup> is a stronger base than Cl<sup>−</sup>, so it displaces chloride
Acetone protonates the chlorine of 1-chlorobutane, making it a better leaving group
h: Both halides are good leaving groups, so the substitution is reversible. What else is happening in the flask?
w: Iodide and chloride can displace each other, so the reaction itself is an equilibrium. NaI dissolves in acetone but NaCl does not; as NaCl precipitates, Le Châtelier's principle drives the reaction to the right. Precipitation of NaCl makes this Finkelstein reaction useful.
x: The C–I bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond, which would push the equilibrium the other way.
Iodide is a weaker base than chloride (HI is the stronger acid); its strength here is nucleophilicity, not basicity.
Acetone is aprotic and not acidic; it cannot protonate chloride.

q: 5-Bromopentanoic acid is stirred with NaHCO<sub>3</sub> in dilute solution. What organic product forms?
h: NaHCO<sub>3</sub> deprotonates the carboxylic acid. Count the atoms between the carboxylate oxygen and the C–Br carbon.
w: Bicarbonate converts the acid to a carboxylate, a modest nucleophile. Its oxygen attacks C5 in an intramolecular SN2. The ring contains O, C1, C2, C3, C4 and C5: six atoms, so the product is the six-membered lactone oxan-2-one (δ-valerolactone). Dilution favors the intramolecular reaction over intermolecular ester formation.
x: This is a seven-membered lactone; that would need one more CH<sub>2</sub> in the chain.
This is a five-membered lactone; it would need the oxygen to attack C4, which has no leaving group.
This is the hydroxy acid from substitution by water or hydroxide. Bicarbonate is not HO<sup>−</sup>, and the intramolecular carboxylate is much closer to the electrophilic carbon.

q: Each ω-bromoalkylamine is warmed in dilute solution and cyclizes by intramolecular SN2. Which cyclizes fastest?
h: Ring closure rates balance ring strain in the transition state against how often the two ends of the chain meet.
w: Intramolecular SN2 rates depend on ring size. Five-membered rings close fastest: little strain, and the chain ends meet often. Three-membered rings are strained but form surprisingly fast (the ends are very close), four-membered rings are slow (strain without the proximity bonus), and seven-membered rings are slow (the chain ends rarely meet). 4-Bromobutan-1-amine gives pyrrolidine, a five-membered ring: A.
x: B gives aziridine, a strained three-membered ring. Its proximity helps, but five-membered ring closure is still faster by orders of magnitude.
C gives azetidine, a four-membered ring, the slowest of the small rings: angle strain without the proximity bonus of the three-membered case.
D gives a seven-membered ring; the floppy chain rarely brings its ends together, so closure is slow.

q: Which sequence converts (R)-butan-2-ol into (R)-2-azidobutane?
h: Check whether the target needs net inversion or net retention. Then count how many steps invert the stereocenter in each sequence.
w: The OH and N3 groups both rank first (then ethyl, then CH3), so keeping the label (R) means net retention: an even number of inversions. PBr3 gives (S)-2-bromobutane with inversion, and azide inverts again by SN2: (R)-2-azidobutane. 1. PBr3 2. NaN3 works.
x: Tosylation keeps the configuration, so this route has only one inversion and gives (S)-2-azidobutane.
HO<sup>−</sup> is far too poor a leaving group; azide cannot displace an unactivated OH.
NaH makes an alkoxide, which is an even worse leaving group than OH; no substitution occurs.

q: 1-Bromo-4-(bromomethyl)benzene is treated with one equivalent of NaCN in DMSO. What is the major product?
c: no reaction: both C–Br bonds are too strong for cyanide to break
h: One bromine is on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, the other on an sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon. Which can undergo backside attack?
w: The CH2Br is a primary benzylic halide, an excellent SN2 substrate. The aryl C–Br cannot react by SN2 (backside attack would pass through the ring) or SN1 (aryl cations are very unstable). Cyanide therefore replaces only the benzylic bromine: 2-(4-bromophenyl)acetonitrile.
x: B has cyanide on the ring carbon. Aryl halides do not undergo S<sub>N</sub>2 or S<sub>N</sub>1.
C needs substitution at the aryl carbon too, which does not occur; it also needs two equivalents of cyanide.
The benzylic C–Br is very reactive toward S<sub>N</sub>2; only the aryl C–Br is inert.

q: Which compound does not react with NaI in acetone, even on heating?
h: S<sub>N</sub>2 requires backside attack on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.
w: (E)-1-Bromoprop-1-ene is a vinylic halide: the C–Br carbon is sp2, the C–Br bond is stronger, and backside attack would have to pass through the π system and the other substituents in the plane. Vinylic halides do not undergo SN2 or SN1, so A does not react.
x: Allyl bromide is a primary allylic halide; π-overlap stabilizes the S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state, so it reacts quickly.
Benzyl bromide is a primary benzylic halide and reacts quickly with iodide.
1-Bromopropane is an unhindered primary halide, a good S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate.

q:
(S)-2-Iodobutane is dissolved in acetone with excess NaI. Which statements are correct?
I. The optical activity of the solution falls toward zero over time.
II. The rate of loss of optical activity does not depend on [I−].
III. Each substitution event converts one molecule of (S)-2-iodobutane into (R)-2-iodobutane.
h: Iodide is both the nucleophile and the leaving group here. What does each S<sub>N</sub>2 event do to the stereocenter?
w: Each SN2 attack by I− inverts the carbon, turning an (S) molecule into (R) (III true). The reverse reaction converts (R) back to (S), so the mixture moves toward a 1:1 racemate and the optical rotation falls to zero (I true). Because each event is bimolecular, the rate depends on [I−] (II false). I and III only.
x: II is false: the racemization happens by S<sub>N</sub>2, which is first order in iodide.
III is also true: every backside substitution inverts the stereocenter, which is exactly why the activity is lost.
I is true: repeated inversions drive the sample toward a racemic mixture, and II is false.

q: Which reaction is fastest?
h: All four are S<sub>N</sub>2 reactions with the same nucleophile. Compare them one variable at a time: substrate, leaving group, solvent.
w: For SN2, each change from the key slows the reaction: a poorer leaving group (Cl instead of Br), a protic solvent that hydrogen-bonds to azide (methanol instead of DMSO), or a more hindered secondary carbon. The combination of an unhindered primary carbon, a good leaving group and a polar aprotic solvent is fastest: 1-bromobutane + NaN3 in DMSO.
x: Chloride is a stronger base and poorer leaving group than bromide, so the C–Cl bond reacts more slowly.
Methanol hydrogen-bonds to azide and lowers its nucleophilicity; the same reaction is much faster in DMSO.
The secondary carbon has an extra methyl group crowding the backside; S<sub>N</sub>2 is slower than at the primary carbon.

q: NaN<sub>3</sub> (0.10 M) is added to a solution of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane in 80% aqueous acetone. Compared with the same reaction without azide, what is observed?
c: The rate of disappearance of the chloride is essentially unchanged, but some 2-azido-2-methylpropane forms
The chloride disappears much faster, because azide attacks it by S<sub>N</sub>2
The chloride disappears much faster, because azide pulls the chloride off
Nothing changes: only 2-methylpropan-2-ol forms, because azide cannot react with a carbocation
h: Separate two questions: what controls how fast the chloride is consumed, and what controls what the cation becomes?
w: This tertiary chloride reacts by SN1. The rate is set by ionization, so adding azide does not change how fast the chloride disappears. Once the cation forms, though, it is trapped by whichever nucleophile it meets: water gives the alcohol, and azide (a much better nucleophile) gives the azide. Same rate; new azide product.
x: Backside attack at a tertiary carbon is blocked; azide cannot speed this reaction by S<sub>N</sub>2.
Azide does not assist ionization; the C–Cl bond breaks on its own in the rate-determining step.
Carbocations react with any available nucleophile, and azide competes very well with water.

q: Sodium propynide (CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C<sup>−</sup> Na<sup>+</sup>) is used to make an internal alkyne by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which alkyl halide gives the best yield of substitution product?
h: Acetylide ions are strong bases as well as nucleophiles. Which substrate gives the base the least chance to eliminate?
w: Acetylides (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 25) are strong bases. With secondary and tertiary halides they mainly cause E2 elimination; only methyl and primary halides give good SN2 yields. Bromoethane gives pent-2-yne cleanly.
x: With 2-bromopropane, the strong base removes a β-H (E2) and propene is the main product.
A tertiary halide cannot be attacked from the back; E2 gives 2-methylpropene.
An aryl halide does not undergo S<sub>N</sub>2 at all.

q: cis-3-Methylcyclopentyl tosylate, as the single enantiomer shown, is treated with NaCN in DMSO. What is the product?
h: Decide cis or trans for the product first, then make sure the carbon that is not attacked keeps its configuration.
w: SN2 at C1 inverts that carbon only. The tosylate was cis to the methyl, so the nitrile ends up trans. C3 (bearing CH3) is untouched and stays R. The starting tosylate is (1S,3R); the product is (1R,3R)-3-methylcyclopentane-1-carbonitrile.
x: This is the cis nitrile with both centers unchanged, the retention product. SN2 inverts C1.
This is trans but is the enantiomer of A: it also inverts C3, which is not attacked.
This is cis and has both carbons inverted relative to the starting material. Only C1 changes.

q: Which reagent converts 1-bromobutane mainly into an ether?
h: A primary halide reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 with a good, unhindered nucleophile. Which reagent is a strong nucleophile that is not too bulky, and whose product is an ether?
w: Methoxide is a strong, small nucleophile. With an unhindered primary bromide, SN2 beats E2, giving 1-methoxybutane: NaOCH3 in CH3OH.
x: tert-Butoxide is too bulky to reach the backside of the carbon easily; with 1-bromobutane it gives mostly but-1-ene by E2.
Neutral methanol is a weak nucleophile, and a primary bromide cannot ionize, so there is essentially no reaction at 25 °C.
Hydroxide gives butan-1-ol, an alcohol, not an ether.

q: Which reagent(s) convert 1-butyne into 2-butanone in one step?
h: Ask which carbon of the triple bond ends up as C=O: the more substituted one (Markovnikov) or the terminal one.
w: Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of a terminal alkyne is Markovnikov: OH adds to the internal carbon, and the enol tautomerizes to the methyl ketone. So HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O gives 2-butanone. Hydroboration with a bulky borane is anti-Markovnikov and gives the aldehyde, and ozonolysis cleaves the triple bond.
x: Hydroboration with a bulky dialkylborane puts the oxygen on the terminal carbon; the enol tautomerizes to butanal, an aldehyde, not the ketone.
Lindlar reduction gives 1-butene, and acid-catalyzed hydration of that alkene gives 2-butanol, an alcohol rather than a ketone.
Ozonolysis cleaves the C≡C bond completely, giving propanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>, not a four-carbon ketone.

q: Which sequence converts 2-methyl-2-butene into 3-methyl-2-butanol (racemic)?
h: The OH must end up on the less substituted alkene carbon. Which addition is anti-Markovnikov and gives an alcohol directly?
w: The target has OH on C2 (the CH end of the alkene), so the addition must be anti-Markovnikov. Boron adds to the less hindered carbon and oxidation replaces B with OH: 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH. Acid hydration is Markovnikov (tertiary alcohol), OsO4 adds two OH groups, and the radical HBr route stops at a secondary bromide that hydroxide mostly eliminates.
x: Acid-catalyzed hydration goes through the tertiary carbocation, giving 2-methyl-2-butanol (Markovnikov), the wrong constitutional isomer.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups (syn dihydroxylation), giving 2-methyl-2,3-butanediol, not a mono-alcohol.
HBr/ROOR does give 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, but this hindered secondary bromide with hydroxide (a strong base) gives mainly E2, back to the alkene, not clean S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: Which sequence converts propyne into (Z)-2-hexene?
h: Build the six-carbon skeleton while you still have a terminal alkyne C–H, then choose the reduction that sets the alkene geometry.
w: Deprotonating propyne (pKa ≈ 25) needs a base whose conjugate acid is weaker, such as NaNH2 (NH3, pKa ≈ 38). The acetylide does SN2 on the primary bromide to give 2-hexyne, and Lindlar hydrogenation adds both H atoms to the same face, giving the cis (Z) alkene: 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2CH2Br 3. H2, Lindlar.
x: Dissolving-metal reduction (Na, NH<sub>3</sub>) goes through a vinyl radical/anion that adopts the trans geometry, so this gives (E)-2-hexene.
Reducing first gives propene, which has no acidic C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 44), so NaNH<sub>2</sub> cannot form a carbon nucleophile and no C–C bond is made.
Hydroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.7) is far too weak to deprotonate a terminal alkyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25); the equilibrium lies almost entirely on the alkyne side.

q: Which sequence converts 2-butyne into meso-2,3-butanediol?
c: 1. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  2. OsO<sub>4</sub>  3. NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  2. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
h: Pair the alkene geometry with the type of dihydroxylation: syn addition to a cis alkene and anti addition to a trans alkene give the same diastereomer.
w: Lindlar reduction gives (Z)-2-butene. OsO4 adds both OH groups to the same face (syn), and syn addition to a cis alkene gives the meso diol, (2R,3S)-2,3-butanediol. So the answer is 1. H2, Lindlar 2. OsO4 3. NaHSO3. Changing either the alkene geometry or the addition mode (syn → anti) switches the product to the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair.
x: Na/NH<sub>3</sub> gives (E)-2-butene; syn dihydroxylation of a trans alkene gives the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) diol, not meso.
Epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition; anti addition to the cis alkene gives the racemic diol, not meso.
Hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the C=C bond, giving two molecules of acetic acid instead of a diol.

q: The dibromide shown is formed as a racemic mixture (only one enantiomer is drawn). Which sequence from 2-pentyne gives it as the major product?
h: Assign R/S to the drawn dibromide. Then remember Br<sub>2</sub> adds anti, and decide which alkene geometry gives that pair of configurations.
w: The drawn compound is (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromopentane, the threo ("like") diastereomer. Bromination is an anti addition through a bromonium ion. Anti addition to a trans alkene gives the erythro (2R,3S)/(2S,3R) pair (the meso-like pattern seen with 2-butene), while anti addition to a cis alkene gives the threo (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair. So the alkyne must first be reduced to the cis alkene: 1. H2, Lindlar 2. Br2, CH2Cl2.
x: Na/NH<sub>3</sub> gives (E)-2-pentene; anti addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to the trans alkene gives the (2R,3S)/(2S,3R) diastereomer, not the one drawn.
HBr with peroxide adds only one Br (radical, anti-Markovnikov), giving a monobromopentane, not a vicinal dibromide.
Two equivalents of HBr add Markovnikov twice to the same carbon, giving geminal dibromides (2,2- and 3,3-dibromopentane), not a 2,3-dibromide.

q: Which sequence moves the double bond of 2-methyl-2-butene to the end of the chain, giving 3-methyl-1-butene as the major product?
h: First put a leaving group on the carbon that must become C2 of the new alkene, then choose a base that removes the less hindered β-H.
w: Radical HBr addition (ROOR) puts Br on the less substituted alkene carbon, giving 2-bromo-3-methylbutane. That bromide has β-H on C1 (CH3) and C3 (one tertiary H). The bulky base t-BuOK removes the more accessible CH3 hydrogen (Hofmann product), giving 3-methyl-1-butene: 1. HBr, ROOR 2. t-BuOK, heat. A small base gives the Zaitsev product, which is just the starting alkene again.
x: Without peroxide HBr adds Markovnikov, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane; Hofmann elimination of that gives 2-methyl-1-butene, the wrong skeleton position.
The bromide is correct, but ethoxide is a small base and gives the Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene, which is 2-methyl-2-butene, the starting material.
Hydroboration gives 3-methyl-2-butanol, but E1 dehydration goes through a secondary cation that undergoes a hydride shift to the tertiary cation and gives 2-methyl-2-butene again.

q: Which sequence converts 1-methylcyclohexene into the racemic alcohol shown?
h: Where is the OH relative to the methyl group, and are H and OH added to the same face?
w: The target, trans-2-methylcyclohexanol, has OH on the less substituted alkene carbon (anti-Markovnikov), and the H added to C1 is cis to the OH (syn addition). Hydroboration adds H and B to the same face and oxidation replaces B with OH with retention, so 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH gives the trans alcohol.
x: Oxymercuration–demercuration is Markovnikov: OH goes to the tertiary carbon, giving 1-methylcyclohexanol.
Acid hydration is also Markovnikov through the tertiary cation, giving 1-methylcyclohexanol.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups, giving 1-methyl-cis-1,2-cyclohexanediol, not a mono-alcohol.

q: Which sequence converts acetylene into the racemic diol shown (one enantiomer drawn)?
c: 1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)  3. OsO<sub>4</sub>, then NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  3. OsO<sub>4</sub>, then NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)  3. mCPBA, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C  3. OsO<sub>4</sub>, then NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
h: The skeleton step is the same in every choice. Assign the drawn diol as meso or chiral, then match alkene geometry with syn or anti dihydroxylation.
w: Two acetylide alkylations with 1-bromopropane give 4-octyne. The drawn diol is (4R,5R)-4,5-octanediol, a chiral (racemic) diastereomer, not the meso form. Racemic comes from syn addition to a trans alkene or anti addition to a cis alkene. Na/NH3 gives (E)-4-octene and OsO4 adds syn, so Na, NH3 then OsO4 gives the (4R,5R)/(4S,5S) pair.
x: Lindlar gives the cis alkene; syn addition to a cis alkene gives meso-4,5-octanediol, not the chiral diol shown.
Na/NH<sub>3</sub> gives the trans alkene, and epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition; anti addition to a trans alkene gives the meso diol.
H<sub>2</sub> over Pd/C reduces the alkyne all the way to octane, which has no π bond for OsO<sub>4</sub> to attack.

q: Which plan gives 4-methyl-2-pentyne in good yield?
h: An acetylide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile. Which disconnection lets it attack a methyl or primary carbon?
w: Disconnecting the target at either alkyne–carbon bond gives two plans: isopropylacetylide + CH3–X, or propynide + isopropyl–X. Acetylides do clean SN2 only on methyl and primary substrates; with a secondary halide the strong base gives mostly E2. So the good plan is 3-methyl-1-butyne, NaNH2, then CH3I.
x: 2-Bromopropane is secondary; the strongly basic acetylide removes a β-H (E2), giving propene and recovering propyne.
Hydroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.7) cannot deprotonate a terminal alkyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25), so almost no acetylide forms.
OH<sup>−</sup> is not a leaving group, and the alcohol O–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 17) simply protonates the acetylide back to propyne.

q: Which sequence converts methylcyclohexane into racemic trans-2-methylcyclohexanol (shown)?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
h: Work backward: which alkene gives this alcohol by hydroboration, which base makes that alkene, and which halogenation puts the leaving group in the right place?
w: Hydroboration–oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene gives trans-2-methylcyclohexanol (anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH). 1-Methylcyclohexene is the Zaitsev product of E2 on 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane with a small base, and that tertiary bromide is the highly selective product of radical bromination. So: 1. Br2, hν 2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat 3. BH3·THF 4. H2O2, NaOH.
x: The bulky base gives the Hofmann alkene, methylenecyclohexane, and hydroboration of that gives cyclohexylmethanol instead.
Radical chlorination is not selective; it chlorinates the primary, secondary and tertiary positions, so the later steps start from a mixture of chlorides.
Acid-catalyzed hydration of 1-methylcyclohexene is Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexanol, the tertiary alcohol.

q: Which C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkene gives heptane-2,6-dione as the only product of ozonolysis (1. O<sub>3</sub>  2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S)?
h: Ozonolysis turns each alkene carbon into a C=O. Reconnect the two carbonyl carbons of the product with a double bond.
w: Heptane-2,6-dione has two ketone carbons (C2 and C6) separated by three CH2 groups, each bearing a CH3. Joining C2 and C6 by a C=C closes a five-membered ring with a methyl on each alkene carbon: 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene. A ring alkene gives one product with two carbonyls; both alkene carbons are fully substituted, so both carbonyls are ketones.
x: 1-Ethylcyclopentene has one alkene C–H, so one end becomes an aldehyde: the product is 5-oxoheptanal.
1,3-Dimethylcyclopentene also has an alkene C–H; it gives 2-methyl-5-oxohexanal, a keto-aldehyde.
1-Methylcyclohexene cleaves to 6-oxoheptanal: the ring is one carbon larger and one end is an aldehyde.

q: Which sequence converts (R)-2-pentanol into the nitrile shown, with the configuration drawn?
c: 1. TsCl, pyridine  2. NaBr, DMSO  3. NaCN, DMSO
h: Assign R/S to the product, then count how many steps break a bond to the stereocenter (each S<sub>N</sub>2 inverts; making a tosylate does not).
w: The product is (S)-2-methylpentanenitrile: the CN has taken the place of the OH with inversion. Tosylation forms the O–S bond and leaves the C–O bond intact (retention), and then cyanide displaces the tosylate by SN2 (one inversion). Net: one inversion, so 1. TsCl, pyridine 2. NaCN, DMSO. Routes with two SN2 steps invert twice and give back the (R) configuration.
x: PBr<sub>3</sub> converts the alcohol to the bromide with inversion, and cyanide inverts again; two inversions give (R)-2-methylpentanenitrile, the enantiomer.
Tosylation retains, bromide displacement inverts and cyanide inverts again: two inversions in total give the (R) nitrile, the enantiomer of the target.
Hydroxide is a very poor leaving group, so cyanide cannot displace OH directly; the alcohol is recovered.

q: Which starting material and reagent give 5-methyl-2-hexanone as essentially the only carbonyl product?
h: Hydration of an alkyne gives a ketone only where the oxygen lands. Which alkyne has only one possible Markovnikov carbon next to the target C=O?
w: Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne puts the oxygen on C2 and gives a methyl ketone: 5-methyl-1-hexyne with HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O gives 5-methyl-2-hexanone. An unsymmetrical internal alkyne has two similar carbons, so its hydration gives a mixture of two ketones.
x: The two alkyne carbons of 5-methyl-2-hexyne are both disubstituted, so oxygen adds to either one: about a 1:1 mixture of 5-methyl-2-hexanone and 5-methyl-3-hexanone.
Hydroboration of a terminal alkyne is anti-Markovnikov and gives the aldehyde, 5-methylhexanal.
Acid hydration of the alkene gives the alcohol 5-methyl-2-hexanol, not a ketone; no oxidation step is present.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexane into 1,3-cyclohexadiene?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH  3. NBS, hν  4. t-BuOK, t-BuOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH  3. NBS, hν  4. H<sub>2</sub>O
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH  3. HBr, ROOR  4. t-BuOK, t-BuOH
h: You need two eliminations, so you need two leaving groups introduced at the right times. Where does NBS put a bromine?
w: Radical bromination and E2 make cyclohexene. NBS then brominates the allylic position (C3) by a radical chain, and a second E2 forms a C=C conjugated with the first: 1. Br2, hν 2. t-BuOK 3. NBS, hν 4. t-BuOK.
x: Water substitutes the allylic bromide (S<sub>N</sub>1 through an allylic cation), giving 2-cyclohexen-1-ol, not the diene.
HBr/ROOR adds across the C=C to give bromocyclohexane again; elimination just returns cyclohexene.
Cyclohexane has no allylic C–H, so NBS is the wrong tool here, and even if one Br were introduced, a single elimination gives only cyclohexene.

q: Using 1-butene and propyne as the only sources of carbon, which plan makes (E)-2-heptene?
c: 1-butene + HBr, ROOR; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)
1-butene + HBr; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)
1-butene + HBr, ROOR; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst
1-butene + HBr, ROOR; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: Find the C–C bond the acetylide makes, decide which halide the acetylide needs (methyl/primary only), then set the alkene geometry.
w: (E)-2-Heptene is CH3CH=CH(CH2)3CH3. The propynide anion supplies C1–C3 and must attack a primary butyl halide. Radical (peroxide) HBr addition to 1-butene gives 1-bromobutane; SN2 gives 2-heptyne; Na/NH3 reduces it to the trans alkene. So the plan is HBr/ROOR, alkylation of propynide, then Na, NH3(l).
x: Markovnikov HBr gives 2-bromobutane, a secondary halide; the acetylide mostly eliminates (E2), and any substitution would give a branched skeleton.
Lindlar hydrogenation gives the cis alkene, (Z)-2-heptene.
H<sub>2</sub> over Pd/C reduces the alkyne completely to heptane.

q: Three of these routes give cyclohexyl ethyl ether in good yield. Which route gives mostly a different product?
h: In a Williamson-type S<sub>N</sub>2, which carbon should be the electrophile: the primary one or the secondary one?
w: An alkoxide is a strong base. Attacking a primary electrophile (ethyl bromide or ethyl tosylate) it does SN2 cleanly. Attacking a secondary cyclohexyl bromide in hot ethanol it mostly removes a β-H (E2), giving cyclohexene. So bromocyclohexane + NaOEt is the poor route. Alkoxymercuration adds EtOH across the alkene Markovnikov-fashion (both alkene carbons of cyclohexene are equivalent) and also gives the ether.
x: This route works: the cyclohexoxide ion attacks unhindered ethyl bromide by S<sub>N</sub>2.
This route works: alkoxymercuration–demercuration adds H and OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> across the C=C without rearrangement.
This route works: ethyl tosylate is a primary substrate with an excellent leaving group, ideal for S<sub>N</sub>2 by the alkoxide.

q: Which starting material and reagent give the racemic bromohydrin shown?
h: Halohydrin formation: where does water attack the bromonium ion, and from which face?
w: In Br2/H2O the alkene forms a bromonium ion, and water (the solvent, present in huge excess) opens it at the more substituted carbon, which carries more δ+, from the face opposite the Br. 1-Methylcyclohexene therefore gives 2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexanol with Br and OH trans: 1-methylcyclohexene; Br2, H2O.
x: Methylenecyclohexane gives 1-(bromomethyl)cyclohexanol: Br on the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>, not on a ring carbon.
In CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> the only nucleophile is bromide, giving trans-1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane, not a bromohydrin.
Methanol as solvent opens the bromonium ion, giving the bromo methyl ether (OCH<sub>3</sub> on C1), not the alcohol.

q: Which sequence converts 1-hexene into 1-hexyne?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv), NH<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O  2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv), NH<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O
h: An alkyne needs two eliminations from the same pair of carbons. How many leaving groups must be placed there, and how strong a base does the second elimination need?
w: Br2 gives the vicinal dibromide (1,2-dibromohexane). Two E2 eliminations with NaNH2 give the alkyne; the third equivalent deprotonates the terminal alkyne, and water workup reprotonates it: 1. Br2 2. NaNH2 (3 equiv) 3. H2O. The second elimination (from a vinyl bromide) needs the very strong amide base.
x: HBr installs only one leaving group, so only one elimination is possible, which simply gives back hexene.
Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O gives a bromohydrin (only one leaving group); strong base turns it into an epoxide, not an alkyne.
Hydroxide can at most remove one HBr to give a vinyl bromide; it is not strong enough for the second elimination to the alkyne.

q: Which sequence converts acetylene into 3-hexanone as a single product?
c: 1. NaNH<sub>2</sub> 2. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br 3. NaNH<sub>2</sub> 4. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br 5. HgSO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub> 2. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br 3. NaNH<sub>2</sub> 4. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br 5. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst 6. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub> 2. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br 3. NaNH<sub>2</sub> 4. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br 5. HBr (2 equiv)
h: Where must the C=O end up? A symmetrical internal alkyne gives only one ketone on hydration.
w: Two alkylations with ethyl bromide build 3-hexyne. Because 3-hexyne is symmetrical, Markovnikov hydration gives the same enol whichever alkyne carbon receives the OH, so double ethylation then HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O gives 3-hexanone as the only product.
x: Monoalkylation with 1-bromobutane gives 1-hexyne; Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne gives the methyl ketone, 2-hexanone.
Lindlar reduction then acid hydration gives 3-hexanol, an alcohol; nothing in the sequence makes a C=O.
Two equivalents of HBr add across the triple bond to give 3,3-dibromohexane, not a ketone.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexanol into racemic trans-1,2-cyclohexanediol (one enantiomer shown)?
h: First make the alkene. Then ask which dihydroxylation puts the two OH groups on opposite faces of the ring.
w: Acid-catalyzed dehydration (E1) gives cyclohexene. Epoxidation followed by acid-catalyzed ring opening is an anti addition: water attacks the protonated epoxide from the face opposite the C–O bond, so the two OH groups end up trans. Attack at either epoxide carbon is equally likely, giving both enantiomers: 1. H2SO4, heat 2. mCPBA 3. H3O+.
x: OsO<sub>4</sub> is a syn dihydroxylation; it gives cis-1,2-cyclohexanediol, the meso diastereomer.
Oxymercuration–demercuration adds only one OH, giving back cyclohexanol.
Ozonolysis cleaves the ring C=C, giving the open-chain dialdehyde hexanedial.

q: Which compound, treated with one equivalent of Br2 in CH2Cl2, gives meso-3,4-dibromohexane (shown)?
h: Br<sub>2</sub> adds anti through a bromonium ion. Which alkene geometry turns anti addition into a meso product?
w: Anti addition of Br2 to a trans alkene with identical ends gives the meso dibromide, and anti addition to the cis isomer gives the racemic (3R,4R)/(3S,4S) pair. So the starting material is (E)-3-hexene.
x: (Z)-3-Hexene undergoes the same anti addition, but from the cis alkene it gives racemic (3R,4R)/(3S,4S)-3,4-dibromohexane.
(E)-2-Hexene has the C=C at C2–C3, so it gives 2,3-dibromohexane, a constitutional isomer.
One equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> adds once to 3-hexyne, giving (E)-3,4-dibromo-3-hexene, which still has a C=C and no stereocenters.

q: Which sequence moves the OH group of 1-methylcyclopentanol to the adjacent ring carbon, giving racemic trans-2-methylcyclopentanol (shown)?
c: 1. HBr  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
h: Remove the OH to make the right alkene, then add H and OH back with the opposite regiochemistry.
w: E1 dehydration of the tertiary alcohol gives the Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene, 1-methylcyclopentene. Hydroboration–oxidation then adds OH to the less substituted carbon (C2) and H to C1 on the same face, so the OH ends up trans to the methyl: 1. H2SO4, heat 2. BH3·THF 3. H2O2, NaOH.
x: The tertiary bromide with bulky t-BuOK gives mainly the Hofmann alkene, methylenecyclopentane, and hydroboration of that gives cyclopentylmethanol.
Oxymercuration is Markovnikov and puts the OH back on the tertiary carbon, regenerating 1-methylcyclopentanol.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups, giving 1-methyl-cis-1,2-cyclopentanediol.

q: The Fischer projection shows one enantiomer of a racemic 2,3-pentanediol. Which sequence from 2-pentyne gives this diastereomer as the major product?
h: Both OH groups on the same side of a Fischer projection means erythro (the meso-like pattern). Which combinations of alkene geometry and syn/anti addition give erythro?
w: With both OH groups on the same side of the Fischer projection, this is erythro-2,3-pentanediol, (2S,3R) as drawn, the analogue of meso-2,3-butanediol. Erythro products come from syn addition to a cis alkene or anti addition to a trans alkene. Of the choices, only Na, NH3 (trans alkene), then mCPBA and H3O+ (anti addition) fits.
x: Syn dihydroxylation of the trans alkene gives the threo (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) diol, with the OH groups on opposite sides of the Fischer projection.
Anti addition to the cis alkene gives the threo diastereomer, not the erythro one shown.
Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O gives a bromohydrin (one Br, one OH), not a diol.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexanol into hexanedial?
h: Ozonolysis needs a C=C, and the workup decides whether you stop at aldehydes.
w: Dehydration gives cyclohexene. Ozonolysis cleaves the ring C=C, and a reductive workup (dimethyl sulfide) leaves both new carbonyls as aldehydes: 1. H2SO4, heat 2. O3 3. (CH3)2S gives OHC(CH2)4CHO.
x: An oxidative workup with H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> converts the aldehydes to carboxylic acids, giving hexanedioic (adipic) acid.
OsO<sub>4</sub> dihydroxylates the alkene without cleaving it, giving cis-1,2-cyclohexanediol.
Cyclohexanol has no C=C, so ozone has nothing to cleave.

q: Hydrocarbon X (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) takes up one equivalent of H<sub>2</sub> over Pt. Ozonolysis of X gives cyclopentanone and acetone. What is X?
h: C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>14</sub> has two degrees of unsaturation but only one C=C. Reconnect the two carbonyl carbons with a double bond.
w: DBE = 2 with one C=C means one ring plus one double bond. Ozonolysis gives two separate products, so the C=C is not inside the ring. Joining the carbonyl carbon of cyclopentanone to the carbonyl carbon of acetone with a C=C gives isopropylidenecyclopentane.
x: 1-Isopropylcyclopentene has its C=C in the ring, so ozonolysis opens the ring and gives one keto-aldehyde, 6-methyl-5-oxoheptanal.
Ethylidenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and acetaldehyde.
2-Cyclopentylpropene gives cyclopentyl methyl ketone and formaldehyde.

q: Which sequence converts 1-butanol into 2-butanol?
c: 1. TsCl, pyridine  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaBH<sub>4</sub>
1. TsCl, pyridine  2. NaOEt, EtOH  3. Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaBH<sub>4</sub>
1. TsCl, pyridine  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
h: Moving an OH one carbon: eliminate to an alkene first, then add water back with the opposite regiochemistry.
w: Tosylation makes a good leaving group, and the bulky base t-BuOK favors E2 over SN2 even on a primary substrate, giving 1-butene. Oxymercuration–demercuration adds OH to the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) without rearrangement: 1. TsCl, pyridine 2. t-BuOK 3. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 4. NaBH4.
x: Ethoxide is a small, strong nucleophile, and with a primary tosylate it does mostly S<sub>N</sub>2, giving butyl ethyl ether instead of the alkene.
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov, so the OH returns to C1 and you get 1-butanol back.
The primary bromide undergoes S<sub>N</sub>2 with hydroxide at the same carbon, regenerating 1-butanol.

q: Which alkene gives meso-3,4-dimethylhexanedial (shown) as the only product of 1. O3 2. (CH3)2S?
h: Ozonolysis does not touch sp<sup>3</sup> stereocenters. Reconnect the two CHO carbons and keep the relative configuration of the methyl groups.
w: Joining the two aldehyde carbons by a C=C closes a six-membered ring with methyls on C4 and C5 (counting the alkene as C1=C2). The stereocenters are carried through unchanged, so a meso product needs a meso alkene: cis-4,5-dimethylcyclohexene, in which both methyls are on the same face and the molecule has a mirror plane.
x: trans-4,5-Dimethylcyclohexene is chiral (no mirror plane), so its ozonolysis gives the chiral (3R,4R) or (3S,4S) dialdehyde, not the meso one.
1,2-Dimethylcyclohexene has its methyls on the alkene carbons, so it gives the diketone octane-2,7-dione.
With the methyls on C3 and C4, cleavage gives 2,3-dimethylhexanedial, a constitutional isomer of the target.

q: Using propene as the only source of carbon, which plan makes 2-hexyne?
c: Portion 1: Br<sub>2</sub>, then NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv). Portion 2: HBr, ROOR. Add the product of portion 2 to the product of portion 1.
Portion 1: Br<sub>2</sub>, then NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv). Portion 2: HBr (no peroxide). Add the product of portion 2 to the product of portion 1.
Portion 1: HBr, ROOR, then NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv). Portion 2: HBr, ROOR. Add the product of portion 2 to the product of portion 1.
Portion 1: Br<sub>2</sub>, then NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv). Portion 2: NBS, hν. Add the product of portion 2 to the product of portion 1.
h: Split 2-hexyne into a three-carbon acetylide and a three-carbon alkyl halide. What does each half need, and which halide will survive a strongly basic nucleophile?
w: 2-Hexyne is CH3C≡C–CH2CH2CH3: propynide plus a primary propyl halide. Propene + Br2 gives 1,2-dibromopropane, and double elimination with NaNH2 (the third equivalent deprotonates the alkyne) gives sodium propynide. Radical HBr addition gives 1-bromopropane, a primary halide that undergoes SN2. So Br2/NaNH2 for one portion and HBr/ROOR for the other.
x: Markovnikov HBr gives 2-bromopropane; the secondary halide mostly undergoes E2 with the acetylide, returning propene and propyne.
1-Bromopropane has only one leaving group, so NaNH<sub>2</sub> can eliminate only once (to propene) or substitute it; no alkyne or acetylide is formed.
NBS gives allyl bromide (3-bromopropene); alkylation gives hex-1-en-4-yne (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>C≡CCH<sub>3</sub>), which still has the extra C=C.

q: Which sequence converts 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene into 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol as the major product?
h: Markovnikov OH is needed, but the secondary carbocation here sits next to a quaternary carbon. Which method avoids a free carbocation?
w: The target has OH on C2, the Markovnikov position. A free secondary carbocation at C2 would undergo a 1,2-methyl shift to the tertiary cation, moving the OH to the wrong carbon. Oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, so no rearrangement occurs: 1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 2. NaBH4.
x: Acid hydration forms the secondary cation, which undergoes a methyl shift; water then traps the tertiary cation to give 2,3-dimethyl-2-butanol.
Hydroboration is anti-Markovnikov and gives the primary alcohol 3,3-dimethyl-1-butanol.
HBr also rearranges, giving 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane; hydroxide then gives mostly E2 (2,3-dimethyl-2-butene), and the skeleton is already wrong.

q: Which sequence converts 2-methylbutane into 2-methyl-1-butanol (racemic)?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
h: Work backward: which alkene gives a primary alcohol on C1 by hydroboration, and which base gives that less substituted alkene?
w: Hydroboration of 2-methyl-1-butene puts OH on the terminal CH2, giving 2-methyl-1-butanol. 2-Methyl-1-butene is the Hofmann product from 2-bromo-2-methylbutane with a bulky base, and that tertiary bromide is the selective product of radical bromination: 1. Br2, hν 2. t-BuOK, heat 3. BH3·THF 4. H2O2, NaOH.
x: Ethoxide gives the Zaitsev alkene, 2-methyl-2-butene; hydroboration of that gives 3-methyl-2-butanol.
Radical chlorination is unselective and gives a mixture of four constitutional isomers of chloro-2-methylbutane, so the later steps give a mixture.
Acid hydration of 2-methyl-1-butene is Markovnikov, giving the tertiary alcohol 2-methyl-2-butanol.

q: Which sequence converts trans-4-methylcyclohexanol into trans-1-azido-4-methylcyclohexane (both shown)?
h: The product has the same cis/trans relationship as the alcohol. Count the S<sub>N</sub>2 steps at the ring carbon; each one flips that substituent to the other face.
w: Retention of the trans relationship needs an even number of inversions at C1. PBr3 converts the alcohol to cis-1-bromo-4-methylcyclohexane with inversion, and azide (a good nucleophile and weak base) displaces bromide with a second inversion, giving the trans azide: 1. PBr3 2. NaN3, DMSO.
x: Tosylation keeps the C–O bond (retention), so azide displacement is the only inversion; the product is the cis azide.
t-BuOK is a bulky strong base; it eliminates the tosylate to 4-methylcyclohexene instead of substituting it.
Hydroxide is a very poor leaving group, so azide cannot displace the OH directly.

q: Which alkyl bromide, heated with NaOEt in ethanol, gives (Z)-3-methyl-2-pentene as the major product?
h: E2 needs the Br and the β-H anti-periplanar. In that conformation, which groups on C2 and C3 end up on the same side of the new double bond?
w: E2 removes the single H on C3 (Zaitsev, trisubstituted alkene) from the conformation where that H is anti to Br. For (2R,3S)-2-bromo-3-methylpentane, that conformation places the C1 methyl gauche to the ethyl group, so they become cis in the alkene. With ethyl (higher priority on C3) cis to CH3 (higher priority on C2), the product is Z. The answer is (2R,3S)-2-bromo-3-methylpentane (its enantiomer would work equally well).
x: In (2R,3R)-2-bromo-3-methylpentane the anti-periplanar H–C3–C2–Br conformation puts the C1 methyl anti to the ethyl group, so stereospecific E2 gives (E)-3-methyl-2-pentene.
(2S,3S) is the enantiomer of (2R,3R); it has the same relative configuration and also gives (E)-3-methyl-2-pentene.
3-Bromo-3-methylpentane has two CH<sub>2</sub> groups, and either H of a CH<sub>2</sub> can be anti to Br, so it gives both E and Z isomers (plus some 2-ethyl-1-butene), not one stereoisomer.

q: Which sequence converts 1-butene into pentanenitrile, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C≡N?
h: The CN carbon attaches to C1 of the butene. Which addition puts a leaving group on C1?
w: Cyanide adds one carbon by SN2, so you need 1-bromobutane. HBr with peroxide adds by a radical chain, placing Br on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov), and the primary bromide reacts cleanly with cyanide in a polar aprotic solvent: 1. HBr, ROOR 2. NaCN, DMSO.
x: Markovnikov HBr gives 2-bromobutane, so cyanide substitution gives the branched nitrile 2-methylbutanenitrile.
Hydroboration does give 1-butanol, but OH<sup>−</sup> is a very poor leaving group, so cyanide cannot displace it without first activating the alcohol.
NBS brominates the allylic carbon and keeps the C=C, so the product would be an unsaturated nitrile (a pentenenitrile).

q: Which sequence converts 2-methylpropane into 2-methyl-1-propanol?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. OsO<sub>4</sub>  4. NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Radical bromination puts Br on the tertiary carbon, but the target OH is on a primary carbon. How do you move it?
w: Bromination is highly selective for the tertiary C–H, giving 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. E2 gives 2-methylpropene (the only possible alkene), and hydroboration–oxidation adds OH anti-Markovnikov to the CH2 end: 1. Br2, hν 2. NaOEt 3. BH3·THF 4. H2O2, NaOH.
x: Substitution on a tertiary bromide cannot occur at a different carbon; aqueous hydroxide gives tert-butyl alcohol (and 2-methylpropene), not the primary alcohol.
Acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov and gives tert-butyl alcohol, 2-methyl-2-propanol.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups, giving 2-methyl-1,2-propanediol.

q: A student proposes the three-step synthesis shown. Which step fails, and why?
c: Step 2: the acetylide is a strong base and the bromide is secondary, so E2 to cyclohexene dominates.
Step 1: radical bromination of cyclohexane gives a mixture of constitutional isomers.
Step 3: hydration of a terminal alkyne gives an aldehyde, not a methyl ketone.
Step 2: acetylide ions are too weakly nucleophilic to displace bromide.
h: Check each step against its requirements: selectivity in step 1, the substrate type for the acetylide in step 2, and the regiochemistry of step 3.
w: Step 1 is fine: all 12 H atoms of cyclohexane are equivalent, so only one monobromide forms. Step 3 is fine: Hg2+-catalyzed hydration of a terminal alkyne is Markovnikov and gives the methyl ketone. Step 2 fails: acetylide ions (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 25) are strong bases, and with a secondary halide such as bromocyclohexane, E2 outcompetes SN2. A workable route would put the acetylide on a primary carbon instead.
x: Every H in cyclohexane is equivalent, so monobromination gives only bromocyclohexane.
HgSO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> hydration is Markovnikov; only hydroboration of a terminal alkyne gives the aldehyde.
Acetylides are good nucleophiles toward methyl and primary halides; the problem here is their basicity toward a secondary halide.

q: Which compound is the strongest acid?
h: Compare the stability of each conjugate base. Where can the negative charge on oxygen spread?
w: Acidity tracks the stability of the conjugate base. A phenoxide ion delocalizes its charge into the ring (phenol pKa ≈ 10), while cyclohexoxide keeps it on one oxygen (pKa ≈ 16–18). A para-nitro group adds one more resonance form that places the negative charge on the nitro oxygens, so 4-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 7.2) is the strongest acid.
x: Phenol is a good deal more acidic than an alcohol, but it lacks the electron-withdrawing nitro group that further stabilizes the phenoxide (pK<sub>a</sub> 10 vs 7.2).
The methyl group is weakly electron-donating, which slightly destabilizes the phenoxide; 4-methylphenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10.3) is a little weaker than phenol.
An alkoxide has no resonance delocalization, so cyclohexanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 18) is the weakest acid of the four.

q: Rank these phenols in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
h: For each para substituent, decide whether its resonance effect or its inductive effect dominates on the phenoxide.
w: Approximate pKa values: 4-methoxyphenol 10.2, phenol 10.0, 4-chlorophenol 9.4, 4-nitrophenol 7.2. A para OCH3 donates lone-pair density by resonance, which outweighs its inductive pull and destabilizes the phenoxide slightly. Chlorine is inductively withdrawing, and that outweighs its weak resonance donation, so it stabilizes the anion a little. NO2 withdraws by both resonance and induction. Order: I < II < III < IV.
x: This treats OCH<sub>3</sub> as electron-withdrawing because oxygen is electronegative; at the para position its resonance donation wins, so 4-methoxyphenol is slightly weaker than phenol.
This makes chlorine stronger than nitro. Nitro can delocalize the phenoxide charge onto its own oxygens by resonance; chlorine only pulls inductively.
This treats chlorine as a net donor. For halogens, induction outweighs resonance, so 4-chlorophenol is more acidic than phenol.

q:
Rank these alcohols in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
I. CH3CH2OH   II. ClCH2CH2OH   III. CF3CH2OH   IV. (CH3)3COH
h: None of these alkoxides has resonance. Think about induction from halogens and about how well the solvent can surround each alkoxide.
w: Electron-withdrawing halogens stabilize the alkoxide by induction, and three fluorines on the adjacent carbon pull far harder than one chlorine one carbon farther away. A bulky tert-butoxide is poorly solvated, which makes tert-butyl alcohol the weakest acid. Approximate pKa: (CH3)3COH 18, CH3CH2OH 16, ClCH2CH2OH 14.3, CF3CH2OH 12.4. Order: IV < I < II < III.
x: This swaps ethanol and tert-butyl alcohol. The crowded tert-butoxide ion is solvated less well, so tert-butyl alcohol is the weaker acid.
One chlorine is not stronger than three fluorines: the CF<sub>3</sub> group exerts a much larger inductive pull on the alkoxide oxygen.
This is the reverse order; halogen substituents make alcohols more acidic, not less.

q: Which base deprotonates phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.0) essentially completely but deprotonates ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> 16) far less than completely? (The pK<sub>a</sub> of each base's conjugate acid is in parentheses.)
h: An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid. Compare each conjugate acid's pK<sub>a</sub> with 10 and with 16.
w: Keq = 10(pKa of conjugate acid of the base − pKa of the acid). For phenol + NaOH, Keq ≈ 105.7, essentially complete. For ethanol + NaOH, Keq ≈ 10−0.3 ≈ 0.5, so ethanol is only partly deprotonated, far from complete. NaOH separates the two; this is why phenols dissolve in aqueous NaOH as phenoxide salts, while ordinary alcohols are not converted to alkoxides there.
x: Bicarbonate is too weak: for phenol, K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>6.4−10</sup> ≈ 10<sup>−3.6</sup>, so phenol is barely deprotonated.
Hydride is so strong (H<sub>2</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 35) that it deprotonates ethanol completely too.
Amide (NH<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> 38) deprotonates both phenol and ethanol essentially completely.

q: Rank these compounds from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: Count the O–H groups first; then, among isomers with one O–H, consider shape and surface area.
w: Butane-1,4-diol has two O–H groups and forms an extended hydrogen-bond network (bp ≈ 230 °C). Butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol each have one O–H, but the straight chain has more surface contact and less steric shielding of the OH (117 °C vs 82 °C). Diethyl ether cannot donate a hydrogen bond (35 °C). Order: I > II > III > IV.
x: A second O–H group roughly doubles the hydrogen bonding, so the diol boils far above butan-1-ol.
Branching lowers the boiling point: the compact tert-butyl alcohol has less surface area and a more hindered OH than butan-1-ol.
Diethyl ether is a hydrogen-bond acceptor only; it cannot donate, so it boils well below tert-butyl alcohol.

q: What is the major organic product of this reaction?
h: Which carbonyl is more electrophilic, the ketone or the ester? How strong a hydride donor is NaBH<sub>4</sub>?
w: NaBH4 is a mild hydride donor. It reduces aldehydes and ketones quickly but leaves esters essentially untouched, because the ester carbonyl is stabilized by donation from the OCH3 oxygen. Only the ketone becomes a secondary alcohol: methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate (racemic).
x: Reducing both groups needs LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; NaBH<sub>4</sub> in methanol does not reduce the ester at a useful rate.
This reverses the selectivity: the ester is the less reactive carbonyl, so it cannot be reduced while the ketone survives.
Removing the oxygen completely (C=O → CH<sub>2</sub>) requires Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner conditions, not a hydride reagent.

q:
Which functional groups are reduced by NaBH4 in methanol at room temperature?
I. aldehyde   II. ketone   III. ester   IV. carboxylic acid
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is the gentle hydride reagent. Which carbonyls are the most electrophilic?
w: NaBH4 reduces the most electrophilic carbonyls, aldehydes (to 1° alcohols) and ketones (to 2° alcohols). Esters are resonance-stabilized and react too slowly, and a carboxylic acid is simply deprotonated to an unreactive carboxylate. Answer: I and II only. LiAlH4 reduces all four.
x: Ketones are reduced by NaBH<sub>4</sub> as well; they are only slightly less reactive than aldehydes.
Esters are not reduced at a useful rate by NaBH<sub>4</sub> in methanol; that takes LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.
A carboxylic acid is deprotonated by the basic hydride to a carboxylate, which is far too electron-rich to accept hydride from NaBH<sub>4</sub>.

q: The ketone below is a single enantiomer. Which statement best describes the product mixture after reduction with NaBH<sub>4</sub>?
c: (2R,3R) and (2S,3R) diastereomers in unequal amounts; optically active
(2R,3R) and (2S,3S) enantiomers in equal amounts; optically inactive
(2R,3S) and (2S,3R) enantiomers in equal amounts; optically inactive
(2R,3R) and (2S,3R) diastereomers in equal amounts; optically inactive
h: Hydride does not touch C3. With C3 fixed, how are the two possible C2 products related?
w: The starting ketone is (R)-3-phenylbutan-2-one. Hydride adds to C2 from either face, creating a new stereocenter, while C3 keeps its (R) configuration. The products, (2R,3R)- and (2S,3R)-3-phenylbutan-2-ol, are diastereomers. The two faces of the carbonyl are diastereotopic (the existing stereocenter makes them different), so the transition states differ in energy and the products form in unequal amounts. A mixture of chiral, non-mirror-image molecules is optically active.
x: C3 is not touched by NaBH4, so it cannot become (S); a (2S,3S) product would require inverting a carbon that never reacts.
This inverts C3, which does not react; every product molecule keeps the (3R) configuration of the starting ketone.

Diastereomers form through transition states of different energy, so equal amounts are not expected; and even a 1:1 mixture of diastereomers would still rotate light because they are not mirror images.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: A lactone is a cyclic ester. What does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> do to both the acyl carbon and the alkoxy oxygen of an ester?
w: LiAlH4 reduces an ester to two alcohols: the acyl carbon becomes a CH2OH and the alkoxy oxygen becomes a second OH. In a lactone both pieces are in the same molecule, so the ring opens to one diol: butane-1,4-diol.
x: The aldehyde formed after the first hydride is more reactive than the ester and is reduced at once; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not stop at the aldehyde.
Tetrahydrofuran would need the carbonyl oxygen removed while the ring stays closed; hydride reduction instead opens the ring at the C–O bond to give a diol.
The ring oxygen is not lost: it becomes an O–H after workup, so the product keeps both oxygens.

q: What is the major organic product after treatment with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> followed by aqueous workup?
