h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both carbonyls. For the amide, which group leaves from the tetrahedral intermediate: oxygen or nitrogen?
w: Excess LiAlH4 reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol. Amides are reduced too, but differently from esters: the oxygen (bound to aluminum) is expelled to give an iminium ion, which takes a second hydride, so C=O becomes CH2 and the nitrogen stays. Product: 1-[4-(dimethylaminomethyl)phenyl]ethan-1-ol.
x: This treats the amide like an ester. In amide reduction nitrogen stays attached and the oxygen is removed, giving an amine, not an alcohol.
Amides are less reactive than ketones but are still reduced by excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; leaving the amide intact is the NaBH<sub>4</sub> result.
The ketone is the most reactive carbonyl present; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> cannot reduce the amide while leaving the ketone untouched.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane reacts with NaOH in DMSO. What is the substitution product?
h: A strong nucleophile, a secondary substrate and a polar aprotic solvent: which substitution mechanism, and what does it do to configuration?
w: Hydroxide is a strong nucleophile and DMSO is polar aprotic, so substitution goes SN2 with backside attack and inversion. OH takes the place of Br, which had the same priority rank (highest), so inversion changes the label: (S)-butan-2-ol.
x: Retention would require frontside attack or two inversions; a single S<sub>N</sub>2 step inverts the stereocenter.
Racemization comes from a planar carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1), which is not favored with a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent.
S<sub>N</sub>2 does not move the functional group; the OH ends up on the carbon that carried the Br.

q: Which reagent sequence turns this alkene into the alcohol shown, in good yield?
h: The OH goes to the more substituted alkene carbon, and the carbon skeleton must not change. Which Markovnikov method avoids a free carbocation?
w: The target has Markovnikov regiochemistry and the same skeleton. Acid hydration would form a secondary carbocation next to a quaternary carbon, which undergoes a methyl shift. Oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, gives Markovnikov addition and does not rearrange. Answer: 1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 2. NaBH4.
x: Acid hydration goes through a free 2° carbocation that undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to a 3° cation, giving mainly 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov and gives the primary alcohol 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.
Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C; reduction of the resulting aldehyde gives 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol, with one carbon fewer.

q: Which compound is the weakest acid?
h: Draw the resonance forms of each phenoxide. In which isomer can the negative charge reach the carbon bearing the nitro group?
w: The phenoxide charge is delocalized to the ortho and para carbons. A nitro group at an ortho or para position can accept that charge onto its own oxygens (pKa ≈ 7.2 for both 2- and 4-nitrophenol), and two such groups do even better (2,4-dinitrophenol, pKa ≈ 4.1). A meta nitro group is never on a carbon that carries the charge, so it helps only by induction: 3-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 8.4) is the weakest acid of the four.
x: In 4-nitrophenol the charge delocalizes onto the nitro oxygens by resonance, which makes it more acidic than the meta isomer.
An ortho nitro group also stabilizes the phenoxide by resonance (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 7.2), so 2-nitrophenol is more acidic than 3-nitrophenol.
Two resonance-withdrawing nitro groups (ortho and para) make 2,4-dinitrophenol the strongest acid here, not the weakest.

q: Acetophenone is treated with NaBD<sub>4</sub> in ether, then with H<sub>2</sub>O. Where are the deuterium atoms in the product?
h: Follow each hydrogen: one comes from the hydride reagent, one from the workup.
w: Borodeuteride delivers D− to the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide. The O–H proton comes later from the H2O workup. Product: PhCD(OH)CH3 (racemic, since D adds equally to both faces).
x: The nucleophile is the deuteride; it bonds to carbon, not oxygen. The oxygen is protonated by H<sub>2</sub>O.
The workup uses H<sub>2</sub>O, not D<sub>2</sub>O, so the O–H ends up as O–H; only the carbon carries D.
Hydride attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, not the methyl carbon; the CH<sub>3</sub> is untouched.

q: Which sequence carries out this conversion?
h: You must reduce the less reactive carbonyl and keep the more reactive one. What can temporarily hide a ketone from LiAlH<sub>4</sub>?
w: Any hydride that reduces an ester also reduces a ketone, so the ketone must be protected. Ethylene glycol and acid convert the ketone to a cyclic acetal, which is inert to LiAlH4. LiAlH4 then reduces the ester to CH2OH, and aqueous acid removes the acetal and restores the ketone. Answer: 1. HOCH2CH2OH, TsOH 2. LiAlH4 3. H3O+.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> has the opposite selectivity: it reduces the ketone to an alcohol and leaves the ester untouched.
Unprotected, both carbonyls are reduced, giving the diol 4-(hydroxymethyl)cyclohexan-1-ol.
PCC re-oxidizes both alcohols of the diol, giving the keto aldehyde (4-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde), not the keto alcohol.

q: Which compound, treated with CH3CH2MgBr in ether and then H3O+, gives a primary alcohol?
h: The carbonyl carbon becomes the carbinol carbon. How many carbon groups will it carry after the Grignard adds?
w: In a Grignard addition the carbonyl carbon becomes the C–OH carbon, carrying the new alkyl group plus whatever it already had. Formaldehyde has only H atoms, so the carbinol carbon ends up with one carbon group: CH3CH2CH2OH, a primary alcohol. Answer: formaldehyde.
x: Acetaldehyde already has one methyl group, so adding ethyl gives the secondary alcohol butan-2-ol.
Acetone carries two methyl groups, so adding ethyl gives the tertiary alcohol 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
An ester takes two equivalents: methyl formate gives pentan-3-ol, a secondary alcohol with two ethyl groups on the carbinol carbon.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: After the first addition, methoxide leaves. What carbonyl is left, and is it more or less reactive than the ester?
w: The first CH3MgBr adds to the ester carbonyl; the tetrahedral intermediate expels CH3O− to give acetophenone. The ketone is more electrophilic than the ester, so it captures a second CH3MgBr at once. Workup gives the tertiary alcohol 2-phenylpropan-2-ol, with two identical methyl groups that both came from the Grignard.
x: The ketone intermediate is more reactive than the starting ester, so it cannot be isolated with excess Grignard; it is converted to the tertiary alcohol.
A secondary alcohol would require a hydride as the second nucleophile; here both nucleophiles are methyl groups.
Grignard reagents add C–C bonds; they do not hydrolyze the ester to benzoic acid.

q: (R)-2-Methyloxirane is treated with phenylmagnesium bromide, followed by H3O+. What is the major product?
h: A Grignard opens an epoxide by an S<sub>N</sub>2-like attack. Which carbon is less hindered, and does any bond to the stereocenter break?
w: Under basic (Grignard) conditions the epoxide opens by backside SN2 attack at the less hindered CH2. No bond to the stereocenter breaks, so it keeps its spatial arrangement. Its priorities stay in the same order (O > CH2R > CH3 > H), so the label stays the same: (R)-1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
x: Inversion happens only at the carbon that is attacked. The CH2 is attacked, so the stereocenter is untouched and stays (R).
Attack at the more substituted carbon is the acid-catalyzed pattern; a strongly basic Grignard attacks the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub>.
This places phenyl on the more substituted carbon (the wrong regiochemistry) and also keeps the old arrangement, which an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack there could not do.

q: Which compound cannot be converted into a useful Grignard reagent by treatment with Mg in dry ether?
h: A Grignard reagent is a very strong base. Look for an acidic hydrogen in the same molecule.
w: A Grignard carbon is strongly basic (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 50). Any O–H, N–H, S–H or CO2H in the same molecule protonates it immediately, destroying the reagent. 4-Bromobutan-1-ol has an O–H (pKa ≈ 16), so its OH must be protected first, for example as a TBS ether.
x: An ether oxygen has no acidic hydrogen; ethers are the usual solvents for Grignard reagents.
Aryl bromides form Grignard reagents readily, and the methoxy group has no acidic hydrogen.
Secondary alkyl bromides such as bromocyclohexane form Grignard reagents without difficulty.

q: Which sequence prepares the diol below from 4-bromobutan-1-ol and benzaldehyde?
c: 1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. PhCHO  4. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, H<sub>2</sub>O  5. TBAF
1. TBSCl, imidazole  2. Mg, ether  3. PhCHO  4. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, H<sub>2</sub>O  5. PCC  6. TBAF
1. TBAF  2. Mg, ether  3. PhCHO  4. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, H<sub>2</sub>O  5. TBSCl, imidazole
h: The Grignard reagent cannot coexist with a free O–H. When must the OH be masked, and when should it be released?
w: The free OH would protonate the Grignard as soon as it formed. So: (1) protect the OH as a TBS ether, (2) form the Grignard, (3) add it to benzaldehyde, (4) protonate the new alkoxide with a mild workup, and (5) remove the silyl group with fluoride (TBAF), which frees the primary OH. Answer: TBSCl/imidazole; Mg; PhCHO; NH4Cl; TBAF.
x: Without protection, the Grignard is quenched by its own O–H as soon as it forms, giving butan-1-ol (as its alkoxide), not the diol.
PCC oxidizes the new secondary alcohol to a ketone, so the product would be 5-hydroxy-1-phenylpentan-1-one, not the diol.
TBAF removes a silyl group; using it first does nothing, so the OH is still free when Mg is added. Protection must come before the Grignard step.

q: Which ester, treated with excess CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr and then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, gives 3-methylpentan-3-ol?
h: Two equivalents of the Grignard end up on the ester carbonyl carbon. Which of the three groups on the carbinol carbon is not ethyl?
w: An ester plus excess RMgX gives a tertiary alcohol in which two of the three groups on the carbinol carbon are the Grignard's R and the third is the ester's acyl group. 3-Methylpentan-3-ol has two ethyls and one methyl on the carbinol carbon, so the acyl group must be acetyl: ethyl acetate.
x: The propanoyl group contributes a third ethyl, giving 3-ethylpentan-3-ol.
Formate contributes H, so two ethyls give the secondary alcohol pentan-3-ol.
A carbonate loses both ethoxy groups and adds three ethyl groups, giving 3-ethylpentan-3-ol.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Treat the lactone as an ester whose alkoxy group is tethered to the same chain. How many methyl groups add?
w: Like any ester, the lactone takes two equivalents of CH3MgBr. The first addition opens the ring (the ring oxygen leaves as an alkoxide, still attached to the chain) and gives a methyl ketone; the second adds to that ketone. Workup protonates both alkoxides: 5-methylhexane-1,5-diol.
x: The ketone formed after ring opening is more reactive than the lactone, so with excess Grignard it does not survive.
The ring oxygen leaves the carbonyl carbon during the reaction and ends up as a free primary OH after workup; it does not stay bonded in a ring.
This product has only one new methyl group and an H on the carbinol carbon, which would need a hydride donor; both added groups here are methyls.

q: Which combination, followed by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup, gives 2-phenylethan-1-ol?
h: Count the carbons between the ring and the OH. Which electrophile adds a two-carbon unit with the OH on the far carbon?
w: A Grignard opens ethylene oxide at a CH2, adding –CH2CH2O−; after protonation the OH sits two carbons from the original nucleophilic carbon. PhMgBr + oxirane gives PhCH2CH2OH.
x: With acetaldehyde the phenyl bonds to the carbonyl carbon, so the OH ends up on the carbon next to the ring: 1-phenylethanol.
Formaldehyde adds only one carbon, giving benzyl alcohol (PhCH<sub>2</sub>OH).
Methyl adds to the benzaldehyde carbonyl carbon, giving the secondary alcohol 1-phenylethanol.

q: 4-Hydroxyacetophenone is treated with 1.0 equivalent of CH3MgBr in THF, followed by H3O+. What is the main organic compound isolated?
h: Before the Grignard can act as a nucleophile, does anything in the molecule react with it faster as a base?
w: Proton transfer is much faster than carbonyl addition. The phenolic O–H (pKa ≈ 8) protonates CH3MgBr, releasing CH4 and using up the single equivalent. The phenoxide salt has no Grignard left to add to the ketone, and workup reprotonates it, so the starting material, 4-hydroxyacetophenone, is recovered.
x: This would need at least two equivalents: the first is consumed by the acidic phenol O–H.
A Grignard reagent does not methylate oxygen; the phenoxide is only reprotonated on workup.
A Grignard reagent delivers a carbon nucleophile, not a hydride; it cannot reduce the ketone to a secondary alcohol.

q: Cyclohexene oxide is treated with CH<sub>3</sub>Li in ether, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>. What is the product?
h: Organolithium opening of an epoxide is S<sub>N</sub>2-like. From which face does the nucleophile attack, relative to the C–O bond that breaks?
w: The methyl anion attacks one epoxide carbon from the backside, opposite the C–O bond that breaks. The oxygen stays on the neighboring carbon, on the face where it started, so CH3 and OH end up anti: trans-2-methylcyclohexanol. The two epoxide carbons are equivalent mirror-image sites in this achiral epoxide, so attack at either gives the two enantiomers equally: racemic.
x: A cis product would require frontside attack; SN2 opening places the nucleophile anti to the departing oxygen.
The methyl bonds to an epoxide carbon, and the oxygen remains on the other carbon; both cannot end up on the same carbon.
Cyclohexylmethanol would need the new carbon inserted between the ring and the oxygen; instead the methyl bonds to a ring carbon and the OH stays on the adjacent ring carbon.

q: Using bromobenzene and reagents with no more than two carbons, which sequence gives 2-phenylbutan-2-ol?
c: 1. Mg, ether  2. CH<sub>3</sub>CHO  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC  5. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr  6. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. Mg, ether  2. oxirane  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC  5. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr  6. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. Mg, ether  2. HCHO  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC  5. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr  6. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: Disconnect one C–C bond at the carbinol carbon. The ketone you need has to be made first; which secondary alcohol oxidizes to it?
w: The target is a tertiary alcohol carrying Ph, CH3 and CH2CH3. Disconnecting the ethyl group leaves acetophenone + EtMgBr. Acetophenone comes from oxidizing 1-phenylethanol, which is PhMgBr + acetaldehyde. Sequence: Mg; CH3CHO; H3O+; PCC; EtMgBr; H3O+.
x: After step 2 the carbinol carbon is an alkoxide, not a carbonyl, so EtMgBr has nothing to add to; workup gives only 1-phenylethanol.
Oxirane puts a CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the new carbinol carbon; the route ends at 1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
Formaldehyde gives benzyl alcohol, then benzaldehyde; adding EtMgBr gives the secondary alcohol 1-phenylpropan-1-ol.

q: Ethyl acetate reacts with only 1.0 equivalent of C6H5MgBr. The mixture contains mostly 1,1-diphenylethanol (after workup) and unreacted ethyl acetate, with little acetophenone. What is the best explanation?
c: Acetophenone, once formed, is more electrophilic than the ester and captures PhMgBr faster than the remaining ester does
Acetophenone is less electrophilic than ethyl acetate but forms in higher concentration, so it reacts first with PhMgBr
PhMgBr adds twice to the same ester molecule in a single concerted step, so no ketone ever forms
The ethoxide released in the first step converts acetophenone back into ethyl acetate
h: Compare the electrophilicity of a ketone and an ester. What does the OR group donate to the ester carbonyl?
w: An ester carbonyl is stabilized by resonance donation from the OR oxygen, which makes it less electrophilic than a ketone. When the first addition expels ethoxide, the ketone formed competes for the remaining Grignard and wins, so most of it goes on to the tertiary alcohol while some ester is left. The ketone is more reactive than the ester. This is why stopping at a ketone requires a different method (for example a Weinreb amide or a nitrile).
x: Ketones are more, not less, electrophilic than esters; a ketone formed in small amounts still reacts faster.
The two additions are separate steps: addition, loss of ethoxide to give the ketone, then a second addition.
Ethoxide does not convert ketones into esters; the observed result comes from the ketone's higher reactivity.

q: Which is a suitable solvent for preparing and using a Grignard reagent?
h: The solvent must not protonate the reagent and must not be attacked by it.
w: A Grignard reagent is both a strong base and a strong nucleophile. Ethers such as diethyl ether and THF have no acidic hydrogen and no electrophilic carbonyl, and their oxygen lone pairs coordinate and stabilize magnesium.
x: Ethanol's O–H protonates RMgX at once, converting it to the alkane R–H.
Acetone's carbonyl is an electrophile; the Grignard would add to the solvent to give a tertiary alcohol.
Ethyl acetate's ester carbonyl reacts with Grignard reagents (two equivalents each), consuming the reagent.

q: What is the major organic product of this sequence?
h: First build the tertiary alcohol. Then ask which alkene E1 dehydration of that alcohol favors.
w: Methyl adds to the carbonyl to give 1,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol. Hot sulfuric acid dehydrates it by E1 through a tertiary carbocation at C1. Loss of the C2 hydrogen gives the most substituted (tetrasubstituted) alkene, which is the Zaitsev product: 1,2-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene.
x: The exocyclic alkene is only disubstituted; under thermodynamic E1 conditions the more substituted endocyclic alkene is favored.
Losing a C6 hydrogen gives a trisubstituted alkene, but removing the C2 hydrogen gives the more stable tetrasubstituted alkene.
This is the alcohol after step 2; hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dehydrates a tertiary alcohol readily.

q:
Which combinations, after H3O+ workup, give 1-phenylpropan-1-ol?
I. C6H5MgBr + propanal
II. CH3CH2MgBr + benzaldehyde
III. C6H5CH2MgBr + acetaldehyde
h: For each pair, the carbonyl carbon becomes the C–OH carbon. Which groups end up on that carbon?
w: The carbinol carbon of the target carries Ph, CH2CH3 and H. Either group can come from the Grignard: Ph adds to propanal (I) or ethyl adds to benzaldehyde (II). In III the carbinol carbon (from acetaldehyde) carries CH3 and CH2Ph, giving 1-phenylpropan-2-ol. Answer: I and II only.
x: II also works: ethyl adds to the benzaldehyde carbonyl carbon, which already carries the phenyl.
III puts a CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the carbinol carbon, giving 1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
III gives the constitutional isomer 1-phenylpropan-2-ol, not the target.

q: What is the product of this two-step sequence, and why?
c: (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile: retention in the TsCl step, inversion in the SN2 step
(R)-2-methylbutanenitrile: inversion in the TsCl step, inversion again in the SN2 step
Racemic 2-methylbutanenitrile: the tosylate ionizes to a carbocation
h: In tosylation, which bond is made: C–O or O–S? Then decide what cyanide does at carbon.
w: Tosylation forms an O–S bond; the C–O bond of the stereocenter is not touched, so the (R) tosylate forms with retention. Cyanide, a good nucleophile in polar aprotic DMSO, then displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion. In the product, CN takes the top priority that OTs had, so the label changes: (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile.
x: Tosylation does not invert: the alcohol oxygen attacks sulfur, and the C–O bond stays intact.
The S<sub>N</sub>2 step with cyanide inverts the stereocenter, so the configuration cannot be retained overall.
A secondary tosylate with a strong nucleophile in DMSO reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2, not through a free carbocation.

q: (S)-Pentan-2-ol is treated with PBr3. What is the major product?
h: PBr<sub>3</sub> turns OH into a leaving group, then bromide attacks. By which mechanism, and from which side?
w: The OH attacks phosphorus, becoming –OPBr2, a good leaving group. Bromide then displaces it by SN2 with backside attack and no carbocation. The stereocenter inverts, and since Br takes the top priority that O had, the label changes: (R)-2-bromopentane.
x: Retention would require frontside attack; the S<sub>N</sub>2 step in the PBr<sub>3</sub> reaction inverts the stereocenter.
PBr<sub>3</sub> does not form a carbocation, so there is no hydride shift to C3.
The bromine replaces the OH on the same carbon (C2); it does not migrate to the chain end.

q: (R)-Butan-2-ol is taken through the sequence below. What is the final product?
h: Track the stereocenter step by step. In ester hydrolysis by hydroxide, which bond breaks: acyl C–O or alkyl C–O?
w: Step 1 makes the (R) tosylate with retention (only the O–S bond forms). Step 2: acetate displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-butan-2-yl acetate. Step 3: saponification attacks the acyl carbon and breaks the acyl C–O bond, so the alkyl C–O bond, and the stereocenter, are untouched. Net result: the alcohol is inverted, giving (S)-butan-2-ol.
x: This assumes the hydrolysis step inverts the stereocenter again. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, not the stereocenter, so there is only one inversion overall.
No step forms a carbocation: the displacement is S<sub>N</sub>2 and the hydrolysis occurs at the acyl carbon.
This is the product after step 2; hot aqueous NaOH saponifies the acetate ester to the alcohol.

q: cis-4-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is treated with PBr3. What is the major product?
h: The ring carbon with the OH reacts by backside attack. If OH was on the same face as CH<sub>3</sub>, where does Br end up?
w: PBr3 converts OH into –OPBr2, and bromide displaces it by SN2 from the opposite face. OH was cis to the methyl, so Br ends up trans: trans-1-bromo-4-methylcyclohexane. Neither compound is chiral; the stereochemistry shows up as cis/trans.
x: Keeping the cis relationship would need retention; PBr<sub>3</sub> reactions proceed with inversion at the carbinol carbon.
Moving Br to the methyl-bearing carbon would need a carbocation and hydride shifts, which do not occur with PBr<sub>3</sub>.
PBr<sub>3</sub> is a substitution reagent; it does not dehydrate the alcohol to an alkene.

q: Why is an alcohol usually converted to a tosylate before an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction with a nucleophile such as N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>?
c: Hydroxide is a strong base and poor leaving group; tosylate is a weak, resonance-stabilized base that leaves easily
The tosyl group makes the carbon less hindered, so the nucleophile can reach it from the back side
Tosylation converts the alcohol into a carbocation, which the nucleophile then traps in a fast second step of the reaction
The tosylate makes the nucleophile stronger by deprotonating it before it attacks the carbon
h: Good leaving groups are the conjugate bases of strong acids. Compare H<sub>2</sub>O (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) with TsOH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −3).
w: A leaving group must be able to carry away the electron pair. HO− is a strong base (conjugate acid H2O, pKa 15.7), so it is a very poor leaving group. TsO− is the conjugate base of a strong acid and spreads its charge over three oxygens. Tosylation turns a poor leaving group into an excellent one without touching the stereocenter.
x: The tosyl group is large; it does not reduce steric hindrance at the carbon.
Tosylation forms a neutral sulfonate ester; no carbocation is formed, which is why stereochemistry is kept in this step.
The tosylate is on the substrate; it does not change the nucleophile.

q: Butane-1,3-diol is taken through the sequence below. What is the final product?
h: The bulky silyl chloride reacts with the least hindered OH first. Which OH is left for PCC?
w: TBSCl is bulky, so one equivalent silylates the primary OH much faster than the secondary one. PCC then oxidizes the free secondary OH to a ketone (the TBS ether is inert). TBAF cleaves the Si–O bond and frees the primary OH: 4-hydroxybutan-2-one.
x: This assumes the secondary OH was protected. The bulky TBS group goes on the less hindered primary OH, so the secondary carbon is the one oxidized.
Only one OH is free during the PCC step; the silyl ether is not oxidized.
PCC does not oxidize alcohols to carboxylic acids, and the primary OH was protected during the oxidation.

q: Why does tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF) remove a TBS protecting group under mild conditions?
c: The Si–F bond formed is much stronger than the Si–O bond broken
Fluoride is a strong base that deprotonates the silyl ether to cleave it
Fluoride reduces silicon, breaking the Si–O bond
TBAF is a strong acid that hydrolyzes the silyl ether
h: Compare bond strengths to silicon.
w: Silicon forms an exceptionally strong bond to fluorine (about 135 kcal/mol for Si–F vs about 110 for Si–O). Fluoride attacks silicon, forming a pentacoordinate intermediate that releases the alkoxide; workup gives the alcohol. The driving force is the strong Si–F bond. Carbon-based groups (esters, ketones, alkenes) are untouched, which makes TBS removal very selective.
x: A silyl ether has no acidic hydrogen to remove; fluoride acts as a nucleophile at silicon.
No redox occurs; silicon stays in the +4 oxidation state.
TBAF is a salt of fluoride, not an acid; acid can also cleave silyl ethers, but that is a different method.

q: Which reagent converts cyclohexylmethanol into cyclohexanecarbaldehyde in good yield?
h: You need an oxidant that stops at the aldehyde. Which oxidants work without water?
w: Primary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes by anhydrous oxidants that cannot form the aldehyde hydrate: PCC, Swern, or Dess–Martin periodinane.
x: Aqueous chromic acid oxidizes the aldehyde (through its hydrate) on to cyclohexanecarboxylic acid.
Hot permanganate is a strong aqueous oxidant that takes a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent; it cannot oxidize an alcohol.

q: What is the major organic product with excess Jones reagent?
h: Classify each OH as 1°, 2° or 3°. Oxidation needs an H on the carbinol carbon.
w: Chromic acid oxidizes a primary alcohol through the aldehyde hydrate all the way to a carboxylic acid. The tertiary alcohol has no H on its carbinol carbon, so it cannot form the C=O and is untouched. Product: 4-hydroxy-4-methylcyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid.
x: Stopping at the aldehyde needs an anhydrous oxidant such as PCC; aqueous Jones reagent goes on to the acid.
Oxidizing the tertiary carbon would require breaking a C–C bond (losing the methyl); Cr(VI) does not do this.
The primary alcohol is readily oxidized; only the tertiary OH is inert.

q: Which alcohol is not oxidized by PCC in CH2Cl2?
h: Look at the carbon carrying the OH. Does it have a hydrogen?
w: Oxidation to a carbonyl removes the H from the carbinol carbon. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol with no such H, so PCC does not react with it.
x: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol; PCC oxidizes it to 3-methylbutan-2-one.
2-Methylbutan-1-ol is primary; PCC oxidizes it to 2-methylbutanal.
Cyclohexanol is secondary; PCC oxidizes it to cyclohexanone.

q: Which sequence carries out this conversion?
c: 1. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, ether  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. H<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>, acetone  2. CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, ether  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
h: Work backward: a methyl ketone comes from oxidizing a secondary alcohol, which comes from CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + an aldehyde.
w: Retrosynthesis: the methyl ketone ⇐ 1-cyclohexylethanol (oxidation) ⇐ cyclohexanecarbaldehyde + CH3MgBr ⇐ cyclohexylmethanol (oxidation that stops at the aldehyde). Forward: PCC; CH3MgBr; H3O+; PCC.
x: Jones reagent takes the primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid, which simply protonates CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr; no ketone or secondary alcohol forms.
This stops at the secondary alcohol 1-cyclohexylethanol; a final oxidation is needed to reach the ketone.
The Grignard reagent is destroyed by the alcohol's O–H before any oxidation is done; Grignard addition needs a carbonyl present.

q: Why does PCC in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> stop at the aldehyde when it oxidizes a primary alcohol, while aqueous Jones reagent gives the carboxylic acid?
c: Without water the aldehyde cannot form its hydrate, the form that Cr(VI) oxidizes to the acid
PCC is too weak to oxidize any C–H bond on a carbon that already bears an oxygen atom
The pyridinium ion reduces the carboxylic acid back to the aldehyde as fast as the acid forms
In CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> the aldehyde evaporates from the flask before it can be oxidized any further
h: Chromium oxidizes an O–H-bearing carbon that also has a C–H. What must happen to the aldehyde before it fits that description?
w: Cr(VI) oxidation requires a carbon that bears both an OH (to form the chromate ester) and an H. An aldehyde becomes such a species only after adding water to form the hydrate, R–CH(OH)2. In aqueous Jones conditions the hydrate forms and is oxidized to the acid; in anhydrous CH2Cl2 it cannot. No water, no hydrate, no over-oxidation.
x: PCC does oxidize a C–H on an oxygen-bearing carbon: that is exactly how it converts the alcohol to the aldehyde.
Pyridinium is not a reducing agent; no acid is formed in the first place.
Most aldehydes made this way are not volatile; the selectivity is chemical, not physical.

q: The racemic trans alcohol below is converted to its tosylate and then heated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. What is the major product?
h: E2 in a cyclohexane needs the leaving group and the β-H both axial (trans-diaxial). Put OTs axial: where is the methyl, and which neighbor still has an axial H?
w: Tosylation keeps the configuration, so the tosylate is trans to the methyl. For E2 the OTs must be axial; in that chair the trans methyl on C2 is also axial, so C2's only H is equatorial and cannot be anti-periplanar. The only axial β-H is on C6, so elimination goes toward C6 and gives the less substituted alkene: 3-methylcyclohexene, not the Zaitsev product.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene needs loss of the C2 hydrogen, which is never anti-periplanar to the OTs in the trans isomer.
An exocyclic alkene would need a C=C to the methyl carbon, which is not β to the leaving group.
A strong base with heat on a secondary tosylate favors E2; the S<sub>N</sub>2 ether is at most a minor product.

q:
Which conditions would remove (cleave) a TBS ether?
I. TBAF in THF
II. aqueous HCl in methanol
III. CH3MgBr in ether
IV. PCC in CH2Cl2
h: Silyl ethers are chosen because they survive bases, nucleophiles and oxidants. What two kinds of reagent do take them off?
w: TBS ethers are cleaved by fluoride (strong Si–F bond) and by aqueous acid (protonation of oxygen, then attack at silicon). They survive strong bases and carbon nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents, and they cannot be oxidized because there is no O–H. Answer: I and II only.
x: Aqueous acid also removes silyl ethers; that is why a mild workup (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is often used when a TBS group must survive.
Grignard reagents do not cleave TBS ethers; that stability is why TBS is used to protect OH groups during Grignard reactions.
Neither a Grignard reagent nor PCC cleaves a TBS ether; PCC needs a free O–H to oxidize.

q: Which reagent converts 3-methylbutan-2-ol into 2-chloro-3-methylbutane without rearrangement?
h: Which method avoids a free carbocation next to a carbon that carries a hydrogen it could shift?
w: With HCl/ZnCl2 a secondary alcohol ionizes to a 2° carbocation, which undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the tertiary cation and gives 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Thionyl chloride with pyridine forms a chlorosulfite ester that chloride displaces by SN2, with no carbocation: SOCl2, pyridine.
x: The Lucas reagent goes through a carbocation; the hydride shift gives mainly the rearranged tertiary chloride.
Radical chlorination replaces C–H bonds, not the OH, and gives a mixture.
Hydroxide is a very poor leaving group, so chloride cannot displace OH without activation.

q: What is the major product when this diol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: After one OH leaves, the neighboring carbon still carries an OH. What can migrate to the cation, and what does the remaining oxygen become?
w: Pinacol rearrangement: protonation and loss of water give a tertiary carbocation. A methyl on the adjacent carbon shifts (1,2-shift) to that cation, leaving a cation on the carbon bearing the OH, which is strongly stabilized as a protonated carbonyl (oxocarbenium ion). Loss of H+ gives 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one (pinacolone).
x: Double dehydration can compete, but the pinacol pathway is favored because the oxygen-stabilized cation formed after the methyl shift is especially stable and leads to a C=O.
An epoxide would form only by the neighboring OH attacking the cation; under hot acid the 1,2-shift to a carbonyl dominates and an epoxide would itself open again.
Forming this alkene would require removing both oxygens; the second oxygen is kept and becomes the ketone C=O.

q: What is the major product of pinacol rearrangement of this diol?
h: Decide first which OH leaves: which carbocation is more stable? Then see which groups are available to migrate from the other carbon.
w: Loss of water from the diphenyl carbon gives a doubly benzylic tertiary cation, much more stable than the dimethyl tertiary cation. The groups on the neighboring carbon are two methyls and an OH, so a methyl migrates. The carbinol carbon becomes the C=O: 3,3-diphenylbutan-2-one.
x: This product comes from ionizing at the dimethyl carbon and then shifting a phenyl. Ionization occurs at the carbon that gives the more stable, diphenyl-stabilized cation.
Simple dehydration is not the main path; the 1,2-shift leads to a strongly stabilized oxocarbenium ion and a ketone.
The epoxide is not the product of this reaction under hot acid; the 1,2-methyl shift and loss of H<sup>+</sup> give the ketone.

q: What is the major product when this diol is treated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Only a C–C bond of the other ring can migrate to the cation. How does the size of that ring change when one of its bonds shifts?
w: Loss of water gives a tertiary cation on one ring carbon. On the neighboring carbinol carbon the migrating group must be a ring C–C bond; when it shifts, that carbon's ring gains the cationic carbon and expands from five to six members. The carbinol carbon becomes the C=O, and the original carbocation carbon becomes the spiro atom: spiro[4.5]decan-6-one.
x: Losing both oxygens is not the main path; the 1,2-shift gives an oxocarbenium ion that becomes a ketone.
This ketone has 11 carbons, but the diol has only 10, so it cannot come from this reaction. In the pinacol shift a ring C–C bond migrates instead, and one ring grows from five to six members.
Simple dehydration of one OH is outcompeted by the alkyl shift, which also relieves ring strain as the five-membered ring grows to six.

q: What is the product of NaIO<sub>4</sub> cleavage of this diol?
h: Periodate breaks the C–C bond between the two OH carbons; each becomes a C=O. Keep every other bond.
w: NaIO4 forms a cyclic periodate ester with the 1,2-diol and cleaves the C1–C2 bond. C1 (bearing CH3) becomes a ketone and C2 (bearing H) becomes an aldehyde, opening the ring: 6-oxoheptanal. Periodate does not oxidize the aldehyde further.
x: Periodate stops at the aldehyde; further oxidation to the acid would need an oxidant such as hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
The methyl group stays attached to C1, so that end becomes a methyl ketone, not an aldehyde.
A ring-contracted or methyl-shifted ketone is a pinacol-type (acid) product; periodate cleaves the C–C bond instead.

q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is treated with excess NaIO<sub>4</sub>. What products form, per mole of glycerol?
h: Two C–C bonds have an OH on both ends. Cleave both, and count how many C–O bonds the middle carbon ends up with.
w: Both C1–C2 and C2–C3 are vicinal-diol bonds, so periodate cleaves both. Each terminal CH2OH becomes formaldehyde. The middle carbon loses both C–C bonds and keeps its H and OH, gaining one more bond to oxygen from each cleavage: it ends at the formic acid oxidation level. Products: 2 HCHO + 1 HCO2H (2 equiv NaIO4 consumed).
x: The middle carbon keeps a C–H bond, so it stops at formic acid; periodate does not oxidize it to CO<sub>2</sub>.
This stops after one cleavage. Both C–C bonds of glycerol are vicinal-diol bonds, so excess periodate cleaves the second one too.
No carbon is reduced in a periodate cleavage, so methanol cannot form; every carbon is oxidized or unchanged.

q: Which alkene gives only cyclohexanone and formaldehyde after 1. OsO4, NMO 2. NaIO4?
h: OsO<sub>4</sub> makes a 1,2-diol at the C=C; NaIO<sub>4</sub> then cuts where the double bond was. Reconnect the two carbonyl carbons with a C=C.
w: Dihydroxylation followed by periodate cleavage splits the C=C into two C=O groups, like ozonolysis. Joining cyclohexanone's carbonyl carbon to formaldehyde's carbon with a double bond gives methylenecyclohexane.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene has its C=C in the ring, so cleavage opens the ring to one product, 6-oxoheptanal.
Vinylcyclopentane gives cyclopentanecarbaldehyde and formaldehyde; the ring is five-membered and the ring carbon becomes an aldehyde, not a ketone.
Ethylidenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and acetaldehyde, not formaldehyde.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol is heated with H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Acid-catalyzed dehydration is E1 and gives the most stable alkene available.
w: Protonation and loss of water give a secondary carbocation (which can also shift a hydride to the tertiary C2 cation). Loss of a proton gives the most substituted, most stable alkene (Zaitsev): 1-methylcyclohexene.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexene is disubstituted and forms only as a minor product under thermodynamic E1 conditions.
The exocyclic alkene is disubstituted and less stable than the trisubstituted ring alkene.
4-Methylcyclohexene cannot form directly from either carbocation; the C=C must include C1 or C2.

q: What is the major alkene formed when 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: The first cation is secondary and sits next to a quaternary carbon. What can shift, and which alkene is most substituted after the shift?
w: Loss of water gives a 2° cation next to a C(CH3)3 group. A 1,2-methyl shift gives the more stable 3° cation, (CH3)2C+–CH(CH3)2. Loss of the H from the isopropyl CH gives the tetrasubstituted alkene: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.
x: 3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene would need loss of a proton before any shift; under E1 conditions the cation rearranges first. (That product comes from E2 methods such as POCl<sub>3</sub>/pyridine.)
2,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene comes from the rearranged cation but is only disubstituted; the tetrasubstituted isomer is favored.
Water capture of the rearranged cation gives this alcohol, but under hot concentrated acid the elimination product is favored.

q: What is the major product when 1-cyclobutylethan-1-ol is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: A cation next to a strained ring can shift a ring bond. What ring size results, and is there a further shift to a better cation?
w: Loss of water gives a secondary cation next to the cyclobutane. A ring C–C bond shifts to it, expanding the four-membered ring to a five-membered ring and relieving strain; the new cation is secondary, on the carbon next to the CH(CH3). A 1,2-hydride shift then gives the tertiary 1-methylcyclopentyl cation, and loss of H+ gives the trisubstituted alkene: 1-methylcyclopentene.
x: Ethylidenecyclobutane keeps the strained four-membered ring; ring expansion is faster than proton loss from the unrearranged cation.
Vinylcyclobutane is a monosubstituted alkene from the unrearranged cation; it is both less stable and kinetically bypassed by ring expansion.
3-Methylcyclopentene is disubstituted; the tertiary cation formed after the hydride shift gives the more substituted 1-methylcyclopentene.

q: What is the major product when 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol is treated with POCl<sub>3</sub> in pyridine?
h: POCl<sub>3</sub> makes the OH a leaving group and pyridine removes a β-H in one step. Is there a carbocation? Which β carbons carry hydrogens?
w: POCl3 converts the OH to a dichlorophosphate leaving group, and pyridine removes a β-H in a concerted E2 step, so no carbocation forms and no methyl shift occurs. The only β-hydrogens are on the CH3 at C1 (C3 is quaternary), so the product is 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.
x: The tetrasubstituted alkene requires a methyl shift through a carbocation, which the E2 pathway avoids.
This also needs the rearranged carbon skeleton, which forms only through a carbocation.
Pyridine is used to promote elimination; under these conditions the dichlorophosphate is eliminated rather than displaced by chloride.

q: Hexan-1-ol was treated with reagent X. The product shows the IR spectrum below and gives no broad band at 2500–3600 cm<sup>−1</sup>. What is X?
h: Read the spectrum: what do the two weak bands near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> indicate?
w: The strong C=O at 1728 cm−1 with the pair of weak aldehyde C–H stretches (about 2820 and 2720 cm−1), and no O–H band, identify an aldehyde, hexanal. An anhydrous oxidant that stops at the aldehyde was used: PCC.
x: Aqueous chromic acid gives hexanoic acid, which shows a very broad O–H band from about 2500 to 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not react with an alcohol; the spectrum would still show the broad O–H stretch near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Hot permanganate also oxidizes to the carboxylic acid, which shows the broad acid O–H band.

q: What is the major organic product of this sequence?
h: Make the alcohol first. In the E1 step, which alkene is most stable: think about conjugation and about E vs Z.
w: Ethyl adds to benzaldehyde to give 1-phenylpropan-1-ol. Hot acid ionizes it to a benzylic cation, and loss of a proton from the adjacent CH2 gives an alkene conjugated with the ring. The E isomer avoids the steric clash between phenyl and methyl and is favored under these equilibrating conditions: (E)-prop-1-en-1-ylbenzene.
x: The Z isomer puts the phenyl and methyl on the same side; under thermodynamic E1 conditions the less hindered E isomer dominates.
Allylbenzene is not conjugated with the ring and would need loss of a proton from a carbon not adjacent to the cation.
This is the alcohol after step 2; hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dehydrates a benzylic alcohol readily.

q: An ether solution of benzoic acid, 4-methylphenol and cyclohexanol is extracted first with aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, then with aqueous NaOH. Where does each compound end up?
c: NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid; NaOH layer: 4-methylphenol; ether: cyclohexanol
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid and 4-methylphenol; NaOH layer: cyclohexanol; ether: nothing
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid; NaOH layer: 4-methylphenol and cyclohexanol; ether: nothing
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: nothing; NaOH layer: benzoic acid and 4-methylphenol; ether: cyclohexanol
h: A compound moves into water only if the base deprotonates it. Compare each pK<sub>a</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (6.4) and H<sub>2</sub>O (15.7).
w: Bicarbonate (conjugate acid H2CO3, pKa 6.4) deprotonates only acids with pKa below about 6, so only benzoic acid moves into that layer as sodium benzoate. Hydroxide (H2O, 15.7) then deprotonates the phenol (10.3) but not cyclohexanol (≈ 18), which stays in the ether. Answer: benzoic acid / 4-methylphenol / cyclohexanol.
x: 4-Methylphenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.3) is far less acidic than H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, so bicarbonate barely deprotonates it.
Cyclohexanol is less acidic than water, so hydroxide leaves it mostly protonated and it stays in the ether.
Bicarbonate is basic enough to deprotonate a carboxylic acid (K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>2</sup>), so benzoic acid is removed in the first extraction.

q: Diol A (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) reacts with NaIO<sub>4</sub> to give a single product, heptane-2,6-dione. Which structure is A?
h: Work backward: join the two carbonyl carbons of the product with a C–C bond and put an OH on each. Is the result a ring?
w: Periodate cleavage turns each carbon of a 1,2-diol into a C=O. Reconnecting C2 and C6 of heptane-2,6-dione gives a five-membered ring with a methyl and an OH on each of the two joined carbons: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane-1,2-diol (C7H14O2). The cis isomer forms the cyclic periodate ester easily.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexane-1,2-diol is cleaved too, but its secondary carbinol carbon becomes an aldehyde: the product is 6-oxoheptanal.
This is a 1,3-diol; periodate cleaves only vicinal (1,2) diols, so it does not react.
Cycloheptane-1,2-diol has only secondary OH carbons, so cleavage gives the dialdehyde heptanedial.

q: Alcohol X (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O) is oxidized by PCC to a ketone. When X is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the major alkene is 2-methylbut-2-ene. What is X?
h: Use each clue to eliminate choices: the PCC result tells you the alcohol class; the alkene skeleton (possibly after a shift) tells you the branching.
w: A ketone from PCC means X is secondary, which rules out the 1° and 3° choices. Of the secondary alcohols, pentan-2-ol has an unbranched chain and gives pent-2-ene. 3-Methylbutan-2-ol ionizes to a 2° cation that undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the 3° cation, and Zaitsev loss of H+ gives 2-methylbut-2-ene. X is 3-methylbutan-2-ol.
x: Pentan-2-ol is secondary but has no branch, so dehydration gives pent-2-ene, not 2-methylbut-2-ene.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol does give 2-methylbut-2-ene, but as a tertiary alcohol it is not oxidized by PCC.
3-Methylbutan-1-ol is primary; PCC gives the aldehyde 3-methylbutanal, not a ketone.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the ether shown?
h: Name an ether as an alkoxy substituent on the larger alkyl group, then find the longest chain of that group.
w: The larger alkyl group (four carbons) is the parent alkane and the smaller group becomes the alkoxy substituent: CH3CH2O– is ethoxy. The four-carbon chain is numbered so the ethoxy carbon gets the lowest number, C2. The name is 2-ethoxybutane (common name: sec-butyl ethyl ether).
x: 1-Ethoxybutane has the oxygen on the end carbon of an unbranched butyl group; here the O is on C2 of the four-carbon chain.
The parent should be the larger alkyl group (butane), with the smaller ethyl group named as ethoxy.
Calling the chain "propane" with a methyl branch misses the longest chain; the C1 methyl plus three more carbons make a butane chain.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Count the ring atoms (including O) and remember that the ring oxygen is position 1.
w: A three-membered ring with one oxygen is an oxirane (epoxide). Numbering starts at the oxygen (O1), so the substituted carbon is C2: 2-methyloxirane (also called propylene oxide or 1,2-epoxypropane).
x: Oxetane is the four-membered cyclic ether; this ring has only two carbons and one oxygen.
The ring oxygen is O1 and numbering goes the short way to the substituent, so the methyl carbon is C2, not C3.
The molecule has three carbons in all, so as an epoxy-alkane it is 1,2-epoxypropane, not epoxybutane.

q: Which pair of reagents gives the best yield of the ether shown by a Williamson synthesis?
h: The Williamson synthesis is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction. Which carbon can be attacked from the back side?
w: A Williamson ether synthesis is SN2: the alkoxide attacks an alkyl halide with a good leaving group. Put the hindered group on the alkoxide and the unhindered group on the halide. tert-Butoxide + bromoethane works because the primary C–Br carbon is open to back-side attack.
x: A tertiary halide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; ethoxide acts as a base and the main product is 2-methylpropene by E2.
An alcohol has no leaving group (OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group), so ethoxide only does an acid–base exchange with it.
Ethanol has no leaving group, so tert-butoxide simply deprotonates it (an acid–base equilibrium), not a substitution.

q: What is the major organic product of this reaction?
h: Can a strong base reach the back side of a tertiary carbon? If not, what else can it do?
w: Ethoxide is a strong base and a good nucleophile, but a tertiary carbon is too hindered for SN2. With a strong base and a 3° halide, E2 wins: ethoxide removes a β-H and bromide leaves, giving 2-methylpropene. This is why a Williamson synthesis must use a methyl or primary halide.
x: This ether would need S<sub>N</sub>2 at a tertiary carbon, which is blocked; it is made instead from tert-butoxide and a primary ethyl halide.
There is no water or hydroxide as a nucleophile, and the strong base favors E2 over the slow S<sub>N</sub>1 path.
Forming this ether would need tert-butoxide and a tertiary electrophile; neither is present, and such a hindered ether is not made by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: Which reagents give the best preparation of the aryl ether shown?
h: One of the two carbons on oxygen is sp<sup>2</sup>. Can that carbon be the S<sub>N</sub>2 electrophile?
w: The Williamson synthesis needs back-side attack on an sp3 carbon. The aryl carbon cannot be the electrophile, so the aryl group must be on the nucleophile: phenoxide (easily made because phenol has pKa ≈ 10) attacks iodoethane by SN2. Sodium phenoxide + iodoethane is the best choice.
x: Aryl halides do not do S<sub>N</sub>2: the ring blocks back-side attack and the C(sp<sup>2</sup>)–Br bond is strong. No ether forms with an unactivated bromobenzene.
Ethoxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) just deprotonates phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10) to give phenoxide and ethanol; no C–O bond forms.
Ethanol has no leaving group, so phenoxide cannot displace anything from it.

q: What is the main product when this bromo alcohol is treated with NaH in THF?
h: NaH makes the alkoxide. Count the atoms that will end up in the ring, including O.
w: NaH deprotonates the OH. The alkoxide then attacks the primary C–Br carbon in the same molecule (intramolecular Williamson, SN2). The new ring holds O plus C1–C5: a six-membered ring, oxane (tetrahydropyran). Five- and six-membered rings form quickly because the chain ends meet easily and there is little ring strain.
x: Oxolane has only four carbons; the ring here includes all five chain carbons plus the oxygen.
Oxepane is a seven-membered ring (six carbons); the chain has only five carbons.
E2 on a primary bromide with an alkoxide is minor; the fast intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2 that forms a six-membered ring wins.

q: (S)-4-Bromopentan-1-ol is treated with NaH in THF. What is the main product?
h: The ring closes by S<sub>N</sub>2 at the carbon bearing Br. What does S<sub>N</sub>2 do to that stereocenter?
w: NaH forms the alkoxide, which attacks C4 from the back side (intramolecular SN2), making a five-membered ring (O + 4 C). Back-side attack inverts C4. The oxygen takes the place of Br as the top-priority group, so the descriptor changes from S to (R)-2-methyloxolane (confirmed with CIP ranking: O > ring CH2 > CH3 > H).
x: Retention would need front-side attack; S<sub>N</sub>2 ring closure inverts the carbon that loses bromide.
Racemization needs a carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1). A secondary bromide with a strong internal nucleophile reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 with clean inversion.
E2 can compete at a secondary bromide, but 5-membered ring closure is intramolecular and fast, so the cyclic ether is the main product.

q: What is the major product of this alkoxymercuration–demercuration?
h: Methanol adds to the alkene carbon that can best carry positive charge in the mercurinium ion.
w: Alkoxymercuration adds RO and H across C=C with Markovnikov regiochemistry and no rearrangement. Methanol opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon (the one with more partial positive charge), and NaBH4 replaces Hg with H. The product is 1-methoxy-1-methylcyclohexane.
x: This is the anti-Markovnikov ether; methanol adds to the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, not the secondary one.
The solvent is methanol, not water, so the nucleophile that adds is CH<sub>3</sub>OH and an ether forms, not an alcohol.
Mercurinium ions do not rearrange, so the methoxy group cannot move to C3.

q: What is the major product?
h: Does a bridged mercurinium ion allow a methyl shift the way a free carbocation would?
w: Ethanol opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon (C2), and NaBH4 replaces Hg by H. Because the mercurinium ion is bridged, there is no free carbocation and no methyl shift. The product is 2-ethoxy-3,3-dimethylbutane. (Acid-catalyzed addition of ethanol would instead give the rearranged 2-ethoxy-2,3-dimethylbutane.)
x: This rearranged ether forms only through a free 2° carbocation and a 1,2-methyl shift, which the bridged mercurinium ion avoids.
This is anti-Markovnikov addition; the alcohol attacks the more substituted carbon of the mercurinium ion.
An alcohol would form with water as solvent (oxymercuration); in ethanol the nucleophile is ethanol, giving an ether.

q: Methoxybenzene (anisole) is heated with excess HI. What are the products?
h: After protonation, iodide must do an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack. Which carbon on oxygen can it attack?
w: HI protonates the ether oxygen. Iodide then attacks by SN2, and it can only attack the sp3 methyl carbon; aryl carbons do not undergo SN2 or SN1. So the aryl C–O bond stays and the products are phenol + iodomethane. Phenol is not converted further, because its C–O bond cannot be broken this way.
x: Cleaving the aryl C–O bond would need S<sub>N</sub>2 or S<sub>N</sub>1 at an sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon, which does not happen.
Phenol cannot be converted to iodobenzene by HI; only the alkyl side of the ether is cleaved.
With excess HI the methyl group leaves as iodomethane (I<sup>−</sup> attacks the methyl carbon directly), not as methanol.

q: Tetrahydrofuran (oxolane) is heated with excess concentrated HBr. What is the final organic product?
h: The first cleavage opens the ring. What happens to the new OH group with more HBr?
w: Protonation of O and SN2 attack by Br− at a primary carbon opens the ring to 4-bromobutan-1-ol. With excess HBr and heat, that primary alcohol is protonated and displaced by a second bromide. The final product is 1,4-dibromobutane.
x: 4-Bromobutan-1-ol is the intermediate after one equivalent; excess HBr converts its OH to Br as well.
HBr does not reduce C–O to C–H; one carbon end would have to lose its oxygen without gaining bromine.
Water is not the nucleophile here; bromide attacks the protonated ether, and diols are converted to dibromides by excess HBr.

q: tert-Butyl methyl ether is treated with one equivalent of HI. Which products form?
h: After protonation, one C–O bond can break without any nucleophile. Which one gives the more stable cation?
w: Protonation makes a good leaving group. The tertiary C–O bond ionizes (SN1) to the stable tert-butyl cation and methanol leaves; iodide then traps the cation. Products: 2-iodo-2-methylpropane + methanol. The methyl C–O bond would need an SN2 attack, which is slower than ionization here.
x: This would be S<sub>N</sub>2 at the methyl group. For ethers with a tertiary group, S<sub>N</sub>1 cleavage at the 3° carbon is faster.
Converting both groups to iodides needs a second equivalent of HI; with one equivalent the methanol remains.
The methyl group leaves as methanol, not iodomethane; and E1 (2-methylpropene) would pair with methanol, not iodomethane.

q: The diether shown is heated with excess HBr. Which set of products forms?
h: Treat each C–O bond separately: which ones have an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon that bromide can attack?
w: Each protonated ether is cleaved by SN2 attack of Br− on an sp3 carbon. The Ar–O bond cannot break, so the aryl side gives phenol. The CH3–O and both CH2–O bonds can be attacked; with excess HBr every alkyl alcohol formed is also converted to its bromide, giving 1,3-dibromopropane and bromomethane.
x: Bromobenzene cannot form: the aryl C–O bond is not cleaved because aryl carbons do not do S<sub>N</sub>1 or S<sub>N</sub>2.
HBr cleavage makes alkyl bromides, not alcohols, once excess acid and heat convert the alkyl OH groups.
The aryl C–O bond stays intact, and with excess HBr the 3-bromopropanol OH is also replaced by Br.

q: The crown ether shown (18-crown-6) binds which cation most strongly?
h: Match the size of the cavity to the size of the ion.
w: Crown ethers bind cations whose diameter fits the ring cavity, with all oxygen lone pairs pointing inward. The 18-membered ring with six oxygens fits K+ best. (15-crown-5 fits Na+, 12-crown-4 fits Li+.)
x: Li<sup>+</sup> is too small for the 18-crown-6 cavity; 12-crown-4 is the better size match.
Na<sup>+</sup> is somewhat small for 18-crown-6; 15-crown-5 fits it better.
Mg<sup>2+</sup> is small and very strongly hydrated, and it does not fit the 18-crown-6 cavity well.

q: KF barely reacts with 1-bromooctane in acetonitrile, but adding a little 18-crown-6 gives 1-fluorooctane quickly. What is the best explanation?
c: The crown ether binds K<sup>+</sup>, bringing KF into solution with a poorly solvated, very reactive F<sup>−</sup>
The crown ether binds F<sup>−</sup> through its oxygens and delivers it directly to the carbon
The crown ether hydrogen-bonds to F<sup>−</sup>, making it a stronger base and nucleophile
The crown ether coordinates the Br, making bromide a better leaving group
h: The oxygen lone pairs of a crown ether point into its cavity. Which ion do they attract?
w: The ring oxygens are Lewis bases that wrap around K+. The large organic-coated complex dissolves in the organic solvent and drags F− with it. That fluoride has no tight cation partner and no hydrogen-bonding shell ("naked" fluoride), so it is a much stronger nucleophile and SN2 is fast. The crown ether binds K+.
x: Oxygen lone pairs attract cations, not anions; the crown ether does not bind fluoride.
A crown ether has no O–H groups, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to fluoride; hydrogen bonding would also make F<sup>−</sup> less reactive.
The crown ether does not interact with the alkyl bromide; its role is to bind the potassium ion.

q: (Z)-Hex-3-ene is treated with mCPBA. Which describes the product?
h: Epoxidation is concerted: both C–O bonds form on the same face at the same time.
w: Peroxyacid epoxidation is a concerted syn addition, so the alkene geometry is kept: a Z alkene gives a cis-epoxide. cis-2,3-Diethyloxirane has two stereocenters (R,S) and a mirror plane, so it is a single meso compound; attack on either face gives the same molecule.
x: trans-Epoxides come from E alkenes; the concerted reaction cannot rotate the C–C bond.
A mixture of cis and trans would need a stepwise path with a rotating intermediate; mCPBA epoxidation is stereospecific.
The cis-epoxide here has identical groups on both carbons and a mirror plane, so it is meso; there is no enantiomer pair.

q: (E)-But-2-ene is treated with Br2 in water, and the product is then treated with NaOH. What is the final product?
h: Follow the stereochemistry of two anti steps: anti halohydrin formation, then back-side ring closure.
w: Step 1 adds Br and OH anti (bromonium ion opened by water), giving the bromohydrin. In step 2 the alkoxide attacks the C–Br carbon from the back side (intramolecular SN2), which needs O− and Br anti. Anti addition followed by an anti (back-side) ring closure puts the oxygen on the same face overall, exactly as mCPBA would. The E alkene therefore gives racemic trans-2,3-dimethyloxirane.
x: A cis-epoxide comes from (Z)-but-2-ene; this two-step route keeps the alkene geometry just like mCPBA.
Hydroxide closes the halohydrin to an epoxide; opening it to the diol would need acid or much harsher conditions.
NaOH deprotonates the bromohydrin OH, and the alkoxide quickly displaces the anti bromide to close the epoxide.

q: What is the major product when 2,2-dimethyloxirane reacts with methanol containing a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: In the protonated epoxide, which C–O bond is longer and carries more positive charge?
w: Acid protonates the epoxide oxygen. The C–O bond to the tertiary carbon is weakened most, and that carbon carries most of the positive charge (SN1-like transition state), so methanol attacks the more substituted carbon. Product: 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol.
x: This is the base-catalyzed regiochemistry (attack at the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub>), which applies with CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>, not with acid.
Methanol, not water, is the solvent and nucleophile, so a methyl ether forms rather than the diol.
Only one equivalent of methanol adds; the new primary alcohol is not converted to a methyl ether under these mild conditions.

q: 2,2-Dimethyloxirane is treated with sodium ethanethiolate (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SNa) in ethanol, followed by water. What is the major product?
h: A strong, unprotonated nucleophile opens an epoxide by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon is easier to reach?
w: Thiolate is a strong nucleophile, so the epoxide opens by SN2 without acid. SN2 attack occurs at the less hindered CH2 carbon, and the alkoxide is then protonated. Product: 1-(ethylsulfanyl)-2-methylpropan-2-ol.
x: Attack at the tertiary carbon is the acid-catalyzed regiochemistry; under basic S<sub>N</sub>2 conditions the hindered carbon is avoided.
Water is added only to protonate the alkoxide after the ring has opened; the thiolate is the nucleophile.
Ethanol is a much weaker nucleophile than ethanethiolate, which is large, polarizable and anionic.

q: The racemic epoxide shown (one enantiomer drawn) is treated with CH<sub>3</sub>OH and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which structure is the major product (formed as a racemate; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: Decide two things: which carbon methanol attacks under acid, and from which face relative to the epoxide oxygen.
w: Under acid the nucleophile attacks the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, which carries more positive charge in the protonated epoxide. The attack is still back-side, so OCH3 ends up trans to the OH (anti opening; on the ring the product first forms with OCH3 and OH trans-diaxial). Product: trans-2-methoxy-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: B has OCH<sub>3</sub> and OH cis; epoxide opening is back-side (anti), so the two groups must be trans.
C has methanol attacking the secondary carbon, the regiochemistry seen with methoxide (base), not with acid.
Methanol, not water, is the nucleophile, so a methyl ether forms rather than a diol.

q: (R)-2-Ethyl-2-methyloxirane is treated with CH3OH and a catalytic amount of H2SO4. What is the major product?
h: Acid sets the regiochemistry (which carbon); the back-side attack sets the configuration at that carbon.
w: Under acid, methanol attacks the tertiary carbon of the protonated epoxide. The attack is back-side, opposite the leaving oxygen (the ring is still bonded, so no free carbocation forms), so that stereocenter is inverted. Ranking the product carbon: OCH3 > CH2OH > CH2CH3 > CH3; with inversion this gives (S)-2-methoxy-2-methylbutan-1-ol (checked with CIP software).
x: Retention of configuration would need front-side attack; acid-catalyzed epoxide opening is back-side even at a tertiary carbon.
This is the product of attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, the regiochemistry for basic conditions (e.g. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>).
The ring oxygen is still bonded when methanol attacks, so there is no free planar carbocation and no racemization.

q: Cyclohexene oxide reacts with HBr to give 2-bromocyclohexan-1-ol. Which describes the product in the chair conformation in which it is first formed?
h: Bromide attacks anti to the C–O bond. In a half-chair, which direction is anti to the epoxide oxygen?
w: Bromide attacks the protonated epoxide from the side opposite the oxygen (anti opening). In the cyclohexane ring that path keeps the nucleophile and the leaving oxygen on a common axis, so the new C–Br bond and the C–OH bond are both axial on opposite faces: the product forms trans-diaxial. It then ring-flips to the more stable diequatorial chair, but it stays trans.
x: The diequatorial chair is the more stable conformer reached after a ring flip; it is not the chair formed directly by anti opening.
Anti (back-side) opening always puts Br and OH on opposite faces, so the product is trans, not cis.
A cis product would need syn delivery of Br; epoxide opening is anti, giving the trans isomer.

q: Cyclohexene oxide is treated with (1) NaN<sub>3</sub> in aqueous ethanol, then (2) LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, then (3) H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the product (racemic; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: Azide is a strong nucleophile. Track the stereochemistry of the ring opening, then ask what LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does to an azide.
w: Azide opens the epoxide by SN2 from the face opposite the oxygen, giving trans-2-azidocyclohexan-1-ol. LiAlH4 reduces the azide (–N3) to a primary amine (–NH2) without touching the stereocenters. Product: trans-2-aminocyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This is the cis isomer; S<sub>N</sub>2 opening of the epoxide is anti, so N and O end up trans.
This is the intermediate after step 1; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the azide to an amine.
Azide is far more nucleophilic than water, so the epoxide is opened by N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, not hydrolyzed to the diol.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Hydride from LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a strong nucleophile. Where does a strong nucleophile open an epoxide?
w: Hydride (from AlH4−) opens the epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered secondary carbon. The oxygen stays on the tertiary carbon, and acid workup protonates it: 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This would need hydride to attack the tertiary carbon, which is too hindered for S<sub>N</sub>2.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> adds one H; it does not add a second oxygen, so no diol forms.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> opens the ring to an alcohol; it does not remove the oxygen to regenerate the alkene.

q: What is the product after phenylmagnesium bromide reacts with oxirane (ethylene oxide) and the mixture is worked up with aqueous acid?
h: The Grignard carbon bonds to a ring carbon; the oxygen ends up two carbons away.
w: The aryl carbanion attacks one CH2 of oxirane by SN2, opening the strained ring. Workup protonates the alkoxide. The phenyl group gains a two-carbon chain ending in OH: 2-phenylethan-1-ol. Grignard + oxirane adds two carbons, with the OH on the second carbon.
x: 1-Phenylethanol would form from PhMgBr + acetaldehyde (or CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + benzaldehyde), not from oxirane.
Benzyl alcohol has only one carbon between ring and OH; it is the product with formaldehyde, which adds one carbon.
Oxirane adds two carbons, not three; three carbons would need oxetane.

q: Which reagents give the alcohol shown as the major product?
h: For each pair, put the Grignard carbon on the less hindered epoxide carbon and draw what results.
w: Grignard reagents open epoxides at the less hindered carbon. Phenyl attacks the CH2 of 2-methyloxirane, and the O stays on the CH(CH3) carbon: C6H5–CH2–CH(OH)–CH3, 1-phenylpropan-2-ol. The answer is C6H5MgBr + 2-methyloxirane.
x: Attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-phenyloxirane gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (OH next to the ring), and attack at the benzylic carbon gives 2-phenylpropan-1-ol; neither is the target.
Benzyl + oxirane gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, a primary alcohol (3-phenylpropan-1-ol).
Methyl adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-benzyloxirane, giving C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, which has one carbon too many (1-phenylbutan-2-ol).

q: (R)-2-Methyloxirane is treated with CH3MgBr, followed by aqueous acid. What is the product?
h: Find which carbon is attacked. Are any bonds to the stereocenter broken?
w: The Grignard attacks the less hindered CH2 carbon, so no bond to the stereocenter is broken and its spatial arrangement is kept. CIP check at that carbon: before, O > CH2(ring, bonded to O) > CH3 > H; after, OH > CH2CH3 > CH3 > H. The priority order maps onto the same positions, so the label stays (R)-butan-2-ol.
x: Inversion happens only at the carbon that is attacked; here the attacked carbon (CH<sub>2</sub>) is not the stereocenter.
Racemization would need the stereocenter to become planar; no bond to it breaks in this S<sub>N</sub>2 opening.
This product would come from attack at the more hindered CH carbon, which Grignard reagents avoid.

q: (2R,3R)-2,3-Dimethyloxirane is treated with NaOCH3 in CH3OH. Which stereoisomer of 3-methoxybutan-2-ol forms?
h: The two epoxide carbons are equivalent here. One carbon is inverted and the other is untouched; then assign R/S.
w: The (R,R) epoxide has C2 symmetry, so attack at either carbon gives the same product. Methoxide attacks one carbon by SN2 and inverts it: that carbon (C3, now bearing OCH3) goes from R to S. The other carbon (C2, keeps the oxygen as OH) is untouched and stays R. Product: (2R,3S)-3-methoxybutan-2-ol as a single enantiomer (assignments checked with CIP software).
x: This is the enantiomer; it would come from the (S,S) epoxide.
Both centers R would mean retention at the attacked carbon; SN2 opening inverts it.
Inverting both centers would need both C–O bonds to break; only one carbon is attacked.

q: With NaOH, trans-2-chlorocyclohexan-1-ol rapidly forms cyclohexene oxide, but the cis isomer does not form an epoxide. What is the best explanation?
c: Ring closure is an internal SN2 that needs O− anti to Cl (both axial); only the trans isomer can do this
The cis isomer would have to give a trans-fused epoxide, which is too strained to form
The cis alcohol is much less acidic, so NaOH cannot form enough of its alkoxide
The trans isomer reacts by E2, which needs an anti-periplanar H that the cis isomer lacks
h: Epoxide closure from a halohydrin is a back-side displacement. Where must the nucleophile sit relative to the leaving group?
w: The alkoxide closes the ring by intramolecular SN2, so it must approach the C–Cl carbon from the back side, anti to Cl. In the trans isomer a ring flip puts OH and Cl trans-diaxial, perfectly anti. In the cis isomer O and Cl are on the same face, so back-side attack is impossible. Only the trans isomer can place O− anti to Cl.
x: Both isomers would give the same cis-fused cyclohexene oxide if they could close; the problem is the approach geometry, not product strain.
Cis and trans chlorohydrins have very similar acidities; both are deprotonated by NaOH.
Epoxide formation is a substitution by oxygen, not an elimination of H and Cl.

q:
Rank these compounds from least acidic to most acidic.
I. CH3CH2OH II. CH3CH2SH III. CF3CH2OH
h: Compare the atom carrying the negative charge first, then the inductive effect.
w: Ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is least acidic. Three fluorines pull electron density away inductively and stabilize CF3CH2O− (pKa ≈ 12.4). Ethanethiol is most acidic (pKa ≈ 10.6) because the charge sits on the larger, more polarizable sulfur atom, and the weaker S–H bond breaks more easily; going down a group outweighs the inductive effect here. Order: I < III < II.
x: Inductive stabilization by CF<sub>3</sub> lowers the pK<sub>a</sub> to about 12, but putting the charge on sulfur lowers it more, to about 10.6.
Fluorination makes the alcohol more acidic than ethanol, not less.
The thiol is the most acidic of the three, not the least: sulfur, being larger, holds the negative charge better than oxygen.

q: 2-Sulfanylethan-1-ol (HSCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is treated with one equivalent of NaOH in water, then one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I. What is the major product?
h: Which proton does one equivalent of hydroxide remove? Which anion is the better nucleophile anyway?
w: The thiol (pKa ≈ 10) is far more acidic than the alcohol (pKa ≈ 16), so one equivalent of NaOH forms the thiolate. Thiolate is also a much better nucleophile than an alcohol or alkoxide in water, because sulfur is large and polarizable. It attacks CH3I by SN2, giving 2-(methylsulfanyl)ethan-1-ol.
x: O-Methylation would need the alkoxide, but NaOH deprotonates the much more acidic SH, and S<sup>−</sup> is the better nucleophile.
Only one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I is used, and the neutral OH does not react with CH<sub>3</sub>I in water.
A sulfonium salt needs a second equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I to alkylate the sulfide; only one is available.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with sodium methanethiolate (CH3SNa) in DMF. What is the major product?
h: Thiolates are excellent nucleophiles but weak bases. Which pathway does that favor at a secondary carbon?
w: CH3S− is a weak base (CH3SH pKa ≈ 10) but a very strong, polarizable nucleophile, and DMF is polar aprotic. So even at a secondary carbon SN2 beats E2. Back-side attack inverts the stereocenter; S replaces Br as top priority, so the product is (S)-2-(methylsulfanyl)butane.
x: Retention would require front-side attack; SN2 gives inversion, and the S group takes Br's priority rank, so the label changes to S.
E2 to (E)-but-2-ene needs a strong base such as ethoxide; methanethiolate is too weak a base to compete with its own SN2.
Hofmann-type alkene formation needs a bulky strong base; thiolate gives substitution.

q: What is the product when ethanethiol is treated with I<sub>2</sub> (a mild oxidant) in the presence of a weak base?
h: Mild oxidation of thiols forms an S–S bond.
w: Two thiol molecules are oxidized by I2, each losing an H, and their sulfur atoms join: 2 RSH → RS–SR + 2 HI. The product is diethyl disulfide. This is the same S–S bond that links cysteine residues in proteins.
x: A sulfide (thioether) has one sulfur bonded to two carbons; forming it would need an alkylation, not an oxidation.
Sulfonic acids need strong oxidants such as HNO<sub>3</sub> or KMnO<sub>4</sub>; I<sub>2</sub> stops at the disulfide.
Iodine does not replace the SH group; the thiol is oxidized at sulfur, not substituted at carbon.

q: The disulfide bond in cystine is cleaved by excess 2-mercaptoethanol (or by Zn/HCl) to give two cysteine molecules. Which statement about the sulfur atoms is correct?
c: Their oxidation state does not change; the S–S bond is hydrolyzed
h: Count each sulfur's bonds: S–S counts as zero; S is slightly more electronegative than C and more than H.
w: In the disulfide each S has one bond to C (S is assigned that electron pair: −1) and one bond to S (0), so each S is −1. In the thiol each S has a bond to C (−1) and a bond to H (−1), so S is −2. Going from disulfide to thiols, each sulfur gains a bond to H: reduction from −1 to −2. The reverse (thiols → disulfide) is an oxidation.
x: That is the reverse reaction, thiol to disulfide; breaking the S–S bond and adding H is a reduction.
The disulfide sulfur is −1, not 0, because each sulfur is also bonded to a carbon.
Each S gains an S–H bond in place of an S–S bond, so the oxidation state changes; water does not cleave disulfides.

q: Methyl phenyl sulfide is treated with excess H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid with heating. What is the final product?
h: Each oxidation adds one oxygen to sulfur. How many times can a sulfide sulfur be oxidized without breaking C–S bonds?
w: Sulfides are oxidized at sulfur in two steps: sulfide → sulfoxide (one O) → sulfone (two O). One equivalent of a mild oxidant (NaIO4, or 1 equiv H2O2 at low temperature) stops at the sulfoxide; excess oxidant with heat continues to the sulfone, methyl phenyl sulfone. The C–S bonds are kept.
x: The sulfoxide is the intermediate; with excess H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and heat it is oxidized again to the sulfone.
A sulfonic acid would require breaking the S–CH<sub>3</sub> bond; peroxide oxidation adds O to S and leaves both C–S bonds.
Oxidation adds oxygen to sulfur; it does not replace sulfur by oxygen.

q: Which compound is chiral and can be isolated as a single enantiomer at room temperature?
h: A sulfoxide sulfur is pyramidal with a lone pair as its fourth "group". Look for four different groups.
w: The sulfoxide sulfur is tetrahedral: O, two carbon groups and a lone pair. Its pyramidal inversion is slow at room temperature (barrier about 160 kJ/mol), so a sulfoxide with two different carbon groups is a stable stereocenter. Methyl phenyl sulfoxide has O, CH3, C6H5 and a lone pair, so it is chiral and resolvable.
x: A sulfone has two identical oxygens on sulfur, so the sulfur is not a stereocenter.
Diphenyl sulfoxide has two identical phenyl groups, so it has a mirror plane and is achiral.
DMSO has two identical methyl groups, so it is achiral.

q: Which compound reacts with CH<sub>3</sub>I at room temperature to give a stable, isolable salt?
h: Compare how nucleophilic, and how basic, sulfur and oxygen lone pairs are.
w: Divalent sulfur is large and polarizable, so sulfides are good nucleophiles even though they are weak bases. Dimethyl sulfide attacks CH3I by SN2 to give trimethylsulfonium iodide, (CH3)3S+ I−, a stable salt. Ethers are poor nucleophiles, and trialkyloxonium ions are too reactive to form this way. The answer is dimethyl sulfide.
x: Dimethyl ether's oxygen is a poor nucleophile; a trimethyloxonium salt does not form from CH<sub>3</sub>I.
Diethyl ether is a common solvent for reactions of alkyl halides precisely because it does not react with them.
THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metals (as in Grignard reagents), but THF is not nucleophilic enough to be alkylated by CH<sub>3</sub>I.

q: Which sequence converts (R)-butan-2-ol into (R)-2-methoxybutane?
h: Decide which C–O bond must stay intact to keep the configuration.
w: To keep the configuration, the C–O bond at the stereocenter must not break. NaH forms the alkoxide (the stereocenter is untouched), and the alkoxide attacks CH3I by SN2 at the methyl carbon. The new bond is O–CH3, so the stereocenter keeps its arrangement: 1. NaH 2. CH3I gives (R)-2-methoxybutane (CIP label confirmed).
x: Tosylation keeps the configuration, but methoxide then displaces OTs by SN2 at the stereocenter, giving (S)-2-methoxybutane (plus some E2 alkene).
Acid with a secondary alcohol gives elimination and S<sub>N</sub>1 mixtures that lose the stereochemistry; it is not a clean route to one enantiomer of the ether.
A neutral alcohol reacts very slowly with CH<sub>3</sub>I; the alkoxide must be formed first, so the order of steps matters.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexene into the product shown (racemic; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: The target has two oxygens on adjacent carbons, trans. Which route adds two oxygens anti?
w: Epoxidation adds one oxygen across the double bond. Ethoxide then opens the epoxide by back-side SN2, placing OCH2CH3 trans to the alkoxide, which ethanol protonates. The sequence 1. mCPBA 2. NaOCH2CH3, CH3CH2OH gives trans-2-ethoxycyclohexan-1-ol.
x: OsO4 adds both OH groups syn, so this route gives the cis ether-alcohol (and mixtures from the diol).
Alkoxymercuration adds only one oxygen (ethoxycyclohexane); the product needs an OH on the next carbon.
Hydroboration–oxidation adds only one OH, so this sequence gives ethoxycyclohexane with no second oxygen.

q: Epoxides are opened by hydroxide or alkoxides under mild conditions, while diethyl ether is inert to them. What is the main reason?
c: The three-membered ring is strained, and opening it releases about 110 kJ/mol of strain
