Epoxide carbons are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized, like a carbonyl carbon, so they are very electrophilic
The epoxide oxygen carries a formal positive charge, like a protonated ether
Epoxides are aromatic, and opening the ring relieves antiaromatic strain
h: Compare the C–O–C bond angle in an epoxide with the normal tetrahedral angle.
w: In an epoxide the ring bond angles are about 60°, far from 109.5°, so the ring holds roughly 110 kJ/mol of angle and torsional strain. Opening the ring releases that strain, which makes the alkoxide leaving group acceptable. An acyclic ether has no such driving force. Answer: ring strain.
x: Epoxide carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>; they have no π bond.
A neutral epoxide oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs, so its formal charge is zero.
An epoxide has no π electrons and cannot be aromatic or antiaromatic.

q: Hydroxide ion reacts with bromoethane by an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this single step?
h: Curved arrows always start where the electrons are (a lone pair or a bond) and end where they go. In one step, a bond forms and a bond breaks.
w: An SN2 step needs two arrows. One starts at a lone pair on the hydroxide oxygen and ends at the carbon bearing Br (the new C–O bond). The second starts at the C–Br bond and ends on Br, which leaves as Br−. So the correct drawing is an arrow from an O lone pair to the CH2 carbon plus an arrow from the C–Br bond onto bromine. Both events happen at once, with the nucleophile entering opposite the leaving group.
x: This arrow starts at the carbon and points to oxygen, which says the carbon gives electrons to hydroxide. The electron-poor carbon is the electrophile; the arrow must start at oxygen's lone pair.
With only the attack arrow, the carbon gains a C–O bond while keeping the C–Br bond, so it would have five bonds. The C–Br bond pair must move onto Br in the same step.
Hydroxide attacks bromine here instead of carbon, and the C–Br electrons are sent to carbon (a carbanion). Nucleophiles attack the δ+ carbon, and the leaving group takes the bond pair.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane undergoes S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis. Which drawing shows the curved arrow for the first (ionization) step?
h: Heterolysis: both bonding electrons leave with the more electronegative atom. Which arrow head (full or fishhook) moves a pair?
w: In the ionization step the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically: the bonding pair goes with bromine, giving Br− and the tertiary carbocation. The arrow is a full (two-electron) arrow from the C–Br bond to Br.
x: An arrow from a Br lone pair to carbon would form a second C–Br bond (a five-bond carbon). It is the reverse of what ionization does.
Sending the C–Br bond pair to carbon would make a carbanion and Br<sup>+</sup>. Bromine is more electronegative, so it takes the pair.
A fishhook moves one electron, which is homolysis (a radical and a Br atom). Ionization in a polar solvent is heterolytic, so it needs a full arrow.

q: In the S<sub>N</sub>1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, water captures the tert-butyl cation. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: The cation is the electron-poor partner. Find the electron pair on water that can make a new bond, and the atom with only six electrons.
w: Water is the nucleophile and the carbocation is the electrophile. The arrow starts at a lone pair on the water oxygen and ends at the positively charged carbon, giving the protonated alcohol (an oxonium ion, R–OH2+). The O–H bonds stay intact in this step; a proton is removed in the next step.
x: This arrow starts at the cation, which has no electrons to give. The positive carbon accepts electrons, so the arrow must point to it, not away from it.
The O–H bonding pair is not used to attack; using it would break an O–H bond and attach H, not O, to carbon. Water attacks with a lone pair.
The arrow ends at a methyl carbon, which already has four bonds; a new bond there would give it five. The attack must be at the electron-deficient C<sup>+</sup>.

q: The last step of the S<sub>N</sub>1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane converts the oxonium ion into 2-methyl-2-propanol. Which set of curved arrows shows this step correctly, with water as the base?
h: A proton transfer needs two arrows: one makes the new bond to H, one breaks the old one. Where must the old bond's electrons go to leave a neutral alcohol?
w: This is a proton transfer. A lone pair on solvent water bonds to one of the O–H protons of the oxonium ion, and the O–H bonding pair moves onto the oxonium oxygen, which becomes the neutral alcohol oxygen. The correct drawing is an arrow from a water lone pair to H, plus an arrow from that O–H bond onto the oxonium oxygen, giving the alcohol and H3O+.
x: With only the first arrow, hydrogen would have two bonds (to both oxygens). The old O–H bond must break, so a second arrow is required.
These arrows show water attacking the tertiary carbon and displacing the other water, an S<sub>N</sub>2 exchange at a hindered 3° carbon. It is not a deprotonation and does not lead to the alcohol.
The second arrow sends the O–H bond pair onto hydrogen, which would make hydride (H:<sup>−</sup>) and leave the oxygen electron-poor. The bond pair stays with the more electronegative oxygen.

q: Treating 4-bromobutan-1-ol with NaH gives an alkoxide that closes to tetrahydrofuran (oxolane). Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the ring-closing step?
h: This is an S<sub>N</sub>2 in which the nucleophile and the leaving group are in the same molecule. Count the ring atoms that the product must have.
w: The alkoxide oxygen attacks the carbon that carries Br from the back side while the C–Br bond pair leaves with bromine, a one-step intramolecular SN2. The ring formed has O plus four carbons, the five-membered tetrahydrofuran. The correct drawing is an arrow from an O− lone pair to the CH2Br carbon and an arrow from the C–Br bond onto Br.
x: Without a leaving-group arrow the carbon would end with five bonds. In S<sub>N</sub>2 the C–Br bond breaks in the same step that the C–O bond forms.
The C–Br bond pair is sent to carbon, which already gains a pair from oxygen. Bromide leaves with the bonding electrons, so the arrow must end on Br.
The oxygen attacks the carbon next to the C–Br carbon (a four-membered ring) while bromine leaves from a different carbon. The nucleophile must attack the same carbon that loses the leaving group.

q: Ethanol is converted to ethyl tosylate with TsCl in pyridine. The first step is drawn as the alcohol oxygen substituting at sulfur. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: In tosylation the C–O bond of the alcohol is not touched. Which atom of TsCl is the electrophile, and what leaves from it?
w: The alcohol oxygen uses a lone pair to bond to the electrophilic sulfur, and the S–Cl bond pair leaves with chloride. The correct drawing is an arrow from an O lone pair to S and an arrow from the S–Cl bond onto Cl. The C–O bond of ethanol is never broken, which is why tosylation keeps the configuration of a chiral alcohol; pyridine then removes the O–H proton.
x: This shows chloride attacking carbon and hydroxide leaving, a direct substitution on the unactivated alcohol. Hydroxide is a poor leaving group; the whole point of TsCl is to make O a good leaving group without breaking C–O.
With only the attack arrow, sulfur would gain a seventh bond. The S–Cl bond must break in the same step, so chloride needs its own arrow.
Oxygen attacks chlorine instead of sulfur, and the S–Cl pair is sent to sulfur. Sulfur, bonded to two oxygens and Cl, is the δ+ atom; chlorine leaves as Cl<sup>−</sup>.

q: Ethanol reacts with PBr<sub>3</sub> to give bromoethane. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the first step, which turns the OH into a good leaving group?
h: The OH must be activated before any C–O bond breaks. Which atom of PBr<sub>3</sub> is electron-poor, and which ion leaves it?
w: The alcohol oxygen attacks phosphorus with a lone pair while one P–Br bond pair leaves as Br−, giving R–O(H)+–PBr2. So the arrows are an O lone pair to P and the P–Br bond onto Br. In the next step bromide attacks the carbon from the back side (SN2, inversion) and HOPBr2 leaves.
x: Oxygen attacks bromine rather than phosphorus, and the P–Br pair is sent to P. Phosphorus is the electrophilic center; bromide leaves with the bond pair.
The attack arrow is right, but the P–Br pair is sent to phosphorus. The departing bromine must take the bonding electrons to leave as Br<sup>−</sup>.

This ionizes the C–O bond of a primary alcohol to give a primary carbocation and HO<sup>−</sup>. That never happens: HO<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group and 1° cations are too unstable, which is why PBr<sub>3</sub> is used.

q: After ethanol attacks TsCl, the intermediate is an O-protonated tosylate. Pyridine then gives neutral ethyl tosylate. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: The positive oxygen needs to lose a proton to become neutral. Which hydrogen is on the positive atom?
w: Pyridine acts as a base. Its nitrogen lone pair bonds to the O–H proton on the positively charged oxygen, and the O–H bond pair moves onto that oxygen, giving neutral ethyl tosylate and pyridinium ion. The O–H proton is by far the most acidic hydrogen because it sits on the cationic oxygen.
x: Pyridine attacking sulfur and expelling ethanol would just reverse the first step (the C–O–S link breaks at O–S). The forward step needed here is removal of a proton.
This removes a C–H proton from the CH<sub>2</sub> group. Those hydrogens are not acidic; the acidic proton is the one on the positive oxygen.
With only one arrow the hydrogen would have two bonds. The O–H bond must break, with its pair going back to oxygen.

q: The drawing shows cyanide ion reacting with (S)-2-bromobutane by an SN2 mechanism in DMSO. What is the organic product?
h: Look at which atom the first arrow starts from and which carbon it ends at. Then think about which face of that carbon the nucleophile must approach.
w: The arrows show the lone pair on cyanide's carbon attacking C2 while bromide leaves from the same carbon in one step. Backside attack inverts C2. Because CN outranks ethyl (as Br did), the priority order is unchanged, so inversion changes the descriptor: the product is (R)-2-methylbutanenitrile.
x: This is the retention product, which would require frontside attack. In S<sub>N</sub>2 the nucleophile approaches opposite the C–Br bond, so the configuration inverts.
Pentanenitrile has the CN on a terminal carbon. The arrow ends at C2, the carbon bearing Br, and S<sub>N</sub>2 does not move the carbon skeleton.
This isonitrile would form if nitrogen attacked. The arrow starts at the carbon lone pair of cyanide (the more nucleophilic end in S<sub>N</sub>2 with alkyl halides), so a C–C bond forms.

q: 2-Methyl-2-propanol reacts with HBr by an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. Which statement correctly describes the step drawn?
c: The C–O bond breaks heterolytically to give a tertiary carbocation and water; this is the rate-determining step
The C–O bond breaks heterolytically to give a tertiary carbocation and hydroxide ion; this is the rate-determining step
The C–O bond breaks heterolytically to give a tertiary carbocation and water; this step is fast, and bromide capture is rate-determining
The C–O bond breaks homolytically to give a tertiary radical and a water radical cation; this is the rate-determining step
h: Count the bonds and charges on oxygen before and after the arrow. Which step in an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction makes the high-energy intermediate?
w: The arrow moves the C–O bonding pair onto the positive oxygen, so the oxonium ion splits into the tert-butyl cation and neutral water. Making the carbocation is the slow, uphill step of an SN1 reaction; bromide then captures the cation quickly. So: heterolysis gives a 3° carbocation and water, and this is the rate-determining step.
x: The oxygen keeps both of its H atoms and gains the bond pair, so it leaves as neutral H<sub>2</sub>O, not HO<sup>−</sup>. Protonation is what turns poor-leaving hydroxide into good-leaving water.
Bromide combining with a carbocation is a fast, downhill ion combination. Forming the carbocation is the slow step.
A full arrow moves two electrons (heterolysis). Homolysis would be drawn with two fishhooks and is not how ionic substitution occurs.

q: A student drew these arrows for the S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction of iodide ion with chloroethane. What is wrong with the drawing?
c: The first arrow should start at a lone pair on iodide and end at the carbon, not start at the carbon
The second arrow should end at the carbon, because the C–Cl electrons stay on carbon
Only one arrow is needed, because chloride leaves in a separate, later step
The first arrow should end at chlorine, because iodide attacks the halogen
h: Ask of each arrow: does it start at electrons, and do those electrons have somewhere legal to go?
w: Arrows show where electrons move. The C–Cl carbon is the electrophile and has no lone pair to give; iodide supplies the pair. So the attack arrow must start at an iodide lone pair and end at the carbon. The second arrow (C–Cl bond pair onto Cl) is drawn correctly.
x: The C–Cl bond pair goes to chlorine, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as Cl<sup>−</sup>. That arrow is already correct.
In S<sub>N</sub>2 the bond to the leaving group breaks in the same step the new bond forms; a separate leaving step describes S<sub>N</sub>1.
Iodide attacks the δ+ carbon. Attack on chlorine would not form a C–I bond and is not the S<sub>N</sub>2 path.

q: (R)-Butan-2-ol is treated with SOCl2 and pyridine. The drawing shows the step in which chloride attacks the alkyl chlorosulfite (the stereocenter is unchanged up to this point). What is the product of this step?
h: Follow the first arrow: from which direction must the chloride approach C2 if the C–O bond breaks in the same step? Then assign R/S, comparing Cl with O.
w: Chloride attacks C2 from the back side as the C–O bond breaks; that pair becomes the S=O π bond of SO2, and the S–Cl pair leaves as Cl−. It is one concerted SN2-type step, so C2 is inverted. Cl takes the top priority that O had, and ethyl > methyl in both, so inverting the geometry changes R to S: (S)-2-chlorobutane, by inversion.
x: Retention is seen when SOCl<sub>2</sub> is used without pyridine (internal delivery of Cl from the same face). The drawn step is backside attack by free chloride, which inverts.
No arrow makes a free carbocation; bond making and bond breaking at C2 happen in one step. A secondary substrate with this good leaving group and Cl<sup>−</sup> reacts by inversion.
Inversion is right, but the descriptor is wrong. Cl has the top priority, as O did, so the same three groups in mirror arrangement give S.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is dissolved in methanol and gives 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane. Each drawing shows a step someone proposed. Which drawn step is the rate-determining step of the actual mechanism?
h: The real mechanism is S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis. Which step creates the least stable species, and does every drawing belong to that mechanism?
w: Solvolysis of a 3° bromide in methanol goes by SN1: ionization, capture of the cation by methanol, and deprotonation of the oxonium ion by a second methanol. Ionization forms the high-energy carbocation and has the highest barrier, so the rate-determining step is heterolysis of the C–Br bond to give the tert-butyl cation and Br−.
x: Methanol adding to the carbocation is a fast ion–molecule combination that comes after the slow step. Its rate does not depend on [CH<sub>3</sub>OH] in the rate law.
Proton transfer between oxygen atoms is very fast. It is the last step, and it only neutralizes the oxonium ion.
A concerted backside attack on a tertiary carbon is blocked by the three methyl groups, so this step is not part of the mechanism at all.

q: During methanolysis of 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane, the step drawn occurs. What species is formed directly by these arrows?
h: One arrow means one new bond and no bond broken. Count the bonds to oxygen afterward.
w: The single arrow gives oxygen a third bond (to the ring carbon) while it keeps its O–H and O–CH3 bonds, so it carries a positive charge. The species formed is the protonated ether (an oxonium ion), C8H17O+. A later proton transfer to solvent gives the neutral ether.
x: This is the final product, but the drawn arrow does not remove the O–H proton. That needs a separate proton-transfer step.
The alkene is the E1 product, formed when a base removes a β-H. The drawn arrow makes a C–O bond, not a C=C bond.
Here oxygen is bonded to a CH<sub>2</sub> next to the ring, which would need attack at a carbon that is not cationic. The arrow ends at the ring C<sup>+</sup>.

q: The trans bromo-alkoxide shown (from trans-2-bromocyclohexanol and NaH) closes rapidly to cyclohexene oxide by the step drawn. The cis isomer gives little epoxide under the same conditions. Why?
c: The O<sup>−</sup> must reach the back side of the C–Br bond; only the trans isomer can place O and Br anti (both axial)
The cis isomer would give a less stable cis epoxide, so it reacts by elimination instead
In the trans isomer bromide leaves first to give a carbocation, which the alkoxide then captures
In the cis isomer, hydrogen bonding between O<sup>−</sup> and Br makes the alkoxide non-nucleophilic
h: The drawn step is an intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2. What geometry does every S<sub>N</sub>2 need between the nucleophile and the leaving group?
w: Ring closure is an intramolecular SN2, so the alkoxide must attack C–Br from the back side, 180° from the leaving group. In the trans isomer, the chair with both groups axial puts O− directly anti to Br and closure is fast. In the cis isomer O and Br are on the same face, so the oxygen can only approach from the front side. Hence only the trans isomer can align O− anti to the C–Br bond.
x: The epoxide fused to a six-membered ring is the same (cis-fused) compound whichever isomer it came from. The problem with the cis isomer is the approach geometry, not product stability.
The drawn arrows are concerted: the C–O bond forms as the C–Br bond breaks. No carbocation forms from a secondary bromide under these basic conditions.
An alkoxide does not form a meaningful hydrogen bond with a C–Br group, and there is no O–H left to donate one. The difference comes from geometry.

q: Propyne is treated with NaNH<sub>2</sub> in liquid NH<sub>3</sub> to make a sodium acetylide. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the deprotonation?
h: Which C–H is most acidic: sp, or sp<sup>3</sup>? Then remember a proton transfer needs a bond-making and a bond-breaking arrow.
w: The terminal ≡C–H (pKa ≈ 25) is far more acidic than the CH3 hydrogens, because its conjugate base holds the pair in an sp orbital (50% s character). The amide nitrogen (NH3 pKa ≈ 38) bonds to that H and the C–H pair stays on carbon. The correct drawing is N lone pair → terminal H, and the ≡C–H bond → the sp carbon.
x: This removes an H from the CH<sub>3</sub> group, whose conjugate base has its pair in an sp<sup>3</sup>-like orbital and is much less stable. Amide removes the sp C–H.
Without the second arrow, hydrogen ends up with two bonds. The C–H bond pair must move onto carbon.
Sending the C–H bond pair to hydrogen would make hydride and a carbocation-like alkyne carbon. The pair stays on carbon, which becomes the acetylide anion.

q: Diethyl ether and boron trifluoride combine to form the complex BF<sub>3</sub>·OEt<sub>2</sub>. Which drawing shows the correct curved arrow?
h: One partner has an empty orbital and the other has a lone pair. Which atom is short of an octet?
w: Boron in BF3 has only six valence electrons and an empty p orbital, so it is the Lewis acid; the ether oxygen is the Lewis base. One arrow, from an oxygen lone pair to boron, forms the O–B bond, giving O a +1 and B a −1 formal charge.
x: This arrow moves a B–F bond pair to oxygen, as if BF<sub>3</sub> were donating electrons. Boron is the electron acceptor here.
Fluorine's lone pairs are held tightly and are not the donor; giving one to oxygen would put five electron pairs around a neutral oxygen. The ether oxygen is the donor.
Fluorine already has an octet, so it cannot accept a new bond. The empty orbital is on boron.

q: Cyclohexanol reacts with concentrated HBr. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the first step, protonation of the alcohol?
h: The alcohol is the base here. Arrows go from the base's lone pair to the proton, and the H–Br pair ends on bromine.
w: The alcohol oxygen uses a lone pair to bond to the proton of HBr, and the H–Br bond pair leaves with bromine as Br−. The correct drawing is an O lone pair → H, plus the H–Br bond → Br, giving the oxonium ion (ROH2+), whose water is a good leaving group.
x: This single arrow sends the H–Br bonding pair to oxygen, as if the acid were donating electrons to the alcohol. The proton is accepted by the oxygen's lone pair; the H–Br pair goes to Br.
Oxygen attacks bromine, and the H–Br pair is sent to H (making hydride). The acidic atom is H, and bromine leaves as bromide.
Without a second arrow, hydrogen would have bonds to both O and Br. The H–Br bond must break.

q: Acetic acid is mixed with aqueous NaOH. Which set of curved arrows shows the fast acid–base reaction?
h: Compare the O–H (pK<sub>a</sub> about 5) with the C–H of the methyl group (pK<sub>a</sub> about 25). Hydroxide removes the more acidic proton.
w: The carboxylic acid O–H (pKa 4.8) is about 20 pKa units more acidic than the α C–H, because the carboxylate is stabilized by resonance over two oxygens. Hydroxide's lone pair bonds to that proton and the O–H pair stays on oxygen: O lone pair of HO− → acidic H, and the O–H bond → O, giving acetate and water.
x: This removes a methyl C–H. That hydrogen is far less acidic than the carboxylic O–H, so hydroxide does not take it.
These arrows add hydroxide to the carbonyl carbon. Proton transfer from the O–H is much faster, and the carboxylate formed then resists nucleophilic attack.
With only one arrow hydrogen would have two bonds. The O–H bond pair must move onto oxygen.

q: The drawing shows the proton transfer between the propynide ion and water. What are the products, and which side of the equilibrium is favored?
c: Propyne and hydroxide ion; products are favored, because water (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) is a stronger acid than propyne (pK<sub>a</sub> 25)
Propyne and hydroxide ion; reactants are favored, because water (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) is a weaker acid than propyne (pK<sub>a</sub> 25)
Prop-1-en-1-ol and nothing else; products are favored, because water adds across the triple bond
Propyne and hydroxide ion; the two sides are about equal, because both acids are neutral
h: Name the acid on each side and compare their pK<sub>a</sub> values. Equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid.
w: The carbanion lone pair takes a proton from water, and the O–H pair stays on oxygen: the products are propyne and hydroxide ion, and products are favored. The acid on the left is water (pKa 15.7); the acid on the right is propyne (pKa about 25). The equilibrium lies toward the weaker acid, propyne, with Keq ≈ 109. This is why acetylide reactions must be kept dry.
x: The pK<sub>a</sub> comparison is reversed: a lower pK<sub>a</sub> means a stronger acid, so water (15.7) is stronger than propyne (25).
The arrows show a proton moving to carbon; no C–O bond forms. Hydration of an alkyne needs acid and Hg<sup>2+</sup> catalysis, not this step.
Charge type does not set the position; the pK<sub>a</sub> values differ by about 9 units, so K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>9</sup>, far from 1.

q: A student drew this single arrow for the reaction of sodium amide with ethanol. What is wrong with it?
c: The O–H bond pair should go to oxygen; a separate arrow from nitrogen's lone pair to H is needed
Nothing is wrong; in a proton transfer the arrow points from the acid to the base
The arrow should start at the hydrogen atom and point to nitrogen
No reaction occurs, because ethanol is a weaker acid than ammonia
h: Curved arrows track electrons, not the proton. Which species supplies the pair that bonds to H, and where does the O–H pair go?
w: The base (NH2−) supplies a lone pair to the proton, and the O–H bond pair stays on oxygen to make ethoxide. The student's arrow sends the O–H pair to nitrogen, which would leave oxygen electron-poor and does not show the new N–H bond. A correct drawing needs N lone pair → H, and the O–H bond → O.
x: A common slip. Arrows show electron flow, which is from the base to the proton; the proton itself moves the opposite way.
A proton has no electrons to give, so an arrow can never start at H. It starts at the electrons that make the new bond.
Ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) is a much stronger acid than ammonia (≈ 38), so the reaction goes essentially to completion.

q: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) and borane form the BH<sub>3</sub>·THF complex by the arrow shown. What are the formal charges on oxygen and boron in the complex?
c: O is 0 and B is 0, because a dative bond carries no charge
h: Use formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − bonds, for O (6 valence) and B (3 valence).
w: After donating a lone pair, oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. Boron now has four bonds and no lone pairs: 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. So O is +1 and B is −1, and the complex is neutral overall. Oxygen is the Lewis base and boron the Lewis acid.
x: The charges are reversed. The donor oxygen loses a share of its pair and becomes positive; the acceptor boron gains one and becomes negative.
Formal charge counts the bonds in the structure, however they formed. Oxygen with three bonds and boron with four always carry +1 and −1.
Boron has 3 valence electrons and four bonds here, so its formal charge is −1. The charges must also sum to the neutral overall charge.

q: 4-Pentyn-1-ol is treated with exactly 1.0 equivalent of NaNH<sub>2</sub>. A student proposes the deprotonation shown as the main reaction. Which evaluation is correct?
c: The arrows are drawn correctly, but the O–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) is removed first, so the main product is the alkoxide
The proposal is correct, because sp-hybridized C–H bonds are the most acidic bonds in the molecule
The arrows are backwards: the C–H bond of the alkyne should donate its pair to nitrogen
The main reaction is removal of an H from the CH<sub>2</sub> next to oxygen, because the electronegative O acidifies it most
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> values of all the acidic hydrogens. With one equivalent of base, which proton goes first?
w: The arrows themselves are drawn correctly (N lone pair → H, C–H pair → C). But with one equivalent of base the most acidic proton reacts first. The alcohol O–H (pKa ≈ 16) is about 9 units more acidic than the terminal alkyne C–H (≈ 25), so the main product is the alkoxide, not the acetylide. A second equivalent of NaNH2 would be needed to form the dianion.
x: sp C–H bonds are the most acidic C–H bonds, but an O–H is more acidic still: oxygen is more electronegative than any carbon, and alkoxide (≈ 16) is a weaker base than acetylide (≈ 25).
The direction is right: arrows start at the base's lone pair. A C–H bond donating to nitrogen would not form an N–H bond.
The CH<sub>2</sub>–O hydrogens are only weakly affected by the oxygen (pK<sub>a</sub> near 50). They are not acidic toward amide.

q: Each drawing shows a correctly drawn proton transfer. For which one does the equilibrium lie on the product side (K<sub>eq</sub> > 1)?
h: For each, name the acid on the left and the acid formed on the right. The equilibrium favors the side with the higher pK<sub>a</sub> acid.
w: An acid–base equilibrium favors the weaker acid (higher pKa). Amide + acetylene: acid on the left is HC≡CH (25), acid on the right is NH3 (38), so the products are favored. In every other drawing the acid formed is stronger than the acid used, so those lie to the left. The answer is amide ion deprotonating acetylene.
x: Hydroxide would form water (15.7) from acetylene (25). Water is the stronger acid, so the reactants are favored by about 10<sup>9</sup>.
Ethoxide would make ethanol (16) from ammonia (38). The product acid is much stronger, so this lies far to the left.
Propynide would make propyne (pK<sub>a</sub> about 25, like acetylene) from methane (50). The alkyne is the stronger acid, so the reactants are favored.

q: A student plans to make sodium hexynide by adding NaNH<sub>2</sub> to 1-hexyne in water. The reaction between amide and the solvent is shown. Why does the plan fail?
c: Amide is converted essentially completely to hydroxide by water, and hydroxide is too weak a base to deprotonate the alkyne
The drawn reaction lies to the left, because ammonia is a stronger acid than water, so amide is never formed in water
Water adds to the triple bond faster than any deprotonation can occur
Amide deprotonates the alkyne, but the acetylide then attacks water's oxygen to give an ether
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of water with that of NH<sub>3</sub>, and then compare the base left over with the alkyne's pK<sub>a</sub>.
w: Water (pKa 15.7) is about 22 units more acidic than ammonia (38), so the drawn proton transfer goes essentially to completion. This is the leveling effect: no base stronger than HO− survives in water. Hydroxide can only remove protons with pKa below about 15.7, and the alkyne's is about 25. So NaNH2 is leveled to hydroxide, which cannot form the acetylide. Even acetylide that did form would be protonated by water. Use liquid NH3 or an aprotic solvent instead.
x: The pK<sub>a</sub> order is reversed: water (15.7) is the stronger acid, not ammonia (38), so the drawn reaction lies far to the right.
Water does not add to an alkyne without an acid and Hg<sup>2+</sup> catalyst. The problem is acid–base: the base is destroyed by the solvent.
An acetylide protonated by water gives back the alkyne and hydroxide. Carbanions take a proton from water much faster than they attack oxygen, and C–O bond formation this way does not occur.

q: Sodium ethoxide converts 3-bromopentane into 2-pentene in a single E2 step. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: E2 is one concerted step: count the bonds that form and break, and give each one its own arrow.
w: In E2 three things happen at once: the ethoxide lone pair forms a bond to a β-hydrogen (the H on the carbon next to C–Br), the electrons of that C–H bond become the new C=C π bond, and the C–Br bond breaks with both electrons going to bromide. The correct drawing therefore has three arrows: O lone pair → β-H, β C–H bond → C–C bond, C–Br bond → Br. Every atom ends with a legal octet: the β carbon trades its C–H for the π bond and the α carbon trades its C–Br for the π bond.
x: This set has no arrow breaking the C–Br bond, so the α carbon would keep Br and gain a π bond: five bonds to carbon. Bromide must leave in the same step.
These are S<sub>N</sub>2 arrows (ethoxide attacks the carbon bearing Br). They give an ether, not 2-pentene, and no C–H bond is broken.
This base takes the H on the carbon that holds Br (the α-H). Those C–H electrons cannot make a π bond to the neighboring carbon; the β carbon would end with five bonds and the α carbon with three.

q: 2-Bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane reacts with sodium ethoxide in ethanol by E2. Which set of curved arrows shows the step that forms the major alkene?
h: Two different β-hydrogens are drawn. Which one leads to the more substituted alkene with a small base? Then check the direction of every arrow.
w: Ethoxide is a small base, so E2 follows Zaitsev's rule and gives the more substituted alkene. Removing the H on C3 (the CH carbon) gives tetrasubstituted 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene; removing a CH3 hydrogen gives only disubstituted 2,3-dimethyl-1-butene. The correct drawing takes the C3–H: O lone pair → C3–H, C3–H bond → C2–C3 bond, C2–Br bond → Br.
x: These arrows are a valid E2, but they remove a methyl hydrogen and give 2,3-dimethyl-1-butene, the minor (Hofmann) alkene. That H is preferred only with a bulky base such as tert-butoxide.
These are S<sub>N</sub>2 arrows at a tertiary carbon. Backside attack at a 3° carbon is blocked by the three alkyl groups, so this step does not occur.

The last arrow points the wrong way: the C–Br bond electrons must end on bromine (it leaves as Br<sup>−</sup>), not on carbon. As drawn, C2 would hold a lone pair plus a π bond, with Br still attached.

q: When 2-iodo-2-methylbutane is warmed in methanol, the E1 reaction begins with the step drawn. What does this step produce?
h: A full-headed arrow moves two electrons. Where do both electrons of the C–I bond end up?
w: The full-headed arrow carries both C–I bonding electrons onto iodine (heterolysis). Iodine leaves as iodide, I−, and the carbon that lost the bond is left with only three bonds and a positive charge. Step 1 gives the tertiary 2-methyl-2-butyl carbocation and iodide; this slow ionization is the rate-determining step of E1.
x: Splitting the bond one electron to each atom (homolysis) gives radicals; that would be drawn with two fishhook arrows, not one full arrow.
This puts both electrons on carbon and leaves iodine electron-poor, the reverse of what the arrow shows. Iodine is the more electronegative atom and the better leaving group.
The alkene and HI form only after a later step (a base removes a β-H from the carbocation). E1 is stepwise; ionization alone cannot make the C=C bond.

q: In the E1 reaction of 2-iodo-2-methylbutane in methanol, a methanol molecule removes a proton from the 2-methyl-2-butyl cation to form the major alkene, 2-methyl-2-butene. Which set of curved arrows shows this step?
h: Two bonds change: one O–H bond forms and one C–H bond breaks. Where must the C–H electrons go to make the alkene?
w: Methanol acts as a weak base. One arrow goes from an oxygen lone pair to the β-hydrogen; the second carries the C–H bonding electrons into the C2–C3 bond, where they fill the empty p orbital of the cation and become the π bond. The correct drawing is O lone pair → β-H, then C–H bond → C–C+ bond. The positive charge moves to oxygen (protonated methanol), and the neutral alkene forms.
x: Arrows never start at a carbocation: it has no electrons to give. The electrons come from methanol, the electron-rich partner.
Methanol attacking the cationic carbon is a real competing step, but it is the S<sub>N</sub>1 step and gives an ether (2-methoxy-2-methylbutane), not the alkene.
If the C–H electrons stayed on C3 as a lone pair, C3 would become a carbanion next to a carbocation; no π bond would form. The bond electrons must move into the C–C bond.

q: The acid-catalyzed dehydration of cyclohexanol begins when the OH group is protonated by hydronium ion. Which set of curved arrows shows this step?
h: Which species is the base here? Its electrons start the first arrow, and a bond to H must also break.
w: Proton transfer takes two arrows. The alcohol oxygen is the base: an arrow from an O lone pair of cyclohexanol to the H of H3O+, and a second arrow from the H–O+ bond onto the hydronium oxygen, which leaves as water. The product is the alkyloxonium ion, which now has a good leaving group (H2O).
x: This arrow sends the H–O bond electrons from hydronium to the alcohol oxygen, as if H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> were donating electrons. The proton is the acceptor; the alcohol lone pair must reach out to the H.
With only one arrow, the H would end up bonded to two oxygens. The H–O<sup>+</sup> bond of hydronium must break in the same step.
The hydronium oxygen is positively charged and acts as the acid, not as the nucleophile; it does not donate its lone pair to the alcohol oxygen. No O–O bond forms.

q: The step drawn is one of the three steps in the acid-catalyzed (E1) dehydration of 1-methylcyclohexanol. Which step of this mechanism is rate-determining?
c: The step drawn: loss of water to form the tertiary carbocation
Protonation of the OH group by hydronium ion
Removal of a β-hydrogen from the carbocation by water
Attack of water on the tertiary carbocation
h: Which step creates a high-energy carbocation, rather than just moving a proton between oxygen atoms?
w: Proton transfers between oxygen atoms are fast. The slow step is the heterolysis of the C–O bond, in which water leaves and an unstable carbocation forms. That step has the highest-energy transition state, so it controls the rate: loss of water to form the tertiary carbocation. This is why 3° alcohols dehydrate fastest: the more stable the cation, the lower that barrier.
x: Protonation of the alcohol is a fast acid–base equilibrium between oxygens; it sets up the leaving group but is not slow.
Deprotonation of the carbocation is fast because the cation is high in energy and reacts quickly with any weak base.
Water adding to the carbocation is the reverse direction (hydration). Under dehydration conditions (heat, removal of the alkene) that step is not part of the forward path, and it is fast anyway.

q: Heating 3-methyl-2-pentanol with H2SO4 forms the secondary carbocation drawn. Which set of curved arrows shows the 1,2-shift that converts it into a more stable carbocation?
h: In a 1,2-shift a group moves with its bonding pair from the carbon next door to the cationic carbon. Which group's move leaves a 3° cation behind?
w: In a 1,2-shift, the electrons of a σ bond on the adjacent carbon swing over to the empty p orbital; the migrating group travels with them, and the carbon it left becomes the new cation. Moving the hydride from C3 to C2 leaves C3 bonded to a methyl, an ethyl and C2: a tertiary cation, drawn as an arrow from the C3–H bond to the cationic C2. That 3° cation then loses a proton to give the alkene.
x: This arrow starts at the carbocation, which has an empty orbital and no electrons to push. The shift is the C–H bond electrons moving toward the cation, not the reverse.
A methyl shift from C3 is drawn correctly as an arrow, but it leaves C3 bonded to only H, ethyl and C2: still a secondary cation. There is no gain in stability, so this shift is not favored.
Moving a hydride from the C1 methyl group would leave a primary cation on C1, which is much less stable than the starting secondary cation.

q: Dehydration of 3,3-dimethyl-2-pentanol in hot H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> forms the secondary carbocation drawn, which undergoes the 1,2-methyl shift shown. What is the major alkene product?
h: Draw the new cation after the methyl moves. Then list every β-hydrogen it can lose and compare how substituted each alkene would be.
w: The methyl moves with its bonding pair from C3 to C2. C3 becomes a tertiary cation bonded to a CH3, an ethyl, and an isopropyl group (old C2 now carries two methyls). Loss of the lone H on the isopropyl CH gives the tetrasubstituted alkene, which is the most stable choice: 2,3-dimethyl-2-pentene. (An ethyl shift instead gives a different 3° cation that loses a proton to the same tetrasubstituted alkene.)
x: 3,3-Dimethyl-1-pentene keeps the original skeleton, as if no shift occurred. A monosubstituted alkene from the 2° cation is minor once the cation can rearrange to 3°.
3,4-Dimethyl-2-pentene comes from the rearranged cation losing an ethyl CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogen; it is only trisubstituted, so it is a minor product.
2-Ethyl-3-methyl-1-butene forms when the rearranged cation loses a methyl hydrogen; that 1,1-disubstituted alkene is the least stable of the rearranged products.

q: trans-1-Bromo-2-methylcyclohexane undergoes E2 with sodium ethoxide. In the drawing, the H on C2 is wedged, on the same face as Br (also wedged), and the H drawn on C6 is the one on the opposite face from Br. Which set of curved arrows shows the E2 step that actually occurs?
h: On a cyclohexane, E2 needs the H and the leaving group trans-diaxial (anti-periplanar). Which β-hydrogens are trans to Br?
w: E2 needs the β C–H and the C–Br bonds anti-periplanar, which on a cyclohexane means both axial, on opposite faces of the ring. In the trans isomer, the only H on C2 is on the same face as Br (cis), so it can never be anti to Br. C6 has an H trans to Br, which becomes axial in the chair where Br is axial. The base therefore removes the C6 hydrogen: O lone pair → C6–H, C6–H bond → C6–C1 bond, C1–Br bond → Br, giving 3-methylcyclohexene even though it is the less substituted (non-Zaitsev) alkene.
x: These arrows would give the Zaitsev product, 1-methylcyclohexene, but the C2–H is cis to Br. A cis H and Br cannot both be axial at once, so they are never anti-periplanar.
The right hydrogen is removed, but no arrow breaks the C–Br bond, so C1 would carry Br plus a new π bond: five bonds to carbon.
These are S<sub>N</sub>2 arrows. Ethoxide is a strong base and the substrate is a hindered secondary halide, so E2 is the main pathway here.

q: Potassium tert-butoxide reacts with 2-bromo-2-methylpentane by the E2 step drawn. What is the major organic product?
h: Follow the arrows: which carbon loses the H and which carbon loses Br? The new π bond joins those two carbons.
w: The bulky tert-butoxide reaches the exposed methyl hydrogens more easily than the hindered CH2 hydrogens inside the chain, so it removes a CH3 hydrogen, as the arrows show. The C–H electrons form the π bond between that CH2 and C2, and bromide leaves: the Hofmann product, 2-methyl-1-pentene.
x: 2-Methyl-2-pentene is the Zaitsev alkene, from removing a C3 hydrogen. That is major with a small base such as ethoxide, but tert-butoxide is too hindered to reach C3 easily, and the arrows drawn remove a methyl H.
This ether would require tert-butoxide to attack a tertiary carbon. Neither S<sub>N</sub>2 (blocked) nor S<sub>N</sub>1 (strong base, E2 is faster) gives it in useful amounts.
An alcohol would need water or hydroxide as the nucleophile; none of the arrows forms a C–O bond.

q: (2R,3S)-2-Bromo-3-methylpentane undergoes E2 with sodium ethoxide, removing the C3 hydrogen drawn. What is the product of the step shown?
h: Rotate the C2–C3 bond until the drawn H and Br are anti-periplanar (a Newman projection helps). Groups that are gauche in that conformation end up cis in the alkene.
w: E2 is stereospecific: the H on C3 and Br on C2 must be anti-periplanar. In that conformation of the (2R,3S) isomer, the C2 methyl is gauche to the C3 ethyl and anti to the C3 methyl. When the π bond forms, gauche groups become cis, so CH3 (C2) and CH2CH3 (C3) are on the same side. On C2 the higher-priority group is CH3; on C3 it is ethyl; both on one side gives (Z)-3-methyl-2-pentene.
x: The E isomer would need the C2 methyl and C3 ethyl anti in the reacting conformation. For this stereoisomer that conformation puts H and Br gauche, not anti, so it cannot react by E2. (The (2R,3R) diastereomer gives the E alkene.)
3-Methyl-1-pentene comes from removing a C1 (methyl) hydrogen. The arrows remove the C3 hydrogen, and a small base favors the more substituted alkene anyway.
This ether is the S<sub>N</sub>2 product. The arrows show the base taking a hydrogen, not attacking carbon, and the hindered 2° substrate with a strong base favors E2.

q: A student drew the E2 reaction of bromocyclohexane with sodium methoxide as shown. What is wrong with the arrows?
c: No arrow breaks the C–Br bond, so the carbon bearing Br would end up with five bonds
Methoxide should attack the carbon bearing Br, not a hydrogen
The first arrow should start at the hydrogen and point to the methoxide oxygen
E2 takes two steps, so the hydrogen cannot be removed until bromide has left
h: Count the bonds on each carbon after the arrows are followed. Does every atom end with a legal number of bonds?
w: The base arrow and the C–H → C=C arrow are fine, but E2 is concerted: the C–Br bond must break in the same step. With only these two arrows, the α carbon gains a π bond while keeping its H, its ring bonds and Br, which is five bonds. The fix is a third arrow from the C–Br bond onto Br. The error is that no arrow breaks the C–Br bond, giving carbon five bonds.
x: Attack at carbon is the S<sub>N</sub>2 path, a different reaction. For an E2 drawing, removing the β-hydrogen is exactly right.
Arrows start at electrons. The methoxide lone pair is the electron source and the hydrogen is the acceptor, so the drawn direction is correct.
Losing bromide first and then the proton describes E1. E2 is a single concerted step in which both bonds break together.

q: Addition of HBr to methylenecyclohexane begins with protonation of the alkene. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this first step?
h: The alkene is the nucleophile here. What is its electrophilic partner, and which bond in that partner must break?
w: The π electrons are the most available electrons in the alkene, and the H of HBr is the electrophile. The first arrow goes from the π bond to H, and the second from the H–Br bond onto Br, which leaves as bromide. The proton goes to the CH2 so that the cation forms on the ring carbon (tertiary). Correct set: π bond → H, H–Br bond → Br.
x: This sends the H–Br electrons toward the alkene, which is backwards: HBr is the electron acceptor here, and the π bond is the electron donor.
With no arrow breaking H–Br, the hydrogen would be bonded to both carbon and bromine (two bonds to H).

Bromine does not attack first. The neutral Br of HBr is not a good nucleophile toward an electron-rich alkene, and pushing the π electrons onto carbon would make a carbanion next to a five-bonded carbon.

q: In the second step of HBr addition to 1-methylcyclohexene, bromide captures the 1-methylcyclohexyl cation. Which set of curved arrows shows this step?
h: Which partner has the electrons, and which atom has the empty orbital?
w: Bromide has four lone pairs and a negative charge; the cationic carbon has an empty p orbital. One full-headed arrow from a lone pair on Br− to the positively charged carbon forms the C–Br bond and neutralizes both charges, giving 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane (the Markovnikov product).
x: An arrow from the carbocation to bromide runs from the electron-poor atom to the electron-rich one, which is backwards. The electrons come from bromide.
The CH<sub>2</sub> next to the cation already has four bonds; a new bond there would give carbon five bonds. Bromide must bond to the carbon with the empty orbital.
A fishhook moves one electron (radical chemistry). Here a two-electron bond forms from a lone pair, which needs a full-headed arrow.

q: HBr adds to 3-methyl-1-pentene. After protonation, the secondary carbocation undergoes the 1,2-shift drawn. What is the major product?
h: Follow the arrow to find which carbon becomes the new cation, then add bromide there.
w: Protonation of C1 gives a 2° cation at C2. The hydride on C3 shifts with its bonding pair to C2 (as drawn), which moves the positive charge to C3. C3 is then bonded to a methyl and two ethyl groups: a 3° cation. Bromide captures it to give 3-bromo-3-methylpentane.
x: 2-Bromo-3-methylpentane is the unrearranged Markovnikov product. Some forms, but the faster 1,2-hydride shift to the 3° cation makes the rearranged bromide major.
1-Bromo-3-methylpentane is the anti-Markovnikov product, which needs peroxides (a radical pathway). The ionic mechanism never makes the primary cation.
3-Bromo-2-methylpentane would come from a methyl shift, which leaves C3 as a secondary cation. That shift gives no gain in stability and is not observed.

q: During acid-catalyzed hydration of 1-methylcyclopentene, water adds to the carbocation intermediate. Which set of curved arrows shows this step?
h: Water is a neutral nucleophile. Which of its electrons are free to make a new bond without breaking anything?
w: Water uses one of its oxygen lone pairs to bond to the empty p orbital of the tertiary carbocation. The correct drawing is a single arrow from an O lone pair to the cationic carbon, giving a protonated alcohol (alkyloxonium ion) that later loses H+ to give 1-methylcyclopentanol.
x: This arrow starts at the carbocation, which has no electrons to donate. The arrow must start at the electron source, water's oxygen.

Using the O–H bond electrons would break that bond and make a C–H bond, not the C–O bond, and would leave oxygen with only six electrons. Water attacks with a lone pair, and the O–H bonds stay intact.
The CH<sub>2</sub> beside the cation already has four bonds, so water cannot bond there without giving carbon five bonds. The nucleophile must go to the carbon bearing the + charge.

q: The last step of the acid-catalyzed hydration of 1-methylcyclopentene is drawn. What species are produced by this step?
h: One arrow moves a proton to water; the other puts the O–H bond electrons back on the ring oxygen. Keep track of the total charge.
w: Water acts as the base: its lone pair takes a proton from the oxonium ion, and the O–H bond electrons return to the ring oxygen as a lone pair. The ring oxygen goes from +1 to neutral and water becomes hydronium, so the products are 1-methylcyclopentanol and H3O+. The acid catalyst is regenerated, and the overall charge (+1) is conserved.
x: An alkoxide would need the oxygen to gain a second lone pair beyond neutral. Starting at +1, receiving one bond's electrons makes it neutral, not −1; this choice also has total charge 0 instead of +1.
Breaking the C–O bond to make a carbocation and water is the reverse of the previous step and would need an arrow from the C–O bond, not from water to H.
An alkene would form only if a C–H bond broke. The arrows break an O–H bond, so the oxygen stays on the ring.

q: Vinylcyclohexane is treated with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in water. The first step is drawn. Assume the carbocation rearranges whenever a shift gives a more stable cation. What is the major product of the overall reaction?
h: Decide where the first cation forms, then ask whether a neighboring hydrogen can move to make it more stable before water arrives.
w: Protonation of the CH2 end gives a secondary cation next to the ring. The ring carbon attached to it carries one H; a 1,2-hydride shift from that ring carbon moves the positive charge onto the ring, where it is tertiary (bonded to two ring carbons and the ethyl group). Water then attacks the 3° cation, and loss of H+ gives 1-ethylcyclohexanol.
x: 1-Cyclohexylethanol is the unrearranged Markovnikov alcohol. It ignores the hydride shift from the ring CH, which turns the 2° cation into a more stable 3° cation before water adds.
2-Cyclohexylethanol is the anti-Markovnikov alcohol (hydroboration–oxidation). Acid-catalyzed hydration never forms the primary cation that this would need.

2-Methylcycloheptanol would need a ring bond to migrate (ring expansion). That gives only another 2° cation and relieves no strain from a six-membered ring, whereas the hydride shift gives a 3° cation.

q: Cyclopentene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> to form a bridged bromonium ion and bromide. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: The product has two new C–Br bonds to the same bromine and one broken Br–Br bond. Each bond that forms or breaks needs an arrow.
w: Three bond changes happen together. The π bond attacks the near bromine (forming one C–Br bond), a lone pair on that same bromine bonds to the other alkene carbon (closing the three-membered ring), and the Br–Br bond breaks with both electrons going to the far bromine, which leaves as Br−. Correct set: π bond → Br, Br lone pair → other carbon, Br–Br bond → far Br. The bridged ion explains why the second bromine later adds anti.
x: These arrows make an open carbocation, not the bridged ion: no lone pair of bromine closes the ring. An open cation would allow syn and anti attack, which does not match the observed anti addition.
A bromine lone pair attacking an alkene carbon while the π bond stays intact would give that carbon five bonds. The π bond must be used.
Without an arrow breaking the Br–Br bond, the near bromine would hold three bonds (two carbons plus the other Br), and no bromide would be released.

q: (E)-3-Hexene reacts with Br2 in CH2Cl2. The trans bromonium ion is opened by bromide as drawn, with Br− approaching from the face opposite the bridging bromine. What is the stereochemical outcome?
c: A mixture of meso and racemic 3,4-dibromohexane
h: Anti addition to a trans alkene: think of (E)-2-butene + Br2. Then check whether the product has an internal mirror plane.
w: Backside opening of the bromonium ion puts the two bromines anti: overall anti addition. For a symmetric alkene, anti addition to the E isomer gives a product with stereocenters of opposite descriptor (3R,4S), which has an internal mirror plane. Attack at either carbon, or on the bromonium from either face of the alkene, gives the same compound: meso-3,4-dibromohexane only.
x: The racemic (R,R)/(S,S) pair comes from anti addition to the Z alkene, (Z)-3-hexene. Mixing up which alkene isomer gives which outcome is the usual trap.
A single enantiomer cannot form from achiral starting materials and reagents; and the E alkene gives the meso compound, not (R,R).
A mixture of meso and racemic products would result from an open carbocation (syn and anti attack). The bridged bromonium ion allows only anti attack, so the addition is stereospecific.

q: In bromohydrin formation from 1-methylcyclopentene (Br<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O), water opens the bromonium ion drawn. Which set of curved arrows shows the step that leads to the major product?
h: In an unsymmetrical bromonium ion, one C–Br bond is longer and that carbon carries more positive charge. Which carbon is it?
w: The bromonium ion is unsymmetrical: the C–Br bond to the tertiary carbon is weaker and that carbon carries more of the positive charge (more SN1-like character). Water attacks there from the back face, and the C–Br bond to that carbon breaks, with its electrons going to bromine. Correct set: water lone pair → tertiary carbon, tertiary C–Br bond → Br. After deprotonation the product is trans-2-bromo-1-methylcyclopentanol (OH on the more substituted carbon, Br and OH anti).
x: Attack at the secondary carbon is the S<sub>N</sub>2-style guess (less hindered), but bromonium opening is controlled by where positive charge builds up, so it puts Br on the tertiary carbon, the minor regiochemistry.
Water bonding to the bromine would give bromine three bonds and does nothing to open the ring. Nucleophiles attack a ring carbon.
With no arrow breaking a C–Br bond, the tertiary carbon would end up with five bonds. The ring must open as the C–O bond forms.

q: 2-Methylpropene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in water. The step in which water opens the bromonium ion is drawn. After a final proton transfer, what is the major product?
h: Water, not bromide, is the main nucleophile because it is the solvent. Which carbon does the drawn arrow send it to?
w: Water is present in large excess, so it outcompetes bromide in opening the bromonium ion. It attacks the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, which carries more positive charge, and the C–Br bond to that carbon breaks. Bromine stays on the CH2. Loss of H+ from the oxonium ion gives the bromohydrin 1-bromo-2-methyl-2-propanol.
x: 2-Bromo-2-methyl-1-propanol has the regiochemistry reversed. The drawn arrow puts oxygen on the tertiary carbon, the more δ+ end of the bromonium ion.
The vicinal dibromide forms when bromide opens the ion, as in an inert solvent. In water the solvent is the far more abundant nucleophile.
A diol would need a second oxygen nucleophile to displace the bromine; Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O stops at the bromohydrin.

q: In the oxymercuration of 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene (Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O), water opens the mercurinium ion. Which set of curved arrows shows this step?
h: The mercurinium ion is bridged, like a bromonium ion. Where is the partial positive charge larger, and does a free carbocation ever form?
w: Like a bromonium ion, the mercurinium ion is opened at the more substituted carbon (here the secondary CH), which carries more partial positive charge, and the C–Hg bond to that carbon breaks. Because the bridge prevents a free carbocation, no methyl shift occurs even with a tert-butyl group next door. Correct set: water lone pair → secondary carbon, that C–Hg bond → Hg. Demercuration (NaBH4) then gives 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol, the unrearranged Markovnikov alcohol.
x: Attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon gives anti-Markovnikov orientation. The CH<sub>2</sub>–Hg bond is the stronger one and that carbon carries less δ+.
A methyl shift needs a free carbocation. The bridged mercurinium ion never opens to one, which is why oxymercuration avoids the rearrangement seen in acid-catalyzed hydration.
Without breaking a C–Hg bond, the attacked carbon would end with five bonds. The ring must open as the C–O bond forms.

q: The first step of HCl addition to 2-methyl-2-butene is drawn. What intermediate does this step form?
h: The arrows move pairs of electrons and give H to one alkene carbon. Put the proton where it leaves the more stable cation.
w: Full-headed arrows mean a polar, two-electron step: the π bond takes H+ and chloride leaves. The proton bonds to the CH carbon (C3), leaving the positive charge on C2, which carries two methyls and an ethyl: the tertiary 2-methyl-2-butyl cation. This is the origin of Markovnikov orientation.
x: Putting H on C2 instead would leave a secondary cation on C3. The proton adds so that the more stable (tertiary) cation forms.
A radical forms only from one-electron (fishhook) steps, as in HBr/peroxide addition. These arrows are two-electron arrows, and HCl does not add by a radical path.

A bridged halonium ion forms from X<sub>2</sub>, where the halogen that bonds to carbon still has lone pairs to share. In HCl addition, the hydrogen bonds to carbon and chloride leaves, so no Cl bridge forms.

q: A student drew water adding to the 2-methyl-2-butyl cation during acid-catalyzed hydration as shown. What is wrong with this drawing?
c: The arrow should start at an oxygen lone pair, not at the electron-poor carbocation
Water cannot react with a carbocation, so hydroxide ion must be used instead
The arrow should be a fishhook because only one new bond forms
The cation must first rearrange to a more stable cation before water can add
h: Curved arrows show where electrons come from. Which species in the drawing actually has electrons to share?
w: A curved arrow must begin at electrons (a lone pair or a bond). The carbocation has an empty p orbital and nothing to donate, while water's oxygen has two lone pairs. The new C–O bond is drawn as a full arrow from an oxygen lone pair to the cationic carbon. The error: the arrow starts at the carbocation instead of at an oxygen lone pair.
x: Water is a fine nucleophile toward a carbocation; acid-catalyzed hydration works this way, and hydroxide would not survive in the acidic solution.
A fishhook means one electron moves. Forming a two-electron C–O bond from a lone pair needs a full-headed arrow.
The 2-methyl-2-butyl cation is already tertiary; no hydride or methyl shift could make it more stable.

q: Light starts the radical bromination of an alkane by breaking the Br–Br bond. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this initiation step?
h: Light breaks this bond homolytically. How many electrons does each bromine atom keep, and which arrow shows one electron moving?
w: Initiation by light is homolysis: the two electrons of the Br–Br σ bond split evenly, one to each atom, giving two Br• radicals. One electron moving is shown by a fishhook (half-headed) arrow, so the correct drawing has two fishhook arrows starting at the Br–Br bond, one ending on each bromine. A single full arrow, or two fishhooks landing on the same atom, describes heterolysis to Br+ and Br−, which does not happen in a nonpolar radical reaction.
x: A single full arrow moves both bond electrons to one bromine: heterolysis to Br<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>−</sup>, not the two Br• radicals that start the chain.
Two full arrows would move four electrons out of a bond that holds only two. Homolysis needs fishhooks, one electron to each atom.
Both fishhooks end on the same bromine, so that atom gets both electrons. That is heterolysis (Br<sup>−</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>) drawn with the wrong arrow type, not homolysis.

q: In the first propagation step of the light-initiated bromination of 2-methylpropane, a bromine atom removes the tertiary hydrogen to give the tert-butyl radical and HBr. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: Hydrogen-atom abstraction makes one new bond (H–Br) and breaks one (C–H). Each of those two-electron bonds needs one electron from each partner.
w: H-atom abstraction is a radical step, so every arrow is a fishhook. The unpaired electron of Br• moves toward H, one electron of the C–H bond moves toward H to pair with it (forming H–Br), and the other C–H electron stays on carbon as the unpaired electron of the 3° radical. That is three fishhooks: Br• → H, C–H bond → H, C–H bond → C. Bromine abstracts the 3° H because it gives the most stable radical and bromination is highly selective.
x: Full arrows describe a polar step: a bromine lone pair attacks H and the C–H pair goes to carbon, giving a carbanion and a cationic bromine species. A radical abstraction moves single electrons.
Here Br• attacks carbon and breaks a C–CH<sub>3</sub> bond. Radicals abstract hydrogen atoms from alkanes; substitution at a crowded sp<sup>3</sup> carbon by Br• does not happen.

The first arrow starts at the hydrogen atom, which has no unpaired electron, and points toward Br•; arrows must start where electrons are. With only two arrows the new H–Br bond also gets just one electron.

q: The fishhook arrows show one step of the light-initiated bromination of 2-methylpropane. What kind of step is it?
c: Second propagation step: it uses one radical and regenerates the Br• chain carrier
Initiation step: it creates two radicals from a molecule with none
First propagation step: it removes a hydrogen atom from the alkane
Termination step: two radicals combine and the chain ends
h: Count the radicals on each side of the step, then ask which radical is made.
w: The left side has one radical (the tert-butyl radical) and the right side has one (Br•), so this is a propagation step. The alkyl radical takes a Br atom from Br2, forming the C–Br bond of the product and releasing Br• to start the next cycle: the second propagation step. The first propagation step is Br• taking an H atom from the alkane.
x: Initiation starts from a nonradical (Br<sub>2</sub> + light) and makes two radicals; here a radical is already on the left.
In the first propagation step Br• abstracts H from the alkane to make HBr. Here the alkyl radical reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> and no H moves.
Termination would combine two radicals and leave none. This step has one radical in and one radical out.

q: With HBr and a peroxide, 2-methylpropene gives 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the step in which the bromine atom adds to the alkene?
h: Which carbon must Br• bond to so that the unpaired electron ends up on the more substituted carbon? And how many electrons move in each arrow?
w: Br• adds to the less substituted CH2 end so that the new radical is tertiary (more stable); this is why the bromine ends up on C1 (anti-Markovnikov). The π bond splits: one π electron pairs with the Br electron to make the C–Br bond, the other stays on C2. So the correct drawing has three fishhooks: Br• → CH2, π bond → CH2, π bond → C2, giving BrCH2–C•(CH3)2.
x: Adding Br• to the more substituted carbon leaves a primary radical on the CH<sub>2</sub>. That radical is much less stable, and it would also lead to the Markovnikov product, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
Full arrows move electron pairs: this drawing would make a C–Br bond from a bromine lone pair and a carbanion at C2. The peroxide reaction is a radical chain, so each arrow moves one electron.

The first arrow starts at an alkene carbon and points to Br•, which reverses the flow; the electron that forms the bond comes from the radical. Two arrows also leave the π bond's split unaccounted for.

q: In the peroxide-initiated addition of HBr to 2-methylpropene, the radical formed when Br• adds to the alkene then reacts with HBr. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this second propagation step?
h: The chain can only continue if this step hands back the same chain carrier that added to the alkene. Which atom must the carbon radical take from HBr?
w: The 3° carbon radical abstracts the hydrogen atom of H–Br (the H–Br bond is weak, 366 kJ/mol, and a C–H bond of about 400 kJ/mol forms), which gives 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and regenerates Br• for the next cycle. Each bond change moves one electron: C• → H, H–Br bond → H, H–Br bond → Br, all fishhooks.
x: Taking the Br atom instead would release H•, a very high-energy radical, and the step would not regenerate Br•, so the chain could not continue.
Full arrows imply ions: the carbon has only one unpaired electron, so it cannot donate a pair, and sending the whole H–Br pair to Br makes bromide ion.
The fishhook from carbon is right, but the full arrow sends both H–Br electrons to bromine (Br<sup>−</sup>). The new C–H bond would then have only one electron, and the charges no longer balance.

q: But-1-ene reacts with NBS and light. Removal of an allylic H gives radical I, which has a second resonance form, II (I and II are resonance forms). Which set of curved arrows on I correctly converts it into II?
h: A radical is an odd-electron species. Count how many electrons move in each arrow, and make sure no σ bond is broken.
w: Radical resonance is shown with fishhooks. The unpaired electron on C3 moves into the C3–C2 bond, one π electron of C1=C2 joins it there to form the new π bond C2=C3, and the other π electron goes to C1 as the new unpaired electron. That is three fishhooks: C3• → C2–C3 bond, π bond → C2–C3 bond, π bond → C1. Only π electrons and the unpaired electron move; every σ bond stays. Because of this delocalization, NBS gives both 3-bromobut-1-ene and 1-bromobut-2-ene.
x: Full arrows move two electrons each, but C3 has only one unpaired electron. Odd-electron resonance needs fishhooks.
This breaks the σ bond to the methyl group, which is never allowed in resonance; the drawing would make a methyl radical, a different species.
One fishhook alone makes C2 part of two π bonds while it keeps its σ bonds: C2 would have five bonds. The C1=C2 π bond must also shift.

q:
The drawing shows a step that can occur in the radical bromination of methane. Which statements about this step are true?
I. It is a termination step: the number of radicals decreases by two.
II. ΔH for this step is negative, because a bond forms and none breaks.
III. It is the rate-determining step of the chain reaction.
h: Count radicals before and after, think about the energy of making a bond, and remember that radicals are present at very low concentration.
w: I is true: CH3• and Br• (two radicals) pair their electrons, shown by two fishhooks, to give CH3Br with no radicals left. II is true: bond formation with no bond breaking releases energy (about −290 kJ/mol for C–Br). III is false: termination is rare because two radicals, each at a tiny concentration, must meet; the rate of the chain is set by the propagation steps (H abstraction for bromination). So the answer is I and II only.
x: Misjudges II: forming a C–Br bond without breaking any bond is exothermic, so ΔH is negative.
Misjudges III: termination steps are rare events that stop chains; they are not the rate-determining step of the propagation cycle.
Misjudges I: two radicals combine into one nonradical molecule, which is the definition of termination.

q: In peroxide-initiated HBr addition, the O–O bond of di-tert-butyl peroxide breaks first. The tert-butoxyl radical then reacts with HBr as shown by the fishhook arrows. What are the products of this step?
h: Follow the arrows: which atom does the oxygen radical bond to, and where does the other H–Br electron end up?
w: The oxygen's unpaired electron and one H–Br electron form a new O–H bond; the other H–Br electron stays on bromine. The products are tert-butyl alcohol and Br•. This second initiation step makes the bromine atom that carries the chain (the strong O–H bond, about 440 kJ/mol, makes the step favorable).
x: The arrow from oxygen ends on H, not Br. Taking Br would leave H•, a very unstable radical, and the drawing does not show it.
No arrow touches the C–O bond, so the tert-butyl group stays on oxygen.
Fishhooks move one electron each, so bromine keeps one electron as Br•. Reading them as full arrows gives bromide, and the charges would then not balance (neutral reactants, one anion product).

q: The enolate ion of acetone has the two resonance forms I and II. Which set of curved arrows on I correctly converts it into II?
h: When a lone pair makes a new π bond to the carbonyl carbon, that carbon must give up a bond. Which bond may move in resonance?
w: Resonance moves only lone pairs and π electrons, two at a time, with full arrows. The carbanion lone pair forms the C=C π bond, and at the same time the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen so the central carbon keeps four bonds: lone pair → C–C bond, C=O π bond → O. This gives II, with the negative charge on the more electronegative oxygen (the major contributor).
x: The second arrow breaks the σ bond to the methyl group. σ bonds never move in resonance; that would make a different species (a methyl anion).
With only the first arrow, the carbonyl carbon would have five bonds (C=C, C=O and C–CH<sub>3</sub>). The C=O π bond must move to oxygen.
Fishhooks move one electron each; the enolate is an even-electron ion, and its lone pair and π bond move as pairs, so full arrows are needed.

q: The arrows on N-methylacetamide (I) generate a second resonance form. Which structure is that resonance form?
h: Apply both arrows: a lone pair becomes a π bond, and a π bond becomes a lone pair. Atoms and H's stay where they are; only charges change.
w: The nitrogen lone pair becomes a C=N π bond (N gains a + charge, since it now has four bonds), and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen (O becomes −). Every atom and every H stays put, so the resonance form is CH3C(O−)=N+HCH3. This contributor explains the planar amide nitrogen, the restricted C–N rotation and the weak basicity of amide N.
x: This is the result of moving only the C=O π electrons; the nitrogen lone pair arrow was ignored, leaving a carbocation.
The imidic acid has the H moved from N to O. Moving an atom makes a tautomer (a different compound), not a resonance form.
This form has lost the N–H hydrogen and carries an overall −1 charge. Resonance forms must have the same atoms and the same net charge (0 here).

q: Each drawing shows curved arrows proposed for drawing a resonance form of the species shown. Which set of arrows is not valid?
h: For each drawing, count the bonds and lone pairs on every atom after the arrows. Can a second-row atom hold more than eight electrons?
w: In nitromethane the O− lone pair is pushed into the N–O bond, but the N=O π bond is not moved away. Nitrogen would then have five bonds (10 electrons), which a second-row atom cannot hold. So the nitromethane drawing is invalid; it needs a second arrow moving the N=O π electrons onto the other oxygen. The acetate arrows (O− lone pair in, C=O π out), the allyl cation arrow (π bond toward the empty p orbital) and the methoxymethyl cation arrow (O lone pair toward C+) all keep every atom within an octet.
x: Valid: the O<sup>−</sup> lone pair forms a C=O π bond while the other C=O π pair moves to oxygen, so carbon keeps four bonds and the charge moves to the other oxygen.
Valid: the π electrons shift toward the cationic carbon, which has an empty p orbital, so the positive charge moves to the other end carbon.
Valid: the oxygen lone pair fills the empty p orbital of the adjacent carbocation, giving an oxocarbenium ion in which every atom has an octet.

q: Nitromethane has two equivalent resonance forms, I and II, which differ in which oxygen (a or b) carries the negative charge. Which set of curved arrows on I correctly converts it into II?
h: Nitrogen already has four bonds in I. If a new π bond forms to it, which of its existing bonds may give up its electrons?
w: The lone pair on Ob forms an N=Ob π bond, and the N=Oa π electrons move onto Oa, so nitrogen keeps four bonds and its + charge while the − charge moves from b to a: lone pair on b → N–Ob bond, N=Oa π bond → Oa. These two equal forms explain why both N–O bonds in nitromethane have the same length.
x: Only the first arrow gives nitrogen five bonds (10 valence electrons), which exceeds the octet of a second-row atom.
The second arrow breaks the C–N σ bond. σ bonds are never broken in resonance, and the drawing does not lead to II.
Moving only the N=Oa π pair onto oxygen leaves nitrogen with three bonds and no lone pair (a +2 formal charge and a sextet) and gives two negative oxygens, not II.

q: But-3-en-2-one (methyl vinyl ketone, I) has the resonance form II, which shows why its terminal carbon is electrophilic. Which set of curved arrows on I correctly converts it into II?
h: Electrons in a conjugated carbonyl flow toward oxygen. Which two π bonds have to move, and in which direction, for the + charge to end up on the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>?
w: The C=O π electrons move onto the electronegative oxygen, and the C=C π electrons shift one bond toward the carbonyl carbon to replace the lost π bond. The carbonyl carbon keeps four bonds, the terminal CH2 loses its π bond and becomes C+, and O becomes O−: C=C π bond → C2–C3 bond, C=O π bond → O. This form shows why nucleophiles add to the β-carbon (conjugate addition).
x: Moving only the C=C π bond toward the carbonyl carbon gives that carbon five bonds. The C=O π pair must leave at the same time.
This arrow alone gives a valid form, but a different one: the + charge sits on the carbonyl carbon, not on the terminal CH<sub>2</sub> as in II.
These arrows push electrons away from oxygen: the carbonyl carbon would get five bonds, oxygen would become positive and the terminal carbon negative, the opposite of II.

q: A student draws the arrows shown on acetone and labels acetone and its enol, prop-1-en-2-ol, as resonance forms. What is wrong with this?
c: A hydrogen atom changes position (a C–H σ bond breaks), so the two are tautomers, not resonance forms
Nothing is wrong: the enol is a minor resonance contributor to acetone
The arrows should be fishhooks, because the forms have no formal charges
The enol drawn has a carbon with five bonds, so it is not a valid structure
h: Compare the positions of all atoms in the two structures. What may change between resonance forms, and what may not?
w: Resonance forms differ only in where π electrons and lone pairs are drawn; every atom stays in the same place and no σ bond breaks. Here the C–H σ bond breaks and the H moves from carbon to oxygen. Acetone and its enol are therefore tautomers: two different compounds in equilibrium, each with its own structure, not two pictures of one molecule. The keto–enol interconversion needs an acid or base catalyst and takes time; resonance does not happen at all in time.
x: Because an atom has moved, the enol is a separate compound, not a contributor to acetone's structure. It is present only in tiny amounts at equilibrium.
Fishhooks are for moving single electrons (radicals). The arrow type has nothing to do with whether the forms carry charges; the real problem is the σ bond broken.
Prop-1-en-2-ol is a valid structure: each carbon has four bonds and oxygen two. The issue is the H shift, not the valence.

q: The curved arrow converts the methoxymethyl cation I into its resonance form II. Which statement about I and II is correct?
c: II is the major contributor, because every atom in II has a complete octet
I is the major contributor, because a positive charge is more stable on carbon than on oxygen
I and II are constitutional isomers that interconvert rapidly
II is not a valid form, because oxygen cannot form three bonds
h: For carbocations next to a lone-pair donor, which matters more: where the charge sits, or whether every atom has an octet?
w: In I the CH2+ carbon has only six electrons. In II the oxygen lone pair has become a C=O π bond, so carbon and oxygen both have octets. A full set of octets outweighs placing + on the more electronegative atom, so II (the oxocarbenium form) is the major contributor. This is why an α-oxygen strongly stabilizes a carbocation (for example in SN1 reactions of α-chloro ethers and in acetal chemistry).
x: Charge placement is a lower priority than complete octets. Carbon in I has only a sextet, so I contributes less.
I and II have the same atoms connected the same way; only electrons are redrawn. They are resonance forms of one ion, not isomers.
Oxygen with three bonds and one lone pair (as in H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) is a normal oxonium oxygen with a +1 formal charge.

q: Each species I–III is drawn with curved arrows. Which arrow sets give a valid resonance form of the species drawn?
h: For each set ask two questions: does any σ bond break, and does any atom end up with more than eight electrons?
w: I is valid: the O− lone pair forms a C=O π bond and the C=C π pair moves to the end carbon, giving the carbanion form of the acetaldehyde enolate; no σ bond breaks and every atom keeps an octet. II is not valid: the arrow starts at a C–H σ bond. Moving σ electrons breaks the bond (the H would leave as H+, which is deprotonation, an E1 step), so this is a reaction, not resonance. III is valid: the C=O+H π pair moves onto oxygen, giving a carbocation and a neutral OH. It is a minor contributor (carbon has a sextet) but a correct resonance form. Answer: I and III only.
x: Misjudges III: moving a π pair onto an electronegative atom is a legal resonance move, even though the resulting form (a carbocation) is minor.
Misjudges II: the arrow starts at a σ bond. Breaking a σ bond changes the atoms' connections, so it is a reaction step, not resonance.
Misjudges I: the enolate oxygen's lone pair and the C=C π bond can both move, which is the standard enolate resonance.

q: The 3-methylbutan-2-yl cation (formed when 3-methylbutan-2-ol is heated with acid) rearranges by a 1,2-shift. Which curved arrow correctly shows the shift that gives a more stable carbocation?
h: A 1,2-shift moves a group with its bonding pair toward the positive carbon. Which group's move leaves the + charge on a more substituted carbon?
w: In a hydride shift the C–H bond on the neighboring carbon moves, with both electrons, to the empty p orbital of C+. The arrow starts at the C3–H bond and ends on the cationic C2. C3 is attached to three carbons, so the shift leaves a 3° cation, (CH3)2C+CH2CH3, which is more stable than the 2° starting cation.
x: The arrow starts at the positive carbon, which has no electrons to give. Arrows begin at the electrons that move: here the C–H bonding pair.
Shifting the methyl from C3 to C2 gives CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, which is the same 2° cation again; nothing is gained. The H shift gives a 3° cation.
Shifting an H from the C1 methyl would leave the + charge on a primary carbon, which is much less stable than the 2° starting cation.

q: When 1-cyclobutylethanol is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the cation shown forms and then undergoes the alkyl shift indicated by the arrow. Which cation forms directly in this step?
h: Follow the bond that moves: which ring carbon stays attached to the old cationic carbon, and which ring carbon loses a bond and becomes positive?
