w: The ring C–C bond shifts its electrons to the cationic carbon. The CH2 at the end of that bond becomes bonded to the old C+, which is now inside the ring, so the four-membered ring grows to five. The ring carbon that lost the bond (the old point of attachment) becomes the new C+, next to the carbon carrying the CH3: the 2-methylcyclopentyl cation. The cation is still 2°, but relieving the large cyclobutane ring strain drives the step. A later hydride shift can give the 3° 1-methylcyclopentyl cation, but that is a second step.
x: The 1-methylcyclopentyl cation forms only after a further 1,2-hydride shift; the alkyl shift itself leaves the charge on the carbon that lost the bond.
One ring bond moves to the side-chain carbon, so the ring gains one atom (4 → 5), not two. The methyl carbon stays outside the ring.
The positive charge ends on the carbon that gave up the migrating bond, which is next to the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) carbon, not one carbon further away.

q: The 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-yl cation rearranges to a tertiary cation. Which curved arrow correctly shows this 1,2-methyl shift?
h: Curved arrows show electrons, not atoms. Where are the electrons that travel with the methyl group?
w: In a 1,2-alkyl shift the methyl group moves with its bonding pair. The arrow must start at the C3–CH3 σ bond and end on the cationic C2. C3, bonded to three carbons after the shift, becomes the new C+: the 3° 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-yl cation.
x: The arrow starts at the positive carbon, which has no electrons to donate; arrows always begin at an electron source.
Drawing the arrow from the methyl carbon atom shows the atom moving. A curved arrow must start at electrons, here the C–CH<sub>3</sub> bonding pair.
This sends the C–CH<sub>3</sub> bonding pair away onto the methyl group, as if CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> left. That would make a second carbocation (a dication) instead of filling the existing one.

q: The step shown occurs in the SN1 hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide. Which species is the nucleophile, and what forms in this step?
c: Water is the nucleophile; the alkyloxonium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> forms
The carbocation is the nucleophile; the alkyloxonium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> forms
Water is the nucleophile; neutral tert-butyl alcohol forms directly in this step
Water acts as a base; 2-methylpropene forms in this step
h: The arrow starts at the electron-pair donor. Then count the bonds on oxygen after it forms the new bond.
w: The arrow starts at a lone pair on water and ends at the empty p orbital of the carbocation, so water is the nucleophile (Lewis base) and the carbocation is the electrophile (Lewis acid). Oxygen now has three bonds and one lone pair, so the product of this step is the alkyloxonium ion, (CH3)3COH2+. A separate step, deprotonation by another water molecule, gives tert-butyl alcohol.
x: The carbocation has an empty orbital and no lone pair; it accepts the electron pair, so it is the electrophile.
Only one arrow is drawn, so no O–H bond breaks in this step. The neutral alcohol appears only after a second water removes a proton.
A base would take a proton from a carbon next to C<sup>+</sup> (E1). Here the arrow goes to the cationic carbon itself, not to an H.

q: A student proposes the hydride shift shown for the 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation. Why is this step not expected to occur to a significant extent?
c: It turns a 3° carbocation into a less stable 2° carbocation, an uphill step
A hydride shift must be drawn with a fishhook arrow, because only one electron moves
The arrow is drawn backwards; it should start at the positive carbon
Only methyl groups, not hydrogens, can undergo 1,2-shifts
h: Classify the cation before and after the shift.
w: The starting cation, (CH3)2C+CH2CH3, is tertiary. After the shift the charge sits on a carbon bonded to only two carbons, a secondary cation. Carbocation shifts go toward greater stability (2° → 3°, or relief of ring strain), so a 3° → 2° shift is uphill and does not compete with capture of the 3° cation. The arrow itself is drawn correctly.
x: A hydride moves with both of its bonding electrons (H:<sup>−</sup>), so a full arrow is correct here.
The arrow correctly starts at the C–H bonding pair; the positive carbon has no electrons to give.
Hydride shifts are common (often faster than alkyl shifts); the problem here is the direction of stability, not the group.

q: Sodium propynide reacts with bromoethane to give pent-2-yne. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this S<sub>N</sub>2 step?
h: Find the nucleophile's lone pair and the electrophilic carbon. What must happen to the C–Br bond as the new C–C bond forms?
w: The acetylide carbon's lone pair attacks the electrophilic CH2 (backside to C–Br), and in the same step the C–Br bonding pair leaves with bromide. Two arrows: acetylide lone pair → CH2, C–Br bond → Br. This forms CH3C≡CCH2CH3 (pent-2-yne). The primary halide matters: with 2° or 3° halides the strongly basic acetylide gives mostly E2.
x: Without the C–Br arrow the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon would have five bonds. The leaving group must take the bonding pair as the new bond forms.
Attack at bromine (with the C–Br pair going to carbon) would make a carbanion and a C–Br bond on the alkyne, not the C–C bond of pent-2-yne.
The arrow starts at the electron-poor CH<sub>2</sub> carbon and points to the anion. Arrows run from the electron-rich nucleophile to the electrophile.

q: Hydration of propyne (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O, HgSO<sub>4</sub>) first gives the enol prop-1-en-2-ol, which tautomerizes to acetone in acid. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows the first step of this acid-catalyzed tautomerization?
h: The overall change puts a new H on the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon and removes the H from oxygen. Which atom of the enol must be protonated first?
w: In acid, the enol's C=C π bond (made electron-rich by the OH) takes a proton from H3O+ at the CH2 carbon, and the H–O bonding pair stays on the water oxygen: π bond → H, H–O bond → O. The cation formed is resonance-stabilized by the oxygen lone pair (protonated acetone). Water then removes the O–H proton to give acetone. Net result: H moves from O to C.
x: Protonating the OH oxygen gives an oxonium ion that does not lead to acetone; the H must be added to carbon for the keto form to result.
Without the H–O arrow, the hydrogen of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> would have two bonds. The O–H bond must break as the C–H bond forms.
This arrow sends the H–O bonding pair toward the alkene, the reverse direction. The alkene π electrons are the electron source; the acidic H is the target.

q: HgSO<sub>4</sub>-catalyzed hydration of but-1-yne goes through an enol that tautomerizes in acid. The arrows show the last step of the tautomerization. What is the organic product of this step?
h: Water removes the proton on oxygen. What is left when the O–H bonding pair returns to oxygen?
w: Water takes the O–H proton, and the O–H bonding pair becomes a lone pair on oxygen, leaving a neutral C=O. The product is the ketone butan-2-one, the Markovnikov hydration product of a terminal alkyne (the OH first went to the more substituted carbon).
x: Butanal is the anti-Markovnikov product, made from but-1-yne by hydroboration–oxidation (via the other enol), not by HgSO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.
The enol is the starting point of tautomerization, not its end. Removing the O–H proton from the protonated ketone gives the C=O, not a C=C.
Butan-2-ol would need two more hydrogens (a reduction). Tautomerization only moves one H from O to C.

q: Sodium amide (NaNH<sub>2</sub>) converts but-1-yne into its acetylide ion. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this step?
h: This is an acid–base reaction. Where does the base attack, and where do the electrons of the broken bond go?
w: The amide ion (conjugate acid NH3, pKa ≈ 38) is strong enough to remove the terminal alkyne H (pKa ≈ 25). The N lone pair forms a bond to the H, and the C–H bonding pair stays on the sp carbon as the acetylide lone pair: N lone pair → H, C–H bond → C.
x: Without the C–H arrow the hydrogen would have two bonds. The C–H pair must move onto carbon as the N–H bond forms.
This shows the amide adding to the triple bond, which gives a vinyl anion. Nonactivated alkynes are not attacked by NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>; it removes the acidic sp C–H instead.
The C–H pair is sent onto the hydrogen, which would then carry four electrons. The bonding pair must stay on carbon to make the acetylide.

q: In which of the species shown is the charge delocalized by resonance?
h: For each species, count the atoms between the charged atom and the nearest C=C. Resonance needs the charged atom to be bonded directly to a π-bonded atom.
w:
Delocalization needs the charged atom (its empty p orbital or its lone pair) to sit directly next to a π bond, so the p orbitals overlap in a row.
I is false: an sp3 CH2 separates the CH2+ from the C=C, so the empty p orbital cannot overlap the π bond and the positive charge stays on one carbon.
II is false: the O− is on an sp3 carbon, one atom away from the C=C. This is an alkoxide, not an enolate, and no resonance form can move the charge.
III is true: in the allyl anion the carbanion carbon is bonded directly to the alkene carbon, so a second contributor puts the negative charge on the other end CH2.
Answer: III only.
x: I is a homoallylic cation. The sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub> between the C=C and the cationic carbon breaks the conjugation, so no resonance form moves the + charge.
II is an alkoxide on a carbon next to the alkene, not an enolate. Its oxygen is not attached to a π-bonded atom, so the charge cannot be delocalized.
Neither I nor II has its charged atom next to the π bond. Only the allyl anion (III) is delocalized.

q:
Consider N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), shown. Which statements are correct?
I. The nitrogen is sp2 hybridized, and its three bonds lie in one plane.
II. At room temperature the two N–CH3 groups are in different environments, because rotation about the C(O)–N bond is slow.
III. The nitrogen of DMF is a much weaker base than the nitrogen of trimethylamine.
h: Draw the second resonance contributor of the amide (N lone pair into the C=O). What does it say about the C–N bond and the N lone pair?
w:
The amide resonance contributor O−–CH=N+(CH3)2 controls all three statements.
I is true: the N lone pair sits in a p orbital so that it can overlap the C=O π system. Nitrogen is sp2 and trigonal planar, not a pyramidal sp3 amine.
II is true: the C–N bond has partial double-bond character (rotation barrier about 80–90 kJ/mol). One CH3 is cis to O and the other is trans, and they do not swap quickly at room temperature (DMF shows two CH3 singlets in its 1H NMR spectrum).
III is true: the lone pair is delocalized onto oxygen, so amide nitrogen is barely basic. A protonated amide has pKa near −0.5, compared with 9.8 for trimethylammonium.
Answer: I, II, and III.
x: Statement III is also true. Delocalization of the N lone pair into the C=O makes amide nitrogen far less basic than an amine nitrogen.
Statement II is also true. Partial C=N double-bond character slows rotation, so the CH3 cis to O and the CH3 trans to O stay distinct at room temperature.
Statement I is also true. The lone pair is in a p orbital overlapping the C=O π bond, so N is sp<sup>2</sup> and planar, not sp<sup>3</sup>.

q:
Which statements about the molecules shown are correct?
I. In I, the three atoms C–C≡N lie on a straight line.
II. In II, the central carbon (bonded to both CH2 and O) is sp2 hybridized.
III. In III, the oxygen is sp3 hybridized and the C–O–C angle is close to 110°.
h: Count electron domains (σ bonds plus lone pairs; a double or triple bond counts once) on each atom named.
w:
Hybridization follows the number of electron domains: 2 → sp (180°), 3 → sp2 (120°), 4 → sp3 (about 109.5°).
I is true: the nitrile carbon has two domains (the C–C single bond and the C≡N triple bond), so it is sp and the C–C≡N unit is linear.
II is false: the central carbon of ketene has two double bonds (C=C and C=O) and no lone pairs, so it has only two domains. It is sp and linear, like the central carbon of CO2 or an allene.
III is true: the ether oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs (four domains), so it is sp3; the C–O–C angle in dimethyl ether is about 111°.
Answer: I and III only.
x: III is also true: oxygen with two σ bonds and two lone pairs has four electron domains (sp<sup>3</sup>), and the C–O–C angle is near 110°.
I is also true: the nitrile carbon has only two electron domains, so the C–C≡N atoms are collinear.
II is false: a carbon with two double bonds has two electron domains and is sp, not sp<sup>2</sup>.

q:
Which statements are correct?
I. The C2–C3 single bond of buta-1,3-diene is shorter than the C–C bond of ethane.
II. The C–H bond of ethyne is longer than a C–H bond of ethane.
III. (E)-1,2-Dichloroethene has a larger dipole moment than (Z)-1,2-dichloroethene.
h: More s character in the hybrid orbitals makes a bond shorter. For dipoles, add the bond dipoles as vectors.
w:
I is true: the C2–C3 bond of butadiene joins two sp2 carbons (and has a little conjugation), so it is about 148 pm long, compared with 154 pm for the sp3–sp3 bond of ethane.
II is false: the ethyne C–H bond uses an sp orbital (50% s), which holds electrons closer to carbon. It is shorter (about 106 pm) and stronger than the sp3 C–H of ethane (about 110 pm).
III is false: in the E isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so its dipole moment is zero. The Z isomer, with both Cl on one side, has a net dipole of about 1.9 D.
Answer: I only.
x: II is false. More s character puts the bonding electrons closer to carbon, so the sp C–H bond of ethyne is shorter than the sp<sup>3</sup> C–H bond of ethane.
III is false. The two C–Cl bond dipoles of the E isomer are antiparallel and cancel; the Z isomer is the polar one.
I is true and II is false. The sp<sup>2</sup>–sp<sup>2</sup> C2–C3 bond of butadiene (about 148 pm) is shorter than the ethane C–C bond, while sp C–H bonds are shorter than sp<sup>3</sup> C–H bonds.

q: The three C5H12O isomers shown have the same molar mass. Rank them in order of increasing boiling point (lowest first).
h: First ask which compounds can donate a hydrogen bond. Then ask how branching changes the contact between molecules.
w:
The ether III has no O–H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other; it boils lowest (1-methoxybutane, about 70 °C). Both alcohols hydrogen bond, so they boil higher. Between them, the compact, branched tertiary alcohol II has less surface contact (weaker London forces) and a more crowded O–H, so it boils lower (2-methylbutan-2-ol, about 102 °C) than the straight-chain pentan-1-ol I (about 138 °C).
Answer: III < II < I.
x: This puts the tertiary alcohol below the ether. II can still donate a hydrogen bond, which the ether III cannot, so II boils well above III.
Branching lowers the boiling point (smaller contact area), so the branched alcohol II boils below the straight-chain alcohol I, not above it.
This is the reverse order. Hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point, so the alcohols boil above the ether, and the straight-chain alcohol boils highest.

q:
Each structure is given a name. Which names are correct IUPAC names for the structure shown?
I. 3-methylpentane
II. (Z)-5-methylhex-2-ene
III. 4-ethylhexane
h: Check three things in each name: the longest chain, the numbering direction (lowest locants), and, for the alkene, which side each chain carbon is on.
w:
I is correct: the longest chain has five carbons and the methyl is on C3 from either end.
II is incorrect: the chain is numbered from the end nearer the double bond (C2=C3, methyl on C5), so 5-methylhex-2-ene is right, but the drawn alkene has C1 and C4 on opposite sides of the double bond. It is (E), not (Z).
III is incorrect: the longest chain has six carbons, and it must be numbered from the end that gives the ethyl group the lower locant, so the name is 3-ethylhexane.
Answer: I only.
x: II has the right chain and locants but the wrong stereodescriptor: the higher-priority groups on C2 and C3 are on opposite sides, so the alkene is E.
III is numbered from the wrong end. Numbering from the other end puts the ethyl on C3, so the name is 3-ethylhexane.
I is correct (3-methylpentane), while II has the wrong E/Z label and III the wrong numbering.

q:
A compound has the molecular formula C5H8O. Which statements are correct?
I. It has two degrees of unsaturation.
II. It could be pentanal.
III. It could be cyclopent-2-en-1-ol.
h: Degrees of unsaturation = (2C + 2 − H)/2; oxygen does not change it. Then count rings and π bonds in each candidate.
w:
I is true: (2 × 5 + 2 − 8)/2 = 2, so the compound has two rings and/or π bonds in total.
II is false: pentanal has only one degree of unsaturation (one C=O) and the formula C5H10O.
III is true: cyclopent-2-en-1-ol has one ring and one C=C (two degrees of unsaturation) and the formula C5H8O.
Answer: I and III only.
x: III is also true: one ring plus one C=C gives two degrees of unsaturation, and cyclopent-2-en-1-ol is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O.
II is false: pentanal has one C=O and no ring, so it is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O, two H more than the formula given.
I is true (DBE = 2), and pentanal (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O) does not fit the formula.

q:
Which statements about the functional groups in the compound shown are correct?
I. It contains an ester.
II. It contains a secondary amide.
III. It contains an aldehyde.
h: Look at what is attached to each oxygen and to each C=O carbon. An ester needs an O–C bond on the carbonyl carbon.
w:
I is false: the OCH3 on the ring is an aryl ether (aryl–O–CH3). Neither carbon on that oxygen is a C=O, so it is not an ester.
II is true: the acetyl C=O is bonded to N, which also carries one H and the ring carbon. An amide whose N bears one carbon substituent besides the acyl group is a secondary (2°) amide (an acetamido group).
III is true: the CHO on the ring is a carbonyl bonded to one H, an aldehyde.
Answer: II and III only.
x: II is also true. The N–H nitrogen bonded to the acetyl C=O and to the ring is a secondary amide, not an amine.
III is also true. The ring CHO has a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, so it is an aldehyde, not a ketone.
I is false. The OCH<sub>3</sub> oxygen is bonded to the ring and to CH<sub>3</sub>, with no C=O on either side, so it is an ether, not an ester.

q:
Which of the names given are correct IUPAC names for the structures shown?
I. pent-1-en-4-ol
II. cyclopentylmethanol
III. 2-methylbutan-3-ol
h: The OH is the principal group: it gets the lowest possible locant, even if that gives a double bond or a methyl group a higher number.
w:
I is incorrect: numbering must give the OH (the principal group) the lowest locant, so number from the CH3 end: OH on C2, C=C starting at C4. The name is pent-4-en-2-ol.
II is correct: the OH is on the CH2 outside the ring, so the parent is methanol with a cyclopentyl substituent.
III is incorrect: numbering from the end nearer the OH puts it on C2 and the methyl on C3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-2-ol.
Answer: II only.
x: I gives the double bond the lower locant, but the OH outranks the C=C for numbering. The correct name is pent-4-en-2-ol.
III gives the methyl the lower locant, but the OH must get the lowest number. The correct name is 3-methylbutan-2-ol.
Only II is right; both I and III number the chain from the end farther from the OH.

q: Rank the compounds in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
h: All three are O–H acids, so compare how well each conjugate base spreads out its negative charge: by resonance, by induction, or not at all.
w:
Each conjugate base is an oxyanion, so the difference lies in what stabilizes the charge. Ethoxide (from III) has the charge localized on O: pKa about 16, weakest acid. 2,2,2-Trifluoroethoxide (from I) is stabilized by the inductive pull of three F atoms two bonds away: pKa about 12.4. Phenoxide (from II) delocalizes the charge by resonance onto the ortho and para ring carbons: pKa about 10, strongest acid.
Answer: III < I < II.
x: This makes trifluoroethanol stronger than phenol. Induction through two σ bonds lowers the pK<sub>a</sub> to about 12.4, but resonance delocalization in phenoxide lowers it further, to about 10.
This makes trifluoroethanol weaker than ethanol. The electron-withdrawing CF<sub>3</sub> group stabilizes the alkoxide, so it makes the alcohol more acidic, not less.
This is the reverse order. Phenol is the strongest acid of the three and ethanol the weakest.

q: Rank the compounds in order of increasing acidity of their most acidic hydrogen (weakest acid first).
h: Find the most acidic H in each, then ask where the negative charge sits in each conjugate base: on which atom, in what orbital, and whether it is delocalized.
w:
Ethyne (I): the acetylide charge sits in an sp orbital on carbon, localized: pKa about 25. Acetone (II): removing an α-H gives an enolate whose charge is shared by carbon and oxygen through resonance: pKa about 19–20. Ethanol (III): the charge of ethoxide sits entirely on oxygen, a much more electronegative atom than carbon: pKa about 16. Here having the charge on oxygen wins over resonance that puts only part of it on oxygen, so ethanol is the strongest acid.
Answer: I < II < III.
x: This puts acetone below ethyne. The enolate spreads its charge onto oxygen by resonance, which beats an sp carbanion (pK<sub>a</sub> 19–20 vs 25).

This makes acetone more acidic than ethanol. The enolate is resonance-stabilized, but ethoxide holds its whole charge on electronegative oxygen; ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> about 16) is more acidic than acetone (19–20).
This is the reverse order. Ethyne is the weakest acid of the three and ethanol the strongest.

q:
A terminal alkyne (pKa ≈ 25) must be converted completely to its acetylide ion. Which bases can do this?
I. NaOH
II. NaNH2
III. CH3Li
h: A base works when its conjugate acid is weaker (higher pK<sub>a</sub>) than the alkyne. Find the conjugate acid of each base.
w:
The equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid, so the base's conjugate acid must have a pKa well above 25.
I fails: hydroxide's conjugate acid is water (pKa 15.7), a stronger acid than the alkyne, so the equilibrium favors the alkyne.
II works: amide's conjugate acid is NH3 (pKa about 38).
III works: methyllithium's conjugate acid is CH4 (pKa about 50).
Answer: II and III only.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>Li also works: its conjugate acid, methane (pK<sub>a</sub> about 50), is far weaker than the alkyne.
NaOH does not work: water (pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) is a stronger acid than the alkyne, so hydroxide leaves the alkyne almost entirely protonated.
NaNH<sub>2</sub> also works: NH<sub>3</sub> (pK<sub>a</sub> about 38) is a much weaker acid than the alkyne, so amide deprotonates it completely.

q:
Which statements about acids and bases in different solvents are correct?
I. CH3Li cannot be used as a base in water, because water protonates it at once to give CH4 and LiOH.
II. In water, HCl and HBr appear equally strong, because both are converted completely to H3O+.
III. In pure acetic acid as the solvent, HCl and HClO4 are equally strong acids.
h: A solvent levels any acid stronger than its own protonated form, and any base stronger than its own deprotonated form. How basic is acetic acid compared with water?
w:
This is the leveling effect.
I is true: CH3− (conjugate acid pKa about 50) is far stronger than OH−, so water protonates it completely; the strongest base that survives in water is hydroxide.
II is true: both acids are much stronger than H3O+, so each ionizes completely and the solution contains only H3O+; their real difference is hidden.
III is false: acetic acid is a much weaker base than water, so it does not ionize strong acids completely. In acetic acid the acids are differentiated, and HClO4 is clearly the stronger acid.
Answer: I and II only.
x: II is also true: in water both HCl and HBr are leveled to H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, so they appear equally strong.
I is also true: any base stronger than hydroxide, such as CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, is protonated by water at once.
III is false: acetic acid is too weakly basic to level strong acids, so it differentiates them; HClO<sub>4</sub> is the stronger acid there.

q: Which of the species shown can act as a Lewis base?
h: A Lewis base donates an electron pair; a Lewis acid accepts one. Look for an available lone pair or an empty orbital on the central atom.
w:
I is not a Lewis base: boron in BF3 has only six valence electrons and an empty p orbital, so it accepts a pair (a Lewis acid).
II is not a Lewis base: the tert-butyl cation also has an empty p orbital on the cationic carbon and accepts a pair from a nucleophile.
III is a Lewis base: the nitrogen of trimethylamine has a lone pair it can donate, for example to BF3 to give F3B–N(CH3)3.
Answer: III only.
x: BF<sub>3</sub> is an electron-pair acceptor (empty p orbital on boron), a Lewis acid, not a base.
A carbocation has an empty p orbital and reacts with electron-pair donors, so it is a Lewis acid.
This swaps acid and base: BF<sub>3</sub> accepts electron pairs, while trimethylamine, with its lone pair, is the Lewis base.

q: Three conformations of butane, viewed along the C2–C3 bond, are shown. Rank them from lowest to highest energy.
h: Decide first which projections are staggered and which is eclipsed. Then look at how close the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are.
w:
I is staggered with the CH3 groups 180° apart (anti): lowest energy. II is staggered with the CH3 groups 60° apart (gauche): about 3.8 kJ/mol higher, from steric strain. III is eclipsed (two CH3/H and one H/H eclipsing interactions): about 16 kJ/mol above anti, because eclipsing adds torsional strain that any staggered form avoids.
Answer: I < II < III.
x: Gauche is higher than anti: the CH<sub>3</sub> groups 60° apart crowd each other, so II lies about 3.8 kJ/mol above I.
Any eclipsed conformation of butane is higher in energy than any staggered one; III (about 16 kJ/mol) is above gauche II (3.8 kJ/mol).
This is the reverse order. The anti conformation is the most stable and the eclipsed one the least.

q:
Three staggered conformations of 2,3-dimethylbutane, viewed along the C2–C3 bond, are shown. Which statements are correct?
I. Conformation II is the most stable of the three.
II. Conformation I has exactly two gauche CH3/CH3 interactions.
III. Conformations I and III have the same energy.
h: In each projection, look at each back CH<sub>3</sub> and count the front CH<sub>3</sub> groups 60° from it. Each such pair is one gauche interaction.
w:
Count gauche CH3/CH3 pairs (each about 3.8 kJ/mol). In I, the back CH3 at upper left sits between both front CH3 groups (2 gauche), and the back CH3 at the bottom is next to one front CH3 (1 gauche): 3 in all. In II, the two H atoms are anti to each other and each back CH3 is gauche to only one front CH3: 2 in all. In III, the count is again 1 + 2 = 3.
I is true: II has the fewest gauche interactions (about 7.6 kJ/mol vs 11.4 kJ/mol).
II is false: conformation I has three gauche interactions, not two.
III is true: I and III each have three gauche interactions; they are mirror-image conformations and have the same energy.
Answer: I and III only.
x: III is also true: conformations I and III each have three gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> interactions (they are mirror images), so their energies are equal.
I is also true: in II the H atoms are anti, leaving only two gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> interactions, the fewest of the three.
II is false: in conformation I the upper-left back CH<sub>3</sub> is gauche to both front CH<sub>3</sub> groups and the bottom back CH<sub>3</sub> to one more, three in all.

q:
The chair shown is one conformation of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane. Which statements are correct?
I. Both CH3 groups in this chair are equatorial.
II. After a ring flip, both CH3 groups are axial.
III. The two chair conformations of this compound are equal in energy.
h: A ring flip changes every axial position to equatorial and back, but keeps each group on the same face. Then compare the strain in the two chairs.
w:
I is true: in the chair shown, the up CH3 on C1 and the down CH3 on C2 both point outward along the ring's equator.
II is true: a ring flip turns every equatorial position axial, so both CH3 groups become axial (still up on C1 and down on C2).
III is false: the diaxial chair has four 1,3-diaxial CH3/H interactions (about 2 × 7.6 = 15.2 kJ/mol), while the diequatorial chair has only one gauche CH3/CH3 interaction (about 3.8 kJ/mol). The diequatorial chair is lower by roughly 11 kJ/mol.
Answer: I and II only.
x: II is also true: trans-1,2 substituents are either both equatorial or both axial, so flipping the diequatorial chair gives the diaxial chair.
I is also true: in the chair drawn, both methyl groups occupy equatorial positions.
III is false: the diaxial chair carries two axial CH<sub>3</sub> groups (four 1,3-diaxial interactions), so it is much less stable than the diequatorial chair.

q:
The chair shown is one conformation of cis-1-tert-butyl-4-methylcyclohexane. Which statements are correct?
I. The chair shown is the more stable chair of this compound.
II. In the more stable chair, the CH3 group is axial.
III. The trans isomer is more stable than the cis isomer.
h: Find which group is axial in the chair drawn. Compare A-values: CH3 about 7.3 kJ/mol, tert-butyl about 21 kJ/mol.
w:
In a cis-1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane one group is axial and the other equatorial in each chair.
I is false: in the chair drawn the tert-butyl group is axial (and the CH3 equatorial). An axial tert-butyl costs about 21 kJ/mol, so this is the less stable chair.
II is true: in the other chair the tert-butyl group is equatorial, which forces the cis CH3 axial (about 7.3 kJ/mol); the bulky group always takes the equatorial position.
III is true: the trans isomer can place both groups equatorial, so it avoids even the 7.3 kJ/mol axial methyl and is more stable than the cis isomer.
Answer: II and III only.
x: II is also true: once the tert-butyl group is equatorial in the cis isomer, the methyl on C4 must be axial.
III is also true: the trans isomer has a diequatorial chair, which has no 1,3-diaxial interactions from either group.
I is false: the chair drawn has the tert-butyl group axial, the worst arrangement possible for this compound.

q: For which compounds does one chair conformation have both CH3 groups equatorial?
h: Identify each as cis or trans from the wedges and dashes. Then use the pattern of up/down axial positions around the ring for 1,3 and 1,4 positions.
w:
I is cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane: both CH3 groups are on the same face. At C1 and C3 the axial positions point the same way, so two groups on the same face can both be equatorial: yes.
II is trans-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane: the CH3 groups are on opposite faces. One CH3 is axial in either chair: no.
III is cis-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane: both CH3 groups are on the same face. At C1 and C4 the axial positions point in opposite directions, so a cis pair is always axial/equatorial: no.
Answer: I only.
x: II is trans-1,3: each chair has one axial and one equatorial CH3.
III is cis-1,4: for 1,4 positions it is the trans isomer that can be diequatorial, not the cis.
"Trans means diequatorial" is true only for 1,2 and 1,4 patterns; for 1,3 it is the cis isomer (I) that can be diequatorial.

q: Which of the compounds shown are chiral?
h: Look for a carbon with four different groups, then check for an internal mirror plane. In a ring, follow the ring in both directions from the carbon.
w:
I is chiral: in 3-methylcyclohexene, C3 carries H, CH3, the alkene carbon C2 and the CH2 C4. Going around the ring the two ways is different (C=C one way, CH2CH2 the other), so C3 is a chirality center and there is no mirror plane.
II is chiral: trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane has two chirality centers and a C2 axis but no mirror plane. (The cis isomer is the meso one.)
III is chiral: in 2,3-dimethylpentane, C3 carries H, CH3, CH2CH3 and CH(CH3)2, four different groups. (C2, with two CH3 groups, is not a stereocenter.)
Answer: I, II, and III.
x: III is also chiral: C3 bears H, methyl, ethyl and isopropyl groups. It is easy to miss because C2 has two identical methyls.
I is also chiral: C3 of 3-methylcyclohexene is a chirality center, since one ring path starts with C=C and the other with CH<sub>2</sub>.
II is also chiral: only the cis-1,2 isomer has a mirror plane; the trans isomer is chiral.

q: Which of the compounds shown are meso compounds?
h: Assign R/S to each chirality center. A meso compound has matching centers of opposite configuration (R,S) and an internal mirror plane.
w:
A meso compound has chirality centers but is achiral because of an internal mirror plane; with two equivalent centers this means one is R and the other S.
I is not meso: it is (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane, a chiral compound (the meso isomer is 2R,3S).
II is not meso: it is trans-1,2-dichlorocyclohexane, (1R,2R), which has a C2 axis but no mirror plane. The cis isomer is meso.
III is meso: it is (2R,4S)-pentane-2,4-diol, and a mirror plane passes through C3.
Answer: III only.
x: I is (2R,3R): the two centers have the same descriptor, so they do not cancel and the compound is chiral.
II is the trans 1,2-ring isomer (1R,2R), which is chiral; only the cis isomer has a mirror plane.
Having two identical-looking stereocenters is not enough: I and II are (R,R) and chiral. Only III, with (R,S) centers, is meso.

q:
The compound shown is (2R,3S)-3-bromobutan-2-ol. Which statements are correct?
I. It is a meso compound.
II. Counting this one, 3-bromobutan-2-ol has four stereoisomers.
III. Its enantiomer is (2S,3S)-3-bromobutan-2-ol.
h: A meso compound needs two stereocenters with the same four groups. For the enantiomer, change every descriptor.
w:
I is false: the two chirality centers carry different groups (C2 has OH, C3 has Br), so no internal mirror plane is possible. An (R,S) label alone does not make a compound meso.
II is true: with two chirality centers and no meso form, there are 22 = 4 stereoisomers: (2R,3R), (2S,3S), (2R,3S) and (2S,3R).
III is false: the enantiomer has every center inverted, so it is (2S,3R). (2S,3S) changes only one center, so it is a diastereomer.
Answer: II only.
x: I is false: meso needs identical substituent sets on the two centers; with OH on one and Br on the other, the molecule is chiral.
III is false: inverting only C2 gives a diastereomer. The enantiomer is (2S,3R).
I and III are both false, and II is true: with no meso form, two chirality centers give four stereoisomers.

q:
The Fischer projection shows (R)-glyceraldehyde. Which operations on this drawing give a Fischer projection of the same compound?
I. Rotating the whole projection 180° in the plane of the page.
II. Swapping the positions of two groups, then swapping two groups a second time.
III. Rotating the whole projection 90° in the plane of the page.
h: In a Fischer projection, horizontal bonds point toward you and vertical bonds point away. Which operations keep that true?
w:
I is true: a 180° turn keeps horizontal groups horizontal (toward the viewer) and vertical groups vertical, so the configuration is unchanged.
III is false: a 90° turn moves the groups that pointed toward you into vertical positions (now read as pointing away), which inverts the center and gives the drawing of (S)-glyceraldehyde.
II is true: each swap of two groups inverts the configuration, so two swaps restore it.
Answer: I and II only.
x: II is also true: one swap gives the enantiomer, and a second swap inverts it back to the original.
I is also true: rotating 180° in the plane keeps the horizontal (toward-you) and vertical (away) bonds where they were.
III is false: a 90° rotation in the plane turns a Fischer projection into its enantiomer.

q: Compound A is (2R,3R)-2,3-dichloropentane. Which of structures I–III are diastereomers of A?
h: Assign R/S to C2 and C3 in each structure, being careful where the chain is drawn in a different direction. Diastereomers differ at some, but not all, centers.
w:
Assigning each center: I is (2R,3S), II is (2S,3R) and III is (2S,3S).
I is a diastereomer of A: only C3 differs.
II is a diastereomer of A: only C2 differs. (I and II are enantiomers of each other, but each is a diastereomer of A.)
III is not a diastereomer: both centers are inverted, so it is the enantiomer of A.
Answer: I and II only.
x: II is also a diastereomer: it is (2S,3R), differing from A at C2 only.
I is also a diastereomer: it is (2R,3S), differing from A at C3 only.
III is (2S,3S): both centers differ from A, so it is A's enantiomer, not a diastereomer.

q:
Which statements about optical activity are correct?
I. A compound with the (R) configuration always rotates plane-polarized light clockwise (+).
II. A racemic mixture shows no net optical rotation.
III. A pair of diastereomers has identical boiling points and solubilities.
h: R/S is a naming rule; the sign of rotation is measured. Which kind of stereoisomers share all physical properties?
w:
I is false: R/S comes from the CIP priority rules and has no fixed link to the sign of rotation, which must be measured; some R compounds are (+) and others (−).
II is true: a racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers, whose equal and opposite rotations cancel.
III is false: diastereomers are not mirror images, so they generally differ in boiling point, solubility and other physical properties (which is why they can be separated by ordinary methods). Only enantiomers share these properties.
Answer: II only.
x: I is false: the CIP label does not predict the sign of rotation; an R compound can be levorotatory.
III is false: diastereomers have different physical properties; only enantiomers have identical boiling points and solubilities (in achiral solvents).
Only II is true. The R/S label does not set the sign of rotation, and diastereomers differ in physical properties.

q:
The energy diagram describes a reaction A → C that goes through intermediate B. Which statements are true?
I. The reaction has exactly one intermediate.
II. The first step is the rate-determining step.
III. By the Hammond postulate, the first transition state resembles B more than it resembles A.
h: Find the highest point on the curve, then ask whether step 1 is uphill or downhill.
w: I is true: there is one energy minimum (B) between reactants and products, so one intermediate. II is false: the rate-determining step is the one whose transition state is highest on the diagram, and TS2 (18) lies above TS1 (12), so the second step limits the rate. III is true: step 1 is endergonic (A at 0 → B at 5), so by the Hammond postulate its transition state is late and resembles the higher-energy species, B. I and III only.
x: This misses III: an endergonic step has a late transition state that looks like its product, intermediate B.
This misses I: the single minimum between reactants and products is one intermediate.
II is false: TS2 is the highest point on the curve, so step 2, not step 1, is rate-determining.

q: Which carbocations I–III would rearrange to a more stable carbocation by a 1,2-shift?
h: A shift only pays off if the new cation is more substituted (or resonance-stabilized) than the old one.
w: I does not rearrange: the 1-methylcyclopentyl cation is already tertiary, and any hydride shift would make a secondary cation. II does not rearrange to anything better: a hydride shift in the cyclohexyl cation just makes another secondary cyclohexyl cation, identical to the first. III rearranges: the 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-yl cation is secondary, and a 1,2-methyl shift from the adjacent quaternary carbon gives the tertiary 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-yl cation. III only.
x: I is already tertiary; no 1,2-shift can make it more stable.
A hydride shift in the cyclohexyl cation gives another secondary cation of the same structure, so there is no driving force.
Neither I (already tertiary) nor II (shift gives an identical secondary cation) gains stability by shifting.

q:
3-Methylbut-1-ene reacts with HBr (no peroxides). Which statements about the mechanism are true?
I. Protonation of the alkene gives a secondary carbocation first.
II. A 1,2-hydride shift converts that cation into a tertiary carbocation.
III. The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
h: Add H<sup>+</sup> by Markovnikov's rule, then look at the carbon next to the cation.
w: I is true: H+ adds to the terminal CH2 (Markovnikov), leaving a secondary cation on C2. II is true: C3 next door is a C–H carbon bearing two methyls, so a 1,2-hydride shift moves the positive charge to C3, a tertiary center. III is true: bromide captures the more stable tertiary cation, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product (2-bromo-3-methylbutane is the minor, unrearranged product). I, II, and III.
x: III is also true: the rearranged tertiary cation is trapped by Br<sup>−</sup>, so the major product carries Br on the tertiary carbon.
II is also true: the hydride shifts from the adjacent tertiary C–H, which is why the product is rearranged.
I is also true: Markovnikov protonation at CH<sub>2</sub> makes the secondary cation before any shift occurs.

q:
1-Bromobutane reacts with NaCN in methanol by SN2. Which changes would increase the rate?
I. Using 1-chlorobutane in place of 1-bromobutane
II. Using DMSO as the solvent in place of methanol
III. Using 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane in place of 1-bromobutane
h: Think about three S<sub>N</sub>2 factors: leaving group, solvent, and crowding at the backside of the carbon.
w: I is false: Cl− is a poorer leaving group than Br− (Br− is the weaker, more polarizable base and its C–Br bond is weaker), so 1-chlorobutane reacts more slowly. II is true: DMSO is polar aprotic; it does not hydrogen-bond to cyanide, so the nucleophile is less solvated and much more reactive. III is false: 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide) is primary but its β-tert-butyl group blocks backside attack, so it reacts far more slowly. II only.
x: I is false: chloride is a worse leaving group than bromide, which slows S<sub>N</sub>2.
III is false: the neopentyl substrate is primary but badly hindered at the backside, so its S<sub>N</sub>2 rate is tiny.
III is false (neopentyl is very hindered) and II is true: a polar aprotic solvent speeds S<sub>N</sub>2 with anionic nucleophiles.

q:
Which reactions give a racemic organic product? (Each substitution follows the mechanism its conditions favor.)
I. Compound I in H2O/acetone, heat
II. Compound II with NaCN in DMSO
III. Compound III with NaCN in DMSO
h: Ask two things for each: does the reaction happen AT the stereocenter, and is the intermediate planar?
w: I is racemic: (S)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is tertiary, so in aqueous acetone it ionizes (SN1) to a planar tertiary carbocation that water attacks from either face, giving racemic 3-methylhexan-3-ol (in practice with at most a slight excess of inversion). II is not racemic: (R)-2-bromobutane is secondary and cyanide in DMSO is a good nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent, so SN2 inverts the center and gives optically active (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile. III is not racemic: in (S)-1-bromo-2-methylbutane the substitution happens at the CH2Br carbon, not at the stereocenter, so the product (S)-3-methylpentanenitrile keeps its configuration. I only.
x: II is not racemic: S<sub>N</sub>2 with cyanide in DMSO gives clean inversion, one enantiomer of the nitrile.
III is not racemic: the stereocenter is not the carbon that reacts, so its configuration is untouched.
III keeps its stereocenter (the reaction is at CH<sub>2</sub>Br), and I does racemize through a planar tertiary carbocation.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert (R)-butan-2-ol into (S)-2-bromobutane?
I. PBr3
II. 1. TsCl, pyridine 2. NaBr, DMSO
III. 1. SOCl2, pyridine 2. NaBr, DMSO
h: Count the inversions. Which steps break a bond to the stereocenter, and which only change the O–H?
w: OH and Br are both the top CIP priority, so each inversion of geometry turns R into S. I works: PBr3 converts the OH into a leaving group that bromide displaces by SN2, one inversion → (S). II works: TsCl reacts at oxygen, so the tosylate keeps the R configuration; then Br− displaces tosylate by SN2, one inversion → (S). III fails: SOCl2 with pyridine gives (S)-2-chlorobutane with inversion, and the SN2 by Br− inverts again, so two inversions give (R)-2-bromobutane. I and II only.
x: II also works: tosylation does not touch the C–O bond, so the one inversion comes in the bromide step.
I also works: PBr<sub>3</sub> converts the alcohol to the bromide with a single S<sub>N</sub>2 inversion.
III fails: it has two inversions (SOCl2/pyridine, then Br−), so it returns the R bromide.

q:
Which of these are better leaving groups than chloride ion in an SN2 reaction?
I. HO−
II. TsO− (tosylate)
III. I−
h: Good leaving groups are weak bases. Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of each conjugate acid with that of HCl.
w: A leaving group is better the weaker it is as a base. I is false: HO− is a strong base (H2O, pKa 15.7), which is why alcohols must be activated before substitution. II is true: tosylate is the conjugate base of a strong sulfonic acid (pKa about −3) and its charge is spread over three oxygens. III is true: HI (pKa about −10) is stronger than HCl, and the large, polarizable I− leaves from a weak C–I bond. II and III only.
x: III is also true: iodide is a weaker base than chloride and the C–I bond is the weakest carbon–halogen bond.
II is also true: tosylate is resonance-stabilized and is one of the best common leaving groups.
I is false: hydroxide is a strong base and a very poor leaving group.

q:
Which substrate/base combinations give 1-methylcyclohexene as the major product?
I. Compound I with NaOCH2CH3
II. Compound II with NaOCH2CH3
III. Compound III with KOC(CH3)3
h: E2 on a cyclohexane needs an axial leaving group and an axial β hydrogen on the neighboring carbon. Then think about base size.
w: I (trans-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane) fails: Br is axial only in the chair where the methyl is also axial, so the H on C2 is equatorial and cannot be anti-periplanar; E2 must use C6 and gives 3-methylcyclohexene. II (cis-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane) works: with Br axial the methyl is equatorial, so C2 has an axial H anti to Br and E2 forms the more substituted 1-methylcyclohexene (Zaitsev). III fails: with bulky tert-butoxide, the tertiary bromide loses a methyl H, giving mainly the less substituted methylenecyclohexane (Hofmann). II only.
x: I fails: in the trans isomer the C2 hydrogen cannot be anti-periplanar to an axial Br, so 3-methylcyclohexene forms.
III fails: the bulky base removes the most accessible H (on CH<sub>3</sub>), so methylenecyclohexane is the major product.
This reverses the two isomers: the cis compound, not the trans, has an axial C2–H anti to an axial Br.

q:
(2S,3S)-2-Bromo-3-phenylbutane is treated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. Which statements are true?
I. The major alkene is (E)-2-phenylbut-2-ene.
II. The (2S,3R) diastereomer gives the same alkene stereoisomer.
III. In the transition state, the H removed and the Br are syn-periplanar.
h: Draw the conformation with H on C3 anti to Br on C2. Which groups end up on the same side of the new π bond?
w: C3 has only one H, so the Zaitsev product (conjugated, trisubstituted 2-phenylbut-2-ene) forms stereospecifically. III is false: E2 requires the C–H and C–Br bonds to be anti-periplanar. I is true: with H(C3) anti to Br in the (2S,3S) isomer, the C1 methyl on C2 and the phenyl on C3 end up on opposite sides of the new double bond; those are the higher-priority groups on each carbon, so the alkene is (E). II is false: the (2S,3R) diastereomer places the methyl and phenyl on the same side in its anti-periplanar conformation, so it gives the (Z) alkene. Diastereomers give different alkenes in a stereospecific E2. I only.
x: II is false: E2 is stereospecific, so the diastereomer with the opposite configuration at C3 gives the (Z) alkene.
III is false: E2 needs the H and the leaving group anti-periplanar (180°), not syn.
I is true (anti elimination puts CH3 and Ph trans, the E alkene), and II is false.

q:
2-Bromopropane reacts with NaOCH3 in methanol to give a mixture of propene and 2-methoxypropane. Which changes increase the fraction of elimination?
I. Running the reaction at a lower temperature
II. Using KOC(CH3)3 in place of NaOCH3
III. Using 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in place of 2-bromopropane
h: Treat each change separately: does it help the base reach a β H, or the nucleophile reach the carbon? And which pathway gains more from heating?
w: I is false: elimination has the larger, more favorable ΔS (more product molecules), so it is favored by higher temperature; cooling increases substitution. II is true: tert-butoxide is a strong but bulky base that cannot easily reach the backside of carbon, so it removes a β H instead. III is true: a tertiary bromide cannot undergo SN2, so a strong base gives almost entirely E2. II and III only.
x: III is also true: tertiary substrates block S<sub>N</sub>2, so a strong base gives E2 almost exclusively.
II is also true: a bulky alkoxide is a poor nucleophile but a strong base, which shifts the ratio toward elimination.
I is false: lowering the temperature favors substitution, because elimination is the entropy-driven pathway.

q: Which alcohols give 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product when heated with concentrated H2SO4?
h: Follow each cation: does it shift to the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation before it loses H<sup>+</sup>?
w: All three funnel to the same tertiary cation, (CH3)2C+CH2CH3, which loses H+ to give the Zaitsev (most substituted) alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene. I (2-methylbutan-2-ol) forms this tertiary cation directly. II (3-methylbutan-2-ol) forms a secondary cation that undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the tertiary cation. III (2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol) cannot form a primary cation; loss of water is assisted by a 1,2-methyl shift that gives the same tertiary cation. I, II, and III.
x: III also works: the neopentyl alcohol undergoes a methyl shift as water leaves, giving the tertiary cation and then 2-methylbut-2-ene.
II also works: the secondary cation from 3-methylbutan-2-ol undergoes a hydride shift to the same tertiary cation.
II and III also work: both rearrange (hydride shift and methyl shift) to the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation.

q:
Which reactions give a meso compound as the product?
I. (Z)-but-2-ene + Br2 in CH2Cl2
II. (E)-but-2-ene + Br2 in CH2Cl2
III. (Z)-but-2-ene + OsO4, then NaHSO3, H2O
h: Decide whether each reagent adds syn or anti, place the two new groups on the cis or trans alkene, and check the product for an internal mirror plane.
w: Br2 adds anti (bromonium ion, backside opening); OsO4 adds syn. I is false: anti addition to the cis alkene gives the chiral (2R,3R)/(2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane pair as a racemate. II is true: anti addition to the trans alkene gives (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane, which has an internal mirror plane (meso). III is true: syn addition to the cis alkene puts both OH groups on the same side, giving meso-butane-2,3-diol (2R,3S). II and III only.
x: III is also meso: syn dihydroxylation of a cis alkene gives the (2R,3S) diol with a mirror plane.
II is also meso: anti addition across a trans alkene gives (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane.
I is not meso: anti addition across a cis alkene gives the chiral (R,R) and (S,S) dibromides as a racemate.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert 1-methylcyclohexene into racemic trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (shown)?
I. H2O, H2SO4
II. 1. mCPBA 2. LiAlH4 3. H3O+
III. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH
h: The OH ends up on the less substituted alkene carbon, and H and OH end up on the same face. Which sequence does both?
w: The target has OH on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov) and is trans. I fails: acid-catalyzed hydration goes through the tertiary carbocation and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (Markovnikov). II fails: hydride from LiAlH4 opens the epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered secondary carbon, so the oxygen stays on the tertiary carbon and the product is again 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol. III works: B and H add syn with B on the less substituted carbon; oxidation replaces B by OH with retention, so H (on C2) and OH (on C1) are cis, which puts the CH3 and OH trans. III only.
x: II fails: hydride attacks the less hindered epoxide carbon, leaving OH on the tertiary carbon (1-methylcyclohexanol).
I fails: acid hydration is Markovnikov through a tertiary cation, giving 1-methylcyclohexanol.
II fails, and III works: hydroboration–oxidation is the only anti-Markovnikov, syn route here.

q:
Which reactions give a racemic mixture of chiral products?
I. But-1-ene + HBr
II. Cyclopentene + OsO4, then NaHSO3, H2O
III. Cyclohexene + Br2 in CH2Cl2
h: For each product ask: is it chiral at all? A product with an internal mirror plane is meso, not racemic.
w: I is racemic: Markovnikov addition gives 2-bromobutane, and Br− attacks the planar secondary carbocation from either face, so (R) and (S) form equally. II is not racemic: syn dihydroxylation gives cis-cyclopentane-1,2-diol, a meso compound (achiral, with a mirror plane). III is racemic: anti addition gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane, which is chiral and forms as the (1R,2R)/(1S,2S) pair. I and III only.
x: III is also racemic: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane is chiral and both enantiomers form equally.
I is also racemic: 2-bromobutane forms from a planar carbocation attacked on both faces.
II is false: cis-cyclopentane-1,2-diol is meso, so there is no pair of enantiomers.

q: Which alkenes give only one organic product when treated with 1. O3 2. (CH3)2S?
h: Ozonolysis cuts the C=C and makes a C=O on each end. When are both ends part of the same molecule?
w: I gives one product: the double bond is in the ring, so cleavage opens the ring and both carbonyls stay in one chain, 5-oxohexanal (CH3CO(CH2)3CHO). II gives two: 2-methylbut-2-ene splits into acetone and acetaldehyde. III gives two: the exocyclic C=C splits into cyclohexanone and formaldehyde. I only.
x: II gives two products: acetone from the disubstituted end and acetaldehyde from the other end.
III gives two products: cyclohexanone plus formaldehyde from the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>.
Only the ring (endocyclic) alkene keeps both new carbonyls in one molecule; III is exocyclic and splits into two compounds.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert propyne into propanal?
I. 1. (Sia)2BH (disiamylborane) 2. H2O2, NaOH
II. H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4
III. 1. H2, Lindlar catalyst 2. BH3·THF 3. H2O2, NaOH 4. PCC
h: An aldehyde needs the oxygen on the terminal carbon: you need an anti-Markovnikov step somewhere.
w: I works: a bulky borane adds once to the terminal alkyne with B on C1; oxidation gives an enol that tautomerizes to propanal. II fails: Hg2+-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov, putting O on C2 and giving acetone. III works: Lindlar gives propene, hydroboration–oxidation gives propan-1-ol (anti-Markovnikov), and PCC oxidizes the primary alcohol to propanal without going on to the acid. I and III only.
x: III also works: propene → propan-1-ol → propanal, and PCC stops at the aldehyde.
I also works: hydroboration of a terminal alkyne with a bulky borane gives the aldehyde after tautomerization.
II fails: mercury-catalyzed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule and gives the methyl ketone, acetone.

q:
Hex-3-yne is converted to an alkene, and the alkene is then treated as shown. Which sequences give a racemic product?
I. 1. Na, NH3(l) 2. Br2, CH2Cl2
II. 1. H2, Lindlar catalyst 2. Br2, CH2Cl2
III. 1. Na, NH3(l) 2. OsO4, then NaHSO3, H2O
h: First decide which alkene each reduction gives (cis or trans), then whether the second step is syn or anti.
w: Na/NH3 gives (E)-hex-3-ene; Lindlar gives (Z)-hex-3-ene. Br2 adds anti; OsO4 adds syn. I is false: trans + anti gives (3R,4S)-3,4-dibromohexane, a meso compound. II is true: cis + anti gives the chiral (3R,4R)/(3S,4S) dibromide as a racemate. III is true: trans + syn gives (3R,4R)/(3S,4S)-hexane-3,4-diol as a racemate. II and III only.
x: III is also racemic: syn dihydroxylation of the trans alkene gives the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) diol pair.
II is also racemic: anti addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to the cis alkene gives the chiral dibromide pair.
I is false: anti addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to the trans alkene gives the meso dibromide.

q:
Hex-2-yne is to be made from propyne in two steps (deprotonation, then alkylation). Which statements about this plan are true?
I. NaOH is a strong enough base to deprotonate propyne almost completely.
II. NaNH2 deprotonates propyne essentially completely.
III. 2-Bromopropane is as good an alkylating agent here as 1-bromopropane.
h: Compare pK<sub>a</sub> values (terminal alkyne ≈ 25, water ≈ 15.7, ammonia ≈ 38), then think about S<sub>N</sub>2 versus E2 for the acetylide.
w: I is false: water (pKa 15.7) is a much stronger acid than propyne (pKa about 25), so hydroxide cannot deprotonate propyne to any useful extent. II is true: ammonia (pKa about 38) is a far weaker acid than propyne, so amide removes the alkyne C–H essentially completely. III is false: the propynide ion is a strong base, and with a secondary halide it mostly causes E2 (giving propene); the plan needs the primary halide 1-bromopropane, and it gives hex-2-yne only from a straight-chain propyl group anyway. II only.
x: I is false: the equilibrium lies far on the side of propyne and hydroxide, because water is the stronger acid.
III is false: acetylide ions are strong bases and give mainly elimination with secondary halides; 2-bromopropane would also put a branched group on the alkyne.
I is false (water is a stronger acid than propyne, so hydroxide fails), and II is true: amide is a much stronger base than the acetylide.

q:
2-Methylbutane is treated with Br2 and light. Which statements are true?
I. The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
II. Each molecule of product requires the absorption of a new photon.
III. Bromination is more selective than chlorination because H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so its transition state is late and radical-like.
h: Think about how a chain reaction keeps going, and apply the Hammond postulate to the H-abstraction step.
w: I is true: Br• abstracts the tertiary H selectively (tertiary radical most stable), giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product. II is false: light only starts the chain by splitting Br2; the two propagation steps (R–H + Br• → R• + HBr; R• + Br2 → R–Br + Br•) regenerate Br•, so one photon can lead to many product molecules. III is true: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so by the Hammond postulate the transition state resembles the alkyl radical, and differences in radical stability (3° > 2° > 1°) show up strongly in the rates; the exothermic Cl• abstraction has an early, reactant-like transition state and is much less selective. I and III only.
x: This misses III: the late, product-like transition state is exactly why bromination is so selective.
This misses I: bromination strongly prefers the tertiary C–H, so the tertiary bromide is the major product.
II is false: propagation regenerates Br•, so one photon starts a chain that makes many product molecules.

q: Which alkenes give a single constitutional isomer of allylic bromide with NBS and light (ignore stereoisomers)?
h: Draw the allylic radical and its resonance form. Bromine can bond at either end of the allylic system.
w: I gives two: removing an allylic H from but-1-ene gives a radical delocalized over C1 and C3, so both 3-bromobut-1-ene and 1-bromobut-2-ene form. II gives several: 1-methylcyclohexene has three different allylic positions (the CH3, ring C3 and ring C6), and their radicals are not equivalent. III gives one: the cyclohexenyl radical is symmetric, so bromine at either end of the allylic system gives the same 3-bromocyclohexene. III only.
x: I gives two products: the allylic radical from but-1-ene has unequal ends, giving 3-bromobut-1-ene and 1-bromobut-2-ene.
II gives several products: 1-methylcyclohexene has three nonequivalent allylic positions.
I is wrong (two products from the unsymmetric allylic radical), and III gives one product because its allylic radical is symmetric.

q:
Which reagents convert cyclohexene into cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol?
I. OsO4 (catalytic), NMO
II. KMnO4, NaOH, H2O, cold
III. 1. mCPBA 2. H3O+
h: Sort the methods into syn and anti dihydroxylations.
w: I works: OsO4 adds both oxygens to one face through a cyclic osmate ester (syn); NMO reoxidizes the osmium so only a catalytic amount is needed. II works: cold, basic KMnO4 also forms a cyclic manganate ester and gives syn addition. III fails: mCPBA gives the epoxide, and acid-catalyzed opening by water occurs from the back face, so the product is trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol. I and II only.
x: II also works: cold, dilute, basic permanganate is a syn dihydroxylation through a cyclic manganate ester.
I also works: catalytic OsO<sub>4</sub> with NMO as the reoxidant is the standard syn dihydroxylation.
III fails: epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition and gives the trans diol.

q:
Which sequences convert acetylene into (E)-hex-3-ene?
I. 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2Br 3. NaNH2 4. CH3CH2Br 5. H2, Lindlar catalyst
II. 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2Br 3. NaNH2 4. CH3CH2Br 5. Na, NH3(l)
III. 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2Br 3. NaNH2 4. CH3CH2Br 5. H2, Pt
h: All three build the same alkyne first. The last step decides the outcome.
w: Steps 1–4 are the same in every route: two deprotonation–alkylation cycles add an ethyl group to each end, giving hex-3-yne. I fails: H2 with Lindlar catalyst adds both H atoms syn, giving (Z)-hex-3-ene. II works: dissolving-metal reduction (Na in NH3) goes through a vinyl radical and vinyl anion that adopt the trans arrangement, giving (E)-hex-3-ene. III fails: H2 over Pt reduces the alkyne all the way to hexane. II only.
x: I fails: Lindlar reduction is syn and gives the Z alkene.
III fails: an unpoisoned Pt catalyst reduces the alkyne completely to the alkane.
This reverses the two partial reductions: Lindlar gives the Z alkene, and Na/NH3 gives the E alkene.

q:
Which reagent sequences convert 1-methylcyclohexene into 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane (ignore which stereoisomer forms)?
I. HBr, ROOR, hν
II. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH 3. PBr3
III. HBr (no peroxides)
h: The Br must end up on the less substituted alkene carbon. Which routes are anti-Markovnikov?
w: I works: under peroxides Br• adds to the less substituted carbon so that the more stable tertiary radical forms; that radical takes H from HBr, putting Br on C2 of the original alkene (anti-Markovnikov). II works: hydroboration–oxidation gives trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, and PBr3 converts the secondary alcohol to the bromide with inversion (so this route gives specifically the cis bromide, but the constitution is right). III fails: ionic HBr addition goes through the tertiary carbocation and gives 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane (Markovnikov). I and II only.
x: II also works: anti-Markovnikov alcohol, then PBr<sub>3</sub>, puts Br on the secondary carbon next to the methyl.
I also works: radical addition of HBr is anti-Markovnikov because the tertiary radical forms on the way.
III fails: without peroxides HBr adds through the tertiary carbocation and gives 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

q:
Which reagents convert pentan-1-ol into pentanal without significant further oxidation?
I. Na2Cr2O7, H2SO4, H2O
II. KMnO4, NaOH, heat; then H3O+
III. PCC, CH2Cl2
h: Over-oxidation of an aldehyde goes through its hydrate, which needs water.
w: I fails: chromic acid in water oxidizes the primary alcohol to the aldehyde, which forms a hydrate and is oxidized on to pentanoic acid. II fails: hot permanganate is a strong oxidant that also takes a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid. III works: PCC in anhydrous CH2Cl2 stops at the aldehyde, because no water is present to form the hydrate that would be oxidized further. III only.
x: I fails: aqueous chromic acid over-oxidizes a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid.
II fails: hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidizes the primary alcohol all the way to pentanoic acid.
I fails (aqueous chromic acid gives the acid), and III works: PCC in dry CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> stops at the aldehyde.

q:
Which methods give tert-butyl ethyl ether, (CH3)3COCH2CH3, as the main product?
I. CH3CH2O− Na+ + (CH3)3CBr
II. 2-Methylpropene + CH3CH2O− Na+ in ethanol
III. (CH3)3CO− K+ + CH3CH2Br
h: In a Williamson synthesis the alkoxide attacks by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon can be attacked from the back? And can an alkoxide add to an ordinary C=C?
w: III works: this is a Williamson ether synthesis with the alkyl group on the primary halide, so SN2 at the unhindered CH2 gives the ether. I fails: SN2 at a tertiary carbon is impossible, and ethoxide acts as a base, so E2 gives 2-methylpropene. II fails: an unactivated alkene is electron-rich and does not react with a nucleophile such as ethoxide (adding ethanol across the C=C needs an electrophile, for example H+ or Hg2+). III only.
x: I fails: a tertiary bromide with a strong base gives E2 (2-methylpropene), not substitution.
II fails: an alkoxide cannot add to an ordinary alkene; the C=C is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.
This reverses the Williamson rule: the tertiary piece must be the alkoxide and the halide must be primary, so III works and I fails.

q: A compound with formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR spectrum shown. There is no absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which compound is it?
h: Find the carbonyl band first, then decide whether an O–H is present and whether there is a strong C–O stretch between 1000 and 1300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
w: The strong band at 1735 cm−1 is a C=O stretch in the saturated-ester range (about 1735–1750 cm−1, a little higher than a ketone at 1715). The two strong bands at 1230 and 1045 cm−1 are the C–O stretches that every ester shows, and there is no O–H band. All four choices are C4H8O2, so the spectrum points to the ester, ethyl acetate.
x: Butanoic acid would show a very broad O–H stretch from about 2500 to 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>; the spectrum has nothing above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
3-Hydroxy-2-butanone has an alcohol O–H (broad, near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and a ketone C=O near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not 1735 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
1,4-Dioxane is a diether with no C=O at all; it would show strong C–O bands near 1120 cm<sup>−1</sup> but nothing near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub> gives the IR spectrum shown. Which compound is it?
h: A sharp band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> in a compound with no oxygen or nitrogen has only one common source.
w: The sharp band at 3320 cm−1 is the ≡C–H stretch of a terminal alkyne (an O–H or N–H band would be broad, and this compound has no O or N). The weak band at 2120 cm−1 is the C≡C stretch, and the strong band near 635 cm−1 is the ≡C–H bend. The compound is 1-pentyne.
x: 2-Pentyne is an internal alkyne with no ≡C–H, so it has no band at 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>; its nearly symmetric C≡C stretch is very weak or absent.
Cyclopentene would show an =C–H stretch just above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> (about 3050) and a C=C stretch near 1610–1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>, with nothing at 3320 or 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
1,3-Pentadiene shows =C–H stretches near 3020–3090 cm<sup>−1</sup> and C=C stretches near 1600–1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>; it has no triple-bond band near 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound with formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> gives the IR spectrum shown. Which compound is it?
h: Bands above 3000 and near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup> show what kind of bond is present. Strong bands below 1000 cm<sup>−1</sup> (=C–H out-of-plane bends) show how many groups are on it.
w: The band at 3090 cm−1 (sp2 =C–H) and the C=C stretch at 1640 cm−1 show an alkene, so the one degree of unsaturation is a C=C, not a ring. The pair at 990 and 905 cm−1 is the out-of-plane =C–H bending pattern of a monosubstituted alkene, RCH=CH2. A 1,1-disubstituted alkene (R2C=CH2) shows one strong band near 890 cm−1 instead. The compound is 1-hexene.
x: 2-Methyl-1-pentene is a 1,1-disubstituted alkene: it has the =C–H stretch and C=C band, but its out-of-plane bend is a single strong band near 890 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not the 990/905 pair.
(E)-3-Hexene is symmetric, so its C=C stretch is essentially IR-inactive (no band near 1640 cm−1); a trans alkene shows one strong bend near 965 cm−1.
Cyclohexane uses its degree of unsaturation as a ring. It has only sp<sup>3</sup> C–H stretches below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=C band.

q: A compound with formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O gives the IR spectrum shown. Which compound is it?
h: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O has one degree of unsaturation. Decide whether it is a C=O or a C=C, then check whether an O–H is present.
w: One degree of unsaturation must be a C=O or a C=C (or a ring). There is no band in the 1700–1750 cm−1 carbonyl region, so it is not a C=O. The =C–H stretch at 3090 cm−1, the C=C stretch at 1645 cm−1 and the 995/920 cm−1 pair (a CH=CH2 group) show a vinyl group. The broad, strong band at 3340 cm−1 is a hydrogen-bonded O–H, and 1020 cm−1 is the C–O stretch of a primary alcohol. The compound is 2-propen-1-ol (allyl alcohol).
x: Propanal would show a strong C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the aldehyde C–H pair near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>; it has no O–H and no C=C.
Acetone shows a strong C=O at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no O–H, no =C–H and no C=C band.
Methyl vinyl ether has the vinyl =C–H and C=C bands, but it has no O–H. It could not give the broad band at 3340 cm<sup>−1</sup>; its C–O band is a strong stretch near 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown? (The band at 3290 cm<sup>−1</sup> is weak and single.)
h: Count the bands between 3300 and 3500 cm<sup>−1</sup> and note how strong and broad they are.
w: A single, weak N–H stretch near 3300 cm−1 is the mark of a secondary amine, R2NH, which has one N–H bond. Primary amines (RNH2) show two bands (symmetric and asymmetric stretches), tertiary amines show none, and an alcohol O–H is strong and broad. The compound is diethylamine.
x: Butylamine is a primary amine; its NH<sub>2</sub> group gives two N–H stretching bands, near 3370 and 3290 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not one.
Triethylamine is a tertiary amine with no N–H bond, so it shows no absorption between 3200 and 3500 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
1-Butanol would show a strong, very broad O–H stretch centered near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a strong C–O stretch near 1050 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not a weak, single band.

q: A compound with formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR spectrum shown. Which compound is it?
h: A C=O is present. Look just to the right of the C–H stretches for a pair of weak bands that only one kind of carbonyl compound shows.
w: The strong band at 1730 cm−1 is a C=O stretch, and the two bands at 2815 and 2715 cm−1 are the C–H stretches of an aldehyde CHO group. No O–H band is present. The compound is pentanal.
x: 2-Pentanone also has a C=O (near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>), but a ketone has no aldehyde C–H, so the 2715/2815 cm<sup>−1</sup> pair would be missing.
Cyclopentanol would show a broad O–H stretch near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=O band at 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Penten-1-ol would show a broad O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, an =C–H stretch near 3080 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=C near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and no C=O.

q: 1-Hexanol is treated with PCC in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>. The isolated product gives the IR spectrum shown. What is the product?
h: Check three regions: the O–H region (3200–3600 and 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>), the C=O region, and 2700–2850 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
w: The broad O–H band of the starting alcohol is gone, a strong C=O appears at 1730 cm−1, and the pair at 2810/2710 cm−1 is the aldehyde C–H stretch. PCC in an anhydrous solvent stops a primary alcohol at the aldehyde, so the product is hexanal.
x: Hexanoic acid (from over-oxidation, as with aqueous chromic acid) would show a very broad O–H from about 2500 to 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no 2710 cm<sup>−1</sup> aldehyde band.
Unreacted 1-hexanol would still show the broad O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=O band at 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
1-Hexene (from dehydration) would show =C–H near 3080 cm<sup>−1</sup> and C=C near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>, with no C=O.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown?
h: Nothing appears above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> or between 1600 and 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>. What does the strong band near 1100 cm<sup>−1</sup> leave?
w: There is no O–H (no broad band near 3350 cm−1), no C=O (nothing near 1715 cm−1) and no alkene (nothing above 3000 cm−1 or near 1640 cm−1). The strongest band besides the sp3 C–H stretches is the C–O stretch at 1120 cm−1, the typical pattern of an ether. The compound is diethyl ether.
x: 1-Butanol has a C–O stretch too, but it would also show a strong, broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
2-Butanone would show a strong C=O stretch near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
1-Butene would show an =C–H stretch near 3080 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a C=C stretch near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup> and strong bends near 990 and 910 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and no C–O band.

q: Which compound gives the mass spectrum shown?
h: Read the molecular-ion pair: its m/z values and the height of M+2 relative to M<sup>+</sup>.
w: The molecular ion appears as two peaks of nearly equal height two mass units apart (m/z 122 and 124). A 1:1 M+/M+2 pair means one bromine (79Br and 81Br are about 50:50). C3H779Br has M = 36 + 7 + 79 = 122. Loss of ·Br leaves the propyl cation, C3H7+, at m/z 43 (the base peak). The compound is 1-bromopropane.
x: Bromoethane also shows a 1:1 pair, but at m/z 108 and 110 (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br).
1-Chloropropane has M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 78, and its M+2 peak (80) is only about one-third as tall, the 3:1 pattern of chlorine.
1-Bromobutane shows the 1:1 bromine pair at m/z 136 and 138, and its alkyl cation is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 57.

q: Which compound gives the mass spectrum shown? (The three small peaks at m/z 186, 188 and 190 are the molecular-ion cluster.)
h: A 1:2:1 molecular-ion triplet and a 1:1 fragment pair each say something about how many heavy halogen atoms are present.
w: Two bromine atoms give an M+ : M+2 : M+4 pattern of about 1:2:1, because the two Br atoms can be 79Br/79Br, 79Br/81Br (two ways) or 81Br/81Br. C2H479Br2 = 24 + 4 + 158 = 186. The base-peak pair at m/z 107/109 (1:1) is BrCH2CH2+, formed when M+ loses one ·Br; it keeps one Br, so it shows the single-bromine 1:1 pattern. The compound is 1,2-dibromoethane.
x: 1-Bromo-2-chloroethane would show its cluster at m/z 142, 144 and 146 in about a 3:4:1 ratio, not 1:2:1 at 186–190.
1,2-Dichloroethane would show M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 98 with M+2 and M+4 in a 9:6:1 pattern, and no 1:1 pair at 107/109.
Bromoethane has only one Br, so its molecular ion is a 1:1 pair at m/z 108/110 with no M+4 peak.

q: An alkyl halide gives the mass spectrum shown; its molecular ion at m/z 104 is very weak. Which compound is it?
h: Use the m/z 76/78 fragment pair to identify the halogen, then work out the formula and its degree of unsaturation from M<sup>+</sup>.
w: M+ is at m/z 104 (too weak for its M+2 partner to show). The fragment pair at m/z 76 and 78, with 78 about one-third as tall, is the 3:1 pattern of one chlorine (C3H5Cl+). Subtracting 35Cl leaves 69, which is C5H9; the formula C5H9Cl has one degree of unsaturation, so with no C=C it is a ring. Loss of ·Cl gives C5H9+ (m/z 69), and loss of HCl gives the base peak at m/z 68. The compound is chlorocyclopentane.
x: 1-Chloropentane is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Cl, with M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 106 (and M+2 at 108); it has no ring, so it has two more hydrogens.
Bromocyclopentane would show a 1:1 pair at m/z 148 and 150, the bromine pattern.
Chlorocyclohexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Cl) has M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 118/120, and its C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub><sup>+</sup> fragment is at m/z 83.

q: An amine C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>15</sub>N gives the mass spectrum shown (M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 101). Which compound is it?
h: Amines fragment by α-cleavage: a C–C bond to the carbon next to N breaks, leaving an iminium ion. Which radical must be lost to reach the base peak?
w: The odd M+ (101) fits the nitrogen rule for one N. The base peak at m/z 86 is M − 15, the loss of a methyl radical. In an amine, α-cleavage breaks the bond between the α-carbon (attached to N) and the β-carbon, so losing ·CH3 requires an N-ethyl group (N–CH2–CH3). In triethylamine, every α-cleavage loses ·CH3 and gives CH2=N+(CH2CH3)2, m/z 86, so this is the base peak.
x: In dipropylamine, α-cleavage loses an ethyl radical (29) from a propyl group, giving CH<sub>2</sub>=N<sup>+</sup>H–C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub> at m/z 72 as the base peak, not 86.
Hexylamine is a primary amine with an unbranched α-carbon; α-cleavage loses the pentyl radical and gives CH<sub>2</sub>=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 30 as the base peak.
In N-ethylbutylamine, the preferred α-cleavage loses the larger propyl radical (43) from the butyl side, giving m/z 58 as the base peak; loss of methyl from the ethyl side is the minor path.

q: An alkane C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub> gives the mass spectrum shown. The molecular ion (m/z 86) is barely detectable. Which compound is it?
h: Alkane molecular ions break most easily at a branch point, where the most stable carbocation forms. What cation is m/z 57, and what loss gives m/z 71?
w: Branched alkanes cleave at the most substituted carbon. The peak at m/z 57, nearly as tall as the base peak at 43, is C4H9+ (M − 29, loss of ethyl), and the strong m/z 71 is M − 15 (loss of methyl). In 2,2-dimethylbutane, both cleavages happen at the quaternary carbon: losing ·CH2CH3 gives the tert-butyl cation (57), and losing ·CH3 gives the tertiary (CH3)2C+CH2CH3 cation (71). Because cleavage there is so easy, almost no M+ survives.
x: Hexane is unbranched; its M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 86 is clearly visible, and M − 15 (71) is weak because losing methyl would form a primary cation.
2-Methylpentane cleaves at C2 to lose a propyl radical and give the isopropyl cation, so its base peak is m/z 43 and its m/z 57 is small (about 10%), not nearly as tall as 43.
3-Methylpentane does give m/z 57 (loss of ethyl at the branch, a secondary cation), but its M − 15 peak at 71 is small, because loss of methyl is less favorable than loss of the larger ethyl radical.

q: A small halogenated compound gives the mass spectrum shown. The molecular-ion cluster at m/z 130, 132, 134 and 136 has heights of about 100 : 96 : 32 : 4. Which halogen atoms does it contain?
h: Each Cl is about 3:1 <sup>35</sup>Cl:<sup>37</sup>Cl and each Br about 1:1 <sup>79</sup>Br:<sup>81</sup>Br. How many peaks does each combination give, and in what ratio?
w: With n chlorine atoms, the cluster has n + 1 peaks spaced 2 apart, with heights from the expansion of (3 + 1)n. For n = 3 that gives 27 : 27 : 9 : 1, or about 100 : 100 : 33 : 4, which matches four peaks (M to M+6) of 100 : 96 : 32 : 4. The answer is three Cl atoms; the compound is trichloroethene, C2HCl3 (24 + 1 + 105 = 130). The fragment cluster at m/z 95/97/99 (about 9 : 6 : 1) is M − Cl, which keeps two Cl.
x: Two Cl atoms give only three peaks (M, M+2, M+4) in a 9 : 6 : 1 ratio (100 : 65 : 11); there would be no M+6 peak, and M+2 would be clearly shorter than M<sup>+</sup>.
One Cl and one Br give three peaks in about a 3 : 4 : 1 ratio, with M+2 the tallest; there would be no M+6.
