Two Br atoms give three peaks in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, with M+2 twice as tall as M<sup>+</sup>, and no M+6.

q: A compound gives the mass spectrum shown, with M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 128 (relative intensity 4.4) and M+1 at m/z 129 (relative intensity 0.44). There is no M+2 peak. Each carbon contributes about 1.1% to M+1. Which compound is it?
h: Divide the M+1 intensity by the M<sup>+</sup> intensity, then divide by 0.011 to estimate the number of carbons.
w: Number of C ≈ (M+1 / M+) ÷ 0.011 = (0.44 / 4.4) ÷ 0.011 = 0.100 ÷ 0.011 ≈ 9 carbons. All four choices have M = 128; nine carbons rules out the C8, C7 and C10 choices. The fragment series 43, 57, 71, 85, 99 (spaced 14, CH2) with a weak M+ is typical of a straight-chain alkane. The compound is nonane.
x: 2-Octanone is C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O, with eight carbons, so its M+1 would be about 8.8% of M<sup>+</sup> (about 0.39 here, not 0.44); a methyl ketone would also show a large m/z 43 acylium and a McLafferty peak at 58.

Naphthalene, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, has ten carbons, so M+1 would be about 11% of M<sup>+</sup> (about 0.48 here, not 0.44); as an aromatic compound its M<sup>+</sup> would also be the base peak, and it would not show the 43, 57, 71, 85 alkyl series.
Butyl acrylate, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, has seven carbons, so M+1 would be only about 7.7% of M<sup>+</sup> (about 0.34 here).

q: An alcohol C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O (M = 102) gives the mass spectrum shown; no peak is seen at m/z 102. Which alcohol is it?
h: Alcohols undergo α-cleavage: a bond from the carbinol carbon (C–OH) to a neighboring carbon breaks, leaving a resonance-stabilized R<sub>2</sub>C=OH<sup>+</sup> ion. Work out the mass of that ion for each choice.
w: Alcohol molecular ions are weak or absent because α-cleavage and loss of water are so fast. The base peak at m/z 45 is CH3CH=OH+ (C2H5O+), formed when the carbinol carbon loses its largest group, a butyl radical (102 − 57 = 45). That ion requires a CH3–CH(OH)– unit, so the compound is 2-hexanol. The small peak at 87 is the other α-cleavage (loss of ·CH3), and 84 is M − H2O.
x: 3-Hexanol undergoes α-cleavage to lose propyl (giving C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH=OH<sup>+</sup>, m/z 59) or ethyl (giving m/z 73); neither gives m/z 45.
1-Hexanol, a primary alcohol, gives CH<sub>2</sub>=OH<sup>+</sup> at m/z 31 by α-cleavage, together with strong M − H<sub>2</sub>O-derived peaks (84, 56).
2-Methyl-2-pentanol loses the propyl group by α-cleavage to give (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=OH<sup>+</sup> at m/z 59 as the base peak.

q: An alcohol C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O (M = 102) gives the mass spectrum shown; no peak is seen at m/z 102. Which ion is responsible for the base peak at m/z 45?
h: The base peak keeps the oxygen, because O can share its lone pair with the cationic carbon. Add up the masses (C 12, H 1, O 16).
w: The base peak comes from α-cleavage of 2-hexanol: the C2–C3 bond breaks, a butyl radical leaves, and the positive charge stays on the oxygen-bearing fragment, where O donates a lone pair to make an oxonium ion with all octets complete. That ion is CH3CH=OH+: 2(12) + 5(1) + 16 = 45.
x: CH<sub>2</sub>=OH<sup>+</sup> has m/z 31 (12 + 3 + 16); it is the α-cleavage ion of a primary alcohol, RCH<sub>2</sub>OH.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=OH<sup>+</sup> has m/z 59; it would come from an alcohol with an ethyl group on the carbinol carbon, such as 3-hexanol.

The butyl cation, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub><sup>+</sup>, has m/z 57. In α-cleavage the butyl group leaves as the neutral radical because the oxygen-stabilized ion is far more stable than a primary carbocation.

q: An alcohol C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O (M = 102) gives the mass spectrum shown; no peak is seen at m/z 102. The compound is 2-hexanol. Which neutral species does the molecular ion lose when it forms the base peak at m/z 45?
h: The molecular ion is a radical cation. When it splits into two pieces, one piece keeps the charge and the other leaves carrying the unpaired electron. Which piece is detected?
w: The molecular ion (102) is a radical cation. α-Cleavage of the C2–C3 bond gives a cation and a radical. The detected cation is CH3CH=OH+ (45), so the neutral fragment, which is never detected, is a butyl radical, ·C4H9 (102 − 45 = 57).
x: A cation cannot be the neutral piece: only one fragment carries the + charge, and here that is the m/z 45 oxonium ion. A butyl cation would itself appear at m/z 57.
Loss of water (102 − 18) gives the small peak at m/z 84, not the base peak at 45.
Loss of a propyl radical would leave m/z 59, which requires an ethyl group on the carbinol carbon; 2-hexanol has a methyl and a butyl group there.

q: A ketone gives the mass spectrum shown: M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 114 (relative intensity 14.4) and M+1 at m/z 115 (relative intensity 1.2). About how many carbon atoms does the compound contain? (Each carbon contributes about 1.1% to M+1.)
h: Carbons ≈ (M+1 ÷ M<sup>+</sup>) ÷ 0.011. If that lands between two whole numbers, check which carbon count can still fit M = 114 for a ketone.
w: (1.2 ÷ 14.4) = 0.083; 0.083 ÷ 0.011 ≈ 7.6, so 7 or 8 carbons. Eight carbons plus one O already make 96 + 16 = 112, leaving only 2 H for M = 114, which is impossible (C8H2O), so the compound has 7 carbons. With M = 114 and one O for a ketone, 114 − 16 − 84 = 14 hydrogens: C7H14O, which has one degree of unsaturation (the C=O).
x: Six carbons would give M+1 ≈ 6.6% of M<sup>+</sup> (about 0.95 here), clearly lower than observed.

Eight carbons would give M+1 ≈ 8.8% of M<sup>+</sup> (about 1.3 here), close to the observed value, but C<sub>8</sub> with one O (112) leaves only 2 H to reach M = 114; no ketone has the formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O.
Nine carbons would give M+1 ≈ 9.9% of M<sup>+</sup> (about 1.4 here), and C<sub>9</sub> with one O cannot reach M = 114 with a sensible H count (108 + 16 = 124 already).

q: A ketone gives the mass spectrum shown: M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 114 (relative intensity 14.4) and M+1 at m/z 115 (relative intensity 1.2). Look closely at the small even-mass peaks at m/z 86 and 58. Which ketone is it?
h: Ketones fragment by α-cleavage (giving acylium ions) and, if a γ-hydrogen is present, by the McLafferty rearrangement (giving an even-mass ion). Predict both for each choice.
w: α-Cleavage of 4-heptanone loses a propyl radical to give CH3CH2CH2C≡O+ (m/z 71, nearly as tall as the base peak); the propyl cation gives the base peak at 43. Each propyl group has a γ-hydrogen, so the McLafferty rearrangement expels ethene (28) and gives the even-mass enol radical cation at m/z 86 (114 − 28); a second McLafferty loses another ethene and gives m/z 58. The even-mass peaks at 86 and 58 rule out 2,4-dimethyl-3-pentanone, which also gives 71 and 43 but has no γ-hydrogen.
x: 2,4-Dimethyl-3-pentanone gives the isobutyryl acylium (71) and isopropyl cation (43) by α-cleavage, but each isopropyl group stops at the β-carbon, so with no γ-hydrogen there are no McLafferty peaks at m/z 86 or 58.

2-Heptanone would also give CH<sub>3</sub>C≡O<sup>+</sup> (43) as the base peak, but its McLafferty peak at m/z 58 would be large (about half the base peak) and its m/z 71 small; here 71 is nearly as tall as 43 and 58 is small.
3-Heptanone would give acylium ions at m/z 57 (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) and 85 (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>), not 71.

q: A ketone gives the mass spectrum shown: M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 114 (relative intensity 14.4) and M+1 at m/z 115 (relative intensity 1.2). The compound is 4-heptanone. Which process gives the peak at m/z 86?
c: McLafferty rearrangement: a γ-H moves to the C=O oxygen and ethene (28) is lost
α-Cleavage: the bond to the carbonyl carbon breaks and a propyl radical (43) is lost
Inductive cleavage: the positive charge goes to the propyl group, giving C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub><sup>+</sup>
Cleavage of the β C–C bond: an ethyl radical (29) is lost from one propyl chain
h: Compare 86 with 114. An even-mass fragment from an even-mass molecular ion (no N) means a neutral molecule, not a radical, was lost.
w: 114 − 86 = 28, an even mass, so a neutral molecule was lost and the ion is still a radical cation. In the McLafferty rearrangement, the C=O oxygen abstracts a hydrogen from the γ-carbon through a six-membered transition state, the Cα–Cβ bond breaks, and ethene (CH2=CH2, 28) is lost, leaving the enol radical cation at m/z 86.
x: α-Cleavage loses a propyl radical (43) and gives the acylium ion at 114 − 43 = 71, not 86.
Inductive cleavage produces the propyl cation at m/z 43; it does not account for an ion at 86.
Losing an ethyl radical would give m/z 114 − 29 = 85, not 86, and this simple β-cleavage is not a favored ketone fragmentation.

q: Which observation would best distinguish 1-bromobutane (I) from 1-chlorobutane (II)?
c: In the mass spectrum, M+2 is about as tall as M<sup>+</sup> for I but about one-third as tall for II
In the IR spectrum, I shows a strong C–X band near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> that II lacks
In the mass spectrum, M<sup>+</sup> appears at an odd m/z value for I and at an even m/z value for II
In the IR spectrum, II shows a broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> that I lacks entirely
h: Think about the natural isotopes of bromine and chlorine and which technique detects masses.
w: Bromine is about 50% 79Br and 50% 81Br, so a monobromide shows M+ and M+2 of nearly equal height (here m/z 136/138). Chlorine is about 75% 35Cl and 25% 37Cl, so a monochloride shows M+2 about one-third of M+ (m/z 92/94). The M+2 pattern in the mass spectrum tells them apart immediately.
x: C–Br and C–Cl stretches lie in the fingerprint region below about 800 cm<sup>−1</sup>; 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> is a C=O stretch, which neither compound has.
Both compounds contain only C, H and halogen and have even molecular masses (136 and 92); the nitrogen rule does not distinguish them.
A broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> is an O–H stretch; neither alkyl halide has an O–H group.

q: Which observation would best distinguish butanal (I) from 2-butanone (II)?
c: In the IR spectrum, only I shows a pair of weak C–H bands near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>
In the IR spectrum, only I shows a strong C=O band between 1700 and 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>
In the mass spectrum, the molecular ions appear at different m/z values
In the mass spectrum, only II shows an M+2 peak about one-third as tall as M<sup>+</sup>
h: Both are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O carbonyl compounds. What does an aldehyde have that a ketone does not?
w: Butanal and 2-butanone are constitutional isomers (C4H8O, M = 72) and both have a strong C=O stretch (about 1730 and 1715 cm−1). Only the aldehyde has a C–H on the carbonyl carbon, whose stretch appears as two weak bands near 2720 and 2820 cm−1 (the 2720 band is the more diagnostic, since it sits clear of the sp3 C–H bands).
x: Both compounds have a strong C=O stretch in this range (aldehyde about 1730, ketone about 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>), so its presence alone does not distinguish them.
Both are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O, so both give M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 72.
An M+2 peak one-third as tall as M<sup>+</sup> is the pattern of chlorine; neither compound contains a halogen.

q: Which method can distinguish the two compounds shown?
c: Polarimetry, because the two rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions
IR spectroscopy, because their O–H stretches appear at different wavenumbers
Mass spectrometry, because their base peaks appear at different m/z values
<sup>13</sup>C NMR, because they give different numbers of carbon signals
h: First decide how the two structures are related. Which properties are identical for that relationship?
w: I is (R)-2-butanol and II is (S)-2-butanol, a pair of enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical IR, mass and NMR spectra (in an achiral environment) because every bond, mass and magnetic environment is the same. They differ only in how they interact with something chiral, such as plane-polarized light: they have specific rotations of equal size and opposite sign. Polarimetry distinguishes them.
x: Enantiomers have identical bond strengths and vibrations, so their IR spectra are superimposable.
Enantiomers have the same mass and fragment in exactly the same way; their mass spectra are identical.
Each enantiomer of 2-butanol gives four <sup>13</sup>C signals at the same shifts; ordinary NMR cannot tell enantiomers apart.

q: Which observation in the mass spectrum would best distinguish 1-propanol (I) from 2-propanol (II)?
c: The α-cleavage base peak is at m/z 31 for I and at m/z 45 for II
The molecular ion appears at m/z 60 for I and at m/z 58 for II
Only I shows a peak for loss of water (M − 18) from the molecular ion
Only II shows an M+2 peak about one-third as tall as M<sup>+</sup>
h: Both have M = 60. Work out the oxonium ion each alcohol forms when the largest group on the carbinol carbon leaves.
w: Both alcohols are C3H8O (M = 60), so the molecular ion does not help. α-Cleavage of 1-propanol loses an ethyl radical and gives CH2=OH+ (m/z 31). α-Cleavage of 2-propanol loses a methyl radical and gives CH3CH=OH+ (m/z 45). The base peak at 31 versus 45 distinguishes them.
x: The two are constitutional isomers with the same formula, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O, so both molecular ions are at m/z 60.
Loss of water (M − 18) is a general alcohol fragmentation; both alcohols can show it, so it does not distinguish them.
An M+2 peak about one-third of M<sup>+</sup> signals chlorine; neither alcohol contains a halogen.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure is it?
h: The broad 3380 cm<sup>−1</sup> band says alcohol. Now look for a signal between 3.3 and 4 ppm: is there any H on the carbon that carries the OH?
w: DBE = 0 and the broad IR band at 3380 cm−1 is an O–H stretch, so this is a saturated alcohol. The 1H spectrum has no signal between 3.3 and 4.0 ppm, so the carbinol carbon has no H: the alcohol is tertiary. The 2H quartet plus 3H triplet is an ethyl group on a carbon with no H, and the 6H singlet is two equivalent CH3 groups on that same carbon. That is (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3, 2-methyl-2-butanol.
x: 3-Methyl-2-butanol is a secondary alcohol: its CH–O hydrogen would appear near 3.5 ppm, and its CH<sub>3</sub> groups would be doublets, not a 6H singlet.
2,2-Dimethyl-1-propanol would show a 2H singlet near 3.3 ppm for CH<sub>2</sub>O and a 9H singlet for the tert-butyl group; there is no ethyl quartet/triplet.
3-Pentanol has a 1H CH–O signal near 3.4 ppm and no singlet methyls; its two ethyl groups give a 6H triplet.

q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure is it?
h: The sharp 3325 and weak 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> bands point to one kind of alkyne. Then ask why the 1H signal near 2 ppm is a doublet.
w: DBE = 2. The sharp band at 3325 cm−1 (≡C–H stretch) and the weak 2120 cm−1 band (C≡C stretch) mean a terminal alkyne. The alkyne H at 2.04 ppm is a doublet (a small four-bond coupling across the triple bond to one H), and a 6H doublet plus a 1H multiplet is an isopropyl group. The structure is HC≡C–CH(CH3)2, 3-methyl-1-butyne.
x: 1-Pentyne is also a terminal alkyne, but its spectrum has four signals, including a 3H triplet near 1.0 ppm and two CH<sub>2</sub> signals; there is no 6H doublet.
2-Pentyne is an internal alkyne: it has no ≡C–H, so no sharp 3325 cm<sup>−1</sup> band, and its <sup>1</sup>H spectrum is a 2H quartet-like multiplet and two 3H triplets.
1,4-Pentadiene has vinyl H at 5–6 ppm and no ≡C–H stretch at 3325 cm<sup>−1</sup> or C≡C band near 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>Br<sub>2</sub> isomer gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: Two singlets mean no H–H neighbors for either group. Which isomer has every CH<sub>n</sub> group attached to a carbon with no H?
w: Only two signals, both singlets, in a 2 : 6 ratio. The 6H singlet is two equivalent CH3 groups on a carbon with no H, and the 2H singlet at 3.88 ppm is a CH2Br also attached to that hydrogen-free carbon. That fits (CH3)2CBr–CH2Br, 1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane. The quaternary C–Br carbon separates every set of H from every other set, so nothing is split.
x: 1,4-Dibromobutane does give two signals, but they are 4H each (BrCH<sub>2</sub> near 3.4 ppm and the inner CH<sub>2</sub> near 2.0 ppm), and both are split by neighboring CH<sub>2</sub> groups.
1,3-Dibromo-2-methylpropane has a CH between the CH<sub>2</sub>Br groups and the CH<sub>3</sub>: it gives a 4H doublet, a 1H multiplet and a 3H doublet.
2,2-Dibromobutane has an ethyl group, so it shows a 2H quartet and a 3H triplet along with a 3H singlet; there is no 6H signal.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O shows no O–H band in its IR spectrum. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. Which structure is it?
h: No O–H means an ether. Which ether has a methyl group with no neighbors and a CH split by six H?
w: DBE = 0, and with no O–H band the oxygen must be an ether. The 3H singlet at 3.33 ppm is an O–CH3 (deshielded by O, no neighbors). The 1H septet at 3.48 ppm is an O–CH next to two CH3 groups (6 neighbors → 7 lines), and those two CH3 groups are the 6H doublet. The compound is CH3O–CH(CH3)2, 2-methoxypropane.
x: 1-Methoxypropane has an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet (2H), a CH<sub>2</sub> sextet and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet besides the OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet; no septet or 6H doublet.
Diethyl ether shows only two signals, a 4H quartet near 3.5 ppm and a 6H triplet; it has no OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet.
2-Butanol is an alcohol: it would show a broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which the stem rules out.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: The 3H singlet near 2.1 ppm is a methyl ketone. Then find what the 2H doublet and 6H doublet together tell you about the rest of the chain.
w: DBE = 1, and 1715 cm−1 with no aldehyde H is a ketone C=O. The 3H singlet at 2.12 ppm is CH3–C=O, so it is a methyl ketone. The 2H doublet at 2.30 ppm is a CH2 next to the C=O (deshielded) with one neighboring H, and the 6H doublet is two CH3 groups on a CH; that CH (1H multiplet) links them. The chain is CH3CO–CH2–CH(CH3)2, 4-methyl-2-pentanone.
x: 3,3-Dimethyl-2-butanone gives just two singlets (3H and 9H); there is no CH<sub>2</sub> doublet or 6H doublet.
2-Hexanone has a straight chain: its α-CH<sub>2</sub> is a triplet, and the chain ends in a 3H triplet, not a 6H doublet.
3-Methyl-2-pentanone has a 1H α-CH next to the C=O, a 3H doublet and a 3H triplet; it has no 6H doublet.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. (The two hydrogens of a =CH<sub>2</sub> group are not equivalent here: one is cis and one is trans to the rest of the molecule, so they give separate signals.) Which structure is it?
h: Count the vinyl H (4.5–6.5 ppm) and check whether any H sits on the carbon bearing the OH (3.3–4.2 ppm).
w: DBE = 1. IR: broad 3380 cm−1 (O–H), 3090 cm−1 (sp2 C–H) and 1645 cm−1 (C=C), so this is an alkenyl alcohol. Three 1H vinyl signals, each a doublet of doublets, are a monosubstituted alkene, –CH=CH2. There is no signal at 3.3–4.2 ppm, so the OH carbon has no H (a tertiary alcohol), and the 6H singlet is two CH3 groups on that carbon. Structure: CH2=CH–C(CH3)2OH, 2-methyl-3-buten-2-ol.
x: 3-Methyl-2-buten-1-ol has only one vinyl H (a triplet near 5.4 ppm), a 2H doublet near 4.1 ppm for CH<sub>2</sub>OH, and two separate 3H methyl singlets.
Cyclopentanol has no C=C: no vinyl H, no 3090 or 1645 cm<sup>−1</sup> bands, and its CH–O hydrogen appears near 4.3 ppm.
4-Penten-1-ol has a CH<sub>2</sub>OH triplet near 3.6 ppm and two CH<sub>2</sub> groups in the chain; it has no 6H singlet.

q: An alkyl halide gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (400 MHz). Which structure is it?
h: A 1H quartet and a 3H doublet belong together. Then ask what pulls the 1H signal so far downfield.
w: A 1H quartet coupled to a 3H doublet is a CH–CH3 unit (the CH sees 3 neighbors → quartet; the CH3 sees 1 → doublet). The CH at 5.89 ppm is far downfield, so it carries two electronegative atoms: CH3–CHCl2, 1,1-dichloroethane.
x: 1,2-Dichloroethane has four equivalent H (ClCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl): one singlet, no splitting.
Chloroethane has a CH<sub>2</sub> (2H quartet near 3.5 ppm) and a 3H triplet; the integrations are 2 : 3, not 1 : 3.
1,1,1-Trichloroethane has only a CH<sub>3</sub> group: one 3H singlet.

q: The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown was recorded on a 400 MHz spectrometer. How far downfield from TMS, in hertz, is the center of the quartet?
h: Chemical shift in ppm means hertz from TMS per MHz of spectrometer frequency.
w: δ (ppm) = Δν (Hz) ÷ spectrometer frequency (MHz), so Δν = δ × MHz. For the quartet, Δν = 5.89 × 400 = 2356 Hz downfield from TMS.
x: 1767 Hz is 5.89 × 300; the spectrum was recorded at 400 MHz, not 300 MHz.
824 Hz is 2.06 × 400, the position of the doublet, not the quartet.
68 Hz comes from dividing 400 by 5.89; hertz = ppm × MHz, not MHz ÷ ppm.

q: In the 400 MHz 1H NMR spectrum shown, the two lines of the doublet are at 827.1 Hz and 821.0 Hz from TMS. What is the coupling constant J, and how far apart are the two lines when the same sample is run at 600 MHz?
c: J = 6.1 Hz; the lines are still 6.1 Hz apart at 600 MHz
J = 6.1 Hz; the lines are 9.2 Hz apart at 600 MHz
J = 6.1 Hz; the lines are 4.1 Hz apart at 600 MHz
J = 3.05 Hz; the lines are still 3.05 Hz apart at 600 MHz
h: For a doublet, J is the distance between its two lines. Does a coupling between nuclei depend on the magnet?
w: The splitting of a doublet equals J: 827.1 − 821.0 = 6.1 Hz (the center, 824.05 Hz ÷ 400 = 2.06 ppm, is the δ value). J comes from the bonds linking the coupled H, not from the applied field, so in hertz it is the same at any spectrometer frequency: at 600 MHz the lines are still 6.1 Hz apart, while the signal's center moves to 2.06 × 600 = 1236 Hz. (In ppm the splitting shrinks, which is why high-field spectra look less crowded.)
x: 9.2 Hz scales J by 600/400 as if it were a chemical shift; chemical shifts in hertz grow with the field, coupling constants do not.
4.1 Hz scales J by 400/600, as if it were fixed in ppm; J is fixed in hertz.
J is the full distance between the two lines of a doublet, not half of it (half is the distance from each line to the center).

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown, with the DEPT result (C, CH, CH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>) written over each peak. Which structure is it?
h: Count signals first (symmetry), then use the DEPT labels to decide what kind of carbon is bonded to oxygen.
w: Three signals for four carbons means two carbons are equivalent. The peak at 69.6 ppm is a carbon bonded to O, and DEPT says it is a CH2, so the compound is a primary alcohol or ether with an O–CH2. The other two signals are a CH and a CH3; with two equivalent CH3 groups on the CH, the structure is (CH3)2CH–CH2OH, 2-methyl-1-propanol.
x: 1-Butanol has no symmetry: four signals, three of them CH<sub>2</sub> and none a CH.
2-Methyl-2-propanol gives only two signals, and its C–O carbon is quaternary (C), not CH<sub>2</sub>.
2-Butanol gives four signals, and its C–O carbon (≈69 ppm) is a CH, not a CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown, with the DEPT result written over each peak. Which describes its DEPT-90 and DEPT-135 spectra? (DEPT-90 shows only CH carbons. In DEPT-135, CH and CH<sub>3</sub> peaks point up, CH<sub>2</sub> peaks point down, and C peaks are absent.)
c: DEPT-90: δ 30.9 only. DEPT-135: δ 30.9 and 18.9 up, δ 69.6 down
DEPT-90: δ 30.9 only. DEPT-135: all three peaks up
DEPT-90: δ 30.9 and 18.9. DEPT-135: δ 30.9 and 18.9 up, δ 69.6 down
DEPT-90: δ 69.6 only. DEPT-135: δ 69.6 up, δ 30.9 and 18.9 down
h: Apply the two rules to each labeled peak one at a time: is it a CH? Is it a CH<sub>2</sub>?
w: DEPT-90 keeps only CH carbons: the δ 30.9 peak. DEPT-135 shows every protonated carbon with CH and CH3 positive and CH2 negative: δ 30.9 (CH) and δ 18.9 (CH3) point up and δ 69.6 (CH2) points down. So: DEPT-90 shows δ 30.9 only; DEPT-135 has δ 30.9 and 18.9 up and δ 69.6 down.
x: The CH<sub>2</sub> at 69.6 ppm is not positive in DEPT-135; CH<sub>2</sub> peaks are the ones that point down.
DEPT-90 shows only CH carbons; the CH<sub>3</sub> at 18.9 ppm does not appear in it.
This reverses the labels: 69.6 ppm is the CH<sub>2</sub> (down in DEPT-135, absent in DEPT-90), and 30.9 ppm is the CH.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown (DEPT results written over the peaks). In its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum, how does the signal of the hydrogens on the carbon bonded to oxygen (near 3.4 ppm) appear? Assume the OH hydrogen exchanges quickly and does not split other signals.
h: First decide the structure from the DEPT labels, then count the H on the carbon next to the O-bearing carbon.
w: The DEPT labels (O–CH2 at 69.6, one CH, equivalent CH3 groups) give (CH3)2CH–CH2OH, 2-methyl-1-propanol. The O–CH2 hydrogens (2H) have one neighboring H, on the CH, and the OH does not couple, so n + 1 = 2: a 2H doublet.
x: A triplet would need two neighboring H (a CH<sub>2</sub> next door, as in 1-butanol); here the neighbor is a CH.
A singlet would need a neighboring carbon with no H, as in 2,2-dimethyl-1-propanol; the DEPT shows the neighbor is a CH.
A 1H septet is the CH of an isopropyl group bonded to O (as in 2-propanol or 2-methoxypropane); here the carbon on O is a CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: A compound C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Cl gives the 500 MHz <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. The δ 5.98 doublet has lines at 2996.7 Hz and 2983.3 Hz from TMS, and the δ 5.80 doublet has the same spacing. Which structure is it?
h: Work out J in hertz from the two lines, then compare it with typical vinyl couplings: trans 12–18 Hz, cis 6–12 Hz, geminal 0–3 Hz.
w: The two vinyl doublets couple only to each other: J = 2996.7 − 2983.3 = 13.4 Hz. A vinyl–vinyl coupling of 12–18 Hz means the two H are trans across a CH=CH bond (cis is about 6–12 Hz; two H on the same sp2 carbon, about 0–3 Hz). With a 9H tert-butyl singlet, the compound is (CH3)3C–CH=CH–Cl with the H trans, which is (E)-1-chloro-3,3-dimethyl-1-butene (Cl and tert-butyl are the higher-priority groups and lie on opposite sides).
x: The Z isomer has the two vinyl H cis to each other; a cis coupling (about 6–12 Hz) is smaller than the 13.4 Hz measured.
2-Chloro-3,3-dimethyl-1-butene has its two vinyl H on the same carbon (=CH<sub>2</sub>); geminal coupling is only about 0–3 Hz, and those H appear near 5.1–5.3 ppm.
Chlorocyclohexane has no vinyl hydrogens; its most downfield signal is the CH–Cl near 4 ppm.

q: The 1H NMR spectrum of bromoethane shown was recorded at 300 MHz, and J = 7.3 Hz. If the same sample is run at 600 MHz, where is the center of the quartet (in Hz from TMS), and how far apart are its neighboring lines?
c: Center at 2058 Hz; lines 7.3 Hz apart
Center at 2058 Hz; lines 14.6 Hz apart
Center at 1029 Hz; lines 7.3 Hz apart
Center at 2058 Hz; lines 3.7 Hz apart
h: Convert ppm to hertz with the new spectrometer frequency. Then decide whether the spacing between lines depends on that frequency.
w: Δν = δ × spectrometer MHz. The quartet stays at δ 3.43 at any field, so at 600 MHz its center is 3.43 × 600 = 2058 Hz from TMS (it was 1029 Hz at 300 MHz). The spacing between lines of a multiplet is J, which is set by the bonds, not by the magnet, so it stays 7.3 Hz. Answer: center at 2058 Hz; lines 7.3 Hz apart.
x: Doubling the field does not double J; coupling constants in hertz are field-independent.
1029 Hz is 3.43 × 300, the position at the old field; at 600 MHz the same δ corresponds to twice as many hertz.
Coupling constants do not shrink at higher field in hertz; only their size in ppm shrinks (7.3 Hz is 0.012 ppm at 600 MHz).

q:
A chemist reruns a sample on a 600 MHz spectrometer that was first recorded at 300 MHz. Which statements are true?
I. The chemical shift (δ, ppm) of each signal is unchanged.
II. Each coupling constant J (Hz) doubles.
III. The separation in hertz between the centers of two different signals doubles.
h: Separate what is measured relative to the field (chemical shift) from what is set by the bonds between nuclei (coupling).
w: I is true: δ = Δν(Hz)/ν(MHz) is defined so that it does not depend on the instrument. II is false: J depends on the bonds between the coupled nuclei, so it is the same number of hertz at any field. III is true: a fixed difference in ppm is twice as many hertz at 600 MHz as at 300 MHz. So I and III only; signals spread apart in hertz while the multiplets keep their width, which is why high-field spectra overlap less.
x: Misjudges III: since Δν = δ × MHz, a 1 ppm gap is 300 Hz at 300 MHz and 600 Hz at 600 MHz, so it does double.
Misjudges II: coupling constants in hertz do not change with the spectrometer frequency.
Misjudges I: chemical shifts in ppm are field-independent; that is the reason the ppm scale is used.

q: A C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub> alkane gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown, with the DEPT result written over each peak. Which isomer is it?
h: Two of the choices give four signals. Use the DEPT labels: which one has a CH but no quaternary C?
w: Four signals for six carbons means symmetry. The DEPT labels show one CH, one CH2 and two different CH3 environments, with no quaternary C. In CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3 the two ethyl groups are equivalent (one CH2 signal, one CH3 signal), plus the branch CH and the branch CH3: four signals of exactly these types. It is 3-methylpentane.
x: 2,2-Dimethylbutane also gives four signals, but one is a quaternary C (absent from DEPT) and it has no CH; the labels here show a CH and no C.
2,3-Dimethylbutane is so symmetric that it gives only two signals (a CH and a CH<sub>3</sub>).
2-Methylpentane has no symmetry across its chain: five signals, including two different CH<sub>2</sub> carbons.

q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub> gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown (DEPT results written over the peaks). Which structure is it?
h: sp carbons appear at about 65–90 ppm. Are the two alkyne carbons here CH or C?
w: Two peaks at 75–82 ppm are sp (alkyne) carbons, and DEPT says neither carries an H, so the triple bond is internal. The remaining carbons are two different CH3 groups and one CH2: one CH3 on one alkyne carbon (the unusually upfield 3.5 ppm methyl) and an ethyl group on the other. This is CH3C≡CCH2CH3, 2-pentyne.
x: 1-Pentyne is a terminal alkyne: one of its sp carbons is a CH (near 68 ppm), and its sp<sup>3</sup> carbons are two CH<sub>2</sub> and one CH<sub>3</sub>, not two CH<sub>3</sub> and one CH<sub>2</sub>.
3-Methyl-1-butyne gives only four signals; its ≡CH carbon is a CH, and its two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent.
Cyclopentene has no sp carbons; its sp<sup>2</sup> CH carbons appear near 130 ppm, and it gives only three signals.

q: Which C5H12O isomer gives exactly two signals in its 1H NMR spectrum?
h: Group the hydrogens by symmetry. Remember that an OH hydrogen counts as its own signal.
w: In tert-butyl methyl ether, (CH3)3C–O–CH3, the nine tert-butyl H are equivalent and the three OCH3 H are a second set: two signals (9H singlet near 1.2 ppm, 3H singlet near 3.2 ppm). So the answer is tert-butyl methyl ether.
x: 2,2-Dimethyl-1-propanol has three signals: the 9H tert-butyl group, the CH<sub>2</sub>O and the OH.
Ethyl propyl ether has no symmetry relating its two alkyl groups: five signals.
3-Pentanol has four signals: the two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> groups, the two equivalent CH<sub>2</sub> groups, the CH–O and the OH.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. Which structure is it?
h: Find the DBE, read the three IR bands above 2000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, then explain why the alkyne H is a singlet.
w: DBE = 2. IR: broad 3365 cm−1 (O–H), sharp 3300 cm−1 (≡C–H) and weak 2115 cm−1 (C≡C): a terminal alkyne and an alcohol, with no C=O. 1H: the 1H singlet at 2.42 ppm is the ≡C–H, the broad 1H singlet is the OH, and the 6H singlet is two equivalent CH3 groups. No H appears at 3.3–4.2 ppm, so the alcohol carbon carries no H. Everything fits HC≡C–C(CH3)2OH, 2-methyl-3-butyn-2-ol.
x: 4-Pentyn-1-ol is a primary alcohol: a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>OH triplet near 3.7 ppm and two more CH<sub>2</sub> signals; no 6H singlet.
4-Pentyn-2-ol has a 1H CH–O multiplet near 3.9 ppm and a 3H doublet, not a 6H singlet.
Cyclopentanone has a strong C=O band near 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no O–H or ≡C–H bands; its <sup>1</sup>H spectrum is two 4H multiplets.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O shows no O–H and no C=O band in its IR spectrum, but has strong bands at 1620 and 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. (The two hydrogens of its =CH<sub>2</sub> group give separate signals.) Which structure is it?
h: DBE = 1 with no C=O means a C=C or a ring. Why is one vinyl H near 6.5 ppm while the other two sit near 4 ppm?
w: DBE = 1. No O–H and no C=O, so the oxygen is an ether, and the 1620 cm−1 band is a C=C (strong because it is polarized by O). The 2H quartet at 3.73 ppm and 3H triplet are an O–CH2CH3 group. The three 1H doublets of doublets are a –CH=CH2 group bonded to O: the O–CH= hydrogen is deshielded to 6.47 ppm, while the =CH2 hydrogens are pushed upfield (3.97, 4.18 ppm) by resonance donation from the oxygen lone pair onto that carbon. The compound is CH2=CH–O–CH2CH3, ethyl vinyl ether.
x: 2-Butanone has a strong C=O band near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which the stem rules out, and no vinyl H.
3-Buten-2-ol is an alcohol (broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and has a 3H doublet and a CH–O near 4.3 ppm, not an ethyl quartet/triplet.
Tetrahydrofuran has no C=C: its spectrum is two 4H multiplets (≈3.7 and 1.8 ppm), with no vinyl signals.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows no O–H band in its IR spectrum. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. Which structure is it?
h: Both signals are singlets in the 3.3–3.6 ppm region. What does that say about every carbon bearing H?
w: DBE = 0, and no O–H band means both oxygens are ethers. Both signals sit at 3.3–3.6 ppm, so every CHn group is bonded to O. The 6H singlet is two equivalent OCH3 groups, and the 4H singlet is two equivalent OCH2 groups; they are not split because equivalent neighbors do not split each other and O separates the CH3 from the CH2. The compound is CH3O–CH2CH2–OCH3, 1,2-dimethoxyethane.
x: 1,1-Dimethoxyethane has a C-methyl that is not on O: a 3H doublet near 1.3 ppm, a 1H quartet near 4.6 ppm (the O–CH–O), and a 6H OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet.
1,4-Butanediol is a diol: a strong broad O–H band, plus an inner CH<sub>2</sub> signal near 1.6 ppm that is not on O.
2-Ethoxyethanol has an O–H (ruled out by IR) and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet near 1.2 ppm.

q: An alkyl chloride gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: A septet means six neighboring H. Where would two CH<sub>3</sub> groups and one H have to be?
w: A 1H septet and a 6H doublet are the classic isopropyl pattern: the CH has six neighbors (two CH3 groups) → 7 lines, and each CH3 has one neighbor → doublet. The CH at 4.16 ppm is on the carbon bearing Cl. The compound is (CH3)2CHCl, 2-chloropropane.
x: 1-Chloropropane gives three signals: a 2H triplet near 3.5 ppm, a 2H sextet and a 3H triplet.
2-Chloro-2-methylpropane has no H on the C–Cl carbon: one 9H singlet near 1.6 ppm.
Chloroethane gives a 2H quartet and a 3H triplet; it has no septet or 6H signal.

q: The broadband-decoupled 13C NMR spectrum of 3-buten-1-ol (shown) is given. Which peak belongs to the tagged carbon a?
h: Sort the carbons into sp<sup>2</sup>, sp<sup>3</sup> bonded to O, and plain sp<sup>3</sup>, and recall the usual shift range of each.
w: Typical ranges: alkene carbons 100–150 ppm, sp3 carbons bonded to O 50–80 ppm, other sp3 carbons 0–45 ppm. Carbon a is the sp3 CH2 bonded to OH, so it is δ 61.5.
x: 135.0 ppm is in the alkene range; it is the internal =CH carbon.
117.3 ppm is the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> alkene carbon.
36.9 ppm is the allylic CH<sub>2</sub>, an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon not bonded to O.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Br gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. (Any =CH<sub>2</sub> group here gives two separate 1H signals, one for each H.) Which structure is it?
h: Every signal is a singlet. Which isomer has no H on any carbon next to a carbon bearing H?
w: DBE = 1. Two 1H vinyl signals with almost no splitting are the two H of a =CH2 on a carbon with no H (geminal coupling is very small). The 2H singlet at 3.95 ppm is a CH2Br that is also allylic, and the 3H singlet at 1.85 ppm is a CH3 on a C=C. Both are attached to the same hydrogen-free sp2 carbon, so nothing splits them: CH2=C(CH3)CH2Br, 3-bromo-2-methylpropene.
x: (E)-1-Bromo-2-butene has two vinyl CH (a 2H multiplet near 5.7 ppm), a 2H doublet for CH2Br and a 3H doublet for the CH3; no singlets.
4-Bromo-1-butene has three vinyl H (one near 5.8 ppm) and a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br chain whose signals are split; it has no CH<sub>3</sub>.
Bromocyclobutane has no C=C, so no vinyl signals; its CH–Br is a multiplet near 4.4 ppm.

q: In the 400 MHz 1H NMR spectrum of chloroethene, the tagged hydrogen a appears as a doublet of doublets with lines at 2514.9, 2507.7, 2500.3 and 2493.1 Hz from TMS. What are its two coupling constants, and which coupling is the larger one?
c: 14.6 Hz (to the =CH2 H trans to a) and 7.2 Hz (to the H cis to a)
14.6 Hz (to the =CH2 H cis to a) and 7.2 Hz (to the H trans to a)
7.2 Hz and 7.4 Hz, the spacings between neighboring lines
21.8 Hz and 7.4 Hz, the outer and inner line separations
h: In a doublet of doublets, the spacing of lines 1 and 2 is the smaller J, and the spacing of lines 1 and 3 is the larger J.
w: A doublet of doublets is a doublet (large J) with each line split again (small J). The small coupling is the spacing of lines 1 and 2 (and of 3 and 4): 2514.9 − 2507.7 = 7.2 Hz. The large coupling is the spacing of lines 1 and 3 (and of 2 and 4): 2514.9 − 2500.3 = 14.6 Hz. Check: the outer lines are 14.6 + 7.2 = 21.8 Hz apart, and the center, 2504.0 Hz, is δ 6.26. Across a C=C, trans H couple more strongly (12–18 Hz) than cis H (6–12 Hz), so the answer is 14.6 Hz to the trans H and 7.2 Hz to the cis H.
x: This swaps the assignment: trans vinyl coupling (12–18 Hz) is larger than cis coupling (6–12 Hz).
Lines 2 and 3 are not split by a real coupling; their 7.4 Hz gap is just the difference of the two J values (14.6 − 7.2).
The outer-line separation is the sum of the two couplings (14.6 + 7.2), and the inner gap is their difference; neither is a J value.

q: Which bond-line formula represents CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Read the condensed formula left to right. A group in parentheses with a subscript hangs off the atom just before it; count every carbon in the main chain.
w: Walk along the formula: CH3CH2– is an ethyl end, C(CH3)2 is a chain carbon carrying two methyl groups, then one CH2, then CH(OH), then a terminal CH3. That is a six-carbon chain with OH on C2 and two methyls on C4 (4,4-dimethylhexan-2-ol), C8H18O. The structure with the gem-dimethyl carbon flanked by an ethyl group and a CH2–CH(OH)–CH3 unit is the match.
x: This chain has no CH<sub>2</sub> between the quaternary carbon and the CH(OH) carbon, so one carbon of the formula is missing (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O).

Here the quaternary carbon carries three methyls (a tert-butyl group) and two CH<sub>2</sub> groups follow it. The formula has an ethyl group, not a methyl, on that carbon and only one CH<sub>2</sub> after it.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> means two methyl groups; this structure shows only one, so the carbon is CH instead of a quaternary C.

q: Which bond-line formula represents C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
h: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>– and C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>– are different rings. In a condensed formula, CO with no H written after it is a carbonyl.
w: C6H11– is a cyclohexyl group (a saturated six-membered ring with one H removed); C6H5– would be phenyl. Next comes CH2, then CO, which is a ketone C=O because no H follows the O, then an isopropyl group CH(CH3)2. So the answer is cyclohexyl–CH2–C(=O)–CH(CH3)2 (1-cyclohexyl-3-methylbutan-2-one).
x: This ring is a benzene ring (phenyl, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), which has six fewer hydrogens than the cyclohexyl group C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>.
This is an alcohol, CH(OH). In a condensed formula CO with nothing after the O is a carbonyl; an alcohol would be written CH(OH).
The CH<sub>2</sub> has moved to the other side of the carbonyl: this is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, a constitutional isomer.

q: What is the condensed structural formula of the compound shown?
h: Start at the branched end, count the vertices between the branch point, the C–Br carbon and the C=O carbon, and add the hydrogens each carbon needs to make four bonds.
w: From the left: an isopropyl end, (CH3)2CH–; one CH2; the carbon bearing Br, CHBr; one CH2; the carbonyl carbon, CO; and a terminal CH3. That gives (CH3)2CHCH2CHBrCH2COCH3 (4-bromo-6-methylheptan-2-one, C8H15BrO).
x: This puts Br on the carbon right next to the isopropyl CH. The drawing has a CH<sub>2</sub> between the branch point and the C–Br carbon.
This formula has two CH<sub>2</sub> groups between CHBr and C=O; the drawing has only one.
This formula branches at the wrong carbon: it describes a sec-butyl group, not an isopropyl group followed by CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: How many hydrogen atoms are bonded to each of the tagged carbons a, b and c?
h: A neutral carbon makes four bonds. Count the bonds you can see (a double bond counts twice); hydrogens fill the rest.
w: Bond-line drawings hide the H atoms on carbon, so count bonds to non-hydrogen atoms and subtract from 4. Carbon a is bonded to the C=O carbon and to a ring carbon: 2 bonds, so 2 H. Carbon b has a double bond (2) to a ring carbon and a single bond to a CH2: 3 bonds, so 1 H. Carbon c is bonded to two ring carbons, Cl and a CH3: 4 bonds, so 0 H. Answer: a 2, b 1, c 0.
x: Carbon b is an alkene carbon: its double bond uses two of its four bonds, leaving room for only one H. Carbon c already has four bonds (two ring C, Cl, CH3).
Carbon a has only two bonds to carbon (C=O carbon and ring carbon), so it carries two hydrogens, not one.
The chlorine counts as one of carbon c's four bonds; with two ring bonds and a methyl, no H is left.

q: Which structure is the same compound as the one shown (only redrawn in a different orientation)?
h: Are the groups 1,2 or 1,3 on the ring? Do OH and CH<sub>3</sub> share a face (cis) or not (trans)? Then use R/S to rule out the mirror image.
w: The given compound is trans-3-methylcyclopentan-1-ol with both stereocenters R, (1R,3R). Turning or flipping a drawing over in the plane changes how it looks, but not the connectivity or the configuration of each stereocenter. The structure that is (1R,3R) with the groups 1,3 and trans is the same compound. Of the others, one is trans but (1S,3S) (the enantiomer), one is cis (a diastereomer) and one has the groups 1,2 (a constitutional isomer).
x: This is trans and 1,3, but both centers are S: it is the mirror image (enantiomer) of the compound shown, not the same compound.
Here the OH and CH<sub>3</sub> are on the same face of the ring (cis), so this is a diastereomer.
The methyl is on the carbon next to the C–OH carbon (a 1,2 pattern), so this is a constitutional isomer, 2-methylcyclopentan-1-ol.

q: In the imine shown, the tagged nitrogen a is sp2 hybridized. How are its five valence electrons distributed among its orbitals?
c: three sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals hold 2, 1 and 1 electrons; the unhybridized 2p orbital holds 1
three sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals hold 1, 1 and 1 electrons; the unhybridized 2p orbital holds 2
four sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals hold 2, 1, 1 and 1 electrons
two sp orbitals hold 2 and 1 electrons; two unhybridized 2p orbitals hold 1 each
h: Decide which orbital forms the π bond to carbon and which orbital holds the lone pair. A π bond needs a p orbital with one electron.
w: An imine N has three electron domains (the σ bond to C, the σ bond to CH3 and a lone pair), so it is sp2. Its 2s and two 2p orbitals mix into three sp2 orbitals; one 2p orbital is left over. The two σ bonds each need one electron in an sp2 orbital, the lone pair sits in the third sp2 orbital, and the remaining 2p orbital holds one electron to form the C=N π bond. So: sp2 orbitals with 2, 1, 1 electrons and the 2p with 1. This is why the imine lone pair lies in the molecular plane and is not part of the π system.
x: With the pair in the p orbital, no singly occupied p orbital is left to make the C=N π bond. A lone pair in p is the situation in amides or pyrrole, not in an imine.
Four sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals leave no p orbital, so nitrogen could not form the C=N π bond. That is the picture for an amine nitrogen.
sp hybridization fits a nitrogen with two electron domains, such as the N of a nitrile. The imine N has three (two σ bonds and a lone pair).

q: The allyl radical, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•, has three π molecular orbitals (ψ<sub>1</sub>, ψ<sub>2</sub>, ψ<sub>3</sub>, in order of increasing energy). Which orbital holds the unpaired electron, and what is its node pattern?
c: ψ<sub>2</sub>, which has one node passing through the central carbon
ψ<sub>1</sub>, which has no nodes between the carbons
ψ<sub>3</sub>, which has two nodes, one between each pair of carbons
ψ<sub>2</sub>, which has one node between C1 and C2 only
h: Three p orbitals give three MOs with 0, 1 and 2 nodes. Fill three π electrons from the bottom, and place each node symmetrically about the central carbon.
w: Three overlapping p orbitals combine into ψ1 (0 nodes, bonding), ψ2 (1 node, nonbonding) and ψ3 (2 nodes, antibonding). The radical has three π electrons: two fill ψ1 and the third goes into ψ2. Because the molecule is symmetric, the single node of ψ2 must lie at the center, so ψ2 has zero coefficient on C2. The answer is ψ2, with its node through the central carbon. That explains why the unpaired electron (and the reactivity) of the allyl radical is found on the two end carbons, matching the two resonance forms.
x: ψ<sub>1</sub> holds two paired electrons. The third electron cannot enter it (Pauli principle), so it goes into ψ<sub>2</sub>.
ψ<sub>3</sub> is the antibonding orbital and is empty in the radical; it is filled only after ψ<sub>1</sub> and ψ<sub>2</sub>.
A node between C1 and C2 only would make the orbital lopsided. In the symmetric allyl system the one node of ψ<sub>2</sub> passes through C2, leaving equal lobes on C1 and C3.

q: What is the hybridization of the tagged atoms a, b and c?
h: Count σ bonds plus lone pairs for each atom, but first ask whether a lone pair next to a C=O is delocalized into the π system.
w: Atom a is the central carbon of an allene (C=C=C): it has two σ bonds and two π bonds at right angles, so it is sp. Atom b is an amide nitrogen; its lone pair is delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen by resonance, so the N is planar and sp2, with the lone pair in a p orbital. Atom c is an ordinary amine nitrogen (three σ bonds and a localized lone pair), so it is sp3. Answer: a sp, b sp2, c sp3.
x: The central allene carbon makes two double bonds, so it needs two unhybridized p orbitals: it is sp, not sp<sup>2</sup>.
Counting the amide N as 3 σ bonds + 1 lone pair = sp<sup>3</sup> ignores resonance. The N lone pair is conjugated with C=O, which makes the nitrogen sp<sup>2</sup> and planar.
Nitrogen c is not next to any π bond, so its lone pair is localized and the N is sp3 (trigonal pyramidal).

q: What are the molecular geometries (VSEPR shapes) at the tagged atoms a, b and c?
h: Count electron domains (σ bonds and lone pairs; a multiple bond counts once) to get the electron geometry, then name the shape from the atoms only.
w: Atom a is a nitrile carbon: two domains (C≡N and C–C), so it is linear. Atom b is an ether oxygen: two bonds and two lone pairs make four domains (tetrahedral electron geometry), but the shape described by the atoms is bent. Atom c is an amine nitrogen: three bonds and one lone pair, so it is trigonal pyramidal. Answer: linear, bent, trigonal pyramidal.
x: VSEPR shapes name only atom positions. The ether O has two lone pairs, so its shape is bent, and the amine N has a lone pair, so it is pyramidal, not planar.
The nitrile carbon has only two electron domains (a triple bond counts as one domain), so it is linear, not trigonal planar.
The ether oxygen has two lone pairs as well as two bonds; four domains give a bent shape. The amine N, with one lone pair, is pyramidal, not tetrahedral.

q: Which of the compounds shown have a net molecular dipole moment?
h: Draw each C–X bond dipole as an arrow and add them as vectors. Only a molecule whose bond dipoles exactly cancel has no net dipole.
w: I is false: in (E)-1,2-dibromoethene the two C–Br dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel, so the net dipole is zero. II is true: in 1,1-dibromoethene both C–Br dipoles point toward the same end of the molecule and add. III is true: in 1,3-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl dipoles are 120° apart; they partly cancel, but a resultant along the line bisecting them remains. Answer: II and III only.
x: Statement III is misjudged: meta C–Cl dipoles are 120° apart, not 180°, so they do not cancel. Only para-dichlorobenzene has zero dipole.
Statement II is misjudged: both C–Br bonds of 1,1-dibromoethene point toward the CBr<sub>2</sub> end, so their dipoles add.
Statement I is misjudged: the trans isomer has a center of symmetry, so its two C–Br dipoles cancel exactly.

q: Which structure is NOT a resonance contributor of the cation shown?
h: Resonance forms keep every atom (and every H) in place and move only π electrons and lone pairs. Compare where the hydrogens are in each structure.
w: Moving the O=C π electrons onto oxygen puts + on C1; then each C=C can shift toward the electron-poor carbon, placing + on C3 and then on C5. All of those keep the same atoms and hydrogens, so they are true contributors. The structure with a CH2 next to oxygen and a terminal =CH+ vinyl cation has moved a hydrogen from C5 to C1. That is a different compound (a constitutional isomer), not a resonance form.
x: This is the form made by moving the O=C π bond onto oxygen: the positive charge sits on C1, next to the OCH<sub>3</sub>. Same atoms, same H positions, so it is a contributor.
Shifting the C2=C3 π bond toward C1 puts the + on C3. No atom moves, so this is a contributor.
Shifting the C4=C5 π bond as well places + on the terminal CH<sub>2</sub> (C5). This is a contributor.

q: The acetyl cation (acylium ion) can be drawn as structures I and II. Which is the major contributor, and why?
c: II, because every atom in II has a complete octet
I, because the positive charge is on the less electronegative atom
Neither; I and II contribute equally because they differ only in charge location
II, because oxygen is more electronegative and stabilizes a positive charge better than carbon
h: Rank the rules for major contributors: first complete octets, then charge placement by electronegativity.
w: The most important rule for judging contributors is that more atoms with full octets (and more bonds) win. In I the cationic carbon has only six electrons. In II the extra C≡O π bond gives every carbon and oxygen an octet, even though the + now sits on oxygen. So II is the major contributor because every atom has a complete octet. This is why acylium ions are linear and relatively stable, and why they form in Friedel–Crafts acylation.
x: Putting + on the less electronegative atom is only a tiebreaker. A full octet on every atom outranks it, so I is the minor form.
Contributors are equal only when they are equally stable. II has one more bond and no electron-deficient atom, so it contributes more.
II is the major form, but not for this reason: a positive charge is less stable on the more electronegative oxygen. II wins in spite of that, because of its complete octets.

q: Rank these carbocations from least stable to most stable.
h: Classify each cation (vinyl, 2°, 3°) and then ask which ones are also allylic. In an allylic cation, look at both resonance forms.
w: II is a vinyl cation: the + is on an sp-like carbon with the empty orbital in the plane, not overlapping any π bond, so it is the least stable. I is a simple secondary cation (hyperconjugation from two alkyl groups). III is tertiary, so it is more stable than I. IV is allylic: its resonance form puts the + on the ring carbon that carries the methyl, so the charge is shared between a 2° and a 3° carbon. Resonance plus a tertiary contributor makes IV the most stable. Ranking: II < I < III < IV.
x: A vinyl cation is less stable than an ordinary secondary cation, so II belongs below I.
IV is allylic and one of its contributors is tertiary; resonance delocalization makes it more stable than the simple tertiary cation III.
The vinyl cation II is the least stable of all; it does not rank above the secondary and tertiary cations.

q: Rank these radicals from least stable to most stable.
h: Where is the unpaired electron: in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital in the ring plane, or in a p orbital that can overlap the ring π system? Then count alkyl groups.
w: I is the phenyl radical: the odd electron is in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, perpendicular to the π system, so it gets no resonance help and is the least stable (the aryl C–H bond is about 113 kcal/mol). II is a secondary alkyl radical, helped only by hyperconjugation. III is benzylic: the odd electron is delocalized into the ring by resonance. IV is benzylic and also tertiary, so it is the most stable. Ranking: I < II < III < IV.
x: The phenyl radical is not stabilized by the ring; its odd electron is in an in-plane sp<sup>2</sup> orbital. A secondary alkyl radical is more stable.
IV is benzylic and tertiary; the two methyl groups add hyperconjugation to the benzylic resonance, so IV is more stable than primary benzylic III.
Phenyl radical I is less stable than the alkyl radical II, not more stable than the benzylic radical III.

q: The 4-nitrobenzyl anion is shown. On which of the tagged atoms does the negative charge appear in at least one resonance contributor?
h: Push the CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> lone pair into the ring one arrow at a time; each arrow moves the charge two atoms. At the C–NO<sub>2</sub> carbon, can N=O accept it?
w: The charge starts on the benzylic carbon a. Forming a C=C to the ring pushes the charge to the ortho carbon b, then to the other ortho carbon and to the para carbon (the one bearing NO2). From the para carbon a C=N bond can form while the N=O π electrons move onto oxygen, so the charge reaches oxygen d. The meta carbon c is never charged, because the charge alternates positions. Answer: a, b and d. The extra delocalization onto the nitro oxygen is why 4-nitrotoluene is far more acidic at CH3 than toluene.
x: The charge alternates around the ring (ortho, para), so the meta carbon c never carries it.
Carbon c is meta to the CH2; the charge skips it. The ortho carbon b and the nitro oxygen d are the charged positions.
This stops at the ring. From the para carbon the charge continues onto the nitro oxygen d, through the C=N / N–O− contributor.

q:
In which species is the tagged central atom trigonal planar?
I. the nitrogen of nitromethane, CH3NO2
II. the boron of trimethyl borate, B(OCH3)3
III. the negatively charged carbon of the tert-butyl anion, (CH3)3C−
h: Count electron domains on each central atom, including any lone pair. Three domains and no lone pair give a trigonal planar shape.
w: I is true: the nitro nitrogen bonds to C and two O atoms (one N=O, one N–O− in each contributor) and has no lone pair, so it has three domains and is trigonal planar (sp2). II is true: boron has three B–O bonds and no lone pair (only six valence electrons), so it is trigonal planar. III is false: the carbanion carbon has three bonds and a lone pair, four domains, so it is trigonal pyramidal like an amine N. Answer: I and II only.
x: Statement I is misjudged: the nitro N has no lone pair (it carries the formal + charge), so its three bonds make it trigonal planar.
Statement II is misjudged: boron in B(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> has only six valence electrons and no lone pair, so its three B–O bonds make it trigonal planar.
Statement III is false: with four electron domains, the tert-butyl anion carbon is pyramidal, not planar.

q: What is the approximate C–O–C bond angle in dimethyl ether, CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count the electron domains on oxygen, including lone pairs.
w: The ether oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs: four electron domains, tetrahedral electron geometry, sp3. The bond angle is therefore near the tetrahedral 109.5°. (The real value is about 112°, slightly wider than in water because the two methyl groups are bulky.) Answer: about 110°; the shape is bent.
x: 120° fits three electron domains, as in a carbonyl carbon. Oxygen here has four (two bonds, two lone pairs).
A 180° angle would need only two electron domains and no lone pairs on oxygen. Its two lone pairs make the molecule bent.
90° would mean bonding through pure, unhybridized p orbitals; the sp<sup>3</sup> oxygen of an ether is close to tetrahedral.

q: Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) is often drawn with an S–O single bond so that sulfur keeps an octet, as shown. What are the formal charges on sulfur and oxygen in this structure?
h: Formal charge = valence electrons − (nonbonding electrons + ½ bonding electrons). Sulfur and oxygen both have 6 valence electrons.
w: Sulfur has three bonds (6 bonding electrons) and one lone pair: 6 − (2 + 3) = +1. Oxygen has one bond and three lone pairs: 6 − (6 + 1) = −1. The charges sum to zero, matching the neutral molecule. Answer: S +1, O −1. This charge separation is why the S–O bond of DMSO is so polar and why DMSO is a strong H-bond acceptor at oxygen.
x: These signs are reversed. Oxygen with three lone pairs and one bond owns 7 electrons, one more than its 6 valence electrons, so it is −1.
Zero charges would need an S=O double bond (sulfur with 10 electrons). In the single-bond octet structure shown, each atom carries a formal charge.
This counts each atom's full share of the shared electrons. Formal charge gives each atom only half of its bonding electrons.

q:
Which statements about the allyl cation, CH2=CH–CH2+, are correct?
I. Its two carbon–carbon bonds have the same length.
II. One of its resonance contributors places the positive charge on the central carbon.
III. Most of the positive charge is located on the central carbon.
h: Draw the second contributor by moving the π bond toward the empty orbital. Which carbons carry + in the two forms?
w: I is true: the two contributors are mirror images (C1=C2–C3+ and +C1–C2=C3), so each C–C bond is an average of single and double and both are the same length. II is false: moving the π bond only shifts the + between the two end carbons; no octet-obeying contributor puts it on C2. III is false: the positive charge is shared by the terminal carbons; the central carbon carries little of it (the LUMO, ψ2, has a node there). Answer: I only.
x: Statement II is false. Shifting the C=C π bond moves the + from one end carbon to the other; the central carbon is never the cationic carbon in a resonance form.
Statement III is false. Both contributors put the + on an end carbon, so the charge sits on C1 and C3, not C2.
Statements II and III are both false; only the equal bond lengths (I) follow from the two equivalent contributors.

q:
Which statements about the reactive intermediates derived from 2-methylpropane are correct?
I. In the tert-butyl cation, the central carbon and the three carbons bonded to it lie in one plane.
II. In the tert-butyl anion, the lone pair is in an unhybridized p orbital and the carbon is planar.
III. The tert-butyl radical is nearly planar, with the unpaired electron in an orbital that is mostly p in character.
h: Count domains: an empty orbital does not count, a lone pair does, and a single electron behaves between those two cases.
w: I is true: the cation has three σ bonds and an empty p orbital, so it is sp2 and planar. II is false: a carbanion's lone pair is a full electron domain, so the carbon is sp3 and trigonal pyramidal (like NH3). III is true: alkyl radicals are flat or very shallow pyramids; the single electron sits in a nearly pure p orbital, which is why radical reactions at a stereocenter give racemic products. Answer: I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: alkyl radicals such as tert-butyl are nearly planar, with the odd electron in a p-type orbital.
Statement II is false: the anion has four electron domains (three bonds and a lone pair) and is pyramidal, not planar.
Statement I is also true: the cation has three σ bonds and an empty p orbital, so it is sp<sup>2</sup> and planar.

q: Which structure is 4-ethyl-2,2,5-trimethylheptane?
h: Draw a seven-carbon chain, number it, and place the groups. Then check each choice: find its longest chain and number it from the end nearer the first branch.
w: Heptane is a seven-carbon chain. C2 carries two methyls, C4 an ethyl and C5 a methyl. In the structure with a tert-butyl end, one CH2, then CH(CH2CH3), then CH(CH3) followed by an ethyl end, the longest chain has seven carbons, and numbering from the tert-butyl end gives locants 2,2,4,5 (the other direction gives 3,4,6,6). Of the others, one swaps the ethyl and methyl positions, one moves the gem-dimethyl to C3, and one has only a six-carbon parent chain.
x: Here the methyl is on C4 and the ethyl on C5: this is 5-ethyl-2,2,4-trimethylheptane.
The two methyls sit on C3, not C2. Numbered properly this is 4-ethyl-3,3,5-trimethylheptane.
The chain ends in an isopropyl group, so the longest chain has only six carbons: 4-ethyl-2,2,5-trimethylhexane.

q: Which condensed formula is 2-bromo-4-methylhexane?
h: Write a six-carbon chain and number it. Put Br on C2 and CH<sub>3</sub> on C4, then name each choice yourself, numbering from the end nearer the first substituent.
w: Hexane is a six-carbon chain; the halogen is named as a prefix (bromo) and listed alphabetically with the alkyl group. Placing Br on C2 and a methyl on C4 gives CH3–CHBr–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH3. Numbered from the other end the locants would be 3 and 5, so 2,4 is the correct numbering: CH3CHBrCH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3.
x: Here the methyl is on C2 and Br on C4 (numbering from the end nearer the first substituent): 4-bromo-2-methylhexane. The two substituents have traded places.
Br and CH<sub>3</sub> are on adjacent carbons C3 and C4: 3-bromo-4-methylhexane.
Br and CH<sub>3</sub> are on adjacent carbons C2 and C3: 2-bromo-3-methylhexane. The methyl must be two carbons away from the C–Br carbon.

q: Which structure is 4-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene?
h: In a cycloalkene, C1 and C2 are the alkene carbons. Number through the double bond in the direction that gives the substituents the lowest locants.
w: The double bond is between C1 and C2, and C1 carries the methyl. Continue around the ring from C2: C3, then C4 carries Cl. The ring with the methyl on an alkene carbon and Cl on the carbon directly across the ring from it (1,4) is the answer. Of the others, one has Cl at C3 (3-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene), one is 5-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene, and one swaps Cl and CH3 (1-chloro-4-methylcyclohexene).
x: Here Cl is on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon right next to the alkene: 3-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene.
Numbering through the double bond from the methyl carbon, Cl lands on C5 (the other direction gives 2,4, which loses at the first locant). This is 5-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene.
The chlorine is on the alkene carbon and the methyl is at C4: this is 1-chloro-4-methylcyclohexene.

q: Haloperidol, an antipsychotic drug, is shown. Which choice correctly describes its functional groups?
c: a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two aryl halides
a ketone, a secondary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two aryl halides
a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a secondary amine and two aryl halides
a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two tertiary alkyl halides
h: Classify an alcohol by the carbons on the C–OH carbon, an amine by the carbons on N, and a halide by the kind of carbon bearing it.
w: The C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons (the aryl ring and a CH2), so it is a ketone. The OH carbon in the piperidine ring is bonded to three carbons (two ring CH2 groups and the aryl ring), so the alcohol is tertiary. The ring nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and the side chain), so the amine is tertiary. F and Cl are bonded directly to benzene carbons, so they are aryl halides. Answer: a ketone, a tertiary alcohol, a tertiary amine and two aryl halides.
x: The C–OH carbon has no H: it is bonded to two ring carbons and the chlorophenyl ring, which makes the alcohol tertiary.
The piperidine N has no N–H; its three bonds all go to carbon, so the amine is tertiary.
Both halogens are on sp<sup>2</sup> benzene carbons, which makes them aryl halides; a tertiary alkyl halide has X on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon bonded to three carbons.

q: Which compound contains both a lactone and a tertiary amine?
h: A lactone is a cyclic ester: the ring contains O bonded to a C=O. A tertiary amine N carries three carbons and no H.
w: The five-membered ring with O–C(=O) in the ring and a CH2N(CH3)2 side chain has both: the ring oxygen bonded to the carbonyl carbon makes a cyclic ester (lactone), and the N bonded to three carbons is a tertiary amine. One distractor has a secondary amine (N–H), one has an N–H in the ring next to C=O (a lactam, a cyclic amide), and one has a ring ether with a ketone carbon that is not bonded to the ring oxygen.
x: The lactone is right, but the side-chain N carries an H and only two carbons, so it is a secondary amine.
The ring contains N–C(=O), which is a lactam (cyclic amide), not a lactone.
In this ring the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone; the ring oxygen is an ether, not part of an ester.

q: Menthol, the cooling compound in mint, is shown. How many tertiary (3°) carbons does it contain? (A tertiary carbon is bonded to exactly three other carbons.)
h: Go carbon by carbon and count carbon neighbors only; the O of the OH does not count.
w: Count C–C bonds at each branch point. The isopropyl CH is bonded to two methyls and a ring carbon (3°). The ring carbon carrying the isopropyl group is bonded to two ring carbons and the isopropyl carbon (3°). The ring carbon carrying the methyl is bonded to two ring carbons and the methyl (3°). The C–OH carbon is bonded to only two carbons (plus O), so it is secondary. Answer: 3.
x: This misses the isopropyl CH, which is bonded to two CH<sub>3</sub> groups and to the ring: three carbons.
This counts the C–OH carbon. It is bonded to only two carbons; the oxygen does not make it tertiary.
Each branching ring carbon also counts; only one of the three tertiary carbons is in the isopropyl group.

q: The artificial sweetener aspartame is shown. Which functional group is NOT present?
h: Look at every C=O and name it by what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon.
w: Aspartame has three C=O groups. One carbonyl carbon is bonded to OCH3 (a methyl ester), one is bonded to N–H (an amide, the peptide bond), and one is bonded to OH (a carboxylic acid). It also has a primary amine and a benzene ring. No carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbons, so there is no ketone.
x: The C(=O)OCH<sub>3</sub> group at the phenylalanine end is a methyl ester.
The C(=O)–NH linking the two amino acids is an amide (peptide bond).
The CH<sub>2</sub>C(=O)OH side chain is a carboxylic acid.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The OH is the principal group: it gets the suffix and the lowest possible locant, even if that gives the C=C a higher number.
w: The six-carbon chain contains the OH, the C=C and the Cl. The alcohol is the highest-priority group, so it is named with the suffix -ol and must get the lowest locant. Numbering from the CH3 end puts OH on C2 (from the other end it would be C5). Then Cl is on C4 and the double bond starts at C5. Name: 4-chlorohex-5-en-2-ol.
x: This numbers from the alkene end. The OH outranks the C=C, so the OH (not the alkene) gets the lower locant.
When an alcohol is present, it must be the suffix (-ol); using the prefix hydroxy- here breaks the principal-group rule.
Counting from the CH<sub>3</sub> end, the Cl carbon is C4 (C2 carries OH, C3 is CH<sub>2</sub>), not C3.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: The carbon bearing OH is C1. Go around the ring in the direction that reaches a methyl soonest.
w: The OH carbon is C1. Going toward the adjacent methyl puts the methyls at C2 and C4; the other direction gives C4 and C6. The set {2,4} is lower, so the name is 2,4-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This goes around the ring the wrong way; {2,4} is lower than {4,6} at the first point of difference.
An OH principal group is named as the suffix -ol on the parent (cyclohexanol), not as a hydroxy prefix.
3,5-Dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol would have no methyl on a carbon next to C1. Here one methyl sits on the carbon directly beside the C–OH carbon, so the locants are 2 and 4.

q: Which structure is N,2-dimethylbutan-1-amine?
h: The locant N means the group is on nitrogen; a number means it is on that carbon of the chain. C1 is the carbon bonded to N.
w: Butan-1-amine has N on C1 of a four-carbon chain. 2-Methyl places a methyl on C2, and N-methyl places a methyl on the nitrogen. The compound CH3NH–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3 fits. The others put the carbon methyl on C3, put both methyls on nitrogen, or put both methyls on C2 with no N-methyl.
x: Here the C-methyl is on C3 (third carbon from N): N,3-dimethylbutan-1-amine.
Both methyls are on nitrogen: N,N-dimethylbutan-1-amine, a tertiary amine.
This is a primary amine with two methyls on C2: 2,2-dimethylbutan-1-amine; it has no N-methyl group.

q:
Which statements about the compound shown are correct?
I. The amine is secondary.
II. The alcohol is secondary.
III. The chlorine is bonded to a primary carbon.
h: Alcohols and halides are classified by the carbon that bears the OH or X; amines by how many carbons are bonded to N.
w: II is true: the C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons (CH3 and CH2), so the alcohol is secondary. I is false: the nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (the CH2 on each side and a CH3) and has no N–H, so it is a tertiary amine. III is true: the C–Cl carbon is bonded to only one other carbon, so it is a primary alkyl chloride. Answer: II and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: the CH<sub>2</sub>Cl carbon is attached to just one carbon, so it is primary.
Statement I is false: amines are classified by the number of carbons on nitrogen, and this N has three, so it is tertiary.
Statement II is also true: the carbinol carbon carries a CH<sub>3</sub> and a CH<sub>2</sub>, two carbons, so the alcohol is secondary.

q: Which intermolecular forces act between molecules in pure liquid triethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N?
c: dispersion, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding
hydrogen bonding and dispersion forces only
h: To donate a hydrogen bond, a molecule needs H bonded directly to N, O or F.
w: All molecules have dispersion forces. Triethylamine is a pyramidal molecule with polar C–N bonds and a lone pair, so it has a net dipole and shows dipole–dipole attractions. It has no N–H bond, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other (the N can only accept an H bond from a donor such as water). Answer: dispersion and dipole–dipole forces only.
x: The pyramidal N with a lone pair gives triethylamine a net dipole moment, so dipole–dipole forces are also present.
Hydrogen bonding between molecules of the pure amine needs an N–H donor; a tertiary amine has none.
A tertiary amine has no N–H, so there is no hydrogen bonding in the pure liquid; its permanent dipole gives dipole–dipole forces instead.

q:
Which of these compounds can form hydrogen bonds between molecules of the same compound in the pure liquid?
I. ethyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2CH3
II. propanamide, CH3CH2CONH2
III. methylamine, CH3NH2
h: A pure liquid can hydrogen-bond to itself only if its molecules have both an acceptor (lone pair on N, O, F) and a donor (H on N, O or F).
w: I is false: ethyl acetate has O acceptors but every H is on carbon, so it has no donor. II is true: the amide NH2 donates and the C=O oxygen accepts, so amides hydrogen-bond strongly. III is true: methylamine has N–H donors and an N lone pair acceptor. Answer: II and III only.
x: Statement III is misjudged: methylamine has two N–H bonds and a lone pair, so it is both donor and acceptor.
Statement II is misjudged: the NH<sub>2</sub> of a primary amide is a good donor and the C=O is a good acceptor.
Statement I is misjudged: an ester can accept hydrogen bonds (from water, for example) but has no O–H or N–H to donate, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to itself.

q: These three isomeric amines (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N) have the same molar mass. Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Count N–H bonds in each isomer, then consider how compact each molecule is.
w: Primary amine I (propan-1-amine) has two N–H donors and the most surface area, so it boils highest (48 °C). Secondary amine II (N-methylethanamine) has one N–H, so it forms fewer hydrogen bonds (36 °C). Tertiary amine III (trimethylamine) has no N–H and cannot hydrogen-bond to itself; it is also the most compact, so it boils far lower (3 °C). Ranking: III < II < I.
x: This is the reverse order. More N–H bonds mean more hydrogen bonding and a higher boiling point, so the primary amine is highest.
Trimethylamine has no N–H and cannot hydrogen-bond to itself, so it must have the lowest boiling point, not a middle one.
The primary amine has two N–H donors versus one for II, so I boils higher than II.

q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
h: Molar mass matters, but the number of O–H groups per molecule matters more when the masses are similar.
w: Propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) (92 g/mol) has three O–H groups, so each molecule forms a dense network of hydrogen bonds; it boils near 290 °C. Ethane-1,2-diol (62 g/mol, two OH) boils at 197 °C, hexan-1-ol (102 g/mol, one OH) at 157 °C, and heptane (100 g/mol, dispersion forces only) at 98 °C.
x: Hexan-1-ol is the heaviest alcohol here, but with only one O–H it forms far fewer hydrogen bonds than glycerol (157 °C vs about 290 °C).
Heptane has the largest molar mass but only dispersion forces, so it boils lowest of the four.
Ethane-1,2-diol has two O–H groups and boils high (197 °C), but glycerol has three and a larger mass.

q: Which compound is least soluble in hexane?
h: Like dissolves like: hexane offers only dispersion forces.
w: Hexane is nonpolar and attracts solutes only by dispersion forces. To dissolve in it, a compound must give up its own attractions. Ethane-1,2-diol is held together by strong hydrogen bonds from two OH groups per molecule, and hexane cannot replace them, so the two liquids are nearly immiscible. Diethyl ether, toluene and 1-chlorobutane are mostly hydrocarbon and mix freely with hexane.
x: Diethyl ether has a small dipole and no O–H; its two ethyl groups make it fully miscible with hexane.
Toluene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon held together by dispersion forces, just like hexane, so it mixes freely.
1-Chlorobutane is only weakly polar and has no hydrogen bonding, so it dissolves readily in hexane.

q: Dodecan-1-amine, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>11</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is insoluble in water but dissolves in dilute aqueous HCl. What is the best explanation?
c: HCl converts it to an alkylammonium chloride, whose ions are held in water by ion–dipole forces
HCl breaks the hydrogen bonds between amine molecules, freeing them to hydrogen-bond with water
HCl adds Cl to the alkyl chain, making the chain polar enough to dissolve
HCl converts the amine into an amide, which hydrogen-bonds strongly to water
h: What does an amine do with a strong acid? Compare a neutral molecule and an ion in water.
w: An amine is a base. HCl protonates the nitrogen to give CH3(CH2)11NH3+ Cl−, an ionic salt. Water molecules orient their partial charges around the ions; these ion–dipole attractions are much stronger than the hydrogen bonds the neutral amine can make, and they pull the long chain into solution. Answer: it becomes an alkylammonium chloride held in water by ion–dipole forces. Basifying the solution with NaOH would bring the neutral amine back out.
x: The neutral amine already can hydrogen-bond with water through its NH<sub>2</sub>; the C<sub>12</sub> chain is what keeps it insoluble. Only forming an ion changes that.
HCl does not react with a saturated alkyl chain; it reacts with the basic nitrogen lone pair.
An amide needs a carbonyl group; HCl only protonates the amine, giving an ammonium salt.

q: These three compounds have nearly the same molar mass (72–74 g/mol). Rank them from least to most soluble in water.
h: Neither ether can donate a hydrogen bond, but both can accept one from water. Which oxygen is easier for water to reach?
w: Pentane (I) has no polar group and is almost insoluble (about 0.04 g/L). Diethyl ether (II) can accept hydrogen bonds from water at its oxygen, so it dissolves moderately (about 69 g/L). Tetrahydrofuran (III) has the same C4O composition, but its alkyl groups are tied back into a ring, so the oxygen lone pairs are exposed and less shielded by flexible ethyl groups; THF is miscible with water in all proportions. Ranking: I < II < III.
x: THF is more soluble than diethyl ether: tying the carbons into a ring leaves its oxygen more exposed for hydrogen bonds from water.
Pentane has no way to interact with water except weak dispersion forces, so it is the least soluble, below diethyl ether.
This is the reverse order; the hydrocarbon is least soluble and the cyclic ether is most soluble.

q: 2-Nitrophenol boils at about 216 °C, while its isomer 4-nitrophenol boils at about 279 °C. What is the best explanation?
c: The O–H of 2-nitrophenol hydrogen-bonds to its own nitro group, so it forms fewer hydrogen bonds to other molecules
4-Nitrophenol has a larger molar mass, so its dispersion forces are stronger
2-Nitrophenol has no net dipole moment because its two groups are next to each other
The nitro group of 4-nitrophenol makes its O–H a weaker acid, so it hydrogen-bonds more strongly
h: The two isomers have the same atoms and the same groups. Look at how close the OH is to the nitro oxygens in each.
w: In 2-nitrophenol the OH and NO2 are on adjacent carbons, so the O–H forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond to a nitro oxygen (a six-membered ring). That H is then mostly unavailable for hydrogen bonds to neighboring molecules. In 4-nitrophenol the groups are too far apart, so each O–H hydrogen-bonds to other molecules, which raises the boiling point. Answer: 2-nitrophenol forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond, leaving fewer intermolecular hydrogen bonds. (The same effect lets 2-nitrophenol be separated from the 4-isomer by steam distillation.)
x: They are isomers (both C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>, 139 g/mol), so molar mass cannot explain the difference.
Ortho-disubstituted benzenes with polar groups do have net dipoles; the OH and NO<sub>2</sub> dipoles do not cancel.
