A para nitro group makes the phenol more acidic, not less; and acidity is not what sets the boiling point here.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Choose a parent chain that contains both C=C bonds, then number to give the double bonds the lowest locants.
w: The longest chain that includes both double bonds has six carbons (it runs from the =CH2 to one of the methyls on the far alkene carbon). Numbering from the =CH2 end gives the double bonds locants 1 and 4 (the other direction gives 2 and 5). The methyls are then on C3 and C5: 3,5-dimethylhexa-1,4-diene.
x: This numbers from the wrong end. The double bonds must get the lowest locants: {1,4} beats {2,5}.
The parent chain must contain both double bonds when possible. Treating the vinyl group as a substituent leaves one alkene out of the chain.
The chain has six carbons, not seven: the far alkene carbon carries two methyls, and only one of them is part of the chain.

q: What is the IUPAC name of this alkene?
h: Find the longest chain that contains both alkene carbons, number from the end nearer the C=C, then compare the higher-priority group on each alkene carbon.
w: The longest chain through the C=C has four carbons, numbered from the Cl end so the alkene starts at C1: 1-chloro-2-methylbut-1-ene. On C1, Cl outranks H. On C2, the ethyl group (C,H,H) outranks the methyl group (H,H,H) at the first point of difference. Cl and the ethyl group are on the same side, so the name is (Z)-1-chloro-2-methylbut-1-ene.
x: Cl and the methyl group are on opposite sides, but the methyl is the lower-priority group on C2; E/Z compares Cl with the ethyl group, which is on the same side as Cl.
The parent chain must be the longest chain containing the C=C; a four-carbon chain (butene) is available, so "2-ethylprop-1-ene" is not allowed.
Numbering must give the C=C the lowest locant; numbering from the Cl end puts it at C1, not C3.

q: Which structure is (2E,4Z)-hexa-2,4-dien-1-ol?
h: Number from the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon (C1). For each C=C, ask whether the two chain carbons attached to it are on the same side (Z) or opposite sides (E).
w: C1 is the CH2OH carbon, so the double bonds are C2=C3 and C4=C5. In each C=C here the higher-priority group on each carbon is the chain carbon (the other group is H). The required compound has the chain trans across C2=C3 (E) and cis across C4=C5 (Z): HOCH2–CH=CH–CH=CH–CH3 drawn trans at C2=C3 and cis at C4=C5.
x: This is the (2Z,4E) isomer: the geometries are swapped, cis at C2=C3 and trans at C4=C5.
This is the (2E,4E) isomer: the chain is trans across both double bonds.
This is the (2Z,4Z) isomer: the chain is cis across both double bonds.

q: What is the configuration of the C=C bond in this alkene, and which comparison decides it?
h: Compare the two groups on the fully substituted alkene carbon atom by atom: list the three atoms attached to each first carbon and compare the highest atom first.
w: On the CH end, CH3 outranks H. On the other alkene carbon, both groups are attached through carbon, so look at the next atoms: –CH2OH has (O,H,H) and –CH(CH3)2 has (C,C,H). The first point of difference is O versus C, so –CH2OH wins even though the isopropyl group is larger. In the drawing the CH3 and the CH2OH are on opposite sides, so the alkene is E.
x: CIP rules compare the highest atom first, not the number of carbons: O in (O,H,H) beats C in (C,C,H), so the isopropyl group is the lower-priority group.
The priority is right, but CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>OH are drawn on opposite sides of the C=C, which is E.
Size does not set priority; with isopropyl wrongly ranked first, the CH<sub>3</sub>/isopropyl pair would be cis and give Z, so this choice is inconsistent as well as wrong.

q: Which alkene can exist as a pair of E/Z isomers?
h: E/Z isomers need two different groups on each alkene carbon.
w: 3-Methylpent-2-ene has H and CH3 on C2, and CH3 and CH2CH3 on C3. Both alkene carbons carry two different groups, so 3-methylpent-2-ene exists as E and Z isomers.
x: In 2-methylbut-2-ene one alkene carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so swapping them gives the same molecule.
In but-1-ene C1 carries two H atoms, so there is no E/Z isomerism.
In 2,3-dimethylpent-2-ene, C2 carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so there is no E/Z isomerism.

q: The Newman projection shows a stereoisomer of 3-aminobutan-2-ol viewed along the C2–C3 bond, with C2 (the carbon bearing OH) in front. What are the configurations of C2 and C3?
h: Treat each carbon separately. The C2–C3 bond is one of its four groups: it points straight back for the front carbon and toward you for the back carbon.
w: A reliable method for a Newman projection: on each carbon, the bond to the other carbon lies along the viewing axis, so mentally swap it with the H, read the sense of priorities 1 → 2 → 3, then reverse once for the swap. C2 (front; OH > C3 > CH3 > H): after the swap H points straight back, and OH → C3 (now lower right) → CH3 runs clockwise, R; undoing the swap gives S. C3 (back; NH2 > C2 > CH3 > H): after the swap H points straight at you, and NH2 → C2 (now upper left) → CH3 runs counterclockwise, which with H toward you means R; undoing the swap gives S. The drawing is (2S,3S)-3-aminobutan-2-ol.
x: This is the enantiomer; it comes from reading each center as drawn without accounting for the group that lies along the viewing axis.
C2 is S, not R: with OH > C3 > CH<sub>3</sub> > H, the C3 bond (priority 2) points straight back, so the drawn sense cannot be read directly.
C3 is S: on the back carbon the C3–C2 bond (priority 2) points at the viewer, so the drawn NH<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub> sense cannot be read directly.

q: How are the compound in the Newman projection (viewed along C2–C3, C2 in front) and compound II related?
h: Both are 2-bromo-3-methylpentane. Assign R/S at C2 and C3 in each drawing and compare.
w: Both drawings have the same connectivity (2-bromo-3-methylpentane), so they are stereoisomers or identical. In the Newman projection, C2 (Br > C3 > CH3 > H) is S and C3 (C2 > CH2CH3 > CH3 > H) is R: (2S,3R). Structure II is (2S,3S). One center matches and one differs, so they are diastereomers.
x: Enantiomers differ at every stereocenter; here C2 is S in both.
Identical compounds have the same configuration at every center; C3 is R in the Newman projection but S in II.
Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity; both are 2-bromo-3-methylpentane.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound in this Fischer projection?
h: Horizontal bonds in a Fischer projection point toward you. If the lowest-priority group is horizontal, reverse the direction you read.
w: The chain has six carbons, numbered from the ethyl end so Cl gets locant 3. Priorities: Cl > CH2CH2CH3 > CH2CH3 > H (propyl beats ethyl at the second carbon). Cl (right) → propyl (bottom) → ethyl (top) runs clockwise, but H is on a horizontal bond pointing toward the viewer, so reverse it: (S)-3-chlorohexane.
x: The clockwise reading must be reversed because the lowest-priority H is on a horizontal bond, toward the viewer.
Numbering must give Cl the lowest locant; from the ethyl end it is C3, not C4.
Both the locant (should be 3) and the configuration (should be S) are wrong.

q: How many chirality centers does this terpene alcohol have?
h: Check each sp<sup>3</sup> carbon for four different groups. For ring carbons, compare the two ring paths away from the carbon.
w: The carbon bearing OH (H, OH, two different ring paths), the carbon bearing CH3 (one path reaches the CHOH next door, the other a CH2), and the carbon bearing the isopropenyl group (one path reaches CHOH in two bonds, the other only CH2 groups) each have four different groups. The ring CH2 carbons, the CH3 carbons and the sp2 carbons do not qualify. There are 3 chirality centers.
x: The ring carbon bearing the isopropenyl group is easy to miss: its two ring paths differ (one meets the CHOH carbon after two bonds), so it is a chirality center too.
Only three carbons qualify; the sp<sup>2</sup> carbon of the isopropenyl group has only three groups and cannot be a chirality center.
The CHOH carbon is not the only one; the ring carbons bearing CH<sub>3</sub> and the isopropenyl group also have four different groups.

q: Which tagged carbon(s) in this compound (terpinen-4-ol) is/are a chirality center?
h: For a ring carbon, walk both ways around the ring and see whether the two paths ever differ.
w: Carbon a carries OH, an isopropyl group and two ring paths. One path reaches the C=C after one CH2; the other passes two CH2 groups before reaching the methyl-bearing alkene carbon. The paths differ, so a has four different groups. Carbon b carries two identical CH3 groups. The answer is a only.
x: Carbon b is the isopropyl CH, which has two identical CH3 groups, so it cannot be a chirality center.
Carbon b has two identical CH3 groups; the chirality center is a.
The ring paths from a are not equivalent, because the C=C is not placed symmetrically, so a is a chirality center.

q: Which of compounds I–III would be optically active as pure samples?
h: Look for a chirality center first, then ask whether the molecule has an internal mirror plane.
w: I (4-methylcyclohexene): C4 carries H, CH3 and two different ring paths (one reaches the C=C after one CH2, the other after two), so it is chiral and optically active. II (cis-cyclopentane-1,2-diol): two chirality centers but a mirror plane between them, so it is meso and inactive. III (3-methylpentane): C3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so it is achiral. I only.
x: II is meso: the cis diol has a mirror plane through C4 and the midpoint of the C1–C2 bond, so its rotations cancel within each molecule.
II is the meso cis diol and is optically inactive, while I is chiral.
III has no chirality center; C3 carries two identical ethyl groups.

q: Which C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> isomer is chiral?
h: None of these has an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon with four different groups. Think about the geometry of an allene: the two CH= ends lie in perpendicular planes.
w: In an allene (C=C=C), the groups on one end lie in a plane perpendicular to the groups on the other end. 1,3-Dichloropropadiene has two different groups (H, Cl) on each end, so the molecule has no mirror plane and is chiral (axial chirality), with no chirality center. It exists as a pair of enantiomers.
x: 1,1-Dichloropropadiene has two identical H atoms on one end, so the plane containing the C=C=C axis and both Cl atoms is a mirror plane: achiral.
In 1,3-dichloropropyne the CH<sub>2</sub>Cl carbon has two identical H atoms and the alkyne is linear, so the molecule has a mirror plane and no chirality center.
3,3-Dichloropropyne has two Cl atoms on the same carbon, so it has a mirror plane and no chirality center.

q: Which description fits (1R,2S)-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol?
h: Read cis/trans from the drawing (same face or opposite faces). The enantiomer inverts every chirality center.
w: In the drawing the OH and the CH3 are on the same face of the ring, so the compound is the cis isomer. Its mirror image inverts both centers: (1S,2R). (1S,2S) and (1R,2R) are the trans pair, diastereomers of this compound.
x: The OH and CH<sub>3</sub> are drawn on the same face of the ring, so this is cis; the enantiomer part is right.
Inverting only one center gives a diastereomer, not the enantiomer; the enantiomer of (1R,2S) is (1S,2R).
(1R,2R) differs at only one center, so it is a diastereomer (the trans compound), and the drawn compound is cis.

q: Which chair is the most stable conformation of trans-1-isopropyl-2-methylcyclohexane?
h: First keep only the chairs that are trans (one group up, one down). Then pick the one with no large axial group.
w: Chairs III and IV have both groups up, so they are the cis isomer and are ruled out. Chairs I and II are the two ring-flip conformers of the trans isomer: in I both groups are axial; in II both are equatorial. The diequatorial chair has no 1,3-diaxial interactions (only one gauche interaction between the adjacent groups), so II is the most stable.
x: Chair I is the trans isomer, but both groups are axial, giving four 1,3-diaxial interactions; it is the less stable chair.
Chair III has both groups up, so it is a conformer of the cis isomer, not the trans compound.
Chair IV puts the isopropyl group equatorial, but both groups are up, so it is the cis isomer.

q: In its most stable chair conformation, which compound has its chlorine axial?
h: A tert-butyl group is far too large to sit axial, so put it equatorial first. Then ask where cis or trans forces the chlorine to go.
w: A tert-butyl group costs about 20 kJ/mol when axial, so it locks the ring with tert-butyl equatorial; chlorine's preference (about 2 kJ/mol) cannot override it. On a chair, cis-1,4 and trans-1,3 pairs are one axial and one equatorial, while trans-1,4, cis-1,3 and trans-1,2 pairs can both be equatorial. So only cis-1-tert-butyl-4-chlorocyclohexane must place Cl axial.
x: trans-1,4 substituents can both be equatorial (one up, one down), so Cl is equatorial along with the tert-butyl group.
cis-1,3 substituents can both be equatorial on the same face, so Cl is equatorial.
trans-1,2 substituents can both be equatorial, so Cl is equatorial next to the equatorial tert-butyl group.

q: These C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> isomers are each burned completely to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. Which releases the least heat per mole?
h: Isomers give the same combustion products, so the difference in heat released comes only from how much strain energy each starts with.
w: All four give 5 CO2 + 5 H2O, so the most stable (least strained) isomer releases the least heat. Cyclopentane has only modest strain (about 26 kJ/mol), cyclobutanes about 110 kJ/mol and cyclopropanes about 115 kJ/mol. Cyclopentane releases the least heat.
x: Methylcyclobutane has a strained four-membered ring (about 110 kJ/mol of ring strain), so it releases more heat than cyclopentane.
Ethylcyclopropane contains the highly strained three-membered ring and releases more heat.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclopropane has the three-membered ring strain plus eclipsed cis CH<sub>3</sub> groups; so it releases more heat than unstrained cyclopentane.

q:
Which statements about ring strain are correct?
I. In chair cyclohexane, the C–H bonds on adjacent carbons are eclipsed.
II. Cyclopropane has both angle strain (60° C–C–C angles) and torsional strain (all C–H bonds on adjacent carbons eclipsed).
III. Cyclopentane puckers into an envelope mainly to relieve torsional strain, even though this slightly changes its C–C–C angles.
h: Decide separately for each ring whether its bonds are staggered or eclipsed and whether its angles are near 109.5°.
w: II is true: a planar three-membered ring forces 60° angles and eclipses every pair of adjacent C–H bonds. I is false: in the chair every C–C bond is perfectly staggered and the angles are about 111°, so it is nearly strain-free. III is true: a flat pentagon would have ideal-looking 108° angles but ten eclipsed C–H pairs; folding one carbon out of the plane relieves much of that torsional strain. II and III only.
x: III is also true: the envelope relieves eclipsing (torsional) strain at a small cost in angle strain.
I is false: all bonds in chair cyclohexane are staggered; eclipsing occurs in the boat, not the chair.
I is false: the chair has no eclipsed bonds.

q: Which structure is (2R,3S)-3-methylhexan-2-ol?
h: Rank the groups at each center (at C3 the CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> branch beats propyl because of the O), then check each drawing one center at a time.
w: C2: OH > C3 > CH3 > H. C3: CH(OH)CH3 (O,C,H) > CH2CH2CH3 (C,H,H) > CH3 > H. Assigning each drawing gives A = (2R,3S), B = (2R,3R), C = (2S,3R), D = (2S,3S). The answer is A.
x: This is (2R,3R): C2 is right, but C3 is inverted.
This is (2S,3R), the enantiomer of the target: both centers are inverted.
This is (2S,3S): C3 is right but C2 is inverted.

q: How are drawings I and II related?
h: Do not compare the pictures by eye. Assign R/S to each chirality center in both drawings, or check whether the two groups are cis or trans in each.
w: Both drawings are 3-methylcyclohexan-1-ol with the OH and CH3 cis. Assigning the centers gives the same result in both: (1S,3R) in I and in II. Drawing II is the same molecule turned over and rotated, which does not change any configuration. They are identical.
x: A mirror-image drawing would invert both centers; here both centers have the same descriptors in I and II.
Diastereomers would differ at one center (cis vs trans); both drawings are cis.
The connectivity is the same: both are 3-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.

q:
Compound I is (2R,3R)-hexane-2,3-diol and compound II is (2R,3S)-hexane-2,3-diol. Which terms correctly describe the pair?
I. diastereomers
II. epimers
III. enantiomers
h: Count how many of the chirality centers differ between the two compounds.
w: The compounds have the same constitution and differ at C3 only. Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers (statement I true). Diastereomers that differ at exactly one of several chirality centers are also called epimers (statement II true). Enantiomers would differ at both centers, (2S,3S) for compound I, so statement III is false. I and II only.
x: Epimers is also correct: the pair differs at exactly one of its two chirality centers.
Enantiomers must have every center inverted; here C2 is R in both.
Epimers are a kind of diastereomer, not of enantiomer; the pair differs at only one center, so III is false and I is true.

q: Why is the chair conformation of cyclohexane nearly free of strain?
c: Its C–C–C angles are close to the tetrahedral angle and every C–C bond is staggered
Its ring is planar, so all six carbons have 120° angles
Its axial hydrogens point away from each other, which removes all steric strain but leaves the bonds eclipsed
Its carbons are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized, which matches the hexagonal shape
h: Think about the two kinds of strain a ring can have: bond-angle strain and eclipsing (torsional) strain.
w: In the chair the C–C–C angles are about 111°, close to 109.5°, so there is almost no angle strain, and looking down any C–C bond shows a staggered arrangement, so there is no torsional strain. Hence angles near tetrahedral and all bonds staggered.
x: A planar hexagon would have 120° angles (too large for sp<sup>3</sup> carbon) and twelve eclipsed C–H pairs; cyclohexane is not planar.
The chair has no eclipsed bonds; the eclipsed boat is a higher-energy conformation.
The ring carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>, not sp<sup>2</sup>; the hexagon in a line drawing does not mean the ring is flat.

q: In this equilibrium, which species act as Brønsted–Lowry acids?
h: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates H<sup>+</sup>. Find the proton donor on each side of the equilibrium.
w: In the forward direction propyne (I) gives its terminal H+ to the amide ion (II), so I is the acid and II the base. In the reverse direction ammonia (IV) gives H+ back to the propynide ion (III), so IV is the acid and III the base. The Brønsted acids are I and IV.
x: III is the conjugate base of I (it has lost the proton); it accepts H<sup>+</sup> in the reverse reaction.
II and III are the two bases: each accepts a proton in one direction.
II is the base in the forward reaction (it accepts the proton from propyne); IV is the acid on the right side.

q: Which species can act as a Lewis acid?
h: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. Look for an electron-poor atom, even one with an octet: can a π bond shift its electrons onto a more electronegative atom?
w: Every atom in CO2 has an octet, but the carbon is bonded to two electronegative oxygens and a resonance contributor puts a positive charge on carbon (O−–C+=O). An electron pair from a base (for example OH− or a carbanion) can add to that carbon while a C=O π bond moves onto oxygen. CO2 is the Lewis acid.
x: Trimethylamine has a lone pair on N and no low-lying empty orbital; it is a Lewis base.
Dimethyl ether donates an oxygen lone pair (for example to BF<sub>3</sub>); it is a Lewis base.
The π bond of ethene is electron-rich; ethene reacts with electrophiles as an electron-pair donor, not as an acceptor.

q: Cyanide ion adds to acetone to form a new C–C bond. Which tagged atom is the electrophilic site that accepts the new bond?
h: The nucleophile brings the electron pair. Which atom of acetone carries a partial positive charge and can let a π bond move away from it?
w: The C=O bond is polarized toward oxygen, so the carbonyl carbon c is δ+. The lone pair on the cyanide carbon (a, the nucleophile) attacks carbon c, and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen to give an alkoxide. The electrophilic site is carbon c.
x: Carbon a is the nucleophilic atom: it carries the lone pair and the negative charge that form the new bond.
Oxygen d is δ− and receives the π electrons; it is where the negative charge ends up, not the electrophile.
Methyl carbon b has no leaving group or π bond to accept electrons, so it is not electrophilic.

q: 4-Hydroxybenzoic acid has pKa values of 4.5 (CO2H) and 9.3 (phenol OH). Which form is the major species in water buffered at pH 8.0?
h: Compare the pH with each pKa: a group is mostly deprotonated when pH > pKa and mostly protonated when pH < pKa.
w: pH 8.0 is 3.5 units above the carboxylic acid pKa, so the CO2H is almost entirely CO2−. pH 8.0 is 1.3 units below the phenol pKa, so the phenol stays mostly protonated (about 95%). The major species is the monoanion with CO2− and a phenol OH.
x: The neutral acid dominates only below pH 4.5; at pH 8.0 the carboxylic acid is about 3000 times more ionized than not.
The phenol (pKa 9.3) is the weaker acid; it would not lose its proton while the much more acidic CO2H keeps its own.
The dianion needs pH above 9.3; at pH 8.0 the phenol is still mostly protonated.

q: Benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) is dissolved in a buffer at pH 6.2. What is the approximate ratio of benzoate ion to benzoic acid?
h: Use log([A−]/[HA]) = pH − pKa.
w: pH − pKa = 6.2 − 4.2 = 2.0, so [A−]/[HA] = 102.0 = 100 : 1. Each pH unit above the pKa multiplies the ratio of conjugate base to acid by 10.
x: This is inverted: above the pKa the deprotonated form (benzoate) dominates.
The ratio depends on 10 raised to the pH difference, not on the difference itself.
A one-unit difference gives 10 : 1; here the pH is two units above the pKa.

q: Rank these nitrogen compounds from weakest to strongest base.
h: In each compound the basic lone pair is on nitrogen. Identify the hybridization of the orbital holding that lone pair.
w: The more s character in the lone-pair orbital, the closer the electrons are held to the nucleus and the weaker the base. Benzonitrile (I) holds its lone pair in an sp orbital (conjugate acid pKa about −10); pyridine (II) in an sp2 orbital (about 5.2); N-methylpiperidine (III) in an sp3 orbital (about 10). Order: I < II < III.
x: The sp nitrogen of the nitrile (50% s character) is the weakest base, weaker than the sp<sup>2</sup> nitrogen of pyridine.
This is the reverse order; the sp<sup>3</sup> amine is the strongest base, not the weakest.
Pyridine (sp<sup>2</sup>) is a weaker base than the sp<sup>3</sup> amine; the pyridine lone pair is not part of the aromatic sextet, but it still sits in an orbital with more s character.

q:
Which side of this equilibrium is favored, and why?
CH3CH2S− + CH3CH2OH ⇌ CH3CH2SH + CH3CH2O−
c: The left side; ethanethiolate is the weaker base because the charge is spread over the larger S atom
The right side; ethoxide is the weaker base because O is more electronegative than S
The left side; ethoxide is the weaker base because O is more electronegative than S
The right side; ethanethiol is the weaker acid because the S–H bond is weaker than O–H
h: Equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base. When the acidic atoms are in the same group, size matters more than electronegativity.
w: S and O are in the same group, so the size of the atom bearing the charge decides: the negative charge on the larger S is spread over a bigger volume, so CH3CH2S− is the weaker base and CH3CH2SH (pKa about 10.6) the stronger acid than ethanol (about 16). The equilibrium lies on the left, with the weaker base ethanethiolate (K about 10−5).
x: Electronegativity decides only within a row; down a group, size wins and the thiolate is the more stable (weaker) base.
The side is right, but ethoxide is the stronger base, not the weaker one; the reason must explain why the left side is lower in energy.
A weaker S–H bond makes ethanethiol a stronger acid, not a weaker one; the stronger acid is on the right, so the right side is disfavored.

q: Rank these carboxylic acids from weakest to strongest acid.
h: Electronegative atoms stabilize the carboxylate by induction. The effect grows with the number of such atoms and falls off quickly with distance from the CO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>.
w: All four conjugate bases are resonance-stabilized carboxylates, so induction decides. Butanoic acid (I) has no fluorine. In II the F is on C4, three bonds from the carboxyl carbon, so its pull is small. In III one F sits on C2, next to the carboxyl, giving a large effect, and in IV two F atoms on C2 give the largest. Order: I < II < III < IV.
x: This is the reverse order: more fluorine closer to the CO<sub>2</sub>H gives a stronger acid, so IV is the strongest.
The F on C4 (II) is much farther from the carboxylate than the F on C2 (III), so II is the weaker acid of the two.
Any electron-withdrawing F increases acidity; II is still a stronger acid than unsubstituted butanoic acid.

q: The curved arrows show one step of an ester-forming reaction. What are the products of this step?
h: Follow each arrow: where a new π bond forms, and which bond breaks. A full arrow moves two electrons, and they go to the atom at the arrowhead.
w: The first arrow moves an oxygen lone pair into the O–C bond, making a C=O π bond. To keep carbon at four bonds, the second arrow breaks the C–Cl bond, and both electrons go to chlorine. The products are methyl acetate and chloride ion; the negative charge has moved from oxygen to chlorine.
x: This would require breaking the C–OCH<sub>3</sub> bond, but the arrow is drawn from the C–Cl bond.
No arrow touches the O–CH<sub>3</sub> bond, so the CH<sub>3</sub> cannot move to chlorine in this step.
A full (double-barbed) arrow gives both bonding electrons to Cl, making chloride ion, not a neutral chlorine atom; the overall −1 charge must be conserved.

q: Which hydrogen in this compound is the most acidic?
h: Compare the stability of each conjugate base. When the atoms are in the same group, atom size outweighs electronegativity.
w: Removing H from S gives a thiolate, with the charge on the large, polarizable sulfur (thiol pKa about 10–11). The alcohol O–H (about 16) and the terminal alkyne C–H (about 25) are weaker acids, and the sp3 C–H at d (about 50) is weakest. The most acidic H is on sulfur a.
x: The sp C–H of the terminal alkyne (pKa about 25) is acidic for a C–H, but far less acidic than S–H or O–H.
O is more electronegative than S, but within a group size dominates: the thiol (about 10–11) is more acidic than the alcohol (about 16).
The sp3 C–H at d gives an unstabilized carbanion (pKa about 50); it is the least acidic of these.

q: What are the conjugate acid and the conjugate base of methylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>?
c: conjugate acid CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>; conjugate base CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>−</sup>
conjugate acid CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>−</sup>; conjugate base CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>
conjugate acid CH<sub>4</sub>; conjugate base NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>
h: A conjugate acid has one more H<sup>+</sup>; a conjugate base has one fewer H<sup>+</sup>. Which H on methylamine is the most acidic?
w: Adding H+ to the nitrogen lone pair gives the methylammonium ion, CH3NH3+ (the conjugate acid). Removing H+ from the N–H (pKa about 40, more acidic than the C–H bonds) gives CH3NH− (the conjugate base). CH3NH3+ and CH3NH−.
x: The labels are swapped: gaining H<sup>+</sup> gives the conjugate acid, and losing H<sup>+</sup> gives the conjugate base.
Removing a C–H proton is far harder than removing the N–H proton, because N is more electronegative than C; the conjugate base is CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>−</sup>.
Breaking the C–N bond is not an acid–base reaction; conjugate pairs differ by exactly one H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Nitromethane, CH3NO2 (pKa about 10), is far more acidic than methane (pKa about 50). What is the main reason?
c: The negative charge of the conjugate base is delocalized by resonance onto the two oxygen atoms
The carbon of nitromethane is sp hybridized, so its C–H bond has more s character
The C–H bond of nitromethane is longer because nitrogen is a large atom
The conjugate base carries its negative charge on nitrogen, which is more electronegative than carbon
h: Draw the conjugate base and look for resonance contributors.
w: Removing a proton from CH3NO2 gives −CH2–NO2. The carbon lone pair can form a C=N π bond while an N=O π bond moves onto oxygen, so the negative charge is shared by the two electronegative oxygens. This resonance stabilization of the conjugate base (with some help from the inductive pull of N+) is the main reason for the large acidity. Methane’s conjugate base has no such stabilization.
x: The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon of nitromethane is sp<sup>3</sup> (four single bonds), the same as in methane.
Bond length to a neighboring atom does not set acidity here; the key is the stability of the anion formed.
In the nitro group, nitrogen already carries a formal + charge; the extra negative charge goes onto carbon and, through resonance, onto the oxygens.

q:
Which statements about curved-arrow notation are correct?
I. A curved arrow starts at the electrons that move: a lone pair or a bond.
II. In a proton transfer, the arrow is drawn from the H atom to the base.
III. A single-barbed (fishhook) arrow shows the movement of one electron.
h: Arrows always follow electrons, never atoms or positive charges.
w: I is true: every curved arrow begins at an electron source (a lone pair or a bond). II is false: in a proton transfer, the arrow goes from the base’s lone pair to the H, and a second arrow moves the old H–A bond onto A. III is true: a fishhook arrow moves a single electron, as in radical reactions. I and III only.
x: III is also true: single-barbed arrows show one-electron movement in radical steps.
II is false: drawing the arrow from H to the base shows the proton moving, but arrows track electrons, which flow from the base to H.
II is false (arrows go from the base to H), and I is true.

q: The curved arrows show amide ion removing a proton from 2-methylcyclohexanone. What is the organic product of this step?
h: Track which C–H bond breaks, where the new C=C π bond forms, and where the C=O π electrons end up.
w: The amide lone pair takes the H drawn on C6 (the CH2 on the side away from the methyl). The C6–H electrons become a C6=C1 π bond, and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. The product is the enolate with the C=C toward the unsubstituted side and the negative charge on oxygen (the kinetic enolate, with NH3 as the other product).
x: The arrows remove the H from C6, the CH<sub>2</sub> drawn with the H; this enolate would require deprotonating the methyl-bearing C2.
No arrow goes from the amide ion to the carbonyl carbon; the base removes a proton rather than adding to C=O.
The C=O π electrons end up on oxygen as a lone pair (an alkoxide-type O<sup>−</sup>); nothing protonates oxygen in this step.

q:
Which statements are correct?
I. H2S is a stronger acid than H2O.
II. NH3 is a stronger acid than H2O.
III. HF is a stronger acid than HCl.
h: Within a row, compare electronegativity of the atom that keeps the electrons. Within a group, compare size.
w: I is true: S is below O, and the larger S stabilizes the negative charge of HS− better (pKa 7.0 vs 15.7). II is false: N is less electronegative than O in the same row, so NH2− is less stable and NH3 (pKa about 38) is a much weaker acid than water. III is false: Cl is larger than F, so HCl (about −7) is far stronger than HF (3.2). I only.
x: II is false: across a row acidity increases with electronegativity, so H<sub>2</sub>O is more acidic than NH<sub>3</sub>.
III is false: down a group size wins over electronegativity, so HCl is the stronger acid.
Both II and III are false, and I (true) is left out.

q: In the first step of the addition of HBr to propene, the alkene is protonated to give a carbocation and bromide ion. Which drawing shows correct curved arrows for this step?
h: The π bond is the electron source (the Lewis base). Every arrow must start at electrons, and H can never have two bonds.
w: The π electrons of propene (the nucleophile) move to the H of HBr, forming the new C–H bond, and the H–Br bonding electrons move onto Br to give Br−. The correct drawing has one arrow from the C=C π bond to H and one from the H–Br bond onto Br; the H goes to the CH2 end so the positive charge ends up on the secondary carbon.
x: The Br lone pair attacks carbon while Br is still bonded to H, and the H–Br bond is never broken: Br would end up with two bonds and H with two bonds. Bromide attacks only after it has formed, in the second step.
The H–Br bond is never broken, so the H would end up with two bonds.
The π electrons attack Br and the H–Br electrons move onto H: this makes H<sup>−</sup> and a C–Br bond, the reverse of the polarity of H<sup>δ+</sup>–Br<sup>δ−</sup>.

q: Acetamide, CH3CONH2 (conjugate acid pKa about −0.5), is a far weaker base than ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2 (conjugate acid pKa about 10.7). What is the main reason?
c: The nitrogen lone pair of acetamide is delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen by resonance
The nitrogen of acetamide has no lone pair because it is bonded to a carbonyl carbon
Acetamide is more sterically hindered around nitrogen than ethylamine
The nitrogen of acetamide is sp hybridized, while the nitrogen of ethylamine is sp<sup>3</sup>
h: Draw a resonance contributor of acetamide that moves the nitrogen lone pair.
w: In acetamide the N lone pair overlaps with the C=O π bond: a contributor with C=N+ and O− shows that the pair is shared with oxygen. Protonating N would remove this stabilization, so the lone pair is much less available. In ethylamine the lone pair is localized on an sp3 nitrogen. The main reason is resonance delocalization of the amide lone pair. (Amides that are protonated at all are protonated on O.)
x: The amide nitrogen still has a lone pair; it is delocalized into the carbonyl, not missing.
The NH2 of acetamide is no more crowded than that of ethylamine; steric effects cannot explain a difference of about 11 pKa units.
The amide nitrogen is nearly planar (sp<sup>2</sup>-like because of resonance), not sp; it forms no triple bond.

q: Rank these anions from weakest to strongest base.
h: The weakest base has the strongest conjugate acid. Ask how much each oxygen anion is stabilized by resonance (onto O or onto C) or by induction.
w: The conjugate acids are acetic acid (pKa 4.8), phenol (10), 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (12.4) and methanol (15.5). Acetate (II) spreads its charge over two oxygens by resonance; phenoxide (III) spreads it onto ring carbons, which is less effective; trifluoroethoxide (IV) has only an inductive effect from three F atoms two bonds away; methoxide (I) has no stabilization. Weakest to strongest base: II < III < IV < I.
x: Phenoxide is a stronger base than acetate: resonance onto carbon atoms stabilizes the charge less than resonance onto a second oxygen.
Trifluoroethoxide has only an inductive effect, which is weaker than phenoxide's resonance, so IV is the stronger base of the two.
This is the order from strongest to weakest; methoxide is the strongest base, not the weakest.

q: When acetone is dissolved in concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, its carbonyl oxygen is protonated. What role does acetone play in this reaction?
h: Which species gives up H<sup>+</sup>, and which accepts it?
w: A lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen accepts H+ from sulfuric acid, so acetone is the proton acceptor: a Brønsted–Lowry base (and, equivalently, a Lewis base). The protonated ketone that forms is a strong acid (pKa about −7).
x: Acetone does not donate a proton here; H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is the acid.
A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair; acetone donates its oxygen lone pair to H<sup>+</sup>.
In this step acetone uses its lone pair to form a bond, so it acts as the electron donor; the protonated ketone formed is what becomes a strong electrophile.

q: Phenol (pKa 10) is a much stronger acid than cyclohexanol (about 16) but a much weaker acid than acetic acid (4.8). Which explanation accounts for both comparisons?
c: The phenoxide charge is delocalized by resonance onto ring carbons; acetate delocalizes its charge onto a second, more electronegative oxygen
The phenol O–H is attached to an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, while the acetic acid O–H is attached to an sp carbon
Phenoxide is stabilized only by induction from the ring, while acetate is stabilized by resonance
Phenol is more acidic than cyclohexanol because its O–H bond is shorter, and less acidic than acetic acid because it is larger
h: Draw the conjugate base of each acid and ask where resonance can put the negative charge.
w: Cyclohexoxide has its charge localized on one oxygen. Phenoxide has resonance contributors with the charge on the ortho and para ring carbons, so it is more stable and phenol is more acidic. Acetate has two equivalent contributors with the charge on two oxygens; oxygen holds negative charge far better than carbon, so acetate is more stable than phenoxide and acetic acid is the stronger acid. Hence resonance onto carbon (phenoxide) helps, but resonance onto a second oxygen (acetate) helps more.
x: The carboxyl carbon of acetic acid is sp<sup>2</sup>, not sp; hybridization of the attached carbon is not the main factor.
Phenoxide is stabilized mainly by resonance into the ring, not just by induction; the difference from acetate is where the charge goes, not whether resonance occurs.
O–H bond lengths are nearly the same in all three; the size of the molecule is not what sets acidity. The conjugate-base stability is the key.

q: A sample of (R)-2-bromopentane with 80% ee is treated with NaSH in DMF, and the substitution goes cleanly by SN2. Enantiopure (R)-pentane-2-thiol has [α]D = −14.0. What is the specific rotation of the thiol product?
h: Decide the configuration of the major thiol enantiomer first, then scale the rotation by the ee.
w: SN2 inverts the stereocenter. SH outranks the other groups just as Br did, so inversion changes the label: the major enantiomer of the bromide (R) gives the (S)-thiol. Each molecule reacts with inversion, so the product keeps the starting 80% ee, now with (S) in excess. (S)-thiol rotates +14.0, so the product shows 0.80 × (+14.0) = +11.2.
x: −11.2 is the right size but the sign of the (R)-thiol; it assumes retention. SN2 gives the (S)-thiol here.
+14.0 is the rotation of pure (S)-thiol. The starting bromide was only 80% ee, and SN2 passes that ee through unchanged.
Zero would mean racemization, which needs a carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1). HS<sup>−</sup> in DMF on a 2° bromide reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: Ethyl (S)-2-bromopropanoate reacts with NaCN in DMSO by SN2. What is the product?
h: Inversion is a change in 3D arrangement. Whether the R/S label changes depends on the new priority order.
w: SN2 always inverts the 3D arrangement: CN− enters opposite Br. The label is a separate question. In the bromide the priorities are Br > CO2Et > CH3 > H. In the nitrile the ester carbon (O,O,O) outranks the nitrile carbon (N,N,N), so the order is CO2Et > CN > CH3 > H. The top-priority group moved from the new position (old Br) to the ester, and that swap cancels the inversion: the product is ethyl (S)-2-cyanopropanoate, formed with inversion.
x: Inversion does not always flip the label. Here the incoming CN ranks second, not first, so the descriptor stays (S).
The label is (S), but the mechanism is not retention. SN2 is backside attack, and the same (S) label arises only because the priorities changed.
A 2° α-bromo ester with cyanide in DMSO reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2; the carbonyl destabilizes a carbocation, so there is no S<sub>N</sub>1 racemization.

q: Which bromide gives essentially no substitution product either on heating in aqueous ethanol (S<sub>N</sub>1 conditions) or with NaI in acetone (S<sub>N</sub>2 conditions)?
h: Think about the backside of the C–Br bond, and whether the carbocation could become planar.
w: 1-Bromobicyclo[2.2.2]octane has Br at a bridgehead. SN2 needs the nucleophile to approach from directly behind C–Br, but that direction points into the cage of the bicyclic ring. SN1 needs a planar (sp2) carbocation, and a bridgehead carbon held in the cage cannot flatten, so the cation is very high in energy. Both pathways shut down.
x: 1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane is 3°: it is blocked for S<sub>N</sub>2 but ionizes readily to a planar 3° cation, so S<sub>N</sub>1 in aqueous ethanol works well.
Bromocyclohexane is 2°: slow, but it does react with NaI in acetone on heating, and it can solvolyze slowly. Its ring carbon can flatten and has an open backside.
3-Bromocyclohexene is allylic: it ionizes fast to a resonance-stabilized cation and also does S<sub>N</sub>2 quickly. It is the most reactive choice, not the least.

q: (E)-1-Chloro-2-butene is warmed in ethanol and gives a mixture of two ethers by SN1. Which other chloride gives essentially the same ether mixture under the same conditions?
h: Draw the carbocation from the starting chloride and both of its resonance forms. Which other chloride would ionize to that cation?
w: Ionization of (E)-1-chloro-2-butene gives an allylic cation with + charge shared between C1 and C3 (CH3CH=CH–CH2+ ↔ CH3CH+–CH=CH2). Ethanol attacks either end, giving 1-ethoxy-2-butene and 3-ethoxy-1-butene. 3-Chloro-1-butene loses Cl− from C3 and forms the same allylic cation, so it gives the same two ethers.
x: 4-Chloro-1-butene is a 1° chloride whose C=C is one carbon too far away; ionization would give a non-allylic 1° cation, which does not form in ethanol.
3-Chloro-2-methylpropene is allylic, but its cation (CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>) is a different, symmetric ion, and it gives only one ether, 3-ethoxy-2-methylpropene.
2-Chloro-2-butene is a vinylic chloride. Loss of Cl<sup>−</sup> would give a vinyl cation, which is far too unstable to form under solvolysis conditions.

q: 1-Cyclobutylpropan-1-ol is heated with concentrated HBr. What is the major alkyl bromide? Assume the carbocation rearranges whenever a shift gives a more stable cation.
h: The first carbocation sits next to a strained four-membered ring. What does a 1,2-shift of a ring bond do, and is the cation then as stable as it could be?
w: Protonation and loss of water give a 2° cation next to the cyclobutane. A ring C–C bond shifts to that carbon (ring expansion), relieving most of the cyclobutane strain and giving a cyclopentyl cation; it is 2° and sits next to the carbon carrying the ethyl group. A 1,2-hydride shift then makes the 3° cation on the ethyl-bearing ring carbon, and bromide traps it: 1-bromo-1-ethylcyclopentane.
x: This is the unrearranged product. A 2° cation beside a cyclobutane expands the ring (strain relief plus a later 3° cation) before bromide traps it.
This product (1-bromo-2-ethylcyclopentane) stops after the ring expansion and traps the 2° cation. A 1,2-hydride shift to the 3° position is faster than capture by bromide.

1-Bromo-1-propylcyclobutane comes from a 1,2-hydride shift from the ring CH, giving a 3° cyclobutyl cation. That cation keeps the four-membered ring strain; ring expansion relieves the strain and still reaches a 3° cation, so it wins.

q: Rank these benzylic chlorides from slowest to fastest S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis in 80% aqueous ethanol.
h: The rate-determining step forms a benzylic cation. How does each para group change the stability of a positive charge delocalized onto the ring?
w: SN1 rate follows carbocation stability. In a 1-arylethyl cation the + charge is delocalized onto the ortho and para ring carbons. A para CH3 donates electron density (hyperconjugation and induction) to the carbon bearing + in one resonance form, so III is fastest. A para NO2 withdraws electron density and puts + next to + in one resonance form, so I is slowest: I < II < III.
x: This reverses the trend. Electron-withdrawing NO<sub>2</sub> destabilizes the cation, so the nitro compound is slowest, not fastest.
NO<sub>2</sub> slows the ionization compared with H; it does not speed it up.
CH<sub>3</sub> is electron-donating and stabilizes the benzylic cation, so III must be faster than the unsubstituted II.

q: Which reagent completes this transformation?
h: Bromide is replaced by a carbon that brings its own C≡N. Which reagent actually supplies a nucleophilic cyanide carbon?
w: The 1° bromide undergoes SN2 with cyanide ion; the cyanide carbon bonds to CH2 and Br− leaves. The reagent must deliver free CN−, so it is an ionic salt: NaCN (Na+ is a spectator).
x: HCN is a weak acid (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 9) and is mostly un-ionized, so it provides very little CN<sup>−</sup>; neutral HCN is a poor nucleophile.
Acetonitrile has no nucleophilic carbon; the nitrile carbon is electrophilic. It is commonly used as a solvent.
In BrCN the cyanide carbon is bonded to bromine and is electrophilic, not nucleophilic. It cannot displace bromide from the alkyl bromide.

q: 1-Chloro-1-methylcyclohexane slowly reacts with ethanol (S<sub>N</sub>1 solvolysis) to give 1-ethoxy-1-methylcyclohexane. The free-energy diagram for the complete reaction is shown. Which numbered point is the protonated ether (oxonium ion) intermediate?
h: List the steps in order: ionization, attack by ethanol, loss of H<sup>+</sup>. Minima between steps are intermediates; maxima are transition states.
w: The reaction has three steps, so the diagram has three maxima (transition states) and two minima between them (intermediates). Point 1 is the transition state for ionization of the C–Cl bond, the highest barrier and the rate-determining step. Point 2 is the 3° carbocation. Point 3 is the transition state for ethanol's oxygen bonding to the cation. Point 4 is the resulting oxonium ion, R–O+(H)CH2CH3, lower in energy than the carbocation because every atom now has an octet. Point 5 is the transition state for proton transfer to a solvent molecule, which gives the neutral ether. Answer: point 4.
x: Point 2 is the first intermediate, the 3° carbocation formed when chloride leaves. Ethanol has not yet bonded to it, so it is not an oxonium ion.
Point 3 is an energy maximum: the transition state in which the C–O bond to ethanol is only partly formed. Intermediates sit in minima.
Point 5 is also a maximum: the transition state for removing H<sup>+</sup> from the oxonium ion. The minimum just before it is the oxonium ion itself.

q: 1,4-Dibromobutane is stirred with one equivalent of Na<sub>2</sub>S in ethanol. What is the major organic product?
h: After the first S<sub>N</sub>2, the sulfur still carries a negative charge. Where is the nearest electrophilic carbon?
w: S2− is an excellent nucleophile. The first SN2 gives −S–CH2CH2CH2CH2Br. The thiolate end then attacks the C–Br carbon four atoms away in an intramolecular SN2; this forms a five-membered ring, which closes much faster than another intermolecular reaction. The product is thiolane (tetrahydrothiophene).
x: A six-membered ring (thiane) has one S and five CH<sub>2</sub> groups, so it would need a five-carbon chain such as 1,5-dibromopentane; 1,4-dibromobutane has only four carbons, so the ring formed has one S and four C.
The intermediate is a thiolate, not a neutral thiol, and it cyclizes rapidly; it is not isolated after the first substitution.
Butane-1,4-dithiol would need two separate sulfur nucleophiles. With one S<sup>2−</sup>, the single sulfur bonds to both ends of the chain.

q: Rank the alkyl bromides from slowest to fastest S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction with NaN<sub>3</sub> in DMF.
h: All except IV are primary. Count the branches on the carbon next to the C–Br carbon (the β carbon).
w: SN2 rate drops as the backside of the C–Br carbon becomes crowded. Bromomethane (IV) is least hindered. All three others are 1°, so the difference comes from branching at the β carbon: none in 1-bromobutane (III), one methyl in 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (II), and two in 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (I, neopentyl), where a methyl group sits in the path of the nucleophile and SN2 is extremely slow. Order: I < II < III < IV.
x: Neopentyl bromide (I) has two β methyls and is far slower than isobutyl bromide (II); it is the slowest of the set.
This is the order for S<sub>N</sub>1 trends, not S<sub>N</sub>2; methyl and 1° halides react fastest by S<sub>N</sub>2.
β-Branching slows S<sub>N</sub>2: the unbranched 1-bromobutane (III) reacts faster than the β-branched II.

q: Which carbocation is the most stable?
h: Count how many π systems share the positive charge, and how substituted the cationic carbon is.
w: The diphenylmethyl (benzhydryl) cation delocalizes the + charge into two benzene rings (seven resonance forms in all, six of them placing + on ortho and para ring carbons), and it is a secondary carbon. Each other cation has at most one π system to share the charge.
x: The benzyl cation is resonance-stabilized by one ring only, and it is primary. Adding a second phenyl, as in the diphenylmethyl cation, doubles the delocalization.
The allyl cation spreads + over two carbons only, both primary. It is less stabilized than a benzylic cation with several resonance forms.
The sec-butyl cation is a simple 2° alkyl cation, stabilized only by hyperconjugation and induction; it has no resonance.

q: Lucas reagent (ZnCl<sub>2</sub> in concentrated HCl) converts alcohols into alkyl chlorides, which make the solution cloudy. Which alcohol turns the reagent cloudy fastest at room temperature?
h: The Lucas test runs through a carbocation once the OH is converted into a leaving group.
w: ZnCl2 (a Lewis acid) and HCl convert OH into a good leaving group; the C–O bond then breaks to give a carbocation, which chloride traps. The rate follows carbocation stability, 3° > 2° ≫ 1°. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol is the only 3° alcohol here and reacts almost at once.
x: Pentan-2-ol is 2°; its cation forms more slowly, so cloudiness takes several minutes.
Pentan-1-ol is 1°; it would need a 1° cation and gives little or no cloudiness at room temperature.
2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol is 1° and also badly hindered for S<sub>N</sub>2, so it is among the slowest, not the fastest.

q: 1-Bromohexane is heated with NaCN in DMSO. The product shows the IR spectrum below. Which compound is the product?
h: Find the one band outside the usual C–H region, then match it to a triple bond.
w: Cyanide attacks through carbon in an SN2 reaction, giving a nitrile with one more carbon: CH3(CH2)5C≡N. The spectrum fits: sp3 C–H just below 3000 cm−1 and a medium, sharp C≡N stretch at 2247 cm−1, with no O–H or =C–H band. The product is heptanenitrile.
x: Hexan-1-ol would show a strong, broad O–H band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which is absent.
Hex-1-ene would show =C–H above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and C=C near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and no band at 2247 cm<sup>−1</sup>. A 1° bromide with cyanide in DMSO gives substitution, not elimination.
An isocyanide (R–N≡C) would form by attack through nitrogen and absorbs near 2140 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Cyanide ion reacts through its carbon with alkyl halides.

q: Butan-1-ol reacts with concentrated HBr. After the OH group is protonated, bromide ion displaces water in one step. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows that step?
h: A 1° oxonium ion reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2. One arrow makes the new bond; one breaks the old bond, and the leaving group takes the electrons.
w: 1° alkyloxonium ions do not ionize (a 1° cation is too unstable), so bromide displaces water by SN2. One arrow runs from a bromide lone pair to the CH2 carbon, and a second runs from the C–O bond onto oxygen, which leaves as neutral H2O. Carbon keeps four bonds throughout.
x: The C–O bond electrons are sent to carbon here. The leaving group must take the bonding pair, otherwise water cannot leave as a neutral molecule and carbon gets too many electrons.
Bromide is drawn attacking oxygen. The electrophilic atom is the carbon bonded to O<sup>+</sup>; bromide does not bond to oxygen.
With only the bromide arrow, carbon would form a fifth bond. The C–O bond must break in the same step.

q: Triethylamine is mixed with iodomethane in acetonitrile, and a white solid forms. What is the solid?
c: Triethylmethylammonium iodide, a quaternary ammonium salt
h: The amine nitrogen has a lone pair, and iodomethane is an excellent S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate.
w: The nitrogen lone pair attacks the CH3 carbon and iodide leaves (SN2). Nitrogen ends with four C–N bonds and a + charge, paired with I−: triethylmethylammonium iodide, (CH3CH2)3N+CH3 I−, an ionic solid that precipitates.
x: Iodomethane has no β carbon and so no β hydrogen; it cannot undergo E2. Triethylamine acts as a nucleophile here.
Nothing breaks an N–ethyl bond. The new bond is N–CH<sub>3</sub>, and all three ethyl groups stay on nitrogen.
Tetraethylammonium iodide would need iodoethane. The carbon added comes from iodomethane, so the new group is methyl.

q: The two stereoisomers of 1-bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane are shown in their preferred chairs. Each is treated with NaSC6H5 in DMF. Which statement is correct?
c: The cis isomer reacts faster: its Br is axial, so the nucleophile can approach along the open equatorial direction
The trans isomer reacts faster: its equatorial Br is less hindered, so it leaves more easily
Both react at the same rate because S<sub>N</sub>2 depends only on the leaving group and the nucleophile
Neither can react by S<sub>N</sub>2, so both give only the S<sub>N</sub>1 product
h: The tert-butyl group locks each chair. For SN2 the nucleophile must approach 180° from C–Br. Where does that path point for axial versus equatorial Br?
w: The bulky tert-butyl group stays equatorial, so in the cis isomer Br is axial and in the trans isomer Br is equatorial. For an axial C–Br, the backside lies along the equatorial direction, which is open, and the product forms directly with SPh equatorial. For an equatorial C–Br, the backside path runs across the ring and is blocked by the axial hydrogens on C3 and C5. So the cis isomer (axial Br) reacts faster, and each reacts with inversion: the cis bromide gives the trans sulfide, and the trans bromide gives the cis sulfide.
x: An equatorial leaving group is not easier to displace. The nucleophile must reach the backside, and for an equatorial Br that path is blocked by the axial H atoms on C3 and C5.
S<sub>N</sub>2 is very sensitive to steric access at the backside, and that access differs between the two locked chairs.
Both are 2° bromides with a strong, weakly basic nucleophile (PhS<sup>−</sup>) in a polar aprotic solvent: classic S<sub>N</sub>2 conditions. No carbocation forms.

q: Which nucleophile reacts fastest with 1-bromobutane by S<sub>N</sub>2 in ethanol?
h: In a protic solvent, the larger, more polarizable nucleophilic atom is less tightly solvated.
w: Going down a group, nucleophilicity in protic solvents rises: sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen, and the thiolate is held less tightly by hydrogen bonds from ethanol. Ethanethiolate is therefore the fastest, even though it is a weaker base than ethoxide.
x: Ethoxide is the strongest base among the oxygen nucleophiles, but in ethanol it is strongly hydrogen-bonded and is less nucleophilic than the larger sulfur anion.
tert-Butoxide is a strong base but a poor nucleophile; its three methyl groups block its approach to carbon.
Acetate is resonance-stabilized; its charge is spread over two oxygens, which makes it a weak base and a weak nucleophile.

q:
Which statements about nucleophilic substitution are correct?
I. Changing the solvent from water to acetone speeds up the SN1 solvolysis of a 3° alkyl chloride.
II. The rate of the reaction of 2-bromobutane with NaN3 in DMSO depends on the azide concentration.
III. SN1 substitution of an enantiopure 3° alkyl bromide gives a product that is mostly racemic.
h: Judge each statement separately: which step is rate-determining, what does the solvent stabilize, and what geometry does the intermediate have?
w: II is true: azide in DMSO with a 2° bromide is SN2, and its rate = k[RBr][N3−]. I is false: the SN1 transition state builds up charge separation, and a polar protic solvent like water stabilizes it (and the departing halide) by hydrogen bonding; acetone is much less able to do this, so the reaction slows. III is true: the planar carbocation is attacked from both faces, so the product is largely racemic (often with a slight excess of inversion). Answer: II and III only.
x: This misses III. A planar carbocation is attacked on both faces, so S<sub>N</sub>1 gives mostly racemic product.
I is false: removing the polar protic solvent destabilizes the ionization transition state and slows S<sub>N</sub>1. It also leaves out true statement III.
I is false: water, not acetone, speeds S<sub>N</sub>1 ionization.

q: Which combination is the best way to prepare (S)-2-methoxybutane in high yield?
h: Two questions: does any bond to the stereocenter break, and does the alkyl halide used invite E2?
w: With NaH, (S)-butan-2-ol becomes its alkoxide; no bond to the stereocenter is touched. The alkoxide then attacks CH3I by SN2, which is fast and cannot eliminate (CH3I has no β H). The O–CH3 bond forms at oxygen, so the configuration is kept: (S)-butan-2-ol + NaH, then CH3I.
x: SN2 inversion of (R)-2-bromobutane would give the (S) ether, so the stereochemistry is right. But a 2° bromide with the strong, unhindered base methoxide gives mostly E2 (butenes), so the yield is poor.
(S)-2-Bromobutane gives the (R) ether by inversion, and it also suffers from extensive E2.
Strong acid and heat with a 2° alcohol give a carbocation (and butenes); any ether formed is racemic, so this cannot give pure (S) product.

q: Rank the solvents from slowest to fastest for the S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction of NaN<sub>3</sub> with 1-bromobutane.
h: The salt must dissolve before it can react; after that, ask what the solvent does to the azide anion.
w: Hexane is nonpolar and cannot dissolve NaN3, so essentially no reaction occurs. Methanol dissolves the salt but surrounds N3− with hydrogen bonds, lowering its energy and its nucleophilicity. DMF is polar aprotic: it solvates Na+ well but leaves the anion poorly solvated and highly reactive. Order: hexane < methanol < DMF.
x: Hydrogen bonding in methanol slows S<sub>N</sub>2 with an anion, but hexane is worse: the ionic NaN<sub>3</sub> does not dissolve in it at all.
This reverses the order. Polar aprotic DMF gives the fastest S<sub>N</sub>2 with an anionic nucleophile.
A protic solvent (methanol) hydrogen-bonds to azide and makes it less reactive than in polar aprotic DMF.

q: 3-Bromo-2-methylhexane is heated with NaOCH2CH3 in ethanol. Counting E and Z isomers separately, how many different alkenes can form by E2?
h: Find every β carbon that carries an H. For each new C=C, check whether both alkene carbons have two different groups.
w: Br is on C3. Its β carbons are C2 (one H) and C4 (two H). Removing the C2 H gives 2-methylhex-2-ene, (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH2CH3; C2 carries two identical CH3 groups, so it has no E/Z isomers. Removing a C4 H gives 2-methylhex-3-ene, (CH3)2CHCH=CHCH2CH3, which exists as E and Z. Total: 3.
x: Two counts the constitutional isomers only. 2-Methylhex-3-ene has two different groups on each alkene carbon, so its E and Z forms are separate products.
Four would give 2-methylhex-2-ene E and Z forms too, but its C2 carries two methyl groups, so there is only one.
Five would include an alkene toward one of the methyl carbons on C2. Those carbons are γ to Br, not β, so they cannot form a C=C with C3.

q: What is the major product when 2-bromo-1-phenylbutane is heated with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol?
h: Both possible C=C positions give disubstituted alkenes. What extra stabilization can one of them have?
w: E2 can remove an H from C1 (benzylic) or from C3. Both alkenes are disubstituted, so substitution does not decide. Removing the benzylic H puts the C=C in conjugation with the benzene ring, which lowers the energy of the alkene and of the E2 transition state leading to it; that H is also the more acidic one. The E isomer avoids the phenyl/ethyl steric clash, so the major product is (E)-1-phenylbut-1-ene.
x: (E)-1-Phenylbut-2-ene is also disubstituted, but its C=C is isolated from the ring; it lacks conjugation, so it is the minor E2 product.
The Z isomer is conjugated but puts the phenyl and ethyl groups on the same side; the E isomer is more stable and forms faster.
Ethoxide with a 2° bromide on heating gives mainly E2; this S<sub>N</sub>2 ether is a minor product.

q: An alkyl chloride is warmed in ethanol with no added base, and the two products shown are formed. Which compound was the starting material?
h: The ether shows where the leaving group was; the alkene shows that a carbocation lost a β proton. Which substrate ionizes easily in ethanol?
w: Both products come from the same 3° carbocation, 1-methylcyclopentyl. Ethanol traps it to give the ether (SN1) or removes a β proton to give 1-methylcyclopentene (E1). The ethoxy group sits on the ring carbon that bears the methyl, so the leaving group was there: the substrate is 1-chloro-1-methylcyclopentane, a 3° chloride that ionizes readily in a polar protic solvent.
x: (Chloromethyl)cyclopentane is 1°. It does not ionize in warm ethanol, and slow S<sub>N</sub>2 with ethanol would put OEt on the CH<sub>2</sub>, not on the ring.
This is a vinylic chloride; loss of Cl<sup>−</sup> would give a vinyl cation, which does not form under these conditions.
1-Methylcyclopentanol has no leaving group without acid: HO<sup>−</sup> is a very poor leaving group, so nothing happens in neutral ethanol.

q: 3-Methylbutan-1-ol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major alkene? Assume the carbocation rearranges whenever a shift gives a more stable cation.
h: A 1° alkyloxonium ion does not ionize to a free 1° cation. But the first alkene formed can be protonated again by the hot acid. Where does that lead?
w: Protonated 3-methylbutan-1-ol loses water with a β H in a concerted E2-like step (a 1° cation is too unstable), giving 3-methylbut-1-ene. In hot concentrated acid this alkene is reprotonated (Markovnikov) to a 2° cation, which undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the 3° cation (CH3)2C+CH2CH3. Loss of a β H gives the most substituted alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene (trisubstituted), as the major product.
x: 3-Methylbut-1-ene is the first-formed, monosubstituted alkene. Under strongly acidic, hot conditions it isomerizes through carbocations to the more stable trisubstituted alkene.
2-Methylbut-1-ene comes from the same 3° cation, but it is disubstituted; Zaitsev loss of the CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogen gives the trisubstituted alkene instead.
Diisopentyl ether forms from 1° alcohols at lower temperatures (S<sub>N</sub>2 of one alcohol on another's oxonium ion); with heat, elimination dominates.

q: The stereoisomer of 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane in which every Cl is trans to both neighbors is shown in its all-equatorial chair. It undergoes E2 with NaOH thousands of times more slowly than the other stereoisomers. What is the best explanation?
c: In either chair, no Cl has an H on a neighboring carbon that is anti-periplanar (trans-diaxial) to it
It has no hydrogens on carbons β to any chlorine
The ring is locked with every Cl equatorial and cannot flip to a diaxial chair
Equatorial C–Cl bonds are stronger than axial C–Cl bonds
h: E2 on a cyclohexane needs the leaving group axial and a β H axial on the opposite face. Flip this chair and look at what sits on the neighboring carbons.
w: E2 in a cyclohexane needs Cl and a β H trans-diaxial. In the drawn chair every Cl is equatorial, so none can leave. The ring can flip, and then every Cl is axial; but each neighboring carbon's axial position, on the opposite face, is also occupied by its own Cl, because adjacent Cl atoms are trans. So every β H is cis to the Cl and equatorial. In neither chair is any Cl anti-periplanar to a neighboring H, so the normal E2 path is blocked.
x: Every carbon carries one H, and each is β to the Cl on the next carbon; the problem is the geometry of those H atoms, not their absence.
The ring is not locked; it can flip to the all-axial chair. Even in that chair the β hydrogens are equatorial, so flipping does not help.
Equatorial and axial C–Cl bonds have essentially the same strength. The rate difference comes from the anti-periplanar requirement of E2.

q: Cyclohexanol reacts with POCl<sub>3</sub> to give a dichlorophosphate ester, and pyridine then removes a β hydrogen in a single E2 step to form cyclohexene. Which set of curved arrows correctly shows this E2 step?
h: E2 makes one bond and breaks two in one step; each change needs its own arrow, and electrons always move toward the atom that ends up holding them.
w: POCl3 converts OH into –OPOCl2, a good leaving group, without forming a carbocation. In the E2 step the pyridine N lone pair takes the β H, the C–H bond electrons form the C=C π bond, and the C–O bond electrons leave with oxygen as the dichlorophosphate anion. Three arrows, all in one step.
x: No arrow breaks the C–O bond, so the carbon bearing oxygen would gain the π bond while keeping four other bonds: five bonds to carbon.
These arrows describe S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of pyridine on carbon, which would give a pyridinium salt rather than cyclohexene; pyridine acts as a base here, and no C–H bond is broken in this drawing.
The C–O bond electrons are sent to carbon. The leaving group must take the bonding pair; carbon is already gaining the π bond.

q: Which reagent best converts 1-bromooctane into oct-1-ene with little substitution product?
h: A 1° bromide strongly prefers S<sub>N</sub>2. What kind of base can still remove a β H but cannot easily reach the carbon?
w: Unhindered 1° bromides undergo SN2 with most nucleophiles. A strong but bulky base, potassium tert-butoxide, cannot easily reach the backside of the C–Br carbon, but it can still take a β H from the end of the chain, so E2 gives oct-1-ene as the main product.
x: Ethoxide is a strong, unhindered nucleophile; with a 1° bromide it mainly gives the S<sub>N</sub>2 product, 1-ethoxyoctane.
Hydroxide in water mainly gives octan-1-ol by S<sub>N</sub>2 (and the alkyl bromide is poorly soluble in water).
Iodide is a good nucleophile and a very weak base; it gives 1-iodooctane by S<sub>N</sub>2, not an alkene.

q: 2-Fluorohexane and 2-iodohexane are each heated with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> in methanol. Which statement correctly describes the alkene products?
c: The iodide gives mainly hex-2-ene, but the fluoride gives mainly hex-1-ene
Both give mainly hex-2-ene, since methoxide is an unhindered base
Both give mainly hex-1-ene, since C2 is a secondary carbon
The fluoride gives mainly hex-2-ene, but the iodide gives mainly hex-1-ene
h: Fluoride leaves poorly. If C–H breaking runs ahead of C–X breaking in the E2 transition state, what charge builds on carbon, and which H is then easiest to remove?
w: With a good leaving group (I), C–I and C–H break together, the transition state has much double-bond character, and the more substituted (Zaitsev) hex-2-ene is favored. With fluoride, the C–F bond breaks late; the transition state has carbanion character on the β carbon. A primary carbanion-like carbon (C1) is more stable than a secondary one (C3), and the C1 hydrogens are also more numerous and accessible. So the iodide gives mainly hex-2-ene, but the fluoride gives mainly hex-1-ene (Hofmann product), even with an unhindered base.
x: Base size is not the only factor. A poor leaving group such as F shifts E2 toward the less substituted alkene.
2-Iodohexane follows Zaitsev with methoxide; only the poor leaving group F reverses the regiochemistry.
This reverses the two substrates. The good leaving group (I) gives Zaitsev; the poor one (F) gives Hofmann.

q: 2-Bromo-2,4,4-trimethylpentane is heated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butyl alcohol. What is the major product?
h: A bulky base removes the most accessible β hydrogen. Compare the exposed CH3 hydrogens on C2 with the CH2 hydrogens tucked beside the tert-butyl group.
w: A 3° bromide with a strong, bulky base reacts by E2. Two kinds of β H are available: nine on the CH3 groups of C2 and two on C3, which sits between C2 and the large tert-butyl group. tert-Butoxide is too bulky to reach the crowded C3 hydrogens, so it removes a methyl hydrogen (Hofmann orientation). The Zaitsev alkene would also be strained, with the tert-butyl group cis to a methyl on the double bond. Major product: 2,4,4-trimethylpent-1-ene.
x: 2,4,4-Trimethylpent-2-ene is the Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene, but forming it requires the bulky base to reach the hindered C3 hydrogens beside the tert-butyl group.
SN2 cannot occur at a 3° carbon, and tert-butoxide is a hindered, poor nucleophile; this di-tert-alkyl ether does not form.
This tetrasubstituted alkene needs a methyl shift, which requires a carbocation. E2 with tert-butoxide is concerted and gives no rearranged products.

q:
3-Bromo-3-ethylpentane reacts slowly in pure ethanol to give a mixture of an ether and an alkene. The experiment is repeated with 1 M NaOCH2CH3 added. Which statements are correct?
I. The bromide is consumed faster in the presence of ethoxide.
II. The ratio of alkene to ether increases.
III. The alkene formed with ethoxide is a different constitutional isomer from the one formed in pure ethanol.
h: Without base, the reaction goes through a carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1/E1). What new pathway does 1 M ethoxide open, and how many different alkenes can this substrate give at all?
w: I is true: in pure ethanol the slow step is ionization, but 1 M ethoxide, a strong base, adds a bimolecular E2 path (rate = k[RBr][EtO−]) that is much faster. II is true: E2 gives only alkene, and ethoxide cannot do SN2 at a 3° carbon, so the share of ether falls. III is false: all three β carbons are equivalent CH2 groups, so E1 and E2 both give the same alkene, 3-ethylpent-2-ene. Answer: I and II only.
x: I is also true. A strong base adds a fast bimolecular E2 pathway, so the bromide disappears faster than by ionization alone.
II is also true. The added E2 pathway gives only alkene, so the alkene-to-ether ratio rises.
III is false: the three ethyl groups are identical, so every β H gives 3-ethylpent-2-ene by either mechanism.

q: 2-Chloro-2-methylpentane is heated with KOC(CH3)3 in tert-butyl alcohol. The major product gives the 1H NMR spectrum below (the two =CH2 protons overlap). Which compound is it?
h: Look at the vinyl region (4.5–5.5 ppm): how many H appear there, and are they split?
w: The signal at 4.68 ppm integrates to 2H and is unsplit: a terminal =CH2 on a carbon with no H. The 1.71 ppm singlet (3H) is a CH3 on the alkene carbon, and the triplet/sextet/triplet set is a propyl chain (CH2 at 2.00 next to the alkene). This is 2-methylpent-1-ene, the Hofmann product expected with the bulky tert-butoxide base.
x: 2-Methylpent-2-ene has one vinyl H (1H, a triplet near 5.1 ppm) and two different CH<sub>3</sub> singlets on the alkene carbon, not a 2H singlet at 4.7 ppm.
(E)-4-Methylpent-2-ene has two vinyl H that couple to each other and to neighbors, plus an isopropyl doublet (6H); it also cannot form from this substrate.
The ether would show no vinyl signal at all and a 9H singlet near 1.2 ppm for the tert-butyl group; a 3° chloride with tert-butoxide eliminates instead.

q: 3-Bromocyclohexene is treated with KOC(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Find the β carbon that has sp<sup>3</sup> hydrogens, and place the new C=C between it and the carbon bearing Br.
w: The carbon bearing Br (C3) has two neighbors: C2, an alkene carbon, and C4, a CH2. The bulky base removes a C4 hydrogen, and the new C=C forms between C3 and C4, next to the existing C1=C2 bond. The product is the conjugated diene cyclohexa-1,3-diene.
x: Cyclohexa-1,4-diene would need the new C=C between C4 and C5, which is not bonded to the carbon carrying Br. E2 always forms the π bond between the α and β carbons.
A bulky, strong base like tert-butoxide gives elimination, not SN2 substitution, especially at a 2° carbon.
Benzene would need the loss of two more hydrogens (an oxidation). One E2 removes only one HBr.

q: Each C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkene is burned completely to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. Which releases the most heat per mole?
h: All four are isomers and give the same combustion products. How does the heat released relate to the stability of the starting alkene?
w: Isomers burn to the same products, so the one that starts highest in energy (least stable) releases the most heat. Alkene stability increases with the number of alkyl groups on the C=C (and with branching): monosubstituted < disubstituted E < trisubstituted < tetrasubstituted. The least stable is the monosubstituted hex-1-ene, so it has the largest heat of combustion.
x: (E)-Hex-2-ene is disubstituted and more stable than hex-1-ene, so it releases less heat.
2-Methylpent-2-ene is trisubstituted and more stable, so it releases less heat.
2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene is tetrasubstituted, the most stable of the four, so it releases the least heat, not the most.

q: Which reaction does this reaction-coordinate diagram (reactants on the left, products on the right) best describe?
h: Count the maxima and the dips between them. Which mechanism has no intermediate?
w: The diagram has one maximum and no intermediate (no energy well between reactants and products), so the reaction is a single concerted step. Of the choices, only E2 of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with ethoxide is one step: the base removes a β H as Br− leaves.
x: With no strong base, the 3° bromide reacts by E1: ionization to a carbocation and then deprotonation, two transition states with an intermediate between them.
Acid-catalyzed dehydration has three steps (protonation, loss of water, deprotonation) and two intermediates.
S<sub>N</sub>1 methanolysis passes through a carbocation and an oxonium ion, so its diagram has three maxima.

q: 2,2-Dimethylcyclopentan-1-ol is heated with H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major alkene?
h: The first cation is secondary and sits next to a carbon bearing two methyl groups. What shift is available, and then which β H gives the most substituted alkene?
w: Loss of water gives a 2° cation at C1. A methyl group on C2 shifts to C1, giving a 3° cation at C2 (which keeps one methyl). Of its β hydrogens, removing the one on C1 gives a C=C with four alkyl substituents: 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene, the Zaitsev product.
x: 3,3-Dimethylcyclopentene is the unrearranged product. A 1,2-methyl shift to a 3° cation is faster than loss of a proton from the 2° cation.
1-Methyl-2-methylidenecyclopentane comes from the 3° cation, but by loss of a methyl H; the exocyclic C=C is only disubstituted.
1,5-Dimethylcyclopentene is trisubstituted (from loss of a ring CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogen); the tetrasubstituted alkene is more stable.

q: Which alkyl bromide gives the same single alkene whether the base is NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> or KOC(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>?
h: The base matters only when there are different kinds of β hydrogens. Look for a substrate whose only β hydrogens are all equivalent.
w: In 2-bromo-2,3,3-trimethylbutane the carbon bearing Br has three neighbors: two equivalent CH3 groups and a quaternary C(CH3)3 carbon with no H. Every β H is on a methyl, so any base gives only 2,3,3-trimethylbut-1-ene; Zaitsev and Hofmann give the same answer.
x: 2-Bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane has a β CH on C3 and β methyl groups; ethoxide gives mainly the tetrasubstituted 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, and tert-butoxide mainly the 1-ene.
2-Bromo-2-methylpentane has β CH3 and β CH2 hydrogens, giving 2-methylpent-2-ene (ethoxide) or 2-methylpent-1-ene (tert-butoxide).
2-Bromo-4-methylpentane can lose an H from C1 or C3, giving 4-methylpent-1-ene and the E/Z 4-methylpent-2-enes in base-dependent ratios.

q: Rank the alkyl bromides from slowest to fastest E2 reaction with NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol.
h: The E2 transition state already has partial C=C character. Which substrate leads to the most substituted alkene, and has the most β H?
w: E2 rates rise from 1° to 2° to 3° halides: the developing C=C is more substituted (and more stable) in the transition state, and the number of β hydrogens grows (2, 6 and 9 here). Steric crowding, which slows SN2, does not hinder removal of an outer β H. Order: II < III < I.
x: This is the S<sub>N</sub>2 order. For E2 the trend is reversed: 3° halides eliminate fastest.
1-Bromopropane is the slowest E2 substrate here; it gives the least substituted alkene and has only two β H.
2-Bromo-2-methylpropane (3°) is faster than 2-bromopropane (2°) in E2; it forms a more substituted alkene and has more β hydrogens.

q: 1-Phenylpropan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major alkene?
h: E1 gives the most stable alkene available. Which position of the C=C gains conjugation with the ring?
w: The 2° cation at C2 can lose a proton from C1 or C3. Loss from C1 puts the C=C in conjugation with the benzene ring, which makes the alkene clearly more stable (and E1 favors the most stable alkene). The E isomer keeps phenyl and methyl apart: (E)-1-phenylprop-1-ene.
x: Allylbenzene (3-phenylprop-1-ene) is monosubstituted and not conjugated; it is a minor product.
The Z isomer is conjugated but places phenyl and methyl on the same side; the E isomer is more stable and predominates.
2-Phenylpropene would need the phenyl group to migrate to C2, which is not the favorable path here; loss of a proton from the cation is fast and gives the conjugated product directly.

q: 2-Bromopentane is stirred with sodium acetate (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na) in DMF at room temperature. What is the major organic product?
h: Classify acetate: how strong a base is it (compare pK<sub>a</sub> of acetic acid), and how good a nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent?
w: Acetate is a weak base (acetic acid pKa ≈ 4.8) but a decent nucleophile, and DMF leaves it poorly solvated. With a 2° bromide, a weakly basic nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent gives SN2: pentan-2-yl acetate (formed with inversion).
x: (E)-Pent-2-ene would need a strong base for E2. Acetate is far too weak a base to compete with substitution at room temperature.
Pent-1-ene would need a bulky strong base (Hofmann E2); acetate is neither.
The alcohol would require hydroxide or water as the nucleophile. Here the oxygen that attacks belongs to acetate, so an ester forms.

q: 3-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpentane is treated in two ways: (I) NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol, heat; (II) ethanol alone, heat. What is the major alkene in each case?
h: Which conditions make a carbocation, and which do not? A concerted E2 cannot rearrange.
w: (I) Ethoxide is a strong base, so the 2° bromide reacts by E2. The β carbon on one side (C2) is quaternary and has no H, so only a C4 hydrogen can be removed, giving 4,4-dimethylpent-2-ene, mainly E. (II) Without base, the bromide ionizes (E1).
