The 2° cation next to a quaternary carbon undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to a 3° cation, which loses a proton to give the tetrasubstituted alkene 2,3-dimethylpent-2-ene. Answer: I: (E)-4,4-dimethylpent-2-ene; II: 2,3-dimethylpent-2-ene.
x: E2 with ethoxide is concerted and has no carbocation, so the methyl shift needed for 2,3-dimethylpent-2-ene cannot happen in (I).
In (II) the reaction goes through a carbocation, and the 2° cation next to a quaternary carbon rearranges to a 3° cation before losing a proton.
This swaps the two mechanisms: the rearranged alkene comes from the carbocation path (II), not from the base (I).

q: The free-energy diagram below is for the acid-catalyzed hydration of methylenecyclopentane (H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) to 1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol. Which labeled point corresponds to the tertiary carbocation?
h: Intermediates sit in energy wells (local minima); transition states sit on peaks. Which well comes first?
w: Hydration takes three steps: (1) the π bond takes a proton from H3O+ to give the tertiary carbocation, (2) water adds to the cation to give an alkyloxonium ion, (3) water removes a proton to give the alcohol. Peaks A, C and E are the three transition states; wells B and D are the two intermediates. The first intermediate formed is the carbocation, so it is point B. It sits high because a carbocation is a reactive, electron-poor species.
x: Point A is a peak: it is the transition state for protonation of the alkene, not an intermediate that can be drawn as a discrete species.
Point D is the second intermediate, the protonated alcohol (alkyloxonium ion) formed after water bonds to the carbocation.
Point C is a peak: the transition state for water attacking the carbocation, partway between B and D.

q:
Use the free-energy diagram for the acid-catalyzed hydration of methylenecyclopentane. Which statements are correct?
I. The step from the alkene to point B is the rate-determining step.
II. Point B is a transition state.
III. The carbocation is found at point C.
h: The rate-determining step has the highest transition state. Then sort every point into peak (transition state) or well (intermediate).
w: I is true: peak A is the highest point on the curve, so protonation of the alkene to form the carbocation has the largest barrier and is rate-determining. II is false: B is a well, a local minimum, so it is an intermediate (the carbocation), not a transition state. III is false: C is a peak, the transition state for water adding to the cation; the carbocation itself is at B. Answer: I only.
x: This accepts II, but B is a local minimum. Transition states are maxima (A, C, E); B is an intermediate.
This accepts III, but C is a peak. The carbocation is the first intermediate, the well at B.
This rejects I, but A is the highest barrier on the diagram, so step 1 is rate-determining; and II and III both mislabel peaks and wells.

q: What is the major product when 1-methylcyclohexene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in methanol as the solvent?
h: Methanol is present in huge excess, so it, not bromide, opens the bromonium ion. Decide where it attacks and from which face.
w: Br2 forms a bridged bromonium ion on one face of the ring. Methanol (the solvent, far more abundant than Br−) opens it from the opposite face. In the bridged ion the C–Br bond to the tertiary carbon is longer and that carbon carries more δ+, so methanol bonds to the methyl-bearing carbon. The result is trans-2-bromo-1-methoxy-1-methylcyclohexane (OCH3 on C1, Br on C2, anti to each other), formed as a racemate.
x: This has the right regiochemistry but OCH<sub>3</sub> and Br on the same face. Opening of the bromonium ion is backside (anti), so syn addition does not occur.
Here Br ends up on the tertiary carbon and OCH<sub>3</sub> on the secondary one. The nucleophile attacks the more substituted carbon of the bromonium ion, which carries more positive charge.
The dibromide forms in an inert solvent such as CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>. In methanol the solvent outcompetes the small amount of Br<sup>−</sup> for the bromonium ion.

q: What is the major product of methylenecyclopentane with Cl<sub>2</sub> in water?
h: Water opens the chloronium ion. Which carbon of the three-membered ring can best carry partial positive charge?
w: Cl2 gives a chloronium ion. Water (the solvent) opens it at the more substituted ring carbon, which carries more δ+ charge. Cl stays on the CH2 and OH ends up on the ring carbon: 1-(chloromethyl)cyclopentan-1-ol. This is Markovnikov-type regiochemistry with Cl acting as the electrophile.
x: This puts OH on the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon. Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the chloronium ion, not the less hindered one.
The vicinal dichloride is the product in an inert solvent. With water as the solvent, water captures the chloronium ion.
A diol needs an oxidant such as OsO<sub>4</sub> or epoxidation then hydrolysis. Cl<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O adds one Cl and one OH.

q: Which structure shows the product of cyclopentene with Br<sub>2</sub> in water?
h: Halohydrin formation goes through a bridged bromonium ion. From which face does water attack?
w: Br2 forms a bromonium ion on one face of the ring; water attacks the other face (backside). Br and OH end up on opposite faces: trans-2-bromocyclopentan-1-ol, as a racemic mixture. Both enantiomers form because the bromonium ion forms equally on either face of the flat alkene.
x: Br and OH on the same face would require syn addition. The bridging Br blocks that face, so water must attack from the back.
trans-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane is the product in an inert solvent. In water, water is the nucleophile that opens the bromonium ion.
cis-Cyclopentane-1,2-diol comes from OsO<sub>4</sub> (syn dihydroxylation). Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O installs one Br and one OH.

q: (Z)-Hex-3-ene is treated with CH<sub>2</sub>I<sub>2</sub> and Zn(Cu) (Simmons–Smith reaction). Which structure is the product?
h: The carbenoid delivers CH<sub>2</sub> to both alkene carbons at once, from one face. What does that do to the cis relationship of the ethyl groups?
w: The Simmons–Smith carbenoid (ICH2ZnI) adds a CH2 group to both carbons of the π bond in one concerted, syn step, so the alkene geometry is preserved. A cis alkene gives a cis-disubstituted cyclopropane: cis-1,2-diethylcyclopropane. It has a mirror plane through the CH2 carbon, so it is a meso compound and no enantiomer forms.
x: trans-1,2-Diethylcyclopropane would come from (E)-hex-3-ene. The reaction is stereospecific: the ethyl groups keep their cis relationship.
1,1-Diethylcyclopropane has both ethyl groups on one carbon. The CH<sub>2</sub> is added across the C=C; no ethyl group moves.
A vinyl iodide would require substitution of an alkene C–H. The carbenoid adds CH<sub>2</sub> across the π bond and the iodine leaves with zinc.

q: 1-Methylcyclopentene is treated with BD<sub>3</sub>·THF, then with H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and NaOH. Which structure shows the product (D = deuterium)?
h: Find where boron goes (regiochemistry) and remember that D and B add to the same face. Oxidation then replaces B with OH with retention.
w: Hydroboration is a concerted syn addition: boron bonds to the less substituted alkene carbon (C2) and D bonds to the more substituted one (C1), both from the same face. Oxidation with H2O2/NaOH replaces C–B with C–OH with retention. So D (on C1) and OH (on C2) are cis, which leaves the methyl trans to OH: D and OH cis on adjacent carbons, CH3 trans to OH (racemic).
x: Here D and OH are on opposite faces, the result of anti addition. B and D are delivered to the same face in a four-center transition state.
This puts OH on the methyl-bearing carbon (Markovnikov). Boron, and therefore OH, goes to the less substituted carbon.
Here D and OH sit on the same carbon. In hydroboration D and B bond to the two different alkene carbons, so D must end up on the methyl-bearing carbon, next to the OH.

q: What is the major product of vinylcyclohexane with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in water? Assume the carbocation rearranges whenever a shift gives a more stable cation.
h: Protonate the alkene to give the more stable cation, then check whether a neighbouring hydrogen can shift to make an even more stable one.
w: Protonation of the CH2 end gives a secondary carbocation next to the ring CH. A 1,2-hydride shift from that ring carbon gives a tertiary carbocation in the ring, which water traps. After loss of H+ the product is 1-ethylcyclohexan-1-ol. To avoid the rearrangement and get 1-cyclohexylethanol, use oxymercuration–demercuration.
x: 1-Cyclohexylethanol is the unrearranged Markovnikov product. The secondary cation next to a tertiary C–H undergoes a hydride shift before water adds.
2-Cyclohexylethanol is the anti-Markovnikov product from hydroboration–oxidation, not from acid-catalyzed hydration.
Ring expansion is an alkyl shift. Here a hydride shift is available and already gives a tertiary cation; the expanded ring would only be secondary.

q: 2-Methylpent-1-ene is heated with concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> in aqueous NaOH, then acidified. What are the products?
h: Hot permanganate cleaves the C=C and oxidizes each piece as far as it can go. How far can a =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon be oxidized?
w: Hot, concentrated KMnO4 cleaves the double bond. A disubstituted alkene carbon (C2, bearing CH3 and propyl) becomes a ketone, which resists further oxidation. A =CH2 carbon is oxidized all the way: formaldehyde → formic acid → CO2. Products: pentan-2-one and CO2.
x: Formaldehyde is what ozonolysis with a reductive workup gives from a =CH<sub>2</sub> group. Hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> does not stop at an aldehyde.
Formic acid is still oxidizable under hot permanganate; the terminal carbon ends as CO<sub>2</sub>.
The 1,2-diol is the product of cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub>. With heat the diol is cleaved.

q: Ozonolysis (1. O<sub>3</sub>; 2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S) of an unknown alkene gives octane-2,7-dione as the only organic product. Which alkene was it?
h: Turn each C=O of the product back into one end of a C=C. If both carbonyls came from the same double bond, the starting alkene was a ring.
w: One product containing two ketones means one C=C was cleaved inside a ring, so the ring opened into a chain. Rejoining the two carbonyl carbons (C2 and C7) with a double bond gives a six-membered ring with a methyl on each alkene carbon: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene. Each alkene carbon carries a methyl group, so each becomes a methyl ketone.
x: 1,6-Dimethylcyclohexene has an alkene C–H, so it gives an aldehyde: 2-methyl-6-oxoheptanal, not a diketone.
1-Ethylcyclohexene also has an alkene C–H; it gives 6-oxooctanal (an aldehyde and an ethyl ketone).
This diene does give octane-2,7-dione, but each =CH<sub>2</sub> end also gives formaldehyde, so the dione would not be the only organic product.

q: Which reagents convert ethynylcyclohexane into 2-cyclohexylacetaldehyde?
h: The oxygen must end up on the terminal carbon. Which alkyne hydration is anti-Markovnikov?
w: Hydroboration of a terminal alkyne with a bulky dialkylborane such as disiamylborane, (sia)2BH, puts boron on the terminal carbon and stops after one addition. Oxidation gives an enol with OH on the terminal carbon, which tautomerizes to the aldehyde: 1. (sia)2BH; 2. H2O2, NaOH.
x: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: OH goes to the internal carbon and the enol tautomerizes to the methyl ketone, 1-cyclohexylethan-1-one.
Lindlar reduction gives vinylcyclohexane, and acid hydration of that gives an alcohol (rearranged to 1-ethylcyclohexanol), not an aldehyde.
Ozonolysis cleaves the triple bond: the product is cyclohexanecarboxylic acid (plus CO<sub>2</sub> from the terminal carbon), which has lost a carbon.

q: Which alkynes give a single ketone (no isomeric ketone) on hydration with H2O, H2SO4 and HgSO4?
h: For each alkyne ask: can water add to either alkyne carbon, and would the two choices give different ketones?
w: I (hex-2-yne) is unsymmetrical internal: the two alkyne carbons are similar (methyl vs propyl side), so water adds to both and a mixture of hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one forms. II (hex-3-yne) is symmetrical: either orientation gives hexan-3-one only. III (hex-1-yne) is terminal: Markovnikov addition puts OH on C2 only, giving hexan-2-one only. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misses III. A terminal alkyne is strongly Markovnikov under Hg<sup>2+</sup> catalysis and gives only the methyl ketone.
This accepts I. Hex-2-yne has a methyl on one side and a propyl on the other; both carbons are internal, so both ketones form.
This accepts I, whose two alkyne carbons both have alkyl groups, so hydration gives a mixture of two ketones.

q: In the HgSO<sub>4</sub>-catalyzed hydration of an alkyne, the enol formed tautomerizes in acid to the ketone. For cyclohex-1-en-1-ol and H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, which drawing shows the first step of that tautomerization (the step that makes the new C–H bond)?
h: The new C–H bond forms at the carbon that is not bonded to oxygen. Which electrons reach out to the proton?
w: In acid, the enol C=C π electrons attack a proton of H3O+, forming the new C–H bond at the β carbon; the H–O bond electrons go to water's oxygen. This gives the resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion (protonated ketone), which loses the O–H proton to give cyclohexanone. Correct arrows: C=C π bond → H, H–O bond → O of water.
x: Protonating the enol oxygen gives an oxonium ion, but it forms no C–H bond and leads back to the enol or to loss of water, not to the ketone.
The π electrons are drawn going to oxygen, and the H–O bond is never broken. Carbon must bond to the proton, and water leaves as the H–O electrons return to oxygen.
The π electrons reach the proton, but the H–O bond is never broken, so hydrogen would end up with two bonds. Water must leave with the H–O bond electrons.

q: Each alkene is hydrogenated with H<sub>2</sub> over Pd/C. Which one gives a meso compound?
h: Both H atoms add to the same face (syn). Draw each product, find its stereocenters, then look for an internal mirror plane.
w: Catalytic hydrogenation delivers both H atoms to one face of the alkene. 1,2-Dimethylcyclopentene therefore gives cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane, (1R,2S). It has two stereocenters with identical sets of groups and a mirror plane through C4 and the middle of the C1–C2 bond, so it is achiral: a meso compound, from 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene.
x: Syn addition to the E alkene gives (2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-2,3-diphenylbutane in equal amounts, a racemic mixture. Only the Z isomer would give the meso compound.
The product, cis-1-methyl-2-propylcyclopentane, has two stereocenters with different groups, so no mirror plane is possible; it is chiral and forms as a racemate.
2,3-Dimethylbutane has no stereocenter. It is achiral, but a meso compound must contain stereocenters.

q: In the reaction of methylenecyclohexane with Br<sub>2</sub> in water, water opens the bromonium ion. Which drawing shows that step correctly?
h: The nucleophile attacks the ring carbon whose bond to Br is weakest and which carries more positive charge; the bond that breaks must be to the carbon attacked.
w: In the bromonium ion the tertiary ring carbon carries more δ+ and has the weaker, longer C–Br bond. Water's lone pair attacks that carbon from the back, and the C–Br bond to the same carbon breaks with its electrons going to Br. Correct: O lone pair → tertiary carbon; C(tertiary)–Br bond → Br. Deprotonation then gives 1-(bromomethyl)cyclohexan-1-ol.
x: Attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon would put OH on the primary carbon. Opening of a halonium ion occurs at the more substituted carbon.
Water bonds to carbon, not to bromine. Attack at Br would give a species with no new C–O bond and Br with too many bonds.
Water attacks the tertiary carbon but the bond broken is the CH<sub>2</sub>–Br bond, so the tertiary carbon would have five bonds and the CH<sub>2</sub> only three.

q: Adding HBr to vinylcyclohexane gives first the secondary carbocation shown, which rearranges before bromide adds. Which arrow shows the rearrangement to the more stable cation?
h: A 1,2-shift moves a group with its bonding electron pair to the cationic carbon. Which neighbour shift gives a tertiary cation?
w: In a 1,2-hydride shift the C–H bond electrons on the ring carbon move, with the hydrogen, to the adjacent cationic carbon. The positive charge moves to the ring carbon, now tertiary (three carbon neighbours). The arrow starts at the C–H bond and ends at the cationic carbon: ring C–H bond → C+. Bromide then adds to give 1-bromo-1-ethylcyclohexane.
x: The arrow starts at the positive carbon, which has no electrons to give. Arrows show electrons moving toward the electron-poor carbon.
This shifts a ring C–C bond (ring expansion), giving a secondary cycloheptyl cation. That is no more stable than the starting cation; the hydride shift gives a tertiary one.
This arrow puts the C–H electrons on the ring carbon as a lone pair, making a carbanion next to a cation. No group moves to the cationic center.

q: What is the major product when but-2-yne reacts with one equivalent of Br2 in CH2Cl2?
h: With one equivalent, one Br<sub>2</sub> adds across the triple bond. Is the addition syn or anti?
w: Like alkenes, alkynes add Br2 through a bridged bromonium ion that bromide opens from the opposite side, so the two Br atoms add anti. One equivalent gives the dibromoalkene with Br atoms trans: (E)-2,3-dibromobut-2-ene.
x: The Z isomer would require syn addition. Anti opening of the bridged bromonium ion places the bromines on opposite sides.
The tetrabromide needs two equivalents of Br<sub>2</sub>. With one equivalent the reaction stops at the dibromoalkene.
2-Bromobut-2-ene is an HBr addition product. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two bromine atoms and no hydrogen.

q: Which sequence converts 4-phenylbut-1-ene into 4-phenylbut-1-yne?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv), NH<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O  2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv), NH<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O
h: A triple bond needs two eliminations, so both alkene carbons must first carry a leaving group. Then count what the base has to do.
w: Br2 adds across the C=C to give the vicinal dibromide, 1,2-dibromo-4-phenylbutane. Two E2 eliminations with the very strong base NaNH2 form the triple bond (the second one, from a vinyl bromide, needs a base this strong). The third equivalent deprotonates the terminal alkyne (pKa ≈ 25) to its acetylide, and water reprotonates it: 1. Br2, CH2Cl2 2. NaNH2 (3 equiv), NH3 3. H2O.
x: HBr puts only one bromine on the chain. One elimination simply regenerates an alkene; there is no second leaving group to form the triple bond.
Br<sub>2</sub> in water gives a bromohydrin (Br and OH). OH<sup>−</sup> is not a leaving group, so base closes the bromohydrin to an epoxide instead of making an alkyne.
One equivalent of hydroxide can remove at most one HBr, giving a vinyl bromide. The second elimination needs a much stronger base such as NaNH<sub>2</sub>.

q:
3-Methylpent-1-ene is treated separately with each reagent set. Which give a product whose carbon skeleton or functional-group position shows a carbocation rearrangement?
I. HBr
II. H2O, H2SO4
III. 1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O; 2. NaBH4
h: Which reagent sets go through a free carbocation? For those, look for a hydride on the carbon next to the first cation.
w: Protonation gives a secondary cation at C2, next to C3, which bears a hydrogen and two alkyl groups. A 1,2-hydride shift gives a more stable tertiary cation at C3. I is true: HBr traps the tertiary cation (3-bromo-3-methylpentane). II is true: acid hydration also goes through the free cation and gives 3-methylpentan-3-ol. III is false: oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, not a free carbocation, so it gives unrearranged 3-methylpentan-2-ol. Answer: I and II only.
x: This leaves out I. HBr addition (no peroxides) also goes through the secondary carbocation, which undergoes the hydride shift.
This reverses the logic: oxymercuration is the one method that avoids rearrangement, because the mercurinium ion is bridged.
This accepts III. The mercurinium ion never becomes a free carbocation, so no hydride shift occurs.

q:
Which reactions of cyclohexene give a meso product?
I. Br2 in CH2Cl2
II. OsO4, then NaHSO3, H2O
III. mCPBA, then H3O+
h: Decide syn or anti addition for each, then ask whether a cis- or trans-1,2-disubstituted cyclohexane with two identical groups has a mirror plane.
w: I gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane (anti addition); with two identical groups on opposite faces it has no mirror plane and forms as a racemate. II gives cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol (syn addition); its mirror plane makes it meso. III: the epoxide is opened by water from the back, giving trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, which is chiral and racemic. Answer: II only.
x: This picks the two anti additions. trans-1,2-Disubstituted cyclohexanes with identical groups are chiral (C<sub>2</sub>-symmetric), so they form as racemates, not meso compounds.
Anti addition of Br<sub>2</sub> gives the trans dibromide, which is chiral. It forms as a racemic mixture.
Only the syn addition gives the cis, meso product. Both anti routes give a chiral trans product.

q: What is the product when methyl 4-formylbenzoate is treated with NaBH<sub>4</sub> in ethanol, followed by aqueous workup?
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a mild hydride donor. Which of the two carbonyl groups is reactive enough for it?
w: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones but reacts only very slowly with esters at room temperature, because the ester carbonyl is stabilized by donation from the OR oxygen. The aldehyde becomes a CH2OH group and the ester is untouched: methyl 4-(hydroxymethyl)benzoate.
x: Reducing both groups to the diol needs a stronger hydride donor such as LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.
This reduces the ester and leaves the aldehyde, the reverse of the real selectivity: aldehydes are far more reactive than esters toward hydride.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> in ethanol does not hydrolyze the ester; ester hydrolysis needs aqueous acid or base with heating.

q: Ethyl 3-phenylpropanoate is treated with one equivalent of DIBAL-H in toluene at −78 °C, then with water. What is the major organic product (besides ethanol)?
h: At −78 °C the first tetrahedral intermediate does not collapse until water is added. What does it give on workup?
w: DIBAL-H delivers one hydride to the ester carbonyl. At −78 °C the aluminum-bound tetrahedral intermediate is stable, so no aldehyde is present to be reduced again. On aqueous workup it collapses, expelling ethanol, to give the aldehyde: 3-phenylpropanal.
x: The primary alcohol forms with LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, or with excess DIBAL-H at higher temperature, where the aldehyde is released in the flask and reduced again.
This hemiacetal is the hydrolyzed tetrahedral intermediate. It is unstable and loses ethanol to give the aldehyde.
DIBAL-H is a reducing agent. Hydrolysis of the ester to the acid would need aqueous acid or base, not a hydride.

q:
Which statements about hydride reducing agents are correct?
I. NaBH4 in methanol reduces a ketone but leaves an ester in the same molecule largely unchanged.
II. LiAlH4, followed by aqueous acid workup, reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol.
III. One equivalent of DIBAL-H at −78 °C reduces an ester to an aldehyde.
h: Rank the reagents by strength and recall which carbonyl groups each one can reach.
w: I is true: NaBH4 is mild and reduces aldehydes and ketones, not esters. II is true: LiAlH4 first deprotonates the acid, then reduces the carboxylate to the primary alcohol. III is true: at −78 °C DIBAL-H stops at a stable tetrahedral intermediate that gives the aldehyde on workup. Answer: I, II, and III.
x: This rejects III, but low-temperature DIBAL-H is the standard way to reduce an ester only to the aldehyde.
This rejects II, but LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is strong enough to reduce carboxylic acids (via the carboxylate) to primary alcohols.
This rejects I, but NaBH<sub>4</sub>'s selectivity for ketones and aldehydes over esters is its main use.

q: What is the product of 3-methylbutane-1,3-diol with PCC in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>?
h: Classify each OH (1°, 2°, 3°) and recall how far PCC oxidizes each kind in the absence of water.
w: PCC in anhydrous CH2Cl2 oxidizes a primary alcohol only to the aldehyde, because no water is present to form the hydrate that would be oxidized further. The tertiary OH has no H on its carbon, so it cannot be oxidized. Product: 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutanal.
x: Oxidation to the carboxylic acid needs aqueous chromic acid (Jones reagent). PCC stops at the aldehyde.
PCC is not a dehydrating reagent, and this structure still contains the primary OH that PCC oxidizes.
The primary OH does react with PCC. Only the tertiary OH is untouched.

q:
Which reagents convert hexan-1-ol into hexanal in good yield?
I. PCC, CH2Cl2
II. CrO3, H2SO4, H2O, acetone (Jones reagent)
III. Dess–Martin periodinane, CH2Cl2
h: Which oxidations happen in water? An aldehyde in water forms a hydrate, which can be oxidized again.
w: I works: PCC in dry CH2Cl2 stops at the aldehyde. II does not: aqueous chromic acid oxidizes the aldehyde (through its hydrate) on to hexanoic acid. III works: Dess–Martin periodinane is a mild, anhydrous oxidant that stops at the aldehyde. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misses III. Dess–Martin periodinane, like PCC, is anhydrous and stops at the aldehyde.
Jones reagent is the one that fails: in water the aldehyde hydrate is oxidized to the carboxylic acid.
This accepts II. Aqueous chromic acid takes a primary alcohol all the way to the carboxylic acid.

q: cis-4-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is treated with SOCl<sub>2</sub> in pyridine. Assuming the substitution occurs by backside (S<sub>N</sub>2) attack of chloride, which product forms?
h: First the OH becomes a chlorosulfite leaving group (C–O bond untouched). Then chloride attacks the carbon from which side?
w: SOCl2 turns the OH into a chlorosulfite (–OS(O)Cl) without breaking the C–O bond, so the configuration is kept at that stage. In pyridine, chloride then displaces the chlorosulfite by backside attack, inverting the carbon. The cis alcohol therefore gives trans-1-chloro-4-methylcyclohexane.
x: The cis chloride would mean retention, which is not the outcome when chloride attacks from the back as stated.
Elimination is a side reaction at best here; pyridine is a weak base and chloride substitution is the main path.
The chlorosulfite is an intermediate. With chloride present it is displaced, releasing SO<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sup>−</sup>.

q: trans-2-Methylcyclopentan-1-ol is treated with TsCl in pyridine, and the product is heated with NaN<sub>3</sub> in DMSO. Which structure shows the major product?
h: Count the inversions: does making the tosylate touch the C–O bond? What does azide do to the carbon bearing OTs?
w: Tosylation forms an O–S bond; the C–O bond is not broken, so the tosylate keeps the trans configuration. Azide is an excellent nucleophile and weak base, and in DMSO it displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion. One inversion turns trans into cis: cis-1-azido-2-methylcyclopentane (racemic, since the starting alcohol was racemic).
x: The trans azide would require two inversions or none. Tosylation goes with retention and the S<sub>N</sub>2 step inverts once.
Azide on the methyl-bearing carbon would need a carbocation and a hydride shift. A secondary tosylate with a strong nucleophile in DMSO reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2, without a cation.
The tosylate is only the intermediate after step 1. Heating with azide, an excellent nucleophile, displaces the tosylate group.

q: What is the final product of this sequence starting from 4-bromobutan-1-ol?
h: Follow the protecting group: why is it needed for step 2, and what does fluoride do at the end?
w: A Grignard reagent is destroyed by an O–H proton, so the alcohol is first protected as a TBS (tert-butyldimethylsilyl) ether. The protected bromide then forms a Grignard reagent, which adds to acetone to give a tertiary alkoxide (protonated on workup). Fluoride (TBAF) cleaves the strong Si–O bond and frees the primary OH. Product: 2-methylhexane-2,6-diol.
x: Butan-1-ol is what results without protection: the Grignard reagent is protonated by an OH group before it can add to acetone.
This structure still carries the TBS group. Step 4, fluoride, removes it because the Si–F bond is stronger than Si–O.
Fluoride removes the silyl group, not the oxygen. The C–O bond of the protected alcohol survives, so the primary OH returns.

q: Cyclohexylmethanol was treated with one reagent. The product's IR spectrum is shown (no absorption from 3200 to 3600 cm<sup>−1</sup>). Which reagent was used?
h: Read the bands at 2815 and 2715 cm<sup>−1</sup> together with the band at 1728 cm<sup>−1</sup>. What functional group shows all three?
w: The strong band at 1728 cm−1 is a C=O stretch, and the pair of weak bands near 2815 and 2715 cm−1 is the aldehyde C–H stretch. There is no O–H band. The product is cyclohexanecarbaldehyde, so the reagent oxidized the primary alcohol and stopped at the aldehyde: PCC in CH2Cl2.
x: Jones reagent gives cyclohexanecarboxylic acid, whose spectrum shows a very broad O–H band from about 2500 to 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not react with an alcohol; the spectrum would still show the broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=O.
Acid and heat dehydrate the alcohol to an alkene (C=C near 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>, =C–H above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>), with no C=O band.

q: What is the product of methyl 5-oxohexanoate with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in ether, followed by aqueous acid workup?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is the strong hydride reagent. Which carbonyl groups can it reduce, and how far?
w: LiAlH4 reduces both the ketone (to a secondary alcohol) and the ester (through the aldehyde to a primary alcohol, with loss of methanol). Product: hexane-1,5-diol.
x: Reducing only the ketone is what NaBH<sub>4</sub> does. LiAlH<sub>4</sub> also reduces the ester.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not leave a ketone untouched; ketones are more reactive than esters toward hydride.
The aldehyde formed from the ester is more reactive than the ester and is reduced at once by LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

q: To prepare sodium ethoxide for a Williamson ether synthesis, which base converts ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) essentially completely into its conjugate base?
h: An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid. Compare each conjugate acid's pK<sub>a</sub> with 16.
w: Deprotonation is complete when the conjugate acid of the base is much weaker than ethanol. H2 (pKa ≈ 35) is about 1019 times weaker, and it leaves as a gas, so NaH converts ethanol fully to sodium ethoxide.
x: Water (15.7) and ethanol (≈16) are about equally acidic, so NaOH gives an equilibrium mixture with much ethanol and hydroxide left.
Carbonic acid (6.4) is a far stronger acid than ethanol; the equilibrium lies almost entirely on the ethanol side.
Acetic acid (4.8) is a much stronger acid than ethanol, so acetate cannot deprotonate ethanol to any useful extent.

q: 2-Methyl-1,1-diphenylpropane-1,2-diol is warmed with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (pinacol rearrangement). What is the major product?
h: Both OH groups are tertiary. Which one leaves to give the more stable carbocation? Then decide which group on the neighbouring carbon shifts to it.
w: Water leaves from the carbon that carries two phenyl groups, because that tertiary cation is also stabilized by resonance into both rings; the (CH3)2C+ alternative has no resonance. A methyl group on the neighbouring C(OH)(CH3)2 carbon then shifts to the cationic carbon, leaving a cation on the carbon bearing OH, which is really a protonated ketone. Loss of H+ gives 3,3-diphenylbutan-2-one, (C6H5)2C(CH3)COCH3.
x: This ketone would form if the OH on the dimethyl carbon left first and a phenyl shifted. That route starts from the less stable carbocation, which has no resonance.
This allylic alcohol needs the (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C<sup>+</sup> cation to lose a methyl H. That cation is not the one formed, and in a 1,2-diol a 1,2-shift to a protonated ketone wins.
Acid does not close a diol to a strained epoxide; acid opens epoxides. The carbocation instead rearranges to the carbonyl compound.

q: Which combination gives the best yield of methoxycyclohexane?
h: The Williamson synthesis is S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon should carry the leaving group?
w: In a Williamson synthesis the alkoxide attacks an alkyl halide by SN2, so the halide should be on the less hindered carbon. Methyl iodide is ideal (no β-H, no hindrance), and the bulky secondary part is supplied as the nucleophile: sodium cyclohexoxide + CH3I.
x: Methoxide with a secondary bromide gives mostly cyclohexene by E2, because methoxide is a strong base and the secondary carbon is hindered.
A neutral alcohol is a poor nucleophile; without a base to make the alkoxide, the reaction is very slow.
Acid-catalyzed condensation of two different alcohols gives a mixture of three ethers plus cyclohexene from dehydration of the secondary alcohol.

q: 2,2-Dimethyloxirane reacts with sodium methoxide in methanol. Which drawing shows the ring-opening step correctly?
h: Under basic conditions the epoxide is not protonated, so the reaction is a plain S<sub>N</sub>2. Which carbon is easier to reach?
w: A strong nucleophile opens an unprotonated epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered carbon, here the CH2. The C–O bond to that same carbon breaks and the ring oxygen becomes an alkoxide: CH3O− → CH2; CH2–O bond → O. Protonation by methanol gives 1-methoxy-2-methylpropan-2-ol.
x: Attack at the tertiary carbon is the acid-catalyzed regiochemistry. Without acid, S<sub>N</sub>2 at the crowded tertiary carbon is much slower.
Methoxide does not bond to the epoxide oxygen; an O–O bond would form and no ring strain would be released.
Methoxide attacks the CH<sub>2</sub> but the bond broken is the other C–O bond, leaving CH<sub>2</sub> with five bonds and the tertiary carbon with three.

q: 1-Methyl-7-oxabicyclo[4.1.0]heptane (1-methylcyclohexene oxide) is treated with CH<sub>3</sub>OH and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Protonation of the epoxide gives the tertiary carbon substantial positive character. Where does methanol attack, and from which face?
w: In acid the epoxide oxygen is protonated first. The C–O bond to the tertiary carbon is weakened most and that carbon carries the most δ+, so methanol attacks it, from the face opposite the oxygen (backside, anti). Product: trans-2-methoxy-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (OCH3 on the methyl-bearing carbon, OH on the neighbouring carbon, trans), as a racemate.
x: Correct regiochemistry, but OCH<sub>3</sub> and OH are cis. Epoxide opening is backside attack, so the two oxygens end up trans.
This is the base-catalyzed regiochemistry (attack at the less hindered secondary carbon). In acid the tertiary carbon is attacked.
This has the base-type regiochemistry and syn stereochemistry; both differ from acid-catalyzed opening.

q: (R)-2-Methyloxirane is treated with sodium propynide (CH<sub>3</sub>C≡C<sup>−</sup> Na<sup>+</sup>) in THF, followed by aqueous NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. What is the product?
h: Find the carbon the acetylide attacks. Are any bonds to the stereocenter made or broken?
w: The acetylide is a strong nucleophile, so it opens the unprotonated epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered CH2. No bond to the stereocenter is broken, so its spatial arrangement is kept. The CIP priorities also keep the same order (O > CH2 > CH3 > H), so the descriptor stays R: (R)-hex-4-yn-2-ol.
x: Inversion happens only at the carbon that is attacked. The CH<sub>2</sub> is attacked; the stereocenter is not touched.
No carbocation forms and the stereocenter is never broken, so its configuration is not scrambled.
Attack at the substituted carbon is the acid-catalyzed regiochemistry. A basic carbon nucleophile attacks the less hindered CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: 2-Ethoxy-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl ethyl ether) is treated with one equivalent of concentrated HI. Which products form?
h: After protonation of the ether oxygen, which C–O bond breaks? Think about which fragment can leave as a stable carbocation.
w: HI protonates the ether oxygen. The C–O bond to the tertiary carbon breaks on its own (SN1), because it gives a stable tertiary carbocation and neutral ethanol leaves. Iodide traps the cation. Products: tert-butyl iodide and ethanol.
x: This is the S<sub>N</sub>2 pattern (iodide attacks the less hindered ethyl group). With a tertiary group present the S<sub>N</sub>1 cleavage at the tertiary carbon is much faster.
Converting ethanol to ethyl iodide needs a second equivalent of HI and heating; with one equivalent the alcohol remains.
HI cleaves a C–O bond; it does not substitute a C–H bond on the ethyl group.

q:
Which routes give 1-methoxy-1-methylcyclopentane as the major product?
I. 1-chloro-1-methylcyclopentane + NaOCH3
II. 1-methylcyclopentene; 1. Hg(OAc)2, CH3OH; 2. NaBH4
III. 1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol; 1. NaH; 2. CH3I
h: For each route, identify the electrophilic carbon. Can a strong base do S<sub>N</sub>2 at a tertiary carbon?
w: I fails: methoxide with a tertiary chloride gives E2 elimination (methylcyclopentenes), because backside attack at a tertiary carbon is blocked. II works: alkoxymercuration adds CH3O to the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) without rearrangement, and NaBH4 replaces Hg with H. III works: the tertiary alkoxide attacks CH3I by SN2 at the unhindered methyl carbon. Answer: II and III only.
x: This accepts I. A tertiary halide with a strong base eliminates; the Williamson synthesis needs the alkyl halide part to be methyl or primary.
This misses II. Alkoxymercuration–demercuration is a reliable Markovnikov route to ethers from alkenes.
This accepts I. Methoxide is a strong base, and with a tertiary chloride E2 dominates.

q:
(Z)-But-2-ene is converted to an epoxide in two steps: 1. Br2, H2O; 2. NaOH. Which statements are correct?
I. The epoxide formed is trans-2,3-dimethyloxirane.
II. Step 1 adds Br and OH anti to each other.
III. In step 2 the alkoxide displaces bromide with inversion at the carbon that held Br.
h: Two stereospecific steps: an anti addition, then a backside intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2. What is the net result relative to the alkene geometry?
w: II is true: water opens the bromonium ion from the back, so Br and OH add anti. III is true: NaOH deprotonates the OH, and the alkoxide displaces bromide intramolecularly by backside attack, which needs O and Br anti and inverts that carbon. I is false: anti addition followed by one inversion is net syn, so the cis relationship of the methyls is kept and the product is cis-2,3-dimethyloxirane (meso), the same as from mCPBA. Answer: II and III only.
x: This accepts I. Anti addition plus an inversion cancel out, so the Z alkene gives the cis epoxide.
This rejects II, but halohydrin formation is an anti addition via the bridged bromonium ion.
This accepts I. The two stereochemical steps cancel, so the epoxide keeps the cis geometry of the alkene.

q: 1-Methyl-4-vinylcyclohex-1-ene is treated with one equivalent of mCPBA in CH2Cl2. What is the major product?
h: A peroxyacid is an electrophile. Which π bond is more electron-rich?
w: Epoxidation by a peroxyacid is an electrophilic addition: the alkene's π electrons attack the electrophilic peroxide oxygen. Alkyl groups donate electron density, so a trisubstituted alkene reacts much faster than a monosubstituted one. With one equivalent the ring alkene is epoxidized and the vinyl group survives: the ring epoxide (1-methyl-7-oxabicyclo[4.1.0]heptane bearing the vinyl group).
x: The monosubstituted vinyl group is the less electron-rich alkene, so it reacts more slowly with the electrophilic peroxyacid.
The diepoxide would need two equivalents of mCPBA; with one equivalent the faster-reacting ring alkene consumes it.
The trans diol forms only if the epoxide is opened by aqueous acid. mCPBA in CH2Cl2 stops at the epoxide.

q: A ketone C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O gives the mass spectrum shown: M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 128, base peak at m/z 57, and strong peaks at m/z 99 and 72. Which ketone is it?
h: α-Cleavage on each side of the C=O gives two acylium ions. A McLafferty rearrangement gives an even-mass ion. Predict all three for each choice.
w: For a ketone R–CO–R′, α-cleavage gives R–C≡O+ and R′–C≡O+, and a γ-hydrogen gives a McLafferty ion at even m/z. 3-Octanone (ethyl pentyl ketone): losing the pentyl radical (71) gives CH3CH2C≡O+ at m/z 57; losing the ethyl radical (29) gives C5H11C≡O+ at m/z 99; and the γ-H on the pentyl side lets 1-butene (56) leave, giving the enol radical cation at m/z 72. All three match: 3-octanone.
x: 4-Octanone gives acylium ions at m/z 71 (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) and 85 (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) and McLafferty ions at 86 and 100, not 57, 99 and 72.
2-Octanone (a methyl ketone) gives CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at m/z 43 as the base peak, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at 113, and a McLafferty ion at 58.
This ketone gives a strong m/z 57 (the tert-butyl cation), but its acylium ions are at 85 and 71 and its McLafferty ion is at 100; it cannot give 99 or 72.

q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of 4′-isopropylacetophenone (shown)?
h: Use the mirror plane through C1 and C4 of the ring. How many kinds of ring H, and are the two isopropyl methyls equivalent?
w: The molecule has a mirror plane through the two ring carbons that carry substituents. Signals: the acetyl CH3 (singlet, 3H); two kinds of aromatic H (2H each, the pair next to C=O and the pair next to the isopropyl); the isopropyl CH (septet, 1H); and the two isopropyl CH3 groups, which are equivalent (doublet, 6H). Total: 5.
x: Four misses one set: the ring H next to the acetyl group and those next to the isopropyl group are in different environments.
Six counts the two isopropyl methyls separately; they are swapped by the mirror plane and give one 6H doublet.
Seven treats all four ring H as different; the mirror plane makes them two pairs.

q: Which C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O ether gives exactly three signals in its broadband-decoupled <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum?
h: Look for symmetry that makes the two sides of the oxygen the same, then count carbons on one side.
w: Dipropyl ether is symmetric about the oxygen, so the two propyl groups are equivalent and each gives three kinds of carbon: OCH2, CH2, CH3. Dipropyl ether shows three 13C signals.
x: Diisopropyl ether is also symmetric, but each isopropyl has only two kinds of carbon (CH and the two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub>), so it gives two signals.
tert-Butyl ethyl ether has four kinds of carbon: OCH2, CH3 of ethyl, the quaternary C and the three equivalent CH3.
1-Methoxypentane has no symmetry; all six carbons are different.

q: The 13C NMR spectrum of 4-methoxy-2-butanone (shown) has peaks at δ 207.0, 67.9, 58.8, 43.6 and 30.4. Which set gives the shifts of the tagged carbons a, b, c and d, in that order?
h: Ketone C=O near 200+; sp<sup>3</sup> carbons bonded to O at 50–70; sp<sup>3</sup> carbons next to C=O at 30–45.
w: The ketone carbon b is the peak at 207.0. The two carbons bonded to O are 67.9 (the OCH2, untagged) and 58.8 (the OCH3, d). Of the carbons next to the C=O, the CH2 c (43.6) is farther downfield than the CH3 a (30.4), because it has an extra carbon attached and is also β to oxygen. a 30.4, b 207.0, c 43.6, d 58.8.
x: This swaps c and d: the OCH<sub>3</sub> is bonded directly to oxygen and belongs in the 50–70 region, while the CH<sub>2</sub> next to the C=O is near 44.
A methyl next to a C=O is not bonded to oxygen, so it is not at 58.8; that shift belongs to the OCH<sub>3</sub> (d).
Carbon d is the methoxy CH<sub>3</sub> (58.8); 67.9 is the OCH<sub>2</sub>, which is not tagged. And the CH<sub>3</sub> (a) is the most upfield carbon, 30.4.

q: Which compounds give a <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum consisting of only one triplet and one quartet (no other signals)?
h: A triplet plus a quartet is one ethyl group. Only one signal pair means every ethyl group must be equivalent.
w: A CH3CH2– group gives a 3H triplet and a 2H quartet. I (3-pentanone) has two ethyl groups made equivalent by symmetry: one triplet, one quartet. II (ethyl propanoate) has two different ethyl groups, the acyl CH2 near 2.3 and the OCH2 near 4.1, so it shows two triplets and two quartets. III (diethyl carbonate) is symmetric: one OCH2 quartet and one CH3 triplet. I and III only.
x: III also qualifies: the two ethoxy groups of diethyl carbonate are equivalent, giving one triplet and one quartet.
II does not qualify: its two ethyl groups are on different sides of the ester and give four signals.
I qualifies (its two ethyls are equivalent), and II does not (four signals).

q: Rank the 1H NMR signals of the hydrogens on the tagged carbons of 3-chloropropanal from lowest to highest chemical shift.
h: Recall the typical ranges: H next to C=O about 2–3 ppm, H on a carbon bearing Cl about 3.5–4, aldehyde H about 9.5–10.
w: The aldehyde H on a is strongly deshielded by the C=O anisotropy and electronegativity (δ ≈ 9.8). The CH2 bonded to Cl, c, appears near 3.8. The CH2 next to the carbonyl, b, appears near 2.9. Lowest to highest: b < c < a.
x: Cl is bonded directly to c, which deshields it more than the C=O deshields the α-CH<sub>2</sub> b, so c lies downfield of b.
This is the reverse order; the aldehyde H is the most downfield signal, not the most upfield.
The aldehyde H (about 9.8) lies far downfield of the CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (about 3.8).

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the 2H signal at δ 4.05 is broad and disappears when D<sub>2</sub>O is added). Which structure is it?
h: Two 2H doublets in the aromatic region point to one substitution pattern. Then decide where the ethyl group is attached from the shift of its quartet.
w: Two aromatic doublets of 2H each mean a para-disubstituted ring. The 2H quartet at 4.32 with a 3H triplet at 1.36 is an ethyl group on an ester oxygen (OCH2, deshielded by O and C=O). The exchangeable 2H broad singlet is an NH2. The doublet at 6.64 is ortho to the electron-donating NH2 (shielded) and the one at 7.86 is ortho to the ester C=O. This is ethyl 4-aminobenzoate (benzocaine).
x: An ortho-disubstituted ring has four different aromatic H (1H each), not two 2H doublets.
An N-ethyl group's CH<sub>2</sub> appears near 3.2, not 4.3; the acid would also show a COOH near 12 ppm and the NH would be 1H, not 2H.
This compound has two methyl singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> and NCH<sub>3</sub>) and no ethyl quartet or triplet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown; the DEPT result (C, CH, CH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>) is written over each peak. Which structure is it?
h: Use the DEPT labels: how many aromatic carbons (and so what ring pattern), and what kinds of sp<sup>3</sup> carbon are present? Which sp<sup>3</sup> carbon is bonded to O (50–80 ppm)?
w: Four aromatic peaks (one C and three CH) mean a monosubstituted benzene ring. The sp3 region has two CH2 carbons and no CH3: one at 63.7 (bonded to O) and one at 39.2 (benzylic, not bonded to O). That is Ph–CH2–CH2–OH, 2-phenylethanol.
x: 1-Phenylethanol would show a CH (bonded to O, near 70) and a CH<sub>3</sub> (near 25), not two CH<sub>2</sub> peaks.
Benzyl methyl ether would show a CH<sub>3</sub> (OCH<sub>3</sub> near 58) and only one CH<sub>2</sub> (near 75).
4-Ethylphenol has a CH<sub>3</sub> and a para-disubstituted ring (two aromatic C peaks, one near 153 for C–OH, and only two CH peaks).

q: An alcohol C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O shows a broad IR band at 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>. With chromic acid (Jones reagent) the orange solution turns green, and the isolated product shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no O–H band. Which alcohol was it?
h: Which kinds of alcohol does chromic acid oxidize, and what does each give? Does the product still have an O–H?
w: Chromic acid (Cr(VI), orange) is reduced to Cr(III) (green) when it oxidizes an alcohol that has an H on the carbinol carbon. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone (C=O near 1715, no O–H), while a primary alcohol is oxidized all the way to a carboxylic acid (C=O plus a very broad O–H at 2500–3300). The product here is a ketone, 2-butanone, so the alcohol was 2-butanol.
x: tert-Butyl alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon, so it does not react with chromic acid (the solution stays orange).
1-Butanol is oxidized by aqueous chromic acid to butanoic acid, which still shows a very broad O–H band.
Diethyl ether has no O–H band to begin with and is not oxidized by chromic acid.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown? (There is no absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.)
h: Identify the band near 2250 and the band near 1715. Then rule out any choice that would add a band the spectrum lacks.
w: The sharp medium band at 2250 cm−1 is a C≡N stretch, and the strong band at 1715 cm−1 is a ketone C=O. Nothing appears above 3000 cm−1, so there is no O–H and no ≡C–H. 5-Oxohexanenitrile (a ketone and a nitrile) fits.
x: A terminal alkyne shows a strong, sharp ≡C–H stretch near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a weak C≡C near 2120, not a band at 2250 with nothing above 3000.
An alcohol would give a broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and this compound has no C=O for the 1715 band.
An ester C=O appears near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, with a strong C–O band near 1240; the spectrum's C=O is at 1715.

q: A compound gives the mass spectrum and IR spectrum shown. MS: m/z 154 and 156 (3 : 1), base peak 139 with a partner at 141 (3 : 1), and 111/113 (3 : 1). IR: strong band at 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>, weak band at 3060 cm<sup>−1</sup>, nothing near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: Each 3 : 1 pair contains one Cl. Which fragment keeps the Cl, and what was lost to make the base peak?
w: The 3 : 1 pairs show one chlorine, and the molecular ion is at 154. The 1685 cm−1 band is a conjugated (aryl) ketone C=O, and 3060 is aromatic C–H. The base peak at 139/141 is M − 15: loss of CH3• by α-cleavage, giving ClC6H4–C≡O+, which still has Cl. Losing CO from it gives ClC6H4+ at 111/113. This is 4′-chloroacetophenone.
x: 2-Chloroacetophenone also has M = 154/156, but α-cleavage loses •CH<sub>2</sub>Cl and gives PhC≡O<sup>+</sup> at m/z 105 with no chlorine partner; the base peak would not be a 139/141 pair.
4-Chlorobenzaldehyde has M = 140/142, not 154/156.
1-(4-Chlorophenyl)ethanol has M = 156/158 and an O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and it has no C=O to absorb at 1685.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O gives these data. Which structure fits?
h: The sharp 3290 band and the 1H triplet go together. A small (2–3 Hz) coupling can pass through a C≡C.
w: The strong, sharp 3290 cm−1 band with a weak 2120 band is a terminal alkyne (≡C–H and C≡C). No broad O–H band and a strong 1100 C–O band mean an ether. In the 1H NMR, the 3H singlet at 3.39 is OCH3; the 2H doublet at 4.13 is an O–CH2 next to the alkyne; the 1H triplet at 2.43 is the ≡C–H. The CH2 and ≡C–H split each other through the triple bond (long-range coupling, J ≈ 2.4 Hz). 3-Methoxyprop-1-yne (methyl propargyl ether).
x: 2-Butyn-1-ol has an O–H (broad band near 3350) and no ≡C–H; its CH<sub>3</sub> would be near 1.8, not an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet at 3.39.
3-Butyn-1-ol has an O–H band and two CH<sub>2</sub> groups, with no OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet.
1-Methoxyprop-1-yne is an internal alkyne with no ≡C–H, so it would have no 3290 band and no 1H signal; it gives two 3H singlets.

q: A compound that contains only C, H and O shows M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 88. Combustion analysis gives 54.5% carbon by mass. What is its molecular formula?
h: Multiply the molar mass by the mass fraction of carbon to find the mass of carbon in one mole, then divide by 12.
w: Mass of C per mole = 0.545 × 88 = 48 g, which is 48/12 = 4 carbons. The remaining 40 mass units must be H and O: 2 O (32) + 8 H (8) = 40. The formula is C4H8O2 (DBE 1, for example an ester or a carboxylic acid). Check: 48.04/88.11 = 54.5% C.
x: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O also has M = 88, but it is 60/88 = 68.1% carbon.
C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>3</sub> also has M = 88, but it is 36/88 = 40.9% carbon.
C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>4</sub> has M = 88 but is 95.4% carbon and contains no oxygen; it is also an unlikely highly unsaturated formula.

q: Hexanal (M = 100) shows a prominent peak at m/z 44 in its mass spectrum, formed by a McLafferty rearrangement. Which ion is it, and what neutral molecule is lost?
h: The C=O oxygen takes the H on the γ-carbon (tag d), and the bond between the α- and β-carbons (b–c) breaks.
w: In a McLafferty rearrangement, the carbonyl O removes a γ-hydrogen (on carbon d) through a six-membered transition state, and the bond between the α-carbon (b) and β-carbon (c) breaks. The β- and γ-carbons and the rest of the chain leave as an alkene, CH2=CH–CH2CH3 (1-butene, 56), and the ion kept is the enol radical cation of acetaldehyde: CH2=CH–OH•+, m/z 44, with loss of 1-butene. 100 − 56 = 44.
x: The H moves to oxygen, so the ion is first formed as the enol, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–OH<sup>•+</sup>, not as the keto form.
The neutral fragment is an alkene (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, 56), not an alkane; 100 − 58 would give m/z 42, not 44.
This ion has lost an H from the wrong place and has m/z 42; the McLafferty ion keeps all the H it started with plus the transferred H.

q: Which compound shows two N–H stretching bands of medium intensity near 3300 and 3380 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
h: Count the H atoms on nitrogen. Two N–H bonds can stretch in phase and out of phase.
w: A primary amine, R–NH2, has two N–H bonds that stretch together in a symmetric and an asymmetric mode, giving two bands near 3300 and 3380 cm−1. Cyclohexylamine is the primary amine.
x: A secondary amine has only one N–H, so it shows a single weak band.
A tertiary amine has no N–H bond and no band in this region.
An alcohol gives one broad, strong O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not two medium N–H bands.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1720 and 1160 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a medium band at 1638 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown (the two vinyl singlets are each 1H, from two different =CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogens). Which structure is it?
h: DBE 2: one C=O and one C=C. All four signals are singlets, so no hydrogen-bearing carbons are neighbors.
w: DBE = 2. The 1720 band is a C=O, 1638 a C=C, and 1160 a C–O, so this is an unsaturated ester. Every signal is a singlet: OCH3 (3.75), a CH3 on an alkene carbon (1.95), and two separate vinyl H (6.10 and 5.56) that are on the same carbon, a =CH2 with no H on the neighboring carbon. That is CH2=C(CH3)CO2CH3, methyl methacrylate. The C=O at 1720 rather than about 1740 fits conjugation with the C=C.
x: Methyl (E)-but-2-enoate has two vinyl H on adjacent carbons; they split each other (large trans J) and are split by the CH3, so they are not singlets, and its CH3 would be a doublet of doublets, not a singlet.
Ethyl acrylate would show an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet, and three vinyl H that split each other.
Allyl acetate has a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near 2.1 but an OCH<sub>2</sub> doublet near 4.6 and three coupled vinyl H; its non-conjugated ester C=O would be near 1740.

q: A compound containing only C, H and N shows M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 69. Its IR spectrum has a sharp, medium band at 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup> and nothing above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shows four signals: δ 119.8, 19.3, 19.1 and 13.4. Which structure fits?
h: An odd molecular mass means an odd number of N atoms. Then use the IR band and the number of <sup>13</sup>C signals.
w: By the nitrogen rule, an odd M+ (69) means an odd number of nitrogens, so C4H7N with one N. The 2250 cm−1 band is a C≡N stretch, and there is no N–H or ≡C–H band above 3000. The 13C peak at 119.8 is the nitrile carbon, and three more signals below 20 ppm mean three different sp3 carbons. Butanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2C≡N, fits.
x: 2-Methylpropanenitrile is also C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>N with a C≡N, but its two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent, so it gives only three <sup>13</sup>C signals.
But-3-yn-1-amine has N–H stretches and a strong ≡C–H band near 3300, and its alkyne carbons appear near 70–85 ppm, not 120.
2-Butyn-1-amine has N–H bands above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its internal alkyne carbons appear near 75–80 ppm; there is no 120 ppm nitrile carbon.

q: Which compound gives a <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of exactly two singlets with integrals in a 3 : 1 ratio?
h: Count the H in each set and reduce the ratio.
w: tert-Butyl methyl ether has nine equivalent H on the tert-butyl group and three on the OCH3. Neither group has H on a neighboring carbon, so both signals are singlets, in a 9 : 3 = 3 : 1 ratio. tert-Butyl methyl ether.
x: Methyl acetate gives two 3H singlets, a 1 : 1 ratio.
2,2-Dimethoxypropane gives two 6H singlets, a 1 : 1 ratio.
1-Chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane gives a 9H singlet and a 2H singlet, a 4.5 : 1 ratio.

q: A chlorotoluene shows two doublets of 2H each in the aromatic region of its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum, plus a 3H singlet near 2.3 ppm. Which isomer is it?
h: Which substitution pattern makes the four ring H into two equivalent pairs?
w: In a para-disubstituted ring with two different groups, a mirror plane makes the four ring H into two pairs. Each H is split by its one ortho neighbor, giving two 2H doublets. 4-Chlorotoluene (para) fits.
x: 2-Chlorotoluene (ortho) has four different ring H, giving a more complex pattern of 1H signals.
3-Chlorotoluene (meta) also has four different ring H, including an isolated H between the two groups.
Benzyl chloride is C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Cl too, but it has five ring H and a CH<sub>2</sub>Cl singlet near 4.6, not a CH<sub>3</sub> at 2.3.

q: How many signals appear in the broadband-decoupled 13C NMR spectrum of 4-tert-butylcyclohexanone (shown)?
h: A mirror plane runs through C1, C4 and the tert-butyl group. Count carbons on one side of it.
w: The mirror plane through C=O (C1), C4 and the tert-butyl group makes C2 and C6 equivalent and C3 and C5 equivalent. Signals: C=O, C2/C6, C3/C5, C4, the quaternary C of tert-butyl, and the three equivalent CH3. Total 6.
x: Five misses one environment, usually by merging the quaternary tert-butyl carbon with the CH3 groups or with C4.
Seven treats the three tert-butyl methyls as two kinds; they are equivalent.
Ten counts every carbon separately and ignores the symmetry.

q: Methylcyclohexane reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> under light to give mainly 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane. Which step of the chain mechanism decides that bromine ends up on the tertiary carbon?
c: Br• removing a hydrogen atom from the alkane, since the weakest C–H bond gives the most stable radical
The alkyl radical removing a Br atom from Br<sub>2</sub>, since that is the step that forms the C–Br bond
Light splitting Br<sub>2</sub> into two Br• atoms, since this step starts every chain in the reaction
Two radicals combining at the end of a chain, since the most stable radicals survive the longest
h: The product's regiochemistry is fixed as soon as one particular carbon becomes a radical. Which step first creates a carbon radical?
w: Initiation (Br2 → 2 Br•) involves no carbon at all. In the first propagation step Br• abstracts a hydrogen atom, and whichever C–H breaks decides where Br will end up. The tertiary C–H is the weakest, and because H abstraction by Br• is endothermic its transition state is late and radical-like (Hammond postulate), so the tertiary radical forms much faster. The second propagation step only transfers Br to the radical already formed, and termination is too rare to make much product. Answer: H-atom abstraction by Br•.
x: This step only caps the radical that already exists; the carbon that gets the Br was chosen when the radical was formed.
Initiation makes Br• atoms from Br<sub>2</sub> and involves no C–H bond, so it cannot distinguish tertiary from secondary carbons.
Termination steps are rare compared with propagation (each initiation drives many cycles), so they make only traces of product and do not set the regiochemistry.

q: Which best describes the tert-butyl radical, (CH3)3C•, at the radical carbon?
c: About sp<sup>2</sup> and nearly planar; the unpaired electron is in a p orbital
sp<sup>3</sup> and tetrahedral; the unpaired electron is in an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital
sp and linear; the unpaired electron is in a p orbital
sp<sup>2</sup> and planar; the unpaired electron is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital
h: Compare it with the carbocation that has the same three groups. Where does the extra electron go?
w: An alkyl radical has three σ bonds and one nonbonding electron. Like a carbocation, the carbon is close to sp2 and trigonal planar (alkyl radicals are only very slightly pyramidal, and they invert rapidly), and the single electron sits in the unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the plane. That p orbital is what lets adjacent C–H bonds stabilize the radical by hyperconjugation. About sp2, nearly planar, electron in a p orbital.
x: A tetrahedral carbon would need a fourth σ bond or a lone pair (a carbanion); one electron is not enough to enforce sp<sup>3</sup> geometry.
sp, linear geometry needs only two σ bonds; this carbon has three.
The three sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals are used for the three C–C σ bonds; the odd electron is in the leftover p orbital.

q: 2-Methylpentane is monochlorinated with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light. Counting stereoisomers as separate products, how many C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>Cl products can form?
h: First find the different kinds of hydrogen (constitutional products). Then ask which of those products has a new stereocenter.
w: 2-Methylpentane has five kinds of H (the two C1 methyls are equivalent), so there are five constitutional isomers: 1-chloro-2-methylpentane (new stereocenter at C2), 2-chloro-2-methylpentane (achiral), 3-chloro-2-methylpentane (stereocenter at C3), 2-chloro-4-methylpentane (stereocenter at C2 of that name) and 1-chloro-4-methylpentane (achiral). Each chiral product forms as a racemic pair through the planar radical, so 3 × 2 + 2 = 8 products.
x: Five is the number of constitutional isomers; three of them are chiral and form as two enantiomers each.
Six counts only one of the chiral products as an enantiomer pair.
Ten counts every product as a pair of enantiomers; 2-chloro-2-methylpentane and 1-chloro-4-methylpentane have no stereocenter.

q: Rank the C–H bonds on the tagged carbons of 4-methyl-1-pentene from weakest to strongest (lowest to highest bond dissociation energy).
h: A weak C–H bond gives a stable radical. Which radical is resonance-stabilized, and which one sits in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital?
w: The bond is weaker when the radical it leaves is more stable. Removing H from b (allylic) gives a resonance-delocalized allylic radical, the most stable, so b is weakest (about 360 kJ/mol). Next is the tertiary C–H at c (about 400), then the primary CH3 at d (about 420). The vinylic C–H at a is strongest (about 460) because the radical would sit in an sp2 orbital with no resonance help. b < c < d < a.
x: A tertiary radical is less stable than an allylic radical, whose electron is spread over two carbons; b is weaker than c.
This is backwards for the vinylic bond: a vinyl radical is very unstable, so the vinylic C–H is the strongest, not the weakest.
The vinylic C–H (a) is stronger than a primary C–H (d); a vinyl radical is less stable than a primary alkyl radical.

q: 4-Isopropyltoluene is treated with 1 equivalent of NBS and light (CCl<sub>4</sub>). What is the major product?
h: NBS with light abstracts the H that gives the most stable radical. Compare the two benzylic positions.
w: NBS/hν brominates by H-atom abstraction followed by Br transfer, so it goes where the C–H bond is weakest. Both the ring CH3 and the isopropyl CH are benzylic, but removing the isopropyl H gives a tertiary benzylic radical (resonance with the ring plus two methyl groups), which is more stable than the primary benzylic radical from the CH3. The major product is 2-bromo-2-(4-methylphenyl)propane.
x: Bromination of the ring methyl goes through a primary benzylic radical, less stable than the tertiary benzylic one.
The isopropyl CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens are not benzylic; that primary radical has no resonance stabilization.
Ring bromination is electrophilic aromatic substitution and needs Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>; NBS with light reacts at benzylic C–H bonds.

q: Which sequence converts methylcyclopentane into racemic trans-2-methylcyclopentanol as the major product?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, ethanol, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, ethanol, heat  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, ethanol, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
h: The OH ends up next to the old tertiary C–H, trans to the methyl. Which step targets the tertiary carbon, and which addition is anti-Markovnikov and syn?
w: Radical bromination is highly selective for the tertiary C–H, giving 1-bromo-1-methylcyclopentane. Ethoxide with heat does E2 toward the more substituted alkene (Zaitsev), 1-methylcyclopentene. Hydroboration–oxidation then adds H and OH syn and anti-Markovnikov: OH goes to the less substituted alkene carbon, and the H added to C1 is on the same face as the OH, so the methyl ends up trans to the OH. Product: racemic trans-2-methylcyclopentanol via Br2/hν, NaOEt, then BH3·THF and H2O2/NaOH.
x: Acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: water adds to the tertiary carbon and gives 1-methylcyclopentanol.
Hydroxide in water substitutes (S<sub>N</sub>1) or eliminates at the tertiary bromide; any alcohol formed is 1-methylcyclopentanol, with OH on the tertiary carbon.
Chlorination is not selective (about 1 : 3.8 : 5 per H), so step 1 gives a mixture of chlorides and the later steps give a mixture of alcohols.

q: (E)-1-Phenylprop-1-ene is treated with HBr in the presence of a peroxide (ROOR). What is the major product?
h: With peroxide, Br• adds first. It adds to the alkene carbon that leaves the most stable radical on the other carbon.
w: In the peroxide (radical chain) mechanism, Br• adds to the C=C first. Adding to C2 leaves the radical on C1, which is benzylic and resonance-stabilized by the ring; adding to C1 would leave a less stable secondary alkyl radical on C2. The benzylic radical then takes H from HBr. Br ends up on C2: 2-bromo-1-phenylpropane (formed racemic). Note that this is not simply 'Br on the less substituted carbon': both alkene carbons carry one substituent, and radical stability decides.
x: Br on the benzylic carbon is the ionic (no peroxide) product, formed through the benzylic cation; with peroxide Br• adds first and ends up on C2.
Br cannot reach C3, which was never part of the alkene; the H and Br add across C1 and C2.
An allylic bromide with the alkene kept is the NBS/hν result (allylic substitution), not HBr addition.

q: AIBN, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(CN)–N=N–C(CN)(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, is a common radical initiator. What happens when it is heated to about 70 °C?
c: Both C–N bonds break, releasing N<sub>2</sub> and two (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C•(CN) radicals
The N=N π bond breaks homolytically, giving a diradical that keeps both C–N bonds
A C≡N bond breaks to give two cyano radicals, •CN
h: Which very stable small molecule can leave, and which radical left behind is stabilized?
w: Azo initiators decompose because loss of N2 (very strong N≡N bond, and a gas, so ΔS is favorable) makes the process strongly downhill. Both C–N bonds break homolytically to give N2 and two tertiary 2-cyano-2-propyl radicals, which are stabilized by the two methyl groups and by resonance with the C≡N. Two (CH3)2C•(CN) radicals + N2. These radicals then start the chain, for example by adding to a monomer or abstracting H from Bu3SnH.
x: Breaking only the π bond gives no driving force; the reaction is driven by forming N<sub>2</sub>, which requires cleaving the C–N bonds.
C≡N triple bonds are very strong and do not break at 70 °C; •CN is also a poorly stabilized radical.
Initiators work by homolysis in nonpolar media, not by forming ions; a tertiary cation next to an electron-withdrawing CN is very unstable.

q: The energy diagram shows the two propagation steps of the chlorination of methane: Cl• + CH<sub>4</sub> → •CH<sub>3</sub> + HCl, then •CH<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl•. Which statement is correct?
c: The hydrogen-abstraction step is rate-determining because A is the highest point on the path
B is a transition state in which the C–H bond is half broken
The second step is rate-determining because it releases the most energy
The overall propagation sequence is endothermic because the first step is uphill
h: Maxima are transition states; minima are intermediates. The step whose transition state is highest controls the rate.
w: On an energy diagram the rate-determining step is the one with the highest-energy transition state. A (the H-abstraction TS) is the highest point, so H abstraction by Cl• is rate-determining. B is a minimum, the methyl radical intermediate plus HCl. The second step has a small barrier (C) and is strongly exothermic, so the overall sequence is downhill even though the first step is slightly uphill.
x: B is an energy minimum, so it is an intermediate (•CH<sub>3</sub> + HCl), not a transition state.
How exothermic a step is does not set the rate; the second step has the lower barrier and is fast.
The products lie far below the reactants, so the sum of the two steps is exothermic despite the small uphill first step.

q: 2,3-Dimethylbutane is monochlorinated with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light at 25 °C. Using relative rates per hydrogen of 1° : 3° = 1 : 5, about what percentage of the monochloride is 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane?
h: Multiply the number of each kind of H by its relative rate, then take the fraction.
w: 2,3-Dimethylbutane has 12 primary H (four CH3) and 2 tertiary H. Relative amounts: primary 12 × 1 = 12; tertiary 2 × 5 = 10. Fraction tertiary = 10/(12 + 10) = 0.45, so about 45% is 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane and 55% is 1-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane. Chlorination's low selectivity means the many primary H win on numbers.
x: 14% (2 of 14 H) is the purely statistical value; it ignores that a tertiary H reacts five times faster.
55% is the share of the primary product, 1-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane.
83% (5/6) compares one tertiary H with one primary H and ignores that there are six times as many primary H.

q: To make chlorocyclohexane by radical chlorination, a chemist uses a large excess of cyclohexane relative to Cl<sub>2</sub>. Why?
c: Cl• then mostly meets cyclohexane, so further chlorination of the product to dichlorocyclohexanes is minimized
Excess alkane speeds up the initiation step
Excess alkane makes chlorination selective for one kind of C–H bond
Excess alkane traps Cl• in termination steps and stops side reactions
h: The product still has C–H bonds. What else could Cl• attack once some product has formed?
w: Chlorocyclohexane still has C–H bonds and can be chlorinated again to dichlorides and beyond. If cyclohexane is in large excess, a Cl• radical is far more likely to hit an unreacted cyclohexane molecule than a product molecule, so polychlorination is suppressed. The unreacted cyclohexane is easy to recover by distillation.
x: Initiation is homolysis of Cl<sub>2</sub> by light; the amount of alkane does not change it.
All twelve H of cyclohexane are equivalent anyway, and the amount of alkane does not change chlorine's intrinsic selectivity.
Alkane molecules are not radicals, so they cannot take part in termination; they react with Cl• in propagation.

q: The copolymer SAN, used in kitchen containers, has the repeat unit –[CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CN)]<sub>n</sub>– and is made by radical polymerization. Which pair of monomers is used?
h: Cut the backbone into two-carbon pieces. Each piece came from a C=C of one monomer.
w: In radical addition polymerization, each monomer's C=C becomes two backbone carbons. Splitting the four-carbon repeat into two-carbon pieces gives CH2–CH(C6H5), from styrene (CH2=CHC6H5), and CH2–CH(CN), from acrylonitrile (CH2=CHCN). Styrene and acrylonitrile.
x: Ethylbenzene and propanenitrile have no C=C, so they cannot undergo addition polymerization.
Allylbenzene puts a CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the backbone, and acetonitrile has no C=C to join the chain.
A diene plus HCN is not a radical chain growth; HCN does not polymerize, and the diene would put a C=C in the backbone.

q: A synthetic rubber has the repeat unit –[CH<sub>2</sub>–C(CH<sub>3</sub>)=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>]<sub>n</sub>–, formed by 1,4-addition of a single monomer. Which monomer is it?
h: In 1,4-addition of a diene, the two end carbons form the new backbone bonds and a C=C appears between C2 and C3.
w: When a conjugated diene polymerizes by 1,4-addition, the radical adds to C1, the resulting allylic radical reacts at C4, and a new C=C forms between C2 and C3. Working backward, the repeat CH2–C(CH3)=CH–CH2 comes from CH2=C(CH3)–CH=CH2, 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene (isoprene), with the methyl on C2.
x: 2-Methyl-2-butene has only one C=C; its polymer would have no C=C in the backbone and would carry methyls on both backbone carbons of each unit.
2-Methyl-1-butene has one C=C; its polymer would be saturated, with a methyl and an ethyl on alternate backbone carbons.
1,3-Pentadiene by 1,4-addition gives –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH=CH–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–, with the methyl on an sp<sup>3</sup> backbone carbon, not on the C=C.

q: Radical polymerization of methyl methacrylate gives poly(methyl methacrylate), used as acrylic glass. Which repeat unit forms (head-to-tail)?
h: Only the C=C reacts. Its two carbons become the backbone, and everything attached to them hangs off as side groups.
w: In addition polymerization only the C=C opens; the CH2 and the substituted carbon become a two-carbon backbone unit. The growing radical adds to the CH2 end, giving a tertiary radical stabilized by the ester (head-to-tail). The methyl and the CO2CH3 both stay on the same backbone carbon: –[CH2–C(CH3)(CO2CH3)]n–.
x: This moves the methyl to the other carbon; that repeat unit would come from methyl crotonate (CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), not methyl methacrylate.
The C=O does not join the chain in radical polymerization, and there is no C=C left in the backbone.
This is a polyester from a condensation or ring-opening; it has lost the methyl and OCH<sub>3</sub> groups of the monomer.

q: BHT (2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol) is added to foods and plastics to slow radical oxidation. How does it work?
c: It gives an H atom to chain-carrying radicals and leaves a stable, hindered aryloxy radical
It absorbs the ultraviolet light that would break bonds and start radical chains
It reacts with O<sub>2</sub> to form a peroxide that starts only harmless chains
Its acidic O–H protonates the chain-carrying radicals and turns them into cations
h: A chain stops when a reactive radical is replaced by one that cannot carry the chain.
w: Radical oxidation (autoxidation) is a chain carried by peroxyl radicals ROO•. The phenol O–H in BHT is weak because the aryloxy radical left behind is delocalized into the ring, so ROO• takes that H (ROO• + ArOH → ROOH + ArO•). ArO• is resonance-stabilized and shielded by the two bulky tert-butyl groups, so it does not abstract H from the food or polymer; the chain stops. BHT donates an H atom and forms an unreactive aryloxy radical.
x: BHT is a radical scavenger, not a UV filter; it acts after radicals have formed.
An antioxidant that made peroxides would start more chains, not stop them.
Radicals are neutral and are not quenched by protonation; the key step is H-atom (not proton) transfer.

q: Each radical below forms when one C–H bond of its parent hydrocarbon breaks homolytically. Which radical comes from the weakest C–H bond (the lowest bond dissociation energy)?
h: A C–H bond is weak when the radical left behind is stabilized. Look for resonance first, then count alkyl groups on the radical carbons.
w: The more stable the radical, the less energy it takes to break the C–H bond that forms it. Resonance delocalization is the larger effect, and alkyl groups add more. The 1,1-dimethylallyl radical is allylic (spread over two carbons) and tertiary at one end, so its C–H bond (in 3-methylbut-1-ene) is the weakest: the tertiary allylic radical. The allyl radical has resonance but no alkyl groups; the tert-pentyl radical is tertiary but has no resonance; the vinyl radical is the least stable, so its C–H bond is the strongest.
x: Propene's allylic C–H is weak because of resonance, but with no alkyl groups on the radical carbons the allyl radical is less stable than the tertiary allylic one.
A tertiary C–H bond is weaker than a primary or secondary one, but hyperconjugation alone stabilizes the radical less than allylic resonance does.
A vinylic C–H bond is the strongest here: the odd electron sits in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital with no resonance.

q:
(S)-2-Bromobutane is monochlorinated with Cl2 and light. Which statements are true?
I. Chlorination at C2 gives 2-bromo-2-chlorobutane as a racemic mixture.
II. Chlorination at C3 gives 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane as two diastereomers in unequal amounts.
III. Chlorination at C4 gives 3-bromo-1-chlorobutane as a racemic mixture.
h: A planar radical loses the configuration only at the carbon where it forms. Is C2 touched in each case?
w: I is true: H abstraction at C2 makes a planar radical at the stereocenter, and Cl adds to either face equally, so the product is racemic. II is true: the radical forms at C3 while C2 keeps its (S) configuration; the existing stereocenter makes the two faces of the C3 radical different, so the two diastereomers form in unequal amounts. III is false: reaction at C4 does not touch C2, so 3-bromo-1-chlorobutane keeps the original configuration and is optically active. I and II only.
x: II is also true: a nearby stereocenter makes the two faces of the C3 radical diastereotopic, giving unequal amounts of two diastereomers.
I is true (C2 radical is planar, racemic product) and III is false (C2 is not touched at C4).
III is false: when the reaction occurs at C4, the C2 stereocenter is never involved and keeps its configuration.

q: Peroxides make HBr add to alkenes anti-Markovnikov, but they have no such effect on HCl or HI. Which statement best explains this?
c: Only for HBr are both propagation steps (X• adding to C=C, then the carbon radical taking H from HX) exothermic
Only HBr can be protonated by the peroxide to start the chain
Cl• and I• are too stable to add to an alkene
HCl and HI react with peroxides by termination steps before they reach the alkene
h: Use bond strengths: compare H–X bond strength with the C–X bond made when X• adds.
w: A radical chain runs well only if both propagation steps are energetically downhill (or nearly so). For HBr, Br• adding to C=C and C• taking H from the fairly weak H–Br bond are both exothermic. For HCl, the strong H–Cl bond makes the H-transfer step endothermic. For HI, the C–I bond formed is so weak that I• adding to the alkene is endothermic. So only HBr has two exothermic propagation steps.
x: The chain is started by homolysis of the O–O bond, not by protonation; any HX could be involved in that.
Cl• is a very reactive radical, not a stable one; for HCl the problem is the second step, breaking the strong H–Cl bond.
This is not the reason; the failing step for each acid is an endothermic propagation step.

q: During radical polymerization of vinyl chloride, the growing chain radical adds to a new monomer to give the more stable radical. Which drawing shows the correct arrows for this step?
h: Radical steps move single electrons (fishhooks). A new σ bond needs one electron from each partner, and the radical should end up on the carbon that carries Cl.
w: Radical addition uses three fishhook (one-electron) arrows: one from the chain radical toward the CH2 end of the monomer, one electron of the π bond also to that CH2 (the two together make the new C–C σ bond), and the other π electron moves onto the CHCl carbon, which becomes the new chain-end radical. Adding at CH2 gives the more stable, secondary radical stabilized by Cl and keeps the head-to-tail pattern. The drawing with three fishhooks attacking the CH2 is correct.
x: Full (two-electron) arrows describe polar steps; the radical has only one electron to give, so fishhooks are needed.
Attack at the CHCl carbon would put the new radical on the unsubstituted CH<sub>2</sub>, a primary radical; it also gives head-to-head linkage.
A new σ bond needs two electrons. With only the radical's electron moving toward CH<sub>2</sub>, the second electron from the π bond is missing.

q: Which C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> isomer gives only one monochlorination product with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light?
h: Chlorination is not selective, so the only way to get one product is to have only one kind of hydrogen.
w: Because Cl• attacks every kind of C–H bond, a single monochloride forms only if all H are equivalent. In 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane all 18 H are on six equivalent CH3 groups, so only (CH3)3C–C(CH3)2CH2Cl can form.
x: 2,3,4-Trimethylpentane has four kinds of H (two kinds of CH<sub>3</sub> and two kinds of CH), so it gives several chlorides.
2,2,4-Trimethylpentane has four kinds of H (two kinds of CH<sub>3</sub>, a CH<sub>2</sub> and a CH).
Octane has four kinds of H (C1, C2, C3, C4 positions), giving four constitutional monochlorides.
